title: Huge crowds, low vaccination rates raise measles alarms as pope visits South America
summary: While millions of Catholics gather to catch a glimpse of Pope Leo XIV in South America, health authorities are watching for a different kind of visitor: measles
story: While millions of Catholics gather to catch a glimpse of Pope Leo XIV in South America, health authorities are watching for a different kind of visitor: measles
While millions of Catholics gather to catch a glimpse of Pope Leo XIV in South America, health authorities are watching for a different kind of visitor: measles.
Cases are already surging in the region this year and mass gatherings provide an opportunity for one of the world's most contagious viruses to spread further.

The Pan American Health Organization, or PAHO, and officials in Uruguay, Argentina and Peru have been preparing for potential problems to different degrees for months, including mounting vaccination campaigns and increasing surveillance to try to limit spread.

Uruguay, where thousands of people attended a prayer vigil and a Mass celebrated by Leo, implemented a nationwide intensified surveillance monitoring period until Nov. 29, three weeks after Leo’s departure from the country, according to Nataly Rodriguez, director of epidemiology at Uruguay’s health ministry. Uruguay has also taken steps to boost its vaccination rate to among the highest in the region.
“As a preventive strategy, the ministry has been emphasizing the importance of keeping vaccination schedules up to date,” Rodriguez said.

The Nov. 6-17 trip to the continent where around 40% of the world’s 1.4 billion Catholics live marks a return home for Leo, who spent two decades ministering in Peru as a missionary priest and then bishop.

Ahead of the visit, PAHO assessed the public health risk of measles in the context of the religious mass gatherings in South America as “very high.” That's in part because there has been a nearly five-fold increase in cases between January and October compared with the same period last year.
“We’re seeing children not going to school, children being hospitalized,” said Daniel Salas Peraza, the head of immunization at PAHO. “It’s a very complex situation.”

Measles spreads easily through the air when an infected person breathes, sneezes or coughs. A person can be contagious even before they show symptoms. The virus first infects the respiratory tract, then spreads throughout the body, causing a high fever, runny nose, cough, red, watery eyes and a rash. It most commonly affects children and while it usually isn’t fatal, it can be.

The vaccine for measles is extremely effective, but the first of two doses is not usually recommended for babies until their first birthday. In order to stop the disease from spreading in a community, to protect infants and others who can't get the vaccine, at least 95% of the population must be fully vaccinated with two doses.

As of 2025, only Uruguay had achieved that number, according to data from the World Health Organization. Peru has reached 90% with one dose and 82% with two doses while Argentina has reached only 84% with one dose and 55% with both doses.

PAHO reported 57,666 confirmed cases of measles in 17 countries and territories in the Americas between January and the end of October, nearly five times the number recorded during the same period in 2025. At least 81 people have died so far this year due to the disease.
With nearly 3,000 cases, Peru has seen the fourth highest number of cases in the Americas after Guatemala, Mexico and the United States.
In the five Peruvian cities Leo will be visiting including Lima, Chiclayo, Cajamarca, Cusco and Pucallpa, a total of 170 measles cases have been identified so far in 2026.

Ahead of the Pope’s visit, Salas Peraza said PAHO had supported efforts to encourage vaccination in Peru, including initiatives targeting adolescents, deploying equipment to strengthen vaccine storage and delivery capacity, and intensifying vaccination along the border with Brazil.

In late October, authorities carried out measles vaccination campaigns in areas with the highest rates of transmission. These included a dose for babies aged six to eleven months, as well as vaccination for people up to 29 years old.
By the end of September, 1.2 million vaccine doses had been administered since April in Peru, with more than two million additional doses available.
Still, with vaccination rates so far below the threshold needed for community protection in parts of the region, experts say conditions are ripe for further spread.

In Argentina, authorities issued a warning in late October about the high risk associated with the pope’s visit, after estimating that they expected up to 4 million people in the province of Buenos Aires.

But Argentina President Javier Milei has slashed Argentina’s healthcare budget, eviscerating agencies tasked with planning, financing and tracking immunization campaigns. The cuts coincided with a measles outbreak that in April 2025 led to Argentina’s first measles death in two decades and some are concerned that efforts are falling short.

Marcela Lopez Yunes, a doctor and pediatric infectious disease specialist, said she hadn’t seen what she considered sufficient public communication to encourage vaccination. “We need to do a little more to give diseases such as measles the attention and importance they deserve,” she said.

A spokesperson for Argentina's health ministry said that while the federal government is in charge of purchasing and distributing vaccines, provinces are in charge of administering them to their populations. They also said that there is an ongoing public service announcement speaking to the importance of vaccination in general.
Leo took aim at Milei’s austerity measures as he arrived in Argentina Sunday, insisting that political leaders must put people, not the economy, first.
Associated Press journalists Ramiro Barreiro in Montevideo, Uruguay, and Franklin Briceño in Lima, Peru, contributed to this report.

title: US, Mexico are on the verge of forfeiting a major health victory. Here's what to know
summary: International health experts are meeting to assess whether the U.S. and Mexico have lost their measles elimination status
story: International health experts are meeting to assess whether the U.S. and Mexico have lost their measles elimination status
NEW YORK -- International health experts are meeting this week to determine if the United States and Mexico have forfeited one of their greatest public health victories — the elimination of measles.

Measles is one of the most contagious diseases known to medicine, but vaccines had safely stopped the virus’ spread in the U.S. for 30 years. Over those decades, measles had become a medical rarity in the U.S., with deaths from the disease virtually unheard of. But in the past two years, large outbreaks have hit multiple states, spawning thousands of illnesses, including about a dozen deaths.

Experts expect that the meeting, convened by the Pan American Health Organization, or PAHO, will show that measles has officially returned to the U.S. and Mexico — that the virus is now continually spreading within the nations' borders.
“It’s a big deal. The decision represents us moving backwards,” said Dr. David Margolius, director of Cleveland’s health department and a leader in a coalition of big U.S. city health departments.
Here's a look at the meeting's deliberations and why it's important.

In a closed-door meeting this week, a PAHO advisory commission is looking at genetic evidence to determine if the same measles virus has been spreading for one year or more in the outbreaks that have torn through North America starting in 2024.
“It’s solely based on genetics,” said Dr. Amesh Adalja, an infectious disease doctor in the Pittsburgh area and a senior scholar at the Johns Hopkins Center for Health Security.

If so, the commission will say the country can no longer be considered to have “eliminated” measles, meaning a return to sustained circulation of the virus. Last year, PAHO stripped Canada of the measles-free designation it had had since 1998.

The commission will present its determination to PAHO Director Dr. Jarbas Barbosa, a former Brazilian health official, who makes the final determination. An announcement of the findings is being scheduled for next week, PAHO officials said.
A PAHO decision to strip the U.S. of its measles elimination status will not change how federal health officials are addressing outbreaks, CDC Director Erica Schwartz said this week.

“The measles elimination designation is not what protects Americans. Vaccination does. We know where transmission is occurring and we’re working with state and local health departments to reach those communities. Losing a designation doesn’t mean we abandon an evidence-based approach. It means we remain focused on stopping outbreaks,” she said in the statement.

But many public health experts say such an occasion demands a stepped-up, full-throated campaign to promote vaccinations and provide more advice to doctors. They fault what they say is a politically fraught, muted federal response, and blame U.S. Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., who was a leading voice in the anti-vaccine movement before President Donald Trump put him in charge of the nation's health agencies.

Kennedy has moved to downsize the childhood vaccination schedule, reshape a key vaccine advisory board, and lauded Trump’s executive order calling for spacing out the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine. Such a move runs counter to medical groups’ recommendations, and likely would result in fewer children getting fully vaccinated, experts say.

Measles typically begins with a high fever followed by a telltale rash that starts on the face and neck. Most people recover, but it’s one of the leading causes of death among young children, according to the World Health Organization. Serious complications, including blindness and swelling of the brain, are more common in young children and adults older than 30.

The U.S. achieved measles elimination status in 2000, after decades of vaccination campaigns brought the childhood measles vaccination rate to above 97%. Health experts say a 95% vaccination rate is needed so that when an infected traveler enters a community, so many people are vaccinated that it will not spark an outbreak.

But U.S. vaccination rates have been slipping for years, in part because of disproven claims that the vaccine can cause autism. Trump claimed earlier this year, without evidence, that the MMR vaccine — which is credited with saving millions of lives globally — is possibly “quite lethal.” Last year, the childhood vaccination rate fell to about 92% nationally, and was much lower in certain states and certain communities.

Measles exploded last year in large outbreaks in Texas, Arizona, Utah and South Carolina. And the more than 5,100 confirmed cases this year are already double the 2025 tally, driven largely by an outbreak in Pennsylvania that has dwarfed the earlier ones. The U.S. has now seen eight measles-associated deaths this year — more than any year in more than three decades — and is enduring its worst year for measles illnesses since 1991.

A measles vaccine did not become available in Mexico until years after a measles vaccine was first licensed — in 1963, in the U.S. — and the U.S. started giving shots. Mexico did not achieve measles elimination status until 2016.

Cases began surging in Mexico early last year. Researchers think an outbreak in the northern border state of Chihuahua stemmed from an unvaccinated Mennonite child from that Mexican state who traveled to Gaines County, Texas, where an outbreak was occurring, and came back infected.
As of this week, more than 20,500 confirmed cases have been reported across the nation. Fifty measles-related deaths have been reported, most of them children younger than 5 years old.

The issue has not been confined to North America. Early this year, the World Health Organization confirmed that Armenia, Austria, Azerbaijan, Spain, the United Kingdom, and Uzbekistan lost their status.
Associated Press writer Megan Janetsky contributed to this story from Mexico City.

title: Preliminary study finds a clue in the quest to help diagnose CTE in the living
summary: Scientists stumbled onto a hint that measuring a toxic protein tied to Alzheimer’s disease just might one day be useful in diagnosing a different brain disease in football players and others who have suffered repeated blows to the head
story: Scientists stumbled onto a hint that measuring a toxic protein tied to Alzheimer’s disease just might one day be useful in diagnosing a different brain disease in football players and others who have suffered repeated blows to the head

WASHINGTON -- Scientists stumbled onto a hint that measuring a toxic protein tied to Alzheimer’s disease just might one day be useful in diagnosing a different brain disease in football players and others who have suffered repeated blows to the head.

Doctors evaluate symptoms such as mood swings and memory loss to try to tell if patients may have CTE, or chronic traumatic encephalopathy, a disease linked to concussions and other brain trauma. But other diseases cause similar symptoms, and a CTE diagnosis can only be confirmed by examining the brain after death.

The new clue involves a protein called tau that normally supports neurons but becomes abnormal in Alzheimer’s, tangling inside those nerve cells. Researchers at Washington University in St. Louis were using autopsy samples to study a tau fragment called eMTBR-tau243 that may help track those tangles when they found something unusual: a patient with high levels of that biomarker even though records showed the person didn’t have Alzheimer’s but advanced CTE instead.
The researchers turned to a larger collection of autopsied brain and other samples, and eventually tested blood stored from 11 people who had been classified as having CTE.

Compared to healthy people, levels of eMTBR-tau243 were higher in those with advanced CTE, said study coauthor Chihiro Sato, a WashU assistant neurology professor. That biomarker couldn’t reliably identify early-stage CTE.

It is an interesting but very preliminary finding, requiring far larger studies to see if there is a real connection, cautioned Dr. Rudolph Castellani, a neuropathologist at Northwestern University who wasn’t involved with the research.

Abnormal tau is found in several brain diseases, many of which can overlap in older adults, adding to the difficulty in teasing apart its role in any one disease, including CTE. Sato, who studies such tauopathies, also stressed much more research is needed.
The findings were published late Friday by the medical journal JAMA and presented at a scientific meeting in Japan.

title: Tokyo protests after two suspected Russian aircraft violate Japanese airspace
summary: Japan has protested to Moscow after two suspected Russian aircraft entered Japanese airspace off the country’s southwestern coast
story: Japan has protested to Moscow after two suspected Russian aircraft entered Japanese airspace off the country’s southwestern coast

TOKYO -- TOKYO (AP) — Japan said it protested to Moscow on Tuesday after two suspected Russian aircraft entered Japan's airspace off the country's southwestern coast, the latest incident fueling escalating tensions between the neighbors.

Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi told reporters the suspected Russian aircraft violated Japanese airspace for about five minutes early Tuesday near Fukuoka, long enough for Japan to scramble fighter jets and send warnings.
Japan's government lodged "an extremely stern protest" and “strongly” demanded preventive measures be taken, Koizumi said. He did not specify the types of aircraft involved.

“The violation of the Japanese airspace by the Russian aircraft is not only a serious violation of our country's sovereignty, but also a threat to our safety,” Koizumi said. “It is absolutely unacceptable.”
The Russian aircraft flew across the Tsushima Strait, then headed south and flew above the waters between Taiwan and Japan's westernmost island of Yonaguni, Koizumi said.

Taiwan's defense ministry said Tuesday it detected two Russian military planes entering the island's air defense identification zone from the northeast and that the planes flew through airspace east of the island before leaving the zone south of Taitung County in southeastern Taiwan.
The ministry said it “employed joint intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance measures to monitor the situation continuously and responded appropriately.”

Separately, South Korea’s military said several Russian military aircraft temporarily entered the country’s air defense identification zone over waters between the Korean Peninsula and Japan on Monday, though they did not violate South Korean airspace.

South Korea’s Joint Chiefs of Staff said the military had detected the aircraft before they entered the zone and scrambled fighter jets. The South’s military did not disclose the number of Russian aircraft it detected or what types of planes they were.
Koizumi did not comment on why the violations took place but said Japan continues to closely monitor Russian military activity “with strong interest."
Japan has raised growing concern over growing joint military activity between Russia and China around the Japanese coasts.

The airspace violation was the latest sign of deteriorating Japan-Russia relations. Tensions have risen since Russian President Vladimir Putin visited Iturup in August, one of four Russian-controlled islands off Japan’s northern coast that Tokyo also claims.

Tensions escalated in mid-October after the arrest of a Japanese journalist in Russia on suspicion of spying. Despite repeated protests and demands for his immediate release, the journalist, who works for the Hokkaido newspaper, remains in custody.

Earlier this month, Russia placed several subsidiaries of Japan Tobacco Inc. under the temporary management of a Russian company following a presidential order issued by Putin. Japan protested and demanded the measure be withdrawn.

The Soviet Union seized the Kuril Islands from Japan in the final days of World War II. The territorial dispute has prevented the two countries from signing a peace treaty formally ending hostilities.
Associated Press writers Kim Tong-hyung in Seoul, South Korea, Kanis Leung in Hong Kong and Taijing Wu in Taipei, Taiwan, contributed to this report.

title: El Salvador's president confirms and celebrates attack on home of key Haitian gang leader
summary: El Salvador’s president says that his troops have demolished the lavish home of a prominent gang leader in Haiti known as Jeff
story: El Salvador’s president says that his troops have demolished the lavish home of a prominent gang leader in Haiti known as Jeff

SAN JUAN, Puerto Rico -- El Salvador’s president, Nayib Bukele, said Wednesday that his troops demolished the lavish home of a prominent gang leader in Haiti known as Jeff. It wasn’t immediately clear if he was killed.

Bukele posted a video on X that depicts an old video of Jeff posing in front of his mansion in the Caribbean country and then cuts to Salvadoran helicopters flying toward it as they fire shot after shot, with big plumes of smoke rising from Jeff’s home.
“My gift to the Haitian people on the anniversary of the Battle of Vertières,” Bukele wrote.
The 1803 battle was critical in helping secure Haiti's independence from France and transforming it into the world's first Black republic.
It wasn’t immediately known if Haiti’s police and army were involved. A U.N.-backed gang suppression force said that it wasn’t involved.

Jeff is considered one of Haiti's most powerful gang leaders. His real name is Jeff Larose, but he's known as Jeff Canaan, Jeff Gwo Lwa and Taliban. He has long controlled a community known as Canaan in northern Port-au-Prince, leading a gang of an estimated 200 members, according to the United Nations. His so-called Taliban gang based in Canaan is a very close ally of 5 Segond, which has provided it with reinforcements.
Diego Da Rin, a Haiti expert with International Crisis Group, said the attack on Jeff’s home was the obvious next step for Bukele’s operations.
Jeff built the home in mid-2024, complete with a pool emblazoned with his logo.
“It’s very easy to identify it by satellite,” Da Rin said. “It was a very defiant act by him.”
He noted that Jeff’s home is very vulnerable to an aerial attack, but it was built in a place where attacking it by land would have been very difficult.
Da Rin said Jeff was among a handful of gang leaders who have built mansions in recent years.
“In a way, they felt untouchable in their territory,” he said.
The use of explosive drones and helicopters, which Haitian police and military lack, has changed that.

Da Rin said he doubts Jeff was staying at the mansion when it was attacked early Wednesday given that on Nov. 8, Salvadoran troops attacked the home of Wilson Joseph, best known as Lanmò San Jou and leader of the 400 Mawozo gang. He wasn’t killed in the attack.
Da Rin said gang leaders have several residences and can always seek shelter in any home within the territory they control.

He noted that Jeff and Lanmò San Jou are allies and control the main roads north and east of Port-au-Prince that lead to other cities and towns, charging tolls that have become their main source of revenue.
Canaan was established as an informal community after a devastating earthquake hit Haiti in January 2010. Tens of thousands of people are estimated to now live there.
The attack comes a day after thousands of Haitians in Port-au-Prince and beyond marched in favor of Bukele, thanking him and his troops for fighting violent gangs.
On Wednesday, Haitians were again celebrating.
“Jeff is a criminal and I hope he died,” said Mario Jean-Pierre, a 45-year-old salesperson in Port-au-Prince. “We asked for help; Bukele answered us.”
Last month, Bukele deployed around 2,500 troops to Haiti after four of their own came under attack on Oct. 18 while deep in gang territory. They remain missing.
Associated Press reporter Evens Sanon in Port-au-Prince, Haiti contributed to this report.

title: A Chinese executive is convicted in a case linked to a Bangkok building collapse
summary: A Thai court has found a Chinese executive and Thai shareholders guilty of illegally operating a business in Thailand
story: A Thai court has found a Chinese executive and Thai shareholders guilty of illegally operating a business in Thailand

BANGKOK -- A court in Thailand on Wednesday found a Chinese executive and Thai shareholders of a Thai subsidiary of a Chinese state-owned construction company guilty of illegally operating a business in Thailand in a case related to the collapse of a Bangkok office building last year.

At least 92 people died on March 28, 2025, when an earthquake struck the partially built high-rise, which was to house the State Audit Office. It was the only building in Thailand to collapse completely due to the 7.7-magnitude quake, which was centered in neighboring Myanmar.

The tower was being built by a joint venture between China Railway No. 10 (Thailand) and Italian-Thai Development. Executives from both companies are also facing separate proceedings over alleged wrongdoing related to the building’s collapse.

China Railway No. 10 (Thailand) and its director, Zhang Chuanling, were found guilty of violating Thailand’s Foreign Business Act by using Thai nominee shareholders to conceal the company’s foreign ownership and operating a construction business without the required permission. The Criminal Court in Bangkok fined the company and Zhang 1 million baht ($29,450) each and sentenced Zhang to three years in prison, while also ordering the company to cease operations.
The defendants had denied the charges and were granted bail.
China Railway No. 10 (Thailand) is a Thai-registered affiliate of China Railway No. 10 Engineering Group, part of the Chinese state-owned China Railway group, which operates internationally.

The court’s action comes after increasing public concern about Chinese influence over local business, especially through the use of Thai citizens as proxies to disguise their real ownership. In some cases, the concern extends to suspicion that such enterprises are fronts for illegal activities, including money laundering and online scams.

The involvement of Chinese companies in the building collapse and other construction-related accidents has drawn considerable attention. The most notable other accident took place in January this year on a line that is part of a Thai-Chinese high-speed railway project linking the capital to northeastern Thailand. At least 32 people were killed and dozens injured when a construction crane crashed onto a moving passenger train, derailing it.
Italian-Thai Development was also the construction contractor for the railway project, and a Chinese company handled design and construction supervision.

After the train accident, China’s ambassador to Thailand, Zhang Jianwei, said that China requires its companies to follow the rules when participating in overseas projects, and that Beijing is willing to “guide Chinese companies to actively cooperate with the Thai authorities’ investigation."

Wednesday’s court case also saw three Thai shareholders found guilty of acting as nominees for China Railway No. 10 (Thailand). Two were sentenced to six years in prison each and fined 2 million baht ($58,900), while the third received a three-year prison term and a 1-million-baht ($29,450) fine. However, the court reduced their sentences and their fines by one-fifth after they confessed to the offenses.

title: Nabeel Rajab, prominent Bahraini human rights activist, dies at 62
summary: Nabeel Rajab, a prominent democracy activist who advocated for the rights of Bahrain’s Shiite majority and spent years in prison for challenging the country’s monarchy, has died
story: Nabeel Rajab, a prominent democracy activist who advocated for the rights of Bahrain’s Shiite majority and spent years in prison for challenging the country’s monarchy, has died

Nabeel Rajab, a prominent democracy activist from Bahrain who helped lead the island nation’s 2011 Arab Spring protests and spent years in prison for challenging its monarchy, died on Tuesday. He was 62.

His family found him unresponsive at their home in Turkey on Tuesday morning, friends and activists said. The Bahrain Center for Human Rights, which Rajab once led as president, confirmed his death in a post on X.

“We extend our sincere condolences and heartfelt sympathy to his esteemed family. We pray that God may encompass him with his vast mercy and reward him abundantly for his efforts and contributions,” the group wrote.

Ebrahim Sharif, an activist and close friend of the family, said Rajab's wife and daughter took him to a hospital in Istanbul, where he was pronounced dead. He said after speaking with Rajab's brother that the family believes Rajab likely died of a heart attack.

Rajab for decades was one of Bahrain's leading human rights activists. He frequently posted on social media about Bahrain's treatment of dissidents, and was an unusually visible figure in a country where voicing criticism can carry enormous risk.

In 2002, Rajab helped establish the Bahrain Center for Human Rights, which became a platform for him and his colleagues to call for democratic reforms in the island nation, where a Sunni monarchy rules over a predominantly Shiite Muslim population.
He rose to international prominence in 2011 as the Arab Spring uprisings swept the region and demonstrations erupted in Bahrain.

As one of the movement’s best-known voices, he joined thousands of demonstrators occupying Manama’s Pearl Roundabout and kept protesting even after a violent crackdown by security forces. He and the protesters described their demands as fair elections, constitutional democracy and an end to preferential treatment for Bahrain’s Sunni minority.
Bahrain ultimately put down the uprising with the help of troops from Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates.

Though Bahrain’s constitution guarantees freedom of speech, Rajab was prosecuted under laws criminalizing remarks that insult foreign countries or government agencies or spread false rumors during wartime.

He was imprisoned on multiple occasions in the years that followed. The detentions drew international criticism from the United Nations, human rights groups and some of Bahrain’s closest allies, including the United States, which bases its Navy’s 5th Fleet in the island kingdom.
He was released to home detention in June 2020 during the coronavirus pandemic while serving a five-year sentence over tweets criticizing the Saudi-led war in Yemen and alleging prison abuse.

“Nabeel really stood out for standing up for the most vulnerable even when he knew the cost would be extremely heavy,” said Sayed Ahmed AlWadaei of the London-based Bahrain Institute for Rights and Democracy.

Rajab left Bahrain with his family early in the Iran war, as authorities cracked down on Shiite-led protests. Rajab accused the government of torturing an imprisoned activist and feared he would be arrested if he returned, he told The Associated Press at the time.
The International Federation for Human Rights, where Rajab served as deputy secretary-general from 2010 to 2020, called him an inspiration.

“The world has lost a truly exceptional human rights defender. He paid for his commitment to a more just world with many years in prison and constant harassment by the Bahraini authorities. This must have taken a toll on his health,” said Alexis Deswaef, the group's president.
___ Schreck reported from Bangkok and Metz from Jerusalem.

title: Japan urges creation of an Asian energy framework to counter oil crises
summary: Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi has proposed the creation of an Asian energy agency to help countries in the region cope with oil crises, such as the shocks from the Iran war
story: Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi has proposed the creation of an Asian energy agency to help countries in the region cope with oil crises, such as the shocks from the Iran war

MANILA, Philippines -- Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi proposed Tuesday the creation of an Asian energy agency to help countries in the region cope with oil crises, such as the shocks from the Iran war.

Takaichi called for setting up an oil security task force and a Japan-based version of the International Energy Agency for the region. She put forward the plan at a meeting on the sidelines of the annual summit of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations in the Philippine capital, Manila.
“We would like to position this as an Asian version of the IEA,” Takaichi said.

The IEA is a multigovernmental but independent agency set up in 1974 in response to a severe oil crisis in the early 1970s. It provides policy recommendations and helps to coordinate oil reserves of its members. The Iran war that began in late February has raised the sense of urgency over energy security, especially in Asia.

Japan would help lead an Asian oil security task force, along with the Indonesia-based Economic Research Institute for ASEAN and East Asia, or ERIA, an energy security research organization, to develop rules for emergency releases and sharing of oil from national stockpiles, Takaichi told a meeting of the Asia Zero Emissions Community.

Japan is one of many Asian countries that depend heavily on imports of oil and gas. Takaichi's proposals follow a Japanese-led initiative announced in April to strengthen energy supply chains and cooperation in the region.
The region also should cooperate in stockpiling oil and set up a joint reserve system for Southeast Asia, Takaichi said. Idled oil storage tanks in Japan could be used for reserves, she said.

Soaring prices for oil and gas and disruptions to the shipping of oil from the Persian Gulf through the Strait of Hormuz due to the war led some countries in Asia to take emergency measures to conserve energy. It also has prompted a faster shift to use of renewable energy such as rooftop solar and electric vehicles.

title: Pope forgives person who nailed him in the eye with a rosary in Peru
summary: Pope Leo XIV has forgiven the person who threw a rosary at him before his final Mass in Peru and nailed him in the eye
story: ABOARD THE PAPAL PLANE -- Pope Leo XIV has forgiven the person who threw a rosary at him before his final Mass in Peru and nailed him in the eye, saying it was merely a sign of the person’s profound faith.

Leo got hit during a popemobile ride Monday through the estimated 1.5 million people who had flooded a Lima air base for the service. Leo grimaced and touched his eye but proceeded as if nothing had happened.

During an in-flight press conference en route home, a Peruvian reporter apologized for the incident. Leo, who lived in Peru for two decades and has Peruvian citizenship, brushed it off as merely someone trying to get close to the pope.
And he also joked about it.

“The nice thing about Peruvians, including the person who with a lot of faith simply wanted to offer me a rosary, are things you carry in your heart – or maybe in your eye – but that mark the life of someone,” he said.
“It tells you that here truly there is enthusiasm. Here there is profound faith. Here there is a desire to receive the blessing of the Lord,” he said.

People often toss rosaries, stuffed animals, sports jerseys and other items toward the pope when he is in the popemobile and he has often wowed crowds with his quick reflexes and ability to catch them. His bodyguards, however, say these tossed items are some of their biggest security concerns when he’s out in public.

title: 4 detained in North Macedonia for alleged Iran-backed assassination plot in Greece
summary: Authorities in North Macedonia say four people have been detained for questioning over an alleged Iran-linked assassination plot in neighboring Greece
story: Authorities in North Macedonia say four people have been detained for questioning over an alleged Iran-linked assassination plot in neighboring Greece
SKOPJE, North Macedonia -- Authorities in North Macedonia have detained four people for questioning over an alleged Iran-linked assassination plot in neighboring Greece, officials said Tuesday.

Bojan Hristovski, director of North Macedonia's domestic security agency, said Tuesday that the suspects are all Macedonian citizens, adding that a fifth person had also been questioned and a sixth remained wanted by the authorities.

Hristovski named one of the Iranian recruiters as Naji Sharifi Zindashti, who is wanted in the United States for allegedly operating a criminal network that targets Iranian dissidents and activists abroad.
He did not give details of the alleged target in Greece, and Greek authorities did not immediately comment on the announcement.
“This concerns the dismantling of an Iranian proxy network involved in planning a terrorist attack,” Hristovski said.

“The network operating in Macedonia consisted of individuals embedded in criminal organizations within the country,” he said. “Acting on direct instructions from an Iranian national, they undertook preparatory and logistical activities for a terrorist act — an assassination targeting a previously identified individual located in Greece.”
Iran's mission to the United Nations did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

title: Pope Leo’s envoy brings message of comfort and unity to Holy Land Christians
summary: The Catholic cardinal who oversees care of the faithful in the Holy Land visited Jerusalem to convey Pope Leo XIV's presence during troubled times for Christians
story: The Catholic cardinal who oversees care of the faithful in the Holy Land visited Jerusalem to convey Pope Leo XIV's presence during troubled times for Christians

JERUSALEM -- The Vatican cardinal who oversees care of the Catholic faithful in the Holy Land visited Jerusalem on Tuesday, saying he wanted to convey the presence of Pope Leo XIV during particularly troubled times for Christians in the region.

Cardinal Claudio Gugerotti, prefect of the Vatican’s Dicastery for the Eastern Churches, prayed before the Holy Edicule inside the Church of the Holy Sepulcher, which marks the site where Christians believe Jesus was buried and rose from the dead.
“Lord, you were here physically,” Gugerotti prayed. “Lord, give hope to the world.”

Leaders of other Christian denominations in Jerusalem listened intently. The incense-filled ceremony, with clergy in solemn robes, offered a show of unity in the basilica where they have sometimes tensely shared worship space in a unique arrangement dating to the 19th century.

Preceded by bagpipers, rows of Franciscan friars and a large cross, Gugerotti and other Christian leaders processed through the narrow stone alleyways of Jerusalem’s Old City to the centuries-old church.
Harassment of clergy and faithful there has been rising. A rare violent attack on a religious sister in April sent shock waves across Israel.
“We know we are not always welcome,” said Sister Marie Reine, a Catholic nun who joined the procession in her white habit. “But our presence can bring peace, too.”

Most of Israel’s Christians are Palestinians, who have been the target of heated rhetoric after Arab-led parties made historic gains in the national elections last month. And neighboring Jordan is reeling from an attack that killed nine worshippers during a service at a Greek Orthodox church.

“We pray that these days may confirm in faith and in hope our priests and religious, who serve with great fidelity in often demanding conditions; our families, who choose, day after day, to remain; and our young people, who need to know that the Church stands beside them as they seek to build a future here,” said Cardinal Pierbattista Pizzaballa, the Latin Patriarch of Jerusalem, in a statement before the visit.

A Catholic father who participated in Tuesday's procession said his children want the family to leave Jerusalem, where many Christians say tensions have grown since the war triggered by the Hamas-led attacks on Oct. 7, 2023.
“To be here is a vocation,” Andre Haddad said. “We can’t just flee our reality.”

Christians’ emigration from across the Holy Land is an intensifying concern, church and lay leaders say. Many Christians in Israel feel especially vulnerable to organized crime because they are a tiny minority and believe the state provides them little protection “because I’m another Arab,” said Wadie Abunassar, a Catholic community leader from the northern Israeli city of Haifa.

Gugerotti’s six-day visit is also scheduled to take him to Bethlehem, where he will visit the Basilica of the Nativity – where Christians believe Jesus was born – and a mosque. The town is in the occupied West Bank, where Palestinian Muslims and members of the dwindling Christian minority have denounced growing violence by Israeli settlers.

He is also planning to meet the leaders of the Greek Orthodox and Armenian churches in Jerusalem, several of whom attended Tuesday's prayers. During his first papal trip to the Middle East last fall, Leo prayed that Christians might again be united after more than 1,000 years of division between Eastern and Western churches.

Gugerotti's public schedule does not include meetings with Israeli leaders. Leo has reached out to Jewish faith leaders since the inauguration of his pontificate last year, raising hopes for a new start after a strained relationship under his predecessor. He has spoken against rising antisemitism while pleading for an end to war and displacement in Gaza.

title: Angry crowds rally against Slovakia's pro-Russian leader on Velvet Revolution anniversary
summary: Crowds have gathered in Slovakia to protest the government of pro-Russian Prime Minister Robert Fico on the anniversary of the 1989 Velvet Revolution, which ended communist rule in Czechoslovakia
story: Crowds have gathered in Slovakia to protest the government of pro-Russian Prime Minister Robert Fico on the anniversary of the 1989 Velvet Revolution, which ended communist rule in Czechoslovakia

BRATISLAVA, Slovakia -- People in Slovakia took to the streets Tuesday to rally against the government of pro-Russian Prime Minister Robert Fico on the anniversary of the 1989 Velvet Revolution that brought an end to decades of communist rule in Czechoslovakia.

Opposition parties organized the protests in dozens of communities across the country, where Fico remains as Europe’s most pro-Russian leader since Hungary’s Viktor Orbán was ousted from power in April.
“We’ve had enough of Fico,” chanted people in Bratislava, where organizers estimated 25,000 gathered in the downtown SNP square. One banner had a message for the prime minister: “Go to hell.”

The capital's rally united the liberal groups Progressive Slovakia and the Democrats with pro-business Freedom and Solidarity, the conservative Christian Democrats and an alliance of ethnic Hungarians. Together they hope to defeat Fico and his coalition government in next year’s parliamentary election.
“Just as in 1989, what unites us must be stronger than what divides us,” said Michal Šimečka, leader of the major opposition Progressive Slovakia party. “We’ll win only if we stick together.”

The government angered opponents by sending Foreign Minister Juraj Blanár to Russia for talks about renewing economic cooperation and other ties between the two countries for the first time since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

Fico agreed on the plan during one of his trips to Moscow to meet with Russian President Vladimir Putin, and held a Cabinet meeting to discuss a report about Blanár’s visit just hours before the rally on Tuesday.
“Shame, shame,” the crowd chanted in condemnation.
Fico has long been a divisive figure in Slovakia, and thousands have repeatedly rallied to protest his policies. Czechoslovakia split into the Czech Republic and Slovakia in 1993.

His views on Russia’s war on Ukraine and other issues sharply differ from the European mainstream. Fico ended Slovakia’s military aid for Ukraine, opposes EU sanctions on Russia, wants to block Ukraine from joining NATO and rejected EU loan guarantees for Ukraine.

title: Iran war dents Middle East sports as events are canceled. F1 bucks the trend
summary: The season-ending Formula 1 races in the Middle East are going ahead despite the war in Iran and retaliatory attacks across the region that have canceled or postponed other large sports events
story: The season-ending Formula 1 races in the Middle East are going ahead despite the war in Iran and retaliatory attacks across the region that have canceled or postponed other large sports events

Two season-ending Formula 1 races in the Middle East are going ahead despite the war in Iran and retaliatory attacks across the region that have canceled or postponed other large sports events. This includes two Formula 1 races earlier this year in Saudi Arabia and Bahrain.

The conflict has upended the region's image as a safe haven where governments and sponsors have kicked in billions to lure mega-sports events. This comes as Europe and North America appear wary of such lavish spending.

“The situation could change but the geography will not change,” Sebastian Sons, who follows sports in the Middle East with the German research institute CARPO, told The Associated Press. “The Middle East and the Gulf region are always a volatile and fragile region.”

Going ahead is an endorsement for doing business in the region, but has also prompted concerns about safety from some teams and staff. Mohammed Ben Sulayem, the president of auto racing's world governing body FIA, has said “we are fully prepared” to pull off the two races: Qatar on Nov. 29 and Abu Dhabi on Dec. 6.
Ben Sulayem is from the United Arab Emirates.
A MotoGP race was held in Qatar on Nov. 8 on the track where F1 races. MotoGP is operated by Liberty Media, which also runs F1.

“Holding the races in Qatar and Abu Dhabi signals that those two are stable and able to host large-scale sporting events. It is important they are seen to be open for business,” Kristian Ulrichsen, a political scientist at Rice University's Baker Institute, told The AP.

“Predictability in long-term decision-making and policy planning,” Ulrichsen added, “made the region so attractive as a host of mega-events at a time when many cities and countries around the world are rethinking the cost of doing so.”

Qatar’s reputation is on the line. It held the 2022 World Cup and is a co-favorite — with India — to land the 2036 Olympics. It’s also host next year to the basketball World Cup (Aug. 27-Sept. 12) and has the 2030 Asian Games.
It took a hit last week when the United States pulled its team from the boys’ under-17 World Cup being played in Qatar.
Saudi Arabia and its Persian Gulf neighbors have spent big to hold major sports events but were cutting back on mega-sports funding before the war began nine months ago.

“For Saudi, the war has accelerated the need to find economies, to maybe reassess what was feasible and what wasn’t,” Ulrichsen said. He said landing the “big prize,” two years ago — the 2034 World Cup — probably honed Saudi's focus.
“Qatar and the UAE will probably have to at some point do the same,” he added.

Major events called off, postponed or relocated include the two Formula 1 races earlier in the season, and the WTA season-ending tennis finals and soccer’s monthlong Asian Cup — both originally scheduled for Saudi Arabia. The 2027 Dakar Rally was also moved from Saudi Arabia to Portugal and Morocco.

The region has been using sports to promote “soft power” to enhance its brand. But Saudi Arabia now faces hard power with Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi rebels having struck Saudi Arabia’s main international airport in Riyadh. Riyadh’s business district has also recently been targeted.
The war has also affected the large Gulf air carriers and changed travel patterns in the region.

“One of the things Iran did during the war was to deliberately attack the connective tissue between Gulf states and the world,” Sascha Bruchmann, an analyst at the International Institute for Strategic Studies, told The AP. “This includes ports, airports, hotels and data centers — signaling that Iran can attack important issues beyond hydrocarbons and challenge the Gulf states’ ambitions to diversify.”

Sons, the researcher at the German think tank, estimated that Saudi Arabia invested more than $6 billion in international sports between 2021 and 2023. Sons said the country hosted more than 100 international sports events between 2019 and 2024.

A visible failure was the bankruptcy of LIV Golf, which reports say was funded by approximately $5 billion from Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund. Saudi Arabia also canceled the 2029 Asian Winter Games, planned for the Trojena ski village in the south of the desert kingdom.
The event has been moved to Almaty, Kazakhstan, which lost to Beijing in a close vote for the 2022 Winter Olympics.

Ulrichsen said Saudi Arabia was backing off what seemed like a “scattergun approach,” backing LIV Golf, planning an unlikely Winter Asian Games, bankrolling soccer star Cristiano Ronaldo, and buying the Premier League team Newcastle. All are varied approaches to “soft power.”
Ronaldo is reported to earn more than $200 million annually with Saudi club Al-Nassr.

Qatar's sovereign wealth fund controls French club Paris Saint-Germain, and Manchester City is controlled by an Abu Dhabi investment group. Ulrichsen argued sports teams are a more effective investment than World Cups or Olympics “because people care more about the teams they support than an event that happens for three or four weeks.”

“When Ronaldo would post on Instagram about the amazing lifestyle he was enjoying in Riyadh, that would reach upward of a half a billion people,” Ulrichsen added. “You simply can't buy that kind of reach with a conventional PR campaign.”

title: St. Peter's Basilica marks 400 years at the heart of Roman Catholicism
summary: St. Peter’s Basilica, the spiritual heart of Roman Catholicism, marks the 400th anniversary of its dedication
story: St. Peter’s Basilica, the spiritual heart of Roman Catholicism, marks the 400th anniversary of its dedication

VATICAN CITY -- VATICAN CITY (AP) — St. Peter’s Basilica, the spiritual heart of Roman Catholicism whose commanding dome defines the Roman skyline, marks the 400th anniversary of its dedication Wednesday, a monument to artistic achievement and perseverance.

Its construction spanned 120 years, 20 pontificates and the work of a succession of 12 architects, enduring the Protestant Reformation and the sack of Rome before Pope Urban VIII dedicated it on Nov. 18, 1626.

“You walk through those doors and you won’t feel the conflicts and the disasters and the setbacks,” said Elizabeth Lev, a Rome-based American art historian. “You walk through those doors and you see continuity and beauty and achievement and triumph.”

A setting for papal ceremonies and a destination for millions of pilgrims each year, the basilica was built over the traditional burial site of the Apostle Peter, replacing a church that had stood for more than a millennium.
Pope Julius II laid the foundation stone on April 18, 1506, launching a project whose architects included Donato Bramante, Michelangelo and Carlo Maderno, who completed its facade.
Even on the day of its dedication, the basilica’s familiar setting was still taking shape.
“The church facade was complete, but the amazing piazza, which is part and parcel of the church we know today, wasn’t there yet,” Lev said.
“As a matter of fact, you would have heard lots of people complaining about the new facade and how it blocked Michelangelo’s dome,” she said.

Gian Lorenzo Bernini’s sweeping oval piazza was completed in 1667, its curving colonnades conceived as the welcoming arms of the Church. Its 284 columns, arranged in four rows, frame an oval space connected to the basilica by a trapezoidal forecourt.

Inside, the basilica’s architecture draws attention toward its spiritual center: Peter’s tomb beneath the main altar, Bernini’s monumental bronze canopy and Michelangelo’s dome rising overhead. Generations of popes have been entombed in the basilica and the Vatican Grottoes below.
“The inside of St. Peter’s Basilica is marked by unity and magnificence,” Lev said. “So for a church that took 120 years, it’s amazing how each part fits together into something of a unified whole.”

The basilica and its square have witnessed the opening of the Second Vatican Council, papal funerals and the first appearances of newly elected pontiffs. Crowds gather in the square for Sunday blessings, while at Christmas and Easter the pope traditionally delivers his message and “Urbi et Orbi” blessing — Latin for “to the city and to the world” — from the basilica’s central balcony.
In one of the defining images of the coronavirus pandemic, Pope Francis stood before the rain-soaked, deserted square to impart an extraordinary blessing on March 27, 2020.
The basilica also provided the setting for a private meeting between U.S. President Donald Trump and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy before Francis’ funeral on April 26, 2025.
For Lev, the basilica's long history offers a message for another unsettled age.

“I think one of the great lessons about St. Peter’s is that people adapt, the church adapts according to the circumstances,” she said. “And yes indeed, many terrible things happened while they were building that church and they forged onwards and they ended up making something beautiful.”
Barry reported from Milan.

title: David Beckham sues after his fragrance is sold in gas stations and discount stores
summary: David Beckham’s company is suing beauty group Coty for at least $41 million, alleging that sales of his perfumes in discount stores breached their licensing agreement and damaged his luxury brand
story: David Beckham’s company is suing beauty group Coty for at least $41 million, alleging that sales of his perfumes in discount stores breached their licensing agreement and damaged his luxury brand
LONDON -- A dispute over the sale of David Beckham perfumes has struck a sour note with the soccer star turned style icon.
Beckham’s commercial company is suing a beauty firm after his “luxury” fragrances were allegedly found for sale in discount stores and a gas station bargain bin.

DB Ventures has filed a claim in the New York Supreme Court against German beauty group Coty, which makes and distributes a range of Beckham-branded fragrances and toiletries. They include the Classic and Instinct lines and the eaux de toilette Intimately and Exquisite Leather.
The claim argues that Beckham’s “world-renowned global brand is synonymous with excellence and refinement,” and “David Beckham products are a symbol of everyday luxury.”

“Imagine, then, the shock and dismay experienced when DB Ventures discovered that David Beckham products were being offered for sale in a gas station,” the legal document says. “How could this possibly have happened? Desperation and greed.”

Lawyers for DB Ventures allege that Beckham-branded products “ended up in the bargain bin inside a gas station” and at British budget retailer Poundland, “allowing the product to be sold for dollar store prices and associating the David Beckham brand with cheap, discount products.”
DB Ventures is seeking at least $41 million in damages for breach of its licensing agreement.

Coty has asked a judge to dismiss the lawsuit, which was filed in April. The company argues that New York courts have no jurisdiction in the case, and says DB Ventures is using the claim to “manufacture its early exit” from its licensing deal and hand over the Beckham contracts to another firm, Interparfums.
Coty and DB Ventures did not immediately respond to requests for comment on Tuesday.

Beckham, the former soccer star for Manchester United and Real Madrid and captain of the England men’s national team, parlayed success on the pitch into a lucrative business career that includes co-ownership of soccer team Inter Miami. He was knighted last year by King Charles III, becoming Sir David.

He also has had a very public persona as a fashion model, “Bend it Like Beckham” movie muse and is husband to Spice Girl-turned-fashion designer Victoria “Posh Spice” Beckham. The couple have four children.
The Sunday Times Rich list earlier this year estimated the Beckhams' wealth at almost 1.2 billion pounds ($1.58 billion).

title: Ukraine criticizes IAEA plan to appoint sanctioned Russian official to senior post
summary: Ukraine has criticized the proposal by the International Atomic Energy Agency to appoint a Russian official, sanctioned by Kyiv, to a senior position
story: Ukraine has criticized the proposal by the International Atomic Energy Agency to appoint a Russian official, sanctioned by Kyiv, to a senior position

VIENNA -- VIENNA (AP) — Ukraine on Wednesday denounced a proposal by the head of the International Atomic Energy Agency to appoint a Russian official sanctioned by Kyiv to a senior position at the U.N. nuclear watchdog in Vienna.

Ukraine’s Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha called the proposed appointment of Alexey Ferapontov as deputy director general “categorically unacceptable” and urged IAEA chief Rafael Mariano Grossi to “abandon this appointment" in a post on X.

In a note sent Nov. 16 to all 35 members of the IAEA Board of Governors, which was seen by The Associated Press, Grossi proposed the nomination of Ferapontov to the position of deputy director general in the Department of Nuclear Energy.

The note also proposed a candidate from the United States to the position of deputy director general in the Department of Management, and a candidate from North Macedonia to become director in the Department of Safeguards.

Grossi suggested holding an informal briefing about the senior appointments with members of the board this week. According to the IAEA’s Statute and staff regulations, the IAEA director general has the authority to appoint staff members.

“Ferapontov is subject to Ukrainian sanctions for his involvement in Russia’s attempts to legitimize the illegal seizure of the Zaporizhzhia Nuclear Power Plant,” Sybiha wrote on X. “Officials implicated in such violations should face accountability, not be rewarded with senior positions in international organizations,” he added.

“Appointing a senior official from the Russian authority complicit in legitimizing Russia’s illegal seizure of the plant would be an unacceptable endorsement of impunity and a serious blow to the Agency’s credibility,” Sybiha noted.
Ferapontov is currently deputy head of Rostechnadzor, Russia’s Federal Environmental, Industrial and Nuclear Supervision Service.
The Russian Foreign Ministry did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The Zaporizhzhia nuclear power plant has been under Russian control since early in Moscow’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Although the plant is not operating, it needs reliable external power to cool its six shut-down reactors and spent fuel to avoid any catastrophic nuclear incidents.
The plant is near the front line and has been occupied by Russia since March 2022. Ukraine and Russia have traded blame for shelling close to the plant.

On Nov. 8 the site experienced its 27th complete loss of off-site power since the start of the conflict, according to the IAEA. The external power line has since been restored, but diesel fuel reserves that are necessary for emergency generators have been reduced at the plant, the IAEA warned.
Sybiha also referred to Grossi’s campaign to become the next U.N. Secretary-General, stressing the importance of the “independence and impartiality” of the IAEA.
“There can be no room for political considerations or external influence in decisions of such importance,” he wrote.

Grossi confirmed his plans to appoint Ferapontov as deputy director general in the IAEA’s Department for Nuclear Energy during a news conference on Wednesday on the first day of a regular meeting of the IAEA Board of Governors in Vienna. Grossi said the criteria in making such appointments relate to the “technical experience and the technical capacities” of the appointees.

“When I appoint somebody, I’m not appointing a country, I am not appointing a policy, I am not appointing preferences in this regard,” Grossi said. “We are appointing the person and individual that has the capacities to fulfill that position.”
Grossi added that in the specific case related to Ferapontov, “it’s a very well-known expert in areas like nuclear safety, nuclear security and others.”

The post of deputy director general in the IAEA’s Department for Nuclear Energy became vacant after the IAEA in September suspended the previous incumbent, Mikhail Chudakov, a Russian senior official who had a decades-long career in Russia’s nuclear industry.

Chudakov reportedly promoted a book he published under a pseudonym among a U.N. youth group that allegedly contained degrading comments about feminism and LGBT people and expressed support for authoritarian government. The IAEA never commented publicly on the suspension. Bloomberg first reported about Chudakov’s suspension.
The IAEA has six deputy director-general posts.
