title: How Europe decided on 'return hubs' for migrants
summary: A group of European countries has announced plans to establish a "migrant hub" in Rwanda for rejected asylum-seekers
story: A group of European countries has announced plans to establish a "migrant hub" in Rwanda for rejected asylum-seekers
BRUSSELS -- A group of European countries announced on Monday that they aim to set up a “migrant hub” in Rwanda where rejected asylum-seekers could be sent from next year.

The European Union has worked for years to tighten migration rules, push down the number of asylum-seekers coming to the 27-nation bloc and increase deportations of migrants who aren’t entitled to stay. Sending people to centers outside Europe has emerged as a central element.
Here's a timeline of events that led to this agreement:
2015: Over 1 million people — the majority from war-stricken Syria — arrive in Europe seeking asylum, in what was at the time the largest migration crisis impacting the continent since World War II.

June 2016: The U.K. votes to leave the European Union in a referendum following a campaign during which those favoring Brexit use images of lines of migrants as a warning of what staying in the EU would entail.

September 2018: Sweden joins Europe's move to the right as voters boost a party that campaigned on anti-migrant sentiment and policies. It follows similar shifts in Germany, Austria and Italy as part of a backlash to the 2015 migration crisis. Denmark floats an idea it later scraps to deport migrants to a remote island once used as a research laboratory for contagious animal diseases.

September 2020: Denmark appoints a special envoy to toughen EU migration policies including setting up migrant reception centers in one or more countries outside the EU to diminish the incentive for migrants to seek asylum in Denmark and improving the deportation of rejected asylum-seekers.

April 2021: After Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen, leading a center-left Social Democratic-led government, rolls out a vision of having “zero asylum-seekers," Denmark begins revoking the residency permits of some Syrian refugees.

April 2022: Britain announces a deal with Rwanda to send some asylum-seekers thousands of miles to the East African country — a plan it says will stop people-smugglers sending desperate migrants on treacherous journeys across the English Channel.

November 2023: The U.K. Supreme Court rules that the deal with Rwanda to return asylum-seekers there is unlawful because they would not be safe there. The Conservative government says it will send migrants to the African country regardless. Italian Premier Giorgia Meloni and her Albanian counterpart, Edi Rama, strike a five-year deal for Albania to shelter up to 3,000 migrants picked up by the Italian coast guard in international waters each month.

June 2024: Far-right parties make major gains in elections to the Parliament of the European Union, rattling traditional political powers. In France, President Emmanuel Macron calls a snap election that results in a boost for the anti-migration far right, weakening his own government.
July 2024: The U.K. scraps the Rwanda migration deal shortly after the Conservatives are defeated in an election, ceding power to the Labour Party under Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer.

October 2024: Italy’s government formally opens two centers in Albania where it plans to process male migrants who are intercepted in international waters. Less than a month later, a court in Italy rules against the right-wing government’s move to detain 12 migrants at the new centers.

January 2025: An Italian appeals court refuses to approve the speedy expulsion of 43 asylum seekers detained in Albania. The migrants were among 49 people who were transferred to Albania on an Italian naval ship under the five-year agreement with Albania.

March 2025: The Meloni government approves a decree expanding the use of the Albanian fast-track processing centers to include the detention of rejected asylum-seekers with deportation orders. The Albanian centers have remained substantially inactive since their opening in October, due to legal hurdles and amid wide opposition from human rights groups.
April 2025: Italian authorities transfer 40 migrants with no permission to remain in the country to the Albanian centers.

March 2026: Rwanda tells an international arbitration panel that Britain still owes it 100 million pounds ($134 million) under the refugee resettlement deal scrapped in 2024. The court dismisses Rwanda's claim.

March 2026: European lawmakers vote to ease the setting up of new migrant detention centers outside the European Union, known as “return hubs.” Any EU nation can start negotiating on its own or in small coalitions to deport migrants not to their home countries but to facilities yet to be built outside the 27-nation bloc.

June 2026: The three main bodies of the EU, the European Parliament, the European Commission and the European Council, reach agreement over migration policy to increase deportations and to allow member nations to make deals for so-called return hubs.

August 2026: A spokesperson for the Rwandan government defends the practice of establishing return hubs, saying it is “natural” for her government to negotiate with European countries and others to potentially host asylum seekers who are not allowed to live elsewhere.
Sept. 2026: Denmark and four other European Union countries agree on a model for “return hubs” in non-EU nations and say they hope to begin sending migrants to the facilities as early as 2027.
Ciobanu reported from Warsaw, Poland.

title: Military jet crashes in Serbia and the pilot is killed, authorities say
summary: Serbia's defense ministry says that a military jet crashed northwest of Belgrade, killing the pilot
story: Serbia's defense ministry says that a military jet crashed northwest of Belgrade, killing the pilot
BELGRADE, Serbia -- A Serbian military jet crashed on Tuesday northwest of Belgrade, killing the pilot, the defense ministry said. The ministry did not immediately give a reason for the crash.
The MIG-29 jet crashed around 8:45 a.m. into a field near the town of Stara Pazova, some 50 kilometers (30 miles) from the Serbian capital, a statement said.
Some local Serbian media published photos of the burning wreckage in the field and an ambulance and police cars parked nearby.

Serbia's defense ministry statement said a special commission will work to determine what happened. The pilot, Maj. Goran Bulajic, was born in 1973 and had joined the army in 1996, it said. No other details were immediately available.

title: Iran-backed group warns Iraqi forces against entering its stronghold near Baghdad
summary: Kataib Hezbollah, a powerful Iran-backed armed group, has vowed to confront Iraqi government forces if they enter its stronghold near Baghdad
story: Kataib Hezbollah, a powerful Iran-backed armed group, has vowed to confront Iraqi government forces if they enter its stronghold near Baghdad

JURF AL-SAKHAR, Iraq -- A powerful Iran-backed armed group in Iraq vowed on Tuesday to confront government forces if they try to enter its main stronghold near Baghdad, denying allegations that it is smuggling oil from the area.
The standoff between Kataib Hezbollah and Iraqi authorities is shaping up to be the first major test of the new government’s resolve to disarm nonstate armed groups.

Abu Taleb al-Saidi of Kataib Hezbollah made the comments a day after Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi said security forces would enter Jurf al-Sakhar, south of Baghdad in Babil province, later this week. Local media reported that the group had until Friday to leave.
Kataib Hezbollah, one of Iraq’s most powerful armed groups, wields considerable influence in Jurf al-Sakhar and has maintained an armed presence there for more than a decade.

The planned move by al-Zaidi is part of his push to disarm powerful Iran-backed groups by mid-2027. The move by both rival sides raises alarms of internal Shiite fighting that has been mostly avoided since the 2003 U.S.-led invasion that removed Saddam Hussein from power.

Two officials from Kataib Hezbollah told The Associated Press that Gen. Esmail Qaani, who heads the foreign wing of Iran’s Revolutionary Guard, arrived in Baghdad on Monday to take part in mediation to end the tension. The officials, who spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to comment publicly, gave no further details.

The United States backs efforts to disarm Iran-backed groups in Iraq as part of its push to reduce Tehran’s influence in the region, including in Iraq and Lebanon. Washington has described Kataib Hezbollah as an “Iran-backed terrorist organization.”

Lebanese authorities will likely be watching the standoff in Jurf al-Sakhar closely. They have made little progress in carrying out their own plan to disarm Lebanon’s Hezbollah militia, which is allied with but separate from Kataib Hezbollah.
Also Tuesday, an Iraqi judicial committee inspected Jurf al-Sakhar following allegations by authorities that Kataib Hezbollah had used the area to smuggle oil worth tens of millions of dollars.

The state news agency quoted an unnamed senior official as saying the judicial committee was accompanied by a government committee. The inspection aimed to examine the circumstances of the alleged smuggling and identify sites where violations had occurred.

The agency quoted al-Zaidi as saying that all suspects involved in the oil smuggling operations will be referred to the judiciary and that legal measures will be taken against them. He also ordered the dismissal of nine security and administrative officials in Babil governorate, including the Babil police chief, commanders and directors of security and intelligence agencies, and the director of the State Company for Oil Pipelines.

Ali al-Nheir, a member of the parliament’s investigative committee, told the state news agency that the investigation that included thermal imaging showed 25 tanker trucks each carrying 36,000 liters.
“The reports reviewed by the committee were shocking, and included evidence and documents proving the existence of smuggling operations,” al-Nheir said about Jurf al-Sakhar.

Another Kataib Hezbollah official, who spoke on condition of anonymity, told journalists touring Jurf al-Sakhar on Tuesday that two facilities in the area refine oil. He said the fuel was used only to run the group’s vehicles and power generators and denied allegations of smuggling.
The official said Jurf al-Sakhar had been hit more than 35 times since the U.S. and Israel began attacking Iran in late February.
He warned that if “a war is imposed on us we will fight.”
Associated Press writer Bassem Mroue contributed to this report from Beirut.

title: Ukraine says it hit 2 Russian oil refineries as Zelenskyy hails weapons produced in the country
summary: Ukraine says it has carried out new strikes on two oil refineries in southern Russia
story: Ukraine says it has carried out new strikes on two oil refineries in southern Russia

KYIV, Ukraine -- Ukraine carried out new strikes on two oil refineries in southern Russia, officials said Wednesday, as Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy praised the effectiveness of Kyiv’s domestically produced weapons that damaged the key Kerch Bridge between Russia and the occupied Crimean Peninsula.

Attacks by both sides have continued even as delegations await word on another round of U.S.-mediated talks. U.S. President Donald Trump says he plans to discuss the nearly five-year war with Presidents Xi Jinping of China and Vladimir Putin of Russia on Thursday during a visit to China.

Ukraine’s General Staff said that storage tanks were hit at the Ilsky refinery and a processing unit was struck at the Afipsky refinery, both in Russia’s Krasnodar region. The two refineries, which were also targeted on Sunday night, can process around 95 million barrels of oil a year and supply Russian forces on the front line in southern and eastern Ukraine, it said.
Russian officials reported attacks on two industrial enterprises in the region, but they gave no details.
Ukraine has repeatedly targeted refineries as Ukraine seeks to hurt Russia’s oil sector, a mainstay of its economy, and Moscow presses on with its all-out invasion of its neighbor.
“Our technologies and companies are developing very well,” Zelenskyy said in a social media post.
Ukraine's cutting-edge long-range drones and missiles were deployed against the Kerch Bridge in a large-scale attack on Monday night that was prepared over weeks, he said.
“Right now, we’re in the top three in the world for tech development. In Europe, I think we’re number one,” Zelenskyy said.
The Pentagon has argued that strikes deep inside Russia are counterproductive, but Ukraine's European backers don't agree.
The Ukrainian leader said that the Kerch Bridge strike, which could hamper Russian deliveries to its front-line troops, was justified by Russia’s relentless bombardment of Ukraine.
Moscow’s forces have focused on knocking out power in Ukraine before the winter, aiming to erode the morale of civilians.

Attacks last month killed at least 372 Ukrainian civilians and wounded 1,981 others — a number 95% higher than in October 2025, the U.N. Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine said on social media Wednesday.
This year, the war has brought “significantly higher” civilian casualties than in previous years, the agency said.

“The first 10 months of this year have seen more civilian deaths than all of 2025, which in turn was worse than the year before,” said Danielle Bell, who heads the U.N. agency in Kyiv. “The world should not become numb to the deadly toll the war exacts on Ukraine’s civilians.”

Russians attacked energy facilities, civilian businesses and residential buildings in five regions with drones overnight into Wednesday and in the morning, Ukrainian Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi said.
Four people were killed in a Russian strike on the southern Ukrainian city of Odesa on Wednesday, local officials said.
The Russian Defense Ministry said Wednesday that its forces used drones overnight to strike the port of Izmail in the Odesa region.
A Russian drone attack on a market in the Kharkiv region wounded 12 people, including an 11-year-old boy, Ukraine’s State Emergency Services said.
Barry Hatton reported from Lisbon, Portugal.
Follow the AP’s coverage of the war in Ukraine at https://apnews.com/hub/russia-ukraine

title: Thousands demonstrate in Haiti’s capital to praise Bukele and Salvadoran troops fighting gangs
summary: Thousands of people in Haiti's capital and beyond are praising El Salvador’s president, Nayib Bukele, and his troops for fighting gangs in the country
story: Thousands of people in Haiti's capital and beyond are praising El Salvador’s president, Nayib Bukele, and his troops for fighting gangs in the country

PORT-AU-PRINCE, Haiti -- Thousands of people poured into the streets of Haiti’s capital and beyond on Tuesday to praise El Salvador’s president, Nayib Bukele, and his troops as they fight gangs in the troubled Caribbean country.
Many in the crowd raised their fists and some clutched Haitian flags and signs in favor of Bukele.
“Bukele is here to free us!” some shouted.

“Give them the drones and the dogs!” others yelled in reference to the explosive drones that have targeted areas controlled by powerful gangs and the newly unveiled robot dogs making their rounds in Port-au-Prince.

Last month, Bukele deployed some 2,500 troops to Haiti after four of their own came under attack on Oct. 18 and remain missing. Fighting between gangs and foreign forces backed by Haitian authorities has only increased since then as Haiti remains mired in violence, with more than 20,000 people killed in the past five years.
While chants of “Bukele!” are spreading across Haiti, experts warn there’s no long-term plan to keep the country safe once the Central American troops pull out.
“This enthusiasm…could turn into anger against the government if the troops withdraw,” said Diego Da Rin, an analyst with International Crisis Group.

The group published a report Tuesday based on more than 100 interviews with officials in Haiti and abroad that reveal government failures and missteps as it urged Haitian officials to develop a plan to prevent their country from imploding once international forces leave.

“The new foreign mission promises temporary relief from the bane of gangs, but its goal is to weaken, not dismantle them," the report said. “Haiti should start preparing now for the day when its own forces are once again summoned to take sole charge of the nation’s security.”

Forces currently fighting gangs include Haiti’s police and soldiers; a U.N.-backed gang suppression force; self-appointed vigilantes; and Vectus Global, a private security firm founded by former U.S. Navy SEAL and Blackwater founder Erik Prince. Fighting gangs on their own are some 2,500 Salvadoran troops deployed when four of their own went missing after they were attacked on Oct. 18 deep in gang-controlled territory.
International Crisis Group warned that authorities “lack a strategy to identify the most pressing threats, coordinate state efforts, and bring a lasting reduction in violence.”

Echoing that sentiment was a recent cartoon in Le Nouvelliste newspaper that depicted Haitians cheering on Bukele as they stood near a table with a piece of paper on which someone had written “PLAN ANTI GANG” with crayons of various colors.
Tuesday’s report noted that plans to establish a National Security Council tasked with creating a long-term strategy to make Haiti safer two years ago never materialized.

Citing interviews with former senior government officials, the report stated that some people were concerned the council would oversee intelligence gathering, which has previously been used by Haitian leaders to target political opponents. Sources also told International Crisis Group that top officials did not want to see intelligence funds redirected because they feared losing that money.

International Crisis Group also said a foreign adviser told it that a lack of national strategy means that various police units “often follow different operational guidelines depending on their foreign donors.”

As of last year, Haiti’s National Police had no more than 8,000 active officers for a country of nearly 12 million people, the report said, citing “sources with first-hand knowledge.” Many of those officers occupy command and administrative positions and are not on the street, “while others are not trained for combat.”
The report said the government shortened training from seven months to less than four to quickly increase the number of police officers.

It also warned that police promotions rarely follow criteria like seniority or merit, with some rank-and-file officers opting to work with gangs or turning to private security or arms trafficking for additional income. Lower-ranking officers in Haiti are paid about $300 a month before mandatory deductions.

International Crisis Group called for improving salaries, benefits and facilities for police officers, as well as offering them specialized training and a “clear promotion system based on performance rather than politics.”
The number of victims is expected to grow as foreign forces increasingly rely on helicopters and explosive drones – two things that Haitian security forces lack – to target gangs.

In the first quarter of 2026, the number of civilians killed or injured by security forces as a fraction of all casualties rose 24%, the report found, and that number is expected to increase, but Bukele is finding fans in Haiti.

“In a security environment as troubled as Haiti’s, it is understandable that many have rallied around the use of explosive drones, particularly as initially the technology had a visible effect on gang leaders’ confidence and their willingness to attack state forces,” the report said.

Among the Haitians celebrating is Cliford Vital, who lives in Port-au-Prince, where gangs control an estimated 70% of the city. He noted that Bukele swiftly deployed more than 2,500 soldiers and helicopters to Haiti while U.N.-backed missions have lagged in his view.
“We’ve seen a wind of change in the country,” he said. “The fear that had persisted for so long has now shifted sides.”
But International Crisis Group said the use of such weapons “has brought diminishing returns…producing no meaningful changes in territorial control” or a change in the balance of power on the ground.
“That said, an immediate outright ban on the use of drones is unrealistic,” the report stated.
This week, Haitian Justice Minister Patrick Pélissier flew to El Salvador for an international conference and is expected to meet behind closed doors with Salvadoran officials.
Salvadoran Vice President Félix Ulloa said Monday that the bilateral agreement with Haiti would not be made public.
“There is a hidden agenda to criticize our operation,” he said when asked whether the deal guarantees respect for human rights and the rule of law.
Ulloa and Salvadoran Security Minister Gustavo Villatoro said that the Salvadoran soldiers would return home as soon as the four missing aviation technicians are found.
“We must begin preparing Haiti for a genuine rule of law, so that its institutions function and its legal frameworks work effectively in the future,” Villatoro said.
Coto reported from San Juan, Puerto Rico. Associated Press reporters Yolanda Magaña in San Salvador, El Salvador and Pierre-Richard Luxama in Port-au-Prince, Haiti contributed to this report.

title: Some Afghan women quietly defy Taliban bans
summary: In the shadows of the Afghan capital’s bustling streets, many women live in a hidden world, secretly defying the laws imposed on them when the Taliban seized power in August 2021
story: In the shadows of the Afghan capital’s bustling streets, many women live in a hidden world, secretly defying the laws imposed on them when the Taliban seized power in August 2021

KABUL, Afghanistan -- In the shadows of the Afghan capital’s bustling streets lies a hidden world: the world of women, quietly defying the draconian bans imposed when the Taliban seized power after the withdrawal of U.S.-led troops in August 2021.

For women, schooling beyond primary grades is banned, except for Islamic religious education and language courses. Parks and gyms are off-limits, beauty salons are outlawed, and a strict head-to-toe dress code applies. Although women can obtain some business licenses, they’re barred from most jobs.
“Being a woman in Afghanistan is a crime,” said a former soccer player whose dreams were shattered by a sports ban.

Rules are enforced by the widely feared morality police from the Ministry for the Promotion of Virtue and Prevention of Vice. They patrol the streets in doctor-like white coats and can detain women violating rules. Some have been beaten.

The ministry is “fully committed” to ensuring the rights of all under Islamic Sharia law, spokesman Mohammad Aslam Badriwal told The Associated Press in response to questions about restrictions on women.

“Our sisters may also conduct their social and commercial affairs, provided they strictly adhere to the principles of Islamic Sharia and the laws currently in force," he said, adding that the ministry's priority is ”to ensure that our sisters are completely safe within society and are able to enjoy all their Sharia-granted rights."
Some women have found ways to defy the bans, despite the risks.
Here is a look at the hidden lives of three such women in Kabul, all speaking on condition of anonymity for fear of arrest.
For years, the 40-year-old worked in one of Kabul’s beauty salons. When authorities banned them, she felt her life contract.

“You just feel a sense of hopelessness; you become completely despondent,” she said. “Right now, in Afghanistan, there’s nothing left to bring any joy or comfort. There’s no travel, no parks, no schools, there’s absolutely nothing.”
Work was all she had left.
“But now, they won’t even allow that," she said. "It’s as if, for women in Afghanistan, working has become a crime.”
Despite the salon ban, she decided to open her own. Demand was high, particularly for weddings, where women are expected to sport elaborate hairstyles and makeup.
She rented an apartment and bought equipment. Soon, she had about 30 clients. With her husband among the millions of Afghan men unable to find work, it was a lifeline.
But authorities found her secret salon. Their raid took all the equipment, nearly all the furniture.

“I felt completely hopeless,” she said. “If my work, the only thing that gave me any sense of purpose, is taken away, what am I left with? How am I supposed to feed my children? How am I supposed to cover household expenses? I reached a point of total despair and thought: ‘I’m just going to leave.’”

But clients kept calling, and she had bills to pay. Eventually, she decided to try again. She rented another apartment and reopened. Now she has seven employees – young women supporting their own families.
One recent October day, the salon was full of women getting wedding makeovers. They lay on cushions on the floor as beauticians brushed powder onto their cheeks.
The atmosphere was light, but with an undercurrent of fear.
“Every time there’s a knock on the door," the salon owner said, "I worry the Taliban might be on the other side.”

As a teenager, all her ambitions were tied up in soccer. And it looked as if her dreams were coming true: She was picked for the national team. But two years later, the ban on women’s sports crushed them.
Plunged into depression, she spent six months barely leaving her room.
Her family was worried, and she knew she had to find a way out. Eventually, she started playing again – not on pitches, but in the cramped confines of her home.
She also started boxing, turning a stack of old car tires into a rudimentary punching bag. It helped her work through her emotions, she said.

Her true love is still soccer. Unable to play properly herself, she's decided to pass on her knowledge and skills to a new generation. She coaches a small group of young boys in her home’s tiny walled courtyard.

“I saw in them the same dreams and the same passion I had held during my own childhood,” she said, tears welling in her eyes. “It feels really good for me to train with them. Sometimes, I see myself in them.”
Between boxing and coaching, she manages to get through the days. But her view of the future is bleak. She wants to leave and find refuge in another country.
“I see no hope for myself in Afghanistan,” she said.
“No doors are open to us.”
Students stagger arrivals to avoid raising suspicion. The door opens just enough to let them in.

Inside, the subjects are ordinary: history, science, geography, math, languages, Quranic studies. But it's no ordinary school. Set up inside a private home, its students are boys but also girls as old as 20. With teenage girls included, classes must be held in secret.
Teachers here — a 20-year-old with help from her teenage sister — aren’t professionally trained. They do the best they can to pass on what they learned before they were banned from school.
“The current situation in Afghanistan is far from ideal. I had been experiencing increasing levels of depression, so I decided to organize this class,” the 20-year-old said.
She started over a year ago, she said, hoping to help girls “by giving them a sense of hope and allowing them to continue their education." Now she has about 30 students.
A room in the house has been converted into a classroom, with students sitting on the floor at low plastic tables. Brightly colored drawings decorate the walls.
The education restrictions have been the most widely disliked of the Taliban's bans. Officials have repeatedly said they're working on a solution.

“Regarding the part (of education) that still has shortcomings, we are striving to resolve it comprehensively,” government spokesman Zabihullah Mujahid said in August. But there's been no sign of progress.
The teenage teaching assistant said many girls have fallen behind, and “we wanted to create an environment where girls can study and strive to reach their goals.”
But with every class they hold, they risk arrest.

“We are very afraid of the Taliban," she said. "We fear that one day, they might come after us, accuse us of violating their rules, arrest us and take us away. We are absolutely terrified of that possibility.”

title: Pope Leo says there is no change to agenda or priorities after his lung cancer surgery
summary: Pope Leo XIV says his recent lung cancer surgery hasn't changed his agenda or outlook
story: Pope Leo XIV says his recent lung cancer surgery hasn't changed his agenda or outlook

ABOARD THE PAPAL PLANE -- ABOARD THE PAPAL PLANE (AP) — Pope Leo XIV said his recent lung cancer surgery has not altered his agenda, outlook or even sense of mortality, as he projected a long pontificate focused on unity and healing within the church.

Leo seemed full of health, energy and jokes during an airborne news conference on Monday while returning to Rome from Peru. The grueling, 12-day trip through three South American countries left several members of the travelling Vatican delegation and press corps sick.
“I’m not 100% but I’m pretty good,” Leo said of his surgical recovery. “Endurance is one of the gifts the Lord gave me.”
Leo, 71, had the lower lobe of his right lung removed Oct. 13 because of a cancerous tumor. He said it was discovered by chance during an annual checkup and appeared at first as a shadow on his lung.

“The first news was a surprise. There were no symptoms. I felt fine,” he said. Once the cancer was confirmed, he decided to proceed immediately to have it removed, and said he hoped his experience would help others not fear having checkups or pursue preventive care.
Prior to going into surgery, Leo said he saw no need to make provisions for the leadership of the Catholic Church if he were left medically impaired and unable to govern.

He said he hadn’t written any instructions, as his predecessors had done, outlining the criteria under which he would resign, which some legal experts believe is necessary if a pope were to end up in an irreversible coma and unable to articulate his resignation.

“Eventually I will do it, I think, but I don’t see the need now,” Leo said, adding that he never doubted he would be in good enough shape afterward to make the South America trip. He credited good doctors, prayer and what he described as a strong sense of determination to recover.

Leo also showed himself in no hurry to appoint new cardinals who will eventually elect his successor, another sign that he is planning to be around for a while. “I will eventually get around to that,” he said.

The pontiff also seemed in no hurry to get things done, saying he still doesn’t know what trips he’ll be taking next year — aside from his previously confirmed trip to South Korea to attend World Youth Day in August.

Leo made it very clear that his No. 1 priority was “unity” and healing in the church, a reference to the polarization that has always existed but in some ways deepened during Pope Francis’ sometimes turbulent pontificate.

Leo was asked, for example, whether he would consider ordaining married men to ease the priest shortage in the Amazon, where remote Indigenous communities can go months or longer without a priest to celebrate the sacraments. Amazonian bishops had asked Francis to allow for such a change but he declined.
Leo said he had no plans to go down that path, either, saying the issue was too divisive.

While ordaining married men is one solution to the priest shortage, Leo said “it’s a solution which in certain areas of the church can cause division because there is not universal, if you will, acceptance.”
“One of my priorities is first to promote unity and communion among us as members in the church,” he said.
“It may be in the future that some things will change. However for right now, for what I believe, an important part of my ministry of the church is to heal, bring people together,” he added.

He similarly said he had no plans to change one of Francis’ most divisive decisions restricting the celebration of the old Latin Mass. Traditionalist Catholics had hoped Leo would be more sympathetic to their cause and would reverse Francis’ crackdown.
But Leo said Francis’ decision already allowed for exceptions and that his decision stands.
Where Leo did hint at some change was on the thorny issue of clergy abuse.
He met with abuse survivors in Argentina and in Peru, and said he recognized that the issue of “spiritual abuse” was a problem in the church that needed to be addressed.

For over two years, a Vatican working group has been studying “spiritual abuse,” given the increasing number of cases of people — often adult women — who accuse priests of using their spiritual authority to psychologically, physically or sexually abuse them.

While the Catholic Church has laws punishing priests who sexually abuse minors, priests who use their spiritual authority to take advantage of people under their care rarely are sanctioned since there are no explicit laws criminalizing the practice.
Leo, a canon lawyer, said he was aware of the loophole in the church’s canon law.

“Spiritual abuse is a very serious topic in the church,” and needs to be addressed canonically, Leo said. “In order to exercise justice, you have to have a codification or a juridical expression of how to apply that, and that’s a very vague concept still,” he said.
At the same time, he conceded that “we all probably could describe either specific cases or kinds of instances where that has happened.”

One recent case of alleged spiritual abuse is expected to land soon on Leo’s desk. A Vatican-appointed tribunal is deciding the fate of the Rev. Marko Rupnik, a once-famous Jesuit mosaic artist accused by two dozen women of spiritual, psychological and sexual abuse.

The women began complaining about his behavior in the 1990s, but nothing was ever done until the victims went public, amid suspicions he was protected by his Jesuit superiors, up to and including Francis.

title: More than 200 people jailed over crackdown on illegal gold mining
summary: A court in Guinea has sentenced 22 former officials and 202 miners to prison over illegal gold mining in the northeast
story: A court in Guinea has sentenced 22 former officials and 202 miners to prison over illegal gold mining in the northeast

A court in Guinea sentenced 22 former local officials and 202 miners to prison over illegal gold mining in the country’s northeast, the latest in a crackdown that has sparked deadly clashes and sent tens of thousands of people fleeing into neighboring Mali.

The government announced a crackdown on unauthorized gold mining earlier this month, saying it aims to curb environmental damage, including the destruction of farmland by heavy machinery and the pollution of rivers by chemicals.
The crackdown turned violent last week, when clashes between protesters and security forces enforcing restrictions on gold mining in northeastern Guinea killed 10 people and injured 13 others.

On Monday, the Court for the Repression of Economic and Financial Offenses in Conakry, Guinea’s capital, sentenced the 22 former officials from Siguiri, a major gold-producing area near Guinea’s border with Mali, to two years in prison each for complicity in environmental degradation, destruction and water pollution. Each official was also fined 10 million Guinean francs (about $1,120).

The 202 illegal miners — who included several foreign nationals — received three-year prison sentences on the same charges, in addition to illegal mining. They were ordered to pay a combined fine of 10 billion Guinean francs ($1.1 million).
The court also banned the foreign nationals involved in the case from Guinean territory for 10 years.
The 224 defendants sentenced on Monday were among more than 1,200 people arrested in Siguiri earlier this month on suspicion of illegal gold mining.

Unauthorized gold mining has been the livelihood of more than 300,000 people in Guinea, according to the U.N. Environment Program. Guinea’s gold mines have long attracted workers from across West Africa.
The crackdown has sent tens of thousands of miners and their families, many originally from Burkina Faso, fleeing into neighboring Mali, according to Malian authorities.

title: Migrants face severe health tolls amid South Africa's anti-illegal migration tensions
summary: Aid groups in South Africa report that anti-illegal migration protests have severely impacted the health of migrants
story: Aid groups in South Africa report that anti-illegal migration protests have severely impacted the health of migrants

JOHANNESBURG -- Migrants affected by protests against illegal immigration in South Africa have suffered devastating impacts to their health as they avoided visiting medical facilities or left the country to avoid violence in recent months, aid groups said Wednesday.
Many migrants who had been receiving medication in South Africa for HIV, tuberculosis and other ailments have had their treatment severely disrupted, they said.

Children, pregnant women and people traveling with newborns have been among the most affected, while others suffered physical injuries and illnesses including respiratory infections, high blood pressure and gastrointestinal issues during rushed journeys home from South Africa, they said.

South Africa has been gripped by anti-illegal migration protests accusing foreigners in the country illegally of committing crimes, stealing jobs amid high unemployment and overburdening public services. Tens of thousands have voluntarily repatriated to their home countries including Malawi, Nigeria and Ghana. Some fled after violent attacks.

Some protesters have blocked foreigners from accessing clinics and other public health facilities, claiming they are exclusively reserved for South Africans even though the law allows foreigners to receive treatment there.

“Many migrants at displacement sites reported not accessing healthcare for many months, and up to a year in some cases, due to fear of being turned away or harmed," said Claire Waterhouse, the Doctors Without Borders advocacy director for Southern Africa.

Patients with chronic infectious diseases including HIV or TB had defaulted or were close to defaulting on their treatment regimens, causing high distress and worsening illness and increasing the risk of resistance in wider populations.
Doctors Without Borders has been among the aid organizations supporting the migrants, setting up sites in Cape Town and Johannesburg and also in the town of Musina near the border with Zimbabwe.
In Zimbabwe, a site was set up at the Beitbridge border post and the Nyamapanda border between Zimbabwe and Mozambique where migrants who had left South Africa received treatment.
Khanyisa Mapipa, an attorney with rights group Section27, said the organization is pursuing a legal case against the Gauteng department of health and the city of Johannesburg.

“In December 2025, we obtained a court order compelling the respondents to put together a plan to ensure that patients are able to enter facilities. The second part of the application is pending," said Mapipa.
Meanwhile, aid groups and district health offices had to create parallel health systems to keep people from going without treatment, especially those with chronic illnesses, she said.

The groups have called on other governments to make adequate arrangements for reintegrating their citizens into their healthcare systems, and for chronically ill people leaving South Africa to be given adequate supplies of medication to maintain continuity of care.

title: Mozambique's Mondlane is the latest opposition leader to go on trial in Africa
summary: Mozambique’s opposition leader will go on trial charged with instigating terrorism and inciting civil disobedience in relation to monthslong anti-government protests that broke out following a disputed 2024 election
story: Mozambique’s opposition leader will go on trial charged with instigating terrorism and inciting civil disobedience in relation to monthslong anti-government protests that broke out following a disputed 2024 election

MAPUTO, Mozambique -- Mozambique's opposition leader will go on trial Tuesday charged with instigating terrorism and inciting civil disobedience in relation to monthslong anti-government protests that broke out following a disputed 2024 election that kept the country's long-ruling party in power.

Venancio Mondlane, who was the runner-up in that presidential election, is the latest opposition figure in Africa to face what some analysts say are politically motivated charges meant to silence or remove criticism.

Mondlane's trial follows the four-year prison sentence given to Tanzanian opposition leader Tundu Lissu this month for inciting people to disrupt a 2025 election. Lissu, who said he was prosecuted for calling for electoral reform, was acquitted of treason in that case.
One of Uganda's veteran opposition figures, Kizza Besigye, is on trial for treason and faces a potential death penalty if convicted.

Zambia's leading opposition figure and several supporters also face treason charges in their southern African country following another troubled election this year that rights groups say was characterized by a campaign of harassment against the opposition.

In Mozambique in eastern Africa, Mondlane lost to President Daniel Chapo of the Frelimo party in the 2024 election. Frelimo has now governed Mozambique for 51 years since independence from Portugal in 1975 and has been accused of rigging elections and suppressing opposition, which it denies.

Mondlane rejected the 2024 results as fraudulent and called for protests and people to stay away from work after the vote. Postelection protests by thousands of people lasted months in the largest popular uprising against Frelimo. They were exacerbated by the killing of Mondlane's lawyer and another official with their opposition Podemos party, who were fatally shot in a car in what Mondlane called political assassinations.
Mondlane left Mozambique for a period following the killings claiming his life was in danger.

Amnesty International, citing local civic groups, said more than 300 people were killed in the protests and criticized the Mozambican authorities for what it called a brutal crackdown on protesters. Human Rights Watch alleged that security forces used live ammunition against protesters.
Election observers including a team from the European Union questioned the validity of the elections and said there were irregularities in counting and the alteration of some results.

Mondlane, who has since formed a new party, has denied the charges against him and said he was advocating for "electoral truth" with his messages on social media calling on people to protest and boycott work.

The charges against him include inciting terrorism and instigating terrorism and he faces up to 24 years in prison if convicted on the most serious charge of instigating terrorism, according to Mozambican legal expert Vítor da Fonseca.
Some legal analysts say the trial, which will be held in Mozambique's Supreme Court, will be a test of the judiciary's impartiality under Frelimo.
Alberto Manhique, a spokesperson for Mondlane's new party, said it is a target of oppression by the government and “there is no shadow of a doubt that Mondlane's trial is purely political.”
The president of the Supreme Court has denied any political influence and said it will rule according to the law.
Mondlane has not been placed under arrest and recently traveled to a democracy and human rights conference in Berlin. He has said he will attend the trial.

title: Police in Bangladesh clash with garment workers demanding higher minimum wages
summary: Police in Bangladesh have clashed with garment workers demanding higher wages
story: Police in Bangladesh have clashed with garment workers demanding higher wages

DHAKA, Bangladesh -- Police in Bangladesh on Wednesday clashed with thousands of garment workers demanding higher basic wages amid weekslong chaos in the main export-earning industry in the country, police and media reports said.

Local media reported that around 20,000 workers at a garment factory took to the streets and blocked the Dhaka-Aricha Highway in Savar, outside the nation’s capital. They clashed with police who used tear gas and stun grenades and charged at them with batons to disperse them. It wasn’t immediately clear how many people were injured.

The violence spread to the nearby area of Ashulia, the country’s leading English-language Daily Star newspaper reported. Local police chief Saiful Alam said that officers took action to disperse them after the protesting workers blocked the highway and threw stones at them. About 25 factories were closed because of the unrest in Ashulia, police said.

Violence was also reported in the district of Gazipur, outside Dhaka, which is a major industrial zone. The protesters also blocked the Dhaka-Mymensingh highway and torched a police vehicle. Police fired tear gas and stun grenades during the violence.
The protests intensified earlier this month, and disruptions to production because of the closure of hundreds of factories and street clashes have become routine in recent weeks.
The industry earns about $40 billion a year from exports through the South Asian nation’s garment factories, which number around 2,500.

Workers are demanding a minimum monthly wage of 30,000 takas ($236), up from 12,500 takas ($98). They say rising living costs and inflation have eroded their purchasing power. About 4 million workers, mostly women from rural Bangladesh, are employed directly in the industry while its backward linkage industry has employed a few million more.
Many factories have remained shut under a “no work, no pay” provision under labor laws allowing the factory owners to suspend operations because of the unrest.

The government has formed a board to set a new wage package, but the efforts have failed to appease the protesters. The Bangladesh Garment Manufacturers and Exporters Association and the Bangladesh Knitwear Manufacturers and Exporters Association demanded protection of their factories.

title: Top UN court to deliver judgment alleging Myanmar committed genocide against Rohingya
summary: The United Nations' top court is set to deliver a judgment Thursday in a case accusing Myanmar of committing genocide against the Rohingya
story: The United Nations' top court is set to deliver a judgment Thursday in a case accusing Myanmar of committing genocide against the Rohingya

THE HAGUE, Netherlands -- The United Nations' top court is due to deliver a judgment Thursday in a case accusing Myanmar of committing genocide against the Muslim minority Rohingya, a ruling that could seek to ease their plight and lay down legal precedents for other politically charged cases.

The Muslim-majority African nation of Gambia launched the proceedings at the International Court of Justice in 2019, asking it to rule that Myanmar has breached the 1948 Genocide Convention, order the nation to put an end to any illegal activities targeting the Rohingya and ensure those responsible for genocide are punished.
In public hearings early last year, Myanmar defended its deadly military campaign, calling it a legitimate counter-terrorism operation that did not amount to genocide.
The judgment comes while the World Court also is handling genocide allegations linked to the Gaza conflict and the war in Ukraine.

“Genocides have similarities in how they are committed so this decision will have an impact on other cases,” said Melanie O’Brien, a professor of international law at the University of Western Australia.

If judges rule that Myanmar committed genocide, it would be the first time the International Court of Justice has passed such a judgment. In 2007, the court said that Serbia “violated the obligation to prevent genocide” in the 1995 Srebrenica massacre, when Bosnian Serb forces murdered some 8,000 mostly Muslim men and boys in the Bosnian region.

Buddhist-majority Myanmar has long considered the Rohingya to be “Bengalis” from Bangladesh even though their families have lived in the country for generations. Nearly all have been denied citizenship since 1982, effectively rendering them stateless. They are also denied freedom of movement and other basic rights.

In August 2017, Myanmar’s military launched what it called a clearance campaign in northern Rakhine State in response to an attack by a Rohingya insurgent group. The campaign forced more than 700,000 Rohingya to flee to neighboring Bangladesh and led to accusations that security forces committed mass rapes and killings and burned thousands of homes.

Now, approximately 1.2 million Rohingya refugees live in Bangladesh, primarily in congested camps across Cox’s Bazar district. Residents endure harsh conditions marked by fire hazards, infectious diseases, monsoon landslides, inadequate sanitation and strict work restrictions.

Severe funding cuts in recent years have made conditions worse, prompting thousands to attempt perilous maritime journeys toward countries such as Malaysia. The U.N. refugee agency recorded over 6,500 attempted crossings in 2025, with nearly 900 people — roughly one in seven — reported dead or missing at sea.

Meanwhile, around 550,000 Rohingya remain in Myanmar, facing heavy restrictions on movement, healthcare and livelihoods. Their situation deteriorated further after Myanmar’s military takeover in 2021.
The Gambia has asked for reparations for the Rohingya, including ordering Myanmar to grant them full citizenship and the right to return home.
The court’s rulings are final and legally binding, but even if the ICJ grants the order in full, the court has no way to enforce it beyond reporting non-compliance to the U.N. Security Council.

Even so, recognition by the U.N.'s top court that what happened to them was a genocide can be meaningful, according to international law professor O’Brien. “A finding of genocide is a form of validation. It is someone publicly acknowledging what happened to them," she told The Associated Press.
“This is a justice process for people who have nowhere else to turn,” she added.

Yasmin Ullah, a Rohingya human rights activist who fled Myanmar as a young child with her mother in the 1990s, said the demands in the case are rooted in her community's desire for recognition and dignity.

“Because so far, we’ve just been pushed around into this limbo state,” she said. "It’s been almost 10 years now that Rohingya have been living in very, very precarious conditions across the Asia Pacific.”
Yousuf Ali, who traveled from his home in a Cox's Bazar camp to witness Thursday's decision, said its significance goes beyond the Rohingya.
“This isn’t just for our community, it is for all communities who have faced this,” he said.
Judges at the Hague-based court have also been asked to weigh in on other allegations of genocide.
South Africa has accused Israel of breaching the genocide convention during its offensive in Gaza, a claim Israel vehemently denies.

At public hearings, Israel insisted that its war in Gaza was a legitimate defense of its people and that it was Hamas militants who were guilty of genocide. The campaign in Gaza was launched after Hamas’ Oct. 7, 2023, attack, when militants stormed through Israeli communities, killing some 1,200 people and taking around 250 people hostage.

That case will take years to reach a judgment. Meanwhile, Nicaragua has accused Germany of breaching the Genocide Convention by selling Israel weapons that were used in the Gaza conflict. Germany denies the claim and has asked the court to toss out the case.

Ukraine also has a case pending against Russia. Shortly after Moscow’s full-scale invasion in February 2022, Kyiv accused Russia of fabricating genocide claims against Ukraine to justify the attack. A final, legally binding decision is likely still years away.
Associated Press writer Grant Peck in Bangkok contributed.

title: Why France is sending soldiers into Ukraine and how Russia is responding
summary: Russia is responding forcefully to France's confirmation that it periodically sends military personnel into Ukraine for training and maintenance help with supplied weaponry
story: Russia is responding forcefully to France's confirmation that it periodically sends military personnel into Ukraine for training and maintenance help with supplied weaponry

PARIS -- Russia is responding forcefully to confirmation from France that it periodically sends military personnel into Ukraine to provide training and maintenance help with some of the weaponry it has supplied for the war.
Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said: “This is no longer ‘support for Ukraine,' but direct participation in the war.”
France says the soldiers and weapons specialists are noncombatants.
“Since we are not at war with Russia, these, in fact, are not combat units,” French Deputy Defense Minister Alice Rufo said.
Here's a closer look:
Speaking on Wednesday to French broadcaster RMC, Rufo said French personnel are “a very long way from the front line. They come to carry out occasional missions.”

She didn't specify their numbers, but said that they are “a few soldiers, specialists, including armaments engineers, who work — or can come to work — on an occasional basis to maintain complex equipment, such as Mirage aircraft or Caesar howitzers, and provide targeted training on certain equipment.”

France first delivered Mirage 2000-5 fighters last year to Ukraine and trained pilots and mechanics for them. The French Defense Ministry says the aircraft have helped fend off missile and drone attacks.
It also says that with donations from allies and purchases, Ukraine's force of high-precision French-made Caesar howitzers has grown to become the largest in the world.
France has also supplied precision bombs, cruise missiles, air defense systems, light tanks and other equipment.

Rufo told French lawmakers on Tuesday that France is “accelerating” its support in light of Russia's air campaign against Ukrainian targets. She spoke of a “complete absence of any intention to engage in combat” and described as “absurd” Lavrov's accusation that France is directly participating in the war.
Only a “very limited" number of French personnel are engaged in “the extremely limited” missions, Rufo said.

Her comments came after French media, including broadcaster RFI and Le Monde newspaper, reported that small contingents of French military officers stay in Ukraine for short rotations as part of the so-called Operation Volia, since at least this summer.

French military personnel have been operating in Ukraine for more than six months and France isn't alone in providing such support, Lavrov said Tuesday at a news conference in Manila, Philippines, where he was attending a summit of Southeast Asian nations.

“We have conveyed our concern through the available channels, warning the relevant countries that this is no longer ‘support for Ukraine,’ but direct participation in the war,” he said, without naming the countries.
“This is just like the assistance with target designation, the provision of satellite data and much else,” he said.

Russian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Maria Zakharova said that Moscow will regard any foreign troops in Ukraine as legitimate targets and it will be up to the Russian military to determine a response.

The United Kingdom has soldiers in Ukraine, but officials haven't disclosed how many or what their role is. The U.K. Defense Ministry confirmed two deaths of British soldiers in Ukraine in the past year, in both cases in accidents.

Since Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine on Feb. 24, 2022, dozens of countries have trained more than 100,000 Ukrainian soldiers, at locations outside the country — in France, the U.K., the United States, Poland, Germany and elsewhere — including on Patriot missile batteries, F-16 combat jets and other equipment. They have also trained recruits, officers, medics and other specialists for combat.
Jill Lawless in London, Sylvie Corbet and Catherine Gaschka in Paris, and Lorne Cook in Brussels, contributed to this report.

title: How three leaders donated the $20 million Melinda French Gates gave them with no strings attached
summary: Philanthropist Melinda French Gates launched a $240 million Global Leaders program in 2024, through her philanthropic organization Pivotal, where she gave $20 million each to 12 luminaries without warning or requirements other than donating the money b...
story: Philanthropist Melinda French Gates launched a $240 million Global Leaders program in 2024, through her philanthropic organization Pivotal, where she gave $20 million each to 12 luminaries without warning or requirements other than donating the money b...
Dr. Alfiee Breland-Noble says she was shocked when philanthropist Melinda French Gates picked her to receive $20 million to donate however she wanted.

The psychologist, author and founder of The AAKOMA Project, a nonprofit supporting the mental health of young people of color, has long admired French Gates’ work, especially in the diversity of her support initiatives. Breland-Noble just never expected to be the focus of one of those initiatives.

“It really was shock and awe,” she said. “My mom just had a knack and a penchant for finding people that nobody else was helping and she would help them. And so for me, the excitement was I get to honor my mother’s legacy by doing the same thing.”

In 2024, through her philanthropic organization Pivotal, French Gates launched the $240 million Global Leaders program, where she gave $20 million each to 12 luminaries, including Breland-Noble, without warning or requirements other than donating the money by the end of 2026. It was part of her plan to donate $1 billion to support women and girls at a time when nonprofits focusing on their issues receive only about 2% of all U.S. philanthropic funding.

Now, with nearly all the money donated, Pivotal has seen enough to call the trust-based philanthropy initiative a “huge success” and is looking for ways to replicate it and encourage other donors to do the same.

“There are so many great ideas out there that might never cross my path but might cross someone else’s,” French Gates said in a statement to The Associated Press. “That’s one reason I started the Global Leaders program: to partner with experts whose firsthand knowledge could broaden Pivotal’s perspective and deepen our impact.”
According to Pivotal, the average grant the Global Leaders handed out was approximately $240,000, with 91% of the donations going to organizations that had not received funding from Pivotal before.

Haven Ley, Pivotal’s chief strategy officer, said a final report on the Global Leaders program will come next year, but that the organization is already looking for ways to build on it. “We did this not just for the impact," Ley said, “but because it was a model that was intriguing to us.”
French Gates said the different vantage points on the world’s challenges have made Pivotal more responsive and helped the Global Leaders be more impactful.
“For me, this is as much about expanding who gets to make decisions about funding as it is about where funding goes,” she said.
For Breland-Noble, being able to donate to others on a grand scale was a meaningful new experience.

Though she has been working in the mental health field for decades, she is relatively new to running her own nonprofit. Breland-Noble established The AAKOMA Project, which stands for African American Knowledge Optimized for Mindfully Healthy Adolescents, in 1999 as an academic research lab, only turning it into a nonprofit in 2018 so that it could put its research findings into action.

To donate the $20 million that French Gates had given her, Breland-Noble created The MATTIE Fund – short for Mindful Advocacy for Totally Transformative Inclusion and Equity, but also named for, and inspired by, her mother Mattie McLeod Breland.

The MATTIE Fund donated to well-established groups like Asian Mental Health Collective. But Breland-Noble made a point of expanding her donations to groups outside her network, searching Google and LinkedIn to find ideas. She asked her Instagram community for recommendations, as well as audiences at her speaking engagements.

Those searches led to her support of BackSpinz Music Academy in North Carolina, which trains young people to use their creativity, and Daddy Stroller Social Club, which helps new fathers deal with postpartum depression.
Breland-Noble said she was thankful to French Gates for the opportunity to give.
“She saw me and supported me and pulled me out – like a needle in a haystack,” said Breland-Noble. “I then had the ability to do that for somebody else.”

Former New Zealand Prime Minister Jacinda Ardern said she is also grateful for the opportunity to make $20 million in donations. And she knows she took the decidedly tougher route by not making large gifts to established organizations.
“I wanted to use this funding to achieve things that otherwise may not have existed were it not for this opportunity,” she said. “That took time.”

She began working with the International Rescue Committee on a program to prevent postpartum hemorrhaging for women in areas affected by war and other humanitarian crises, where 58% of maternal mortality occurs. The resulting Safer Births in Crises Consortium now focuses on preventing the deaths of mothers in South Sudan, Burkina Faso and Papua New Guinea.

What Ardern did not anticipate was that her donations through The Matariki Fund for Women would coincide with funding cuts for international aid. As a former prime minister who previously dispatched such aid, she said she had two distinct reactions to seeing life-saving programs cut.

“One is we’ve just got to get on with it. What do we do? How can we help?” Ardern said. “And then I think about how I can advocate for the restoration. How we can lift the profile of this collective approach to voters? Because ultimately, they’re the ones that demand from their leaders that we keep having this impact.”
Ardern said she has no plans to become a full-time philanthropist. She prefers her new job at the University of Sydney as a professor, announced last month.

“I’ll be working on empathetic leadership, but I’m also attached to the School of Public Health," she said, adding that she intends to continue working on global health issues. “My view is there is absolutely a role for political leadership to rebuild trust, reduce insularity, and reduce the grievance that people feel. Actually, what’s interesting is that the public think that it’s their job too.”
Gary Barker, on the other hand, not only used the $20 million he received from French Gates to expand his philanthropic work, he used it to convince other funders to also support his nonprofit.

Barker is the founder and CEO of the Equimundo Center for Masculinities and Social Justice, which engages men and boys in promoting gender equality, and launched the Caring Masculinity Fund to distribute French Gates’ donation.

“The Minderoo Foundation in Australia looked at what Melinda funded us to do and said, ‘Would you come do the same at the country level in Australia?’,” said Barker. “Her voice saying, ‘This is worth investing in and that this is not taking funds or attention away from women and girls’ is a political boost in addition to boosting our credibility as an organization.”
Barker said the experience has made him seek similar relationships with funders.
“We don’t want to go back to piecemeal fundraising,” he said. “We’re not gonna wanna do it any differently from here on out.”

The Associated Press receives financial support for news coverage of women in the workforce and state governments from Pivotal.
