The AP is solely responsible for this content. For all of AP’s philanthropy coverage, visit https://apnews.com/hub/philanthropy.

title: Target will take momentum from strong third quarter into the holiday shopping season
summary: Target is reporting its strong quarterly sales gains in roughly five years, fueled by a revitalized product lineup, expanded same-day deliveries and price cuts that brought in customers battered by inflation
story: Target is reporting its strong quarterly sales gains in roughly five years, fueled by a revitalized product lineup, expanded same-day deliveries and price cuts that brought in customers battered by inflation

NEW YORK -- Target delivered its strong quarterly sales gains in roughly five years, fueled by a revitalized product lineup, expanded same-day deliveries and price cuts that brought in customers battered by inflation.
The company raised its annual earnings and sales outlook again on Wednesday after an encouraging third quarter.

Target reported a better-than-expected 7.1% increase in net sales, the best performance since the fourth quarter of 2021. The company also posted its third straight quarter of quarterly comparable sales, which include sales from online and its physical stores.

Sales made through digital channels operating for at least 12 months increased 9.8% from the same quarter last year, while comparable sales at established stores rose 4.6%. The three-month period that ended Oct. 31 overlapped with back-to-school shopping season.
Shares were essentially flat before the opening bell.

The Minneapolis retailer reported growth in a majority of its six core merchandise categories, led by electronics, gaming equipment, sporting goods, toys, trading cards and collectibles, a category Target refers to as "Fun 101.” It also cited higher sales of beauty products, food and beverages.

But Target CEO Michael Fiddelke, a 20-year company veteran who became chief executive in February, told reporters this week that the sales momentum was not limited to certain categories or based on any one initiative. He said Target has seen business pick up across its markets among shoppers of all incomes.
“It’s the cumulative impact of changes across our business that is driving this guest preference for Target,” Fiddelke said.
The company said November net sales so far are in line with the full-year outlook.

Together, comparable store and digital sales in August, September and October increased 5.6% though that figure is being compared to a 2.7% drop in the year-ago period. The retailer also reported a 5.6% gain in the first quarter and a 3.8% uptick in the second quarter of this year.

In March, Fiddelke unveiled a multibillion dollar investment plan aimed at reversing a post-pandemic sales slump. The overhaul included a focus on stocking products and brands that would help restore Target's reputation as a place to go for affordable yet stylish items.

Target launched a new Target Beauty Studio concept in more than 600 locations in September. The new area, which features upscale beauty products and staff trained to offer advice, partly replaced the Ulta shops that were in some stores before Target and Ulta Beauty ended their partnership in August.
Company executives said work to improve the offerings in Target's clothing and home goods departments was ongoing.

With U.S. consumers expressing concerns about the U.S. economy and their own finances, Target also has promoted price reductions this year, including cuts on nearly 2,000 additional items during the third quarter.
The company said most of the new items it has for the holiday shopping season cost $20 or less, including thousands priced at $5 and under.

Target is one of the first big retailers to report third-quarter earnings. The results could give industry analysts and economists another read on how U.S. consumers responded to ongoing inflation pressure before the end-of-year holidays.

Target said it earned $1.21 billion, or $2.65 per share, including a 50-cent benefit from a government tariff refund. In the third quarter of 2025, the company reported $689 million, or $1.51 per share.
Net sales rose 7.1% to $27.07 billion compared to $25.27 billion in the year-ago period.
Analysts were expecting $2.08 per share on net sales of $26.5 billion, according to FactSet.
Target now expects net sales for the full year to be up roughly 6%, one percentage point higher than the guidance it gave in August.
The company projected full-year earnings per share of $10.65 to $11.40. That includes a $2.14 tariff refund benefit. In August, the company expected earnings of $9.90 to $10.90 per share.
Analysts were projecting profits of $10.25 per share on sales of $110.27 billion.

title: After a 13-year wait, 'Grand Theft Auto VI' arrives with enormous hype and expectations
summary: “Grand Theft Auto VI” has begun rolling out worldwide, bringing players back to Rockstar Games’ Vice City
story: “Grand Theft Auto VI” has begun rolling out worldwide, bringing players back to Rockstar Games’ Vice City
LOS ANGELES -- After a 13-year wait, one of entertainment’s biggest releases is finally here.

“Grand Theft Auto VI” launches Thursday, sending players back to Vice City and testing whether Rockstar Games can follow one of the bestselling video games ever made with another cultural and commercial phenomenon.
The latest installment becomes playable at midnight local time on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X'S, meaning players in Asia and other regions can start playing hours before its U.S. release.
New Zealand was among the first countries where players could access the game, and internet providers prepared for a surge in downloads as midnight approached.

“The game file size at 212 gigabytes is unprecedented,” said Kurt Rodgers, network strategy manager for Chorus New Zealand. “That’s more than a quarter of the average household’s data usage in an entire month, all in one go.”
In the capital, Wellington, players stayed up to be among the first to try “Grand Theft Auto VI.”
Among them was Adam Simmons, 50, a director of photography who launched the game in his living room as soon as it unlocked, keeping the volume low to avoid waking his wife and daughters.

“The gameplay dynamics are just amazing and the graphics are great and you can tell that the storytelling is really deep, which is impressive,” he said after half an hour of shooting, car theft and jokes about Florida.
“You really feel like you are in a world,” he added. “The places and how they’re put together feel right.”
Simmons moved to New Zealand from Portland, Oregon, five months ago — a decision he joked had been influenced by the prospect of playing “Grand Theft Auto” before his friends.
He praised the game’s emotional connection with its characters and said he expected its expansive world to offer hours of play long after he finished the story.
By 1 a.m., he reluctantly admitted he should go to bed, though he expected to put in plenty of hours in the coming days.
“I have my own company that I have to run,” he said. “So I’m the boss, but also I’m just going to lose sales because a video game came out.”

The “Grand Theft Auto” franchise has sold more than 470 million units worldwide. “Grand Theft Auto V,” released in 2013, accounts for more than 230 million of those sales and generated $1 billion in retail sales in just three days.

Rockstar returns to Vice City, its fictionalized version of Miami, with two new protagonists, a sprawling Florida-inspired world and the pressure of following one of the most successful entertainment products ever released.

At the center of “GTA VI” are Lucia Caminos and Jason Duval, a couple whose attempts to improve their lives pull them deeper into the criminal underworld of Leonida, Rockstar’s fictionalized version of Florida.

Lucia has recently been released from prison, while Jason is a former soldier who became involved with drug runners in the Leonida Keys. When a criminal job goes wrong, the pair become entangled in a wider conspiracy.
The focus on their relationship marks a major departure from “Grand Theft Auto V,” which followed three playable protagonists.

Rockstar has promoted Leonida as its largest and most detailed open world yet, extending beyond Vice City to beaches, highways, wetlands, nightlife districts and smaller communities inspired by South Florida.

Developers immersed themselves in the region while building the game, driving through Miami, the Florida Keys and surrounding communities, flying over the Everglades and researching the area’s history and architecture.

Miami and surrounding communities have leaned into their connection to Vice City ahead of the release, with businesses, sports teams and local governments using the game’s arrival as a marketing opportunity.

Miami-Dade County entered into a $3.9 million promotional deal with Rockstar that includes a giant “Welcome to Vice City” display atop the Miami Heat’s Kaseya Center. The NBA team is also scheduled to wear black-and-pink Vice City uniforms on the eve of the game’s release.

The campaign has not been universally welcomed. Some South Florida officials have questioned whether public resources should be used to promote a franchise known for car theft, gunplay and other criminal activity.
Supporters have argued that the enormous attention surrounding “GTA VI” gives the region an opportunity to capitalize on a global spotlight.
In Seoul, a giant advertisement draped the side of a building, while Warner Music will host a party at a bar Thursday themed around the game’s soundtrack.
Few entertainment releases arrive with this much anticipation.

The first “GTA VI” trailer drew more than 93 million YouTube views in its first 24 hours, while Take-Two Interactive, Rockstar’s parent company, has said the second trailer generated more than 475 million views across platforms in a day.
The game also has attracted awards attention before most players have had a chance to explore it.

“GTA VI” received eight nominations Tuesday for the Game Awards, including game of the year, game direction, narrative, art direction, score and music, audio design, action/adventure and performance. The awards will be presented Dec. 10.

The long wait is partly a product of the extraordinary staying power of its predecessor. “Grand Theft Auto Online,” the multiplayer component of “GTA V,” has kept players engaged for years through updates, activities and in-game purchases.
Music has long been woven into the “Grand Theft Auto” experience, with fictional radio stations and carefully curated soundtracks accompanying players as they drive through the series’ cities.

For “GTA VI,” Rockstar commissioned an original adaptive score from Grammy-winning French electronic duo Justice. The music is designed to shift depending on where players are and what they are doing. A 30-track “Grand Theft Auto VI: Original Score” is scheduled for release Dec. 11 and includes collaborations involving Tame Impala, SZA, King Gizzard & The Lizard Wizard and Gesaffelstein.
Despite years of trailers and promotional material, Rockstar has kept significant portions of “GTA VI” under wraps.

The full voice cast has not been revealed, including the performers behind Lucia and Jason. Actor Stephen Root has confirmed to The Associated Press that he appears in the game, though Rockstar has not publicly identified his role.
Questions also remain about the full range of characters, locations, activities and gameplay systems waiting inside Leonida.
Those answers will begin emerging first from players in Asia and Europe as midnight arrives in their regions, followed by North America hours later.
Associated Press journalists Charlotte Graham-McLay in Wellington, New Zealand, and Tong-hyung Kim in Seoul contributed to this report.

title: US futures point higher led by rebound for Nvidia
summary: Tech stocks are leading U.S. futures higher after Nvidia easily exceeded Wall Street expectations as it deals with the abrupt departure of CEO Jensen Huang
story: Tech stocks are leading U.S. futures higher after Nvidia easily exceeded Wall Street expectations as it deals with the abrupt departure of CEO Jensen Huang
HONG KONG -- Tech stocks are leading U.S. futures higher Wednesday after Nvidia easily exceeded Wall Street expectations as it deals with the abrupt departure of CEO Jensen Huang.
Futures for the S&P 500 rose 0.6%, while those for the Dow Jones Industrial Average gained 0.2%. Futures on the tech-heavy Nasdaq advanced 1%.
Oil prices are continuing on a downward trajectory despite new attacks by Iran that threaten to disrupt the shipment of Middle East crude through the crucial Strait of Hormuz.
Prices declined after the American Petroleum Institute said that U.S. crude inventories rose by 5.3% last week, a boost that far exceeded projections from energy analysts.

Chipmakers are surging early after Nvidia reported that its revenue doubled from last year to $116 billion. Nvidia shares are up 4% in premarket trading. Broadcom, Arm Holdings and Advanced Micro Devices are following closely behind.

Retail stocks are mixed after Target raised its outlook for the year following its strongest sales growth in nearly five years. Despite the strong performance, shares dipped 3% and Walmart, which reports quarterly earnings Thursday, fell more than 1%.

President Donald Trump landed in China on Wednesday with trade likely to be the focus of talks with China's leader, Xi Jinping, but a distressing series of technical outages back home has left the administration scrambling to calm the American public.
Later on Wednesday, the U.S. Federal Reserve will release minutes from its most recent meeting, with new indications that it has yet to tame inflation.

The persistence of elevated inflation makes it highly likely that the Fed will raise benchmark interest rates at its next meeting in December. It kept rates unchanged late last month, after raising them in September. The Fed increases borrowing costs in an effort to cool spending and bring down inflation.
The 10-year Treasury yield climbed toward 5.15% early Wednesday.
In midday European trading, Germany’s DAX slipped 0.1% to 26,045.57, while France’s CAC 40 edged 0.1% lower to 8,210.70. Britain’s FTSE 100 fell 0.6% to 10,621.79.

U.K. inflation in October rose to 3.6%, the highest level in a year, according to the Office for National Statistics on Wednesday. Rising fuel costs drove much of the increase, adding pressure on the Bank of England to raise the interest rate.
In Asia, the Kospi in Seoul closed 2% higher at 5,067.44 as memory chipmaker SK Hynix jumped 4.2% and Samsung Electronics gained 2.3%.
In Hong Kong, the Hang Seng fell 0.9% to 23,294.75, while the Shanghai Composite index edged 0.1% lower to 3,587.83.
The price for a barrel of Brent crude oil is down slightly to $93.10. U.S. benchmark crude oil dropped less than a percent to $85.50 per barrel.
The U.S. dollar edged up to 159.38 Japanese yen from 159.37 yen late Tuesday. The euro fell to $1.0966 from $1.0999.

title: Long-lost Georgia O’Keeffe painting found in Manhattan closet sells for $4.8M
summary: A painting dug out of a New York City closet this year after being stashed away since the 1980s has sold at auction for $4.8 million
story: A painting dug out of a New York City closet this year after being stashed away since the 1980s has sold at auction for $4.8 million
NEW YORK -- A long-lost Georgia O’Keeffe painting that had been buried in the closet of a Manhattan apartment for decades sold at auction Tuesday for $4.8 million.

The 1930 landscape painting “Near Abiquiu, New Mexico I” is likely the first in a series of three works depicting Lobo Peak in northern New Mexico, according to Christie’s auction house. Its existence was known from a 1931 photograph, but its whereabouts had been kept secret until recently.

A Manhattan woman in her 90s nonchalantly told her niece one day in 2022, “Oh, by the way, there’s a Georgia O’Keeffe in the closet.” Her family believes she received the painting as a graduation gift from her mother, who had purchased it in 1963 from a New York gallery for $3,800.

The woman, who died recently, displayed it in her East Village apartment for many years until the mid-’80s when she noticed a guest looking at it a little too closely. From then on she kept it in her closet, safely hidden behind coats and boxes.

When the family finally unboxed it this year, they discovered it has all the hallmarks of O’Keeffe’s work, including her signature marking on the back: a star with her initials scrawled in the middle.

The 10-x-24-inch (25.4-x-61-centimeter) oil painting is among O’Keeffe's early love letters to New Mexico, where she settled and lived for decades. The identity of the winning bidder was not disclosed; it sold for $4,878,000.

Known as the “mother of American modernism,” O’Keeffe maintained a home and studio in Abiquiu and a nearby summer residence tucked between the red-rock cliffs of Ghost Ranch. She died in 1986 at age 98 and is best known for her paintings of flowers and American Southwest landscapes.
The second piece in the “Near Abiquiu, New Mexico” collection is at New York’s Metropolitan Museum of Art, and the other, for many years, was in the collection of the Rockefeller family.

title: Should court filings related to the search of Ilhan Omar's home be released? A judge will decide
summary: It's been more than a month after federal agents searched the home of U.S. Rep. Ilhan Omar
story: It's been more than a month after federal agents searched the home of U.S. Rep. Ilhan Omar

WASHINGTON -- More than a month after federal agents searched the home of U.S. Rep. Ilhan Omar, a federal judge heard arguments Tuesday on a request by media organizations to unseal court records related to the search — and to an immigration-fraud investigation that the Minnesota Democrat claims is politically motivated.

Over a dozen news organizations, including The Associated Press, maintain that the public has a First Amendment right to access the search warrant and other court filings that led to the Oct. 12 search of Omar's Washington, D.C., home by Department of Homeland Security agents.

During a hearing on the request, Chief Judge James Boasberg said he agrees with Justice Department attorneys that it's premature to unseal a search warrant affidavit containing sensitive details of the government's investigation. But the judge said he will privately review other sealed court filings for possible public release as soon as next week.

Omar, a naturalized U.S. citizen born in Somalia, has been a target of anti-immigrant rhetoric by President Donald Trump and many Republican allies. Omar, who has denied wrongdoing, said in a social media post that the search was an “attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement.”

Federal authorities are investigating potential fraud in her family’s immigration paperwork and have issued grand jury subpoenas to some of her relatives, a person briefed on the investigation told The AP last month on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to discuss an ongoing investigation.

Agents conducted the court-authorized search less than a month before the Nov. 3 midterm elections, when Omar won her reelection bid. The Justice Department historically has avoided public investigative actions involving a candidate within 60 days of an election.
Omar has said DHS agents seized 17 items, including phones, notebooks, a Somali-language children’s book and a vintage camera that her husband had received as a gift.

Boasberg gave the government until Friday to provide him with proposed redactions to sealed court filings that could shed light on some of the underlying legal arguments involved in the Omar investigation. The judge said redacted versions of those documents could be released as soon as next Monday.

The 67-page search warrant affidavit, which contains information about witnesses and other details of the investigation, will remain under wraps for now. In a court filing last month, the government argued that it would jeopardize the investigation to unseal the court records before a charging decision is made.

The news organizations' attorneys argue that the government's privacy concerns are outweighed by the “enormous public interest in and historic significance of a search warrant executed at the home of a sitting member of Congress.”
Justice Department attorney Alessandra Serano said the government isn't trying to keep the affidavit under seal permanently.
“It's not our position. It's never been our position,” she told the judge.

Boasberg noted that Vice President JD Vance and DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin already have publicly commented on the contours of the Omar investigation. Serano said she can't control what others in the Trump administration say about the case.
“It seems to be a common refrain,” Boasberg replied.

Boasberg, who was nominated to the bench by Democratic President Barack Obama, is himself a frequent target of Trump's ire. Trump called for Boasberg's impeachment last year after the judge blocked the president's administration from deporting planeloads of Venezuelan migrants to El Salvador under the Alien Enemies Act.
___ Associated Press writer Alanna Durkin Richer contributed to this report.

title: Anthropic forges ahead with its IPO even as AI fears mount and markets wobble
summary: Anthropic is preparing to sell stock to the public in a shaky moment for artificial intelligence companies
story: Anthropic is preparing to sell stock to the public in a shaky moment for artificial intelligence companies
NEW YORK -- Investors fearing an AI bubble are getting jittery. Financing costs are rising. Democrats are vowing to crack down on the industry.
It's not an ideal time for an artificial intelligence company to sell stock, but Anthropic is pressing ahead with its blockbuster initial public offering anyway.
No ordinary sale, the Claude chatbot maker's IPO could raise more than $60 billion on Thursday, a massive haul that, depending on the ultimate pricing and other issues, could rival SpaceX's in June.
But Anthropic is facing headwinds as it prepares for its coming-out party.
Tech stocks have done well so far this year, but the path higher has been rocky, especially for AI-related companies. That's not a reassuring setup for the IPO.

One particularly volatile AI stock, CoreWeave, plunged 15.5% on Oct. 14 over fears it wouldn't be able to borrow enough, cheaply enough to fund its growth. The stock then swung wildly. On Wednesday, the company, which buys chips and then rents out access to them to customers over the cloud, surged 25% after an encouraging earnings report, only to plunge 7% the next day.
Most stocks move no more than 2% on the average trading day.

Adding to the sector volatility recently has been the abrupt departure of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang over extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy. Huang, a high-profile AI booster, built Nvidia into a linchpin of the industry and a major financial backer of other AI companies. Stock in the AI chip designer dropped 4% Monday, dragging the broader S&P 500 down for a third day in a row.
Nvidia has agreed to buy an estimated $10 billion of Anthropic stock after the IPO. It also sells chips to Anthropic but the latter also buys from AMD and others.

As to whether the gyration in AI-tied stocks argues for an IPO delay, note that volatility can cut both ways: It might be signaling the much debated AI bubble could burst soon so it's better to sell stock now, fast. And history shows demand for IPOs can disappear quickly.
In 2021, nearly 400 companies went public in the U.S., but then investors got scared of a possible recession the next year and demand dried up with only 71 making market debuts.

Another reason to sell stock now is that the other way to raise money — borrowing — has gotten more expensive. That's partly due to inflation fears and partly due to the sector’s massive cash needs, which have drawn comparisons to the Gilded Age splurge on railroads. Lenders fear AI companies have taken on too much debt to expand while having no clear path to profitability.

Anthropic already has taken on $6.2 billion in debt, which it acknowledges in financial filings is “substantial." Adding to the strain, the company is unprofitable, at least under standard accounting rules, suggesting its resources are limited to pay interest and principal.

On the plus side, it has ample cash, although it will likely run through it quickly if it can't raise more soon given its outsized spending plans. The company said it has already signed leases and other deals requiring it to spend $900 billion in computing and infrastructure in the coming years, including $70 billion in the next 12 months.
Higher interest rates are not the only problem. Politics threatens to slow growth, too.

Newly elected Democrats are vowing to crack down on the industry amid a national backlash against data centers, giving new impetus to a Congressional effort last year to enact a national moratorium on new ones.
And two big states offering incentives for data centers, Texas and Georgia, just elected Democrat governors vowing to stop new construction.
It wouldn't be unprecedented for Anthropic to postpone its IPO at the last minute.

After a bout of volatility following President Donald Trump’s “Liberation Day” tariffs in April 2025, several companies postponed their initial offerings, including the online ticket marketplace StubHub and Klarna, a buy now, pay later business. And an Australian data center company, Firmus, called off its IPO last month because of jitters in the market.
But newly elected Democrats don't take office until January. Anthropic could be betting that selling now is best before the feared crackdown begins in earnest.

If the company does go ahead as expected, it will beat rival OpenAI to the market. That's an important advantage should investors suddenly fear they have too much exposure to the sector and decide they don't want to buy stock in the next public AI company.
And despite the jitters, companies on public markets are still fetching top prices. One measure of investor enthusiasm shows they are paying nearly as much as ever to buy stocks.

The measure championed by the famed American economist Robert Shiller comparing share prices to corporate profits over the previous decade shows shares have been more expensive only once before — the 2000 dot-com crash — and are higher now than on the eve of the 2008-09 Financial Crisis.
Stocks currently trade at 40 times their long term earnings, according to Shiller's measure. That is a third higher — meaning more expensive — than the average going back before 1900.
That's good news for Anthropic, meaning it may be able to fetch top dollars for its shares this week, though maybe not so good for its IPO investors.

title: Outage math at the airport: When a four-hour Uber beats waiting out a ground stop
summary: Flight delays are becoming more common, causing financial and emotional stress for travelers
story: Flight delays are becoming more common, causing financial and emotional stress for travelers
CHICAGO -- New airline tickets: $300. Hours waiting for luggage: four. And the topper: a four-hour Uber ride from Detroit to Chicago that cost $400.
Call it outage math, a hellish calculation spawned by ever-more-common flight delays. This one was part of Angelina and Kyle Phoenix's anniversary trip to Chicago.

On Friday, they flew from Jacksonville, Florida, into the maw of the Great Ground Stoppage of 2026 with as many as a million other travelers. Instantly, the financial and emotional toll of the four-hour flight outage radiated outward from the airports as everyone involved scrambled for costly workarounds to a crisis no one expected, can fully explain or wants to pay for.
Emergency child care. Outrageous taxi ride fees. Rebooked tickets, lost vacation rentals and little idea what expenses might be reimbursed.

But beyond finances, travelers told The Associated Press on Monday, perhaps the most consequential cost is also the most intimate: Stress and grief over time lost — a cumulative toll that is generally not, as customer service might say, eligible for reimbursement.

Kyle Phoenix got a whiff of it more than 12 hours and hundreds of dollars of unexpected expenses into the couple’s journey, as he watched chaos unfold in the baggage claim area of Detroit airport. Officials, he noticed, had stopped announcing which canceled flights would disgorge checked baggage onto which turnstiles.
Answers were hard to come by. That made decisions about what to do next increasingly difficult.
“A lot of confusion, a lot of scrambling from a lot of people,” Kyle recalls of the scene. “I think that was probably the roughest part, not knowing anything.”

When the couple finally retrieved their luggage at midnight, the $400 Uber ride began to look like the best option. They forfeited their rebooked flight — as well as a hotel room they would have stayed in for a few hours — and embarked on the four-hour ride to Chicago.
“We just took the loss,” Angelina Phoenix said.
Dread lingers around such events because they're getting more commonplace, with no end in sight.

Even as travelers spoke to the AP about Friday's ground stop, United Airlines suffered a malfunction and halted its flights for 90 minutes. Several top U.S. banks reported significant slowdowns. And that was after AI chaos and Microsoft’s global meltdown just a few days earlier. Ahead loomed the busy Thanksgiving travel week, when TSA agents typically screen more than 2 million passengers nationwide.
It was enough to make any thinking person ask: Could everything be broken? And it forced humanity to reckon once again with the fragility of the systems that anchor modern life.

Delays are accelerating faster than the increase of scheduled passenger flights since the COVID-19 pandemic, the International Air Transport Association reported in July. Between 2015 and 2025, delays affecting scheduled passenger flights generated about $10.9 billion in costs for airlines and travelers, with sharp increases in holdups starting in 2021.
The issues are costing travelers time, which even the Federal Aviation Administration agrees is worth money.

Federal guidance issued a decade ago valued airline passengers’ time at $47.10 an hour, expressed in 2015 dollars. That's about $66 an hour today. The figure accounted for travel time that would otherwise be available for work or leisure.

More recently, an economist at the Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond estimated that last year’s 43-day federal government shutdown caused roughly 1 million additional hours of passenger delays at six airports. Economist Russell Wong calculated the lost time’s value at $66 million, based on metro area wage data and the higher-than-average incomes of people who take flights. Wong excluded canceled flights.
Harder to measure is the loss absorbed by the population downstream from the airports, including hourly workers, freelancers and caregivers — in short, everyone affected by the ripples.
Another cost: Trust in government, which has been low for years.

The nationwide shutdown, the nation's longest in 25 years, could cost billions of dollars, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said over the weekend. He blamed a contractor and aging infrastructure. President Donald Trump testily pointed to Democrats, who in turn demanded answers about how the administration has spent billions it’s already been given and why its funding request has soared to $50 billion.
Downplaying the event as a glitch with a faulty router raised questions, if not suspicions, one communications expert says.

“It wasn’t simply a crisis, it was an actual emergency of impending disaster-level scale,” Shannon A. Bowen, a journalism and mass communications professor at the University of South Carolina told “The Conversation.”
Inside airports, travelers weren't easily accepting the official explanation.

“I’m super skeptical about what we’re being told as to why this event happened at all,” said Sonia Saini Simpson, 56, whose flight from Orlando, Florida, landed in Philadelphia after hours of uncertainty, during which she said she considered renting a car to drive the nearly 1,000 miles (1,587 kilometers). “I look forward to getting some answers that are believable.”
Days after the stoppage, questions arose among some travelers about delays that sound like routine maintenance issues.
Glenn Anthony Cooper, a disc jockey, said he was told his flight from Philadelphia to Toronto on Monday had been delayed nine hours for “a hole in the tire.”

“It’s like, what’s really going on, you know? Is there something behind it, or what are they doing?” he said in an interview at the Philadelphia airport. “It’s just a bummer to just have these types of situations happen and you can’t really control it.”

The most cursory scroll through social media reveals the nightmare of Friday's historic stoppage in all its dramatic detail, much of it posted live: The 10-hour drives, the epic Uber rides, the lost wages, the stunned faces.

There's advice, too: Buy travel insurance, advised some. Don't check luggage if it's avoidable. Be nice to airline and security workers. And skip, if you can, to the acceptance phase of grief — because there's a limit to what you can control.

For young father William Ware, 24, the peak of stress may have been the moment he realized the shutdown created overwhelming traffic outside LAX that was keeping his Uber from dropping him off in time to make his flight home to Chicago to care for his child.

Ware was rebooked for the next day and could only find a hotel in Long Beach more than 20 miles away — “scary, but that was the only hotel that was available.” That meant another two Uber rides round trip back to the airport.
Maybe, Ware thinks, he'll get a refund for the ticket. But there was another cost: his time.

“I actually had to get home to my kid and I couldn’t, so it was horrible for me,” he told the AP Monday, back in Chicago at last. “I got a great support system, so my family was able to watch my child.”
Kellman reported from London. AP writers Lisa Leff in London and Mingson Lau in Philadelphia contributed to this report.

title: Federal Reserve's Cook refuses to participate in White House hearing
summary: Federal Reserve governor Lisa Cook declined through her lawyers to appear next month before a Trump administration committee that is considering whether she should be fired, calling the process unfair and committed to a predetermined outcome
story: Federal Reserve governor Lisa Cook declined through her lawyers to appear next month before a Trump administration committee that is considering whether she should be fired, calling the process unfair and committed to a predetermined outcome

WASHINGTON -- Federal Reserve governor Lisa Cook declined through her lawyers to appear next month before a Trump administration committee that is considering whether she should be fired, calling the process unfair and committed to a predetermined outcome.

The refusal extends the wrangling between the White House and Cook's lawyers regarding her appearance before the committee, which the administration initially demanded for Nov. 6. Trump administration officials have demanded that Cook appear before the committee to address allegations she committed mortgage fraud in 2021, before she joined the Fed's board of governors, a charge she denies.

President Donald Trump has sought to fire Cook since August 2025, and she has argued that the president's efforts to do so represent a threat to the Fed's independence and reflect Trump's desire to force the central bank to reduce borrowing costs.

“Governor Cook has no legal obligation to participate in an unfair hearing — and indeed, has a duty to the Federal Reserve to decline to participate in any proceeding that would undermine the institution’s unique status and independence,” Abbe David Lowell, Cook's lawyer, wrote in a letter released Tuesday to White House counsel William Scharf. The three-person panel set up by the White House to consider the allegations “appears to be a façade designed to obscure a predetermined decision to fire Governor Cook.”

In June, the Supreme Court blocked the Trump from removing Cook while litigation over the attempted firing continues, finding that "the fact of independence but also the appearance of independence is key to the Federal Reserve’s design.”

Trump officials have threatened to move ahead with the hearing even without Cook, and in a Nov. 3 letter said that the three-member committee “reserves the right to draw adverse inferences against you” for not participating.

The unusual “committee of inquiry” set up by the White House consists of Kevin Hassett, Trump’s top economic adviser; Andrea Lucas, whom Trump appointed to lead the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission; and Keith Sonderling, Trump’s pick for Labor Secretary.

The Supreme Court said in a footnote to its June ruling that Trump could try again to fire her if the administration provided her adequate notice and an opportunity to respond. The committee of inquiry is an effort to meet those conditions.

Under the law governing the Fed, the president can only fire a Fed governor “for cause,” but the Supreme Court didn’t address whether Cook’s actions met that standard. The committee will ultimately recommend whether there is cause to fire Cook, the White House has said.
Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh was asked at a press conference Oct. 28 if he or the Fed would be involved in the hearing against Cook, and he said, “not to my knowledge.”

title: Shoppers slowed spending in October with high prices leading to caution
summary: Shoppers increased spending more slowly in October as economic uncertainty and high prices led more Americans to become cautious with their moneyRetail sales rose 0.2% in October, down from a revised 0.8% gain in September, according to the Commerce De...
story: Shoppers increased spending more slowly in October as economic uncertainty and high prices led more Americans to become cautious with their moneyRetail sales rose 0.2% in October, down from a revised 0.8% gain in September, according to the Commerce De...

NEW YORK -- Shoppers increased spending more slowly in October as economic uncertainty and high prices led more Americans to become cautious with their money ahead of the unofficial start to the holiday shopping season.
Retail sales rose 0.2% in October, down from a 0.8% gain in September, according to the Commerce Department's report released Tuesday.
Sales at gas stations rose 1.5% last month after spiking 30.3% in September, according to the Commerce Department. Excluding gas stations, retail sales rose just 0.1%.

Overall retail sales were pulled down by decline in sales at motor vehicle and parts dealers. Auto vehicles and parts dealers had a 1.6% drop in sales in October, reversing a 1.3% increase in September.

“There are hints of weakening consumer spending as prices rise," wrote Carl B. Weinberg, chief economist at High Frequency Economics. “Let’s call this report a mixed report card on the health of the consumer."
Spending was mixed across different sectors.

Business at furniture and home furnishings stores fell 2.3%, while clothing and accessories stores declined 0.7%. Sales at consumer electronics and appliance stores were unchanged. Sales at online retailers rose 1.2%.
The data offers only a snapshot of consumer spending and doesn’t include activities like travel and hotel stays. But the lone services category – restaurants registered a 0.2% increase.
The weaker sales data followed new evidence that inflation continued to weigh on Americans last month.

Higher energy prices are ricocheting into other parts of the economy, with airfares, public transportation and shipping all jumping in price. Grocery prices, for example, increased 0.4%, a painful uptick after years of increases, according to new Labor Department data.
Massive investments in artificial intelligence have exacerbated inflation by driving up computer chip prices and, in turn, prices for laptops, phones and other consumer electronics.

Retailers are preparing for a surge in business over the Thanksgiving weekend, the unofficial start of the holiday shopping period. Stores have heavily advertised deals to lure customers who increasingly buy when they think prices have dropped.
Companies like Kohl’s and Target and Walmart are trying to drive the affordability message home through marketing.

Target said it’s offering more than 8,000 new gifts for the winter holidays, with more than half exclusive to the retailer. Most of the new holiday items at Target are $20 or less, including thousands of items that are priced at $5 and under. Kohl’s has increased the number of gift sets across different types of merchandise.
Americans, despite the rising cost of credit, continue to rely on cards to finance spending, and credit experts say that defaults have been stable.
“More Americans are carrying credit cards than ever, and they’re handling them well,” said Charles Wise, head of global research and consulting at the credit reporting agency TransUnion.

Wise noted that outstanding credit card balances as of last month hit $1.17 trillion, up 5.1% from the year-ago period, based on data covering 178.5 million consumers who held an active credit card as of last month. Yet serious delinquency rates held steady, he said.
That signals that “consumers remain disciplined borrowers heading into the holidays,” he added.

title: Malaysia-France rare earths project to begin operations in early 2027, Macron says
summary: A joint rare earths mining and processing venture between Malaysia and France is expected to begin operations in early 2027
story: A joint rare earths mining and processing venture between Malaysia and France is expected to begin operations in early 2027

KUALA LUMPUR, Malaysia -- A joint rare earths mining and processing venture between Malaysia and France is expected to begin operations in early 2027 as the two nations agreed to deepen cooperation and elevate ties to a strategic partnership, French President Emmanuel Macron said Tuesday.

The project, which involves French company Carester and Malaysian firm Malaco Mining Sendirian Berhad, would cover the extraction and processing of rare earths in Malaysia, with reserved volumes and the possibility of refining in France, Macron said.

“Operations are due to begin in early 2027,” he said at a joint news conference after talks with Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim. “This will allow us to proceed ... involving not only extraction, but also processing here, with reserved volumes and capacity, including the possibility of refining in France, which is crucial for our entire value chain.”

The arrangement reflects Malaysia’s move to build domestic processing capabilities, while France seeks to secure and diversify supplies of critical minerals used in a wide range of products from electric vehicles, electronics and renewable energy to defense industries.

The two leaders said that they agreed to elevate bilateral ties to a broader strategic partnership, focusing cooperation on defense, energy, semiconductors and digital connectivity, among other areas.

Anwar said that Malaysia has made an exception in its policy against exporting rare earth minerals in return for collaboration with France in developing its rare earths industry. He didn’t provide further details. He said that cooperation with France demonstrated how resource-rich countries could work with foreign partners while securing technology transfer, training and industrial expertise.
“We do not export raw materials, but with France we have done so, because you are committed to that processing and working with the Malaysians as a team,” Anwar said.
Macron said that the partnership reflected a shared commitment to national sovereignty and greater independence in a world increasingly shaped by competing major powers.

Plans for defense cooperation will include a new industrial road map, support for a regional center to counter hybrid threats and Malaysia's procurement of combat search-and-rescue helicopters from Airbus, he said. For semiconductors, Macron said that Malaysian firm SkyeChip and French company SiPearl will collaborate to develop a high-performance computing platform.
More than 300 French companies operate in Malaysia, making France its second-largest European investor, he said.

Macron's visit was the third by a French president since diplomatic relations were established in 1957. He earlier visited Cambodia to attend a summit of French-speaking nations, before arriving late Monday in Malaysia.

title: Turkish authorities carry out a raid on another opposition TV station and appoint trustees
summary: Turkish authorities have raided the headquarters of one of the country's last major opposition-aligned television stations, Sozcu TV
story: Turkish authorities have raided the headquarters of one of the country's last major opposition-aligned television stations, Sozcu TV

ANKARA, Turkey -- ANKARA, Turkey (AP) — Turkish authorities raided the headquarters of one of the country's last major opposition-aligned television stations on Tuesday, detaining several executives and appointing trustees to manage operations in a move critics described as the latest step in a crackdown on independent media.

The predawn raid against Sozcu TV came just weeks after trustees similarly took control of another opposition-leaning news channel, Halk TV, in an alleged corruption investigation that critics said was politically motivated.

Press freedoms in Turkey have steadily eroded during the more than two decades that President Recep Tayyip Erdogan has been in power, and a majority of media outlets are either under government control or aligned with it. The country ranks 163rd out of 180 countries in the Reporters Without Borders’ world press freedom index.

A statement from the Istanbul Chief Public Prosecutor’s office said the move against Sozcu TV was part of an investigation into the channel’s alleged violation of Turkey’s anti-terror financing laws and suspected links to a network that was led by the late U.S.-based cleric Fethullah Gulen.

The cleric, who died in 2024, was accused by Turkey of orchestrating a failed military coup in 2016 and his network of supporters has been branded a terrorist organization. Gulen had denied the accusations.
The prosecutors' office cited suspicion that Sozcu TV and other media outlets linked to its owner, Burak Akbay, were being financed by overseas accounts.

Tuesday's raid follows a widening crackdown on the opposition, with dozens of mayors from the main opposition party arrested on corruption charges since 2024, including former Istanbul mayor Ekrem Imamoglu. The popular politician was widely regarded as a possible challenger to Erdogan.
The government denies any involvement in legal moves against the opposition, insisting that Turkey’s courts operate independently.

The action against Sozcu TV drew condemnation from opposition parties and media groups. Some critics linked the decision to impose a trusteeship to the channel devoting extensive coverage to an investment fund scandal that led to the resignation and subsequent arrest of a senior member of Erdogan’s ruling party.
Main opposition New Party leader Ozgur Ozel accused Erdogan’s government of intolerance toward “even the smallest criticism or a single inconvenient truth being heard.”
He vowed not to “surrender to these would-be dictators.”

Musavat Dervisoglu, the leader of the center-right opposition Good Party, described the move as “an overt assault on democracy, the rule of law, the sense of justice, and the public’s right to be informed.”
“Turkey will speak, and the voice of the truth cannot be silenced!” he wrote on X.
In a joint statement, Turkish journalism associations expressed solidarity with Sozcu TV journalists and called for the decision to appoint trustees to be reversed.
“Following Halk TV, the appointment of trustees to Sozcu shows that the media climate in Turkey has entered a dark winter,” the statement read.
On Tuesday, Sozcu TV’s regular early morning news program was replaced by a recorded discussion about longevity.
Other television stations, including HaberTurk and Tele1, have similarly been placed under trusteeship.

title: As outages persist, Puerto Rico finds a way to help keep the lights on with 'virtual power plant'
summary: Hector Ríos is part of Puerto Rico's innovative “virtual power plant” system, which uses household batteries to support the island's electric grid
story: Hector Ríos is part of Puerto Rico's innovative “virtual power plant” system, which uses household batteries to support the island's electric grid

SAN JUAN, Puerto Rico -- On nearly 20 days in October, an electric utility took energy from a battery attached to Hector Ríos’ house in Cabo Rojo, on the southwest corner of Puerto Rico, and used it to support the power grid.
Ríos was happy to share.

With the U.S. territory's frequent power outages that disrupt daily life and restrain its economy, he likes the idea of helping prevent blackouts for other people. He's also compensated for the energy.
“It just seems like a good deal, to contribute to the community and make money at the same time,” Ríos said.

Ríos, 75, is part of what has become one of Puerto Rico's most effective tools for energy resilience amid nearly a decade of electricity woes: a “virtual power plant,” or VPP, that harnesses batteries from nearly 115,000 households to bolster the grid when its aging and fickle power plants can't meet demand.

Nine years after Puerto Rico's public power utility filed for bankruptcy and Hurricane Maria ravaged its already dilapidated energy grid, residents still face unpredictable blackouts and electricity rates higher than in almost any state. Few new utility-scale power sources have been built since Maria, and most of the federal dollars promised for grid recovery have not yet reached the territory.

But the VPP — the first of its kind in Latin America and the Caribbean, and the U.S.' second largest in terms of capacity — showed its potential this summer, preventing or mitigating outages more than 60 times since June 1, according to Luma Energy, its transmission and distribution utility.
“There’s nothing virtual about it,” said Javier Rúa Jovet, chief policy officer at the Solar and Energy Storage Association of Puerto Rico. “It’s real, and it’s better than a power plant.”

Dozens of states now operate similar networks of distributed energy sources like battery storage systems, electric vehicles and smart thermostats to help manage the grid. Experts expect their role to grow in the U.S. amid energy constraints, rising utility prices, and tech companies’ push to build power-hungry data centers.

As President Donald Trump’s administration promotes fossil fuel expansion and redirects dollars away from solar adoption in Puerto Rico, proponents of the territory's system say it highlights the value of distributed solar and storage, and shows how these systems can bolster resilience for other energy-vulnerable communities.

“There’s a way for this technology to benefit not just the individual buildings that they’re on,” but instead be “in service to the community all the time,” said Nathalie Jordi, community solar lead at Together New Orleans, a nonprofit that championed an upcoming $23 million city program to provide and network over 1,000 batteries on homes and businesses across New Orleans.

The opportunity to harness a vast network of residential batteries arose after Hurricane Maria in 2017, which left some communities without electricity for nearly a year. Experts linked the infrastructure failure to thousands of post-hurricane deaths.
“We had to procure resiliency in some other way,” said Rúa Jovet, “not a centralized system that will completely fail for a whole year.”

There are now over 207,000 rooftop solar systems on an archipelago of fewer than 3.2 million people, a 20-fold increase from before Maria that was propelled by households who could afford installations, philanthropy, and some federal dollars. Because of the territory's unique need for resiliency, nearly every installation includes at least one battery, a necessary add-on to keep the system running in a blackout.

“The mindset was, get yourself ready for everything,” recalled Ríos, who after Maria bought a diesel generator for his house, then installed panels and a Tesla Powerwall battery in 2023. The system also cut his utility bill in half, from about $400 to $200 in the summer.

Solar panels create an energy boon during the day, charging batteries and sending excess power to the grid. But when the sun sets and demand rises, Puerto Rico barely has enough power to meet the need. Any power plant malfunction can prompt an outage.

In late 2023, Luma launched a small pilot program that would leverage residential battery capacity to offset the shortages. Ríos was among the first to enroll; now over half of solar customers participate.

If Luma predicts an energy deficit, customers are digitally notified that a battery sharing event is coming. They can opt out via app, or adjust how much of their battery — enrollees typically offer 30% — they make available.

The experiment has faced challenges. In a 2026 survey of solar customers by the nonprofit Solar United Neighbors, some participants criticized the compensation structure, which varies by solar provider. Others expressed hesitation to enroll in the program because they did not understand it or feared losing backup power.
Ríos said he’s only had that problem once — when a storm knocked out power right after he shared his battery. He now skips battery sharing events if there's bad weather forecast.
He acknowledged the payment system is “a little vague.” He and his wife received $162 last year, which they happily redeemed as a Marshalls gift card.

Luma told The Associated Press that relying so often on battery sharing has contributed in part to recent rate increases. The utility pays solar providers three times the residential electricity price for the battery energy it takes, recovering the costs through rates.

Rúa Jovet says that expense doesn’t compare to the societywide economic losses of frequent power outages that spoil food, endanger health and shutter schools and businesses. The territory is also set to spend more than $1.7 billion this year importing fuel for most of its power generation.

Luma said each battery sharing event, typically about four hours, supports the equivalent of about 80,000 residential customers. Enrolling more households would enable supplemental power for more hours.
But experts believe Puerto Rico can think bigger.

“The VPP in Puerto Rico is like an emergency escape valve, but the batteries should be a grid asset,” said Jigar Shah, director of the Department of Energy’s Loan Programs Office under former President Joe Biden and comanaging director of the advisory firm Multiplier.

Instead of only being tapped in an emergency, Shah said, the batteries could dispatch power every day — offsetting the need to burn fossil fuels — and help absorb excess energy across the grid when solar panels are producing at their peak. Several states, including California and Texas, use solar and batteries this way.

VPPs “could potentially play a larger role in Puerto Rico’s energy future,” Alejandro Figueroa, Luma chief regulatory officer, told The Associated Press. But, he said, a program used daily would require a different design and compensation structure to be sustainable.

Providing daily power is a natural next step, Rúa Jovet said, and could help Puerto Rico meet its own legal mandate that the archipelago reach 100% renewable energy by 2050. But a virtual power plant alone cannot solve the territory’s energy crisis.
That will require deploying billions of unspent federal recovery dollars, continuing improvements to transmission and distribution infrastructure and building new large-scale generation and storage.
“You don’t want the situation to be a persistent emergency forever,” he said.
