title: Xi and Carney call for deeper ties as Canada looks beyond US for trade
summary: The leaders of China and Canada have called for deeper ties as Ottawa navigates strained relations with the United States and seeks closer cooperation with Beijing
story: The leaders of China and Canada have called for deeper ties as Ottawa navigates strained relations with the United States and seeks closer cooperation with Beijing
SHENZHEN, China -- The leaders of China and Canada  called for deeper ties Tuesday as Ottawa navigates strained relations with the United States and seeks closer cooperation with Beijing.

Chinese President Xi Jinping and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney met ahead of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation leaders’ summit, and both praised the strategic partnership they agreed to pursue this year and pointed to improving economic ties.
The meeting came a day after Carney said Canada could turn to Chinese automakers if trade negotiations with U.S. President Donald Trump fail to maintain an integrated North American auto industry.

“Improving and developing China-Canada relations serves the interests of the people of both countries and is also conducive to safeguarding world peace, stability, development and prosperity,” said Xi. “This is the right choice.”
Carney said that the exchanges between Canada and China have increased in the past months and praised that now there is “greater predictability and stability” in their relationship.
“The stabilization of our bilateral trade arrangement is indicative of how we can work together more broadly, pragmatically, to solve problems,” he said.
Xi and Carney reached an agreement in January allowing tens of thousands of Chinese electric vehicles into Canada at reduced tariffs.

Under the January agreement, Canada reduced its 100% tariff on Chinese electric vehicles to 6.1%, initially allowing up to 49,000 vehicles annually, with the cap increasing over time. In exchange, China agreed to lower tariffs on Canadian agricultural products, including canola.

title: Taiwan may take a backseat when Xi and Trump meet for a third time at an APEC summit
summary: Presidents Xi Jinping and Donald Trump are expected to meet at the Asia Pacific Economic Forum this week
story: Presidents Xi Jinping and Donald Trump are expected to meet at the Asia Pacific Economic Forum this week

TAIPEI, Taiwan -- Taiwan is likely to be overshadowed as presidents Xi Jinping and Donald Trump are expected to meet on the sidelines of the Asia Pacific Economic Forum this week, even as the threat from China evolves and grows stronger.

Leaders from China, the U.S. and some 21 other economies will gather at the APEC summit this week in Shenzhen, China. Recent events like the scandal that forced Nvidia's CEO to resign, export controls and the ongoing trade dispute have made the tech competition between Beijing and Washington all the more pressing.

Few expect major breakthroughs on Taiwan, a self-ruled island that is claimed by Beijing. While the U.S. does not formally recognize Taiwan, it is the island’s biggest informal ally and seller of arms.
“For the Trump administration, this isn’t a core issue between the U.S. and China,” said Arthur Zhin-Sheng Wang, an expert on cross-Straits relations at Taiwan’s Central Police University.
Experts largely say that cooperation with the U.S. remains strong below the level of rhetoric, despite Trump’s public ambivalence toward Taiwan.

One sign of this came from the summer, when the de facto United States embassy in Taiwan posted a photo showing joint patrols between the two coast guards, a rare occurrence, as the U.S. does not usually acknowledge it has direct cooperation with Taiwan in any defense capacity.

“This also is proof of the decades that Taiwan and U.S. have had of cooperation and training. I was also surprised,” said Kuo Yu-jen, a defense studies expert and director of the Institute for National Policy Research in Taiwan.

The U.S. is obligated by law to help Taiwan defend itself, which has manifested in the form of arms sales, while the government officially adopts a stance of ambiguity on whether it would intervene militarily in the case of a Chinese invasion.

The Taiwanese public is used to the continued uncertainties of the island’s relationship with the U.S. Research from the Institute of National Defense and Security Research in Taiwan, a government-funded think tank, showed that public attitudes toward the U.S. remain around the same. Polls conducted in the past five years show that about half of the public believes the U.S. will send soldiers to support Taiwan in the event of a Chinese invasion, and about half don’t.

“I do think they will take some actions, though it may not be sending soldiers,” said Allen Hsieh, a 28-year-old media professional in Taipei. “I think Taiwan’s importance to the U.S. is even more important than Ukraine.”
Since starting his second term, Trump called for Taiwan to spend more on its own defense and Taiwan responded that it would commit to 5% of its GDP on defense.

Arms sales are ongoing. While much media attention has focused on a $14 billion package that remains stalled, an earlier package of $11 billion approved at the end of last year is in progress. Some of the stalled arms packages have been delayed since before Trump came into office, experts have also said.

Those include fighter jets. Taiwan received the first two of long-delayed F-16V fighter jets from the U.S. in October, and three more jets earlier this month. The aircraft are a part of a long list of backlogged U.S. orders worth almost $30 billion, according to the Taiwan Security Monitor research project which tracks defense-related developments on the island at George Mason University.

But the delays are not necessarily because of political considerations with China, a concern that was raised when Trump said he discussed arms sales with Xi earlier this year. Instead, it may be more of an issue with manufacturing capacity, particularly for future sales.

Congress approved the sale of long-range precision strike systems to Taiwan in December 2025, but Taiwan faces competition because of limited supplies. Kuo noted that among the missiles approved for sale are the same ones being used by the U.S. military in the ongoing Iran war, such as the HIMARS rockets and supplies were low.
“I don’t think this is a political issue. They just can’t produce so many of these missiles in a short period,” he said.

Meanwhile, China has intensified its military and nonmilitary pressure on Taiwan. In 2025, the People’s Liberation Army flew about 5,448 fighter jet sorties toward the island during military exercises, according to Skyfaring, an open-source website that compiles public data from Taiwan’s Ministry of Defense. That marked a sharp increase from the years before 2023, when such flights were sporadic.

Beijing also recently held unannounced military drills in the Western Pacific, deploying more than 100 vessels in waters near Taiwan and Japan, Taiwan’s National Security Council chief Joseph Wu said in a Nov. 3 post on X.
The number of PLA flights recorded this year stood at 2,401 as of Nov. 12, below the full-year total for 2025.

“I think the threat is transforming ... for example, more of its exercises are now about blockading and sealing off” Taiwan, Wang said, rather than firing live missiles. He said Beijing was expanding its gray-zone tactics — aggressive actions that fall short of open warfare.

These include greater use of the coast guard to assert China’s claims, mirroring its approach elsewhere. In June, the Chinese coast guard began patrolling off Taiwan’s east coast, which faces the open Pacific, extending its activities beyond Taiwan’s outlying islands closer to China.

Wang compared the approach to Beijing’s tactics in the South China Sea, where Chinese coast guard vessels patrol waters disputed with the Philippines. China has also designated a shoal claimed by the Philippines as a nature reserve under Chinese protection.
“It’s telling the whole world it has sovereignty here.”
Wu reported from Bangkok.

title: A top Puerto Rico government official resigns as corruption allegations swirl
summary: Puerto Rico’s embattled secretary of the Department of Family has announced that she would resign by year’s end as she denies the corruption allegations swirling around her
story: Puerto Rico’s embattled secretary of the Department of Family has announced that she would resign by year’s end as she denies the corruption allegations swirling around her
SAN JUAN, Puerto Rico -- Puerto Rico’s embattled secretary of the Department of Family announced Monday that she would resign by year’s end as she denied corruption allegations swirling around her.

Lawmakers in the U.S. territory had demanded for months that Suzanne Roig step down over the latest political scandal to hit the administration of Gov. Jenniffer González, which has seen several high-ranking officials resign or be fired in recent years.
Roig is under investigation by Puerto Rico’s Senate, the island’s Justice Department and its Office of the Inspector General.

In recent months, Blanca Medina Díaz, who was dismissed as head of the Administration for the Socioeconomic Development of the Family, which is within the department Roig oversees, publicly accused Roig of pressuring her to approve a nearly $40 million contract that Medina alleges was illegal and would have used federal funds from the Temporary Assistance for Needy Families program. The alleged push came after Roig and other officials visited Louisiana.
Roig and NOLA Education LLC, a Louisiana-based education company, have said that no contract was signed.
Medina, who has met with U.S. federal authorities, also accused Roig of pressuring her to approve an unrelated contract worth more than $300,000.
Roig has been under fire, as has the governor, who has publicly supported her.
Roig testified before Puerto Rico’s Senate in recent weeks as certain lawmakers who are members of the governor’s pro-statehood party called for her to step down.
Puerto Rico Senate President Thomas Rivera Schatz, also a member of the governor’s New Progressive Party, has said that ongoing legislative investigations would continue even if Roig resigned.
As Roig faced increasing scrutiny, she alleged in recent months that she was being stalked and persecuted as she denied all accusations.
In a statement Monday, Roig said that nobody asked her to resign as she thanked the governor for “the time and space that allowed me to defend my reputation against attacks full of falsehoods.”
Her decision to step down on Dec. 31 angered many.

“The resignation should have been immediate,” said Puerto Rico Sen. Juan Oscar Morales, majority whip and a member of the governor’s party. “The Department of the Family needs leadership focused on addressing the agency’s problems and ensuring services for those who depend on it.”

Roig’s announcement came nearly four months after the governor’s chief of staff and deputy chief of staff announced their resignations as they, too, denied corruption allegations. The governor stood by them as she has by Roig.

title: 1.5-hour-long system outage forces United Airlines to delay departing flights
summary: A system outage that lasted more than 90 minutes forced United Airlines to delay departing flights
story: A system outage that lasted more than 90 minutes forced United Airlines to delay departing flights

A system outage that lasted more than 90 minutes forced United Airlines to delay departing flights Monday, just days after a malfunction in the Federal Aviation Administration's network prompted a nationwide ground stop.

Chicago-based United said in a statement that flights that were in the air and flights on its United Express regional network were not affected. The airline also said there was “no indication that this was a cybersecurity-related issue.”
United apologized on social media to customers for the inconvenience. It resolved the issue about one hour and 40 minutes after pilots first began reporting problems to air traffic controllers.

United did not immediately provide details about which of its systems were affected, but pilots told air traffic controllers that the problem was related to a system that helps them determine a plane's final weight.

Before every departure, pilots use performance software, often on a cockpit tablet, to check that the aircraft can safely take off under current weather and runway conditions. The preflight calculations include the aircraft's weight along with information about the fuel, baggage, cargo and passengers the plane is carrying.
The information is also used to guide the autopilot system and the decisions pilots make, aviation safety expert Steve Arroyo said.

“It is extremely important to have all of these numbers accurate and precise,” said Arroyo, who flew for United. “Pilots use that information to establish guidance and performance for their flights from takeoff to landing.”
Arroyo said he has seen problems with the weight and balance system before in his career, but the airline did the right thing by delaying flights to ensure safety.

Years ago, pilots used to do all those weight calculations manually with a pencil and paper and then radio in the numbers, but today it is all calculated electronically and then loaded into the plane’s computers.

In August 2025, United grounded planes at major U.S. airports, delaying more than 1,000 flights because of an hourslong outage of a system called Unimatic, which houses flight information that is fed to other systems including those that calculate weight and balance and track flight times.
United said in response to a message from The Associated Press that it had no further information to provide about whether the same system was affected by Monday’s outage.

A recording posted Monday on the ATC app showed a United pilot in Houston asking the tower for permission to stay put at the gate until the system was working again. The app combines live air traffic control radio feeds with real-time visual aircraft tracking.
The flight-tracking website FlightAware showed United with about 600 delayed flights Monday evening, though it was unclear how many were directly related to the system outage.
The United computer problem is just the latest high-profile technology meltdown in recent days.
Earlier Monday, thousands of people reported being unable to access their online accounts at several major U.S. banks after JPMorgan Chase had a technical problem.
On Friday, the FAA ordered every flight grounded because a newly installed router malfunctioned, overwhelming the aging air traffic control system.
And one day earlier, Microsoft experienced a major disruption to its Outlook email service. Microsoft said Saturday that services were fully restored.

title: Amazon vows to fight the company's first North American union contract at a Canadian warehouse
summary: Hundreds of Amazon workers at a warehouse in Delta, British Columbia, are now being covered by a union contract, marking the company’s first site in North America under a collective bargaining agreement
story: Hundreds of Amazon workers at a warehouse in Delta, British Columbia, are now being covered by a union contract, marking the company’s first site in North America under a collective bargaining agreement

NEW YORK -- Hundreds of Amazon workers at a warehouse in Delta, British Columbia, are now being covered by a union contract, marking the company's first site in North America under a collective bargaining agreement.

The terms of the contract, which is set to run until Nov. 13, 2029, were imposed by an independent arbitrator between Canadian union Unifor and Amazon. Amazon said the facility employs more than 700 workers.

In a statement on Friday, Unifor's National President Lana Payne praised the workers who "stood up to one of the most powerful companies on earth and won rights in writing that Amazon cannot take away.”

But the Seattle-based online giant argued that the arbitrator set the terms without giving its workers “the chance to ratify or vote on it." It also said that the terms were imposed despite a pending effort by some of Amazon's employees to decertify the union.
Amazon said in a blog posted late Friday that the agreement sets terms for wages, scheduling, layoffs, and benefits that are largely similar to what the workers had already.

Amazon said the contract requires every employee in the unit to join the union, whether they want to or not, and to have union dues of up to C$1,064 ($744.03 US) deducted from their pay in the first year. That means they could actually take home less money than they did before, Amazon said.
“We believe that this process was improper, unfair, and defies common sense,” J. Ofori Agboka, Amazon's vice president of people, wrote in the blog post.

Unifor and Amazon have been locked in a fight since 2024 when employees at the facility started an organizing drive. In July 2025, the British Labour Relations Board certified the worker union for the warehouse through a rare process called “remedial certification” after it found that Amazon committed unfair labor practices including what it described as an unnecessary hiring spree to stop the certification process. The regulatory board said in its decision that Amazon pursued a “lengthy and pervasive anti-union campaign." Amazon had filed an appeal.
Remedial certification is used when an employer pursues unfair labor practices during an organizing drive that makes a fair vote unlikely.

Amazon said that it has filed a request for judicial review in the British Columbia Supreme Court, asking to halt implementation of the collective agreement until its decertification application is resolved and to overturn the board’s order imposing a contract through arbitration.

“We think the best workplace is one where associates have direct input and we work together to make progress quickly, and where nobody should have to pay dues or go through a third party to be heard,” Amazon's Agboka said.

In 2022, Amazon workers in Staten Island, New York, voted to unionize, marking the first successful U.S. organizing effort in the retail giant’s history. The workers were represented by Amazon Labor Union, which affiliated with the International Brotherhood of Teamsters two years later.
But workers don't have a contract yet, with the National Labor Relations Board ordering Amazon to negotiate and Amazon continuing to fight the union certification in court.

title: Trump administration moves to block China from indirect access to American AI technology
summary: The Trump administration has issued new rules to restrict remote access to advanced U.S. computing chips and servers
story: The Trump administration has issued new rules to restrict remote access to advanced U.S. computing chips and servers

WASHINGTON -- The Trump administration on Monday issued new rules to restrict remote access to advanced U.S. computing chips and servers, marking the latest step to limit China’s abilities to use U.S. chips to train their best artificial intelligence models.

Last week, Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang resigned as CEO following scrutiny of his ties to a Chinese executive who used to lead Singapore-based Megaspeed International, which is suspected of diverting advanced Nvidia chips to China in violation of U.S. export controls. The company provides computing power to Chinese companies using chips housed in Southeast Asian data centers, including facilities in Malaysia.

“The rule is designed to ensure that existing restrictions on access to sensitive American technology cannot be circumvented through remote computing arrangements involving data centers in third countries,” the Bureau of Industry and Security under the Commerce Department said in issuing the rule that took effect immediately.
The rule came on the same day President Donald Trump departed for a trip to Asia, where he expects to meet Chinese leader Xi Jinping for the third time this year amid a fragile truce on trade.

Under the new rule, overseas data centers that serve companies in countries including China, Russia, Iran and Cuba are required to identify their end users. There also will be additional licensing requirements for sales of chips for Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand or Brazil — countries that “present a higher-than-normal risk of diversion" to unauthorized destinations, the rule says.

In Beijing, China's foreign ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun accused Washington of arbitrarily interfering with China's trade and technological cooperation with other countries and suppressing the development of China's high-tech industries.

“This is a typical example of economic coercion and long-arm jurisdiction, runs counter to the common understanding between the two sides,” he told reporter, adding that it infringes upon the rights of Chinese companies and disrupts the stability of global supply chains.
He said China would take necessary measures to safeguard its interests.

The U.S. bans sales of the country's most advanced AI chips to China, seeking to maintain an edge in its rivalry with China for predominance in artificial intelligence. However, many lawmakers and policymakers believe the country's export control rules are not tough enough and filled with loopholes such as cloud computing that allows China to rent processing power built on American technology.

Last year, U.S. Rep. Michael Lawler, a New York Republican, introduced a bill to broaden the U.S. export controls to include remote access. He told Congress “physical export controls” under current rules do not apply to remote access, allowing China to “access our tech through the cloud” and giving it “a real tool to sidestep” U.S. export restrictions. The bill has passed the House.

In the Senate, lawmakers also are seeking tougher legislation to prevent China from accessing advanced U.S. chip and AI technologies. Bills include proposals that would let Congress review licenses to sell advanced AI chips to China, ask the Department of Commerce to track AI chips to ensure they are not diverted to unauthorized regions, and compel U.S. allies such as the Netherlands and Japan to match U.S. restrictions on exports to Chinese chipmakers.
Last week, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick came under pressure when Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the Commerce Department was late to place restrictions on Nvidia chip exports to Megaspeed.

On Monday, Trump acknowledged tension between Treasury and Commerce on the matter. He suggested that Lutnick may have delayed placing the export restrictions to avoid a “blow up” in the fragile U.S.-China relationship.
“We’re having a very good relationship with China right now, and I understand both sides of it, Trump said.

In a joint statement late Monday by the Commerce and Justice departments, it said Commerce initiated an investigation into Megaspeed for potential export control violations in 2024, which was followed by requests to Nvidia for records in May 2025 related to sales to Megaspeed. The following month, it said, Nvidia placed Megaspeed on its “no sell” list, and agents from the Commerce Department in conjunction with Singapore law enforcement conducted on-site checks of Megaspeed and interviewed Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang. The Justice Department then took the lead role in the criminal probe of Megaspeed, the statement said.

“The Department of Justice and the Department of Commerce’s Bureau of Industry and Security working together will bring the full extent of the law against Megaspeed for any criminal conduct that may have occurred,” the statement said.

Last week, the Singapore government confirmed that it had investigated Megaspeed over “potential false declarations" involving servers that were exported through Singapore to Malaysia but might have “subsequently been routed from Malaysia to another destination, contrary to declaration made in Singapore.”
The Malaysian government also said last week that it was investigating if chips brought into Malaysia have been re-exported to other countries as permitted by its own law.

“Malaysia welcomes investment in data centers and technology, but will not allow itself to be used to get around export controls,” read the Friday statement by Malaysia's Ministry of Investment, Trade and Industry.

title: Warren Buffett says kindness 'compounds' as he gifts over $5B to family's foundations
summary: Warren Buffett upped his annual Thanksgiving donation as he advances plans to give away his entire wealth
story: Warren Buffett upped his annual Thanksgiving donation as he advances plans to give away his entire wealth
NEW YORK -- NEW YORK (AP) — Warren Buffett upped his annual Thanksgiving donation as he advances plans to give away his entire fortune.

The billionaire investor pledged Monday to donate about $5.5 billion worth of Berkshire Hathaway shares to his family's foundations — an estimated value more than four times as large as recent years' November stock gifts.

The goal, he reiterated Monday, is to grow the grants each year as he donates all his shares by 2034 to four charitable foundations associated with his three children. He emphasized his faith in his children Monday, writing that they “have given thoughtfully to worthy causes for decades” and that he trusts “their abilities and their fidelity.”

In brief comments, Buffett wrote that kindness “compounds” as he reflected on the “costless benefits” he and his longtime business partner received from their teachers. His good fortune, he said, “has come in the form of people who were kind to me and expected nothing in return.”
“This Thanksgiving, thank one of the selfless people in your own life,” Buffett wrote. “Better yet, be a benefactor for someone else.”

Buffett donated 9,225,000 Class B shares of Berkshire Hathaway stock to the foundations — 3,690,000 shares to The Susan Thompson Buffett Foundation and 1,845,000 shares each to The Sherwood Foundation, The Howard G. Buffett Foundation and NoVo Foundation. Berkshire Hathaway Class B shares opened trading Monday at $594 a share.

The next generation of Buffetts tends to fly under the radar even as the children have grown poised to join the ranks of the country's largest donors. The Susan Thompson Buffett Foundation, named after Warren Buffett’s first wife, has supported reproductive healthcare organizations in the U.S. and internationally.

The Sherwood Foundation, Susie Buffett's organization, has been a stalwart funder for early childhood education within the U.S. Much of Howard Buffett's grantmaking supports food security and conflict mitigation internationally — with a recent focus on Ukraine. Peter Buffett and his wife, Jennifer, have largely sought to empower women and girls around the world through the NoVo Foundation.

The Thanksgiving donations have, in recent years, come in addition to the main gifts made every summer by Warren Buffett. This year he cut off the Gates Foundation, the longtime beneficiary of the bulk of his charity, from all future gifts. He said the decision was driven more so by his belief in his three kids' readiness than Bill Gates' ties to convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

This year's Thanksgiving stock gift is Buffett's first since stepping down as the chairman and CEO of the $1 trillion conglomerate he built. He wrote Monday that his confidence in Berkshire Hathaway is “as strong as ever.” The third quarter saw the company repurchase $9.6 billion worth of its own shares and a return to growth for its massive cash pile.

title: More drops for Nvidia and other AI stocks drag the US market lower
summary: More drops for AI stocks are dragging the U.S. market lower, led by Nvidia
story: More drops for AI stocks are dragging the U.S. market lower, led by Nvidia
NEW YORK -- NEW YORK (AP) — More drops for stocks in the artificial-intelligence industry are dragging the U.S. market lower on Monday, led by Nvidia.

The S&P 500 fell 1.1% and was on track for a third straight loss. The weakness for tech stocks pulled the Nasdaq composite down a market-leading 1.6%, and the Dow Jones Industrial Average was down 289 points, or 0.6%, as of 11 a.m. Eastern time.

Nvidia sank 2.5% and was again the heaviest weight on Wall Street following its crisis of leadership. Nvidia is one of the most influential companies in the world not only because its chips are powering much of the world’s move into AI technology but also because its cash has helped companies across the industry to grow.

Now, following Jensen Huang’s resignation as Nvidia’s CEO last week, both the chip company and the broad industry are facing a more uncertain future without the leather-jacketed man who became one of AI’s biggest celebrities.

It’s the latest challenge for the AI industry, which had already been shaky because of criticism that stock prices in the industry shot too high and were in a bubble. The sweeping victories for Democrats in this month’s U.S. midterm elections also raised worries about possible restrictions on further construction of AI data centers.

“The market was already worried about this risk before what happened at Nvidia,” Zhiwei Zhang, president and chief economist at Pinpoint Asset Management, said in a commentary. “Now the risk has become even more serious.”

Outside of Nvidia, other chip companies also fell. They had climbed in the earlier days of Nvidia’s fall on hopes that they could gain a competitive advantage. But Broadcom dropped 3.8% and was on track for a second straight loss on concerns about the broader industry. So was Advanced Micro Devices, which fell 4.5%.
CoreWeave, which buys Nvidia chips and then rents out access to them to customers over the cloud, sank 5%. GE Vernova, which is helping to power AI data centers, fell 3.3%.

The next big milestone for the AI industry may arrive Tuesday after trading in the U.S. stock market ends for the day. That’s when Nvidia will report its latest quarterly results, and interim CEO Colette Kress is set to speak to Wall Street. Investors have become accustomed to Nvidia not only reporting stronger results than analysts expected for each quarter but also giving a forecast for upcoming revenue that’s well above expectations.

Elsewhere on Wall Street, L3Harris Technologies fell 2.5% after officials in President Donald Trump’s administration suggested the contractor for the Federal Aviation Administration may be at fault for a nationwide ground stop Friday. L3Harris said Saturday that it’s supporting the FAA in its investigation.

Summit Therapeutics sank 13.4% after the biopharmaceutical company said the U.S. Food and Drug Administration indicated it cannot approve its application for a therapy to treat certain patients with lung cancer.

Tyson Foods helped to limit the market’s losses and rose 7.5% after reporting a stronger profit for the latest quarter than analysts expected. The company behind the Jimmy Dean and Hillshire Farm brands, though, also reported weaker revenue than expected after selling less beef than it did a year earlier.

The recent swings for AI stocks have overshadowed what's been another strong earnings reporting season for U.S. companies. The big businesses in the S&P 500 index are on track to deliver earnings per share for the summer nearly 32% higher than a year earlier, according to FactSet.

It's the third straight quarter of growth above 25% for the index, which is important because corporate profits are one of the two big levers that set stock prices over the long term, along with interest rates.
In the bond market, Treasury yields eased back following last week's jump due to a worse-than-expected report on U.S. inflation.

The yield on the 10-year Treasury fell to 5.13% from 5.15% late Friday, though it remains well above a low of 4.80% reached earlier this month. Higher yields make borrowing money more expensive for everyone, and they’ve already hurt the housing industry through expensive mortgage rates.

Yields fell as oil prices sank, which took away some of the upward pressure on inflation. The price for a barrel of Brent crude oil fell 2.1% to $93.81. It’s been yo-yoing amid uncertainty about what will happen in the war with Iran.
In stock markets abroad, indexes were mixed in Europe and Asia.

South Korea’s Kospi dropped 3.6%, and Japan’s Nikkei 225 fell 2.4% for two of the world’s sharpest losses because of weakness for tech and AI-related stocks. A report also showed that Japan’s economy contracted in the latest quarter.
AP Business Writers Chan Ho-him and Michelle Chapman contributed to this report.

title: Carney says Canada could turn to Chinese automakers if Trump trade talks fail
summary: Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney says Canada could turn to Chinese automakers if trade negotiations with U.S. President Donald Trump fail to preserve an integrated North American auto industry
story: Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney says Canada could turn to Chinese automakers if trade negotiations with U.S. President Donald Trump fail to preserve an integrated North American auto industry

PHNOM PENH, Cambodia -- Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said that Canada could turn to Chinese automakers if trade negotiations with U.S. President Donald Trump fail to preserve an integrated North American auto industry.

Carney’s comments in Cambodia on Monday came ahead of a planned meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping this week in Shenzhen, China, where Chinese auto manufacturing is expected to be discussed. The two leaders reached an agreement in January allowing tens of thousands of Chinese electric vehicles into Canada at reduced tariffs.

“We have the best auto workers in the world, and we want them fully deployed, full opportunity, in an integrated North American market,” Carney told reporters in Cambodia. “That market has become less integrated because of U.S. trade actions.”

Carney said Saturday in Manila, Philippines, that any trade agreement with Washington must leave Canada with a viable auto industry. He said Monday that negotiations with the United States remain his priority, but their outcome could determine whether Canada pursues alternatives involving European, Chinese or Japanese automakers.
Asked whether potential Chinese investment was leverage in the U.S. negotiations, Carney replied: “It’s not leverage. But action, reaction.”

“If they’re not fully utilized in a North American context, that provides other opportunities,” Carney said of Canada’s auto workers and manufacturing assets. “Canada is going to move forward either way.”

The Detroit Three — Ford, General Motors and Stellantis — operate factories across Canada, the United States and Mexico, with parts sometimes crossing borders multiple times before a vehicle is completed. Trump has repeatedly pushed automakers to move production to the United States from Canada.

Carney said any Chinese investment would have to involve substantial manufacturing in Canada rather than simply assembling imported parts. He said it would require proper labor standards, manufacturing facilities and domestic supply chains that expand over time, including Canadian critical minerals used in electric vehicles.
“It’s not just about kit cars,” he said. “There has to be a manufacturing aspect involved.”

Under the January agreement, Canada reduced its 100% tariff on Chinese electric vehicles to 6.1%, initially allowing up to 49,000 vehicles annually, with the cap increasing over time. In exchange, China agreed to lower tariffs on Canadian agricultural products, including canola.
Carney said at the time that he expected the agreement to attract Chinese investment in Canada’s auto industry and create jobs.

The deal drew criticism from Ontario Premier Doug Ford, whose province is the center of Canada’s auto industry. Ford warned that allowing Chinese electric vehicles into Canada could threaten Canadian jobs and jeopardize access to the U.S. market.

Trump’s tariffs have disrupted Canada’s auto industry, which relies heavily on cross-border production. Canada recently threatened to sue Stellantis after the automaker shifted planned Jeep Compass production from Brampton, Ontario, to Illinois and agreed to sell its idled Canadian assembly plant.

Carney said Saturday that he had spoken at length with Trump and senior U.S. officials and that the two countries were making progress toward a possible trade agreement, although differences remained.

title: 2 planes collide on the ground in Miami, only minor injuries reported
summary: Federal aviation safety officials are investigating a minor collision between two planes at a taxiway intersection at Miami International Airport
story: Federal aviation safety officials are investigating a minor collision between two planes at a taxiway intersection at Miami International Airport

MIAMI -- Federal aviation safety officials on Sunday were investigating a minor collision between two planes at a taxiway intersection at Miami International Airport, where one aircraft's wingtip struck the nose of another, authorities said. Two people reported minor injuries.

The accident happened at about 9 p.m. Saturday and involved a Copa Airlines Boeing 737 aircraft with 172 people aboard and a UPS Boeing 767 cargo plane, according to the National Transportation Safety Board and Copa Airlines. The wing of the Copa flight and the nose of the UPS plane collided, the NTSB said.
Photos taken at the scene show the UPS plane nose with a horizontal gash on one side and a larger hole in the middle.

On audio recorded by ATC.com, a pilot on the UPS plane told air traffic control that he went too far at the intersection and his plane was clipped by the Copa flight. Air traffic control told the UPS pilot that he was supposed to yield to the Copa aircraft.

The NTSB said Sunday that preliminary information showed the UPS plane was instructed to give way to the Copa Airlines flight but did not stop. The UPS aircraft had substantial damage, while an assessment of the Copa plane had not been completed, it said. The NTSB said it opened an investigation and expected a preliminary report to be released within 30 days.
The Copa plane had just arrived from Panama City and the UPS plane was headed to Bogota, Colombia, officials said.
In a statement on social media, Copa called the collision minor and said two of its passengers were treated at the scene for minor injuries.
UPS said it was working with authorities to determine what happened.

“We cannot speculate on the details of the incident,” UPS said in a statement. “The National Transportation Safety Board is responsible for investigating incidents like this and will control the flow of information.”
The mishap came two months after an Amazon cargo plane careened off a runway at Miami International and smashed into a van carrying workers for a company that cleans airplanes, killing five people.

title: Czechs gather in big numbers to reject government's plan to overhaul funding of public media
summary: Hundreds of thousands of people rallied in Prague against the Czech government's plan to overhaul funding for public broadcasters
story: Hundreds of thousands of people rallied in Prague against the Czech government's plan to overhaul funding for public broadcasters

PRAGUE -- Hundreds of thousands of people rallied in Prague on Sunday against a plan by the government of Czech billionaire Andrej Babiš to overhaul funding for public broadcasters that many say will erode media independence and democracy.
The massive protest took place at the capital's Letná Park, where huge crowds gathered during the 1989 Velvet Revolution, which ended more than 40 years of communist rule in the country.

The rally, just two days before the anniversary of the 1989 protests, drew an estimated 350,000 people, said Mikuláš Minář, the lead organizer from the Million Moments for Democracy group. They demanded that the government withdraw its plan and expressed concern that Babiš and his coalition partners pose a threat to democracy.
“We do witness here something extraordinary today,” Minář said. “It's just a beginning.”

Under the plan, the country’s public radio and television broadcasters would be financed from the state budget, replacing the existing system of regular fees paid by individuals, households and businesses. The broadcasters would receive about 15% less money than they do now, which could lead to layoffs, limited production and program cancellations.

Critics say the overhaul would give the three-party coalition the means to take control of the media, similar to what populist governments did in Slovakia under Prime Minister Robert Fico and in Hungary, before former Prime Minister Viktor Orbán was ousted from power in April.
“We refuse the Slovak scenario,” one protest banner read. “Hands off the media,” said another.

One of the protesters, singer Šarka Dumišincová, said that for her “the media represent freedom. And the fact that someone here is trying to control that freedom is unacceptable to me. That’s why I’m here today.”

The ruling coalition unexpectedly moved ahead with the plan in the lower house of Parliament on Oct. 24. Its lawmakers limited the opposition's speaking time before voting at 4:36 a.m. to advance the bill through the first of three parliamentary readings.

Thousands took to the streets the following day to protest the rushed process, and public media employees went on strike on Nov. 3. The strike was backed by labor unions, universities, students, churches, artists, athletes and international media organizations, among others.
“We are here to stand up against the rule by force in the style of 4:36,” Minář said Sunday, referring to the time the bill cleared its first reading.

Media freedom and the rule of law in the Czech Republic were debated Wednesday in the European Parliament. EU Justice Commissioner Michael McGrath said national legislation must ensure that funding for public service iis based on transparent and objective criteria and guarantees "adequate, sustainable and predictable financial resources.”
Babiš vowed to press ahead with the plan despite the protests and denied that it would affect media freedom.

He returned to power in the Czech Republic after his ANO, or YES, movement, won the country’s election last year and formed a coalition with two small political groups — the anti-migrant and pro-Russian party Freedom and Direct Democracy, and the right-wing Motorists for Themselves.
Babiš has opposed some key European Union policies on environment and migration and rejected financial aid for Ukraine and guarantees for EU loans to help it fight the Russian invasion.

His government has been under fire from NATO allies for failing to spend enough on defense. Protesters also condemned its defense policy and demanded the resignation of the Freedom party leader, parliamentary Speaker Tomio Okamura, and Defense Minister Jaromír Zůna. The party is in charge of the ministry.

"While (Russia's President Vladimir) Putin threatens Europe, the pro-Russian (party) is systematically undermining the state’s defensive capability and endangering national security,” Minář, the main protest organizer, said.
Associated Press video journalist Stanislav Hodina contributed to this report.

title: French soccer leader Diallo set to challenge Infantino for FIFA presidency
summary: French soccer leader Philippe Diallo wants to restore “broken” trust in the sport's governance and rid the game of the “poison of division” after having confirmed his intention to challenge Gianni Infantino for the FIFA presidency
story: French soccer leader Philippe Diallo wants to restore “broken” trust in the sport's governance and rid the game of the “poison of division” after having confirmed his intention to challenge Gianni Infantino for the FIFA presidency

PARIS -- French soccer leader Philippe Diallo wants to restore “broken” trust in the sport's governance and rid the game of the “poison of division” after confirming his intention on Tuesday to challenge Gianni Infantino for the FIFA presidency.
His candidacy was ratified following an executive committee meeting at the French soccer federation’s headquarters in Paris.

“A few days ago, my colleagues from the UEFA Executive Committee asked me if I could carry this voice in the world of football," Diallo, 63, said. “I wasn’t initially a candidate, but the insistence of my European colleagues led me to accept the offer to be the candidate for the FIFA presidency.”

UEFA is pursuing legal action in U.S. courts and seeks discovery of evidence for a possible criminal complaint against Infantino in his and FIFA’s home country Switzerland alleging financial mismanagement.
FIFA accused UEFA of a “smear campaign” against its president in a court filing in Colorado.

Concerns include Infantino seeming to act alone in creating a peace prize for U.S. President Donald Trump last year and, at the World Cup, letting United States forward Folarin Balogun avoid a mandatory ban for a red card after Trump intervened.

“Since a few months there have been a series of decisions taken inside FIFA: I think of the peace prize, I think of the distribution of revenue of television rights in the United States, the red card for Balogun, the length of the halftime break in the final and the private investors (sell-off plan),” Diallo said.
“All of these decisions shocked the world of football in a very big way, the fans, the clubs, the sponsors, the federations.”
Diallo said “there are a lot of questions” for Infantino and that the turmoil and fall-out has seriously damaged the game.
“It created a situation this summer whereby the trust placed in FIFA and it’s president was broken," he said. “They have damaged the image of football and have introduced the poison of division.”
UEFA, European soccer’s ruling body, proposed Diallo on Monday after a meeting of its 21-member executive committee that includes the French Football Federation president.

“It was important that another voice can carry another vision, more respectful toward what we love in football," Diallo added on Tuesday. “I could not shy away from the demands. I think I have the experience, the convictions and the values which offer a credible alternative.

“I think with my candidature comes hope of a change. It is support of my European colleagues and my executive committee which allows me to say this. Football deserves a credible change which I represent. I am candidate for the FIFA presidency. What happened in recent months was shocking.”
Diallo sat smiling alongside Zinedine Zidane when he was announced as France’s new national team coach in late July.

Diallo is a long-time soccer administrator with French clubs, and the league, who rose to interim president at the FFF in January 2023, before being fast-tracked in an election of UEFA member federations to join the European body’s executive committee.
Diallo has worked for world soccer's ruling body FIFA as a judge on its Dispute Resolution Chamber, handling contract disputes between players and clubs.

Until his emergence, speculation on a candidate focused on Qatari soccer and broadcast executive Nasser Al-Khelaïfi, the president of Champions League titleholder Paris Saint-Germain and a UEFA executive committee member. He said he would not run against Infantino, who has backing from Qatar.
Focus them shifted onto former Arsenal coach Arsène Wenger, hired by FIFA since 2019 as the global head of developing the game. He made it clear he would not stand.

When the World Cup ended on July 19, Infantino was set to be re-elected unopposed effectively by a coronation. FIFA said he had about 200 letters of support from the 211 member federations who will vote in March in Rabat, Morocco.
One of those letters was from France.

But Diallo formally withdrew the FFF in September, citing that trust in Infantino was broken by the World Cup sell-off plan secretly devised with Joshua Kushner, the younger brother of Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner.

“The last time I saw him (Infantino) was at the World Cup, he came to a few France games. I have known him for a long time," Diallo said. “I regret, as others did, that he did not share the ideas of his projects ... it was an unacceptable act of defiance."

Diallo said the 48-team men’s 2026 World Cup generated record profits of $15-16 million, vastly more than the 2022 edition of 32 teams in Qatar. Therefore the sell-off plan, which “no one really understands", was totally baffling.
“FIFA’s (cash) reserves are $5-6 million,” Diallo said. “We find it hard to understand ... the need to find private investors to bring further billions, when these billions are already here.”
Infantino has promised at least $25 million in development funds to each member federation through 2030.

“On the basis of (cash) reserves that had lay dormant for years and would still be dormant in FIFA accounts if we had not intervened,” Diallo said. “There are a lot of things that need answering, there is no clarity regarding this and there are curious strategies.”
Germany coach Jürgen Klopp said he’d welcome a new FIFA president and that Infantino has turned out worse than Blatter.

“To beat him I need 106 votes, the absolute majority,” said Diallo, who will announce his campaign team in Belfast in early December. “I will have a clear program of solidarity and excellence, and guarantee those who love soccer that these values will be respected.”
He can count on the support, too, of French President Emmanuel Macron.

“The President supports my candidature,” he said, adding that he has been “pleasantly surprised” by the number of people from the African and Asian soccer federations who have offered him their support since his candidacy became known.

title: PGA Tour in no hurry to decide on future of LIV players
summary: The PGA Tour is not in a rush to figure out whether LIV Golf players can return
story: The PGA Tour is not in a rush to figure out whether LIV Golf players can return
The PGA Tour board had “thoughtful discussions” on Monday about the future of players at LIV Golf but otherwise seemed to be in no hurry to decide if there is room for them next season.
CEO Brian Rolapp only repeated his position that rules exist for a membership organization to ensure fairness and a competitive balance.
“Rules matter and they will be enforced,” he said.
Rolapp said the “ returning member program ” that allowed Brooks Koepka to return to the PGA Tour this year with financial penalties was not on the table.
“There are no plans for that currently, no,” Rolapp said in a conference call to discuss the tour's changes to its developmental system.

LIV Golf, which loss the financial support of Saudi Arabia and filed for bankruptcy on Sept. 8, told a bankruptcy court earlier this month it had abandoned plans for a new version of the league and had begun winding down its business.
It hopes to finalize the bankruptcy plan sometime in January.

“We engaged in thoughtful discussion on the top of LIV players with both boards today,” Rolapp said, referring to the PGA Tour and the commercial PGA Tour Enterprises. “As far as we have read, bankruptcy proceedings are ongoing and the process is complex. I hope to have more to say in the beginning of the new year.”
Jon Rahm and Bryson DeChambeau are the most attractive stars. DeChambeau has yet to indicate his plans while Rahm, who won two weeks ago in Abu Dhabi, remains a European tour member.

Rahm has said he has yet to speak with the PGA Tour but would take the deal Koepka got if offered. Rolapp in January offered that deal to Rahm, DeChambeau and Cameron Smith — before there was any indication Saudi Arabia would stop funding the rival league — and said there was no guarantee the offer would be available in the future.

Rahm told the Spanish site “Ten Golf,” “I imagine they have their boards, their meetings to hold for whatever is coming at the end of the year, and I imagine one of those points will be me. I just don't know if it'll be this November or December. I have no idea.
“At the very least, I'll be here in January, here in Dubai,” Rahm said. “So I jokingly tell everyone this: I will either be here or in Palm Springs in January, one of the two.”
The 2027 season on the PGA Tour starts with The American Express in the California desert.

Several players, such as Joaquin Niemann, are planning to play in Australia, where the two biggest events are co-sanctioned with the European tour. DeChambeau had already said he would be playing the Nedbank Golf Challenge in South Africa, also co-sanctioned by the European tour.

Rolapp said the PGA Tour is still discussing a renewed alliance with the European tour. That alliance would determine how many players — currently 10 — will be awarded PGA Tour cards from the season “Race to Dubai” points list.

title: Bryson DeChambeau heads slew of former LIV players on European tour for 2027 season
summary: Bryson DeChambeau will play on the European tour for the 2027 season following the demise of LIV Golf
story: Bryson DeChambeau will play on the European tour for the 2027 season following the demise of LIV Golf

Bryson DeChambeau headlined an influx of former LIV players who will compete on the European tour in the 2027 season, marking a realignment of the golfing landscape following the demise of the breakaway circuit.

DeChambeau, a two-time major champion and social-media influencer with 3 million subscribers on his YouTube channel, will add heft to a circuit that has trailed in the wake of the PGA Tour but now has a sprinkling of new — or returning — talent to raise its profile.

Courtesy of his second U.S. Open title in 2024, the 33-year-old American has taken Category 1 status for the first time on the European tour, the highest priority ranking, which means he can play in whichever tournament he chooses.
DeChambeau was planning to play the Nedbank Golf Challenge in South Africa — an event co-sanctioned by the European tour — on Dec. 4-7.
He was a star name on LIV, which announced two weeks ago in bankruptcy court it planned to wind down operations instead of launching a new version after losing the financial support of Saudi Arabia.
A return to the PGA Tour, which typically has a one-year ban on players dating to their most recent LIV appearance, will have to wait.
On Monday, PGA Tour CEO Brian Rolapp said his board had “thoughtful discussions” about the future of players at LIV Golf, adding: "I hope to have more to say in the beginning of the new year.”
That meant departing LIV players instead were flocking to the DP World Tour — the title name of the European circuit — that is now golf's global tour.

Eighteen players competing on LIV in 2026 are now on the European tour and they include one-time stalwarts of the circuit like former Ryder Cup stars Lee Westwood, Sergio Garcia, Henrik Stenson and Ian Poulter, via a category related to career earnings.
Jon Rahm and Tyrrell Hatton — winners of the last two events of the 2026 European tour season — already had announced they would be returning to the tour after the collapse of LIV.

The tour added that major champions Dustin Johnson and Cameron Smith were among nine players coming off LIV to have signed agreements to receive invites to a specific number of tournaments next season.
They would not be the high-profile, lucrative Rolex Series events, but smaller tournaments where the presence of these former LIV players would “add value,” the European tour said.
The other seven players on that nine-man list were Bubba Watson, Abraham Ancer, Lucas Herbert, Michael La Sasso, Joaquin Niemann, Carlos Ortiz and Thomas Pieters.
Guy Kinnings, CEO of the European tour, said the decision to offer these invites had to be “carefully managed” by the circuit “to ensure and preserve playing opportunities for existing members.”

“There has been significant change in the landscape of men’s professional golf over the past 12 months,” Kinnings said. “As golf’s global tour, we have taken a pragmatic approach to this unique and unprecedented situation as we go into next year, always with the best interests of our entire membership at the forefront of our minds.”
Kinnings said the 2027 season was set to be “one of the most keenly contested campaigns in our 55-year history.”
The season starts next week at the BMW Australian PGA Championship.

title: Christian Pulisic stuns with a bicycle kick as the US sends off Mauricio Pochettino with a 2-0 win
summary: Christian Pulisic scored on a sensational bicycle kick as the United States sent coach Mauricio Pochettino out on a successful note, defeating Haiti 2-0 in the second leg of the Nations League quarterfinals
story: Christian Pulisic scored on a sensational bicycle kick as the United States sent coach Mauricio Pochettino out on a successful note, defeating Haiti 2-0 in the second leg of the Nations League quarterfinals

CINCINNATI -- Mauricio Pochettino spent the three days before his final match as coach of the United States national team focusing on what he needed to do to keep his squad focused on beating Haiti and advancing in the CONCACAF Nations League.

After the final whistle sounded in the Americans' 2-0 victory in the second leg of the Nations League quarterfinals on Tuesday night, Pochettino's emotions took over as he concluded his two-year tenure on a successful note.
The 54-year-old Argentine hugged his now-former players and plenty of tears flowed in the locker room before Pochettino boarded a plane for Manchester, England, to take over at Manchester United.
“I was good until we met for the last time. It is impossible not to cry because we care about the people and they care about us,” Pochettino said.

The win over Haiti showed a mix of the current and future talent the U.S. has in its ranks. Christian Pulisic scored on a sensational bicycle kick and 18-year-old Julian Hall scored in the first half.

“I am sure that this group of players will achieve big things on the future. I have no doubt the experienced players with a mix of younger and the talent that is coming is a perfect combination, and in the way that they are leading all the things now,” Pochettino said.

Pochettino received a standing ovation from the crowd of 24,001 at TQL Stadium after the game. He begins his new job as Manchester United's coach on Wednesday after agreeing last Friday to replace Michael Carrick.

Goalkeeper coach Toni Jiménez, top assistant Jesús Pérez and fitness coach Sebastiano Pochettino — Mauricio Pochettino's son — have been in England since Sunday. They departed after the U.S. defeated Haiti 6-0 on Saturday in the first leg.
Assistant coach Miguel D’Agostino, fitness coach Sylvia Tuyà Viñas and analyst Alex Scott stayed for Tuesday's match and are also headed to Manchester with Pochettino.

Pochettino had a 23-12-2 record with the U.S., including a run to the round of 16 at this year’s World Cup before a 4-1 loss to Belgium. His tenure began with a 2-0 win over Panama on Oct. 12, 2024, in Austin, Texas.
During Pochettino's tenure, 78 players earned caps, including 31 who made their national team debuts. Nine teenagers also earned playing time, including Hall.

“He said that fell in love with the country. He didn’t know exactly what to expect when he took the job. He fell in love with the people, he fell in love with the football, and he fell in love with our team. That’s special,” U.S. captain Tyler Adams said.
The Americans won the series by an aggregate score of 8-0 to advance to the four-match knockout CONCACAF Nations League Finals in March in Los Angeles.

Pulisic had three goals in the matches against Haiti. He lined up and directed a bicycle kick off the far post in the 25th minute after McKennie lobbed a crossing pass. Pulisic said it was the first time in a professional or international game that he had attempted a bicycle kick.

“It was a good back post ball. I know moments like that don’t happen a lot. I saw it and I just had to go for it. It came off really well,” said Pulisic, who has 36 goals for the U.S. and was subbed out in the 65th minute.
Hall, who scored for the fifth time in six U.S. appearances, controlled a pass from McKennie before directing it past Haiti goalkeeper Alexandre Pierre in the 43rd minute.

Pochettino will have his work cut out for him at Manchester United, which is in 18th place in the Premier League and facing potential relegation. He will have only a couple of days to work with his new squad before United visits Liverpool on Sunday.
Pochettino — who previously coached in the Premier League at Southampton, Tottenham and Chelsea — is United’s eighth permanent coach or manager since Alex Ferguson retired in 2013.
United has a chance to turn things around. After Liverpool, the club faces Brentford, Newcastle United, Crystal Palace and Coventry City.

“Our job is to unlock the brain of the people and try to change the idea that you cannot run. You can play comfort-free and express your talent,” Pochettino said. “Soccer is about attitude, approach and communication.”

U.S. Soccer CEO JT Batson said in a prematch interview with TNT Sports that Pochettino has shown everyone the benefits of coming to America as well as his confidence in being able to attract a world-class coach.

“For us to win, we need to be great at a lot of things, and we need someone who cares about youth development, cares about our youth national team programs, our relationships with our clubs and the success of the federation more broadly,” Batson said. “We know that is a key part of our success, and it’s also a key part of how we’ve been able to attract great people because they get to do big things.”

Pochettino said during a roundtable with reporters on Monday that Pep Guardiola should be his successor if offered the job. Guardiola won 12 domestic trophies and two UEFA Champions League titles at Barcelona, Bayern Munich and Manchester City.
However, Pochettino said after Tuesday's match he would not give any recommendations to Batson or U.S. Soccer president Cindy Parlow Cone.
'It’s not my job and for sure they have the capacity and know how to find the right people with the right profile,” Pochettino said. “I don’t know how to measure my colleagues.”

title: Embattled Cowboys defensive coordinator Christian Parker's role could change, Jerry Jones says
summary: Dallas Cowboys defensive coordinator Christian Parker’s play-calling duties could be in question after owner Jerry Jones said the team was discussing changes to his role or responsibilities
story: Dallas Cowboys defensive coordinator Christian Parker’s play-calling duties could be in question after owner Jerry Jones said the team was discussing changes to his role or responsibilities

FRISCO, Texas -- Dallas Cowboys defensive coordinator Christian Parker's play-calling duties could be in question after owner Jerry Jones said Tuesday the club was discussing changes to his role or responsibilities.
“We’re talking about that, but I’m not going to talk about it here,” Jones said on his radio show on 105.3 The Fan. “But we are talking about those things.”

The 34-year-old Parker is a first-time defensive coordinator and the youngest to have that title in franchise history. The Cowboys just gave up their most-ever yards in a home game, allowing 584 in a 46-40 loss to San Francisco on Sunday.
It's the second consecutive year Dallas has had one of the worst defenses in the NFL. Matt Eberflus was fired after the 2025 season, his only season as the defensive coordinator.

Jones' comments came a day after coach Brian Schottenheimer was noncommittal about any changes involving Parker, saying they were “taking a deep dive and looking at everything.” Schottenheimer was pressed on whether that meant a change in the play-calling role would happen.

“I’m not saying that,” said Schottenheimer, who offered firm support for Parker when criticism mounted earlier in the season. “I’m saying we’re still in the process of going through all the film and the evaluation of where we stand today.”

The Cowboys gave up touchdown catches of 74 and 66 yards to star 49ers running back Christian McCaffrey and a 70-yard TD on a reverse to Deebo Samuel. Dallas has allowed at least one touchdown of 50-plus yards in three consecutive games.

Jones referenced nearly 25 years ago when Sean Payton, now Denver's head coach, had play-calling duties taken away with the New York Giants before joining the Cowboys. Payton then had those duties stripped in Dallas as well.

The uncertainty surrounding Parker's role comes a month after the Cowboys hired Mike Pettine, a former NFL defensive coordinator and head coach, as a consultant. Parker and Pettine had worked together before in Green Bay.
Jones said changes could happen before the Cowboys (4-6) play Tennessee (1-8) at home Sunday.

“Some of the best coaches you’ll ever see have had their turn and had to take another run at it on play-calling,” Jones said. “You can (have) a little bit on a seasoned coach of, when you’re hot, you’re hot, when you’re not, you’re not. It’s pretty hard to get specific as to when someone’s doing it right and when they’re not. We’ve got to address it, and we are addressing it.”

Parker was criticized over San Francisco's clinching touchdown for having 37-year-old edge rusher Von Miller trying to cover McCaffrey, who ran untouched most of the 66 yards for the score. Schottenheimer said Parker wanted that call back, but Miller showed support for his defensive coordinator in the locker room Monday.

“That had nothing to do with Christian Parker,” Miller said, adding he still believes he's one of the NFL's best edge rushers in pass coverage. “I had been coached on how to play that route. I’ve had examples of that route, went over that play in practice. I was more than prepared, but for some reason I didn’t make the play.”

summary: Miro Heiskanen scored from the left circle at 3:36 of overtime to cap a furious comeback by the Dallas Stars, who rallied from two goals down late in regulation and stunned the Vegas Golden Knights 4-3
story: Miro Heiskanen scored from the left circle at 3:36 of overtime to cap a furious comeback by the Dallas Stars, who rallied from two goals down late in regulation and stunned the Vegas Golden Knights 4-3

LAS VEGAS -- Miro Heiskanen scored from the left circle at 3:36 of overtime to cap a furious comeback by the Dallas Stars, who rallied from two goals down late in regulation and stunned the Vegas Golden Knights 4-3 on Tuesday night.

Wyatt Johnston scored for Dallas with 1:18 left in the third period and Mikko Rantanen with 4.6 seconds remaining — both at 6-on-5 — as the Stars extended their road point streak to seven games (5-0-2).
It was the second head-scratching defeat in a row for the Golden Knights, who lost 6-3 to last-place Vancouver on Sunday.

Rantanen had a goal and three assists, and Nils Lundkvist scored the other Stars goal. Roope Hintz, playing on his 30th birthday, had two assists, as did Jason Robertson. Jake Oettinger stopped 24 shots.

William Karlsson scored twice for the Golden Knights, and Brett Howden had the other Vegas goal. Trevor Connelly posted two assists. Brayden McNabb picked up his 200th career point on a secondary assist in the third period.
Adin Hill took a shutout midway into the third period before the Dallas scoring outburst, finishing with 18 saves.
Mark Stone was left off the scoresheet, leaving him tied with Jonathan Marchessault for the most points in Golden Knights history with 417.
The Golden Knights took a 1-0 lead 40 seconds into the second period when Karlsson scored from the slot.
The game opened up in the third as Karlsson scored with 9:33 left, Lundkvist hit the back of the net just 32 seconds later and Howden got his goal with 7:17 remaining.
That set up one of the wildest finishes early in this NHL season.
The teams play again Thursday night in Las Vegas.

title: Ten-man Portugal wins with a goal from new No. 7 in Nations League and Norway stuns Denmark
summary: Portugal had a goal from its new No. 7 and the grit to hold on with 10 players in a 3-2 win against Wales in the Nations League
story: Portugal had a goal from its new No. 7 and the grit to hold on with 10 players in a 3-2 win against Wales in the Nations League

Portugal had a goal from its new No. 7 and the grit to hold on with 10 players in a 3-2 win against Wales in the Nations League on Tuesday, but it was another shaky display following Cristiano Ronaldo's retirement from the national team.

Erling Haaland scored a last-chance penalty winner as Norway stunned Denmark 3-2 for the last quarterfinal spot. That set off wild celebrations as the Manchester City striker tore off his shirt and rushed toward the fans.

Poor defending and discipline were issues for Portugal, but there were still far more positives than in Saturday's 4-1 loss to Denmark. Portugal finished its Nations League group with five wins from six games in a campaign overshadowed by the absence of Ronaldo.
Tribute banners were again on show among the Portugal fans in Cardiff, nearly two months after Ronaldo's last game for Portugal, a 1-0 win over Wales in September.

Ronaldo fell out with coach Jorge Jesus when he was an unused substitute for the following game against Norway, and then walked out on the squad. He declared his retirement from the national team Nov. 5.

Bruno Fernandes gave Portugal the lead when he curled the ball into the top corner but it lasted just two minutes before David Brooks leveled for Wales. When Sorba Thomas put Wales ahead on a rapid counter just before halftime, it was Portugal's turn for a quickfire equalizer from Pedro Neto.
Wearing the No. 7 shirt that was for so long Ronaldo's — with a line across the number to honor Ronaldo — Carlos Forbs scored the winner in the 70th with smart movement to set up a low shot.
The 22-year-old winger is a very different player to “CR7,” not least because he's still making his name in the Belgian league with Brugge and all his three Portugal games have been off the bench.
It looked like Portugal might give the lead away again after Chelsea winger Neto was sent off for two reckless tackles in as many minutes, but Wales struggled to create many chances after that.
Denmark needed a draw against Norway to keep hold of second place and a quarterfinal place, but Haaland had other plans.
Denmark raced into an early 2-0 lead, cut by Haaland to 2-1 just before halftime. Martin Odegaard leveled the score in the 84th to ensure a nervous finish.

There was more drama at the very end with a penalty for handball against Danish defender Joachim Andersen and a lengthy video review ended with Haaland sending the goalkeeper the wrong way from the spot in the 96th minute to push Norway into second above the Danes and into the quarterfinals.
It was his 68th goal in 61 games for Norway and his 25th in the Nations League, where he is by far the competition's highest-ever scorer.
Portugal tops the group and will be one of the four seeded teams in Friday's draw along with France, Germany and England. The non-seeded teams are Norway, Belgium, the Netherlands and Spain.
The quarterfinals are played over two legs in March, with the winners heading to a final four tournament in June.

title: Several teams without a Super Bowl win are positioned for a title run, led by the Bills and Jaguars
summary: Several NFL teams that have never won a Super Bowl are in strong positions to change that this season
story: Several NFL teams that have never won a Super Bowl are in strong positions to change that this season
The Super Bowl title drought club might be shrinking come Valentine's Day.

Several NFL teams that have never lifted a Lombardi Trophy are positioned to make a run at their first Super Bowl title, much like the Milwaukee Brewers recently left the ranks of Major League Baseball teams that hadn't won a World Series championship — and celebrated by doing the Lambeau Leap at a Packers game.

The Brew Crew's dominance of Tampa Bay in five games left four MLB teams that have never won it all — the Rays, Padres, Rockies and Mariners, with Seattle being the only team that hasn't reached a World Series.
There are a dozen NFL teams that haven't won the Super Bowl, including four that have never reached the big game: Cleveland, Detroit, Houston and Jacksonville.

Three of those teams are off to good starts — the Jaguars (7-2), Lions (7-2) and Browns (6-4). So are the Buffalo Bills (8-1) — who famously lost four consecutive Super Bowls in the 1990s — and Cincinnati Bengals (7-2), two other teams that have never had a Super Bowl victory parade.

A snapshot of the NFC playoff picture shows the Lions atop the ultra-competitive NFC North and the Minnesota Vikings — losers of four early Super Bowls — in fifth place with the same 7-2 record. The Carolina Panthers lead the middling NFC South at 4-5.
The Super Bowl is on Feb. 14 at SoFi Stadium in Inglewood, California.

Although no teams have been officially eliminated from playoff contention yet, five teams all but certainly will have to wait for another year to break free from the Super Bowl wannabe's list: the Texans (3-6), Atlanta Falcons (3-7), Arizona Cardinals (3-7), Tennessee Titans (1-8) and Los Angeles Chargers (1-8).

The Bills' only loss was 29-26 to New England in Week 4. Josh Allen is having another MVP-type season and a defense that surrendered 30 or more points to four teams early on has allowed just 9.3 points per game since their early bye in Week 7.

After hosting the Dolphins next Sunday, the Bills face a tough five-game stretch featuring home games against the Chiefs and Bears and road games at Green Bay and Denver along with a trip to New England that appears a lot less daunting with Drake Maye injured.

Trevor Lawrence and the Jaguars have been on a heater since the bye week last year, which followed a humiliating 35-7 loss to the Rams in Week 7. Since then, they've gone 16-4, and their losses have been by seven and three points to Houston, seven points to Denver and three points to Buffalo in the playoffs.
The schedule favors the Jaguars, who face five teams with losing records at the moment, including their last four: Houston, Dallas, Washington, Indianapolis.
After back-to-back losses to Pittsburgh and Jacksonville, the Bengals have won five straight, bullying their way back into the playoff picture after an extended stay on the outside looking in.
They've averaged 36.2 points during their winning streak and their remaining schedule features just two teams — Cleveland and Kansas City — with winning records.
First-year head coach Todd Monken has led the Browns to their first 4-0 start at home since 1963. After a bye this weekend, they play three in a row at home, against the Raiders, Bengals and Falcons.
That means they'll have a 42-day stretch without a road game by the time they visit the Giants on Dec. 20, their only game left aside from Cincinnati twice against an opponent with a winning record.
The downer of Detroit's big win in Munich was star Aiden Hutchinson injuring his right knee while celebrating a sack of Drake Maye in the Lions' 35-10 rout of New England on Sunday.

The Lions have a brutal upcoming schedule with two games against Chicago and trips to Minnesota and Green Bay to go with a home game against the Giants. Only three of their remaining games are against teams with losing records.

The Vikings looked like frauds in a 23-6 loss to Buffalo with Carson Wentz under center two weeks ago. Enter Kirk Cousins via a trade with Las Vegas for a third-rounder and voila, Minnesota is magic again as evidenced by its 30-10 clobbering of Jordan Love and the Packers at Lambeau Field.

Now for the hard part: they play the 49ers in Mexico City on Sunday and only three of their remaining opponents have losing records. The good news: they get Carolina, Detroit and Chicago at home down the stretch.
Carolina's 4-5 record would be good for last place in three other divisions but fortunately for the Panthers they reside in the awful NFC South, where they're the cream of a bad crop.

Half of their eight remaining games are against winning teams and the opponents that aren't above .500 include banged-up Baltimore and all three of the Panthers' division foes. Win the division crown and they'll host a playoff game against a team with a better record, renewing another round of debate about seeding the playoffs.

title: Eastern Washington beats Utah 71-67 for program's first win against the Big 12

story: Alton Hamilton IV scores 16 of his 24 points in the second half, leading Eastern Washington to a 71-67 victory over Utah on Tuesday

SALT LAKE CITY -- Alton Hamilton IV scored 16 of his 24 points in the second half to lead Eastern Washington to a 71-67 victory over Utah on Tuesday night for the Eagles' first program win against a Big 12 Conference opponent.

Eastern Washington (2-3) built a five-point halftime lead, but Utah opened the second half on a 24-9 run for a 49-38 advantage with 12:13 remaining. The Eagles answered with 14-0 run and led the rest of the way. Emmett Marquardt and reserve Cole Scherer each hit a 3 for the Eagles during the stretch.

Hamilton shot 7 of 14 from the floor, 8 of 10 from the free-throw line and made both 3-point attempts. Jamil Miller scored 16 points and grabbed 10 rebounds for Eastern Washington. Marquardt chipped in with with 13 points and eight rebounds. Scherer scored eight.
Alec Anigbata scored 16 points and grabbed 10 rebounds to lead Utah (3-1). Trey Campbell added 15 points. Jackson Holcombe finished with 13 points, nine rebounds and four assists.
Utah opened the game on a 12-2 run, but Hamilton answered with eight points to help Eastern Washington build a 30-25 halftime lead.

story: Miles Rubin and DeWayne Brown II each scored 14 points and No. 14 Tennessee held No. 2 Michigan State without a field goal for 10 minutes bridging the first and second halves on the way to a 61-46 victory

KNOXVILLE, Tenn. -- Miles Rubin and DeWayne Brown II each scored 14 points and No. 14 Tennessee held No. 2 Michigan State without a field goal for 10 minutes bridging the first and second halves on the way to a 61-46 victory on Tuesday night.

The Volunteers (4-0) held the Spartans (4-1) without a field goal for the last 5:02 of the first half and the first 4:58 of the second. Tennessee opened the second half by scoring 12 straight points, including six by Rubin, and extended its lead to 14 points.
Michigan State hit 1 of 12 shots to open the second half. The Spartans shot 11.5% (3 of 26) in the second half.
Jeremy Fears, Jr. led Michigan State with 16 points, all from the free throw line. Cam Ward added 12 points.
Tennessee went almost seven minutes without a basket in the second half. The Spartans scored eight straight, including four by Fears, during that stretch.

Tennessee held Michigan State without a basket for the last 5:02 of the first half while building a 27-25 edge at the break. The Spartans shot just 25% (6 of 24) in the half. The Vols hit 44% (11 for 25) of their shots and held an 18-14 rebounding edge.
Tennessee trailed by as many as 10 early in the first half and used a late 11-0 run to take the lead.
Michigan State entered the game against Tennessee after setting a program record by making 18 3-point shots last week against Northern Iowa.
The Spartans struggled shooting the entire game against Tennessee.

For the first time this season, Tennessee's crowd embraced the eight new faces that arrived via the transfer portal. Up until this game, the Vols had trouble defending and playing with the toughness it takes to control rebounds.
