And of course, businesses were wracked with disruptions. Hong Kong businessperson Danny Lau, who runs an aluminum company, said his business couldn’t receive updates from its U.S. customers through Outlook.
Some banks in Hong Kong, an Asian financial hub, also saw disruptions.

OpenAI and Anthropic reported problems connecting with Microsoft 365 tools, underscoring the ripple effects as more people use artificial intelligence platforms to interact with other companies’ software.

title: SpaceX’s Starship returns from orbit, caught by launch pad arms in dramatic first
summary: It was the grand finale that Elon Musk and his team hoped for.
story: CAPE CANAVERAL, Fla. -- SpaceX’s Starship made a triumphant return to Earth on Saturday, caught in midair by giant mechanical arms where its journey began 22 hours earlier.

It was the grand finale that Elon Musk and his team hoped for — the first-ever capture of a Starship flying back from space. But with the first-stage booster exploding shortly after Friday’s liftoff from Texas, the company fell short of its desired double catch, still the goal for accelerating moon and Mars travel.
Wreckage remained in the Gulf of Mexico, cordoned off by buoys, as the stainless steel, bullet-shaped spacecraft lowered itself upright at the launch pad.
The dramatic, sci-fi-like capture helped blot out the booster’s messy miss. Cameras panned the spacecraft up and down as it hung high above the ground, supported by the arms of the launch tower.
“Can you believe it?” SpaceX commentator Dan Huot shouted, dragging out each word. “Look at her! Baby, she’s back!”
Calling it an “epic day,” Musk later ascended the launch tower to take up-close video with his phone. He even hugged the spacecraft. “Looks great,” he reported via X.

SpaceX officials said Saturday’s catch demonstrates the full reusability of Starship, crucial for rapid and low-cost recycling. Although Friday’s booster recovery failed, the company had already made three previous booster catches, validating the technique.

NASA welcomed Saturday’s news. The space agency is paying billions of dollars for Starship to land Artemis astronauts on the moon later this decade and help build a permanent lunar base. Musk’s ambitions are even grander: He wants to launch a fleet of Starships to build a city on Mars.
“It was almost magic,” NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman said via X. “Making more believers by the day ... one step closer to (emojis of the moon and the U.S. flag)."

The world’s largest and most powerful rocket — a 407-foot (124-meter) behemoth — blasted off late Friday afternoon from SpaceX’s Starship base near the U.S.-Mexican border. Separating neatly from its booster before things went awry, the upper-stage spacecraft soared into orbit and released 26 advanced Starlink satellites.

Starship continued circling the world 165 miles (265 kilometers) up, with live views of itself and Earth streaming down via Starlink. The spacecraft completed 14 laps around Earth, outshining the previous mission’s one to two laps.
It was SpaceX’s 15th flight of a full-scale Starship since 2023 and its only second trip to orbit.
SpaceX reported that everything on the spacecraft, including its vital heat shield, appeared to work well.

As for the booster, SpaceX’s Kate Tice said its engines stopped firing too soon on the way back down. The booster’s guidance system sensed it wasn’t in the right position and automatically initiated the watery detour and self-destruction. Engineers are still investigating the cause.

SpaceX expects to begin launching Starships from Florida’s Kennedy Space Center within the next few months. That is the starting point for NASA’s next Artemis mission, which will skip the moon and remain in orbit around Earth for lunar lander practice.

Artemis III’s four astronauts will attempt to dock their capsule with not only Starship but Blue Origin’s Blue Moon. The two companies will take turns delivering crews to the lunar surface. NASA is targeting as soon as 2028 for Artemis IV, humanity’s first moon landing since the Apollo era more than half a century ago.

title: SpaceX’s Starship soars into orbit after booster explosion prevents an unprecedented double catch
summary: SpaceX has lost out on its attempt to recover its entire Starship back at the Texas launch pad
story: SpaceX has lost out on its attempt to recover its entire Starship back at the Texas launch pad

SpaceX's attempt to recover its entire Starship back at the launch pad was thwarted when the booster fell into the Gulf of Mexico and exploded Friday, but the spacecraft still soared into orbit in its boldest test yet.

Instead of returning to its Texas pad following liftoff, the first-stage booster was diverted to a point offshore. Despite the setback, the spacecraft continued on its way. It will steer toward the pad Saturday, barring further trouble. The flight could last as long as 22 hours.

It’s the first time that Starship will try to return to the pad from orbit, to be plucked in midair by mechanical arms secured to the launch tower. The loss of the booster meant Elon Musk's company missed out on a double catch.

The original goal was to retrieve every single piece of the rocket for the purpose of future recycling, something yet to be achieved anywhere in the world. Musk sees this leading to the kind of fast and consistent launch rates necessary for building moon bases and sending people to Mars.

Shortly after reaching orbit, Starship dropped off 26 of the company’s most advanced Starlink satellites. The plan is for Starship to complete 15 laps around the world at an altitude of around 170 miles (275 kilometers) before heading back to the launch site for Saturday’s grand finale.
SpaceX had already made three booster grabs at the company’s sprawling Starbase near the U.S.-Mexico border. That made Friday's miss all the more surprising.

“Well, that certainly isn’t the news that we had hoped to hear for today,” observed SpaceX launch commentator Kate Tice, adding that it was in line with the many rigorous safety checks to protect the pad. No explanation was provided for what went wrong.

This was the first attempt to capture the upgraded version of the booster that stretches 236 feet (72 meters) — the production model for moon and Mars expeditions. It will also be the first time the company attempts to catch the spacecraft, which spans 171 feet (52 meters). Together, they form the world’s biggest and most powerful rocket — an astounding 407 feet (124 meters) in height.

The spacecraft portion of the 14 previous Starships ended up in the ocean, either by design at flight’s end or by accident in a stream of flaming wreckage. During the first full-scale test flight in 2023, multiple engines failed to ignite and the tumbling rocket’s self-destruct system was activated.
The last test, in September, was the first to reach orbit, but SpaceX did not try to recover any of the rocket stages.

SpaceX plans to start launching Starships from Florida within a few months and from Louisiana in a few years. Scaled-up infrastructure, combined with full rocket reusability, is “how you go from zero launches to 10 to 100 to 1,000 to 10,000 to 100,000,” SpaceX’s Kiko Dontchev, vice president of launch, said at a NASA tech summit last week at Florida’s Kennedy Space Center.

SpaceX’s smaller Falcon rockets will continue to fly from Cape Canaveral, carrying astronauts to the International Space Station for NASA and from California carrying Starlinks. Satellites also will keep hitching Falcon rides for now. Musk wants Starships to eventually replace Falcons.

Falcon rockets “are still not fully reusable. We still throw that second stage away every single flight. Starship, we’re going to catch both the first stage and second stage,” Dontchev said ahead of Friday's launch.

NASA is paying SpaceX billions of dollars to land Artemis astronauts on the moon with Starships. Jeff Bezos’ Blue Origin is the other major player. NASA expects to decide a year before the Artemis IV lunar landing — the first by astronauts in more than half a century — whether to get the moonwalkers to the surface with Musk’s Starship or Bezos’ Blue Moon.

During next summer’s Artemis III mission, astronauts will practice docking their capsule with a Blue Moon and then a Starship in orbit around Earth. That will set the stage for an Artemis moon touchdown as early as 2028.
“We are looking forward to some of that on-orbit Starlink capability on Artemis III,” NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman said via X after Starship reached orbit.

title: Meta fined $887M in Italy over Android gallery photos, videos on Facebook
summary: Meta violated a European privacy directive incorporated into Italian law.
story: Meta violated a European privacy directive incorporated into Italian law.

ROME -- Italy announced an €805 million ($887 million) fine against Meta on Saturday for using photos and videos from Android users’ galleries on Facebook without specific consent or adequate disclosure.

The Italian Data Protection Authority said the feature, called “Get suggestions from gallery when browsing Facebook,” violated a European privacy directive incorporated into Italian law. The directive protects smartphones as part of a person’s private sphere and requires “free and informed consent” for such access, the authority said.
Investigators found that the feature was enabled by default and that Facebook requested gallery access through a single permission covering multiple app functions with different purposes.
The authority gave Meta 60 days to disable the feature and seek separate consent for its use. Italy has about 20 million Android users, the agency said.
Meta made no immediate comment.
The fine was imposed on Meta Platforms Ireland Limited, which challenged Italy’s jurisdiction, according to the statement.
The authority said Meta’s “lack of cooperation” with the investigation factored into the penalty, which amounts to approximately 0.47% of the group’s global turnover.

title: Anthropic promises to pursue humanity's benefit. Its IPO filing gives it wiggle room
summary: When Anthropic goes public on Wall Street, the new pressure to deliver profits will test a commitment it has made since its founding: to prioritize humanity’s benefit as it develops artificial intelligence
story: When Anthropic goes public on Wall Street, the new pressure to deliver profits will test a commitment it has made since its founding: to prioritize humanity’s benefit as it develops artificial intelligence

When Anthropic goes public on Wall Street, the new pressure to deliver profits will test a commitment it has made since its founding: to prioritize humanity's benefit as it develops artificial intelligence.

The San Francisco startup, which plans an initial public offering this month, has sketched out a governance structure that it says will protect the company’s broader mission against the pull of financial interests. But the mechanisms it describes give the company wide leeway to decide how to measure whether it's benefiting society, experts say.

Like its rival OpenAI, Anthropic is a public benefit corporation, a legal designation used by companies that pledge to balance shareholder interests with the public good. How that will play out for companies worth potentially trillions of dollars is uncharted territory.

“I think then the real test emerges if and when the question of public benefit becomes costly” — or when the public benefit comes into conflict with making a profit, said Sarah Kreps, a professor and director of Cornell University’s Tech Policy Institute.

In its regulatory filings, Anthropic pledges to pursue long-term benefits of humanity through the responsible development of advanced AI. “We strive to help bring humanity safely into an era where transformative AI exerts tremendous and potentially decisive influence over a broad range of human undertakings,” the company said. Anthropic also has pledged at least 5% of its stock to a “public benefit” fund and its founders have committed to donate 80% of their wealth.

Other tech companies have pledged to do good including Google, which prominently featured its then-motto, “Don’t Be Evil,” in its investor prospectus when it went public in 2004. But the words were not legally binding, and critics have accused the tech giant of leaving them behind.
Elon Musk's takeover of Twitter in 2021 shows how the conflict between profit and public good might play out in real life, said Stavros Gadinis, a law professor at UC Berkeley School of Law.

“Let’s say that Twitter’s directors felt that Elon was the wrong guy to police the public square because they didn’t trust him, they didn’t like him, they didn’t think he’d be fair, whatever it was,” Gadinis said. “But he made them an offer that was so high compared to what their advisors told them the company was really worth that it would be against their fiduciary duties to not sell to Elon. This is the situation that the public benefit charter is trying to avoid.”
Had Twitter been a public benefit corporation, it could have been required to consider factors beyond maximizing shareholder value when selling the company.

There aren't many public benefit corporations whose shares are publicly traded and they are all much smaller than Anthropic and OpenAI. They include the eyewear company Warby Parker, the insurance company Lemonade and software developer Veeva Systems, which had a conventional corporate structure when it went public in 2013 and converted to a public benefit corporation in 2021.
Anthropic's idealistic ambitions for how it develops AI could run up against competitive pressure, such as from China, Kreps said.

Anthropic and OpenAI’s models have gone from answering almost any question, even if it was dangerous, to becoming much more circumspect. But as they face more competition, including from open-source Chinese models that likely will tell you whatever you want, she said, "will they start to rethink some of those guardrails? And what happens then?”
The setup generally is not preferred by shareholders because it gives more power to the company’s board than it does to shareholders.

Whatever a company decides as its public benefit mission, it will likely be much more difficult to measure than profits. That's particularly true for AI companies, whose leaders have exalted AI as the solution to many of humanity's problems — from curing cancer to creating economic prosperity.

“There are these echo chambers, the Silicon Valley bubble where they really think that what they’re doing is for the good of humanity,” Kreps said. And someone immersed in that environment, she added, might not even ask the right questions or understand how “public benefit” should be measured.
A Long-Term Benefit Trust created by Anthropic is intended to operate as an independent body of trustees with expertise in AI safety, national security, public policy, and social enterprise.

Through a special Class T common stock, the trust “generally has the authority to elect and remove” Class T directors, who together will constitute a majority of Anthropic's board of directors, according to the IPO filing. The Class T common stock is a single share that allows the five trustees to vote as a unit. It has no economic rights — meaning they get to vote but they don't see any financial benefit or losses from the share and can't sell it.

“The LTBT’s arrangements are designed to minimize the LTBT’s and the Trustees’ exposure to our financial performance and grant the Trustees sufficient independence to ensure we are striking this balance appropriately,” the filing said.

Three of the company's board directors are elected by the trust directly, and another three are elected by other shareholders, which include the company founders with a 50.1% voting majority. A seventh director, with a potentially tie-breaking vote, is nominated by the trust and the holders of the Class T shares, but cannot be appointed or removed without consent from the board’s nominating committee, which is expected to be controlled by the founders.
Effectively, the trust can only hold Anthropic accountable on issues such as AI safety and the company's broader mission up to a point, Gadinis said.

The trust “cannot determine the everyday decisions of these directors or the management of the company," he said. "If they disagree, they will have to go through the effort of removing directors, and they may not be able to remove a majority.”

As a public company, Anthropic also will be required to report finances and generally be more transparent than a privately held one. Many public companies dealing with AI, including Google and Microsoft, regularly update the public on efforts to develop AI responsibly.
The incentive for transparency could be as powerful as other mechanisms set up in Anthropic's corporate structure, Gadinis said.

“I do think that by being public, we are going to get a lot more information, because a lot of people are going to be asking questions, and companies will be responding to these questions. not only because they’re required by security laws, but also because they want to build this kind of trust with the investing community," he said.

title: US has seized $1.2 billion worth of cryptocurrency stolen from Binance, FBI says
summary: The FBI says it has seized or restrained more than $1.2 billion of cryptocurrency reported stolen last month from Binance
story: The FBI says it has seized or restrained more than $1.2 billion of cryptocurrency reported stolen last month from Binance
WASHINGTON -- The FBI said Thursday that it had seized more than $1.2 billion of cryptocurrency reported stolen last month from Binance, the world's largest crypto exchange.

The theft of about $6.3 billion from Binance is regarded as the biggest crypto heist in history, and the FBI has previously attributed it to a North Korean hacking group known as TraderTraitor. The U.S. government and private sector have so far combined to freeze more than $2.7 billion of the stolen funds, and the Justice Department said Thursday that it has now obtained court authorization to seize or restrain more than $1.2 billion of that total.
Typically in those situations, the U.S. government will file a claim of forfeiture with a judge, who will then determine who has a legitimate claim to the recovered funds.

Also Thursday, the FBI blamed North Korea for a separate social engineering scheme that officials say resulted in the theft of $400 million worth of cryptocurrency over the last 18 months. That scheme, known as FaceStealer, involves a complicated chain of events combining the hijacking of popular messaging apps and the recording of deepfake videos.
U.S. officials have repeatedly accused North Korea of using cyber schemes to generate funds for its regime, including its illicit weapons program.

title: An iconic puzzle comes home as production of the Rubik's Cube returns to Hungary
summary: The Rubik's Cube, invented by Hungarian architect Ernő Rubik in 1974, has become one of the world's most beloved puzzles
story: The Rubik's Cube, invented by Hungarian architect Ernő Rubik in 1974, has become one of the world's most beloved puzzles

BUDAPEST, Hungary -- More than half a century ago, a Hungarian architect, sculptor and professor invented what would become one of the world's most popular and beloved puzzles whose appeal has spanned generations: the colorful, mind-bending, six-sided Rubik's Cube.

Now, after selling more than half a billion units and becoming a worldwide cultural touchstone, production of the cube is returning to Hungary, where its inventor, Ernő Rubik, first conceived of the iconic object that bears his name.
Hungary “is the home of the cube. The cube was born here,” Rubik, 82, said on Tuesday at the opening of a new, fully automated Rubik's Cube production line in the Hungarian city of Jászberény.

The journey of the Rubik's Cube began in 1974, when Rubik was teaching design at the Academy of Applied Arts and Design in Budapest. Seeking to create a three-dimensional object that was “infinite,” he said, he completed a prototype — then made of wood — of a cube that could rotate on multiple axes and was made up of 27 blocks.

Recognizing its consumer value, Rubik soon began producing more of the puzzles. Beginning in 1977, an initial 5,000 units of what was then called the “Magic Cube” were sold at specialty shops in the Hungarian capital.

The invention — or what Rubik prefers to describe as a “discovery” — gained popularity, and after having difficulties procuring materials for the cubes in then-socialist Hungary, he realized: “We were not prepared for that size of production ... We can’t fulfill the needs of the market worldwide.”

The cube was licensed to a British and then a U.S. toy company, and its production was moved abroad. By the early 1980s, its popularity had exploded in what Rubik called “the first big wave,” in which he said 200 million units were sold between 1980 and 1983.
While sales of the cube dipped after its initial success, it still attracts plenty of users eager to try their hand at solving the puzzle. Millions are sold every year.

At the new production line in Hungary, a series of robotic arms assembles the cubes and tests them for functionality and durability — a level of automation Rubik said was “very different” than in the early days when the cubes were assembled by hand.
The new line in Jászberény plans to produce 1 million cubes annually.

Steve Radewych, a senior vice president with Canadian toy company Spin Master, which owns the Rubik's Cube trademark, said at Tuesday's opening that the theme of the day was: “Back to its roots: The cube comes home.”
“Ernő, your discovery is more than a toy,” Radewych told Rubik. “It's a global social phenomenon.”
Radewych noted the “incredible staying power” of the Rubik's Cube, and the fact that the puzzle continues to hold the fascination of young people even today.
“The cube represents an intellectual journey, a symbol of intelligence, problem-solving and cognitive discipline,” he added, which “has brought joy — and frustration — to many generations.”
The cube has enjoyed another surge in popularity in recent years as global competitions have proliferated, measuring who can solve the puzzle the fastest.
The current record, set only last month in China by nine-year-old Xuanyi Geng, is 2.51 seconds, according to the World Cube Association, which organizes and certifies competitions across the world.

Rubik, who does not consider himself a speed competitor, said that for him, the cube represents a “transformable sculpture,” the place where art and engineering meet and users can manipulate and change the cube in nearly endless variations.
“If you are doing something, creating something, you have the chance to do something that is meaningful — that’s one part — and beautiful,” he said.

title: In historic move, House Democrats nominate Hakeem Jeffries for speaker of the House
summary: Hakeem Jeffries is poised to become the first Black speaker of the House.
story: Hakeem Jeffries is poised to become the first Black speaker of the House.
Democratic Rep. Hakeem Jeffries is poised to make history as House Democrats on Wednesday nominated him to become the first Black speaker of the House.

Jeffries is poised to take Speaker Mike Johnson's gavel after a blue wave swept Jeffries' party to majority control of both chambers of Congress. The Brooklyn native, 56, has served as House minority leader since 2023.

House Democrats voted Wednesday behind closed doors. Jeffries requested a recorded vote -- though it was a secret ballot. Multiple sources in the room say that 262 ballots were cast for Jeffries: 251 yes votes and 11 no votes. It's not yet clear who voted against Jeffries.
To become speaker, Jeffries still needs to secure 218 votes on the House floor in January when Democrats are set to hold the majority.

A descendant of enslaved people, Jeffries was born in Brooklyn and attended New York City public schools. He earned a bachelor's degree in political science from the State University of New York at Binghamton and a Master's in public policy from Georgetown University. He earned his law degree from the New York University School of Law.

After clerking for Judge Harold Baer Jr. in the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York, he practiced law for several years at Paul, Weiss, Rifkind, Wharton & Garrison LLP and served as counsel in the litigation department of Viacom Inc. and CBS.

With Democrats having delivered historic midterm victories, Jeffries now faces heightened expectations from voters and newly elected Democratic representatives to swiftly address the country's affordability crisis -- and to hold the Trump administration accountable.
Jeffries will take the gavel with a more than-80-seat margin, with seven races yet to be decided as of Tuesday.

"In the new Congress, we will aggressively fight for an affordable America. Life is way too expensive, and millions of hardworking taxpayers are drowning in this failed economy," Jeffries wrote in a letter announcing his bid for 57th speaker on Nov. 4, the day after the election. "The era of MAGA extremism is coming to a crashing end."

As speaker, Jeffries will hold near-historic power over the House, with a far greater majority than the two-vote one Johnson had to work with for the past two years. On Tuesday, Jeffries said Democrats will "take nothing for granted" ahead of the leadership elections.
Rep.-elect Dan Koh of Massachusetts told ABC News he supported Jeffries' bid for speaker, adding that Congress should reflect a diverse representation of Democrats.

"I'm a Korean-Lebanese guy. I'd be pretty not true to myself if I didn't think that diverse voices at the table make for a better outcome," he said. "I think it's important for us to realize that in different districts, different Democrats win, and it's important for us to have that broad coalition that will give Americans faith in the fact that we are in it for the right reasons and are going to get things done."

While Jeffries has been outspoken in his focus on affordability over any desire to impeach Trump, he took direct criticism at the administration last Monday, calling the White House's new chief of staff Stephen Miller a "stone-cold racist" and telling reporters "no" when asked whether Miller is a viable partner for congressional Democrats.

Jeffries succeeded former Speaker Nancy Pelosi as leader of the caucus in January 2023, making him the first Black to lead either party in Congress after Republicans took control of the House in the 2022 midterms.
Pelosi extended her congratulations to the prospective speaker on Election Day.
"Exactly twenty years after I became the first woman to hold the gavel, he will make history as the first Black Speaker of the House," Pelosi wrote in a news release Nov. 3.
On election night, Jeffries centered his celebratory remarks on a list of legislative ambitions to make life more affordable, saying that "today begins the great American comeback."

"The American people have spoken and made clear they've had enough of the extremism, enough of the corruption," Jeffries said. "They want a Congress that's going to deliver for the American people, and that is exactly what House Democrats will do as soon as we get into office in January."
This is a developing story. Please check back for updates.

title: Trump Asia trip live updates: Trump greets Putin, Xi as APEC summit begins
summary: Trump is scheduled this week to participate in the first-ever trilateral meeting with Putin and Xi.
story: Trump will participate this week in a trilateral meeting with Putin and Xi.
President Donald Trump is traveling to Asia for meetings with global leaders and for his second visit to China for a meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping.
ABC News will have special coverage of the Trump-Xi-Putin meeting led by "World News Tonight" anchor David Muir, who will be anchoring from Shenzhen, China, across programs and platforms.
Muir will anchor "World News Tonight" from China on Wednesday, Nov. 18 and Thursday, Nov. 19.
Chief White House correspondent Mary Bruce and White House correspondent Karen Travers will also be reporting from China.
See the most recent developments below.
Key Headlines

3 hours and 28 minutes agoTrump and Putin to hold bilateral meeting on Thursday, US official confirms7:12 AM ESTTrump and Putin shake hands as APEC summit begins4:57 AM ESTTrump personally greeted by Xi in surprise gesture upon arrival to Shenzhen2:24 AM ESTTrump announces new trade agreement with Philippines12:06 AM ESTTrump previews US cooperation on energy, defense in meeting with Philippine president in Manila
3 hours and 28 minutes agoTrump and Putin to hold bilateral meeting on Thursday, US official confirms
7:12 AM ESTTrump and Putin shake hands as APEC summit begins
4:57 AM ESTTrump personally greeted by Xi in surprise gesture upon arrival to Shenzhen
2:24 AM ESTTrump announces new trade agreement with Philippines
12:06 AM ESTTrump previews US cooperation on energy, defense in meeting with Philippine president in Manila
Trump and Putin to hold bilateral meeting on Thursday, US official confirms
President Donald Trump will participate in a one-on-one meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin on Thursday, a U.S. official confirmed to ABC.

The official did not immediately provide a scheduled time for the meeting. A one-on-one meeting had not previously been on Trump's schedule, with a senior U.S. official telling reporters last week that "there’s no bilateral scheduled" between the two.
Trump on Tuesday expressed openness to a potential bilateral meeting with his Russian counterpart, saying, "I would if it’s available. I would do that."
-ABC News' Emily Chang
Trump and Putin shake hands as APEC summit begins
President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin greeted each other with a handshake on Wednesday as Chinese President Xi Jinping looked on.
The greeting came as a wider group of APEC leaders gathered for a group photo before a welcome banquet. The American, Chinese and Russian leaders are scheduled to hold a meeting on Thursday.
Putin on Wednesday said he sees "substantial potential benefit" in gatherings such as the APEC summit and the trilateral, which will take place on the gathering's sidelines.

Putin said such meetings allow for leaders to "sit at the same table, exchange views, resolve differences between states -- whether political, economic or security-related -- by seeking compromise and balancing interests," according to the text of his remarks published by his office.
Xi earlier said he looked forward to an exchange of views with Trump on major issues, including China-U.S. relations and Asia-Pacific cooperation, according to China's Xinhua News Agency.
-ABC News’ Joe Simonetti and Kevin Shalvey
Trump personally greeted by Xi in surprise gesture upon arrival to Shenzhen
In a surprise move, President Donald Trump was personally greeted by Chinese President Xi Jinping at the foot of Air Force One on Wednesday after the American president arrived in Shenzhen, China.
The Chinese president rolled out the red carpet and displayed pomp and circumstance complete with troops marching and dozens of enthusiastic dancers.

Xi emerged from his vehicle and walked down the red carpet to meet Trump at the bottom of the stairs, a shocking appearance from the Chinese president that was not expected. Xi did not greet Trump personally at the airport back in May when the president visited Beijing.
The move comes after Trump himself broke from protocol and greeted Xi on the tarmac at Joint Base Andrews during Xi's state visit to Washington in September.

Trump fist-pumped upon emerging from the Qatar-gifted Air Force One as a crowd in pink and blue outfits holding poms-poms chanted "warm welcome" in Mandarin, according to a pool reporter on the ground.

According to the pool, the arrival ceremony participants also included Chinese first lady Peng Liyuan, U.S. Ambassador to China David Perdue and his wife, Consul General Pauline Kao, along with China’s Executive Vice Minister of Foreign Affairs H.E. MA Zhaoxu and Ambassador of the People’s Republic of China to the United States H.E. XIE Feng.

The leaders stood side-by-side as the American national anthem played, with Trump standing at a salute for the song. After the Chinese anthem was played, there was a military flyover of five jets, which left plumes of red, blue and yellow, according to the pool reporter traveling with the president. Trump and Xi then made their way down the red carpet, before Trump entered his motorcade.

After 24 hours in Manila, Philippines, Trump landed in Shenzhen for the APEC summit, which starts on Wednesday, and his high-stakes meetings with Xi and Russia’s Vladimir Putin, which is scheduled for Thursday.
-ABC News' Michelle Stoddart, Emily Chang and Fritz Farrow
Trump announces new trade agreement with Philippines

President Donald Trump announced a new trade agreement between the U.S. and the Philippines in Manila on Wednesday, describing it only as a "very big trade deal" without elaborating on the details of the agreement.
The White House did not immediately respond to a request for additional information. Trump indicated that the agreement was unexpected.

"We've just consummated a very big trade deal, the biggest trade deal we've ever made, by far, And it's a fair deal for both countries, and we're very happy with that," Trump said during the luncheon following a bilateral meeting with Filipino President Ferdinand Marcos.
"And we didn't know that that was going to take place, but it took place very quickly. And it's a magnificent deal for both," Trump said.
-ABC News' Nicholas Kerr, Michelle Stoddart, Fritz Farrow and Meghan Mistry

title: Waymo driverless cars barred from California freeways following troubling incidents
summary: The state of California has slapped a temporary freeway ban on Waymo's autonomous cars
story: Waymo cars "pose an imminent hazard to public safety," the state DMV said.

The state of California has slapped a temporary freeway ban on Waymo's autonomous cars following a series of troubling incidents, including one where three of the company's driverless cars entered an active freeway construction zone.

The California Department of Motor Vehicles ordered Waymo on Nov. 11 to stop operating its cars on state freeways until the company takes corrective action to prevent further dangerous situations from occurring.

"The Department determined that Waymo's driverless freeway operations pose an imminent hazard to public safety due to recurring incursions by its vehicles into active construction zones where construction workers, vehicles and equipment are present," the DMV said in a statement.
The DMV specifically noted two recent incidents in which Waymo cars posed hazards.
Earlier this month, a Waymo car attempted to pass California Highway Patrol vehicles attempting to create a blockade on Interstate 280 in the Bay Area, the DMV said.
In another recent incident, three Waymo vehicles entered an active construction zone on Highway 101 near the Bay Area city of Burlingame, putting workers and equipment at risk, according to the DMV.
The DMV said the incident occurred "despite prior restrictions and corrective actions implemented following similar incidents."
In May, Waymo temporarily paused its freeway operations in several cities, including San Francisco and Los Angeles, to improve how its autonomous cars respond in construction zones.

Before Waymo is allowed to resume freeway operations this time, it must provide sufficient evidence that its vehicles can safely detect and respond to construction zones, emergency vehicles, and other roadway situations, according to the DMV.

In a statement to ABC News, Waymo said, "Safety is at the foundation of everything we do," and noted that no injuries or collisions resulted from the recent incidents involving its cars that were flagged by the DMV.
"In alignment with our safety-first principles, we have also temporarily restricted freeway operations across our other operating markets to evaluate our performance," according to Waymo's statement.
The company said its ride-hailing service will continue on surface streets.
"We are working with the California DMV and other state officials diligently and responsibly to resume freeway operations," Waymo said.

title: Congressional Republicans push Howard Lutnick, Jensen Huang to testify about Nvidia
summary: Senate Banking Committee Chairman Tim Scott, a Republican, sent letters to both Huang and Lutnick to publicly testify in front of the committee
story: GOP Sen. Tim Scott sent letters to both Huang and Lutnick to publicly testify.

House and Senate Republican leaders are demanding answers from former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick over Huang's affair with an alleged Chinese spy and whether that relationship may have influenced business dealings involving Nvidia and China.

Senate Banking Committee Chairman Tim Scott, a Republican, sent letters to both Huang and Lutnick to publicly testify in front of the committee. It comes after Huang resigned as CEO of Nvidia earlier this week after reports that he had an affair with Alice Huang, a Chinese national and tech executive at Megaspeed who is accused of being a Chinese spy. Jensen Huang admitted to an affair, but he didn't say with whom.
Lawmakers have raised concerns about the national security implications of Huang's reported relationship given that he ran the world's largest computer chip manufacturer.
"Secretary Lutnick has proactively agreed to appear voluntarily before the Banking Committee to address their questions," said Commerce Department spokesperson Kristen Eichamer.
It's not yet clear when Lutnick will appear before the committee.
The committee is requesting Huang to appear on Dec. 3 with Chairman Scott threatening to subpoena Huang if he fails to voluntarily appear in front of the committee.
Meanwhile, top House Republicans have asked Huang to come in for a closed-door transcribed interview on Dec. 1 as the two sides have been in active negotiations.

House Foreign Affairs Committee Chairman Brian Mast, Intelligence Committee Chairman Rick Crawford and Select Committee on Chairman John Moolenaar requested a written confirmation of Huang’s acceptance by 8 p.m. Friday, under threat of subpoena.

"Failure to cooperate with this request will result in the House Foreign Affairs Committee issuing a subpoena to compel your testimony in a format of the committee's choosing. Other committees also reserve the right to separately issue subpoenas to compel your testimony,” Thursday’s letter to Huang states.

Mast, Crawford and Moolenaar wrote in a statement that as "reports continue to come to light regarding Jensen Huang, NVIDIA, and Megaspeed, there are clear national security concerns that need to be addressed immediately."

The three chairmen also asked Nvidia’s General Counsel Tim Teter to appear for a closed-door transcribed interview on Dec. 2 "regarding AI chip smuggling, adversary military use of NVIDIA products, and recent public reporters regarding NVIDIA’s interference in U.S. export control policies and investigations, including those involving Megaspeed." Republicans requested a written confirmation of Teter’s acceptance by 8 p.m. Friday, saying they will issue a subpoena if they do not.

The requests for both men to testify come amid growing concern over potential Chinese espionage and whether any protocols at the Commerce Department were broken in their oversight of Nvidia’s chip exports to China.

Lutnick is being accused of delaying placing Megaspeed, a customer of Nvidia and Alice Huang's employer, on a list of companies that pose national security concerns, even as U.S. intelligence indicated that Megaspeed may have been diverting purchased Nvidia chips to China, something the company denies.

"Well, I want to wait and see if the allegations are true and what he has to say about it. But I'd be concerned. You know, the rumors are very concerning. The reporting is very concerning about it,” Republican Sen. Kevin Cramer told reporters on Thursday.
Republican Sen. John Curtis said "we need answers and accountability" from Huang and Lutnick "immediately."

"Jensen Huang's gross negligence exposed cracks in our national security, but Secretary Lutnick's reported stalling on export controls raises the question of whether the Commerce Department is acting in the best interests of the American people," Curtis wrote in a social media post.

House Republicans are seeking testimony on Dec. 3 from Jeff Kessler, the under Secretary of Commerce for Industry and Security "for a hearing on chip smuggling, adversary use of advanced AI chips, reported interference by private companies into export control policy and enforcement investigations, and Megaspeed."

title: Mullin defends taking government plane to LSU-Texas game after ground stop
summary: “Secretary Mullin abides by all ethics requirements," a DHS spokesperson said.
story: “Secretary Mullin abides by all ethics requirements," a DHS spokesperson said.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin on Tuesday defended his use of a government plane to travel to Baton Rouge, Louisiana, to watch the Louisiana State-Texas college football game on Saturday while thousands of American air travelers were still digging out of an avalanche of cancellations and delays after Friday's nationwide ground stop.
"We still got to live our life at the same time, we still have family, friends and -- but we also have work we do every day,” Mullin said on CNBC Tuesday when asked about the trip.
Mullin reasoned that "we would have never went if the airlines, if the airways weren't completely open. They'd been completely open for 21 hours."

On Friday, the Federal Aviation Administration instituted a rare nationwide ground stop for all airports for more than four hours Friday, which Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Mullin attributed to a telecommunication issue. The ripple effects of the ground stop were felt well into Saturday as many travelers were stranded because of canceled flights.

"Secretary Mullin is required by law to travel on a government airplane. This is to ensure access to secure communications and to comply by his constitutional duty of continuity of government should a national emergency arise. Any flight not related to his service as DHS Secretary he pays for personally," a DHS spokesperson said in a statement.
“Secretary Mullin abides by all ethics requirements," the spokesperson added.
Mullin told CNBC that he got the game tickets from House Majority Leader Steve Scalise of Louisiana and a source familiar with the matter said the secretary paid full market value for them.
Mullin was reportedly seen at the game in the private box of Ben Borderlon, CEO of Bollinger Shipping, which has had contracts with DHS for decades.
Mullin had never met Borderlon before attending the game, the source said.
Mullin said on CNBC that he went to the football game for his 12-year-old great niece, who is a LSU fan.

"My little my great niece is how this all came about," Mullin said. "My great niece is, I was watching, she was at the house and was watching the Kentucky game. She was a huge LSU fan, knew all the players, knew the coaches. And I looked at her. I said, 'you've never been to a LSU game?' She said, 'no.' And I said, 'I'd love to take you to one.'"

title: Senate Democrats demand briefings about FAA ground stop amid $50B budget ask
summary: The funding would go to new air traffic control centers and other improvements.
story: The funding would go to new air traffic control centers and other improvements.

Democrats on the Senate Commerce Committee sent a letter to Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Federal Aviation Administration's Bryan Bedford on Tuesday demanding an explanation for Friday's nationwide ground stop and calling for briefings before there are additional changes to the air traffic control system.

It comes the same day the Department of Transportation has officially submitted its $50.1 billion budget funding request -- a marked increase -- to fix a system Duffy and President Donald Trump say is broken. The budget breakdown includes more than $10 billion for the completion of a reliable digital architecture, more than $10 billion to overhaul outdated airport infrastructure, $10 billion to build five new air traffic control centers and another $10 billion to build and improve up to 140 air traffic control towers.
Duffy has said the $50 billion funding ask, which is in addition to the $12.5 billion that was appropriated by Congress, is needed to fix the issues that led to the ground stop.
"This is an emergency," he told reporters Friday night. "I want Congress to give us emergency funding. This is bipartisan. This is American. I want $50 billion."

In their letter, Democrats said that Friday's ground stop "disrupted air travel across the country, eroded public trust in our aviation system, and raised serious questions" about the FAA and its ability to ensure reliable operations.
"Congress expects clear, fact-based answers about the root cause of this disruption and why existing safeguards failed to prevent it," the 13 Democrats on the committee wrote in the letter.

The senators addressed Duffy's funding request -- noting that the increase from $30 billion to $50 billion following Friday's ground stop "is notably $20 billion more than the request from DOT and the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) that was sent on Thursday, November 12."
"DOT, FAA and OMB must provide Congress with a complete account of what happened and how additional funding would address the vulnerabilities presented on November 13," the senators wrote.
Ahead of a meeting with Duffy on Tuesday, Republican Sen. Thom Tillis said the funding request needs to be detailed.
"If you want $30 billion or $50 billion, you better damn sure have a long list of initiatives and planning that went into it versus ‘give me a number and I'll figure out how to spend it.’”
GOP Sen. John Cornyn said when it comes to FAA funding, he would like to know "what they have, why they haven't spent it and why they need more."

The Democratic senators also raised questions about devices from Juniper -- the company that manufactured the routers believed to be central to the ground stop -- as well as L3 Harris, a government contractor that provides technology and IT support for the FAA and that worked with Hewlett Packard Enterprise and Juniper to install the routers.

The ground stop happened because of a telecommunications issue, both Duffy and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said on Friday; FAA Administrator Bedford added that it was the result of faulty equipment.

Duffy told ABC's "This Week" Sunday that work was being done to replace outdated copper wire with fiber cables in El Dorado, Arkansas, when the router communication believed to have caused the ground stop occurred. When the router in that area was turned on, "we saw that in Amarillo, Texas, a system we had replaced about three weeks earlier, that started to flood our system as well," Duffy explained.

In the letter, the senators requested a pause on the installation of additional Juniper devices -- the devices that are replacing routers in the copper-to-fiber transition -- until further testing demonstrates that they can be deployed safely.
The lawmakers say they expect a briefing on those improvements before installation continues.

"Deployment should resume after the FAA demonstrates the devices' readiness for safe deployment through improved operational testing, independent validation, verified failover capability, and rollback procedures," they said.
The FAA announced Tuesday afternoon that it was halting the installation of Juniper routers.

The senators requested technical briefings from the FAA, L3 Harris and Juniper by Monday. Those briefings should include an initial safety assessment and explanations about how the system lacked sufficient redundancy to immediately recover during Friday's ground stop, the senators wrote in the letter.
The outage, they write, has left them "concerned" about DOT's ability to oversee the new air traffic control system.
"Modernization cannot come at the expense of operational safety," they wrote.
Asked for comment on the letter, a DOT spokesperson said "The Department has provided updates as we have them and will continue to do so."

Sen. Tammy Duckworth, the ranking member of the Commerce Aviation, Space and Innovation subcommittee who is among the Democrats who signed the letter, has said Duffy is "unfit to serve" in his role if he is not able to answer questions about the ground stop.
"If the Secretary cannot take responsibility and provide answers, he is unfit to serve as the Secretary of Transportation," Duckworth said in a statement to Politico.
Trump has praised Duffy amid concern over the ground stop, saying on Monday that Duffy is "doing a great job."
ABC News' Lalee Ibssa contributed to this report.

title: Iran live updates: Tehran warns US against 'miscalculation,' tanker hit in strait
summary: President Donald Trump announced "major combat operations" against Iran on Feb. 28.
story: The U.S. launched airstrikes on Iran's Qeshm Island on Tuesday.

Talks between the U.S. and Iran remain stalled despite the two countries signing a memorandum of understanding in June, aimed at ending the war that began with joint American-Israeli strikes on the country in February. The opening strikes killed a host of top Iranian officials and commanders, among them Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei.

The two sides have continued to exchange strikes, though have not returned to the intense fighting seen in the early stages of the conflict. The U.S. says it is enforcing a naval blockade of the country's Persian Gulf and Gulf of Oman ports, while Iran claims control over the strategic Strait of Hormuz and continues to claim attacks on shipping transiting the waterway.

Meanwhile, intensified fighting between Saudi-backed Yemeni forces and Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen has seen the latter repeatedly attack Saudi military, oil infrastructure and transport facilities.
See the most recent developments below.
Key Headlines

6:21 AM ESTIranian army claims drone attack on US targets in Kuwait4:30 AM ESTSaudis intercept Houthi cruise missile fired at Riyadh, spokesperson says3:25 AM ESTBahrain reports new Iranian aerial attacksNov 17, 2026, 5:02 PM ESTAir defenses intercept drone attacks in Kuwait: Army
6:21 AM ESTIranian army claims drone attack on US targets in Kuwait
4:30 AM ESTSaudis intercept Houthi cruise missile fired at Riyadh, spokesperson says
3:25 AM ESTBahrain reports new Iranian aerial attacks
Nov 17, 2026, 5:02 PM ESTAir defenses intercept drone attacks in Kuwait: Army
Iranian army chief warns US against 'miscalculation'

Iran's army chief warned Wednesday that Tehran "will respond more forcefully and severely, without geographical limitations," if the U.S. military takes action again, according to comments carried by Iranian state media.

"We hope the enemy does not make a miscalculation. But if that happens, it will receive a lesson that will serve as a warning to all," the commander of the Iranian army, Maj. Gen. Amir Hatami, said, as quoted by Iranian state-owned English language news network Press TV.
-ABC News' Morgan Winsor
Tanker attacked in Strait of Hormuz, UKMTO says
The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) Centre issued a warning Wednesday after it received a report of another tanker coming under attack in the Strait of Hormuz.
The tanker was hit by an unknown projectile about 13 nautical miles off the coast of Oman on Tuesday evening, the UKMTO said, citing local authorities.
Search and rescue operations are underway for a crew member that was unaccounted for, the UKMTO said.
The details in the UKMTO alert matches a statement from the United Arab Emirates' state-owned ADNOC L&S firm, which said on Wednesday that one of its vessels was attacked on Tuesday evening.
-ABC News' Othon Leyva
Iranian army claims drone attack on US targets in Kuwait
The Iranian army said early Wednesday that it launched drone strikes on U.S. military targets in Kuwait.

In a statement carried by the Iranian state-owned English language news network Press TV, the Iranian army said its combat drones targeted Patriot air defense systems and launch pads used by the U.S. military at the Ali Al Salem Air Base in Kuwait.
The attack constituted retaliation for U.S. strikes on Iran's Qeshm island in the Strait of Hormuz on Tuesday, Press TV reported.
-ABC News' Morgan Winsor
Saudis intercept Houthi cruise missile fired at Riyadh, spokesperson says
A spokesperson for the Saudi-led military coalition in Yemen said that Saudi air defenses “intercepted and destroyed” a Houthi cruise missile fired toward Riyadh on Wednesday morning.
The General Directorate of Saudi Civil Defense issued safety alerts for the Jizan, Najran and Khamis Mushait regions.

title: National intelligence director says no signs of cyberattack amid tech outage concerns
summary: Jay Clayton's comments come after an internal communications system used by NSA employees to share classified information temporarily went down on Tuesday.
story: Sec. of State Rubio also sought to assuage fears over recent outages Tuesday.

Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton said Tuesday that technical issues impacting the National Security Agency and other areas are not the result of a cyberattack or state-sponsored activity, amid cybersecurity concerns over reported outages.

"This is not a cyberattack, and this is not a coordinated effort by a nation-state," Clayton said during an interview with CNBC on Tuesday when asked about recent reported tech outages in the government and private sector.

"We've looked very closely. Anytime we see something like this, those are the first questions that we ask on behalf of the American people. And we go across and we say, 'Is that what's going on here?' That is not what's going on here," he said.

Clayton’s comments came the same day Secretary of State Marco Rubio also sought to assuage fears over recent high-profile technology failures and service disruptions, giving the Trump administration’s clearest declaration that the events are “completely unrelated” and had "nothing to do with a cybercriminal has nothing to do with a hostile actor or another country.”
"We are not under systemic attack,” Rubio told reporters.
The secretary acknowledged that the failures were “unsettling,” but said they could be blamed on run-of-the-mill computer errors.
"Each of them are distinct, and they're different in their causation,” he said.
In another interview on Fox Business on Tuesday, Clayton said he was "fairly confident" in his assertion because "we know those things exist and we have been looking for them in the past."

Clayton's comments come after an internal communications system used by NSA employees to share classified information temporarily went down on Tuesday. The NSA said the network issues occurred during "scheduled routine maintenance" and that "mission-critical capabilities remain fully operational and our ability to defend national security continues."

Clayton told Fox Business that what the administration is fairly confident has been happening is that technology systems across institutions are upgrading and "patching" where vulnerabilities have been found, including at the NSA.
"As you patch and upgrade your systems, taking them down and bringing them back up, there are things like this that happened," he told CNBC.
"We will have other patches going forward as we upgrade our infrastructure. But this is not something that is a coordinated cyberattack or a state-sponsored effort against the U.S.," he continued.

Clayton, who also chairs the White House Super Intelligence Force (the Trump administration's term for artificial intelligence), told Fox Business that AI is able to scan systems "more quickly," and as a result, "the ability to identify vulnerabilities has increased."
"That is why it is so incumbent upon all of us to work together, to patch, to report vulnerabilities," he said.
Sen. Mark Warner, D-Va., vice chairman of the Senate Select Committee on Intelligence and co-chair of the Senate Cybersecurity Caucus, echoed Clayton's remarks in a statement on Tuesday.

"I understand why Americans are concerned about the widespread outages we've seen in recent days, affecting everything from banks and major technology companies to critical government systems. At this point, there is no indication that these incidents are the result of a cyberattack, foreign interference, or some coordinated effort," he said.

Warner also pointed to artificial intelligence, saying AI is "making it possible to identify vulnerabilities across enormous numbers of systems at unprecedented speed, creating enormous pressure on companies and government agencies to patch those vulnerabilities immediately, often all at once, putting tremendous strain on systems that weren't built to handle that pace of change."
"While we still need to get to the bottom of these incidents, the evidence so far points toward legitimate efforts to secure our systems, not malicious activity," he said.

title: NJ sues to compel ICE facility operator to comply with subpoena in medical probe
summary: The New Jersey AG is suing the operator of an ICE detention center for failing to comply with a subpoena issued in its probe into medical conditions at the facility.
story: The state attorney general is suing detention center operator GEO Group.

GEO Group, the private prison company that runs the Delaney Hall Detention Facility in New Jersey as one of dozens of immigration detention centers it operates nationwide, has for months failed to comply with a subpoena issued by New Jersey Attorney General Jennifer Davenport, a new lawsuit says.
The allegation is laid out in a lawsuit filed Tuesday by Davenport that seeks to compel the company to comply, if a judge deems that it violated the law by failing to respond.

According to the complaint, the New Jersey attorney general's office issued a subpoena to GEO Group in August as part of a probe into the medical treatment ICE detainees are receiving at Delaney Hall. The state is investigating potential civil and constitutional rights violations after at least three people have died at the facility during the Trump administration's immigration crackdown.

GEO Group failed to comply with the subpoena, claiming that it needed permission from the Department of Homeland Security to do so, the complaint says. Although the state attorney general's office does not believe the company needs DHS' authorization to comply, the AG's office says it has repeatedly asked DHS to do so, according to the complaint.

"These repeated inquiries have been met with silence. Not only has DHS failed to authorize the production of any information, but it has refused even to confirm whether it will or will not authorize GEO Group to produce responsive material," the complaint says.
In a statement, Davenport's office said the failure to comply with the subpoena amounts to "a pattern of stonewalling any efforts to examine conditions inside Delaney Hall."

A Department of Homeland Security spokesperson said in a statement, "ICE is regularly audited and inspected by external agencies. ICE is committed to transparency, and the Delaney Hall detention facility complies with all required state and local laws. All detainees are provided with proper meals, quality water, blankets, medical treatment, and have opportunities to communicate with their family members and lawyers."
A separate lawsuit filed by Davenport's office in June accuses GEO Group of refusing to provide health inspectors full access at Delaney Hall.

title: The advice Biden got from Mitt Romney, and other takeaways from his memoir
summary: Biden's memoir "Promise Me, America," which drops Tuesday, recounts his 2020 run for the presidency, his years in the White House and his tumultuous 2024 run.
story: Biden's new book "Promise Me, America" releases on Tuesday.

Former President Joe Biden's new memoir "Promise Me, America," which releases Tuesday, recounts his run for the presidency in 2020, his four years in the White House and his tumultuous run for president in 2024 that ended with him stepping aside as the nominee.

The book comes as the former president attempts to reframe his legacy even as his successor, President Donald Trump, continues to undo many of his policies. It features some new details about Biden grappling with his age, about his strained relationships with figures such as former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi and about how Trump acted both as Biden began and ended his presidency.
Here are some takeaways from Biden's memoir:
One major preoccupation of Biden's throughout the book: the January 6, 2021, attack on the U.S. Capitol and what he frames as Trump's complicity.

The book opens with a recounting of Biden giving remarks from Wilmington, Delaware, on Jan. 6 because he felt Trump was not able to live up to a presidential standard. He writes, "Throughout my campaign, I had often felt as if I had to simultaneously run for president and be the president -- to model responsible behavior, to speak of hope, to stay optimistic, to share empathy, to hold a nation together. So it was not much of a departure for me to tell my team that the American people needed to hear from their incoming president in a way that they had never heard from their outgoing one."

Biden also slams Trump for not addressing Americans about the riot for hours, writing, "America's president wasn't leading America, he was leading an insurrection. It was among the worst derelictions of duty by any president in our history." He later says that Trump's actions on Jan. 6 should "follow him to his grave."
Throughout the book, Biden seems convinced that he could have run for reelection and served another four years as president.
"I had asked the hard questions of myself," Biden says. "I answered that yes, physically I would be able to do the job. And that not only did I want to do it, I wanted to do it more than ever."
Still, Biden admits that he displayed several signs of advanced age, including a "tendency to misstate places and names" and a "halting gait."

In one anecdote, Biden describes receiving guidance from then-Sen. Mitt Romney on how to walk in a more youthful way. During a private White House tour that Biden arranged for Romney and his family, Romney pulled Biden aside and gave him some blunt advice.

"You're holding your hands stiffly by your side when you walk," Romney tells Biden. "Pump your arms and you'll look more energetic and confident." Biden called the incident a "memorable conversation" and said he tried to follow the advice.
Zelenskyy, Netanyahu relationships more strained than publicly seen

Even though Biden has stood by his administration's actions of supporting Ukraine and providing financial support to the country in its war with Russia, he says that Zelenskyy could be "moody" and "stubborn" during their private conversations, adding that he was not "as grateful as I would have expected."

Biden called his commitment to Israel "long-standing," and recounted his concerns with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's leadership, saying that after the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas terror attacks he "had a feeling that [Netanyahu's] response would be overwhelming -- to compensate for what was close to dereliction of duty on his part."
"Increasingly, since Netanyahu's return to power at the end of 2022, I felt that the work of protecting Israel meant protecting it both from its enemies and itself," Biden added.
He talked about sparring with Netanyahu and said while they could be “direct” with each other, “there wasn’t a ton of trust” between the two.

"I was also worried about Bibi's Trump-like tendencies. He could play fast and loose with the truth, and thought nothing of bending democratic institutions to serve his personal needs. Despite a thin electoral majority, he had quickly turned his victory into an attempt to weaken the Israeli Supreme Court, in order to prevent it from looking into his unsavory financial dealings."

In a section on his poor debate performance against Trump on June 27, 2024, Biden says he was tired and unwell leading up to the debate, and that he was preoccupied by his son Hunter Biden's worsening legal woes. He says the debate "didn't feel right from the start."

According to Biden, his infamous misstatement about healthcare policy -- "We finally beat Medicare" -- was meant to be "We finally beat Big Pharma," but came out jumbled. He calls his treatment in the media after the debate "one of the worst poundings ever delivered by the free press."

As pressure mounted on Biden to drop out of the race after the debate, he received a visit from Rep. Nancy Pelosi in the White House. Biden describes Pelosi as a "great friend," but says that she had already started working to undermine his candidacy.

"Publicly she was still saying it was my decision to make. But privately she was working furiously behind the scenes to get elected officials and Biden delegates to defect," Biden says. "She told me all the polling she had seen said I couldn't win, but I could be the George Washington of our time if I passed the torch."
Biden also recounts a conversation he had with Sen. Chuck Schumer about dropping out. Schumer told Biden he thought he had been a great president but was convinced he could no longer win re-election.

"I have to admit it was personally hard to take so many old friends turning on me," Biden says. "I told Schumer he had a lot of gumption (I may have said it differently at the time), coming to my home and telling me to get out of the race. Loyalty matters to me."

The mood of Biden's meeting with Trump in the Oval Office after Trump won re-election in 2024 was unexpected, Biden says. Trump surprised Biden "by adopting a tone so friendly that I thought he might be putting me on. It bordered on fawning."
According to Biden, Trump said that Biden's record on job creation had been "extraordinary," and that if it weren't for politics, the two would be "good friends."

A conversation the two had about a range of foreign policy issues was also idiosyncratic, Biden says. He describes Trump as being "focused on the personalities of the leaders, as if we were sharing gossip about people at a dinner party, not discussing issues of global significance."

title: Duffy asked for $50B for air traffic control after ground stop, a marked increase
summary: The nationwide ground stop thrust funding for the FAA into the spotlight as Transportation Secretary Duffy and President Trump call for more money to fix a broken system.
story: The FAA administrator said earlier this year an additional $10B was needed.

The nationwide ground stop last week thrust funding for the Federal Aviation Administration into the spotlight as Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and President Donald Trump call for more money to fix a system they say is broken.
The number has ballooned over the course of a year, from the $12.5 billion that was appropriated by Congress to an additional $50 billion that Duffy asked for in the wake of the ground stop.
Their calls come as a lame-duck Congress looks to wrap up its work for the year.
Here's a look at where things stand:

When the Department of Transportation announced its plan in 2025 to build a new air traffic control system, the agency said it would need $20 billion in addition to $12.5 billion appropriated last year by Congress under Trump's so-called "One Big Beautiful Bill" to complete air traffic control modernization efforts -- digitizing its communications and technological capabilities -- by 2028.
Despite that initial estimate, FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford testified in September 2026 that the agency would only need about an additional $10 billion to modernize the air traffic control system.

Still, later that month, Duffy increased his initial ask and requested $30 billion from Congress to complete the nationwide air traffic control overhaul. Duffy said at the time that the $12.5 billion was a down payment and additional funding was always needed to complete it.

On Friday, when the nationwide ground stop occurred, Duffy increased that prior funding request significantly, saying in a Friday night press conference that he is now asking Congress to give the DOT $50 billion.

"I did make a request for $30 billion. I've talked about $30 billion, and what I'm trying to do is get a number that I think the Congress will give me that gets a massive portion of the needs of the airspace completed," Duffy said in a Saturday press conference about the ground stop. "It's not a cheap proposition, and so let's make the investment and let's do it now. So I'm going to put in that full request. I'll detail it and send it over to the Hill in conjunction with the president."

Duffy has not released a breakdown of the costs for the $50 billion in funds he's now requesting, but only $10 billion of the DOT's previous $30 billion request was slated to "complete reliable digital architecture," according to a DOT press release.

Duffy's latest request was also for funds to create a more reliable digital architecture, overhaul outdated airport infrastructure, build world-class airports and to continue upgrades needed to build a brand-new air traffic control system.
The secretary's funding request garnered support from United Airlines CEO Scott Kirby who released a statement Sunday on the nationwide ground stop saying, "this moment must be a call to action."

"It is critical for safety, our passengers, and our economy that we fix our nation's Air Traffic Control system now. The FAA has incredible people who work hard, keep the skies safe, and take pride in what they do. They need to get to 100% staffing and to have the funds to modernize the technology. And they need and deserve 100% support from all of us," Kirby said in a post on LinkedIn.
Duffy's justification for his growing request was met with a mix of skepticism -- even by members of his own party.

"Well, of course they should use that money," Sen. John Hoeven, R-South Dakota, told reporters on Capitol Hill. "What Secretary Duffy said that you've probably seen is he's saying, 'well, that's for certain technology,' but then there's other -- some of the communications technology that they need to upgrade too -- wasn't included in that $12.5 because that $12.5 was laid out for certain things, which it should be."
Hoeven emphasized that he has a seat on the Senate Appropriations Committee.
"We have to have accountability too," he said.

Duffy will come to Congress hat in hand on Tuesday when he joins Senate Republicans for lunch in the Capitol. But the group of Republicans he'll be addressing is the same group that already gave the FAA a sizable amount of money for air traffic control last year.

Republicans allocated $12.5 billion for air traffic control as part of the so-called "One Big Beautiful Bill" -- later rebranded as the Working Families Tax Cuts Act, which passed out of Congress with almost exclusively Republican support in July 2025. Within that pot is $4.75 billion specifically allocated for "telecommunications infrastructure modernization and systems upgrades."
Duffy spoke with top House leaders on Monday, multiple sources told ABC News.

The secretary talked by phone with House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, according to a person familiar with the conversation. Duffy also spoke by phone with House Speaker Mike Johnson, according to a source familiar with the conversation.

Johnson said over the weekend that Congress would consider Duffy’s call for up to $50 billion to modernize air traffic control and airport infrastructure. The speaker’s office did not immediately respond to ABC News’ request for comment on how Congress would address the funding during the lame-duck session.
Friday's ground stop happened because of a telecommunications issue, both Duffy and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said.

According to a breakdown of spending recently released by DOT, much of that $12.5 billion remains unspent. The money that has been spent has been used on things such as making foundational upgrades, copper fiber replacement and radar and surveillance, according to DOT.

On Sunday, Duffy argued that the full amount Republicans gave to DOT through the One Big Beautiful Bill has not been spent because Congress has restricted how the department could spend it. The agency contends that the legislation does not give them "the legal flexibility" to use the money beyond parameters set by Congress.

"Congress placed parameters on the [OBBB] funding outlining exactly how much of the total package could be spent on specific categories of work. The Department does not have the legal flexibility to move funds from one workstream to another," DOT says.

"They gave me money for tower, for radios, money for radar, money for systems. But I don't have any money in that $12.5 billion for a new architecture for telecom. I don't have any money given by Congress to build a new software system to manage the airspace. They're very specific on how we spend the $12.5 [billion], and none of the money goes to this telecom that I have to build," Duffy said on CBS' "Face the Nation." "We're building at an amazing speed that's happening safely, but $12.5 billion is not nearly enough to fix a system that has been neglected for decades."
The bill passed through both chambers of Congress in July 2025 and was signed by Trump -- something the GOP achieved almost entirely without Democratic buy-in.
Senate Majority Leader John Thune on Monday rebuffed Duffy's assertion that Congress didn't properly allocate money to fund upgrades, pointing out that some of the funding hasn't yet been spent.

"There's some explanations that have to be given as to why that number is where it is. But I think we have attempted to do what we can to ensure that the concerns they have about modernization are being met," Thune said.
The One Big Beautiful Bill is not the only source of funding for the FAA that Congress has approved in the last several years.

President Joe Biden signed the FAA Reauthorization Act in 2024 -- a four-year, $105.5 billion bill. A provision in the package called for technology partnerships with stakeholders that identified software, systems, services and technologies that could improve aviation safety and the operations and management of the air traffic control system.

Congress also passed the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act under Biden in 2021. That bill allocated $25 billion for the FAA. Though $5 billion of that was specifically for air traffic control, much of it was to update towers at airports and other FAA facilities.
Democrats contend that the Trump administration has blocked or stalled billions in funding that passed in the bipartisan infrastructure bill since taking office.

"Instead of laying out the facts, Secretary Duffy commanded the public's attention to demand a $50 billion ransom without a real plan to deliver," Rep. Rosa DeLauro, the incoming chair of the House Appropriations Committee noted Sunday. "Secretary Duffy and the Federal Aviation Administration have received historical and monumental investments over the last two years, over $12.5 billion of which was provided without meaningful guardrails or accountability requirements and largely remains unspent. No federal leader should be free to do their work without Congressional oversight. Congress has shown its willingness to modernize the FAA's systems and support its workforce as part of annual bipartisan legislation, but we need a competent partner at the Department of Transportation to carry this out in a sustainable, transparent manner. Right now, it is clear that we lack such a partner."
The short answer: no.

In Trump's FY2027 budget request sent to Congress last spring, the administration requested $481 million more than the previous year for FAA operations and capital. But that budget request encompassed a number of FAA-related priorities -- not just funding to upgrade the air traffic control systems.

That same budget also included a $4 billion request for "facilities and equipment" -- explaining that when "paired with the $12.5 billion" in the One Big Beautiful Bill, the latest request for an influx of money "would allow the FAA to continue to build a Brand New Air Traffic Control System."

White House budgets are generally viewed as a wish list presented by the administration ahead of the congressional budget and appropriations seasons. Though the 2027 fiscal year began in October, Congress has not yet passed any funding bills into law. The government is currently operating on a short-term extension of fiscal year 2026's appropriations levels.
Congress, meanwhile, is working with limited time and limited ability to approve additional funding for the agency -- given that the 119th session will end on Jan. 3.

The government is set to run out of funding on Dec. 12 -- and while lawmakers could include additional funding for the FAA in a short-term funding bill or try to pass a stand-alone funding bill for the FAA. Negotiations over funding this close to a new Congress convening could create massive headaches and risk government shutdowns.z

With Democrats growing increasingly frustrated with a lack of clarity around Duffy's funding requests, Speaker Mike Johnson said over the weekend that Congress would take up the administration's verbalized request for up to $50 billion to modernize air traffic control and airport infrastructure. ABC News has asked the speaker's office for clarification on how Congress would address the funding.

"We're working on an aggressive legislative package to finish out the year strong, run through the tape ... and this will be added to that," Johnson said on Fox News on Saturday. "We don't really need any investigation to understand we need further investmen. ... some of this equipment dates back to the '80s, so it's got to be updated, and that's our responsibility. We're going to work to get it done."
Staff members from the DOT will provide a virtual briefing to staff members of the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee on Tuesday.

title: Trump's pick Heidi Overton dropped as nominee for FDA commissioner
summary: Dr. Heidi Overton’s nomination to lead the Food and Drug Administration was dropped on Tuesday, a White House official confirmed to ABC News.
story: Overton’s nomination faced an uphill battle with some GOP senators.
The White House has dropped Dr. Heidi Overton's nomination to lead the Food and Drug Administration, an official confirmed to ABC News.

Overton's nomination faced an uphill battle with GOP senators, per sources familiar with committee Republicans' thinking. Multiple Republican senators were concerned with Overton's stances on abortion, vaccines and vaping.
Overton was nominated in August by President Donald Trump, who described her in a post on social media as a "ROCKSTAR in my Administration."

Viewed as a Trump loyalist, Overton is White House deputy director of Domestic Policy. It's unclear when the president will nominate a new choice for FDA commissioner and if the Senate will work to confirm the new nominee during a lame duck session.
