title: The Latest: Trump arrives in China, seeking to reinforce US's status as world’s leading tech power
summary: President Donald Trump has landed in China, aiming to reinforce the United States' status as a leading technology power
story: President Donald Trump has landed in China, aiming to reinforce the United States' status as a leading technology power

President Donald Trump landed in China on Wednesday, seeking to reinforce the United States' status as the world’s leading technology power, but a distressing series of technical outages back home has left the administration scrambling to calm the American public. The issues put the administration on the defensive at a moment when the president wants to project strength and certainty ahead of a potentially complicated trilateral meeting with the presidents of China and Russia, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin.

Trump on Wednesday reunited with longtime friend Imelda Marcos, the widow of an ousted dictator and mother of the incumbent Philippine president, who is known for her vast shoe collection. The brief meeting took place in the Philippine capital, Manila, at the Malacañang Presidential Palace, where Trump held a bilateral meeting with President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., who received him with a red-carpet welcome and full military honors, said Philippine Ambassador to Washington Jose Manuel Romualdez.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin is set to appear Wednesday at a congressional hearing about threats facing the U.S. at a time of looming questions over cyber infrastructure, the future of immigration enforcement and his decision to fly to the LSU-Texas college football game as travelers across the country were still stuck at airports after the nationwide grounding of flights.
Here's the latest:

The Trump administration’s director of national intelligence, Jay Clayton, says recent computer systems service disruptions in the government and private sector are “not a coordinated or state-sponsored attack.”
Clayton told the House Homeland Security Committee the outages instead appear to be separate and “associated with maintenance and technical changes.”

The testimony was the latest effort by the Trump administration to offer reassurances after technical outages that have affected everything from Microsoft to the Federal Aviation Administration, the banking industry to United Airlines and a classified internal communications network at the National Security Agency.
Clayton said in interviews Tuesday that the outages appeared to be connected to recent efforts to upgrade systems and patch vulnerabilities.
The Homeland Security Secretary offered a new defense Wednesday for his weekend flight to the LSU-Texas college football game, saying canceling the trip could have sent a confusing message.

Markwayne Mullin, speaking at the House Homeland Security Committee’s worldwide threats hearing, said the trip had been planned for weeks so that he could take his nieces to the game and there was discussion beforehand about whether to forgo it.

“If we canceled something with the airspace completely open, it could bring confusion because I was meeting the governor there. I was meeting other people there that would show maybe distrust that we’re not even willing to fly,” Mullin said.
Mullin said Tuesday and reiterated Wednesday that he is required to fly on government planes and that he personally paid for the trip.

His comments, delivered in a forceful tone, came after Democratic Rep. Bennie Thompson faulted him for the trip while others were stranded because of the nationwide ground stop, which had been lifted before his flight.
Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said that when the FAA ordered the ground stop, the entire cabinet worked together.
“The whole of government went to work — every aspect of it,” he said.
More than 4,000 planes landed safely and the response was a great success, Mullin added.
Mullin said the government was able to get planes back in the air safely within a matter of hours.

The top ranking Democrat on the House Homeland Security Committee criticized Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin for taking a government flight to a college football game shortly after a nationwide ground stop.
Rep. Bennie Thompson, speaking during a committee hearing on worldwide threats, addressed Mullin’s weekend travel at the start of the meeting.

“While Americans were stranded in airports across the country, with many sleeping on the floor at their gates, the secretary boarded a luxury jet, flew to a college football game and visited the private suite of a company that DHS had awarded a $2.2 billion contract for the secretary of Homeland Security,” Thompson said.
Thompson said the Trump administration was failing to take responsibility for that and other recent technological disruptions.
Democrats nominated Hakeem Jeffries on Wednesday to be speaker of the House, as he brushed past skeptics and was on track to make history as the nation’s first Black American with the gavel.
Jeffries, of New York, secured the nod during closed-door voting, ahead of a full House vote when the new Congress convenes in January.

He ran unopposed but faces a restive party eager for a change after voters ousted Republicans in a rebuke of President Donald Trump and the party in power. Jeffries is part of a leadership trio with Rep. Katherine Clark of Massachusetts and Rep. Pete Aguilar of California, who would all be historic firsts — Clark as the first female majority leader and Aguilar as the first Latino to serve as the majority whip. They also ran unopposed.
Jeffries will face a separate roll call of the whole House to become speaker when the new Congress convenes on Jan. 3, 2027.

Rep. Andrew Garbarino, a New York Republican and chairperson of the House Homeland Security Committee, said the panel had made repeated efforts to line up FBI Director Kash Patel’s appearance at Wednesday’s worldwide threats hearing but that he made it clear “he had no intention” of being present.
Garbarino said Patel’s absence marked a significant departure from committee precedent. He said the committee has been clear about its expectation that the FBI director appear in person to testify.
The committee’s top Democrat, Rep. Bennie Thompson, also joined in the criticism.
The FBI sent Deputy Director Christopher Raia in Patel’s place.
Also testifying were Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin and Jay Clayton, the Trump administration’s director of national intelligence.
Sen. Bill Cassidy, who chairs the Senate health committee, said they would not consider Jim O’Neill, the White House’s pick to lead the science organization.

Cassidy said O’Neill “did not do enough to stand up for science” during his time as acting director of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, raising concerns about how he might lead the National Science Foundation.
It’s not yet clear why the vote did not happen. In an email, the White House confirmed it has not pulled O’Neill’s nomination.
O’Neill does not have an advanced science degree or research experience.

Earlier this year, around 50 scientific institutions and groups signed an open letter urging the Senate to hold a confirmation hearing for O’Neill so they could learn more about his vision for NSF prior to a vote.
The science foundation’s staff has been gutted over the past year, and more than $1 billion of its allotted funding sat unused when the fiscal year ended last month.
Democrats are voting in a closed-door meeting nominating Jeffries to become the House speaker when the new Congress convenes.
If nominated by his colleagues, Jeffries would face a vote of the whole House on Jan. 3, 2027.
The New York Times said that Vice President JD Vance has canceled his scheduled Wednesday appearance at the news organization’s DealBook Summit.
Vance’s office declined to directly address his decision to skip the event and instead referred to DealBook’s “tweets on the matter.”
The Times reported Vance has been called to stay in Washington to take part in meetings to address tech outages that have impacted airlines and banks.
Five Democrats essentially representing all corners of the caucus will nominate Hakeem Jeffries for House speaker.
Among them is Rep. James Clyburn, the legendary lawmaker from South Carolina.
Democrats are meeting to elect their leaders for the new Congress in January.
A congressional hearing on worldwide threats is underway in Washington, with Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin set to testify.
The hearing before the House Homeland Security Committee is aimed at assessing threats 25 years after the Sept. 11 attacks.
It also comes amid disruptive technological outages, including a rare nationwide ground stop of flights last week.
Also appearing are FBI deputy director Christopher Raia and Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton.
Mullin, along with Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy, took the lead briefing the public after the outage, which the Trump administration has said likely is not the result of an attack.
Mullin has also been in the news because he took a government flight — which he said he personally paid for — to an LSU-Texas college football match Saturday, hours after the upheaval at airports.
House Democrats are gathering behind closed doors to nominate the House speaker and choose other top leadership positions.

Leader Hakeem Jeffries faces a key test on his path to becoming House speaker, and is expected to easily clear the majority threshold from Democrats during the private caucus election. He and the other top leaders are running unopposed.
In first voting, Rep. Ted Lieu of California has been elected the caucus chairman.
The House elects its speaker when the new Congress convenes on Jan. 3, 2027. Jeffries would make history as the nation’s first Black American to become speaker of the House.

Trump plans to meet separately with Russian President Vladimir Putin on Thursday in China, in addition to his already scheduled three-way meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping, a U.S. official confirmed.
Trump’s meeting with Putin would be the first time the pair have sat down since they met in 2025 in Alaska, conducting talks that failed to broker a deal to ease Russia’s war in Ukraine.

The distressing series of technical outages back home has put the Trump administration on the defensive at a moment when the president wants to project strength and certainty ahead of a potentially complicated trilateral meeting on Thursday with Xi and Putin.
Trump on Wednesday reunited with longtime friend Imelda Marcos, the widow of an ousted dictator and mother of the incumbent Philippine president, who is known for her vast shoe collection.

The brief meeting took place in the Philippine capital, Manila, at the Malacañang presidential palace, where Trump held a bilateral meeting with President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., who received him with a red-carpet welcome and full military honors, Philippine Ambassador to Washington Jose Manuel Romualdez said.

Trump arrived in Manila on Tuesday night to join leaders of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations in their annual summit meetings with major Asian and Western counterparts. In a speech before ASEAN and other Asian leaders over dinner Tuesday, Trump praised Marcos and his parents.
“I just don’t wanna date myself, but I knew your parents very well,” Trump said, addressing the Philippine president. “They were great. I believe in genetics, and they did a good job.”
▶ Read more
Before leaders got into position for the traditional summit family photo, Russian President Vladimir Putin approached President Donald Trump, and they shook hands and exchanged greetings.
Trump had said before departing Washington that he was open to a formal one-on-one meeting with Putin, but it appeared that it might not come to pass while both are in China.
Instead, Trump, Putin and Xi will meet as a group on Thursday on the summit sidelines.
Marcos said he sent Trump a Jollibee delivery so he could have a “taste of Manila” during his short stay in the capital.
Marcos said it was intended as a pick-me-up of sorts for a president who works hard.

“Jollibee … is a very, very popular chain. And one of their main products is fried chicken. And we are very proud to say that we have surpassed KFC in the United States in terms of popularity,” Marcos said at their palace meeting.
“Oh wow,” Trump said upon hearing the claim. “Fantastic.”

“You have been working very hard, Mr. President, so just think of it as providing extra energy for all the work that you have to do that you have done and continue to do, and that is in front of you,” Marcos said.
Trump, who enjoys McDonald’s, didn’t say whether he had tried the chicken. Neither did the White House.
Trump was led by Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. on a rather lengthy red-carpet stroll around the lush grounds of the Malacañang presidential palace after they reviewed the troops.
They stopped at one point to listen as musicians using bamboo instruments played Elvis Presley’s “It’s Now or Never” and a Filipino folk song.
For a few seconds, Trump moved his forearms from side to side in a windshield-wiper-type motion.
Once seated inside the sprawling palace for their meeting, Trump told Marcos their countries’ people have a lot in common and stressed “architectural tastes.”
“I love what you’ve done here,” Trump said, referring to the palace. “You’ve done a fantastic job.”
Trump is a former real estate developer and builder who has been putting those skills to work on numerous renovations at the White House.

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney on Wednesday said that Canada ’s growing trade relations with China are not a top priority for Trump, pointing out that Canada primarily exports commodities to China rather than sensitive technologies such as advanced semiconductors.

“In my conversation with the president, he’s tried to understand where we are with China, where we’re going with China,” said Carney during a news conference in Shenzhen, ahead of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation leaders’ summit. “I shouldn’t speak for him, but in his hierarchy of issues, it’s not the top issue at all.”

Carney’s comments came amid criticism from White House trade adviser Peter Navarro over Canada’s willingness to pursue closer economic relations with Beijing, including potentially bringing Chinese automakers to Canada.

Canada and the U.S. have one of the world’s largest trading relationships, but Trump’s tariffs have strained ties and pushed Ottawa to seek other markets. After negotiations collapsed in August, Washington imposed 50% tariffs on about $20 billion in Canadian goods, prompting retaliation from Ottawa.
▶ Read more

The Asia-Pacific must pursue more open trade and equitable growth if it is to remain stable and dynamic, Chinese President Xi Jinping told business executives gathered Wednesday in the southern Chinese technology and financial hub of Shenzhen, on the sidelines of the annual Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit.

Trump’s “America First” approach of tariff hikes and other moves runs counter to APEC’s aim of eventually forming a Pacific Rim free trade zone. U.S. limits on Chinese access to leading-edge American technology, such as the Nvidia computer chips that help to power artificial intelligence, are a constant source of strain with Beijing.
Xi and other APEC leaders called for a more open approach, without directly criticizing the U.S. shift toward protecting its own markets.
Xi faces pressure at home from slowing growth as retail spending and investment have dragged as China endures a prolonged property market slump.
Still, Trump’s emphasis on friendly relations with Xi may lead to an extension of the trade truce reached last year after a series of tariff escalations.
▶ Read more
Chinese President Xi Jinping welcomed Trump to Shenzhen at an airport, a rare courtesy for Xi that highlights the importance Beijing attaches to its relationship with Washington.
During Xi’s state visit to Washington in September, Trump had also taken the unusual step of greeting Xi on the tarmac.
Chinese official news agency Xinhua reported that Xi recalled Trump’s gesture and said: “China is a nation of etiquette, with a tradition of reciprocating courtesy.”
Xi and Trump greeted each other at the foot of the airplane’s stairs and shared a brief hug as an ensemble of young people chanted, “Welcome! Welcome! Warmly welcome!”
Xi said he looked forward to talking with Trump on major issues concerning China-U.S. relations, Asia-Pacific cooperation and the global landscape to advance “strategic stability,” Xinhua said.

President Donald Trump landed in China on Wednesday, seeking to reinforce the U.S. status as the world’s leading technology power, but a distressing series of technical outages back home has left the administration scrambling to calm the American public.

The issues put the administration on the defensive at a moment when the president wants to project strength and certainty ahead of a potentially complicated trilateral meeting on Thursday with the presidents of China and Russia, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin.

As he began his trip to Asia, Trump initially had been nonchalant about the outages that left people in the United States worried about accessing their email, checking their bank accounts or safely flying on an airplane.

But then the outages involving Microsoft, the Federal Aviation Administration, JPMorgan Chase and the National Security Agency’s communications network began to overshadow Trump’s visit. They raised the specter that artificial intelligence can disrupt daily life, as new cyber vulnerabilities identified require software to be constantly upgraded to fix flaws or other security holes, known as patching, which is supposed to improve how the technology runs.

title: Trump faces GOP pushback to his order to use steam to launch jets from aircraft carriers
summary: Senators are pushing back against President Donald Trump's order to retrofit new aircraft carriers with old steam catapults
story: Senators are pushing back against President Donald Trump's order to retrofit new aircraft carriers with old steam catapults

WASHINGTON -- Senators want to scuttle President Donald Trump's order to retrofit new aircraft carriers with old steam catapults to launch fighter jets, a directive that would cost billions of taxpayer dollars and could even blunt the lethality of America's most advanced warships.

Sen. Roger Wicker, the Mississippi Republican who chairs the Senate Armed Services Committee, put it plainly at a hearing Tuesday: "Returning to steam is a nonstarter, and everybody needs to understand that."

Republicans on the Senate Appropriations Committee also made clear their opposition to Trump’s steam catapult directive in the 2027 defense appropriations bill, which was released Monday. The bill would direct the Navy to provide a report on the effectiveness of the new, magnetically powered catapult system that shoots fighter jets off the deck of carriers versus the old steam-powered one.

“The Committee is concerned that such a major redesign would result in many billions of dollars in additional costs and many years in program schedule delays,” Republican lawmakers wrote in an explanatory statement about Trump's order.

The pushback in the waning days of the Republican-controlled Congress is a notable rebuke to one of Trump's pet issues. He claimed that the magnetic catapults “didn’t work” during remarks in the Oval Office last year, issued the memo in August directing a return to the old steam system and has a long history of railing against the technology.

It comes as the Republican president tries to convince Congress to pass his $1.5 trillion defense budget before the end of the year. Democrats will take control of the House and Senate on Jan. 3, setting the stage for battles over spending in Washington.

In a statement accompanying the defense spending bill, Republicans on the Appropriations Committee targeted Trump's steam catapult order and warned against "such significant programmatic shifts without substantive analysis, justification, and Congressional approval.”

The statement also noted what lawmakers and experts have been saying: The fighting in Iran appeared to show that the new electromagnetic system on the nation's most advanced aircraft carrier, the USS Gerald R. Ford, launched more planes in less time and with fewer sailors than the steam catapults of older carriers.
The new technology also appeared to demonstrate greater “combat lethality than previous generation carriers,” the GOP lawmakers said.

The steam catapult issue came up Tuesday before the Senate Armed Services Committee, which is considering Trump’s nomination of acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao to permanently take the top civilian job.

Under questioning from Sen. Tim Kaine, a Democrat from Virginia, Cao appeared to stand behind Trump's directive, arguing that including the new system, along with electromagnetically driven elevators, was “delaying our carriers by seven years.”
“I’m trying to accelerate that,” he added.

While the new systems experienced development delays during the USS Ford’s construction, Navy leaders have praised their performance and maintenance following the carrier’s recent deployment to the Middle East.

Imposing changes to the Ford-class design appears to continue what the administration’s own assessment found to be one of the issues facing American shipbuilding. Trump’s August memo noted that the Navy’s constant design changes “have resulted in cost growth, delays, and cancellations.”
“The Navy shall not impose iterative design changes upon the original mature parent designs,” the memo declared.

When asked about the pushback to the directive, White House spokesperson Olivia Wales said: “President Trump has revitalized America’s shipbuilding industry, which is essential to the national security and economic prosperity of the United States. President Trump has fixed critical long-term issues in Navy shipbuilding, and will continue to restore American maritime dominance.”

Cao's support for Trump's order seemed in contrast to the acting Navy secretary's arguments earlier in the hearing, when he touted his decision to halt all engineering changes to the Navy's new frigates to keep that program on track.

When asked about the contradicting testimony, Lt. Cmdr. Adagray Willis, a spokeswoman for Cao, said Cao would work with the White House, Pentagon, Congress and the defense industry "to ensure ours remains the fiercest Navy in the world.”

At the hearing, Kaine spoke out against Trump’s steam directive and noted his conversations with sailors on the flight deck of the USS Ford who spoke “very highly” of the new system. Kaine represents the Ford’s homeport of Norfolk as well as the city headquartering the only company building U.S. aircraft carriers, Newport News Shipbuilding.

“I do hope you’ll consider the experience of those who’ve been operating these launches on the Ford before you decide to go down on a path that will be more expensive and less capable,” Kaine told Cao.

Trump's August directive to remove the electromagnetic system and return to steam raised concerns about costs as well as the difficulty of maintaining the older systems, which need more sailors to operate them.
His ire with the new technology goes back to at least 2017 in his first term, when he claimed the new system is “not good” and “doesn’t have the power” of the older, steam systems.
“You’re going to goddamned steam,” Trump said in an interview with Time magazine. The topic has frequently come up since then at rallies and other events.

In April, Cao's predecessor, Secretary John Phelan, announced the Navy was reviewing the design and costs of the Ford-class aircraft carrier and was not ruling out canceling future versions of its design.
The newest Chinese aircraft carriers employ electromagnetic catapults, and France said it plans to use the system on its new carrier.

title: Deep-sea mining auctions spark environmental concerns
summary: The Trump administration has taken a major step forward this year in promoting deep-sea mining by scheduling a series of auctions of the U.S. seafloor
story: The Trump administration has taken a major step forward this year in promoting deep-sea mining by scheduling a series of auctions of the U.S. seafloor

PAGO PAGO, American Samoa -- Sabrina Suluai-Mahuka sat in the shallows at Fatumafuti Beach as her 4-year-old daughter, Erhys, splashed through the clear water on a Little Mermaid kickboard. Below, iridescent blue and rainbow-streaked fish wove through fields of coral.

It was a rare moment of calm before a long journey. Soon, Suluai-Mahuka would travel from American Samoa to California to protest the Trump administration’s efforts to lease areas near her island for deep-sea mining. She planned to pack a bottle of seawater that would give members of the Samoan diaspora a chance to touch and connect with the waters she’s fighting to protect.

The administration has taken a major step forward this year in promoting deep-sea mining by scheduling a series of auctions of the U.S. seafloor. The first waters it is targeting are some of the most pristine areas of the Pacific Ocean near American Samoa and the Northern Mariana Islands, two U.S. territories thousands of miles from where decisions for their islands are being made.

Despite its status as an experimental and controversial industry, deep-sea mining has become a pillar of President Donald Trump’s campaign to expand U.S. control over minerals critical to the technology and defense industries. In April last year, the president directed his administration to expedite the search for those metals on the ocean floor, both within and beyond U.S. borders. Auctions for the seabed near Virginia and Alaska could take place next year, while the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration is reviewing permit applications from companies that seek to mine in international waters.

The minerals companies are after include nickel, cobalt, manganese and copper — useful to making everything from smartphones to electric vehicles — that have concentrated over millions of years along the ocean floor and the volcanic crusts of seamounts. It’s unclear how abundant they are near American Samoa and the Northern Marianas.

In granting a lease, the U.S. would be joining a handful of other countries that have allowed companies to start exploring their waters for deep-sea minerals. Most mining techniques involve deploying underwater vehicles thousands of feet deep to vacuum up rocks and sediment from the ocean floor. Under most proposals, those rocks are filtered and returned to a mining ship, with unwanted debris released back into the ocean.

Suluai-Mahuka and other opponents have tried to stall the auctions of the nearby ocean, rallying public comments criticizing the move. They are prepared to work against the obstacles that come with living in territories dependent on federal aid, where residents have neither a voting representative in Congress nor the right to vote for president.

“When they ask us for public comments, it always feels like we’re just screaming at a moving train,” said David Cabrera, who leads a group seeking to revive Indigenous forms of fishing in Saipan, the main island of the Northern Marianas.

Located in the Pacific Ocean between Hawaii and Australia, American Samoa and the Northern Mariana Islands are two separate chains of volcanic islands that both endured occupations by colonial powers before becoming U.S. territories.

Despite economic challenges and a diaspora that is slowly shrinking their populations of 50,000 people, the territories have kept alive traditions that tie them to the ocean and remain sacred to the Indigenous peoples who first made the region’s islands home.

The U.S. waters surrounding American Samoa include Rose Atoll, an uninhabited island named for the pinkish hue of its coral reefs that is an important habitat for seabirds. The U.S. waters around the Northern Marianas include parts of the Mariana Trench, the deepest place on earth. Both are protected by marine monuments that now border the proposed mining areas.

If a lease is granted, it will be difficult to undo under a different administration, said former Bureau of Ocean Energy Management Director Elizabeth Klein. The government would have to justify the cancellation at a hearing and face potential litigation.

In response to the mounting opposition, the newly formed Marine Minerals Administration has emphasized that the upcoming auctions will only grant companies the right to take initial steps to explore for seafloor minerals. Any testing or commercial mining proposals will go through further public comment and a more intensive environmental review.

“It’s cold comfort,” said Zeno Camacho Deleon Guerrero Jr., a resident of the Northern Mariana Islands and a board member of the Micronesia Climate Change Alliance, a nonprofit focused on protecting the region’s environment and people. “Once you find what you want, you’re going to get it. You’re going to start mining.”
The first auction for deep-sea mining - in waters near American Samoa - was scheduled to take place Thursday in the Southern California city of Thousand Oaks.

Suluai-Mahuka had decided to be in California, despite the long hours it would take to get there. She and her team at Finafinau, the environmental group she founded, were working to bring people from across the Pacific community to protest alongside them.
“If these people are going to be selling our ocean, they’re going to see our faces when they do these bids,” she said.

A legal battle now makes it unclear whether the auction will proceed. On Monday, a judge ruled the government violated the Endangered Species Act by failing to consider the full impacts of a deep-sea mining lease. By Wednesday morning, the Trump administration had yet to delay the auction. Two other lawsuits are pending.

For an opening bid of $3 million, the administration was offering companies the chance to vie for 20-year leases granting them the exclusive right to mine commercially if approved in further environmental reviews. Two areas of the seafloor, each more than 15 million acres in size, were available for bidding.
The administration has proposed another auction for five parcels of the seafloor near the Northern Mariana Islands in December.

Deep-sea mining goes against everything Suluai-Mahuka stands for, she said, and against the Samoan way of life that revolves around the ocean — whether it’s diving among corals, swimming and relaxing, fishing for local delicacies, or the commercial tuna industry that sustains the local economy. All of that, to her, is at risk.
“We would be giving up a piece of ourselves that we cannot get back,” she said. Her group, Finafinau, takes its name from the Samoan word for resilience.
In Samoan legend, the world began as only the heavens and the ocean. “The ocean is life. It’s sacred to us,” said Malouamaua Tuiolosega. “We lose the ocean, we lose life.”

Tuiolosega represents the ancient governing council of Manu’a, a district of American Samoa that makes up the closest inhabited areas to where deep-sea mining leases could be granted, about 100 nautical miles from its shores. Populated by just 800 people across three islands, and isolated by infrequent transportation to the capital city of Pago Pago, Manu’a residents depend even more heavily on the environment for survival.
Since long before American Samoa became part of the United States, the council’s chiefs have overseen the islands’ resources, which they understand are in delicate balance with people.
If more is taken from the islands than is needed to survive, Tuiolosega said, “you violate the relationship and the trust between the people and its resource, and then it disappears.”

He sees the same push toward exploiting the oceans behind deep-sea mining as he does the Trump administration’s efforts to open up marine monuments in the Pacific Ocean to commercial fishing. The governing council, the Faleula o le Manu’atele, has joined one of the lawsuits against the Trump administration over the upcoming lease sale.

“President Trump recognizes the enormous potential of America’s offshore critical minerals to drive technological innovation, economic prosperity, and national security,” Taylor Rogers, a White House spokesperson, said in a statement to The Associated Press.
“A lease sale is not a mandate to mine. Any future extraction would require additional environmental review and regulatory approvals, informed by engagement with local communities,” Rogers said.

Although no company worldwide has started commercial mining operations in the deep sea, a crop of U.S. startups, buoyed by the president’s policies, hopes to soon change that. Some supporters believe deep-sea mining could be an important income stream for American Samoa if it were to become an industry hub.

“If we don’t look for some kind of manufacturing process, something that people will buy, we’re going to be destitute. We’re going to be broke,” said John Wasko, executive director of the American Samoa Economic Development Council, a group promoting industry on the islands.
The deep-sea mining startup Impossible Metals, which has signaled interest in the upcoming auction, has offered to share 1% of any future profits with the American Samoan community.
Suluai-Mahuka and others don’t buy the promises of jobs and investments.

The leases offered by the Marine Minerals Administration will ask companies to “make every reasonable effort” to hire employees from the territories and support “community well-being,” but the regulations don’t include any binding requirements or numeric targets.

There is also no guarantee of economic gains. While the federal government would collect the winning bid amount, along with regular rent payments and royalties over the life of the lease, there are no mandates for the government to share earnings from deep-sea mining with local territories or states. That’s different from offshore oil and gas drilling, where Gulf states receive 37.5% of revenue.

A major question for local government is whether a deep-sea mining lease will hurt American Samoa’s tuna fishery and force the closure of the last remaining cannery. Purse seine and longline fleets supply tuna for the local StarKist plant, with the longline fleet fishing entirely in U.S. waters — including the areas up for leasing.

Nathan Ilaoa, director of the American Samoa Department of Marine and Wildlife Resources, said his agency was hoping for a “more exhaustive” review of the potential impacts to the fishery before the auction. He said he doesn’t yet have answers on whether contaminants or sediment plumes from disrupting the ocean floor will alter the tuna’s migratory patterns.
“We’re extremely concerned that the disappearance of our longline fleet could translate into the cannery leaving American Samoa, which would be an economic disaster for the territory,” Ilaoa said.

American Samoa’s leadership opposed deep-sea mining when word of company interest started reaching its shores. In 2024, the territory issued a moratorium on deep-sea mining in the waters it controls, which extend from shore out to 3 nautical miles (5.5 kms). But the territory has little say over the activities that take place in federal waters beyond that line.

When the auction was proposed last year, American Samoa Gov. Pulaali’i Nikolao Pula, a Republican, wrote to the Bureau of Ocean Energy Management that he and all chambers of local government unanimously opposed deep-sea mining, as did the vast majority of residents. But the governor now welcomes the auction, according to a Monday statement.
“This is a historic moment for American Samoa and for our nation,” he said.

A spokesperson for the Marine Minerals Administration said it has carefully considered feedback from the governor of American Samoa, and will incorporate it into the agency's process “to the maximum extent practicable,” including sharing the locations of deep-sea mining ships, coordinating with fishing vessels, and reviewing any impacts to fish habitat.

The agency said it supports sharing deep-sea mining revenues with territories, and is working with lawmakers and Department of the Interior leadership to support changes that would grant it the authority to do so.
It did not respond to questions about why the auction was arranged to be thousands of miles from American Samoa, or how it factored in local opposition to its policies on deep-sea mining.

Residents of the Northern Mariana Islands are closely watching the events in American Samoa as they brace for a potential auction of the seabed near their islands. The proposal has come at a challenging time for the territory, which was battered by two super typhoons in April and July.

The territory’s government is in fiscal crisis, with Gov. David M. Apatang warning of austerity measures after a five-day shutdown in October. Many public schools suffered broken windows and damaged roofs from the storms, while residents face rising electricity costs from the territory’s sole energy provider.

“It’s very overwhelming for everybody here in this region right now,” said Cabrera, the advocate for traditional fishing. “You just want to worry about keeping your lights on and putting food on the table, so it’s a challenge to get support for anything other than that.”

Born and raised in Saipan, and descended from the Indigenous Carolinian and Chamorro peoples, Cabrera served in the U.S. Navy for seven years and worked in the United States mainland before returning home. He founded his group, Talaya Club, to teach people on the island how to fish with traditional fishing nets known as talayas that are cast out in the ocean surf.

His long-term goal is to help island families become less dependent on imported food through traditional fishing. Sediment plumes from deep-sea mining near the Northern Mariana Islands could endanger that mission, he said.
“That will inevitably impact our fisheries and the health of our fisheries, and thus the health of our people,” Cabrera said.

Residents of Saipan have already waged many fights against the U.S. government. Most recently, islanders objected to U.S. Navy plans to turn the territory’s beloved island of Pagan into a firing range for thousands of troops. The agency formally abandoned those plans in July after more than a decade of community pushback.

When the deep-sea mining auction was proposed, the Northern Marianas government initially reacted with a measured tone. Both Apatang, an independent, and Kimberlyn King-Hinds, the Republican nonvoting congressional delegate, said they neither supported nor opposed deep-sea mining.

But after the federal government doubled the leasing area in March to include waters both east and west of the territory, Apatang opposed the auction, according to Henry Hofschneider, the governor’s chief of staff. The expanded leasing area is just 57 miles from Saipan and 46 miles from the U.S. territory of Guam.

Still, the governor said in a statement to the AP that he has faith in the rule of law and believes federal regulations will protect the marine environment from harm. He has asked the Marine Minerals Administration to consider pausing the auction until the various lawsuits have been heard and decided. In September, King-Hinds introduced a bill in the U.S. House that seeks to distribute 50% of federal deep-sea mining revenues to the nearest territories.
Cecilio Raiukiulipiy worries that deep-sea mining threatens another tradition in the Northern Marianas — navigation by the sea and stars.

Raiukiulipiy was granted the title of navigator in a special ceremony in 2018. Once you accept the title, he said, “it’s your responsibility to keep the knowledge, to pass it on, and to take care of your people, all the people in the islands and also the environment.”

Several times per year, his voyages take him across the Mariana Trench, adjacent to where the Trump administration could green-light seabed mining. On the western side of the trench, he said, the water is colder and the waves churn like a washing machine. It’s an area home to “all kinds of whales,” and where seafood come to spawn, he said. He has seen baby eels swimming north toward the waters of Japan.
“Those are indicators that we are on the right course,” he said. Known as seamarks, or living waypoints, they are derived from a deep-seated knowledge of the seaways in his part of the world.
Raiukiulipiy belongs to one of the groups suing the Trump administration to try to stop the auction off the Northern Marianas next month.

“They don’t understand how we live,” Raiukiulipiy said of the federal government in Washington. “They’re looking at it with a dollar sign. Us, we look at how we’re going to survive, how we are going to live, how we are going to eat.”
Like many around him, the ocean is also sacred to Raiukiulipiy. His community believes their ancestors come from deep in the ocean.
“We usually do our burials in the ocean,” he said. “We bury them back.”
Wieffering reported from Washington, D.C.

title: Ethanol plant trainee charged in connection with bomb at Illinois facility
summary: An Illinois man who worked as a trainee at a Peoria ethanol plant has been charged by a federal grand jury with two felonies related to a bomb that was found at the facility, resulting in a mass evacuation
story: An Illinois man who worked as a trainee at a Peoria ethanol plant has been charged by a federal grand jury with two felonies related to a bomb that was found at the facility, resulting in a mass evacuation

An Illinois man who worked as a trainee at a Peoria ethanol plant was charged Tuesday by a federal grand jury with two felonies related to a bomb that was found at the facility, resulting in a mass evacuation.

Police said they found a bomb on Friday at the BioUrja facility and “rendered it safe” before allowing residents who had been evacuated to return on Saturday. Hundreds of people who live within a 1-mile radius of the industrial site were evacuated.

Andrew Kozak, 41, of Chillicothe, Illinois, was charged by the grand jury in federal court with making threats involving explosives, a felony punishable by 10 to 25 years in prison. He was also charged with making that threat to BioUrja Renewables over email, a felony punishable by five to 10 years in prison.
Kozak has been a trainee at the facility for 10 months, according to his LinkedIn page.
“Learning how to operate an ethanol plant,” Kozak wrote under his job description.
Police said the suspect was arrested at the BioUrja facility on Monday morning. They did not name Kozak at the time of his arrest.
No attorney was listed for Kozak on the federal court website. He was scheduled to make his initial appearance in federal court in Peoria on Tuesday afternoon.
The criminal complaint detailing the charges against Kozak was sealed. The U.S. attorney's office in Peoria did not immediately return a message seeking comment.

Kozak has a criminal record in Nebraska, where prison records show he served two years in prison on burglary charges in three counties. He was released in 2008. Kozak went back to prison in 2013 on a burglary charge in a fourth county and was released in 2014, records show.
The BioUrja plant contains ethanol and “other highly combustible types of chemicals,” Peoria Mayor Rita Ali told WMBD-TV on Friday.

It is not unusual for law enforcement to receive bomb threats and suspicious package calls, but they often don’t result in a credible threat even though such calls are taken seriously by officials who must assess and investigate the claims.
Peoria, with a population of around 110,000, is located about 150 miles (about 240 kilometers) southwest of Chicago. Kozak lives about 15 miles north of Peoria.

title: Trump faces criticism as allies press the White House for answers on tech problems
summary: President Donald Trump faces criticism over service outages affecting travel, banking, and communications
story: President Donald Trump faces criticism over service outages affecting travel, banking, and communications

President Donald Trump faced a groundswell of criticism Tuesday as friends and foes alike said the White House must answer for a cascade of service outages that snarled travel, cut off work, limited bank access and disrupted classified communications.

Even staunch Trump allies accused the administration of lying to Americans or hiding information about the true cause of the disruptions. In recent days, Microsoft, Chase Bank, air traffic control and the National Security Agency have all been affected.

Each outage has been blamed on internal technical problems, with the companies and government agencies involved denying that they were the result of cyberattacks or rogue artificial intelligence systems. Trump was nonchalant after arriving in Asia on Tuesday, declaring that “things like that happen," a response that did little to calm the country.
Karoline Leavitt, Trump’s former press secretary, offered advice for her old colleagues in the administration.

“What I would say to the White House is transparency is key,” Leavitt said on Fox News. She said the president or someone else at the White House should explain what they know after Trump returns from Asia “to really calm the temperature.”

She later praised the White House for having Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton address the outages in an interview on Fox Business Network. “Looking very diligently across the landscape, we are not seeing this as a cyber attack incident,” Clayton said in a clip that Leavitt shared on X. He said the U.S. government believes the incidents are caused by organizations making security upgrades that are taking longer than planned and encountering unexpected hiccups.
Tricia McLaughlin, a former spokesperson for Trump’s Department of Homeland Security, was skeptical about the lack of information coming out of the federal government.
“Americans aren’t stupid," she posted on social media. "We want and deserve to know what’s really going on.”
Meghan McCain, who is sometimes at odds with Trump and his allies, had similar advice.
“Someone high in the administration needs to get on tv and tell the American people NOW what is going on,” McCain wrote on X. “No one who lived through Covid is believing this is all a coincidence.”
The White House did not respond to a request for comment.
Some prominent figures in Trump’s Make America Great Again movement expressed alarm.

“Our leaders are lying to us. This is very clearly a coordinated cyber attack,” Laura Loomer wrote on social media. “President Trump should come back to the United States.” She did not present any evidence of an attack.

The series of outages began on Thursday, when Microsoft's email and other tools went down, paralyzing millions of workers who rely on them. Microsoft traced the issue to “an earlier network capacity upgrade.”
Flights across the country were grounded the next day in the longest so-called ground stop since 9/11. The Federal Aviation Administration blamed a router upgrade.

By Monday, the banks were in the spotlight, as customers reported difficulty accessing online accounts at several major financial institutions and the money transfer service Zelle after a technical issue at JPMorgan Chase caused ripple effects throughout the financial system. Chase said it was caused by “a software bug” and was “not cyber-related.”
The same day, United Airlines said that it had resolved an internal system outage that delayed departing flights.
And on Tuesday, an internal network that the National Security Agency uses to communicate classified information was offline after what the agency described as “routine maintenance.”
Trump was dismissive when asked whether he was concerned about the Chase outage.
“It's life. When you're big and powerful and you have all the money, things like that happen. It's fine,” Trump said in Manila, Philippines, where he began a three-day Asian trip on Tuesday.

Trump's nonchalance was not shared by those already distrustful of the government and big institutions. And for Americans across the political spectrum, the drip-drip-drip of alarming and frustrating outages is an unsettling reminder of perils posed by interconnected tech networks.

“Where is the transparency? Where is the accountability?” conservative commentator Kylie Jane Kremer wrote on X. “And why does it feel like we’re being told everything is fine while the very systems our country depends on are experiencing serious failures?”

title: Mullin defends use of government plane to go to college football game after ground stop
summary: Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin defends using a government plane to attend a college football game after a nationwide ground stop caused travel chaos
story: Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin defends using a government plane to attend a college football game after a nationwide ground stop caused travel chaos

WASHINGTON -- Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin on Tuesday defended his use of a government plane to fly to a college football game the day after a nationwide ground stop which caused massive travel disruptions and left people stranded across the country.
Mullin, speaking on CNBC, acknowledged earlier reporting in the New York Post that he flew to the LSU-Texas college football game a day after all planes were grounded.
Asked whether he is required to fly on government planes and whether he paid for the trip personally, Mullin said yes.
“We would have never went if the airways weren’t completely open,” he said on CNBC. “They’d been completely open for 21 hours.”
He added: “We would have never taken airspace if airspace wasn't open. And we still gotta live our lives at the same time.”
The Department of Homeland Security did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the flight.
The day before his flight, Mullin was at the White House alongside Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy giving updates on the ground stop.
The longest flight stoppage in 25 years lasted more than four hours and ended around 8:15 p.m. ET Friday, allowing some domestic flights to take off from U.S. airports.

President Donald Trump's administration has said last week’s air traffic snarls were caused by a router issue in the aging air traffic control system. Trump on Monday got defensive during a lengthy — sometimes testy — exchange with reporters as he left the White House for his trip to Asia.
He faulted old technology and Democrats for the incident that caused upheaval at the country’s airports — especially his predecessor, President Joe Biden.
“I don’t take any responsibility” for Friday’s ground stop, Trump said,
“What you saw on Friday was very, very old equipment that had a heart attack,” the president said. He later noted: “Incredibly, everybody was safe. Nobody was hurt. No crashes, no nothing.”
Trump was silent on the chaos until Sunday, when he posted on social media blasting his Democratic predecessor and asking Congress for more money to cover the cost of system improvements.

title: Muslims are projected to outnumber Christians by 2035 as the world's largest religion
summary: The Pew Research Center has released new projections that show that Islam will surpass Christianity as the world's largest religion by 2035
story: The Pew Research Center has released new projections that show that Islam will surpass Christianity as the world's largest religion by 2035
NEW YORK -- Islam is expected to surpass Christianity as the world’s largest religion by 2035, according to detailed projections released Wednesday by the Pew Research Center.

Pew, which has been issuing authoritative reports on religious demography for 25 years, said both Islam and Christianity are growing, but Islam is growing much faster. A key reason, Pew said, is that Muslims tend to have more children than other major religious groups.
“It's the babies,” said Pew senior demographer Conrad Hackett, explaining that conversion and other ways of changing religious identity are much smaller factors than fertility rates.

During 2020-2025, the fertility rate for Muslims was 3.1 children per woman, followed by the rate for Christians at 2.5, according to Pew. The average fertility rate for all other women was 1.6, below the level of 2.1 that's considered necessary for each generation to replace itself.

According to Pew's latest estimates, there were 2.27 billion Christians and 2.02 billion Muslims worldwide in 2020. Pew's new projections forecast that there will be 2.57 billion Muslims and 2.52 billion Christians by 2035. By 2070, if recent trends continue, there will be more than 3.6 billion Muslims and just under 3 billion Christians worldwide.

The estimates are part of a broader Pew project examining how the size of major religious groups could change between 2020 and 2070. The projections take into account recent differences between religious groups’ age profiles, fertility rates, and patterns of religious switching and migration.

Among the many notable findings: Pew projects that the United States, within 40 years, will no longer have a Christian majority. Christians now account for 62% of the population, according to Pew, and will fall below 50% by 2065.
In neighboring Canada, Christians are expected to drop below 50% by 2030, Pew said.

In both countries, a significant reason for the drop is the concurrent increase in the number of people with no religious affiliation. By 2070, they are projected to account for 41% of the U.S. population and to outnumber Christians in Canada.

The world’s population is projected to increase by 29% between 2020 and 2070, Pew said. Of the religious groups it analyzed, Muslims and Christians are the only ones expected to keep pace, with Christians growing by 30% and Muslims by 80%.

Although Hindus and Jews are growing in absolute numbers, they are projected to decline as a percentage of the global population, Pew said. It forecasts that Buddhists would shrink both in number and as a portion of the world’s population, in part due to expected declines in the overall populations of China, South Korea and Japan.

Over the coming decades, Pew said, most of the world’s population growth is expected to occur in Africa, particularly south of the Sahara Desert, where most people are Christians or Muslims. The region’s high fertility and rising life expectancy will boost the global numbers of both faiths, Pew predicted.

By 2070, Pew said, more than half of the world’s Christians will live in sub-Saharan Africa, and Congo will surpass the United States as the country with the most Christians, with their ranks increasing threefold to 270 million.
The populations of other major regions are expected to grow more modestly, or even decline.

For example, the number of people living in Europe will shrink by 17% by 2070, Pew said, and the number of Christians there will drop by a third, from 505 million to 324 million. Over the same period, the percentage of Europe's population that is Muslim is expected to increase from 6% to 13%.
In the U.S., Pew projects that the number of Christians will decline from about 217 million in 2020 to about 174 million in 2070.

Several mainline Protestant denominations in the U.S. have faced declining membership over many years. However, Jeffrey Brodd, a religious studies professor at California State-Sacramento, suggested a rebound was possible following congressional election victories this month by several Democrats active in these moderate-to-liberal denominations.

By Pew’s estimates, Muslim women gave birth to more babies than women in any other religion during 2020-2025. About 252 million babies were born to Muslim mothers, compared with 208 million born to Christian mothers.

Muslims are the only major religious group expected to have growing numbers of births in the decades ahead. The other groups are projected either to have steady numbers of births or to experience gradual decline.
If recent trends continue, according to Pew, Pakistan will have the largest Muslim population by 2070, followed by India, Nigeria and Indonesia — which currently has the most Muslims.
Gina Zurlo, a senior researcher at Harvard Divinity School specializing in religious demographics, said Christian-Muslim relations are “extremely important” in light of the evolving trends.

“The ‘clash of civilization’ theory still looms large in some religious communities and there is a lot of misunderstanding of both religions from both sides,” she said via email. “Many Christians are not happy to see that Islam will be the world’s largest religion and it’s causing even more angst.”

“I hope people seek opportunities for greater interreligious education,” she added. “Personal contact is important — when people have personal relationships across religious differences, it ‘humanizes’ the ‘other’ in fruitful ways.”

Alan Cooperman, Pew's director of religion research, noted that most of the projected proliferation of Muslims and Christians was occurring in countries where they already are the majority — with conversion playing only a minor role.

“I don’t think this is a situation in which the growth of Muslims is coming at the expense of Christians,” he added. “I do worry about mischief being made with headlines or narratives that take this finding and portray it as sort of a clash where Christians are losing to Muslims.”
Many countries have seen a steady proliferation of the “nones” — people who are atheist, agnostic or religiously unaffiliated.
Excluding China, which has a high proportion of “nones” but faces a sharp decline in overall population, the ranks of “nones” elsewhere will grow by more than 180 million by 2070, Pew said.

The “nones” already account for a majority of the population in 10 countries, including the Czech Republic, Japan, the Netherlands, New Zealand, Uruguay and Vietnam, according to Pew. South Korea, France and the United Kingdom are forecast to join this group by 2070.

title: Americans will pay more for Thanksgiving dinners this year, Farm Bureau says
summary: Record turkey prices and higher fuel costs could make Thanksgiving dinner more expensive this year, according to a survey released Wednesday
story: Record turkey prices and higher fuel costs could make Thanksgiving dinner more expensive this year, according to a survey released Wednesday
Record turkey prices and higher fuel costs could make Thanksgiving dinner more expensive this year, according to a survey released Wednesday.

The American Farm Bureau Federation said the cost of an average Thanksgiving feast for 10 will rise 6% from last year to $58.63. The group tracks grocery prices using hundreds of volunteers in all 50 states and Puerto Rico.

The Farm Bureau, which has been tracking Thanksgiving costs for 40 years, said it's the first time since 2022 that Americans will see the price of the meal increase. The price hit a high of $64.05 in 2022.
High diesel prices have made it more expensive for farmers to process and transport Thanksgiving staples like milk, dinner rolls, potatoes, frozen peas and cranberries, the Farm Bureau said.

And turkey prices have risen sharply as more Americans seek out protein even as the industry continues to recover from bird flu cases. The U.S. Department of Agriculture has forecast the wholesale price of a whole frozen turkey hen will average $1.76 per pound this year, up 29% from last year.

title: Do school phone bans help students learn? So far, gains are 'modest'
summary: Phone bans have now become common at U.S. schools
story: Phone bans have now become common at U.S. schools
The argument for school cellphone bans is simple: Phones offer endless distraction. Take them away and students can focus on classwork, engage with peers and, ultimately, learn more.
But the reality is more complicated, as emerging research shows. Schools can lock phones away in pouches or banish them to backpacks, but they can’t shut out the digital world.

In the past few years, more than 40 U.S. states have passed laws that restrict cellphones at schools, according to the Phone Free Schools State Report Card, which tracks state phone legislation. But those laws vary widely and often let schools design their own policies, resulting in a patchwork of rules and enforcement across the country.

A large-scale study published Tuesday found strict cellphone restrictions — ones that require students to put phones in locked pouches for the entire school day — result in small academic gains. But, the researchers said, the gains can add up if schools continue banning phones.

The study, led by Harvard’s Center for Education Policy Research, found the schools with strict phone restrictions saw “modest” improvements in academic growth, compared with students in similar schools without those restrictions. The study, which analyzed test scores of 3.3 million students at 4,600 schools nationally, estimates the academic gains were equivalent to about an additional week or two of learning over a school year.

Student achievement has been falling globally since 2013, which is roughly when social media-enabled smartphones took off. The researchers sought to determine if the decline is being reversed now that schools have started taking phones away, said Harvard professor Thomas Kane, one of the study’s authors.

“Our answer is yes, phone bans do have a positive effect on growth. But it’s not a panacea,” Kane said. Learning loss was gradual over a decade, he notes, and it’s not surprising that gains would also be gradual. The study used math and reading test data for grades four through 10 from the past five academic years.

“While schools should not expect large boosts in achievement immediately, storing students' phones seems to be a cost-effective way to add 1-2 weeks of instruction each year, which could add up over time, just as the initial declines did,” the study says.
The boost is equal to about half the annual decline in test scores since smartphones became mainstream, the study said.
Still, the connection between phones and learning is not clear-cut.
A different study published in May concluded strict school phone bans had “close to zero” effect on test scores. It compared schools with bans with tens of thousands of other schools.

The National Bureau of Economic Research study looked at a different set of standardized test scores than Harvard’s study, as well as GPS phone activity, teacher surveys and data from Yondr, the leading provider of lockable phone pouches, at 4,600 schools that use the pouches.

The study had found “modest positive effects” in high school test scores over three years, particularly in math. But the report’s authors, researchers at Stanford, the University of Michigan, Duke and the University of Pennsylvania, were hesitant to conclude overall learning benefits from the bans.

Both studies point to a similar conclusion, said Stanford education economist Thomas Dee, an author of the NBER study. “The early results from school phone bans are largely disappointing and raise unresolved questions,” Dee said.

Noting that the Harvard study showed learning gains may accumulate over time, Dee said: "I hope they're right. However, I’m not comfortable making that extrapolation from estimates that are small, sensitive and based on just a few years of phone bans.”

The reasons, Dee said, could be that students are still distracted on other devices at school. Or, he said, "it may be that we see these disappointing results because out-of-school phone use is harming child development.”

Just because schools or states have phone bans does not mean they’re being enforced, said Jean Twenge, a psychologist at San Diego State University and author of “10 Rules for Raising Kids in a High-Tech World.”

Ask any teacher — or teenager — and they’ll tell you that some phone bans are largely cosmetic. Teens come up with creative workarounds, including stowing burner phones or even phone-shaped rocks in their locked pouches. At schools that rely on students to keep phones in backpacks, adherence to the ban can be spotty.
“It happens pretty often that there’s a policy of no phones during the school day, bell-to-bell, and you go into the school and phones are everywhere,” Twenge said.
Even without phones, "Do they have laptops at school? Are they just doing social media on laptops instead?” Twenge said.
Phone use outside of school affects academics too, Twenge said. “If they have that phone available when they’re studying, how much are they really taking in?”

Kane, of the Harvard study, agrees the effect of cellphone use outside of school is “the big question.” But researchers have not been able to investigate parents and educators’ suspicions that late-night binges on YouTube and other platforms are costly for students.

“I find it astonishing that social media companies know how much time kids spend on their platforms, but that data has never been linked to student outcomes,” Kane said. “We can’t provide answers until the social media companies share data.”

title: Pearl Harbor survivor Gebhard Galle dies at 105, remembered for saving 4 shipmates
summary: Gebhard “Geb” Galle, a Pearl Harbor survivor who saved four shipmates from a sinking vessel in a later battle, has died at 105
story: Gebhard “Geb” Galle, a Pearl Harbor survivor who saved four shipmates from a sinking vessel in a later battle, has died at 105
Gebhard “Geb” Galle, one of the few remaining Pearl Harbor survivors who later saved four shipmates from a sinking vessel in battle, has died.
Galle died Saturday at his home in Moses Lake, Washington. He was 105, according to the Pacific Historic Parks, an organization that helps preserve Pearl Harbor’s history.

“Your humility, quick thinking and selfless actions remain a shining example of Navy valor,” then-Acting Chief of Naval Operations Adm. James Kilby wrote in a letter to Galle for his 104th birthday in 2025.
Galle died the same day as the oldest known Pearl Harbor survivor, Freeman Johnson, of Centerville, Massachusetts, who was 106.
Galle and Johnson were among the estimated 87,000 military personnel on Oahu on Dec. 7, 1941.
The list of surviving veterans from the attack had stood at about a dozen names after the December 2025 death of Ira “Ike” Schab, who was 105.
Galle was born in Germany. He came to North Dakota with his family in 1928 at age 7. He joined the U.S. Navy in 1939 at age 18.
On Dec. 7, 1941, Galle, then 20, was a machinist's mate aboard the USS Nevada, waiting below deck to be taken ashore for church services. He looked out of a porthole and saw planes approaching.
Galle went down to his battle station two decks below in the engineering section.

A torpedo hit the Nevada, allowing water to enter the ship, but officers were able to get it moving, the Navy said. The ship was attacked again, causing more leaks in the hull and fires. The Nevada ran aground.
Galle could not see what was happening.
“Of course, we felt a couple jolts, and that’s when we got hit with the torpedo, and we had a few bomb hits,” he told the Columbia Basin Herald in 2020.
“After we were beached and everything, and we got up to topside, then we saw all the mess that took place,” including the capsized USS Oklahoma and the partially submerged USS Arizona, he said.
“A pretty sad lookout,” Galle said.
Galle was reassigned to the USS Northampton after the Pearl Harbor attack. That ship came under fire on Nov. 30, 1942, by Japanese torpedoes during the Battle of Tassafaronga.

Galle told the Columbia Basin Herald, a newspaper based in Moses Lake, that he was ordered to close the hatch behind four sailors who would've been trapped when the ship was sinking. The officer left, but Galle defied the order, opening the hatch. He closed and secured it after the sailors escaped.
The Northampton sank, and Galle and other sailors spent more than a day adrift in life rafts before they were rescued.

“From the decks of the USS Nevada to the battles of the Pacific aboard the USS Northampton and USS Mobile, your courage under fire and steadfast dedication were extraordinary,” Kilby wrote in his letter to Galle. “You helped save shipmates from a sinking vessel, witnessed the launch of the Doolittle Raid, and fought in 19 of 20 Pacific naval engagements.”

In December 2016, Galle attended a 75th anniversary service at Pearl Harbor to honor and commemorate the USS Nevada and those who served on it. A total of 76 sailors and Marines lost their lives as a result of that attack, the Navy said.

“You can carry your hatred all of your life,” Galle said of the attack at the event. “You have to remember, they had a leader who led them astray. We’re at peace now and I feel comfortable. I have no qualm. We’re all good people.”

After the war, Galle got married and opened a refrigeration and air-conditioning business in North Dakota. He then served as a civil engineer with the Air Force and U.S. Army Corps of Engineers. He retired in the 1980s.

title: Bezos says he was "heavily involved" in casting Pattinson as 007
summary: Amazon founder Jeff Bezos says "it was obvious" to him and others that Robert Pattinson should be the next James Bond.
story: Amazon founder and executive chairman Jeff Bezos said Tuesday that he was "heavily involved" in casting Robert Pattinson as the next James Bond.

Speaking at Semafor's Silicon Valley and The World forum in California, the head of the retail and entertainment giant that now owns the rights to the 007 franchise spoke about what he called the "real old-fashioned screen tests" for five Bond finalists, complete with "full costume, real sets."

On Friday, the team of selectors spent several hours going over the screen tests of each actor, Bezos said in remarks reported by Semafor, adding that while they were all "extraordinarily talented … there was something special about Rob."
Bezos said the group was initially biased against Pattinson, "because he's already so famous," and they had been inclined to choose someone "a little more unknown."
The role of the iconic British spy has historically gone to lesser-known actors, who have then made their name doing the Bond movies.
"But in the screening tests, it was so obvious he is James Bond," Bezos said of Pattinson, who shot to fame with his starring role in the "Twilight" vampire movies.

Amazon bought MGM, which co-owns the rights to the Bond franchise, in 2022. Pattinson will be the first Bond not forged under the creative stewardship of the Broccoli family, who had run the franchise since 1962, when the first movie featuring 007, "Dr. No," was released.

"James Bond is one of the most legendary characters in cinema, and to be entrusted with 007 is the honor of a lifetime," Pattinson said in a statement after he was unveiled as the seventh actor to take on the role. "To say this role is a dream come true is an understatement. I couldn't be more excited about this partnership and the work ahead with this fantastic team."

He will step into the shoes of Hollywood leading men Sean Connery, George Lazenby, Roger Moore, Timothy Dalton, Pierce Brosnan and Daniel Craig to star in the 26th Bond movie, which will be directed by Denis Villeneuve. It is expected to hit screens in 2028.

title: New James Bond is announced after rampant speculation
summary: After rampant online speculation about who would take over the iconic spy character from Daniel Craig, the franchise announced who the new 007 will be.
story: Robert Pattinson is the new 007. After rampant online speculation about who would take over the iconic spy character from Daniel Craig, the franchise announced Monday that Pattinson will be the next James Bond.
He will be the seventh actor to play the role since the first Bond film, "Dr. No," was released in 1962.

"James Bond is one of the most legendary characters in cinema, and to be entrusted with 007 is the honour of a lifetime," Pattinson said in a statement. "... To say this role is a dream come true is an understatement. I couldn't be more excited about this partnership and the work ahead with this fantastic team."

The naming of Pattinson comes five years after the beloved franchise's last film, 2021's "No Time to Die," which marked the first time in Bond's 64-year history on the silver screen to end with the character's death.
But 007 will be reborn in the 26th Bond film, directed by Denis Villeneuve. It will be the first since Amazon MGM took over the franchise.
For months, fans had been debating the merits of other potential 007s, including names like Callum Turner, Josh O'Connor, Jack Lowden and Nicholas Hoult.
Pattinson only entered the rumor mill recently after the revelation that he screen-tested for the role, the Associated Press reported, along with a few other finalists.

"Before anything else, I want to express my deep gratitude to the remarkable actors who joined us on this journey," Villeneuve said in a statement. "We were surrounded by extraordinary talent, but there can only be one 007. I am overjoyed to welcome Robert Pattinson as our new James Bond. He has the timeless soul of 007 and brings a spirit that is completely new. I cannot wait to begin."
Pattinson is already associated with three mega-franchises: "The Batman," "Twilight" and "Harry Potter."

Since his breakthrough in "Twilight," Pattinson has also worked in more independent films such as "Good Time," "The Lighthouse" and "Mickey 17." Earlier this year, he drew rave reviews for his villainous performance in Christopher Nolan's "The Odyssey."
The British royal family responded to the news on social media, saying: "Welcome to His Majesty's Secret Service, Mr Bond."
Now in the Bond role, Pattinson follows in the footsteps of Sean Connery, George Lazenby, Roger Moore, Timothy Dalton, Pierce Brosnan and Craig.

title: Raye leads the 2027 Grammy nominations. See the list.
summary: English singer-songwriter Raye is up for 11 awards at the 2027 Grammys, followed by Spanish singer Rosalía​ with nine nominations.
story: English singer-songwriter Raye leads the 2027 Grammy Award nominations, the Recording Academy announced Monday.

Raye is up for 11 awards at February's ceremony: record, song and album of the year — the first time she's been nominated in those big categories — as well as songwriter of the year non-classical, a variety of pop categories and music video.
Her 11 nods also mean she has tied Beyoncé's record at the 2025 Grammys for the most nominations in a single year by a female artist.
Speaking of Bey: She continues her reign as the most-nominated artist in Grammy history, scoring her 100th nod for "Morning Dew (Donk)" in the R&B solo performance category.

Raye, who is riding the success of her critically acclaimed album "This Music May Contain Hope," has 15 Grammy nominations across her career. She's never won one, though she was previously recognized by the Recording Academy with the noncompetitive Harry Belafonte best song for social change award.

Spanish singer Rosalía, fresh off her album of the year win at the 27th annual Latin Grammy Awards on Thursday for her avant-garde "Lux," follows Raye with nine nominations. She's a first-time nominee in all the categories she's up for: record, song and album of the year as well as pop solo performance, alternative music performance, alternative music album, Latin song, global music performance and music video.

Following her are Miranda Lambert, Olivia Rodrigo, Phoebe Bridgers and first-time nominee Ella Langley, who are tied with seven nods each. Bruno Mars, Leon Thomas and 2026's best new artist winner Olivia Dean have six nominations each.
Taylor Swift's nomination is her fifth consecutive studio album to be nominated for album of the year, something only one other artist has ever done: Kendrick Lamar.

Only recordings commercially released in the U.S. between Aug. 31, 2025, and Aug. 28, 2026, were eligible for nominations. The final round of Grammy voting, which determines the winners, will take place between Dec. 10 and Jan. 7.
The 2027 Grammy Awards will air Feb. 7 at 7 p.m. Eastern, live on ABC for the first time since 1972, from the Crypto.com Arena in Los Angeles. It will also stream on Disney+ and Hulu.
