title: Jeffries wins Democratic nomination for House speaker
summary: Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries easily won his party's nomination for the next speaker of the House on Wednesday.
story: Washington — Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries easily won his party's nomination for the next speaker of the House on Wednesday, paving the way for his election when Democrats take control of the chamber in January.

Jeffries' current and incoming Democratic colleagues voted 251 to 11 to back his nomination for the gavel during a closed-door meeting where members were also choosing the rest of the House Democratic leadership. The caucus also voted to elevate Rep. Katherine Clark of Massachusetts as the next majority leader, the first woman to hold that position.

The speaker is ultimately elected by the full House chamber, a vote that will occur at the beginning of the new Congress. With Democrats on track to control more than 250 seats, Jeffries' path to gaining the 218 votes needed for the speakership is all but secured. Jeffries would be the first Black House speaker in U.S. history.

The New York Democrat faced some hesitance from new progressive members heading into Wednesday's leadership vote. Seven incoming progressives who voted against him said in a statement that they were hoping to secure policy commitments from Jeffries on a number of fronts.

"Whether on Medicare for All, stopping ICE terror, getting money out of politics, or ending the genocide in Gaza, our constituents sent us to Congress with a mandate on these issues. We have worked to secure commitments from Leader Jeffries in good-faith conversations," the new members said. "While we have seen meaningful progress, there is still work to be done to ensure that the direction our party takes this coming Congress reflects what our constituents are demanding of leadership."

The members who released the statement were Darializa Avila Chevalier of New York, Adam Hamawy of New Jersey, Frederick Haynes of Texas, Melat Kiros of Colorado, Donavan McKinney of Michigan, Chris Rabb of Pennsylvania and Claire Valdez of New York.
But no other Democrat put their name forward to directly challenge Jeffries' bid. And with the wide Democratic majority, individual members have limited leverage to push for concessions.

Jeffries said he wanted a tallied vote during the internal election rather than ask for a vote by acclamation. He told reporters Tuesday that it was the same approach Democrats used in their leadership elections in 2018, when they transitioned from the minority to the majority.

"Certainly seems to me it would be appropriate that we take exactly the same approach to give every single person the opportunity to weigh in one way or the other on who the caucus feels is best positioned based on track record, experience, vision," Jeffries said.
House Democrats also voted Wednesday to fill the roles of whip, assistant leader and caucus chair in the new Congress.
Rep. Pete Aguilar of California was elected whip, Joe Neguse of Colorado won assistant speaker and Rep. Ted Lieu of California won the vote for chair of the Democratic caucus.

House Democrats' leadership election was far less contentious than that of their colleagues in the Senate, where longtime Democratic leader Chuck Schumer is facing a challenge from Sen. Chris Van Hollen. Schumer has expressed confidence that he has the votes to be elected majority leader in elections early next month.

title: "No indication" outages are related to cyberattacks, officials say
summary: Officials are testifying at a House committee hearing on worldwide threats as a series of network outages, including Microsoft Outlook and several banking institutions, have rattled Americans.
story: Washington — Top U.S. national security officials told Congress they have found no evidence that a string of technology outages affecting airlines, banks, Microsoft services and national security communications systems were connected or caused by malicious cyberattacks, even as lawmakers pressed for answers about an outage at the National Security Agency and reports of potential Iranian attacks on U.S. soil.

At Wednesday's House Homeland Security Committee hearing, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton and FBI Deputy Director Christopher Raia attempted to reassure lawmakers that federal agencies were investigating the disruptions and monitoring possible threats.
"We have seen nothing that would indicate that they are related," Mullin said, adding that DHS had contacted private industry while reviewing the outages.
Clayton said intelligence officials had reached a similar assessment after reviewing the incidents with government agencies and cybersecurity experts in the private sector.
"These are separate service outages associated with maintenance and technical changes. They are not a coordinated or state-sponsored attack," Clayton said.
Raia said FBI cybersecurity specialists had been involved in examining the incidents from the beginning.

"At this point, there is no indication whatsoever that there is any cyber malicious activity related to any of those incidents," Raia said. He added that the FBI would continue working with private-sector partners "in an abundance of caution."

Rep. Dan Goldman, a New York Democrat, challenged Clayton's characterization of the recent NSA outage, repeatedly asking whether the disruption had resulted from internal software updates or other technical work.
"It's your testimony today that the technological problems that the NSA faced on Monday were from internal software and technological upgrades," Goldman said.
Clayton responded that officials had found no evidence of outside interference.
"We have no indication that they have come from external threat actors," Clayton said.
Goldman pressed for a more definitive explanation.
"It's a pretty binary. It's either external or internal, right?" Goldman asked.
Clayton described routine maintenance procedures, including software patches, system upgrades and hardware replacement, which can require systems to be taken offline and restarted.
Goldman accused Clayton of avoiding the question.
"You're a very smart person, and you're clearly not answering my direct questions," Goldman rebutted.
Clayton separately warned that advances in computing power and increasingly capable software were placing new demands on older government technology systems.
"The speed of compute and the level of capability of applications that use that compute is increasing substantially," Clayton said.

He warned that the accelerating pace of technological development was making legacy systems obsolete more quickly, suggesting that infrastructure considered outdated only months earlier could fall even further behind as computing capabilities advance.

Mullin has already faced significant backlash for taking a government plane to a college football game one day after a FAA ground stop while the nation's airports remained chaotic. Mullin said Wednesday that it would have shown "distrust" in the nation's airspace if he had not flown.

Lawmakers also raised concerns about reports that Iranian-linked actors could be developing plans to target senior Trump administration officials using a radiological weapon, commonly called a dirty bomb, or chemical weapons.

Rep. Michael Guest, a Mississippi Republican, raised concerns about the possibility of Iranian sleeper cells operating within the United States and asked whether federal authorities were equipped to identify and disrupt potential attacks.
"Are we concerned about the possibility of sleeper cells?" Guest asked Mullin.
"Is it a concern? Of course. Are we fighting it and stomping it down every single day? Absolutely," Mullin responded.
Mullin said DHS personnel were working closely with intelligence and Justice Department officials to identify threats and prevent attacks.
Clayton also emphasized the danger posed by online radicalization, describing how foreign extremist networks can influence individuals already living inside the United States.
"That's not theoretical; it's real. We saw it in New York. We've seen it in other cases," Clayton said.
Raia cautioned that intelligence reporting about possible plots does not necessarily mean attackers possess the capability to carry them out.
"A lot of the reporting is largely aspirational," Raia said. "But that does not mean that does not mean we do not take it seriously."

He said authorities had revamped their Iranian threat mission center to strengthen efforts against potential attacks, pointing to previously disclosed investigations involving plots against dissidents.
The officials did not publicly confirm that Iranian sleeper cells were preparing attacks within the United States or that the reported dirty bomb or chemical weapons plans were operational.
Clayton said Iranian threats inside and outside of the U.S. have "dramatically increased."

"We remain committed to detecting, deterring and combatting the Iranian lethal plotting outside the United States and inside the United States," Clayton said. "These threats have dramatically increased."

title: Top Dem sends letters to people close to Trump ahead of probes
summary: Rep. Robert Garcia, who is expected to chair the House Oversight Committee in the next Congress, sent letters to 12 people close to President Trump ahead of expected investigations into his second term.
story: Washington — The top Democrat on the House Oversight and Government Reform Committee sent letters Wednesday to a dozen people close to President Trump ahead of expected investigations into alleged corruption, misconduct by the Department of Homeland Security and the White House's handling of files from the investigation into convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

The letters from Rep. Robert Garcia of California, who is expected to chair the Oversight Committee when Democrats take control of the House in January, went to members of the president's family, as well as former and current administration officials, and instructed them to preserve documents relevant to Democrats' future investigations.

Garcia sent notices to Donald Trump Jr., Eric Trump, Jared Kushner, former U.S. Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle, Trust for the National Mall CEO Catherine Townsend, White House chief of staff Stephen Miller, former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem, former Homeland Security senior adviser Corey Lewandowski, Vice President J.D. Vance, former White House chief of staff Susie Wiles, Attorney General Todd Blanche and Bureau of Prisons Director WIlliam Marshall.

"Voters gave Congressional Democrats a sweeping mandate to root out corruption and ensure that the government is accountable to the people," Garcia said in the letters. "We intend to act on that mandate in the 120th Congress by conducting the critically important oversight essential for legislative reform."

Garcia told Donald Trump Jr., and Eric Trump that the committee will investigate alleged conflicts of interest and their stakes in World Liberty Financial, the Trump family's crypto business. He told Trump Jr. that the Oversight panel is also interested in a Russian oligarch's funding of his post-wedding festivities at a private island in the Bahamas in May.

The letter to Kushner focuses on his personal business dealings and role representing the U.S. government as a negotiator in talks in the Middle East and Russia, which Garcia said raise concerns about "transparency, conflicts of interest and the abuse of" a government position for personal profit.

His document preservation notices to Vance, Wiles, Blanche and Marshall all center around the Trump administration's handling of the release of files from the federal investigation into Epstein, or the transfer of Ghislaine Maxwell, his longtime associate, to a minimum-security prison camp in Texas last year.

Letters to Miller, Noem and Lewandowski indicate that the committee will focus on immigration enforcement operations, and for Noem and Lewandowski, specifically, allegations of corruption and pay-to-play schemes at the department.

Garcia told Guilfoyle that the committee will be investigating alleged pay-to-play schemes surrounding her ambassadorship, and notified Townsend he will be examining private donations to fund construction of the new White House ballroom.

"Oversight Democrats are fighting to put an end to this Administration's self-dealing, misconduct, and abuse. These investigations will lay the groundwork for legislation which helps all Americans. This is just the beginning," the California Democrat said in a statement.

Garcia and congressional Democrats are poised to launch investigations into numerous matters arising during Mr. Trump's second term once they officially take control of the House and Senate in January and will have subpoena power.
But the White House has indicated it intends to fight back against the probes.

White House counsel Will Scharf sent a letter to Garcia last week warning that their investigations "may cross the line into blatant criminality," and said any investigative acts by Congress must support a legitimate legislative purpose.
But Garcia dismissed Scharf's threat and said Congress has "wide latitude" to conduct investigations and oversight.

In addition to Scharf's letter, a U.S. attorney in southern Texas, Aaron Reitz, has sent notices to at least five House and Senate Democrats about remarks they've made about forthcoming investigations and ordered them to preserve documents.

title: China's Xi greets Trump at airport ahead of planned summit with Putin
summary: President Trump arrived Wednesday in China, where the Kremlin said he had an informal meeting with Vladimir Putin.
story: President Trump arrived in China on Wednesday after starting a multiday Asia swing in the Philippines. He's scheduled to meet in Shenzhen, a hub of China's tech industry, with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping in a highly anticipated summit on Thursday.
Mr. Trump said he may meet with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, with Secretary of State Marco Rubio saying such a meeting "may not be possible" but the president is "prepared" for one.
Xi greeted Mr. Trump on a red carpet as he walked off Air Force One in Shenzhen.

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Mr. Trump and Putin had an informal meeting Wednesday ahead of the planned trilateral summit. Peskov also said Putin had already held a meeting with Xi, during which they discussed the war in Ukraine. Mr. Trump and Putin may also discuss Ukraine, Peskov said.
Putin mentioned his recent discussions in Moscow with Mr. Trump's envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner during his meeting with Xi on Wednesday, Peskov said.

"The three leaders have a lot to discuss, given the unstable situation in the world," Putin's senior aide Yury Ushakov told reporters in Shenzhen, according to Russian state broadcaster Vesti. He did not confirm the plan for an initial bilateral meeting between Putin and Mr. Trump on Wednesday, but said they might meet during an formal dinner.
It "will not be a single event" Ushakov said of the possibility of Trump-Putin encounters on Wednesday. "It will take place both standing, on the steps, and while seated."

In Manila, Mr. Trump visited the Malacañang Presidential Palace on Wednesday and met with his Philippine counterpart, Ferdinand "Bongbong" Marcos Jr., before his flight to China. In a public bilateral meeting, the two leaders lauded the U.S.-Philippine relationship, which Mr. Trump called "one of America's oldest and most important alliances in the Pacific." The U.S. president suggested the two countries could cooperate further on technology, energy and defense.

In a banquet luncheon before departing for China, Mr. Trump announced that he and Marcos "just consummated a very big trade deal, the biggest trade deal we've ever made, by far, and it's a fair deal for both countries, and we're very happy with that. And we didn't know that that was going to take place, but it took place very quickly, and it's a magnificent deal for both."
Later, in a social media post, Mr. Trump said the deal "will be a true landmark and, in particular, a Deal that will be great for our Farmers and those in the business of "Energy."

A day earlier, after landing in the Philippine capital of Manila, Mr. Trump met with the leaders of the Quad, a group of nations that have sought to counter China's influence in the Asia Pacific region. The president described the relationship with the Quad — made up of the U.S., Australia, India and Japan — as "very special."
Mr. Trump announced an $85 million investment in artificial intelligence software, describing it as the "greatest opportunity for economic growth since the Industrial Revolution."

There were protests in Manila ahead of Mr. Trump's trip, with demonstrators holding signs reading "Trump Out," drawings of him as a clown or devil, and signs calling on the public to reject an AI hub named Pax Silica.

Ahead of his departure from Washington Monday, Mr. Trump called it a "big trip" and said he may also meet with North Korea's Kim in China. After arriving in the Philippines, he said Kim "would like to" come, but "we'll see what happens."

The meeting between Mr. Trump, Xi and Putin, which marks the first among the three leaders, is expected to center on decreasing the proliferation of nuclear weapons, the White House said, and comes as the wars in Iran and Ukraine remain in focus.

Mr. Trump said Monday they would discuss denuclearization, which he called a "tough subject," as well as Iran and Ukraine, although an official said over the weekend that Ukraine was not expected to be discussed.

In Manila, the president will attend the annual Association of Southeast Asian Nations summit. He will meet with leaders of Japan, India and Australia on security in the Indo-Pacific on Tuesday. He's also scheduled to sign a trade deal with Thailand and attend a dinner with leaders of the Southeast Asian nations and other regional leaders, the White House said.

On Wednesday, the president is set to hold a state visit and lunch banquet with Philippine President Bongbong Marcos at the presidential palace, before departing for Shenzhen, China. There, he'll meet on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit with APEC leaders, and on Thursday, hold the meeting with Putin and Xi. Mr. Trump said Tuesday that he would be open to a one-on-one meeting with Putin, but he didn't know if it had been scheduled.
Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk is expected to join the president on the trip, according to a senior White House official, but will not be part of the meeting with Putin and Xi.

Mr. Trump's trip to Asia comes after he visited China in May for a summit with Xi, where he touted making "fantastic trade deals" and acknowledged a shared desire to end the U.S.-Iran conflict. Xi also visited the U.S. in September, marking his first visit to the White House in over a decade, as the two countries extended a tariff truce.

"I think the president does intend to talk about Iran in the trilateral meeting with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin," a senior U.S. official, speaking on condition of anonymity, told reporters on a call.
It will be Mr. Trump's third face-to-face meeting with Xi this year.

As for Putin, Mr. Trump and the Russian president last met in Alaska in August 2025 for a high-stakes summit on ending the war in Ukraine. But the talks failed to yield a ceasefire that the U.S. was seeking.

Mr. Trump's trip to Asia also coincides with issues back at home, including the recent revelations regarding an affair between Jensen Huang, the former CEO of chipmaker Nvidia, and a suspected Chinese spy. Beijing has said it was not involved.

Huang, who has a relationship with Mr. Trump, traveled on Air Force One during his May trip to China, and he and his wife were at the head table when Mr. Trump hosted Xi in Washington for a state dinner in September. White House officials said they do not think the Nvidia situation will loom over the trip.

"We do not negotiate American export controls. These are national security matters that we develop in the administration ... and we don't expect it to figure at all in any of our conversations with the Chinese while we're there," an official said.

When asked Monday if Rubio had told him that the woman with whom Huang was having an affair, Alice Huang, was suspected of being a spy, Mr. Trump said he didn't know if she was, saying, "I haven't heard that." Mr. Trump also said it "isn't a bad idea" for Jensen Huang to be reinstated at Nvidia, but he also added that he recommended Apple's Tim Cook for the job.
Mr. Trump acknowledged that Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent have "two lines of thought" on how to handle China, adding that "they handled that very well."
Bessent last week accused Lutnick of failing to prevent China from getting some of Nvidia's most advanced chips. Both Bessent and Lutnick are traveling with the president.
Mr. Trump told reporters before he left that he was not considering replacing Lutnick.

The Nvidia Board of Directors announced Tuesday morning that it would be creating a National Security and Export Control Oversight Committee. Mr. Trump said on Tuesday that he believed that is a "good idea."

title: AI platforms planned U.S. terror attack when asked to
summary: The incoming chair of the Senate Homeland Security Committee is preparing hearings on AI after government watchdogs found the four most-used platforms all created proposals for a U.S. terrorist attack when prompted by investigators.
story: Washington — The incoming chair of the Senate Homeland Security Committee is preparing hearings on AI after government watchdogs found the four most-used platforms — ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and Grok — all created proposals for a terrorist attack in the U.S. when prompted by investigators.

Democratic Sen. Maggie Hassan, who will head the panel in the new year, tasked the Government Accountability Office with investigating how commercially available AI could be used for malicious purposes, posing national security risks.

According to a report released Wednesday, the GAO found that within 12 hours of its covert testing, the platforms were able to create viable plans to use explosive devices for attacks with mass casualties in U.S. cities or to attack parts of the nation's electrical grid to create economic harm.
"We need to act now," Hassan said on a conference call with reporters.
The senator announced that one of the first hearings she will hold when the new Congress takes over in January will focus on AI risks and ways to improve safety.

"The AI public safety threat is no longer theoretical," Hassan said in a statement. "If Congress does not act, it is a question of when — not if — a bad actor will use AI to plan and carry out a major attack."

The 61-page report from the GAO includes responses from the tech companies — Anthropic, Google, OpenAI and SpaceXAI — which largely said they are continuing to refine their platforms to ensure security.

"The details behind the information provided by the AI platforms were not novel," the GAO wrote. "Many of the specifics are available on the internet. However, the generation of plans that could have taken weeks or months were instead completed in hours with the assistance of AI. These platforms could also raise ideas or methods that would not have been readily surfaced by basic research."
"The potential benefits of this technology are immense, but they can also benefit malicious actors," the GAO added.

"As AI capabilities evolve, AI providers will continue to refine their safeguards," the GAO said. "However, in its current state, this technology can potentially be dangerous and its misuse represents a growing risk to national and economic security."
The plans the AI platforms came up with
GAO investigators conducted the performance audit from December 2025 to October 2026, including testing in the spring of 2026.

In response to prompts, two of the AI platforms produced plans for constructing and detonating an improvised explosive device (IED) to cause mass casualties, while two other platforms produced plans for using drones or firearms to target the electrical grid, the report said.

"Each of these platforms provided detailed information that could be used to carry out attacks, such as specific targets, locations, timing, and attack methods," the GAO found. "Each platform took less than 12 hours to generate the attack plans."

In one of the tests, the platform suggested renting a vehicle and picking up supplies from a store along a route to the location. It recommended a specific date and time of attack, the report said, because public events likely to have large crowds were scheduled.

While the GAO said the platform initially refused to comply with requests for detailed information about how to construct and detonate the explosive device, it said it was able to circumvent its guardrails and get the platform to provide the information.
The other tests had similar outcomes.

For the tests involving attacks on electrical substations, one of the platforms suggested a drone attack while the other suggested using firearms to attack substations near a U.S. airport — both designed to inflict economic harm. The platforms presented maps and images.
The GAO investigators consulted with experts and engaged in site visits to check out the accuracy of the plans provided by the AI platforms.
In one case, they noted that the roads were incorrectly placed, and in another, they noted the presence of high walls that would make it difficult to see the targets.
AI companies say they're updating their models
In their responses to the GAO report, the major tech companies largely said their products continue to be refined.

Anthropic, in a letter to the GAO included in the report, said it does not dispute that a determined tester could get harmful content out of an AI system by misrepresenting the purpose of a request, "and we take the finding seriously." But it said it's not able to verify the findings in the GAO's report.
Google said the GAO's testing occurred on earlier models, and "we continue to improve our models."
OpenAI said it welcomes the opportunity to respond to the GAO's findings, "as well as the work that remains."
SpaceXAI said it "continues to work diligently" to improve safety with each model release.

title: Groups raise concerns over DOJ's new Civil Rights Division chief
summary: Eighteen civil rights organizations asked President Trump to withdraw his appointment of Craig Trainor as the new acting head of the Justice Department's Civil Rights Division.
story: Washington — Eighteen civil rights organizations asked President Trump on Tuesday to withdraw his appointment of Craig Trainor as the new acting assistant attorney general for the Justice Department's Civil Rights Division, saying he has a track record of undermining the laws he is tasked with enforcing.
Trainor was appointed last week to replace Harmeet Dhillon, who resigned from her post shortly after the midterm elections.

Trainor most recently served as assistant secretary for fair housing and equal opportunity at the Department of Housing and Urban Development. Prior to that, he held several senior roles at the Department of Education.

He also previously served as a senior special counsel to GOP Rep. Jim Jordan of Ohio on the House Judiciary Committee as well as the Select Subcommittee on the Weaponization of the Federal Government.

Tuesday's statement opposing his appointment was signed by a variety of organizations, including the National Center for Youth Law, the Leadership Conference on Civil and Human Rights, National Council of Jewish Women, Human Rights Campaign, the Sikh Coalition and Stop Sexual Assault in Schools, among others.
"In the midterm elections, the American people rejected an agenda to divide, discriminate against, and diminish our communities," the groups said.

"Instead of rebuilding a Civil Rights Division decimated under Harmeet Dhillon, the Administration has chosen to elevate the official behind a court-blocked classroom censorship agenda who seeks to undermine the rights of survivors and equal opportunity in our schools and communities," they added.

In response, the Justice Department told CBS News that the accusations against Trainor are "politically motivated and factually wrong," and alleged the groups who lodged the complaint are more interested in "preserving their preferred ideological status quo than ensuring that civil rights laws are applied as written."

"The Civil Rights Division exists to protect the civil rights of every American and enforce federal law equally—not to defend entrenched interests or advance the agendas of activist organizations," the Justice Department said. "Craig Trainor will carry out that mission without apology or intimidation, ensuring that every American's civil rights are protected and that the law is applied fairly, consistently, and as written."
The civil rights groups said that Trainor took action in his prior roles at the Department of Education and HUD that scaled back civil liberties.

After a court struck down a Department of Education rule that broadened the definition of what constitutes sexual harassment under Title IX of the Civil Rights Act, Trainor issued a directive to schools in February 2025 that ordered them to revert to less-stringent standards that were adopted in 2020.
Many civil rights groups have long criticized the 2020 standards and referred to them as "anti-survivor" rules because the definition of what constitutes sexual harassment is narrower.
The 2020 rules also only require schools to investigate allegations of sexual assault or harassment under Title IX that occur on school grounds, excluding conduct that may occur abroad or off campus.

The groups also pointed to threats that Trainor directed toward schools in a Feb. 14, 2025, letter, in which he threatened to withhold federal funding if they had diversity, equity and inclusion programs.
Several federal courts later enjoined the Department of Education from following through on its threats to withhold the funds.
After he left and went to HUD, Trainor also shuttered many discrimination investigations under the Fair Housing Act, the groups said.
In announcing his appointment, Attorney General Todd Blanche praised his actions at HUD, saying he helped to "cut the Biden-era Fair Housing case backlog in half."
Trainor is taking over the helm of a Civil Rights Division that was largely gutted under Dhillon's leadership, as more than 75% of its staff left since January 2025.
Although Dhillon later hired more attorneys, the staffing level is still not what it once was.

Dhillon reoriented the division away from its historical mission of protecting some of society's most vulnerable and marginalized groups. She shifted its focus to other priorities that included protecting gun owners' rights, curbing the use of equity, diversity and inclusion policies at universities, and adopting legal positions that oppose civil rights protections for transgender people.

title: These are the last midterm races to be decided
summary: Democrats won sizable House and Senate majorities in the 2026 midterm elections, but the exact margins are unclear because some races haven't been projected yet. Here's where the results stand.
story: Washington — The makeup of Congress shifted dramatically in the 2026 midterm elections, as Democrats decisively won control of the Senate, 56 to 44, and picked up dozens of House seats in what's on track to be one of the largest midterm routs in recent decades.

The exact margins in the House are not yet clear, as winners have not yet been projected in a few races. Here's a look at the congressional races that CBS News has not yet projected, including where the results stand:
Democrats on Defense

The dozens of red districts that Democrats flipped were the primary story of election night, but a few Republican House candidates tried to swim against the tide, either due to redistricting or a favorable local political makeup.

Louisiana's 6th District: This formerly blue-leaning, majority-Black district was redrawn after the Supreme Court voided the state's maps, finding that mapmakers relied too heavily on race and narrowing the Voting Rights Act. It's now significantly redder, but since no candidate won a majority under the state's "jungle" primary system, it will go to a runoff between Democrat Chauna Banks and Republican Blake Miguez.
GOP-Held Battlegrounds
Several races held by Republicans didn't have projections in the immediate aftermath of election night — including in districts that Democrats were hoping to flip.

Minnesota's 1st District: Republican Rep. Brad Finstad is facing off against Democrat Jake Johnson, after Finstad won by 17.2 points in 2024. Under state law, candidates who are behind by less than 0.25 points can request a recount.
Tennessee's 4th District: GOP Rep. Scott DesJarlais is defending his seat against Democrat Victoria Broderick. It's a red district, though it was made somewhat less red in redistricting.
North Carolina's 3rd District: GOP Rep. Greg Murphy is running against Democrat Raymond Smith. The district was made slightly bluer during redistricting last year, but it still favors Republicans.

North Carolina's 5th District: GOP Rep. Virginia Foxx is facing Democrat Chuck Hubbard. First elected over 20 years ago, Foxx is the longest-serving member of the Tar Heel State's congressional delegation, which was shaken up in the midterms, with Democrats flipping several House seats and a Senate seat.
North Carolina's 7th District: Republican Rep. David Rouzer is running against Democrat Kimberly Hardy.
North Carolina's 10th District: Republican Rep. Pat Harrigan faces Democrat Ashley Bell.
Please hold...

Results could take a while in some House districts, either because ballots still need to be counted or because of runoffs. In some California districts, both candidates belong to the same party, so they don't have any implications for the makeup of Congress.

Alaska's At-Large District: Republican Rep. Nick Begich is running against Bill Hill, an independent endorsed by Democrats, and a few other candidates. Remember: Alaska has ranked-choice elections, so further tabulation may be needed.
California's 23rd District: Republican Rep. Jay Obernolte is running against Democrat Tessa Hodge.

Louisiana's 5th District: Democrat Patricia Moore and Republican Gabe Firment are headed to a December runoff in this deeply conservative district. It's currently held by GOP Rep. Julia Letlow, who was elected to the Senate.

title: Mystery firm spending millions to attend Trump crypto gala
summary: The firm FastX, which has ties to Singapore, claims to have amassed more than $2 million in $TRUMP coin in the past two months and aims to secure a spot at the president's gala dinner.
story: A mysterious digital finance firm with a CEO who goes by one name and plans to build a "Chinese $TRUMP coin community" appears to have rocketed into the top spot in the competition to attend President Trump's upcoming cryptocurrency gala dinner.

The firm FastX, which has ties to Singapore, claims to have amassed more than $2 million in $TRUMP coin in the past two months. The CEO of its parent company, who goes by Addy, is now boasting on social media about the potential to rub elbows with the American president.

"We are the number one Trump holder now. We have over 2 million tokens," a woman identified as Addy said in a video posted to X on Nov. 11. "So later this month our team will attend a VIP reception with President Trump. So it's a big moment for us and the FastX community."

The opaque nature of the event, in which those competing for access to the presidential gala do so by acquiring large quantities of the Trump-branded meme coin, has renewed questions about the potential for corruption as the president's family venture does business with investors from across the globe.

The event on Sunday, Nov. 22, will be held at the Trump National Golf Club outside Washington, D.C., and will seat the 185 largest holders of the $TRUMP coin — a novelty product whose value rises and falls with the interest of buyers.

The website of the Trump company that sells the digital coins, Fight Fight Fight LLC, displays a public leaderboard for the event. The list identifies the top 130 holders only by usernames and crypto wallets, but does not disclose who is behind them.
On its website marketing the dinner, the company says, "No attendees will be granted a private meet & greet with the President," but Mr. Trump is advertised as the featured speaker at the event.

Little is known about FastX or Addy. The company, a subsidiary of something called GA Ventures Ltd., appears to be less than one year old. Early in October, FastX threw a yacht party during the TOKEN2049 crypto conference in Singapore. Eric Trump spoke at the conference, where he promoted the growth of crypto during his father's presidency.

"America is doing so great right now," Eric Trump said on stage during the crypto event at the Marina Bay Sands. "The way it's embraced cryptocurrency under my father's administration has been amazing."

Just a few weeks after the Singapore conference, FastX landed on the $TRUMP coin leaderboard. FastX's main wallet now holds nearly 1.8 million $TRUMP tokens, about 66% more than the next closest holder.

The company boasted about it in another video posted on X, which appears to have been filmed in an office in Centennial Tower in the Marina Bay area of Singapore. CBS News determined the location based on the facades of buildings appearing in the background and an address previously listed in an archived version of the FastX website.
"We hold Trump coins because we believe in it," Addy said in the video.
CEO of GA Ventures,$TRUMP on FastX. The $TRUMP Hour. What it all means for FastX traders.Everything you need to know. Watch below. https://t.co/tj4dLdUEIO 🔥 pic.twitter.com/nJBqLl5Iak
This comes as congressional Democrats, newly emboldened by sweeping midterm election victories, say they are preparing investigations into the president's crypto businesses.

Mr. Trump has earned more than $1 billion from his crypto ventures during his second term, according to financial disclosures, including at least $635 million in royalties last year from a licensing deal tied to the meme coin.

"Foreign nationals and bad actors are apparently only too happy to seek access and favors by buying into Trump's meme coin scheme," said Sen. Richard Blumenthal, a Democrat from Connecticut, in a statement to CBS News. "He has put a 'For Sale' sign on the White House through the  $TRUMP coin and other crypto dealings." Blumenthal is set to chair the Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations when Democrats take control of the Senate in January.
Earlier this month, Mr. Trump addressed his crypto profits during an interview with "60 Minutes," saying he has left those ventures in the hands of his sons, who oversee the Trump Organization.
"I have a company. My sons run the company," he said. "It's hard to say to them, 'Don't do anything anymore for four years because I'm president.'"

Regardless of the scrutiny, planning for the gala is forging ahead. Last week, Fight Fight Fight — the meme coin's parent company tied to the Trump family — announced that four "legends" will be joining the president for the event: Professional boxer Floyd Mayweather, "Shark Tank" star Kevin O'Leary, NBA champion Tristan Thompson and mentalist Lior Surchard. VIP attendees of the dinner are told to expect commemorative items including a Trump-branded watch and Trump-branded fragrance.
FastX representatives plan to attend the gala this weekend in Virginia, according to the video.
"It's a chance to meet the people who also support the Trump coin community," Addy said.

FastX also encourages users to join the company's "Chinese $TRUMP coin community," which is a curated feed of information about the meme coin, hosted by the cryptocurrency company Binance. Binance, whose CEO Chenpeng Zhao was pardoned by Mr. Trump in 2025, bars U.S.-based users from its platform. CBS News was automatically blocked from signing up on a U.S.-based computer.
FastX and GA Ventures did not respond to CBS News' request for comment.

Last month, CBS News reported that more than half of the crypto wallets on the Trump gala leaderboard at the time had used Binance or other crypto exchanges that prohibit U.S. users, suggesting many of the users were foreign-based.

At the time the gala contest closed Monday morning, 79 of the top 130 wallets had used a crypto exchange that bars U.S. users. Together, they hold about $8.8 million of the board's $9.5 million worth of $TRUMP coin.
"Got a question for Trump? Comment it below."
FastX has touted its prospective access to the U.S. president, offering followers the chance to submit questions that FastX claims it will pose to the president at the gala dinner.

In posts on X last month, FastX said, "Got a question for Trump? Comment it below," and said it "will put 10 randomly selected questions forward at the upcoming dinner." FastX later added the disclaimer, "Questions are not guaranteed to be asked."
Followers responded with questions focused on the U.S. war with Iran, the increase in prices of goods, and concerns about the stability of the crypto markets.
"Mr. President, you called yourself the first Crypto President," one X user wrote. "What's the one crypto law you want to get signed before this dinner ends?"

"Clearly this FastX $TRUMP coin promotion is a way to get their company a direct audience with the president," said Corey Frayer, the director of investor protection for the Consumer Federation of America.

"It's incredibly corrosive to people's faith in our democracy when the highest ranking official and most powerful person in the world is selling away government decisions to line his pockets, not to do what's best for Americans."
Neither the White House nor Fight Fight Fight responded to requests for comment.

Since the midterm elections earlier this month, crypto products tied to the Trump family have been trading at an all-time low. The price of $TRUMP coin fell to around 92 cents this week, down significantly from its 2025 high of $74 a coin.
This story published first on CBS News at 6:00 a.m. on Nov. 18, 2026.

title: Democrats have flipped 46 House seats. Here's the breakdown.
summary: Democrats won control of the House by flipping more than 40 Republican-held seats, picking up perennial swing districts and seats that were once considered deep red.
story: Washington — Democrats won control of the House of Representatives on Nov. 3 by flipping more than 40 Republican-held seats, picking up perennial swing districts and seats that were once considered deep red. The party's wins ranged from suburban areas in the northeastern United States to areas of South Texas that were once viewed as increasingly GOP-friendly.

The 2026 midterm elections were also shaken up by last year's nationwide mid-decade redistricting gambit, with Texas Republicans shifting several districts rightward at President Trump's behest, California Democrats moving districts to the left and several other states tweaking their House maps for partisan purposes. Democrats notched several wins under the new maps, while the GOP's pickups have been more limited so far.
Winners in a handful of House races have yet to be projected by CBS News.
So far, 46 districts have shifted to Democrats and three have shifted to Republicans. Here's a look at the seats that swung:
Upsets
In several districts, Democrats ousted GOP lawmakers who won by double digits two years ago.

New Jersey's 2nd District: Republican Rep. Jeff Van Drew lost to Democrat Zack Mullock in a South Jersey district that was widely seen as solid red. Van Drew, who won by 16.9 points in 2024, is known for switching from the Democratic Party during the first Trump impeachment saga in 2019. Ohio's 10th District: GOP Rep. Mike Turner was ousted by Democrat Kristina Knickerbocker, ending Turner's nearly quarter-century tenure in Congress just two years after he won reelection by more than 18 points.Missouri's 2nd District: Democrat Fred Wellman unseated GOP Rep. Ann Wagner, who won by 12 points in 2024. Republicans tried to make the St. Louis-area seat slightly redder last year, but the new maps were tossed out in the courts. As recently as September, the Cook Political Report viewed it as solid-red.Indiana's 5th District: Republican Rep. Victoria Spartz lost to Democrat J.D. Ford in one of several election night surprises. Spartz won reelection by just over 18 points in 2024.Kentucky's 6th District: The race between Democrat Zach Dembo and Republican Ralph Alvarado for the open seat was not expected to be competitive, but the election forecasters moved the GOP-held seat toward Democrats in recent weeks. Outgoing Rep. Andy Barr won it by 26 points two years ago.Wisconsin's 1st District: Republican Rep. Bryan Steil, who was first elected in 2018, lost his race to Democrat Mitchell Berman. A Democrat has not represented the district in more than 30 years. Steil won his last reelection by just over 10 points, outperforming Mr. Trump, and the Cook Political Report rated it "Likely Republican" until late September.Nevada's 2nd District: Teresa Benitez-Thompson will be the first Democrat to represent Northern Nevada in decades, after she defeated Republican David Flippo. The seat was left open by the retirement of longtime GOP Rep. Mark Amodei, who won by a nearly 19-point margin in 2024.Ohio's 15th District: Democrat Don Leonard defeated GOP Rep. Mike Carey, who won reelection by 13 points in 2024.

Ohio's 15th District: Democrat Don Leonard defeated GOP Rep. Mike Carey, who won reelection by 13 points in 2024.
Rematches
A few Democrats won against Republicans who they'd faced before — in one case, multiple times.

Both parties invested in districts in the Northeast, including seats with a history of swinging from one party to another, and a competitive Pennsylvania seat that was held by an overperforming Republican for a decade.

title: Mary Peltola wins Alaska Senate race, flipping seat for Dems
summary: Mary Peltola, 53, defeated incumbent GOP Sen. Dan Sullivan and will be the first Alaska Native to serve in the U.S. Senate.
story: Washington — Former Democratic Rep. Mary Peltola defeated GOP Sen. Dan Sullivan in the Alaska Senate race, CBS News projects, adding to the new Democratic majority in the Senate two weeks after Election Day.
With the Alaska race now decided, Democrats will control 56 Senate seats to Republicans' 44.

Peltola, 53, was the first Democrat to represent Alaska in the House in 50 years in 2022. She is now set to become the first Alaska Native to be elected to the Senate, and the first Democrat to be elected to the Senate in the state since 2008.

"As a lifelong Alaskan who has dedicated my life to serving our state, there is no greater honor than having Alaskans' support in our fight to take on corporate greed, lower costs, and put Alaska first," Peltola said in a statement Tuesday night. " As our next United States Senator, I will stand up to anyone to take on the rigged system in DC and deliver results for Alaska's working families."
"Thank you Alaska. Let's get to work," she added.

Sullivan, a second-term senator and a Marine veteran, was fighting to hold on to the seat. Peltola successfully portrayed herself as an independent voice for the state. She lost her reelection bid for Alaska's sole House seat in 2024 by less than 3 points, while President Trump won the state by 13 points. But the dynamics were more favorable for her this cycle, with the unpopular war in Iran and high gas and diesel prices hanging over Republican candidates.

The contest was decided by ranked-choice voting. In addition to Sullivan, Peltola faced off against another candidate with nearly the same name as the incumbent, Daniel J. Sullivan, and Republican Gerald Heikes.

The second Dan Sullivan, a former teacher, added a wrinkle to the race. He announced he was challenging the sitting senator in June, prompting an unsuccessful push to remove him from the ballot. But both Dan Sullivans ultimately appeared on the ballot, in a development that Republicans argued could impact the incumbent senator's chances.

About a week and a half before Election Day, the Trump administration sued to prevent the Alaska Senate election from being certified if Sen. Sullivan were to lose to Peltola because of the other Daniel Sullivan.
But in the end, Peltola's margin was large enough that those votes wouldn't have made a difference.

Heading into election night, polls showed a dead heat between Peltola and Sen. Sullivan. Republicans sent their biggest names to stump for Sullivan, including Vice President JD Vance. And the Senate GOP's main super PAC, the Senate Leadership Fund, spent heavily in the race.

Republicans had hoped to retain the seat and their GOP majority in an unexpectedly competitive environment this cycle. Though Democrats initially faced steep headwinds, competitive races opened up in several states that Mr. Trump had won in 2024 by double digits, including Alaska.

title: White House drops its nomination for FDA commissioner
summary: The White House has dropped the nomination of Dr. Heidi Overton, President Trump's pick for FDA commissioner, CBS News has confirmed.
story: The White House has dropped the nomination of Dr. Heidi Overton, President Trump's pick for Food and Drug Administration commissioner, according to a senior administration official and other people familiar with the decision.
The Senate Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee had been scheduled to vote on Overton's nomination Wednesday.
Axios was first to report that Overton was dropped.

Overton had struggled to shore up support among Senate Republicans, CBS News had previously reported. Some lawmakers and administration allies had expressed skepticism of Overton, partly due to her testimony regarding the FDA-approved abortion drug mifepristone and her execution of Mr. Trump's pro-vape policies.

Republican Sen. Bill Cassidy of Louisiana, the outgoing chair of the Senate HELP Committee, argued late Tuesday the issue was not that Overton lacked the votes to get confirmed. He said the "White House abandoned a viable confirmation path."

Cassidy wrote in a statement that "pro-life Senators sought final assurances from the Administration regarding the Administration's commitment to life issues," but the Trump administration withdrew Overton instead.

"I believe she would have had the votes to pass out of committee and pass the full Senate. My conversations with her convinced me she would follow the science and push back against decisions that put Americans' health at risk," he said.

Two sources familiar with the matter said the White House shared its decision to withdraw Overton's nomination Tuesday evening. At the time, whip efforts were still underway to garner enough Republican votes to advance Overton.

Mr. Trump nominated Overton — a physician and White House domestic policy staffer — to the FDA role over the summer. The agency, which regulates products that account for about 20% of U.S. consumer spending, has not had a Senate-confirmed leader since Dr. Marty Makary was forced out in May.
Overton was seen as close to former White House chief of staff Susie Wiles, who departed her role earlier this month.

Prior to the decision to withdraw Overton, the White House had begun talking to other potential candidates for FDA chief, including some who could serve in an acting capacity and thus forgo Senate confirmation, a source told CBS News earlier Tuesday. The agency is currently run by acting Commissioner Kyle Diamantas.
Two sources indicated Sen. Roger Marshall of Kansas, a doctor, is making a play for the FDA post. He lost his reelection bid to Democrat Adam Hamilton earlier this month.
Any Senate-confirmed FDA commissioner would need to be confirmed during a narrow window before Democrats take control of the chamber in January.
Cassidy told CBS News on Tuesday that "with the limited time left, confirming a permanent FDA Commissioner will fall to Senate Democrats."
In an interview with "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan" on Sunday, Cassidy expressed concern that an acting FDA administer would have less independence than a Senate-confirmed leader.

"The question is, do we want a series of short-term administrators who probably will have more influence from the secretary, as opposed to someone who may be not, you know, the perfect candidate in somebody's mind, but at least would be a permanent one and have the ability to establish some independence?" he said.

title: Ex-Nvidia CEO agrees to testify to Congress amid affair probe
summary: The former Nvidia chief will appear for public and closed-door hearings after Republicans threatened to subpoena him.
story: Washington — Jensen Huang, who resigned last week as the CEO of Nvidia, has agreed to answer questions from House and Senate lawmakers under the threat of a subpoena, amid an investigation into his affair with a woman believed to be a Chinese spy.

Huang will testify publicly before the Senate Banking Committee, though the hearing's date has not been determined, according to a spokesperson for the committee's chairman, GOP Sen. Tim Scott of South Carolina. He will also sit for a closed-door transcribed interview with three House committees on Dec. 1.

"The American people need answers on Mr. Huang and Nvidia's role in allowing dangerous [People's Republic of China] actors to access our most advanced chips, as well as the role of a potential Chinese intelligence asset in this scandal," House Foreign Affairs Committee Chairman Brian Mast, a Florida Republican, said in a joint statement announcing the date of the hearing. Mast issued the statement with GOP Rep. John Moolenaar of Michigan, the chair of the House China Committee, and House Intelligence Committee Chair Rep. Rick Crawford of Arkansas.
Nvidia general counsel Tim Teter voluntarily agreed to appear before the House committees on Dec. 2, the lawmakers said.
"We look forward to hearing from Jensen Huang and Tim Teter on their roles in a potential breach of our national security," the lawmakers added.
A representative for Huang declined to comment.

The chairmen had given Huang until 8 p.m. Nov. 13 to respond to their request for a closed-door, transcribed interview after Thanksgiving. Negotiations for the interview continued past the deadline into this week.

In a Nov. 12 letter, the lawmakers warned that "failure to cooperate with this request will result in the House Foreign Affairs Committee issuing a subpoena to compel your testimony in a format of the committee's choosing."
"Other committees also reserve the right to separately issue subpoenas to compel your testimony," they wrote.
Moolenaar and Crawford signed the letter with Mast.

In an initial letter to Huang on Nov. 4, the lawmakers sought a briefing on Nvidia's security protocols against espionage from foreign adversaries and on his relationship with former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, who is not related to him.

The Singapore-based data center company gained access to Nvidia's highly prized chips that are banned from export to China under U.S. law. Megaspeed is under investigation in the U.S. and Singapore for allegedly smuggling those chips into China — allegations Megaspeed has denied.
"It is vital that Congress determines the extent to which U.S. national security has been placed at risk," the lawmakers wrote in their initial letter to Jensen Huang.

title: Rubio says there's "zero evidence" recent tech outages are related
summary: Secretary of State Marco Rubio acknowledged that people are fearful and uncertain, saying he wanted to be clear that the United States is not under systemic attack.
story: Secretary of State Marco Rubio said there's "zero evidence" that recent tech outages in U.S. air travel, banking and other systems are connected.

"The Microsoft incident has nothing to do with what we saw with the FAA. The FAA has nothing to do with what we saw with the banks a few days ago. These issues that we've seen from a technical standpoint are completely unrelated one from another," Rubio said Wednesday morning local time during a news conference in the Philippines.
Rubio acknowledged that people are fearful and uncertain, saying he wanted to be clear that the United States is not under systemic attack.

"We have zero evidence or any reason to believe that any of these isolated or individual instances have anything to do with nefarious actors, with cyber hackers, with criminals, with another nation state, with a malign actor of any kind," Rubio said.

Rubio, who is traveling with President Trump ahead of a trilateral meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping this week, added that the administration is "always on the lookout" for any potential attacks and reiterated multiple times that reports of technical issues are not interconnected.
"Each of them are distinct, and they're different in their causation," he said.

On Thursday, Microsoft said it experienced a worldwide outage affecting services like Outlook and Teams, impacting users, companies and government operations worldwide. The company said the outage was linked to a technical issue, not malicious or cyber activity.

The following day, the Federal Aviation Administration issued a nationwide ground stop on all departing U.S. flights for several hours, throwing the aviation industry into turmoil. Federal officials identified a contractor performing maintenance updates as the cause of Friday's disruption, but key questions remain about the underlying cause of the systemwide failure.

Other recent outages that have since been resolved include disruptions to major banks like JPMorgan Chase, Bank of America and U.S. Bank, and issues with Apple's services. On Tuesday, the National Security Agency's internal network used to store and share classified information went offline, multiple U.S. officials familiar told CBS News.

Democratic Sen. Mark Warner, vice chair of the Senate Intelligence Committee, also said on Tuesday that there's no indication these incidents are the result of an attack, but noted that artificial intelligence is creating pressure for companies to deal with vulnerabilities.

"AI is making it possible to identify vulnerabilities across enormous numbers of systems at unprecedented speed, creating enormous pressure on companies and government agencies to patch those vulnerabilities immediately, often all at once, putting tremendous strain on systems that weren't built to handle that pace of change," Warner said in a post on X. "It feels like every day brings another reminder that AI is moving faster than our ability to manage its consequences.   This is exactly why I've been pushing for commonsense guardrails on AI and stronger cybersecurity protections."
When asked Wednesday about the role of AI in recent incidents, Rubio said he didn't want to speculate because every incident is unique and referred to individual companies.

title: Trump FDA nominee Heidi Overton struggling to win GOP support
summary: Heidi Overton, Trump's pick to be FDA commissioner, is having trouble finding enough Republican support to advance her nomination, which could be pulled if she falls short.
story: Update: The White House has withdrawn Dr. Heidi Overton's nomination, CBS News confirmed Tuesday. Read more here.

Dr. Heidi Overton, President Trump's pick to be FDA commissioner, is struggling to shore up enough support in the Senate Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee as it prepares to vote on her nomination Wednesday.

Sources tell CBS News that she's having trouble finding enough Republicans on the committee to vote to advance her nomination, which could be pulled if she can't muster the support. None of the Democrats on the committee are expected to back her.

The White House knows it has a problem, one source said, and has already begun looking for a new candidate. A second source confirmed that the White House has been talking to potential candidates, including some who could serve in an acting capacity and thus forgo Senate confirmation.
CBS News has reached out to the White House for comment.

Overton's nomination has run aground over her testimony regarding the FDA-approved chemical abortion drug mifepristone and her execution of President Trump's pro-vaping policies while she served on the Domestic Policy Council.

Missouri Republican Sen. Josh Hawley has emerged as one of the skeptics. Overton sidestepped questions on how she would handle a safety study long promised by the Trump administration into mifepristone, which Hawley has pressed for as well. The anti-abortion group Susan B. Anthony urged the Senate to delay her confirmation, and wants the FDA to commit to banning mail orders of mifepristone.

And two pro-abortion-access Republicans on the committee — Sens. Susan Collins of Maine and Lisa Murkowski of Alaska — have also not said whether they'll vote to advance her nomination. During Overton's confirmation hearing, Murkowski asked her whether she would restrict mifepristone, which is used in more than half of abortions in the U.S.

The administration has spoken with candidates about taking the FDA commissioner role in an acting capacity. That's one route to avoiding the Senate confirmation process during the narrow three-week legislative window ahead. The FDA oversees products that account for roughly 20% of consumer spending.
Two sources indicated Sen. Roger Marshall of Kansas, a doctor, is making a play for the FDA post. He lost his reelection bid to Democrat Adam Hamilton earlier this month.
Overton is arguably the Trump nominee with the highest profile who is struggling to shore up sufficient support in the closing weeks of GOP congressional control.

On Tuesday, Hung Cao, Mr. Trump's pick to serve as secretary of the Navy, faced a bipartisan grilling over his management of wartime operations and the Pentagon's decision to block Democrats from some classified military briefings. And retiring North Carolina Republican Sen. Thom Tillis said Tuesday he opposes the nomination of Eric Ueland, currently the deputy director of the Office of Management and Budget, to lead the Government Accountability Office, because of the involvement of Ueland and OMB in implementing DOGE cuts.

The FDA has been helmed by acting Commissioner Kyle Diamantas since the last Senate-confirmed chief, Marty Makary, was forced out by the White House last spring. Multiple sources familiar with his ouster told CBS News that ongoing White House pressure over flavored vapes caused significant friction.

Dr. Makary told CBS News in a statement on Nov. 8 that "big tobacco exploited their connections to administration and HHS officials to put repeated pressure on me to approve fruit-flavored vapes that appeal to children – I wouldn't do it."
Mr. Trump campaigned in 2024 on a promise to save vaping, a smoking alternative that can help with breaking the smoking habit, but also has been found to have serious health side effects.

CBS News' "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan" asked outgoing HELP Chairman Sen. Bill Cassidy, Republican of Louisiana, about whether Republicans would be able to install a Senate-confirmed FDA commissioner in these last weeks that they control the Senate. He raised the concern that the alternative would mean installing acting commissioners.

"Do we want a series of short-term administrators who probably will have more influence from the secretary, as opposed to someone who may be not, you know, the perfect candidate in somebody's mind, but at least would be a permanent one and have the ability to establish some independence. And that's part of the thought process there. That weighs on one side, and of course other things weigh on the other," Cassidy said Sunday.

Asked by "Face the Nation" about his own past remarks that Overton's association with Mr. Trump's efforts around reducing childhood vaccine uptake was "almost disqualifying," Cassidy acknowledged he was still working the phones and uncertain about whether Overton's nomination would be advanced by the HELP Committee he chairs, and he also did not say which way he would vote.

Overton stood beside Mr. Trump in the Oval Office as he signed an executive order on vaccines this summer — and the president twice erroneously referred to the measles or MMR vaccine as "lethal." None of the health officials present corrected Mr. Trump.

Recently resigned MAHA leader Calley Means, a former top adviser to Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., has also urged his followers to help block Overton's confirmation. He told "Face the Nation," "Heidi Overton was the biggest block to MAHA policies I encountered in the government."

Defenders of Overton dismissed criticism of her compliance with Mr. Trump's policies, and point to her medical background and her endorsement by two former FDA commissioners as a sign that she will be a professional.
At this hour, the vote to confirm Overton and a handful of other health officials is still scheduled to take place Wednesday morning.

title: Man convicted in Iran-backed plot to kill Trump is sentenced
summary: A man who was convicted of attempted terrorism and murder-for-hire plots, with potential targets including President Trump and former President Joe Biden, was sentenced to 27 1/2 years in federal prison.
story: A Pakistani man who was convicted of attempted terrorism and orchestrating a murder-for-hire plot at the direction of Iran's Revolutionary Guard Corps, with potential targets including President Trump and former President Joe Biden, was sentenced to 27 1/2 years in federal prison on Tuesday.

Asif Merchant was convicted in March — shortly after the start of the Iran war — on terrorism and murder-for-hire charges and faced up to life in prison. Merchant shuffled into court with a serious expression and shackled ankles, peering around the room. He had wavy gray hair and wore a tan prison outfit. He pressed a headphone to his ear, for an Urdu translation of the proceedings, watching the judge intently and bobbing in his chair as he learned his fate.

"This was an exceptionally severe crime, an extreme instance of terroristic violence," said Brooklyn-based U.S. District Judge Eric R. Komitee, a Trump appointee. "No crimes are more serious than the targeted killing of a U.S. president or other U.S. officials."

Komitee called the "overlay of foreign influence" from Iran an aggravating factor, noting that Iran is the largest state sponsor of terrorism in the world. "The conduct we see here is not an isolated episode for that foreign actor," he said.

Merchant was accused of traveling to the United States to recruit criminal associates and hire hit men to carry out his scheme. The plot involved the assassination of a politician, stealing documents from a target's home and arranging a protest as a distraction after the murder occurred, according to court documents.
He was charged with one count of attempting to commit an act of terrorism transcending national boundaries and one count of murder for hire.

He testified in his own defense during the trial, and admitted that he had been recruited by a member of the Revolutionary Guard Corps, Iran's elite military branch that answers to the supreme leader. In addition to Mr. Trump and Biden, he testified that former U.N. Ambassador Nikki Haley was also a potential target of the plot.

To carry out the plot, Merchant reached out to a contact in the U.S. for assistance, but that person turned out to be a confidential source working with law enforcement. That confidential source, known by the pseudonym Nadeem Ali, ultimately connected Merchant with two alleged hit men who were actually undercover FBI agents. He paid them $5,000 each as down payments for the assassinations.

On the stand, Merchant claimed that he carried out the plot under duress, out of fear his wife and child in Iran would be harmed if he didn't comply. Merchant also has a wife and children in Pakistan. Prosecutors disputed his claim, saying there was no evidence that he had "fear for relatives." Iran has denied plotting to kill Mr. Trump or other high-ranking U.S. officials.

During sentencing, Komitee said the evidence was clear that Merchant was "highly motivated himself to do harm to this country." He said it was possible Merchant had some concern for his family's well-being in Iran, but did not accept the defense's characterization that was the sole motivation behind his actions.
The government pointed to Merchant's own social media posts as evidence, including a post of Mr. Trump's severed head with the words "coming soon" and "severe revenge."
According to trial exhibits, Merchant had searched for Trump campaign rally locations in 2024 and searched the address of at least one rally on Google Maps.

As a front for the plot, Merchant set up a garment business, and used terms related to articles of clothing as code words to communicate about the plan. He instructed the confidential source, who he thought was his associate, that "T-shirt" meant protest, "flannel shirt" meant stealing and "fleece jacket" was to "commit the act of the game," indicating murder.

Merchant's lawyer Christopher Neff disputed that the garment business was a front during sentencing, calling it a real business. The prosecution pointed to a video of Merchant, played at trial, in which he told Ali that "the goal is not to make a profit, the goal is to launder money for the IRGC murder plot."

Neff told the judge that Merchant's plot was "never particularly likely to succeed," since the IRGC sent him to "kill a politician with Secret Service protection and extraordinarily tight security yet gave him almost no resources to carry it out."
"Mr. Merchant is simply not the monster that the government would like you to believe," said Neff. "He is an ordinary guy."
The government countered that the plot was "not farfetched … it was straight out of the IRGC playbook."
Merchant was arrested on July 12, 2024, the day before the attempted assassination of Mr. Trump in Butler, Pennsylvania.
When Merchant was told about the Butler assassination attempt, he responded that what occurred at the rally was "the same thing he was sent here to do."

As the sentencing ended, Komitee wished Merchant the best, telling him: "No matter how serious the crimes of conviction, no human is to be judged entirely by the biggest mistakes they've made in their lives."

Attorney General Todd Blanche said in a statement after Merchant's sentencing: "The Department of Justice will not tolerate foreign terrorist plots against our leaders and will not stop until those responsible are held accountable."

Neff told reporters after court, "While we're upset with the verdict and will appeal and are disappointed with the length of the sentence, we are grateful that Judge Komitee did not impose the draconian sentence that was requested by the government."

When asked what he thought of a Trump-appointed judge not giving Merchant a life sentence for a plot potentially targeting the president, Neff replied, "I think what it shows is that our judiciary remains independent, thankfully."

title: NSA's classified internal network goes down, sources say
summary: Two U.S. officials tell CBS News that so far there is no evidence of a cyberattack.
story: Washington — The National Security Agency's internal network used to store and share classified information went offline Tuesday, according to multiple U.S. officials familiar with the situation, prompting the agency to stagger arrival times for some personnel at its headquarters at Fort Meade, Maryland.
The network, dubbed "NSA Net," is used for classified communications and information sharing within the nation's largest intelligence agency.

An NSA spokesperson said in a statement that the agency experienced a "temporary degradation during scheduled routine maintenance." The statement continued that "while some internal systems were affected, mission/critical capabilities remain fully operational and our ability to defend National Security continues."
The spokesperson said that the agency's infrastructure is designed with multiple layers of redundancy to maintain operations during planned maintenance or unexpected events.

Two U.S. officials told CBS News that, at this point, there is no evidence the disruption was caused by a cyberattack. Two sources familiar with the situation said the outage resulted from routine system patching, though the precise circumstances surrounding the disruption remain unclear.
The NSA has also implemented staggered arrival times for non-emergency personnel at Fort Meade, according to two sources familiar with the measure.
The news was first reported by CNN.

Multiple sources told CBS News that the agency was seeking to avoid having large numbers of employees log on to their computers simultaneously while the network was experiencing problems, which is why they decided to stagger arrivals. Sources referred to this as "Code Gray," part of a modified reporting schedule.

Sources familiar with Fort Meade's operations said the installation remains under normal operating conditions, with gates and campus-wide services unaffected. The sources explained that the NSA operates within its own secured campus and can establish unique reporting requirements for its personnel, independent of the larger installation.
In the meantime, some activities are being redirected to other NSA facilities around the country, according to sources familiar with the situation.
It was not immediately clear how long the network had been offline or when full service might be restored.

The NSA, home to one of the largest workforces in the U.S. intelligence community, is responsible for collecting and analyzing foreign signals intelligence, identifying and countering cyber threats, and protecting U.S. government communications.
CBS News has reached out to the White House, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency and the Pentagon for comment.

title: Outcome of Alaska Senate race could take weeks to determine
summary: The Senate race in Alaska, which has garnered widespread attention with two candidates named Dan Sullivan, remains in limbo.
story: Update: Democrat Mary Peltola is projected to win the Alaska Senate race. Read the latest here. Our earlier coverage is below.

Washington — The Senate race in Alaska remains unresolved more than two weeks after Election Day as a contest that has garnered widespread attention over the two candidates named Dan Sullivan faces a lengthy ballot-counting process.

Incumbent Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan and Democrat Mary Peltola are facing off in the race, which also has two other candidates on the ballot: an independent candidate and retired teacher Daniel J. Sullivan, and another Republican, Gerald Heikes.
With 98% of the vote in as of Tuesday, Nov. 17, the race is leaning Democratic, according to CBS News estimates, with Peltola's lead growing to about 4 percentage points ahead of Sen. Sullivan.

The count in Alaska could stretch on. Alaska has a ranked-choice voting system, which allows voters to rank as many or as few candidates as they'd like in order of preference. If no candidate secures support from more than 50% of voters as their top choice, the count goes to a second round.

The ranked-choice tabulation doesn't occur until the last counting of ballots 15 days after Election Day, meaning the process could drag on for weeks if one candidate does not secure more than 50% of first-place support on the ballot.

The results in Alaska will come after Democrats already secured enough seats to take control of the Senate, winning in several states that President Trump won by double digits in 2024. It is the final Senate race to be decided, after the seat in Mississippi went to Democrat Scott Colom by a narrow margin.
Speaking to reporters in the early hours after Election Day, Peltola said, "The results are not going to be fast."
"But Alaskans are patient," she said. "We just want to make sure the folks [in] the Lower 48 know it won't be hours, it won't be days, it will be weeks."
Sen. Sullivan likewise emphasized to supporters, "We're going to have a long night," adding, "We're probably going to have some long weeks."
