title: 8-year-old Haitian boy released from federal custody in San Diego
summary: The Department of Homeland Security previously confirmed that ICE agents placed the child in federal care after he attended a check-in appointment with a man the agency said claimed to be the boy's uncle.
story: An 8-year-old Haitian boy who was placed in federal custody earlier this month after an immigration appointment in San Diego has been released, according to an advocacy group and the boy's school.

Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents had placed the boy in federal care on Nov. 5 after he attended a check-in appointment with a man the agency says claimed to be the boy's uncle, Homeland Security confirmed at the time.

"School leadership, and counselors had a meeting with the student when he returned to school this morning to ensure he had all the supports he and his family needed, and then he went off to class," the San Diego Unified School District said in a statement.
Haitian Bridge Alliance, which had advocated for the boy's release, said it welcomed the development.

"An eight-year-old child belongs in a classroom, on a playground, and surrounded by love—not in immigration detention," said Guerline Jozef, executive director of Haitian Bridge Alliance, in a statement. "We welcome his release, but his freedom should never have required a public outcry."

Haitian Bridge Alliance said the boy, a third grader, has been living with relatives since his father was deported in 2025. In August of this year, following a legal victory for the Trump administration, some 350,000 Haitians living in the U.S. lost Temporary Protected Status, stripping them of deportation protections and work permits.

Advocates recorded and documented the moment when the 8-year-old was escorted by at least one ICE agent inside the Edward J. Schwartz building in San Diego, with Haitian Bridge Alliance saying the detention left the boy's cousins "in tears."
DHS said at the time that the agents designated the child an unaccompanied minor because "the alleged uncle could not establish legal guardianship of the minor."

"Out of an abundance of caution and to ensure the child's safety, ICE determined it was best to remove the child from the household and place him in the care of the Office of Refugee Resettlement," DHS added.

The Office of Refugee Resettlement is an agency within the Department of Health and Human Services that is responsible for housing minors who lack a valid immigration status and who are taken into custody without their parents or legal guardians.

Haitian Bridge Alliance said in a previous statement that "when parents are taken into custody by ICE, they are not provided an opportunity to return home to see their children or to be able to transfer guardianship."
"ICE just incarcerated then deported without taking into account the wellbeing of the children left behind," it said.

title: Apple restores services after internal update caused outages
summary: The company's system status shows that all Apple services, including iCloud sign-in, have been restored after experiencing issues earlier Tuesday.
story: Apple said it has restored all services after users reported issues with Apple Pay, Apple Support, iCloud and other products on Tuesday.
A spokesperson for the company told CBS News in an email that its services are "green across the board," referring to the System Status page on Apple's website, as of approximately 5:46 p.m. ET.

Thousands of people reported issues with Apple services on Tuesday, according to the tracking site Downdetector.com. The reports started to spike before noon ET and lasted several hours before tapering off in the afternoon, the site shows.

By 4:45 p.m. ET, Apple's system status page showed problems with iCloud sign-in and "AppleCare on device" had been resolved. However, some services, including Apple Business and Apple School Manager, were still experiencing issues, according to the tech giant.
The issues were not the result of a cyberattack, according to the spokesperson.

Apple is the latest company to experience service disruptions following a string of outages that affected everything from air travel to Microsoft email. On Monday, customers at JPMorgan Chase, Bank of America and other major financial institutions also reported service issues affecting bank deposits and Zelle transfers.

Users also reported issues accessing Gmail on Tuesday. In a statement shared on X, Google said it isn't "currently seeing evidence of a broad Gmail service disruption" and encouraged users to check its workplace status dashboard for updates.

title: Groups raise concerns over DOJ's new Civil Rights Division chief
summary: Eighteen civil rights organizations asked President Trump to withdraw his appointment of Craig Trainor as the new acting head of the Justice Department's Civil Rights Division.
story: Washington — Eighteen civil rights organizations asked President Trump on Tuesday to withdraw his appointment of Craig Trainor as the new acting assistant attorney general for the Justice Department's Civil Rights Division, saying he has a track record of undermining the laws he is tasked with enforcing.
Trainor was appointed last week to replace Harmeet Dhillon, who resigned from her post shortly after the midterm elections.

Trainor most recently served as assistant secretary for fair housing and equal opportunity at the Department of Housing and Urban Development. Prior to that, he held several senior roles at the Department of Education.

He also previously served as a senior special counsel to GOP Rep. Jim Jordan of Ohio on the House Judiciary Committee as well as the Select Subcommittee on the Weaponization of the Federal Government.

Tuesday's statement opposing his appointment was signed by a variety of organizations, including the National Center for Youth Law, the Leadership Conference on Civil and Human Rights, National Council of Jewish Women, Human Rights Campaign, the Sikh Coalition and Stop Sexual Assault in Schools, among others.
"In the midterm elections, the American people rejected an agenda to divide, discriminate against, and diminish our communities," the groups said.

"Instead of rebuilding a Civil Rights Division decimated under Harmeet Dhillon, the Administration has chosen to elevate the official behind a court-blocked classroom censorship agenda who seeks to undermine the rights of survivors and equal opportunity in our schools and communities," they added.

In response, the Justice Department told CBS News that the accusations against Trainor are "politically motivated and factually wrong," and alleged the groups who lodged the complaint are more interested in "preserving their preferred ideological status quo than ensuring that civil rights laws are applied as written."

"The Civil Rights Division exists to protect the civil rights of every American and enforce federal law equally—not to defend entrenched interests or advance the agendas of activist organizations," the Justice Department said. "Craig Trainor will carry out that mission without apology or intimidation, ensuring that every American's civil rights are protected and that the law is applied fairly, consistently, and as written."
The civil rights groups said that Trainor took action in his prior roles at the Department of Education and HUD that scaled back civil liberties.

After a court struck down a Department of Education rule that broadened the definition of what constitutes sexual harassment under Title IX of the Civil Rights Act, Trainor issued a directive to schools in February 2025 that ordered them to revert to less-stringent standards that were adopted in 2020.
Many civil rights groups have long criticized the 2020 standards and referred to them as "anti-survivor" rules because the definition of what constitutes sexual harassment is narrower.
The 2020 rules also only require schools to investigate allegations of sexual assault or harassment under Title IX that occur on school grounds, excluding conduct that may occur abroad or off campus.

The groups also pointed to threats that Trainor directed toward schools in a Feb. 14, 2025, letter, in which he threatened to withhold federal funding if they had diversity, equity and inclusion programs.
Several federal courts later enjoined the Department of Education from following through on its threats to withhold the funds.
After he left and went to HUD, Trainor also shuttered many discrimination investigations under the Fair Housing Act, the groups said.
In announcing his appointment, Attorney General Todd Blanche praised his actions at HUD, saying he helped to "cut the Biden-era Fair Housing case backlog in half."
Trainor is taking over the helm of a Civil Rights Division that was largely gutted under Dhillon's leadership, as more than 75% of its staff left since January 2025.
Although Dhillon later hired more attorneys, the staffing level is still not what it once was.

Dhillon reoriented the division away from its historical mission of protecting some of society's most vulnerable and marginalized groups. She shifted its focus to other priorities that included protecting gun owners' rights, curbing the use of equity, diversity and inclusion policies at universities, and adopting legal positions that oppose civil rights protections for transgender people.

title: Democrats have flipped 46 House seats. Here's the breakdown.
summary: Democrats won control of the House by flipping more than 40 Republican-held seats, picking up perennial swing districts and seats that were once considered deep red.
story: Washington — Democrats won control of the House of Representatives on Nov. 3 by flipping more than 40 Republican-held seats, picking up perennial swing districts and seats that were once considered deep red. The party's wins ranged from suburban areas in the northeastern United States to areas of South Texas that were once viewed as increasingly GOP-friendly.

The 2026 midterm elections were also shaken up by last year's nationwide mid-decade redistricting gambit, with Texas Republicans shifting several districts rightward at President Trump's behest, California Democrats moving districts to the left and several other states tweaking their House maps for partisan purposes. Democrats notched several wins under the new maps, while the GOP's pickups have been more limited so far.
Winners in a handful of House races have yet to be projected by CBS News.
So far, 46 districts have shifted to Democrats and three have shifted to Republicans. Here's a look at the seats that swung:
Upsets
In several districts, Democrats ousted GOP lawmakers who won by double digits two years ago.

New Jersey's 2nd District: Republican Rep. Jeff Van Drew lost to Democrat Zack Mullock in a South Jersey district that was widely seen as solid red. Van Drew, who won by 16.9 points in 2024, is known for switching from the Democratic Party during the first Trump impeachment saga in 2019. Ohio's 10th District: GOP Rep. Mike Turner was ousted by Democrat Kristina Knickerbocker, ending Turner's nearly quarter-century tenure in Congress just two years after he won reelection by more than 18 points.Missouri's 2nd District: Democrat Fred Wellman unseated GOP Rep. Ann Wagner, who won by 12 points in 2024. Republicans tried to make the St. Louis-area seat slightly redder last year, but the new maps were tossed out in the courts. As recently as September, the Cook Political Report viewed it as solid-red.Indiana's 5th District: Republican Rep. Victoria Spartz lost to Democrat J.D. Ford in one of several election night surprises. Spartz won reelection by just over 18 points in 2024.Kentucky's 6th District: The race between Democrat Zach Dembo and Republican Ralph Alvarado for the open seat was not expected to be competitive, but the election forecasters moved the GOP-held seat toward Democrats in recent weeks. Outgoing Rep. Andy Barr won it by 26 points two years ago.Wisconsin's 1st District: Republican Rep. Bryan Steil, who was first elected in 2018, lost his race to Democrat Mitchell Berman. A Democrat has not represented the district in more than 30 years. title: Mary Peltola wins Alaska Senate race, flipping seat for Dems
summary: Mary Peltola, 53, defeated incumbent GOP Sen. Dan Sullivan and will be the first Alaska Native to serve in the U.S. Senate.
story: Washington — Former Democratic Rep. Mary Peltola defeated GOP Sen. Dan Sullivan in the Alaska Senate race, CBS News projects, adding to the new Democratic majority in the Senate two weeks after Election Day.
With the Alaska race now decided, Democrats will control 56 Senate seats to Republicans' 44.

Peltola, 53, was the first Democrat to represent Alaska in the House in 50 years in 2022. She is now set to become the first Alaska Native to be elected to the Senate, and the first Democrat to be elected to the Senate in the state since 2008.

"As a lifelong Alaskan who has dedicated my life to serving our state, there is no greater honor than having Alaskans' support in our fight to take on corporate greed, lower costs, and put Alaska first," Peltola said in a statement Tuesday night. " As our next United States Senator, I will stand up to anyone to take on the rigged system in DC and deliver results for Alaska's working families."
"Thank you Alaska. Let's get to work," she added.

Sullivan, a second-term senator and a Marine veteran, was fighting to hold on to the seat. Peltola successfully portrayed herself as an independent voice for the state. She lost her reelection bid for Alaska's sole House seat in 2024 by less than 3 points, while President Trump won the state by 13 points. But the dynamics were more favorable for her this cycle, with the unpopular war in Iran and high gas and diesel prices hanging over Republican candidates.

The contest was decided by ranked-choice voting. In addition to Sullivan, Peltola faced off against another candidate with nearly the same name as the incumbent, Daniel J. Sullivan, and Republican Gerald Heikes.

The second Dan Sullivan, a former teacher, added a wrinkle to the race. He announced he was challenging the sitting senator in June, prompting an unsuccessful push to remove him from the ballot. But both Dan Sullivans ultimately appeared on the ballot, in a development that Republicans argued could impact the incumbent senator's chances.

About a week and a half before Election Day, the Trump administration sued to prevent the Alaska Senate election from being certified if Sen. Sullivan were to lose to Peltola because of the other Daniel Sullivan.
But in the end, Peltola's margin was large enough that those votes wouldn't have made a difference.

Heading into election night, polls showed a dead heat between Peltola and Sen. Sullivan. Republicans sent their biggest names to stump for Sullivan, including Vice President JD Vance. And the Senate GOP's main super PAC, the Senate Leadership Fund, spent heavily in the race.

Republicans had hoped to retain the seat and their GOP majority in an unexpectedly competitive environment this cycle. Though Democrats initially faced steep headwinds, competitive races opened up in several states that Mr. Trump had won in 2024 by double digits, including Alaska.

title: Rubio says there's "zero evidence" recent tech outages are related
summary: Secretary of State Marco Rubio acknowledged that people are fearful and uncertain, saying he wanted to be clear that the United States is not under systemic attack.
story: Secretary of State Marco Rubio said there's "zero evidence" that recent tech outages in U.S. air travel, banking and other systems are connected.

"The Microsoft incident has nothing to do with what we saw with the FAA. The FAA has nothing to do with what we saw with the banks a few days ago. These issues that we've seen from a technical standpoint are completely unrelated one from another," Rubio said Wednesday morning local time during a news conference in the Philippines.
Rubio acknowledged that people are fearful and uncertain, saying he wanted to be clear that the United States is not under systemic attack.

"We have zero evidence or any reason to believe that any of these isolated or individual instances have anything to do with nefarious actors, with cyber hackers, with criminals, with another nation state, with a malign actor of any kind," Rubio said.

Rubio, who is traveling with President Trump ahead of a trilateral meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping this week, added that the administration is "always on the lookout" for any potential attacks and reiterated multiple times that reports of technical issues are not interconnected.
"Each of them are distinct, and they're different in their causation," he said.

On Thursday, Microsoft said it experienced a worldwide outage affecting services like Outlook and Teams, impacting users, companies and government operations worldwide. The company said the outage was linked to a technical issue, not malicious or cyber activity.

The following day, the Federal Aviation Administration issued a nationwide ground stop on all departing U.S. flights for several hours, throwing the aviation industry into turmoil. Federal officials identified a contractor performing maintenance updates as the cause of Friday's disruption, but key questions remain about the underlying cause of the systemwide failure.

Other recent outages that have since been resolved include disruptions to major banks like JPMorgan Chase, Bank of America and U.S. Bank, and issues with Apple's services. On Tuesday, the National Security Agency's internal network used to store and share classified information went offline, multiple U.S. officials familiar told CBS News.

Democratic Sen. Mark Warner, vice chair of the Senate Intelligence Committee, also said on Tuesday that there's no indication these incidents are the result of an attack, but noted that artificial intelligence is creating pressure for companies to deal with vulnerabilities.

"AI is making it possible to identify vulnerabilities across enormous numbers of systems at unprecedented speed, creating enormous pressure on companies and government agencies to patch those vulnerabilities immediately, often all at once, putting tremendous strain on systems that weren't built to handle that pace of change," Warner said in a post on X. "It feels like every day brings another reminder that AI is moving faster than our ability to manage its consequences.   This is exactly why I've been pushing for commonsense guardrails on AI and stronger cybersecurity protections."
When asked Wednesday about the role of AI in recent incidents, Rubio said he didn't want to speculate because every incident is unique and referred to individual companies.

title: Airline schedules returning to normal after ground stop, FAA says
summary: Officials attributed the ground stop to aging system infrastructure and legacy technology.
story: Operations were slowly returning to normal or close to it at most major airlines Monday after a rare nationwide ground stop that lasted more than four hours on Friday, causing chaos in the nation's airports with thousands of flights canceled and travelers stranded.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy told CBS News' "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan" on Sunday that travelers should expect delays to continue but "we should be running at full capacity" heading into Monday.

"What happens with a ground stop, like on Friday, we have airplanes and crews that are out of position, so it takes a little bit of time for the airlines to get back and choreographed and at full capacity and operations, but we're well on our way," he said.

Still, more than 2,300 flights within, into or out of the U.S. were canceled Sunday, according to flight tracking website FlightAware, and more than 10,400 were delayed, though not necessarily as a result of ripple effects from the ground stop.
FlightAware said more than 250 Monday flights had been canceled and 850 delayed as of 6:30 a.m. EST.
How did the FAA ground stop happen?
The ground stop began at 3:36 p.m. ET Friday when the FAA ordered the stoppage while approximately 3,500 flights were in the air.
"The FAA issued a ground stop out of an abundance of caution while 3,500+ planes were in the air," Duffy said. All airborne planes were able to land safely.
It was lifted around 8:20 p.m. ET Friday.
This marked the first nationwide ground stop since January 2023, when a key FAA computer system malfunctioned. Before that, the last national ground stop occurred after the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks.
Around 9,159 flights were canceled on Friday and 7,190 were delayed, according to FlightAware, stranding passengers at major airports across the country.
Officials attributed the ground stop to aging system infrastructure and legacy technology.
"It's just the FAA is still using this really old telecom network that has to be updated, upgraded, and I think built brand new," Duffy said on "Face the Nation" on Sunday.

Duffy told reporters on Saturday that a preliminary investigation found that a contractor for L3Harris, a technology and defense company, was working in a remote FAA location and switching old copper wire to fiber while replacing a router. The router that was being switched then started flooding other routers, overloading the system. There were 1,000 attempts to log on every four to five seconds, he said.

It took L3Harris, which owns the network that runs the nation's air traffic control system, several hours to pinpoint the source of the frequency outage, delaying the lifting of Friday's nationwide ground stop, according to a person familiar with the investigation.

The transportation secretary said the FAA is working to determine if the issue was human error or if a faulty router was installed. Duffy said that many contractors "take our money and provide really poor service."
L3Harris said Saturday that the company has been modernizing the communications infrastructure supporting the National Airspace System in close coordination with the FAA.

"We are supporting the FAA in its investigation to understand the conditions that led to the Nov. 13 ground stop of our nation's air travel," the company said in a statement, adding that it takes the nationwide ground stop and "its impact" seriously.

Federal Aviation Administration Administrator Bryan Bedford told reporters on Saturday that updating the wires was a routine maintenance issue that the agency had been working on for years. About 70% of the system has been transferred from copper wires to fiber. After the router began flooding the system for 45 minutes, the FAA could not determine the cause of the instability. The instability then spread to 17 facilities, he said.
"Out of an abundance of caution," the FAA decided to issue a ground stop, Bedford said. He said he stands behind that call.
Bedford said there was zero evidence of anything nefarious or anything AI-related.
Senior government sources told CBS News on Friday that the issue was isolated to specific hardware: Cisco 600 series routers manufactured between 2001 and 2006.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said in a Friday briefing there were no indications the ground stop was the result of a cyberattack. Duffy said Saturday he doesn't believe it was a cyberattack, but that it was an FAA system that didn't "meet the moment."
Request for more FAA funding
Duffy said in a social media post on Friday that the FAA is working to modernize "this aging infrastructure thanks to a $12.5 billion down payment secured by President Trump, but that isn't ENOUGH."

"I've been talking about this for almost two years, and I've been asking the Congress for money. I've asked for a lot of money," he said Saturday. "Now, the Congress gave me a partial payment. They gave me 12 and a half billion dollars. And one of the problems that we had was they weren't quite sure that we would spend the money well and we'd build with the money."
The Trump administration boosted its request for air traffic control funding to $30 billion late Friday.

President Trump, who broke his silence Sunday on the ground stop, said in a new post on Truth Social that his administration has begun upgrading that system, but that the task should not be done in "drips and drabs."

"If Congress approves the desperately needed money for Air Traffic Control, we can get it built quickly and efficiently," Mr. Trump wrote on social media Sunday. "It will be the BEST SYSTEM anywhere in the World. Much of our current air control system is 50 years old - RIDICULOUS!"

In another post, he complained about how his Democratic predecessor had maintained the FAA and the air traffic control system, accusing the Biden administration of making an "old and broken system worse than when they began."

Rep. Rick Larsen, the ranking member of the House Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure, and Rep. Andre Carson, the ranking member of the Subcommittee on Aviation, said in a joint statement Saturday that FAA and DOT staff will brief the committees on Monday about the additional $30 billion requested by the Trump administration.

"This ground stop left the flying public and aviation workforce in disarray and seeking answers that the Trump administration waited hours to share," the two Democrats said. "The safe travel of the flying public must always be our top priority. Our committee, on behalf of the flying public, will hold the administration accountable for what happened to make sure this chaos does not happen again."
The pair said the Trump administration has only used $1 billion of the $12.5 billion approved by Congress.
"Explain to Congress, again, why they need more money," they said.
Can Americans still travel safely?
Several U.S. officials said it is completely safe for Americans to fly.
"Our top priority right now is making sure travelers get home safely to their families as quickly as possible," Duffy said Friday.

The FAA administrator said on Saturday there were 50,000 flights scheduled for Friday and by the time the ground stop happened, 30,000 flights had been completed. Due to the ground stop, about 12,000 flights were not able to be completed — around 3,000 of those were private flights, while the rest were commercial, Bedford said.
Delays remain possible at major airports nationwide, including those in Boston, Atlanta, Miami, Pittsburgh, New York City, Los Angeles and Baltimore.

Duffy said travelers should check with their airlines before heading to the airport. Delta said on Saturday it would offer customers flexible rebooking options. The airline said it was continuing to restore operations after a four-hour ground stop.
"Customers traveling today should expect delays and additional schedule adjustments as we work to reposition flight crews and aircraft, " Delta said.
American Airlines said on Saturday the airline has taken a number of steps toward recovery, but travelers should continue to monitor the situation as operations return to normal.

"While we are taking every step to limit the impact on our customers and team members, the lingering effects of this major disruption to the national airspace system will continue today, including additional delays and cancellations."
Southwest said Saturday the airline instituted a waiver to allow customers to cancel their flights or rebook them at a later date without penalty.
"We are working to get our Customers to their destinations as quickly as possible," Southwest said.

Olivia  Rinaldi, 
                                                  
                                  Pat  Milton, 
                                                  
                                  Kris  Van Cleave and

title: Trump FDA nominee Heidi Overton struggling to win GOP support
summary: Heidi Overton, Trump's pick to be FDA commissioner, is having trouble finding enough Republican support to advance her nomination, which could be pulled if she falls short.
story: Update: The White House has withdrawn Dr. Heidi Overton's nomination, CBS News confirmed Tuesday. Read more here.

Dr. Heidi Overton, President Trump's pick to be FDA commissioner, is struggling to shore up enough support in the Senate Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee as it prepares to vote on her nomination Wednesday.

Sources tell CBS News that she's having trouble finding enough Republicans on the committee to vote to advance her nomination, which could be pulled if she can't muster the support. None of the Democrats on the committee are expected to back her.

The White House knows it has a problem, one source said, and has already begun looking for a new candidate. A second source confirmed that the White House has been talking to potential candidates, including some who could serve in an acting capacity and thus forgo Senate confirmation.
CBS News has reached out to the White House for comment.

Overton's nomination has run aground over her testimony regarding the FDA-approved chemical abortion drug mifepristone and her execution of President Trump's pro-vaping policies while she served on the Domestic Policy Council.

Missouri Republican Sen. Josh Hawley has emerged as one of the skeptics. Overton sidestepped questions on how she would handle a safety study long promised by the Trump administration into mifepristone, which Hawley has pressed for as well. The anti-abortion group Susan B. Anthony urged the Senate to delay her confirmation, and wants the FDA to commit to banning mail orders of mifepristone.

And two pro-abortion-access Republicans on the committee — Sens. Susan Collins of Maine and Lisa Murkowski of Alaska — have also not said whether they'll vote to advance her nomination. During Overton's confirmation hearing, Murkowski asked her whether she would restrict mifepristone, which is used in more than half of abortions in the U.S.

The administration has spoken with candidates about taking the FDA commissioner role in an acting capacity. That's one route to avoiding the Senate confirmation process during the narrow three-week legislative window ahead. The FDA oversees products that account for roughly 20% of consumer spending.
Two sources indicated Sen. Roger Marshall of Kansas, a doctor, is making a play for the FDA post. He lost his reelection bid to Democrat Adam Hamilton earlier this month.
Overton is arguably the Trump nominee with the highest profile who is struggling to shore up sufficient support in the closing weeks of GOP congressional control.

On Tuesday, Hung Cao, Mr. Trump's pick to serve as secretary of the Navy, faced a bipartisan grilling over his management of wartime operations and the Pentagon's decision to block Democrats from some classified military briefings. And retiring North Carolina Republican Sen. Thom Tillis said Tuesday he opposes the nomination of Eric Ueland, currently the deputy director of the Office of Management and Budget, to lead the Government Accountability Office, because of the involvement of Ueland and OMB in implementing DOGE cuts.

The FDA has been helmed by acting Commissioner Kyle Diamantas since the last Senate-confirmed chief, Marty Makary, was forced out by the White House last spring. Multiple sources familiar with his ouster told CBS News that ongoing White House pressure over flavored vapes caused significant friction.

Dr. Makary told CBS News in a statement on Nov. 8 that "big tobacco exploited their connections to administration and HHS officials to put repeated pressure on me to approve fruit-flavored vapes that appeal to children – I wouldn't do it."
Mr. Trump campaigned in 2024 on a promise to save vaping, a smoking alternative that can help with breaking the smoking habit, but also has been found to have serious health side effects.

CBS News' "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan" asked outgoing HELP Chairman Sen. Bill Cassidy, Republican of Louisiana, about whether Republicans would be able to install a Senate-confirmed FDA commissioner in these last weeks that they control the Senate. He raised the concern that the alternative would mean installing acting commissioners.

"Do we want a series of short-term administrators who probably will have more influence from the secretary, as opposed to someone who may be not, you know, the perfect candidate in somebody's mind, but at least would be a permanent one and have the ability to establish some independence. And that's part of the thought process there. That weighs on one side, and of course other things weigh on the other," Cassidy said Sunday.

Asked by "Face the Nation" about his own past remarks that Overton's association with Mr. Trump's efforts around reducing childhood vaccine uptake was "almost disqualifying," Cassidy acknowledged he was still working the phones and uncertain about whether Overton's nomination would be advanced by the HELP Committee he chairs, and he also did not say which way he would vote.

Overton stood beside Mr. Trump in the Oval Office as he signed an executive order on vaccines this summer — and the president twice erroneously referred to the measles or MMR vaccine as "lethal." None of the health officials present corrected Mr. Trump.

Recently resigned MAHA leader Calley Means, a former top adviser to Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., has also urged his followers to help block Overton's confirmation. He told "Face the Nation," "Heidi Overton was the biggest block to MAHA policies I encountered in the government."

Defenders of Overton dismissed criticism of her compliance with Mr. Trump's policies, and point to her medical background and her endorsement by two former FDA commissioners as a sign that she will be a professional.
At this hour, the vote to confirm Overton and a handful of other health officials is still scheduled to take place Wednesday morning.

title: Outcome of Alaska Senate race could take weeks to determine
summary: The Senate race in Alaska, which has garnered widespread attention with two candidates named Dan Sullivan, remains in limbo.
story: Update: Democrat Mary Peltola is projected to win the Alaska Senate race. Read the latest here. Our earlier coverage is below.

Washington — The Senate race in Alaska remains unresolved more than two weeks after Election Day as a contest that has garnered widespread attention over the two candidates named Dan Sullivan faces a lengthy ballot-counting process.

Incumbent Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan and Democrat Mary Peltola are facing off in the race, which also has two other candidates on the ballot: an independent candidate and retired teacher Daniel J. Sullivan, and another Republican, Gerald Heikes.
With 98% of the vote in as of Tuesday, Nov. 17, the race is leaning Democratic, according to CBS News estimates, with Peltola's lead growing to about 4 percentage points ahead of Sen. Sullivan.

The count in Alaska could stretch on. Alaska has a ranked-choice voting system, which allows voters to rank as many or as few candidates as they'd like in order of preference. If no candidate secures support from more than 50% of voters as their top choice, the count goes to a second round.

The ranked-choice tabulation doesn't occur until the last counting of ballots 15 days after Election Day, meaning the process could drag on for weeks if one candidate does not secure more than 50% of first-place support on the ballot.

The results in Alaska will come after Democrats already secured enough seats to take control of the Senate, winning in several states that President Trump won by double digits in 2024. It is the final Senate race to be decided, after the seat in Mississippi went to Democrat Scott Colom by a narrow margin.
Speaking to reporters in the early hours after Election Day, Peltola said, "The results are not going to be fast."
"But Alaskans are patient," she said. "We just want to make sure the folks [in] the Lower 48 know it won't be hours, it won't be days, it will be weeks."
Sen. Sullivan likewise emphasized to supporters, "We're going to have a long night," adding, "We're probably going to have some long weeks."

title: Duffy pitches Senate GOP on $50 billion for FAA after ground stop
summary: Senate Republicans appeared skeptical after Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy made the case for tens of billions of more dollars for the Federal Aviation Administration.
story: Washington — Senate Republicans appeared skeptical Tuesday after Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy made the case for tens of billions of more dollars for the Federal Aviation Administration following a telecommunication outage that prompted a rare nationwide ground stop last week.
Overloaded routers prompted the FAA to issue the ground stop on Friday, resulting in thousands of canceled flights and stranded travelers.

Duffy is seeking $50 billion to overhaul the FAA's systems, some of which still rely on technology that is decades old. There was widespread concern among lawmakers about the problem, but GOP senators questioned the funding figure — and how the money could get approved.

Speaking at a news conference following a closed-door lunch meeting with Duffy, Senate Majority Leader John Thune said the secretary "fielded a lot of questions" about the funding and how it would be utilized.
"How we deal with that issue remains to be seen," Thune said. "There are ways in which we could do it with Republicans only, there are also ways in which we could do it with Democrats."

Senate Republicans have been considering pursuing another reconciliation bill, which would allow them to move forward without help from across the aisle. But the legislative maneuver is complicated and time-consuming. Thune said Republicans are continuing to have conversations, which will stretch into Wednesday, but he acknowledged that "the clock is ticking" down to the end of the current Congress.

Congress allocated $12.5 billion for the FAA in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act just last year. Duffy said the bulk of that money has been set aside for various projects, and Thune pointed to the funds on Tuesday, acknowledging that "we needed air traffic modernization."
"We did that then — there's more that's required," Thune said. "How that gets done is still an open question."

Thune suggested some senators have concerns about the $50 billion figure. He said the total the administration initially sought before the ground stop — $30 billion — reflected "not just the immediate needs," but also "a number of other things that they want to do." He said some of those projects should be funded through the normal government funding process, not reconciliation.
When asked about the $20 billion difference, Duffy told CBS News that he "decided to put everything on the table."
"There's been a historic underinvestment in aviation," Duffy said. "I hope we get the full investment."
GOP Sen. John Kennedy of Louisiana told reporters he was "furious when they went from $30 billion to $50 billion."
"I mean, I'm not Bambi's baby brother," Kennedy said.
Sen. Rick Scott of Florida thanked Duffy in a post on X, while expressing support for a smaller investment.

"We absolutely need to update our air traffic control system, which would cost about $10 billion," Scott wrote, while stressing that "the airlines need to put up money and have skin in this game too."

But other Senate Republicans were entirely supportive of the transportation secretary's pitch. Sen. Eric Schmitt of Missouri, who's been working with the administration on proposed aviation infrastructure funding, told reporters that "the needs are pretty broad and pretty deep" for tech upgrades.
"So my position is: Let's go fix this on behalf of the American people," he said. "They saw what happened. I think they would want us to be responsive to that."
Schmitt advocated for approving the funds through reconciliation. He said he doesn't want to "make this partisan," but "some of my Democrat colleagues, I think, are taking a different tack."

"I was advocating for this before Friday, and then what we saw Friday, I just think this is something that we should do," Schmitt said. "I can't think of anything more important than the safety of the millions of Americans that fly."

Speaking after the meeting, Duffy said the engagement from Republicans was "fantastic." He said the GOP plans to "work through what they think is the right approach, the right funding levels, to make sure we have the resources to address the needs of the American airspace."

Duffy outlined his new request to Congress, saying the U.S. needs a new network that is "resilient," and an investment in infrastructure, like air traffic control towers, new runways and for airports more broadly. Asked about a piecemeal approach, Duffy said he'll take what he can get. But he said if the status quo continues, "I will replace every single tower in America in 300 years."
"So we have to do something different," Duffy said.

Caitlin  Huey-Burns
                  
        contributed to this report.

title: U.S. officially loses measles elimination status: "What a tragedy"
summary: The United States has lost its official measles elimination status for the first time in 26 years. Here's what to know.
story: The United States has officially lost its measles elimination status, global health officials announced Tuesday.

The decision from the Pan American Health Organization came after the U.S. recorded over 5,400 measles cases so far this year — more than double last year's total. The Pan American Health Organization is a regional office for the World Health Organization, covering North and South America. Researchers with knowledge of the decision had previously confirmed it to CBS News partner KFF Health News on Saturday.
A country is considered as having eliminated the measles if there are "no locally transmitted measles infections or outbreaks lasting 12 months or longer," according to the World Health Organization.

The United States did not meet that standard for the first time since 2000. According to data from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, about a third of this year's measles cases are linked to outbreaks that began in 2025 and continued to spread.

After a 30-year record of 2,242 cases last year, the CDC has tallied 5,412 cases to date in 2026, resulting in more than 590 hospitalizations and at least six measles-related deaths, with some states reporting additional fatalities.

"It's profoundly sad and disappointing," Dr. William Schaffner, a professor of preventive medicine and infectious diseases at the Vanderbilt University Medical Center, told CBS News. "What a tragedy. We have had children die of measles this past year. That should never have happened. Those deaths and all those cases, 5,000-plus, were completely preventable."

The biggest outbreak has been in Pennsylvania, where state health officials have reported more than 1,500 cases and seven deaths associated with the disease this year. Wisconsin reports two children have died and New York had its first measles death in more than 30 years.
Measles cases have been confirmed so far this year in 45 states and Washington, D.C.

"The measles elimination designation is not what protects Americans. Vaccination does," CDC Director Dr. Erica Schwartz said in a statement. "We know where transmission is occurring and we've invested $100 million in state and local health departments to reach those communities." She said the CDC remains focused on stopping outbreaks.

Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. said Tuesday on social media, "We will stop measles outbreaks, protect American families, and work to regain U.S. measles elimination status. I continue to recommend MMR vaccination as the most effective way to prevent measles."
Kennedy pointed to "COVID-era disruptions" in childhood vaccinations and cited other countries, including Canada, Mexico, Spain and the United Kingdom, that have also lost measles elimination status.

Sen. Bill Cassidy, a Republican from Louisiana who is also a doctor, said health officials, including Kennedy, should be doing more to promote the importance of vaccination to protect against measles.

"Speaking as a physician, you may decide not to be vaccinated because it's your free will, but the child who's too young to be vaccinated is vulnerable if you come into that child's presence, and we're seeing children die from measles who are too young to be vaccinated," Cassidy said on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan."
"So if you've not been vaccinated, you could be the person that brings death to another. That's something to remember."
What does it mean to lose measles elimination status?

A country or region loses its measles elimination status once its population immunity lowers enough that there is sustained spread of the disease, CBS News medical correspondent Dr. Céline Gounder explained. When a country has measles elimination status and a high rate of vaccination, a case of measles or small outbreak will soon fizzle out. But when there are this many gaps in the population's immunity, there can be "ongoing chains of transmission," Gounder said.

"It means that we're at risk of being exposed to measles and getting measles if we're not vaccinated," Gounder said. "It means ERs and pediatricians need to consider measles in anyone with a fever and rash, whether they've traveled overseas or not. And we may now become an exporter of measles to other countries."
Dr. Omer Awan, a trained epidemiologist and senior public health contributor for Forbes, said that the loss of measles elimination status is a setback to the nation's public health infrastructure.

"It's frustrating and heartbreaking ... because we have the tools to fight this. The tool is the MMR vaccine, which we know is 97% effective at preventing the onset of measles," Awan said. "It'd be one thing if we didn't have the tools to fight this, but the tools are at our disposal, we just aren't using the tools that can help us mitigate the spread and beat measles."
How can the U.S. regain measles elimination status?
A country earns measles elimination status by ensuring there is no local spread of the disease or outbreaks that last for more than a year.

PAHO says that the best way to maintain the elimination of measles is maintaining a vaccination rate of 95% or higher. Countries should also have sensitive surveillance systems to detect cases quickly, laboratory capacity and a guaranteed rapid response to outbreaks. Data about these trends must be submitted to and verified by the organization.

For the U.S. to curb outbreaks and regain measles elimination status, it needs to return to higher rates of vaccination, Awan said. He said battling misinformation and ramping up vaccination campaigns would be key to that effort.
Data shows childhood vaccination rates have declined in many communities around the U.S. in recent years, often below the threshold needed to help ward off measles outbreaks.
Gounder also noted that lawmakers can create policies that lead to increased vaccination rates.

"States set the school vaccine rules. Nine states made opting out of vaccination easier in 2025. States ending nonmedical exemptions saw kindergarten vaccination rise 2 to 4 points," Gounder said. "Most legislatures reconvene in January. Your state lawmakers will write next year's exemption rules."
Measles in the U.S.

The United States started collecting national data on measles in 1912, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. About 6,000 measles-related deaths were reported each year in the first decade of that data collection.

In the decade between 1953 and 1963, nearly all children in the U.S. caught measles before they turned 15, with an estimated 3 to 4 million people infected each year and tens of thousands hospitalized, according to the CDC. In those years, 400 to 500 people, mostly children, died of measles annually.
Then in 1963, the measles vaccine first became widely available. The numbers began a sharp decline and several generations of Americans grew up without ever encountering measles.
By 1981, reported measles cases had dropped by 80% compared to the previous year, the CDC said. The country was officially declared as having eliminated measles in 2000.

The U.S. maintained its elimination status for over 25 years. That didn't mean there were no cases at all — in 2015, an outbreak that spread among unvaccinated people was traced back to overseas visitors at Disneyland in Southern California, and a 2018-19 outbreak in New York was eventually contained by public health measures including curtailing vaccine exemptions. But those spikes were just a fraction of the spread now being seen in the U.S.

The nation recorded 2,242 measles cases in 2025, according to CDC data, linked to 48 separate outbreaks. The CDC reported 245 hospitalizations, mostly in children, and three measles deaths last year. Infections were confirmed in at least 44 states. It was the most cases the country had seen in over three decades.
That record was shattered in 2026, when the U.S. recorded more than double that number of cases by October — a total that topped 5,000 earlier this month.
Almost all of the cases have been in people who were not vaccinated. Measles-related deaths have been reported in Pennsylvania, New York and Wisconsin.

The CDC said 43 new outbreaks — defined as three or more related cases — have been reported so far in 2026, while about a third of the cases reported this year are tied to outbreaks that have been ongoing since 2025.
Who is at risk from measles?

Measles is one of the most contagious infectious diseases. Those who are unvaccinated for the disease are most at risk of getting it. CDC data shows that 96% of people infected with measles in 2026 had not been vaccinated for measles or were unsure of their vaccination status; only 2% of cases were in people who'd been fully vaccinated.
Medical research has shown that two doses of the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine is extremely safe and effective at protecting against measles.
But some people — including babies, pregnant women or people with weakened immune systems — cannot get vaccinated and must rely on population immunity to keep the disease from spreading.
"They will be the ones that are most vulnerable to getting infected and experiencing the complications," such as pneumonia or encephalitis, Awan said.
Many of the recent cases have been occurring in tight-knit and largely unvaccinated Amish or Mennonite communities.

"It really shows you who's vulnerable because these are totally unvaccinated communities," said Dr. Deborah Birx, a longtime public health official who was a leader of the White House Coronavirus Task Force during the pandemic. "You can see it in who's hospitalized. The largest percentage are children under 4 and adults over 50."

"I hope this is a wake-up call to every parent," Birx told CBS News. "If you had decided to not vaccinate your children, you've been relatively protected by all of us and all of our grandchildren and other children who got vaccinated. But that protection and that shield is going away" as vaccination rates slip. "And so your child is now vulnerable at a level they never were vulnerable before."

Measles is known for causing a rash, but Schaffner said that's the least of it. "What's bothersome is children, even with uncomplicated measles, are miserable for a week or a week and a half with red eyes, runny nose, cough, and just debilitating fever and diarrhea. And then you have the complications of dehydration, pneumonia, and on occasion, encephalitis."

There can be other lingering health consequences, Birx warned. Measles patients "can end up with what we call immune suppression, so that they're more susceptible to all other diseases after they've had measles."
While many people recover, measles can cause severe infections in the lungs and brain that can lead to cognitive issues, deafness or death.
"Measles is a nasty, nasty virus," Schaffner said. "In contrast, the vaccine is wonderfully effective."

title: Inside China's race to get humanoid robot helpers into our homes
summary: China is racing to make humanoid robot helpers common home appliances, and one industry insider says they have an "edge globally."
story: Wuhan, China — In the large lobby of a three story building in Wuhan, China, a child-size yellow robot greets visitors with a dance. It sways along to traditional Chinese music while robots twice the size stand on either side of the stage, beating loud drums to the rhythm. The little robot then moves on to another dance, bopping along to a pop tune that makes people smile and laugh.
The small humanoid robot's agility makes it look almost lifelike. Then it stops, and the crowd is ushered on to see the real wonders inside the Hubei Humanoid Robotics Innovation Center.

On the top floor, more than 100 computer science and engineering graduates toil at individual work stations wearing gloves and outfits equipped with motion and tactile sensors, while cameras record their every movement.
One pours water into a jug; another places cutlery and chopsticks into a container. The graduate at the next table unscrews a flashlight and removes the battery, then replaces it.

All the movements are done slowly, meticulously and repeated over and over again, with the actions recorded as valuable data from the cameras and sensors that can be used to train the company's humanoid robots.
"It was fun at first," said 22-year-old intern Mei. "It gets a little boring in the middle. But it's such a proud moment when we get the model trained."

Mei is one of nearly 1 million engineering graduates China's universities are estimated to be churning out every year. The U.S., by comparison, sends about 140,000 young engineers into the job market annually.
Another graduate sits with a remote control in his hand and a humanoid robot next to him. As he moves his hand, the robot mimics his motions.

"Right now I'm capturing the motion of pouring water into a cup. We're training this action and gathering data for the model. It's controlled by this hand controller. It moves exactly how the hand moves," he explains. "We need to run this hundreds or thousands of times. We have only completed 500 iterations so far."

At the G20 summit in September, Elon Musk made a bold statement, declaring that within 10 years, "there will be well over a billion humanoid robots, and productivity of a robot will be five-times that of a human."
The world's richest man may believe robots will replace human productivity within a decade, but many in China take a different view.

"Our main goal is for these robots to serve humans in household and industrial settings," Prof. Jiyin Cao, who runs the Hubei robotics center, told CBS News, clearly oozing pride over the work they are doing. "We train them to carry out tasks for industrial applications. This is why we train these robots — to help them integrate better into human life."

China is under enormous pressure to make that happen. The country has an aging, shrinking population. It's one of the fastest demographic shifts playing out anywhere in the world, and it is lending urgency to efforts to get humanoid robots into labor-intensive sectors such as manufacturing, logistics, retail and healthcare.

"I believe future robots will be deployed across all industries. They will work in factory workshops, homes, nuclear energy sites, provide elderly care services, and serve as our personal assistants," Cao told CBS News. "They can help us with all these things."
Training the humanoids, however, takes an enormous amount of time, especially for more complex tasks.
Robot soldiers likely only 5-10 years away, Chinese developer tells CBS News
Robot soldiers likely only 5-10 years away, Chinese developer tells CBS News
Cao laughed off any suggestion that most people could have humanoid helpers in their homes anytime soon.

"It still requires extensive training and learning," he said. "Home environments are unstructured, far from simple. Early robots mostly perform actions in simple, fixed, structured settings. But every household is unique, making home environments highly complex. It could be three to five years away before one is in our home. But it could also take 10 years."

The timescale may be up for debate, but China is working at breakneck speed and on a monumental scale to bring robots into the mainstream consumer world — and to ensure it is Chinese companies developing and making them.
"China has the world's strongest industrial manufacturing system and a full supply chain for upstream and downstream robotics products," Cao said. "That is our greatest edge globally."

title: China's Xi greets Trump at airport ahead of planned summit with Putin
summary: President Trump arrived Wednesday in China, where the Kremlin said he had an informal meeting with Vladimir Putin.
story: President Trump arrived in China on Wednesday after starting a multiday Asia swing in the Philippines. He's scheduled to meet in Shenzhen, a hub of China's tech industry, with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping in a highly anticipated summit on Thursday.
Mr. Trump said he may meet with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, with Secretary of State Marco Rubio saying such a meeting "may not be possible" but the president is "prepared" for one.
Xi greeted Mr. Trump on a red carpet as he walked off Air Force One in Shenzhen.

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Mr. Trump and Putin had an informal meeting Wednesday ahead of the planned trilateral summit. Peskov also said Putin had already held a meeting with Xi, during which they discussed the war in Ukraine. Mr. Trump and Putin may also discuss Ukraine, Peskov said.
Putin mentioned his recent discussions in Moscow with Mr. Trump's envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner during his meeting with Xi on Wednesday, Peskov said.

"The three leaders have a lot to discuss, given the unstable situation in the world," Putin's senior aide Yury Ushakov told reporters in Shenzhen, according to Russian state broadcaster Vesti. He did not confirm the plan for an initial bilateral meeting between Putin and Mr. Trump on Wednesday, but said they might meet during an formal dinner.
It "will not be a single event" Ushakov said of the possibility of Trump-Putin encounters on Wednesday. "It will take place both standing, on the steps, and while seated."

In Manila, Mr. Trump visited the Malacañang Presidential Palace on Wednesday and met with his Philippine counterpart, Ferdinand "Bongbong" Marcos Jr., before his flight to China. In a public bilateral meeting, the two leaders lauded the U.S.-Philippine relationship, which Mr. Trump called "one of America's oldest and most important alliances in the Pacific." The U.S. president suggested the two countries could cooperate further on technology, energy and defense.

In a banquet luncheon before departing for China, Mr. Trump announced that he and Marcos "just consummated a very big trade deal, the biggest trade deal we've ever made, by far, and it's a fair deal for both countries, and we're very happy with that. And we didn't know that that was going to take place, but it took place very quickly, and it's a magnificent deal for both."
Later, in a social media post, Mr. Trump said the deal "will be a true landmark and, in particular, a Deal that will be great for our Farmers and those in the business of "Energy."

A day earlier, after landing in the Philippine capital of Manila, Mr. Trump met with the leaders of the Quad, a group of nations that have sought to counter China's influence in the Asia Pacific region. The president described the relationship with the Quad — made up of the U.S., Australia, India and Japan — as "very special."
Mr. Trump announced an $85 million investment in artificial intelligence software, describing it as the "greatest opportunity for economic growth since the Industrial Revolution."

There were protests in Manila ahead of Mr. Trump's trip, with demonstrators holding signs reading "Trump Out," drawings of him as a clown or devil, and signs calling on the public to reject an AI hub named Pax Silica.

Ahead of his departure from Washington Monday, Mr. Trump called it a "big trip" and said he may also meet with North Korea's Kim in China. After arriving in the Philippines, he said Kim "would like to" come, but "we'll see what happens."

The meeting between Mr. Trump, Xi and Putin, which marks the first among the three leaders, is expected to center on decreasing the proliferation of nuclear weapons, the White House said, and comes as the wars in Iran and Ukraine remain in focus.

Mr. Trump said Monday they would discuss denuclearization, which he called a "tough subject," as well as Iran and Ukraine, although an official said over the weekend that Ukraine was not expected to be discussed.

In Manila, the president will attend the annual Association of Southeast Asian Nations summit. He will meet with leaders of Japan, India and Australia on security in the Indo-Pacific on Tuesday. He's also scheduled to sign a trade deal with Thailand and attend a dinner with leaders of the Southeast Asian nations and other regional leaders, the White House said.

On Wednesday, the president is set to hold a state visit and lunch banquet with Philippine President Bongbong Marcos at the presidential palace, before departing for Shenzhen, China. There, he'll meet on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit with APEC leaders, and on Thursday, hold the meeting with Putin and Xi. Mr. Trump said Tuesday that he would be open to a one-on-one meeting with Putin, but he didn't know if it had been scheduled.
Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk is expected to join the president on the trip, according to a senior White House official, but will not be part of the meeting with Putin and Xi.

Mr. Trump's trip to Asia comes after he visited China in May for a summit with Xi, where he touted making "fantastic trade deals" and acknowledged a shared desire to end the U.S.-Iran conflict. Xi also visited the U.S. in September, marking his first visit to the White House in over a decade, as the two countries extended a tariff truce.

"I think the president does intend to talk about Iran in the trilateral meeting with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin," a senior U.S. official, speaking on condition of anonymity, told reporters on a call.
It will be Mr. Trump's third face-to-face meeting with Xi this year.

As for Putin, Mr. Trump and the Russian president last met in Alaska in August 2025 for a high-stakes summit on ending the war in Ukraine. But the talks failed to yield a ceasefire that the U.S. was seeking.

Mr. Trump's trip to Asia also coincides with issues back at home, including the recent revelations regarding an affair between Jensen Huang, the former CEO of chipmaker Nvidia, and a suspected Chinese spy. Beijing has said it was not involved.

Huang, who has a relationship with Mr. Trump, traveled on Air Force One during his May trip to China, and he and his wife were at the head table when Mr. Trump hosted Xi in Washington for a state dinner in September. White House officials said they do not think the Nvidia situation will loom over the trip.

"We do not negotiate American export controls. These are national security matters that we develop in the administration ... and we don't expect it to figure at all in any of our conversations with the Chinese while we're there," an official said.

When asked Monday if Rubio had told him that the woman with whom Huang was having an affair, Alice Huang, was suspected of being a spy, Mr. Trump said he didn't know if she was, saying, "I haven't heard that." Mr. Trump also said it "isn't a bad idea" for Jensen Huang to be reinstated at Nvidia, but he also added that he recommended Apple's Tim Cook for the job.
Mr. Trump acknowledged that Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent have "two lines of thought" on how to handle China, adding that "they handled that very well."
Bessent last week accused Lutnick of failing to prevent China from getting some of Nvidia's most advanced chips. Both Bessent and Lutnick are traveling with the president.
Mr. Trump told reporters before he left that he was not considering replacing Lutnick.

The Nvidia Board of Directors announced Tuesday morning that it would be creating a National Security and Export Control Oversight Committee. Mr. Trump said on Tuesday that he believed that is a "good idea."

title: 2,000-year-old bog woman was beheaded in possible ritual killing
summary: The "Ballymacombs More Woman," whose body lay in a Northern Ireland bog for 2,000 years, was beheaded, possibly in a "ritualized killing," researchers say.
story: London — An investigation into the death of a young Iron Age woman whose remains were preserved in a Northern Ireland bog for more than 2,000 years has found that she was beheaded, possibly in a "ritualized killing," when she was between 15 and 22 years old.

The enquiry into the remains known as the "Ballymacombs More Woman," discovered in a peat bog in central Northern Ireland in October 2023, determined that she was decapitated from behind, most likely with a bladed weapon.

"While the precise circumstances surrounding her death remain unknown, the evidence suggested that she may form part of a wider tradition of ritualized killing and sacrifice," said the Ulster Museum, which hosted a coroner's investigation into the two-millennia-old killing. It said the woman's death appeared similar to others documented among  Iron Age bodies discovered in bogs across northwest Europe.
The More Woman's body dates from between 343 to 1 B.C., from the prehistoric Iron Age period.

"Finds like this that are women are incredibly rare," Hannah Crowdy, head of curatorial for Northern Ireland's National Museums, told CBS News partner network BBC News. "She's the first of her kind in Northern Ireland."

"This helps us piece together a part of history that is quite mysterious," Crowdy added. "There's been a really intensive period of research … To honor her, it's important to tell her story and bring that to the fore."

The team that carried out what the Ulster Museum called a "unique public event modelled on a modern coroner's investigation into the remains" used scientific mapping techniques, 3D imaging and analyses of bone, hair, skin and nails to gain evidence of the woman's age, health, diet, physical condition and the injuries that led to her death.

Niamh Baker, the Ulster Museum's curator of archaeology, told the BBC that an osteoarchaeologist — someone who studies archaeological human bones —   reviewed the remains and found cut marks on the woman's neck.
"It would appear she was intentionally decapitated in the bog," said Baker. "No skull was recovered with further investigation."

"There are examples of some Iron Age remains in the Republic of Ireland that are male that similarly met violent deaths and some of those are thought to be associated with kingship and sovereignty," said Baker. "Was she a female sovereign? Or it may be that it was related to an agricultural or weather issue at the time."
Residents of the nearby town of Balleghy have named the woman Aine.

"We feel that Aine is one of our own," said Séamus Mac an Fhirléighinn, from the town's historical society, who attended the coroner's investigation."This is her inquest. She needed her people, her family there with her to act on her behalf as advocates."
"Local people are very interested," he said. "We wanted to know who this person was, how she died, how she lived."

title: Voyager 1 sets distance record of 1 "light day" from Earth
summary: Voyager 1 and its sister ship Voyager 2 are still beaming back data from interstellar space as they near their 50th anniversary next year.
story: NASA's Voyager 1 probe, launched nearly a half century ago in 1977 to provide the first close-up views of Jupiter, Saturn and their assortment of moons, reached a distance from Earth early Wednesday of one light day — more than 16 billion miles — the farthest any human artifact has ever ventured from the home planet.

Its sister ship Voyager 2, on a different trajectory, added Uranus and Neptune to the outer planets "Grand Tour" before following its sibling out of the solar system and into interstellar space in 2018, six years after Voyager 1.

Both spacecraft continue to beam back data about the magnetic fields, charged particles and plasma waves in the space between the stars as their power steadily declines and their signals grow weaker and weaker.

As of 5:16 a.m. EST Wednesday, Voyager 1, sailing through space at nearly 38,000 mph, was expected to pass the one-light-day milestone, so far away that radio signals, traveling at 186,000 miles every second, need 24 hours to reach flight controllers at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory.
That means the 13-member team will have to wait until Thursday for Voyager 1's first post-light-day signal to confirm the achievement.

And what an achievement it is: No other space agency in the world has matched or even attempted a mission rivaling Voyager, one that many believe ranks with the Apollo moon landings as one of the greatest feats of American space flight.

"It's difficult to describe, difficult to put into words," said Voyager Interstellar Mission Manager Kareem Badaruddin, one of just three full-time team members keeping the aging Voyagers healthy and their antennas aimed at Earth. "I feel like this mission is one of the great things that people have ever done, that humans have ever done.
"All of us, every person, whether they've worked on this mission or not, can take some pride in it and can feel like this is a part of what our civilization has accomplished."

It's not known how long the Voyagers will continue to function as the plutonium in their nuclear power packs steadily decays. With luck and clever management, engineers hope to keep the data flowing for several more years before the signals finally stop.

Voyager 1 started out with about 470 watts of power. That's down to a little more than 210 watts now, enough to run just two of its 10 instruments while keeping the spacecraft properly oriented so it can beam magnetometer and plasma wave data back to Earth. Voyager 2 has a slightly more powerful generator and is operating on a bit more than 230 watts, enough to keep three instruments running.

But even after the power is exhausted, both Voyagers will continue on their way, expected to remain roughly intact, if powerless, for a billion years or more, almost certainly outlasting human civilization.

On the remote chance any aliens might one day stumble upon a Voyager in the cold reaches between the stars, both spacecraft are carrying what amount to messages in a bottle, gold phonograph records encoded with the sights and sounds of planet Earth.

The records include greetings in 55 languages, 115 photos of Earth's people, wildlife and technology, representative natural sounds and carefully selected art and music from multiple cultures, everything from J.S. Bach to Navajo chants to Chuck Berry singing "Johnny B. Goode."

"If Voyager should, sometime in its distant future, encounter beings from some other civilization in space, it bears a message, a phonograph record ... with instructions for use," Carl Sagan, the late astronomer who led the golden record project, said in the 1980 "Cosmos" television series.

"And on this record are a sampling of pictures, sounds, greetings and an hour and a half of exquisite music, the Earth's greatest hits, a gift across the cosmic ocean from one island of civilization to another."

Now beyond the confines of Earth's solar system, the stream of ones and zeros describing the interstellar environment leaves Voyager 1's 12-foot-wide dish antenna with less than half the power used by a typical 40-watt refrigerator bulb.

By the time the signal reaches Earth 24 hours later, its strength is a tiny fraction of a trillionth of a watt, vastly less than the power needed to run a wristwatch — a signal so weak that giant 230-foot-wide antennas in NASA's globe-spanning Deep Space Network are needed to pull in the faint whispers.

Commands from flight controllers at JPL now take a full day to reach the spacecraft with another 24 hours required to find out if the commands were received and acted upon. Fixing a problem is a glacial, nail-biting affair.

"If you want to say 'hello' to Voyager, you send your message and then you go home and you wait two days before you finally get a response," Suzanne Dodd, the Voyager project manager at JPL, said in a web posting.
Voyager 1 and Voyager 2 are powered by electricity generated through the decay of radioactive plutonium 238 in compact nuclear power plants known as radioisotope thermoelectric generators, or RTGs.

Both spacecraft have slowly but steadily lost power as the plutonium in their RTGs has decayed. Flight controllers closely manage the available power and the resulting heat needed to keep fuel lines from freezing so thrusters can fire when needed to keep the spacecraft — and their dish antennas — locked onto Earth.
Badaruddin said the small flight control team feels the weight of responsibility for keeping the Voyagers alive.

"If ever you get that sense that oh, I made a mistake, I'm the one who caused a problem for the spacecraft, that's crushing," he said. "Every one of the team members feels they're committed to doing everything in our power to do our best for these spacecraft. We're doing everything we can to keep them going for as long as we can."

Only three of the 13 Voyager team members are full-time JPL employees. Two are retirees who worked on the project at launch and came back to help during the interstellar voyage while the rest split their time between Voyager and other projects.

"I've been at JPL for 32 years, and everybody loves their spacecraft, and everybody feels like it's a family member and gives everything they've got for it," said Badaruddin. "And Voyager is no different in that regard. And these two retirees have come back and given a tremendous amount of effort and time."

The Voyager program was approved in the early 1970s when the outer planets were lined up in a way that would permit a so-called "Grand Tour" of them, enabling spacecraft to make velocity-boosting flybys to jump from one planet to the next, shaving years off the time needed to explore them all.
But to reduce costs, the project was only funded for flybys of Jupiter and Saturn. Voyager 2 was launched first, on Aug. 20, 1977. Voyager 1 followed on Sept. 5.

Voyager 1 was on a faster trajectory and reached Jupiter first as planned, flying past the giant planet in 1979, sending back spectacular images of its Great Red Spot — a storm that has been churning for centuries, the planet's turbulent atmosphere and its major moons, including detailed looks at Europa, where an icy crust is thought to shield a global ocean, and Io, found to be the most volcanic world in the solar system.

It then flew on to Saturn, wowing astronomers with fantastically detailed photos of the solar system's most spectacular planet, sending back never-before-seen views of its rings, small moons that shepherd the ring particles along, the planet's atmosphere and, as it departed, cloud-shrouded Titan.

With the successful Titan flyby and the completion of the mission's major objectives, NASA approved sending Voyager 2 on a gravitational slingshot past Saturn and on to Uranus and Neptune in 1986 and 1989, respectively.

On Valentine's Day 1990, Voyager 1's cameras were used a final time to take a family portrait of the six largest planets — Venus, Earth, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune — from a distance of 3.7 billion miles. Earth appeared as little more than a blue dot in the pinkish glow of reflected light within the camera.

"Consider again that dot. That's here. That's home. That's us," Sagan said of the photo. "On it everyone you love, everyone you know, everyone you ever heard of, every human being who ever was, lived out their lives ... on a mote of dust suspended in a sunbeam."

He concluded by saying "there is perhaps no better demonstration of the folly of human conceits than this distant image of our tiny world. To me, it underscores our responsibility to deal more kindly with one another, and to preserve and cherish the pale blue dot, the only home we've ever known."
Voyager 1's cameras have been powered down ever since.

In 2012, Voyager 1 flew through the outer edge of the bubble around the solar system defined by the solar wind and the sun's magnetic field, sailing out into interstellar space. It is now in what Carolyn Porco, a well-known planetary scientist and member of the Voyager imaging team, calls "the realm of deep time."

In about 18,000 years, she writes on her Substack page, Voyager 1 will reach another major milestone: passing through a distance of one light-year from Earth, roughly 5.8 trillion miles, only a quarter of the way to the nearest star and "still well within the zone where the sun is the dominant gravitational influence."

But in a million years, the silent spacecraft will have passed well beyond the confines of the solar system, reaching a distance of 56 light-years while "remaining within the sun's local interstellar neighborhood — a low density region filled with diffuse hydrogen and helium gas and scattered stars: most are very dim, some are sun-like, and comparatively few are luminous."

In 100 million years, Voyager 1 will be about 2,000 light years from Earth as the spacecraft and the distant solar system are carried along by the galaxy's rotation. "Still not very far," Porco writes. "But at this time, it will find itself among cold, dense molecular clouds, star-forming regions and nebulae and supernova remnants formed by the deaths of stars."

Finally, 1 billion years from now, the spacecraft will have sailed about 20,000 light-years from home, making four trips around the galactic core in the process. "By then, the sun's growing luminosity will have sufficiently heated the Earth to destroy atmospheric carbon dioxide, halt oxygen production and exterminate plant life and the complex lifeforms that depend on it."
"By that time, both robot and maker will be extinct."

The cosmic travelogue concludes with a personal observation: "The foretelling of Voyager's galactic wanderings leaves one to contemplate the impermanence of all existence and the preciousness of life. And that just might be Voyager's greatest gift of all."
