title: Man with ax destroys $60M U.S. military plane, prosecutors say
summary: Daithi O'Corrain, 48, is charged in the U.S. with destruction of U.S. government property in connection with the April incident at Shannon Airport.
story: An ax-wielding man breached a security perimeter and destroyed an American military plane while it was parked overnight at an Irish airport, cutting hydraulic lines, smashing cockpit gauges and pouring ball bearings into fuel tanks, U.S. prosecutors said. The man's supporters attributed the attack to his anger at the United States' involvement in Middle East conflicts.

An indictment unsealed Tuesday in Manhattan charges Daithi O'Corrain, 48, with destruction of U.S. government property in connection with the April incident at Shannon Airport, an international gateway in the west of Ireland that serves as a hub for American troops and military equipment.

O'Corrain isn't in U.S. custody and his arraignment on the new charge hasn't been scheduled. If convicted, he faces up to 10 years in prison. Online court records do not list an attorney who might speak on his behalf.

The plane, a $60 million U.S. Air National Guard C-130 Hercules that had been en route to a military assignment in another country, was rendered inoperable and won't fly again, U.S. prosecutors said. The attack jeopardized critical military operations, the FBI said.

O'Corrain, described by supporters as an independent peace activist, was arrested immediately after the attack by Ireland's police force, An Garda Síochána. He was charged there with causing criminal damage and trespassing. The Limerick Post reported he is from Cork, about 60 miles southeast of Shannon.
Manhattan U.S. Attorney Jamie McDonald said the indictment sends "a clear and powerful message that attacks on U.S. military assets — and thus our national security — will not be tolerated."

An online fundraiser organized by people describing themselves as O'Corrain's friends and comrades said he disarmed the C-130 in protest of the U.S.'s war with Iran and support for Israel's war in Gaza — a flashpoint in Ireland, where many people have expressed solidarity with Palestinians.

"An inspiring act of direct action was carried out at Shannon Airport to resist the unwanted presence of the US Military in Ireland in the face of their illegal war & support of Israel's genocide," organizer Tracey Ryan wrote.

O'Corrain plotted the attack for months, U.S. prosecutors said. He searched online for information about the construction of the C-130, a quad-engine turboprop mainly used for transporting equipment and personnel, and looked up coordinates for sneaking onto the airport's grounds, prosecutors said.

He subscribed to a cellphone app that provided live flight tracking, including for military aircraft, and ordered capsules of gallium, a chemical that can corrode steel and break down aluminum, the primary material used to build the C-130, prosecutors said.
He even tried to get in touch with someone who had been involved in a prior breach at Shannon Airport, prosecutors said.
"This was not an act of spontaneous vandalism," James Barnacle, the head of the FBI's New York office, said in a statement.

O'Corrain attacked on April 11, breaching the airport's perimeter at around 4:40 a.m. and breaking into the C-130 as it was parked on a taxiway by destroying a locking mechanism on the rear crew door, his indictment said.

He used the crew's hammocks to cover the plane's windows but left the cockpit windshield exposed, the indictment said. He then barricaded himself inside the aircraft, securing the doors with straps, brackets and screws, and putting ball bearings mixed with epoxy in door tracks to prevent doors from being opened or closed, the indictment said.

O'Corrain laid waste to the plane over the next few hours, pulling, snipping and otherwise disabling its key components, the indictment said. He sliced wire bundles, crimped a liquid oxygen line, punctured air ducts and shattered every gauge in the cockpit, the indictment said.
Had O'Corrain cut the oxygen line instead, he would've risked blowing up the plane, prosecutors said.
Returning to the airport after resting elsewhere, the C-130 crew spotted O'Corrain through the uncovered cockpit at around 9:40 a.m. and alerted security, the indictment said.

Crew members then saw him emerging through a roof hatch and swinging an ax at the plane's exterior, according to the indictment, which included images taken from a video recording that show a man standing on the roof of the plane. O'Corrain then poured substances and objects into the fuel tanks, including ball bearings, before being arrested.

Shannon Airport, which was used by President Trump and Air Force One during his visit to Ireland in September, has had several security breaches in the last 18 months, including three people who were accused of spray-painting a U.S. military plane and three others who drove to a restricted area where a U.S. military jet was parked.

title: American soldier accused of spying in U.S. custody after U.K. arrest
summary: Federal Bureau of Investigation director Kash Patel said that the soldier was "a potential threat to national security."
story: A United States Army soldier arrested in the United Kingdom on suspicion that he engaged in espionage linked to Russia has been taken into the custody of the U.S. military, British and American officials said Tuesday.

A U.S. official previously identified the suspect as Lt. Col. Brandon Tyner, a senior human resources officer based at Imjin Barracks, home to the headquarters of NATO's Allied Rapid Reaction Corps. Tyner, 41, joined the Army in 2008 and has been deployed to Afghanistan, Qatar and Iraq.
Assistant Commissioner Laurence Taylor, head of Counter Terrorism Policing, said in a news release that U.S. authorities will continue the investigation. The suspect is expected to be charged soon.

"These are extremely serious allegations, and our collective response should send a strong message that we will act swiftly and robustly where we suspect this kind of espionage activity taking place," Taylor said.

The soldier is suspected of violating the U.K.'s National Security Act of 2023 to obtain or disclose protected information and to assist a foreign intelligence service. The London Metropolitan Police said the suspected activity relates to Russia. Federal Bureau of Investigation director Kash Patel said that the soldier was "a potential threat to national security."

He was arrested by the the London Metropolitan Police during a sting operation in Gloucester, about 100 miles west of London, on November 10. The operation involved the Met Police's Counter Terrorism Policing Unit, the U.S. military and the FBI.
"This FBI has zero tolerance for anyone who betrays their oath to the United States or puts our national security at risk," FBI Director Kash Patel said in a statement on Tuesday.
Officials have carried out further searches in Gloucestershire, the county where Gloucester is located, related to the investigation, the Metropolitan Police Department said.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters in Moscow last week that Russia had "nothing to do with" the soldier's detention.

U.K. police said the arrest is not related to "any other ongoing Counter Terrorism Policing investigations." The unit is investigating a recent suspected plot at RAF Fairford, a British Royal Air Force base where U.S. troops and aircraft are stationed. The U.S. military removed its bombers from that base after the security incident.

Five British men and one U.K.-Iranian national were arrested in late September. Last week, the U.S. Justice Department announced that three people it accuses of being Iran-backed operatives were charged with plotting a terrorist attack at the site. One suspect is in custody in New York, and the other two are not in custody, two sources familiar with the matter told CBS News.

title: U.S. identifies remains of 6 soldiers killed in Korean War, including teens
summary: The identifications are part of an ongoing effort to locate and identify the remains of U.S. soldiers killed in the Korean War.
story: Six soldiers who died in the Korean War, including two teenagers, have been accounted for decades after their deaths, the Defense POW/MIA Accounting Agency announced Monday.

The identifications are part of an ongoing effort to locate and identify the remains of those killed in the Korean War. When a soldier is marked as accounted for, they receive a burial with full military honors.

U.S. Army Cpl. Jackie Lee Thurman was a member of Battery B, 99th Field Artillery Battalion, 1st Cavalry Division. Thurman, 18, was a forward observer near Waegwan, South Korea, when his post came under heavy attack, according to the agency, and was last seen trying to evacuate a shell-shocked officer from the area while under heavy enemy fire.
Afterward, Thurman was reported missing in action. A presumptive finding of death was issued on Dec. 31, 1953. His remains were declared unrecoverable two years later, in January 1956.

The agency said that a set of remains, designated X-5814 Tanggok, was recovered by the Quartermaster Graves Registration Company near Kumhwa-dong, South Korea, in October 1952. The remains were interred as unknowns at the National Memorial Cemetery of the Pacific in Honolulu, Hawaii. In November 2022, the agency disinterred the remains. Analysis allowed the agency's scientists to identify the remains as Thurman's. He was marked as accounted for by the agency on May 18, 2026.

U.S. Army 1st Lt. Raymond Banker Gilbert was a member of B Battery, 503rd Field Artillery Battalion, 2nd Infantry Division, who was reported missing during the battle of the Ch'ongch'on River in North Korea, according to the agency. Witness statements allowed the Army to determine that Gilbert, 23, had been taken as a prisoner of war by the Chinese People's Volunteer Army and died from battlefield wounds in a POW camp on Jan. 31, 1951.

After the war, a recovered set of remains was returned to U.S. custody as part of a 1954 exchange known as Operation Glory, the agency said. The remains could not be identified at the time and were buried as an unknown at the National Memorial Cemetery of the Pacific. They were disinterred on July 1, 2024, and sent to the agency's laboratory. Analysis, circumstantial and historical evidence allowed the agency to identify the remains as Gilbert's. His remains were marked as accounted for on June 4, 2026.

U.S. Army Cpl. William R. Laughlin Jr. was a member of Company D, 1st Battalion, 32nd Infantry Regiment, 7th Infantry Division, attached to the 31st Regimental Combat Team, according to the agency. Laughlin, 21, was among the U.S. soldiers ambushed by the Chinese People's Volunteer Army at the Chosin Reservoir in North Korea.

The ambush sparked a 17-day battle in frigid weather. Each side took thousands of casualties. U.S. and United Nations forces eventually retreated south toward the supply base of Hagaru-ri. Laughlin could not be located after the battle and was reported missing in action on Dec. 2, 1950. A presumptive finding of death was issued on Dec. 31, 1953.

A pair of remains returned during Operation Glory were connected to an isolated burial east of the Chosin Reservoir. They could not be identified and were interred as unknowns at the National Memorial Cemetery of the Pacific. The agency disinterred the remains in July 2022 and used modern forensic techniques at its laboratory to identify them as Laughlin's. He was marked as accounted for by the agency on Sept. 28, 2026.

U.S. Army Sgt. Joseph A. Platzkoester, a member of Company H, 2nd Battalion, 38th Infantry Regiment, 2nd Infantry Division, was last seen during an ambush near Inje in South Korea. Platzkoester, 28, was part of a convoy doing counteroffensive clearing operations at the time, the agency said. The convoy encountered an enemy roadblock. While his battalion pushed through, Platzkoester could not be found after the fight and was reported missing in action.
The area was searched, but Platzkoester's remains were not found. A presumptive finding of death was issued on Dec. 31, 1953, and his remains were declared nonrecoverable in January 1956.

In 1951, the 148th Quartermaster Graves Registration Company found a set of remains that could not be identified. They were interred as an unknown at the National Memorial Cemetery of the Pacific. In November 2023, the set of remains was disinterred and sent to the agency's laboratory, where analysis identified them as Platzkoester's. He was marked as accounted for by the agency on May 29, 2026. A photo of Platzkoester was not available.

U.S. Army Cpl. Andrew R. Tischler, 21, was assigned to Company F, 2nd Battalion, 15th Infantry Regiment, 3rd Infantry Division, and was reported missing in action during a road march near Taewol Village in South Korea, according to the agency. The agency said it was able to account for him on May 5, 2026. Information about how his remains were found and identified was not available. A photo was not shared by the agency.

The other teen soldier, U.S. Army Cpl. Richard N. Lennox, 18, was accounted for on Aug. 7, 2025, the agency said. He was a member of Company C, 1st Battalion, 7th Infantry Regiment, 3rd Infantry Division reported missing in action after his unit was attacked by enemy forces near Sachang-ni, North Korea, on Nov. 28, 1950. He was captured and marched to a prisoner-of-war camp in Changsong, where he died in October 1951.

Lennox's remains were among those handed over during Operation Glory, the agency said. They could not be identified at the time and were buried as an unknown at the National Memorial Cemetery of the Pacific. The remains were disinterred on June 13, 2016. The agency analyzed the remains and said that Lennox had been accounted for on Aug. 7, 2025. A photo of Lennox was not available.

Each missing soldier's name was engraved on the Walls of the Missing at the National Memorial Cemetery of the Pacific. Now that they have been accounted for, rosettes will be placed alongside their names.

More information about each soldier, including how they were identified, may be shared after their families are briefed by the agency. The agency told CBS News in 2024 that history, diplomacy and science all come into each investigation. First, researchers start with archival records. Investigators then search for surviving witnesses and clues. Once the potential location of a set of remains is identified, a recovery mission is sent to bring those remains to the agency's laboratory.

At the lab, scientists use dental evidence and other records to study the remains. For soldiers who disappeared during the Korean War, experts can use tuberculosis skin test results taken before someone shipped out. The remains also undergo X-rays, DNA analysis and isotope analysis. Finally, a reference sample of DNA from a family member is compared to the remains. The process can take decades, the agency told CBS News.

About 7,500 Americans are still unaccounted for from the Korean War, the agency says. Efforts to bring home fallen soldiers from the conflict are complicated by relations with North Korea: While the agency operates in 46 countries, North Korea is an outlier. Sometimes, war dead are recovered during exchanges like Operation Glory.

title: Ukraine says underground gas pipeline used to mount sneak attack
summary: Ukraine says troops spent weeks crawling through an old underground gas pipeline to get behind enemy lines and launch a surprise attack.
story: Ukrainian soldiers spent weeks navigating a decommissioned, underground Soviet-era gas pipeline to sneak behind enemy lines and launch a surprise attack on Russian troops this autumn as part of an operation to prevent the invading forces from reaching the eastern city of Kupiansk, according to the Ukrainian unit involved.

The operation forced the soldiers to get past barricades laid by Russian forces — including the bodies of fallen troops —   and involved close-quarters combat inside the roughly three-foot-wide pipeline, Ukraine's military said.

"Operation Veles" was carried out by members of the Ukrainian National Guard's Khartiia Corps in the Kharkiv region within the last couple of months, according to a series of posts by the unit on social media. The unit said troops crawled and were pulled on wheeled carts some nine miles through the underground pipeline before emerging behind Russian positions.

The operation was part of a broader Ukrainian effort, more than four and a half years into Russia's full-scale invasion, to prevent the invading forces from advancing toward the front-line city of Kupiansk.

The unit's social media posts quoted soldiers saying they engaged in close combat with grenades and small arms inside the pipe, where the cramped space came with pooled freezing water and traces of natural gas lingering years after the pipeline was decommissioned. Some Ukrainian forces spent as long as a month underground during the operation, the Khartiia Corps said.

"They used electric winches to move through the pipe, and transported ammunition and equipment on small wheelbarrows," the unit said in one post. It called the conditions "extremely harsh," and noted that the troops "constantly moving on their knees caused injuries, and dirt clogged the mechanisms of their weapons and caused malfunctions."

Russian troops had laid obstacles in some sections of the pipeline, with Ukrainian soldiers saying that some of those barricades included the bodies of other Russian soldiers. The claims by the Ukrainian forces about the battle have not been independently verified by CBS News.
Russian authorities have acknowledged the operation, referring to a Ukrainian raid.

The Khartiia Corps has not confirmed any Ukrainian casualties, but at least one report on the battle, by Britain's Telegraph newspaper, mentioned Ukrainian forces recovering the body of a fallen comrade from inside an underground gas pipeline.

The pipeline offered a way for Ukrainian forces to conceal their movements in one of the most heavily monitored sectors of the nearly 1,000-mile front line that stretches from the far north to the far south of eastern Ukraine.

Both sides have sought to exploit underground infrastructure to evade increasingly sophisticated aerial surveillance in a conflict shaped by drone warfare. In September 2025, Russian forces similarly attempted to use sections of underground pipeline to move troops closer to Ukrainian positions around the northern outskirts of Kupiansk without being detected by drones.

Military analysts say operations like the underground pipeline assault highlight how the widespread use of drones in Russia's ongoing full-scale invasion, and Ukraine's defense, have transformed modern warfare. Both sides rely heavily on surveillance and attack drones to find and strike troops and hardware moving in the open.
As a result, even short movements above ground can expose soldiers to near real-time observation and attack.

While underground operations present their own dangers, including limited ventilation, restricted movement, navigational challenges and the risk of entrapment, soldiers involved in the Ukrainian mission suggested the hazards were outweighed by the dangers posed above ground, where they could have been spotted by Russian drones.
"It's damp, it's dark, it reeks. There are corpses lying around, but I felt safer there," one Khartiia Corps member, using the callsign "Sgt. Santa," was quoted as saying in a post by the unit.

The operation came ahead of what could prove a critical juncture in the war. President Trump, who campaigned on ending the war quickly, has pushed hard for Ukraine and Russia to agree to a peace deal. Kyiv and its European allies fear, however, that the White House appears to be offering Vladimir Putin and Russia too much — including the prospect of major energy deals, with no significant concessions in return,  while putting pressure on Ukraine to make major territorial concessions without any concrete security guarantees.
Ukraine says the operation in the gas pipeline helped stop Russian forces from gaining more ground near Kupiansk, a city that Ukrainian forces recaptured from Russia's invading troops in 2022.

title: Pope Leo calls for "less controversy, less war, less division"
summary: The Catholic Church's first U.S.-born leader, returning from a major Latin America tour, spoke about American unity, his health, and the prospect of married priests.
story: Rome — Speaking to reporters on his return trip to Rome after an extensive tour of Latin America, Pope Leo XIV called for less political polarization in the United States following the recent midterm elections.

"I would like to see a greater capacity for dialogue, building bridges, reconciliation, less controversy, less war, less division," the Chicago-born leader of the Catholic Church told reporters. "I know this is also a dream, but I know it is possible, so we shall see."

Leo, who confirmed earlier this month that he had voted in the 2026 midterms and was proud to "exercise my right" to do so, said it was the duty of all American citizens to participate in elections. He spoke on the flight back to Italy about his American identity, calling himself "a gringo in many ways."
"My deep faith in democracy, of democratic participation, is also part of being a North American," he said.
The pontiff said being American was also likely why he had been forthcoming about his recent health issues.
"Not at 100%, but I'm doing quite well"

"When I speak in general, I am very direct. I say things as they are," he told reporters. "The issue of my health and the fact of openly speaking about it … it's not so typical in many countries and cultures. In U.S. society, it is a bit more of a common attitude."
"I'm not at 100%, but I'm doing quite well," he said, crediting his doctors, prayers and personal determination for his recovery, calling stamina "one of the gifts the Lord gave me."

Leo underwent surgery in October after doctors discovered a lung tumor and diagnosed him with cancer. His medical team said the cancer was confined to a lobe of one lung that was removed, and that no further treatment was necessary. The tumor was discovered during a routine annual medical examination.
"The initial news was a surprise," the pope said. "I had no symptoms and felt fine."

Leo, who set off on the trip to Latin America just 24 days after his operation, said he had decided to proceed quickly with the surgery because he was determined to stick to the plans for his Latin American tour. He said the diagnosis did not change his agenda, or his priorities.
Asked whether he had signed a conditional resignation letter in the event of permanent incapacity, as previous popes have done, Leo said he had not.
"For now, I don't see the need," he said.
Pope doesn't rule out married priests
Leo also addressed one of the most divisive issues in the Catholic Church on the return flight —   the ordination of married men to the priesthood.

He acknowledged that allowing married priests could help address severe shortages in remote regions such as the Amazon, but cautioned that the issue was "complicated" and could create division within the church.
"It's a solution which, in certain areas of the church, can cause division because there is not universal, if you will, acceptance, of that concept," he said.
Leo did not completely rule out the possibility, but made it sound unlikely any time soon.
"It may be in the future that some things will change. However, for right now, what I believe, an important part of my ministry of the church is to heal, bring people together," he said.
The pope also joked with reporters about being hit in the face with a flying rosary during his final mass in Lima.
"The affection of Peruvians —   including that person who, with great faith, simply wanted to offer me a rosary — these are things one carries in one's heart, perhaps in one's eye," he quipped.

title: Scientist fired after 6-year-old girl dies in gene-editing trial
summary: The girl died last year after receiving experimental gene therapy to correct a non-life-threatening condition, an investigation found.
story: A Chinese scientist who concealed the death of a 6-year-old girl in a gene-editing trial has been fired following a government probe, according to state media.
The girl died last year after receiving experimental gene therapy to correct a non-life-threatening condition — which was not disclosed in published research, an investigation found in July.

Neuroscientist Zilong Qiu, the trial's lead researcher, had made no mention of the girl in a paper published in the prestigious journal Nature, according to the joint investigation by Science and Retraction Watch.

"According to official documents and accounts provided by the girl's parents, the hospital had allowed Qiu's experimental treatment to proceed under a regulatory provision that does not require approval from national regulators," Science reported in July. "After the child's death, the hospital paid a modest fine to a local health authority but Qiu was not publicly sanctioned."

Qiu was dismissed as deputy director of the Songjiang Research Institute affiliated with Shanghai Jiao Tong University, state broadcaster CCTV said Friday, citing a statement from Shanghai authorities.
The reported statement included only Qiu's surname, but referenced the Nature study published on Feb. 18.
Qiu was given a five-year suspension from participating in scientific projects and recorded in a database for "serious breaches of research integrity," the report said.
Another researcher on Qiu's team was fired and handed a five-year suspension, while several others with ties to the hospital where the trial took place were also punished.
The child who died had a rare neurodevelopmental condition called Snijders Blok-Campeau syndrome, according to the report.
The hospital's ethics committee had approved a gene-editing trial to treat the disorder in January 2025, the report said.
The committee terminated the study after the girl died in March due to complications from gene therapy.
"Unusual and dangerous"
Shanghai authorities found that Qiu's team failed to properly inform the hospital of possible safety issues from earlier tests on primates, according to the report.
AFP has reached out to Qiu for comment.
The July investigation by Science and Retraction Watch found that the girl's parents, who paid more than $800,000 to fund the experiment, were not adequately informed about the risks.

"Learning the reality of these missing safeguards has fundamentally changed how we now view the entire project," the girl's father, told Science. "We did not realize how unusual and dangerous many of the arrangements were."

The scandal is a blow to China's ambitions to rival the United States as a biotech power following the 2018 scandal around He Jiankui, a biophysicist who secretly produced gene-edited babies. He was later sentenced to three years in prison.

title: Dead racehorse found in dumpster days after prestigious race
summary: The dead body of So You Are was found in a waste facility less than two weeks after competing in the most prestigious event in Australian horse racing.
story: The dead body of Melbourne Cup horse So You Are was found in a waste facility in Sydney less than two weeks after competing in the most prestigious event in Australian horse racing.

The Sydney Morning Herald newspaper reported Tuesday that racing stewards were investigating after a construction worker saw a dead horse in a dumpster at a licensed waste center and posted a video on Facebook.

Trainer Bjorn Baker had released a statement Monday saying So You Are died following a severe bout of colic. The 5-year-old gelding was rushed to a specialist equine hospital for emergency veterinary treatment but couldn't be saved.
Baker posted an update Tuesday after discovering So You Are hadn't been properly buried.

"Like everyone who has seen the footage, I am deeply distressed by the handling of So You Are's remains," Baker said in a statement. "He was a much-loved horse, and he deserved to be treated with dignity and respect after his death."

"I understand the specialist hospital facility REC Equine Specialists are investigating the circumstances, and I expect a full explanation of what occurred," he added. "My thoughts remain with the Ramsey family [owners], and with all my staff, for whom this has compounded an already devastating loss."
So You Are placed eighth in the Melbourne Cup on Nov. 3, with Point of Law winning the 166th running of the 2-mile classic.
REC Equine Specialists managing partner Dr. Jonathan Lumsden issued a statement saying So You Are had been "humanely euthanized under anesthesia" after receiving emergency treatment.

"After his death, So You Are was collected by our contracted service provider and taken to a licensed landfill. He should have been promptly and respectfully buried," Lumsden said. "What happened was unacceptable and disrespectful to So You Are and to everyone who cared for him. We are deeply sorry."
Lumsden said he was working with the service provider and the state's horse racing authority, Racing NSW, to establish what went wrong and to put in processes to ensure it never happens again.

"So You Are was in our care. We did not carry out the burial ourselves, but we chose the provider and the arrangements, and we take full responsibility for that," he said. "We should have known exactly how horses were handled after leaving our hospital, and we did not. That process is not good enough, and it must change.
"No owner should have to go through what So You Are's connections have experienced this week."
Waste management company Cleanaway, which runs the landfill, told national broadcaster ABC the horse's body was moved to a permitted area of the site.

"Cleanaway's Lucas Heights landfill is licensed to accept and dispose of animal carcasses," a spokesperson told ABC. "The horse carcass delivered to the facility arrived in a small tipper truck, which is not permitted on the landfill tipping face for safety reasons. In accordance with established procedures, the carcass was transferred into a skip bin to enable its safe disposal at the landfill."
"These images are distressing"
Racing NSW said So You Are was being held temporarily, awaiting burial, when the video was recorded.

"These images are distressing for all involved and for all of us who care deeply about our horses," Racing NSW said in a statement. "The way in which So You Are's body was left is distressing and completely unacceptable. So You Are deserved to be treated with dignity and respect."

The state's racing regulator said under industry guidelines — now under review — a licensed landfill was the preferred option for animals that have been euthanized because of the chemicals involved in the process.

"That burial, however, should have occurred in a timely and respectful manner," the statement continued. "If through the course of our ongoing investigation any wrongdoing is found, Racing NSW will not hesitate to take appropriate action."
Australian politician Emma Hurst called the news "absolutely heartbreaking," but not surprising, ABC reported.

"This horse has been treated as though he is nothing more than a piece of rubbish," she said. "To be completely honest, I'm not entirely surprised. We've had complaints about the racing industry for the entire eight years that I have been in parliament."

title: Protests flare in Philippines over Trump's visit and planned AI hub
summary: Protests against President Trump's visit to the Philippines have popped up around the country, as local residents criticize a Trump administration project to build an artificial intelligence hub.
story: Manila, Philippines — Protests against President Trump's visit to the Philippines have popped up around the country, as local residents criticize a Trump administration project to build an artificial intelligence and manufacturing hub just north of the country's capital of Manila.

In the opening salvo for Pax Silica, a U.S. State Department-led international initiative to secure non-Chinese supply chains for high-tech manufacturing, a more than 4,000-acre manufacturing hub is planned to be built in the Philippines.
Protesters in Manila on Monday held signs reading "Trump Out," drawings of him as a clown or a devil, and signs calling on the public to reject the Pax Silica initiative.
Critics argue the proposed industrial hub will displace farming communities and the Indigenous Aeta tribe, harm the country's water supply and represent U.S. imperialism over the Philippines.
"They have been grabbing our lands. They have been grabbing our economy. … Pax Silica is just for the U.S. It's not for us," said Maninging Vilog, a teacher and advocate for Aeta communities.

"If you look at the farmers, what do they care about AI? The people selling water … selling cigarettes, the people who drive buses. What do they care about AI?" said Kaiser Cortina, a 20-year-old protester.

Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., also a subject of the protests this week, supports the hub. He said in October he is "terribly excited" about the project's economic benefits, framing it as a "grand opportunity" for the country to move up the "value chain" by shifting into advanced manufacturing and research, according to PhilStar Global.
Marcos' administration has claimed the project could create 100,000 to 130,000 jobs.

A proposed 4,000-acre artificial intelligence hub north of Manila is drawing opposition ahead of President Trump’s visit to the Philippines.The project is part of Pax Silica, a U.S.-led initiative aimed at reducing reliance on China for critical technology supply chains.… pic.twitter.com/9BQJFClqL8

Over 25 countries have signed on to the Pax Silica initiative since it was announced by the U.S. State Department in December 2025, including the United Kingdom, Israel, Japan and India. The Philippines joined the initiative in April, leading the U.S. and the Philippines to announce plans for a manufacturing hub.

A State Department spokesman said that the Philippines proposed the site of the hub, and that it is up to them to decide under its own laws and timetable, whether and how to proceed. They added that the U.S. remains committed to their set goal to create skilled manufacturing jobs in the Philippines and a more reliable supply chain for both countries.

The U.S. has raised concerns for years about supply chains for the hardware that powers AI, including worries that China could get access to advanced chips. The issue has drawn new attention in recent weeks, amid revelations that now-former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had an affair with a businesswoman and suspected Chinese intelligence asset whose company was under investigation for smuggling chips. (The company has denied chip smuggling.)

Pax Silica participants signed a declaration on Sunday that sets out a "common understanding of the sensitive technologies and critical infrastructure that underpin" artificial intelligence supply chains.

U.S. and Filipino officials have said there aren't expected to be any big announcements about Pax Silica this week during Mr. Trump's visit during the ASEAN summit in Manila. The U.S. president is expected to meet with Marcos on Wednesday before flying to China.
CBS News has reached out to the State Department for comment.

Antonio Tinio, a member of the Philippine House of Representatives, said there aren't any specific votes on Pax Silica planned in the country's legislature, and claimed "it's far from certain" that the Pax Silica hub will start construction and be successful.
And he added that the critiques of the Manila hub mirror the anti-AI data center sentiment in the U.S.

"The opposition to AI data centers is global. … That was one of the big issues in your election. It's a big issue. There's a lot of opposition throughout Southeast Asia, including Malaysia and Indonesia, and also in the Philippines," Tinio said.

title: Well-known journalist who reported death threats is killed on street
summary: Costa Rican independent journalist Camilo Rodriguez had called out alleged ties between drug traffickers and politicians on social media.
story: Costa Rican independent journalist Camilo Rodriguez, who had called out alleged ties between drug traffickers and politicians on social media, was shot dead Monday outside the capital San Jose, authorities said.

Two men riding on a motorcycle opened fire on Rodriguez as he was driving through the town of Santo Domingo de Heredia, police chief Raul Rivera said. Rodriguez was attacked at around 3:20 p.m. local time amid heavy traffic on a main highway, Reuters reported, citing the Red Cross.
Rodriguez, 50, had reported receiving several death threats from drug trafficking groups.

He would name drug lords by their full names and claimed to have provided reports to the U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration regarding links between drug traffickers and powerful figures in politics and business.

When President Laura Fernandez was running for office last year, she sued Rodriguez for defamation after he posted a video claiming her home had been built with money allegedly provided by a drug trafficker.
"Regardless of the content of his statements, what happened today in our country is a stain on freedom of expression," Fernandez said in a video released by her office.
Rodriguez ran for president in 2022, but his nomination was rejected by electoral authorities on technical grounds.
He also accused his ex-wife of being involved in drug trafficking. She has filed a complaint alleging he sexually abused their children.
The Costa Rican Journalists' Association condemned his killing and demanded "a swift investigation."

"All evidence so far points to the silencing of a dissenting voice in Costa Rica -- a person who published information about organized crime in the country," the association's president, Yanancy Noguera, told AFP.
In recent years, Costa Rica has gone from being a drug transit point to a logistics hub for trafficking, and has lost its status as one of the safest countries in Central America.
Fernandez, who took office in May, campaigned on a promise to crack down on the crime wave, and said she is drawing inspiration from El Salvador's iron-fisted President Nayib Bukele.
Fernandez herself that she has received intelligence reports showing that jailed gang members have ordered her assassination, the Tico Times reported on Monday.

Attorney General Carlo Diaz announced an investigation into the murder, adding that Rodriguez -- who had contributed to various Costan Rican print, radio and television media outlets and more recently turned to social media -- had declined to enter a witness protection program.
Diaz told local media the crime scene resembled a contract killing, Reuters reported.

"We know he was a communicator who publicly identified people for alleged links to drug trafficking," Diaz said. "Silencing someone who reports on drug trafficking or corruption, in this case a communicator, is a signal we cannot tolerate in a democratic society."
According to Reporters Without Borders, more than half of the world's countries now fall into the "difficult" or "very serious" categories for press freedom.

title: U.S. gave Singapore scant help with Alice Huang probe, source says
summary: Singapore held Alice Huang's passport for 8 months and asked the U.S. to help investigate her firm's suspected Nvidia chip sales, but received little help, sources say.
story: Singaporean authorities seized the passport of then-Megaspeed chief executive Alice Huang in June 2025 and held it for eight months, preventing her departure while trying to engage the U.S. government to support their investigation into advanced Nvidia chips possibly being shipped to China.

One source with knowledge of the matter told CBS News on Friday the Singaporean government received no meaningful help from Washington during the time she was in the Asian city-state. This source said officials in Washington were "not forthcoming" in response to Singapore's requests for help, and no substantive assistance has been provided to date.
Singapore's government confirmed in a statement this week that it reached out to both the U.S. Department of Justice and the FBI for assistance with its investigation.
Alice Huang is the suspected Chinese spy at the center of the extramarital affair scandal that toppled Nvidia founder Jensen Huang from the helm of the global tech giant he built over three decades.

Since February 2025, Singaporean authorities have been investigating whether Alice Huang and Megaspeed worked with California-based Supermicro to ship the Silicon Valley firm's computer servers — equipped with advanced Nvidia chips — to China, the source told CBS News.
Alice Huang flew into Singapore in June 2025 for a voluntary interview with Singapore-based investigators from the U.S. Bureau of Industry and Security, according to the source.

The agency sits within the U.S. Department of Commerce and regulates the export of sensitive products on national security and economic grounds. The American authorities requested the interview, according to a Thursday statement by Singapore's Home Affairs Ministry, as part of a post-shipment verification check, a process used to determine whether imported products have reached their declared recipient.
Singaporean police also interviewed Huang on the same day as the U.S. officials, and made the decision to impound her passport.
The source said it was not known where Huang, a Chinese national, arrived in Singapore from in June 2025.

By February 2026, however, the Singapore Police Force had not charged Huang with any crime and had no option but to return her passport, the source told CBS News. She was barred from ever returning to Singapore, as authorities assessed that she had given "inaccurate information" to downplay her role at Megaspeed, as noted in the statement from the home ministry.
That statement was released four days after Jensen Huang admitted to having an affair with a woman who sources confirmed to CBS News was Alice Huang.

Singapore's investigation has focused on whether the then-Megaspeed CEO may have broken domestic law by lying about the details of purchases of computer servers from Supermicro, a San Jose-based technology company. The company's servers use Nvidia's advanced chips to run artificial intelligence software, data centers and cloud computing.

"The suspected domestic offenses pertained to potential false declarations in relation to the purchase of servers and other related offenses," Singapore's Home Affairs Ministry said in its statement this week.
Singaporean investigators have tried to determine the true ultimate destination of the Supermicro servers ordered by Megaspeed.

A second source familiar with the investigation told CBS News it is believed they may have been sent to Malaysia, but Singaporean investigators suspect "some or all" of them may then have been shipped onward to China. Megaspeed has denied any wrongdoing.
Singapore's home ministry attempted to contact Supermicro, but the U.S. company only "provided limited cooperation," according to the home ministry statement.

A spokesperson for the California firm told CBS News that Megaspeed "is not, and has never been, a Supermicro customer,"  adding that the company had "been responsive to inquiries and has fully cooperated with U.S. and Taiwanese officials, while also voluntarily providing information and engaging with all requests from Singapore authorities to date."

The New York Times reported Wednesday that Malaysia kept Nvidia's chips and installed them in its own data centers, but then rented use of those centers to China, rather than physically shipping any chips to China.
Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim said Friday that there was "no indication" any chips linked to the Nvidia-Megaspeed issue had been re-exported out of the country.

Beijing has dismissed the claims that Alice Huang is a Chinese spy as "groundless speculation" and "nothing more than an attempt to smear China." Asked Thursday about a Bloomberg report that she had returned to China, Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning told reporters: "I do not have information on what you mentioned."
Since 2022, the U.S. has restricted the export of Nvidia's most powerful chips to China over national security concerns as the world's two biggest economies race for dominance in the AI sector.

The Singapore police first raised the issue with U.S. authorities in July 2025 to try to secure Supermicro's cooperation in revealing where its servers were ultimately ending up, repeating requests "on several occasions to the U.S. Department of Justice and the Federal Bureau of Investigation," according to the Home Affairs Ministry's Thursday statement.

The second source confirmed to CBS News that Washington did not meaningfully engage with the requests for help on the investigation and said it "would be useful to know" what Supermicro declared about its exports to fulfill orders by Megaspeed, whether those products were registered as being bound for Malaysia, and whether some or all of those products were actually "bound for somewhere else," such as China.

The Singapore home ministry said in its statement that six other individuals linked to Megaspeed, in addition to Alice Huang, are wanted for questioning, but none have been in the country since the government launched its investigation in February 2025.
"One is a Singaporean citizen and the rest are foreigners," said the first person familiar with the case.

Singapore has charged five other people in a wider fraud conspiracy case related to the suspected transfer of Nvidia chips, including one Chinese man charged on Friday. The case was launched at the same time as the probe into Alice Huang and Megaspeed, the first source told CBS News, but it is separate.

"Singapore is committed to upholding our reputation as a trusted and reliable business hub. We will not allow companies or individuals to misuse Singapore's business environment to engage in fraud or dishonest practices," the home ministry said in its statement, adding that it would "conduct its own investigations independently, in accordance with our laws and based on the evidence available. We will cooperate with foreign authorities where appropriate, and take firm enforcement action wherever the evidence warrants it."
This story published first on CBS News at 12:16 p.m. on Nov. 13, 2026.

title: Ukraine and Russia trade major strikes as Trump set to meet Putin
summary: Ukraine has struck the Kerch Bridge, which connects Russian-occupied Crimea and Russia, twice, taking it out of service, as Moscow attacks bridges in Kyiv.
story: Ukraine struck a major bridge connecting Russian-occupied Crimea and the Russian mainland Tuesday for the second night in a row, while Russia hit two major bridges in the Ukrainian capital Kyiv.

Traffic was halted for hours across the Kerch Bridge, which carries both automobile and rail traffic, after it was hit shortly after midnight on Tuesday. The bridge has been a target of previous Ukrainian attacks and holds symbolic value as it was built following Russia's annexation of Crimea in 2014.
There was no official comment on the damage, but unverified social media images appeared to show a section of the road bridge completely collapsed and in the water.

Russian military blogger Alexander Kots called the damage "significant" and said cars would not be able to cross it for a month. Kots also said the train service that runs across the bridge had been suspended, citing Russia's Ministry of Transport, but added the railway's tracks were intact.

Meanwhile, Russia's defense ministry said it shot down 1,441 Ukrainian drones during a major overnight barrage — the second-highest one-day figure this year. Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin reported that more than 800 had been headed to the capital itself, while officials reported attacks across 19 regions of the country.
In Kyiv, Russian ballistic missiles hit the Northern and Southern bridges — two major arteries that cross the Dnipro River.
Traffic was suspended, causing gridlock early on Tuesday morning. Russia's army confirmed it had hit both bridges in a "massive attack" on Ukraine's infrastructure.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy had warned of a major Russian attack in the days leading up to a meeting in China on Thursday of Presidents Trump, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin.
Ukraine's Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said the meeting would "only encourage Putin to continue this war."
The White House had earlier signaled that the Ukraine war would not be addressed by the leaders, but Mr. Trump said Monday as he prepared to fly to Asia that it would be among the topics discussed.
"We'll talk about my favorite subject, Ukraine," he told reporters.
China has said only that "safeguarding world peace" and "promoting strategic stability in major power relations" will be on the agenda for the trilateral summit.

title: U.K. mulls changing sexual consent laws after Russell Brand case
summary: Britain's government will consider adopting staggered ages for sexual consent in the wake of "appalling" stories of "abuse of power by powerful men."
story: London —  Britain's government is considering changing the U.K.'s laws on the legal age of sexual consent as a woman who claims she was raped by convicted sex offender Russell Brand campaigns to criminalize sex between adults and 16- or 17-year-olds.

British Work and Pensions Secretary Pat McFadden said over the weekend that "appalling" stories of "abuse of power by powerful men" had emerged last week, warranting consideration of a new law that would set out different ages of consent depending on the ages of the individuals involved.

Already practiced by several other nations, the merits of this staggered age of consent approach have "been raised and will be discussed" by the government, McFadden said, adding that he "can't tell you what the conclusion of that would be, but the last week has certainly put that up in lights."

A day after Brand was sentenced to 10-and-a-half years in prison for rape and sexual assault, fellow British television personality and author David Walliams was named as the subject of multiple allegations of grooming young girls and harassing female colleagues.

Under current U.K. law, an adult of any age can have sex with a consenting person 16 years old or older. If a staggered system were imposed, it could make it illegal for anyone 18 or older, for instance, to have sex with individuals aged between 16 and 18, regardless of whether they gave verbal consent.

There is plenty of precedent: In eight U.S. states —   Idaho, Louisiana, Massachusetts, Mississippi, Missouri, Nevada, North Dakota and Florida, where Brand was living before he was jailed — the age of consent varies depending on the age gap between the two people.

In Idaho, for example, if one person is under 16 and the other is 18 or older, or if the victim is 16 or 17 years old and the perpetrator is at least three years older, it is classed as rape. "Lewd contact with a child" younger than 16 is a crime regardless of the perpetrator's age.
In most U.S. states, the age of consent has a "close-in-age" exception for people under 18 who engage in mutually consentual sexual acts.

In Canada, where the age of consent is 16, the staggered-age system includes more detailed, age-dependent exemptions. For people aged 12-13, the partner must be less than two years older; age 14-15, the partner must be less than five years older, and between 16-17, people are generally seen as able to give consent, unless their sexual partner is in a position of trust or authority toward them.
Austria, Belgium, France, Ireland and South Africa also have close-in-age exemptions.
Mia Latter, now 37, has accused Brand of raping her when she was 16 and he was 30, and she is now campaigning for a staggered age of consent to be introduced in Britain.

Latter, whose allegations were not part of the case that saw Brand convicted last week of raping and sexually assaulting other women, abandoned her anonymity as an accuser of the celebrity in an interview published over the weekend by The Sunday Times. She told the newspaper she was speaking out to help "protect teenagers from being groomed by older men or women."

"I don't want to criminalize teenagers having sex with each other," she said. "If you're between the ages of 16 and 18, it seems reasonable that you can have relationships with each other, and [teenagers] are always going to. But … if you're in your thirties, forties and fifties and you're trying to have a relationship with someone under the age of 18, it [should be] a criminal offense."
Brand protested his innocence from jail on Sunday in a statement read out by his wife Laura.

The prime minister's office said Monday that the comments were under investigation, as "prisoners are strictly banned from making statements that cause distress to victims and speaking to the media is only permitted in exceptional circumstances."

title: Drawing China close, is Kim Jong Un bracing to confront the U.S.?
summary: As North Korea and China draw closer together, is Kim Jong Un ramping up for a confrontation with the U.S.?
story: Dandong, China — With a pair of binoculars and a camera hanging around his neck, retired Chinese government official Mr. Yang leaned against a fence on a boardwalk that meanders through the city of Dandong, peering across the wide Yalu River that separates China from North Korea.

He came to visit from Dalian, about 200 miles away, despite the temperature hovering just above freezing, to catch a glimpse of life inside China's heavily sanctioned, nuclear armed neighbor nation. But the main attraction he came to see is the massive new bridge towering over Dandong, which now links the two countries.
"The bridge is good, but it's only for trucks and cars, not for the trains," he complained. "But this is good for trade, and I do hope this means relations improve with North Korea."

At almost two miles long and four lanes across, the new Yalu River Bridge is a feat of engineering. The Chinese side was finished 12 years ago, but North Korea only recently completed its section, with leader Kim Jong Un making a surprise appearance for the official opening on Oct. 24.

As CBS News visited the new river crossing, a large group of tourists arrived from Fujian province, more than 1,000 miles to the south, to pose for photos in front of the impressive piece of infrastructure.

"This will enhance the friendship between China and North Korea for sure, but we hope that North Korea will open up to the West," tour group leader Mr. Sun told CBS News. "North Korea was an isolated country, and this shows they're trying to join the world."
That may be a message China's government is keen to encourage, but the recent actions and rhetoric from the Kim regime in Pyongyang suggests otherwise.
Kim Jong Un ramping up for a confrontation?
Since the beginning of October alone, North Korea has test-fired more than a dozen missiles — the most concentrated series of such launches by Pyongyang since 2023.
Kim has personally observed some of the launches, accompanied by his teenage daughter Kim Ju Ae, widely viewed as his potential successor.

Former U.S. State Department official Robert Carlin, who has half of a century of experience as a North Korea analyst, believes Kim could be preparing to take steps that will inevitably end in confrontation with the U.S.

"It's part of a pattern of preparations to get ready for what he (Kim) thinks he wants to do. So he's testing new systems, and there's been a flurry of them. They can test in private — they do it all the time —   so they want to make these visible for some reason," Carlin told CBS News. "When you put that together with the pretty aggressive probing along the demarcation line, the high-level statements with warnings and threats … we have to take seriously the possibility that KJU [Kim] is preparing something, putting himself into position for the moment he thinks the winds are at his back, the situation is ripe for him to make some sort of move against U.S. assets in the region and against South Korea."

President Trump has been pushing for a new meeting with Kim for months, citing what he considers his good personal rapport with the North Korean leader, and there has been speculation the two leaders could meet while Mr. Trump is in China this week to attend the APEC summit.

He fueled that speculation himself Monday as he departed for Asia, saying it would be up to the Chinese hosts of the summit, but telling reporters when asked about a possible meeting: "Yes, we might have Kim Jong Un."

Mr. Trump met three times with Kim during his first term, including two historic summits aimed at getting the North Korean leader to agree to steps toward his nuclear-armed country denuclearizing, but the discussions went nowhere.

Since then, Kim has only expanded his nuclear arsenal. South Korean intelligence agencies believe Pyongyang could now have as many as 120 nuclear warheads. Kim has made it clear, meanwhile, that he will only agree to a new round of negotiations if the U.S. first and formally recognizes North Korea as a nuclear state.
Burgeoning ties with Russia and China

While longstanding international sanctions against his country over its nuclear weapons program remain in place, since the failed talks with Mr. Trump, Kim has projected a sense of being emboldened — of no longer leading a nation ubiquitously dismissed as an international pariah.
The relationship with China, while at times strained, has been a constant, and it has helped Kim push the image of North Korea as a global player, rather than a "hermit kingdom."

Since Vladimir Putin ordered the ongoing, full-scale invasion of Ukraine more than four years ago, Pyongyang has also proven a dependable ally to Russia. North Korea has sent a constant stream of munitions to replenish Moscow's depleted stocks, as well as thousands of soldiers to fight on the front lines. In return, Moscow has sent financial and technological assistance, helping North Korea further develop its nuclear weapons program.

The city of Dandong is a symbol of the China-North Korea bond. Hundreds of thousands of Chinese troops marched across the original Yalu River bridge to fight alongside North Korean soldiers in the Korean War. Almost 3 million Chinese soldiers were deployed to fight in that conflict between 1950 and 1953.

The city was bombed by U.S. forces due to its strategic position on the vital North Korean supply line, and the old Yalu River Bridge was destroyed. Renamed "Broken Bridge," it became a war relic and tourist attraction in its own right.

In the center of Dandong, overlooking the old Broken Bridge and the nearby Sino-Korean Friendship Bridge, a smaller piece of infrastructure that facilitates cross-border rail and one-lane road traffic with the North Korean city of Sinuiju, local businesses sell Korean outfits along with trinkets and souvenirs, cashing in on Chinese fascination with the neighbors.

Grocery stores sell liquor in bottles that look like grenades, mortars and bullets, while hotels positioned along the river, facing North Korea, offer telescopes and binoculars in bedrooms for guests to peer across the Yalu into apartments and farmland on the far side. On some sections of the river, North Korea is only about 1,000 feet away.

Using our own long lens, CBS News was able to see people in North Korean apartments at night. At first light, the North Korean side became a hive of activity as people headed out to the fields and greenhouses to work.
George, a 16-year-old student, said he was visiting Dandong because of his passion for Chinese and North Korean history.

"North Korea is trying to get better connections with China, and China is opening to Western countries more and more, and if those things continue to happen, maybe North Korea will be opening to Western countries the same as China," he said.
As for the increasing tension on the Korean Peninsula, George dismissed the concerns.
Kim Jong Un, he said, is just "trying to tell the Western countries and the whole world that the DPRK is powerful enough to join the global stage right now."

While in Dandong, CBS News visited a restaurant and met a North Korean waitress who said she had been living in China for a year — one of as many as 80,000 North Koreans living and working in the city, all of whom are strictly monitored and not permitted to assimilate with the local Chinese population.
She told CBS News she missed home and hopes to return one day to North Korea, and she praised Kim Jong Un as a father to her country.

title: Women in U.K. are getting automatic pardons for past abortion convictions
summary: Women who have received a caution from police will also be pardoned, and women arrested or investigated for ending their own pregnancy will have those details removed from their criminal records.
story: Women in the United Kingdom who were convicted of illegally terminating their pregnancies under a Victorian-era law will receive automatic pardons on Monday, the government said.
This follows the passage of a landmark vote by Parliament last year to decriminalize abortion by repealing a section of the 1861 Offences Against the Person Act.

Women who have received a caution from police will also be pardoned, and women arrested or investigated for ending their own pregnancy will have those details removed from their criminal records. They will not have to apply for pardons, and some will be issued posthumously.

The government did not provide the number of women affected. But Tonia Antoniazzi, the Labour member of Parliament who introduced the decriminalization amendment, said police have investigated more than 100 women suspected of illegal abortions in the five years preceding last year's vote. That included some who suffered natural miscarriages and stillbirths.
Antoniazzi described how women suspected of illegally aborting a fetus were once "dragged from hospital beds to police cells" and interrogated when they should have been cared for.

"This trauma cannot be erased, but I hope that this offers some alleviation of the pain these women have endured, enabling them to participate fully in society again, living their lives to the full, working the jobs they've always wanted to," she said.

Under current law, doctors can legally carry out abortions in England, Scotland and Wales up to 24 weeks, and beyond that under special circumstances, such as when the life of the mother is in danger. Abortion in Northern Ireland was decriminalized in 2019.
Under the Crime and Policing Act that took effect this spring, women who terminate a pregnancy at any stage will not face criminal charges.
The measure was opposed by anti-abortion groups that argued it would open the door to abortion on demand at any stage of pregnancy.

"While no pardon can undo the distress and trauma these women have experienced, this historic change in the law recognizes the profound harm caused by their criminalization and represents a meaningful step towards justice," said Heidi Stewart, with the British Pregnancy Advisory Service, according to CBS News partner BBC News.
The law was changed after high-profile prosecutions, including the jailing of a mother of three that caused an outcry from abortion rights supporters.

Carla Foster was sentenced to more than two years in prison in 2023 for medically inducing an abortion about eight months into her pregnancy. An appeals court freed her a month later, saying the case called for "compassion, not punishment."

Another woman, Nicola Packer, was acquitted on a charge of unlawfully self-administering poison or a noxious thing with intent to procure a miscarriage. Packer, who took abortion medicine when she was about 26 weeks pregnant, testified that she did not know she had been pregnant for more than 10 weeks, which was the legal limit.
Her friend Helle Tumbridge, with Packer's consent, told BBC News that the whole incident has been "incredibly traumatic."
She said it took five years of investigations before a trial eventually found Packer not guilty.
"Of course, by that point the damage had been done," Tumbridge said, "and she'll live with that trauma for the rest of her life."

title: Trump says he may meet with North Korea's Kim Jong Un in China
summary: President Trump said he may meet with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un on his China trip this week.
story: Washington — President Trump said he may meet with North Korean dictator Kim Jong Un during his trip to Asia this week.

As he left the White House Monday morning for a summit in the Philippines, which will be followed by a trip to China, Mr. Trump told reporters the meeting with Kim would take place in China — if it happens. No meeting with Kim has been confirmed by the White House. The president said whether the meeting happens is up to Chinese President Xi Jinping. Mr. Trump will meet with Xi, along with Russian President Vladimir Putin, later this week.

"We'll be with President Xi," the president told reporters on the White House South Lawn. "He was here a month ago. And we're also going to meet with President Putin. And we may meet with Kim Jong Un, also. So that'll be good. We could — we have a chance to accomplish a lot."
The president said he doesn't know if Kim will come.
"He may come," Mr. Trump said of Kim. "I don't know. That's up to President Xi."
Mr. Trump has met with the North Korean leader in person three times, all during his first term in office. He is the only sitting U.S. president to have met with Kim.
This is a developing story and will be updated.

title: Drug lord who orchestrated murder of U.S. agent dies at 80
summary: Miguel Angel Felix Gallardo, the architect of modern Mexican drug trafficking, was known as "the boss of bosses."
story: Miguel Angel Felix Gallardo, the architect of modern Mexican drug trafficking known as "the boss of bosses," who transformed the global cocaine trade and orchestrated the murder of a U.S. agent, died Sunday at age 80, officials said.

The notorious drug kingpin, a former police officer who played a key role in forging alliances with Colombian traffickers, died in a hospital where he had been transferred from prison two days earlier.

"After remaining under observation with a guarded prognosis, he died on November 15 at the medical facility" after "he suffered multiple organ failure," according to a statement from the security ministry of the state of Jalisco, where he was being held.
Felix Gallardo's health had deteriorated markedly in recent years, with conditions including high blood pressure, diabetes and deafness.

In 2022, then-president Andres Manuel Lopez Obrador said he was "in very poor health." A judge granted him house arrest, but technical problems with electronic ankle monitoring prevented his transfer.
One of the founders of the Guadalajara cartel, from which the Sinaloa cartel would later emerge, Felix Gallardo had been incarcerated since 1989 and was serving a 40-year sentence.

He was convicted for the 1985 murder of an undercover U.S. Drug Enforcement Agency officer, Enrique "Kiki" Camarena Salazar, which outraged the United States. Last year, Camarena's alleged killer,  Rafael Caro Quintero, was transferred to the U.S. along with 28 other prisoners requested by the U.S. government.

Camarena, a father of three sons, was living in Guadalajara, Mexico, with his family working as an undercover DEA agent, his son told CBS News in a 2017 interview. He had been stationed there for four years on the trail of the country's biggest marijuana and cocaine traffickers.
A memorial was created in Camarena's honor in Los Angeles in 2014.
His son Enrique, who became a judge in 2014 in San Diego, told CBS News he carries his father's lessons into the courtroom. "He taught us to treat everyone fairly."
Rise of the cartels
Felix Gallardo was a native of Sinaloa state, where he was born on Jan. 8, 1946, according to public records.
His involvement in crime went virtually hand in hand with his career in the state and federal police.
He even served as a bodyguard to a Sinaloa governor, a role that experts say may have helped him secure the complicity and protection of powerful politicians.
He partnered with another veteran kingpin, Rafael Caro Quintero. Together with other crime bosses, they united gangs trafficking drugs to the United States and formed the Guadalajara cartel.
The cartel was formed around a "hegemonic model" and laid "the roots for nearly all of today's drug trafficking activities," according to InSight Crime, a website specializing in the drug trade.
Felix Gallardo "partnered with Colombian traffickers like Pablo Escobar, and became Escobar's most important Mexico associate," the publication said.
The Guadalajara gang controlled the country's underworld, earning Felix Gallardo the nicknames "El jefe de jefes" and "El Padrino" -- which translate to "the boss of bosses" and "the Godfather."
Downfall
Felix Gallardo was convicted for the February 1985 murder of Camarena Salazar, who was kidnapped and tortured.
The agent's death remains an open wound for the United States.
Intense pressure from Washington led to the arrest in 1985 of Caro Quintero, who is now imprisoned in the United States on charges of drug trafficking and the agent's murder.
Felix Gallardo was arrested in April 1989 but continued to control the criminal business from prison, according to experts.
He was serving his sentence at Puente Grande prison in Jalisco state.

The Guadalajara cartel imploded in the 1990s, and its local leaders formed regional cartels, including the Sinaloa cartel, built up by Joaquin "El Chapo" Guzman and Ismael "El Mayo" Zambada, both sentenced to life in prison in the United States.

Felix Gallardo remained in the popular imagination through narcocorridos, or drug ballads, such as "El jefe de jefes," which is banned in public spaces, and Netflix dramas about drug trafficking, with Mexican actor Diego Luna portraying the kingpin.

title: John Madden role pushes Nicolas Cage to dramatic physical transformation with ‘brutal’ diet, prosthetics
summary: Nicolas Cage gained over 25 pounds on pasta and bread, then added 30 more with prosthetics to physically transform into John Madden for the biopic.
story: Nicolas Cage discussed which one of his former roles was his favorite to play, listing Castor Troy in "Face/Off" as one of the top ones.
Nicolas Cage's radical transformation to portray John Madden in the upcoming biopic about the NFL legend included packing on the pounds and the prosthetics.
In addition to a number of prosthetics, Cage, 62, admitted he gained more than 25 pounds to physically embody his character for Prime Video's "Madden."
"I just enjoyed my pasta and my sourdough bread, which I don’t normally do," Cage told People magazine.
THE CAST OF 'MADDEN' HITS THE RED CARPET TO TALK ABOUT WHETHER THEY'VE CHOWED DOWN ON TURDUCKEN
Nicolas Cage gained weight and wore a slew of prosthetics to portray NFL legend John Madden. (Chuck Zlotnick/Prime © Amazon Content Services LLC)
"I mean, it’s pretty brutal. Two premier protein shakes and one meal a day. It’s usually a Caesar salad."
He added, "But with that, I got to enjoy the pasta and then I added — look, I’m 62, so I’m not going to gain 60 pounds. That’s dangerous. But I added the other 30 with [prosthetics]."
NICOLAS CAGE TURNED DOWN PARTS IN TWO BIG FRANCHISE MOVIES FOR ROLES HE THOUGHT WERE BETTER
Cage admitted that while he enjoyed packing on the pounds, returning to his pre-Madden size was slightly more challenging.
"Not really," Cage said, when asked if the weight came off easily. "A lot of days in the gym on the elliptical. I still do it. I’m always on the elliptical for a couple of hours a day."
Nicolas Cage portrays John Madden while Christian Bale got into character as his best friend, Raiders icon Al Davis. (2026 Amazon Content Services LLC)

Directed by David O. Russell, the film follows Madden from Super Bowl-winning coach of the Oakland Raiders to his role in creating arguably one of the most influential video game franchises – Madden NFL ​with Electronic Arts.

The "Con Air" actor brought Madden to life with makeup artist Adrien Morot, who previously helped create Brendan Fraser's physical transformation on his Academy Award-winning role in the 2023 flick "The Whale."
'THE ODYSSEY' STAR MATT DAMON REVEALS BRUTAL SIX-MONTH TRANSFORMATION BEHIND CHRISTOPHER NOLAN FILM
"It was the same approach, a hybrid approach," Cage said. "That was, to me, the sweet spot."
Kathryn Hahn said Cage's transformation didn't stop once the prosthetics were on. (Chuck Zlotnick/Prime)

He admitted that it took time to understand his character, but everything clicked "when I realized that the root of John Madden was his love for life and his high energy and his sense of humor, and that he was a teacher first and foremost, because that was what meant the most to him."
Cage revealed that his own father worked in education as a professor of comparative literature, and he "grew to love" Madden even more after realizing that John was "a teacher first."

title: 'The Vow' host Chris Harrison says young people are ditching dating apps, turning to church
summary: Chris Harrison says young people are rejecting dating apps and turning to faith, inspiring his new Fox Nation series "Chris Harrison's The Vow."
story: The host of "Chris Harrison's The Vow" told Fox News Digital why he believes younger generations are turning toward faith and seeking deeper connections as his new dating series premieres on Fox Nation.
Chris Harrison believes young people are turning away from dating apps and looking toward faith as they search for meaningful relationships.

The television host, who returned to reality dating television with the premiere of "Chris Harrison's The Vow" on Fox Nation, told Fox News Digital that he and the show's producers have noticed what he describes as a growing movement among younger generations seeking something deeper than modern dating culture offers.
"Young people searching for something, going to church more than their parents are," Harrison said.

Chris Harrison returned to reality television as the host of Fox Nation's "The Vow," which takes a different approach to modern dating. (Getty Images)

"Attending youth nights in incredible numbers at churches and temples and all these organizations getting together around faith. So clearly they're searching for something, looking for something, and at the same time, dating apps are being rejected."
Harrison suggested that technology, while making it easier to meet people, may also be contributing to less meaningful relationships.

"So, you know, maybe this world, technologically speaking, that's moving so fast and trying to make our lives easier, and maybe trying to make connections easier, but are also less meaningful," he said.
