The new series follows Jace Cates, a 30-year-old mortgage loan officer from Oregon, as he meets 10 women hoping to find a husband. Set in the Texas Hill Country, the show focuses on faith, family values and the possibility of building a lasting marriage.
The first two episodes premiered Nov. 11, with new episodes scheduled to debut every Wednesday.
For Harrison, returning to television with a project centered on relationships has been a rewarding experience.
"If I'm being honest, it has felt very, very good to step back into the world of not just reality TV, but dating and love and helping people find love," he told Fox News Digital.
"I just feel more than ever, we need love."
Harrison said the early response to the series has been encouraging.
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

"But with the early returns that we have seen, the response from fans, people are loving it, and they seem to be enjoying the fact that I'm back on their TVs, which feels really good. It's kind of cathartic."
The television personality explained that he wanted to create a dating experience that reflected the changing priorities he believes younger generations are embracing.

"I think seeing the need for a show that is truly about love and romance, and seeing again this societal movement by the young people in this generation kind of asking for something deeper, more meaningful," he said.
Harrison said he and the producers wanted to create an environment where participants could have serious conversations about their futures.
"And so we've tried to make the most authentic, intentional environment so these people can really find love."
Jace Cates, 30, is searching for his future wife among 10 women on Fox Nation's faith-focused dating series "Chris Harrison's The Vow." (Fox Nation)
The series has already sparked conversations about traditional marriage, with several women expressing interest in becoming stay-at-home mothers while others hope to continue pursuing their careers.
Harrison said he welcomed the different perspectives, particularly because the contestants felt comfortable discussing their faith and expectations for marriage.
"I'm really glad the ladies and Jace felt really comfortable speaking of their faith and speaking of what they want and hope in a marriage, in a family," he said.
"They're asking those questions that you should be."
He explained that the women represent a wide range of expectations for their future relationships.
"There are some women that want to be stay-at-home moms. They want to just be a supportive wife. Then there are some that want to be CEOs and run the world."
CHRIS HARRISON WEIGHS IN ON CONTROVERSY SURROUNDING TRADITIONAL MARRIAGE: 'IT'S GOING TO BE DIFFERENT FOR EVERYBODY'
Harrison praised Jace for approaching the subject with an open mind.
"And what I love about Jace is, when he was talking about what he thought about traditional marriage, it was all of that," he said.
CHRIS HARRISON RETURNS TO REALITY TV WITH 'THE VOW,' FOX NATION'S FIRST-EVER DATING SHOW
"It was just being a champion for my partner, just being there for my wife, whatever that looks like."
The host acknowledged that the phrase "traditional marriage" can carry different meanings depending on the person.
"Well, I think, you know, many things in this day and age become fragmented and political," he said.
"And in this context, and I hope you'll watch 'The Vow,' because in this context, it really is more about faith and about their values and morals."
Harrison said the show isn't meant to tell viewers what a marriage should look like, but rather to encourage conversations about what works for different couples.
"I like leaning into the debate. I like leading into the conversation and maybe leaning into the uncomfortable a little bit, pushing ourselves."
Faith also plays a central role in the series, with contestants openly discussing prayer, abstinence and their religious beliefs.
Harrison said the decision to cast people of faith was intentional, but emphasized that the women have different perspectives when it comes to intimacy and relationships.
"Some are kind of born again, celibate. Some are, you know, saving themselves," he said.
He added that the variety of experiences allows viewers to connect with different contestants.
"It's not just one size fits all. That's not the real world."
Harrison also reflected on his own marriage to Lauren Zima, explaining that finding love when he least expected it reinforced his belief that people shouldn't give up on relationships.
The couple recently celebrated their third wedding anniversary after exchanging vows in Napa Valley and later hosting a larger celebration in Austin, Texas.
Chris Harrison and wife Lauren Zima recently celebrated three years of marriage. The couple worked together as executive producers on Fox Nation's "The Vow." (Getty Images)
"Maybe that's the lesson, is never give up. When you least expect it, maybe expect it the most, but have faith," he said.
"And I hope that's what 'The Vow' will do, is give people faith that love still exists."
Harrison, who serves as an executive producer of the series alongside his wife, said working together has made the project especially meaningful.
"You know, I think doing the show with the love of your life, first of all, it's an honor and a privilege to get to do that," he said.

He explained that the goal was to raise expectations by focusing on genuine commitment rather than casual dating.
"And the reaction so far has been, 'Thank you. Thank you for providing this environment. Thank you for doing a show like this.'"

title: Robert Pattinson’s James Bond casting could bring 'darker,' 'moodier' twist as fans crave classic 007: expert
summary: Robert Pattinson calls his James Bond casting "the honor of a lifetime," but critics say his brooding Batman past makes him a risky pick for 007.
story: Former Bond girl Alison Papworth shares why she wants the next 007 to stay true to the books as speculation swirls over the role.
James Bond may never miss, but Robert Pattinson's casting as the next iconic British secret agent was positively shocking to fans across the world.

Pattinson, 40, called the role "the honor of a lifetime," in a statement released Monday where "Dune" director Denis Villeneuve was also tapped to bring Bond back to the big screen following Daniel Craig's 15-year reign as 007.
Fox News contributor Raymond Arroyo admitted he was "shaken, not stirred" by the casting choice.
ROBERT PATTINSON NAMED NEXT JAMES BOND
Actor Robert Pattinson at the screening of the film "Primetime" at the 83rd Venice International Film Festival in Italy, on Sept. 5. (Laurent KOFFEL/Gamma-Rapho via Getty Images)

"As a huge fan of the Ian Fleming novels, Pattinson isn’t quite what I envisioned or what I think fans were hoping for," Arroyo told Fox News Digital. "After five Bond films with Daniel Craig in the lead, it was probably time to bring back some of the fun and charm that Pierce Brosnan and Roger Moore brought to the franchise."
He noted how Pattinson was known for his "brooding and dark qualities," a contrast to the more masculine qualities a Bond character usually brings to the screen.
FORMER BOND GIRL SAYS NEXT 007 SHOULD BE 'ANOTHER GORGEOUS MAN' AS JAMES BOND DECISION
"As a huge fan of the Ian Fleming novels, Pattinson isn’t quite what I envisioned or what I think fans were hoping for."

"Fun and a light touch is not the first thing that comes to mind when you think of his filmography," Arroyo said. "His Batman was a pretty dreary affair, the sequel of which I could care less about seeing. Bond also requires a certain physicality and strength – he is an assassin after all."
Arroyo believed Henry Cavill "would have been a much better choice all round."
Sean Connery starred as James Bond 007 in the '64 film "Goldfinger." (Screen Archives/Getty Images)

"But it sounds like MGM/Amazon wants to give audiences a darker, moodier Bond – just when the public is craving a good, old-fashioned escape. We’ll see if audiences wish this new Bond to ‘Live or Let Die.’"
Amazon MGM Studios announced Pattinson’s casting on social media with a brief snippet of the actor emerging from the shadows with a gun.
PIERCE BROSNAN BACKS 'FANTASTIC BEASTS' STAR FOR NEXT JAMES BOND, PREDICTS FANS WILL BE 'BLOWN AWAY'

"Before anything else, I want to express my deep gratitude to the remarkable actors who joined us on this journey. We were surrounded by extraordinary talent, but there can only be one 007," Villeneuve said in a statement.
"I am overjoyed to welcome Robert Pattinson as our new James Bond. He has the timeless soul of 007 and brings a spirit that is completely new. I cannot wait to begin."
Daniel Craig starred as the British secret agent from 2006–21. (Greg Williams/Eon Productions via Getty Images)
Adrienne Uthe, founder of Kronus Communications, exclusively told Fox News Digital that Pattinson was a "risk" to the franchise.

"He's going in as the underdog, period," Uthe said. "To win over the Connery people, the Brosnan people, the Craig people, he can’t just be good — he has to do it better than what’s been done before. That’s the bar when you take a role this iconic, you have to prove you’re actually worth it."
Pattinson found global fame years ago as telepathic vampire Edward Cullen in the "Twilight" series, which collectively grossed more than $3.3 billion worldwide.

"He can’t just be good – He has to do it better than what’s been done before. That’s the bar when you take a role this iconic, you have to prove you’re actually worth it."
Uthe noted that while a younger audience already knows his face and therein may show up to watch him as Bond, there's still a risk of "watering down the brand."
Pierce Brosnan stars as 007 opposite Denise Richards as Dr. Christmas Jones in the '99 James Bond film "The World Is Not Enough." (Keith Hamshere/Getty Images)
"Bond is established, seasoned, it’s got pedigree — so he has to bring pedigree to it too," Uthe said. "He has to prove he can be taken seriously in a role like Bond."

She added, "Now, underdogs can win. People forget Daniel Craig got torn apart when he was cast — too blonde, too rough, wrong guy — and then 'Casino Royale' came out and that was the end of that conversation. So it’s doable. But he has to earn it on screen, nobody’s handing it to him."

Seven actors have starred as the legendary British spy over the years, a role which first originated on television with Barry Nelson before Sean Connery was tapped to play the secret service agent in the '62 film "Dr. No."

Brand expert Eric Schiffer explained that the franchise may face a fan exodus with a "painfully boring" 007, a contrast to the previous Bonds played by David Niven, George Lazenby, Roger Moore, Timothy Dalton and Pierce Brosnan.
English actor Roger Moore poses for a portrait in London, England, on July 20, 1979. Moore portrayed James Bond in the Bond series. (Getty Images)
"Pattinson as Bond is a slap in the face to James, to 007's character, and largely because of his prior history and the Bond character himself," Schiffer told Fox News Digital.
"He failed as Batman. It was a horror show, and prior to that he was the 'Twilight' guy with too much makeup. We're now James Bond? Well, what happened?"

title: ‘24’ star Kiefer Sutherland claims self-defense in Uber driver assault lawsuit, calls suit ‘frivolous’
summary: Kiefer Sutherland claims self-defense in his response to an Uber driver's assault lawsuit, calling the allegations frivolous and filed to harass him.
story: Constitutional law attorney Katie Cherkasky joins 'Fox & Friends First' to weigh in on actor Kiefer Sutherland's first court appearance for an alleged attack on a Los Angeles ride-share driver.
Kiefer Sutherland is pushing back against an Uber driver’s assault allegations, arguing that any actions he took were in self-defense and accusing the driver of pursuing the lawsuit to harass him.

In court documents filed on Nov. 10 and obtained by Fox News Digital, the "24" actor denied wrongdoing in the case brought by Rafael Manvelyan in Los Angeles Superior Court. His attorneys argued that Sutherland reasonably believed he faced an imminent threat and asked that the amended complaint be dismissed with prejudice.

The response comes months after Sutherland’s Jan. 12 arrest following an alleged altercation with a rideshare driver near Sunset Boulevard and Fairfax Avenue in Los Angeles. According to arrest records obtained by Fox News Digital, the 59-year-old actor was released later that day on $50,000 bond.

In dispatch audio previously obtained by Fox News Digital, police could be heard discussing an alleged chase involving the suspect, believed to be Sutherland, and the person reporting the incident. title: Prince William draws hard line on Harry, Meghan’s royal future as King Charles leaves door open: experts
summary: King Charles may keep a personal bond with Prince Harry, but Prince William reportedly sees no path to a working royal return for the Sussexes.
story: Royal commentator Kinsey Schofield explains why Prince William is reportedly not prioritizing reconciliation with Prince Harry and Meghan Markle amid lingering trust issues.
King Charles may leave the door open to Prince Harry personally while ruling out a royal return.
The monarch and his heir, Prince William, are reportedly drawing a firm line on Harry and Meghan Markle returning to royal duties, despite hopes among royal watchers for a family reconciliation.
"There is no half in, half out concession," Kinsey Schofield, host of the YouTube show "Kinsey Schofield Unfiltered," told Fox News Digital.
PRINCE WILLIAM HAS 'LEARNED' TO LIVE WITHOUT PRINCE HARRY AS ROYAL FEUD REACHES BREAKING POINT: EXPERT
King Charles III and Prince William are reportedly in agreement that Prince Harry and Meghan Markle should not be working royals again. (Getty Images)

"The Sussexes moving back to Britain does not turn the clock back to January 2020 or reopen negotiations. King Charles may want a personal relationship with his son and grandchildren. William recognizes that his father is entitled to make that decision, but William is entitled to make his own."

"William's responsibilities today extend beyond this family feud," Schofield said. "He's preparing for the future. He's focused on the future. He's raising three children and supporting not only his wife, but his father. So maybe the question isn't when will William reconcile with Harry. Maybe it's whether William believes reconciliation would bring peace and stability into his life. And right now ... Prince William is not convinced that Harry is a peaceful presence."
Prince William, Prince of Wales, departs the Amos Bursary in Hoxton, London, on Oct. 14, 2026, after meeting scholars and alumni. (SOPA Images/LightRocket via Getty Images)
Schofield's comments came after royal author Russell Myers told People magazine that Charles and William are united in their opposition to the Sussexes representing the royal family.
WATCH: PRINCE WILLIAM SEES NO PATH TO PRINCE HARRY REUNION, EXPERT SAYS
"The king and William are completely united on the Sussexes not representing the royal family," Myers told People. "It's without a doubt how in sync they are on this matter."

The Duke and Duchess of Sussex returned to Britain on Aug. 26, about a week after reports emerged that they planned to relocate to the U.K. for an extended stay with their children, Prince Archie and Princess Lilibet. Harry has expressed a desire for his children to learn more about their British heritage.

Prince William, Prince of Wales, left, and Prince Harry, Duke of Sussex, join the Procession following the State Hearse carrying the coffin of Queen Elizabeth II towards St George's Chapel on Sept. 19, 2022, in Windsor, England. A source recently told People magazine that Harry wants to heal his rift with William. (Justin Setterfield/Getty Images)

On Sept. 7, Buckingham Palace released a letter sent on behalf of the king confirming that Harry and Meghan remain nonworking royals. The guidance reaffirmed the terms of the couple's 2020 departure from official royal duties. The letter also clarified that the Sussexes' charitable activities remain private and that their royal highness styles are not used.

Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, and Prince Harry, Duke of Sussex, arrive at The Community Recording Studio, a youth and community charity, during their visit to Nottingham on Oct. 15, 2026, in Nottingham, England. (Getty Images)
Fox News Digital reached out to Buckingham Palace and Kensington Palace for comment.
Schofield said her sources indicated that while the king is open to mending his relationship with Harry, William is more focused on protecting the monarchy and avoiding further family conflict.
Prince William, Prince of Wales, attends Earthshot's "Cricket On The Mall" on Oct. 13, 2026, in London. (Getty Images)
"My sources tell me that reconciliation with Harry and Meghan is simply not a priority for the Prince of Wales," Schofield said.

Prince William, Prince of Wales, attends the 2026 Tusk Conservation Awards at Raffles London at The OWO on Nov. 11, 2026, in London, England. As Royal Patron of Tusk, Prince William helped launch the awards in 2013 to recognize dedicated, forward-thinking individuals who are conservation leaders and wildlife rangers across Africa. (Getty Images)

"That doesn't mean William spends his days angry with Harry. Quite the opposite. William has a packed agenda. He has his family, his responsibilities as the Prince of Wales and an increasingly significant role supporting the king. And when Harry and Meghan walked away from royal life, other members of the family had to absorb some of the responsibility they'd left behind."

"William also has personally been through an incredibly difficult six years," Schofield said. "He lost Prince Philip. He lost Queen Elizabeth. His father was diagnosed with cancer. His wife Catherine was diagnosed with cancer. Meanwhile, Harry was absent and publicly hurling accusations at the royal family. Trust was damaged and trust isn't magically restored because Harry and Meghan have moved back to Britain."

Britain's Prince William, Prince of Wales, reacts as he meets with scholars and alumni of The Amos Bursary in London on Oct. 14, 2026. Founded by Baroness Valerie Amos and Colleen Amos in 2009, The Amos Bursary is a charity that supports high-achieving young people of African and Caribbean heritage. (POOL/AFP via Getty Images)
"If Prince William can't trust Harry as a brother, he certainly can't trust him as a representative of the monarchy he will one day inherit," Schofield added.

Prince Harry attends the opening of the Lost Screen Memorial exhibition at the European Parliament in Brussels, Belgium, on Nov. 10, 2026. The exhibition honors children who lost their lives due to online harms and aims to amplify the voices of bereaved families. (Anadolu via Getty Images)

Harry has had a strained relationship with members of the royal family since he and Meghan stepped back as senior working royals in 2020 and moved to California. While he has been in contact with his father and privately met with the king and Queen Camilla at Highgrove in July, his relationship with William remains strained, People reported. According to the outlet, the brothers have not been in contact.
People reported that the king and his younger son have spoken "at least once" since Harry's return to Britain.

King Charles III makes his way through gathered crowds during a visit to Surrey Street Market in Croydon, England, on Nov. 13, 2026. The visit marks both His Majesty's 78th birthday and the market's 750th anniversary. (Getty Images)

"William's view is clear — any relationship his father has with Harry or the Sussexes as a family is entirely up to him," Myers said. "But looking toward the future, he will have no relationship with them, in a working or private capacity whatsoever."

The Prince and Princess of Wales have been supporting the monarch. (Samir Hussein/WireImage)

"Prince William has publicly pledged his loyalty and allegiance to King Charles," Chard said. "Obviously, King Charles has loyalty to his son, Prince William, heir to the throne. He realizes that William is concentrating on his future kingship."
"Prince William has strict personal and institutional boundaries in place," Chard noted.
Prince William, Prince of Wales, looks on following a visit to Aberfan Memorial Garden to mark the 60th anniversary of the Aberfan disaster on Oct. 21, 2026, in Merthyr Tydfil, Wales. (Getty Images)
Royal broadcaster Ian Pelham Turner told Fox News Digital that his sources said William has made his feelings about Harry and Meghan's potential return to royal duties clear in private.

Prince Harry, Duke of Sussex, and Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, arrive at the European Parliament for the opening of the Lost Screen Memorial in Brussels, Belgium, on Nov. 10, 2026. (Getty Images)

"In many ways, Harry wants to see the issues with his brother resolved," Turner said. "But my understanding is when William becomes king, the royal family will be a very tight circle. William takes the monarchy to heart."

Prince William, Prince of Wales, and Catherine, Princess of Wales, visit The Commons, a project transforming a church into a self-sustaining community centre, during their visit to Northern Ireland on Oct. 9, 2026, in Belfast, Northern Ireland. (WireImage)
Royal author Simon Vigar told People that William and his wife, Kate Middleton, are taking a "keep calm and carry on" approach to headlines surrounding the Sussexes' return to the U.K.
"They see it as a sideshow and ancient history," Vigar told People.
British royals expert Hilary Fordwich previously told Fox News Digital there's no feud between Prince William and his father, King Charles III. (Max Mumby/Indigo/Getty Images)

"They are shining a light on things that are important to them," Ailsa Anderson, a former press secretary to Queen Elizabeth II, told People. "What they don't want is all this other noise becoming a distraction."

Britain's Prince William, Prince of Wales and Britain's Catherine, Princess of Wales arrive for a state banquet at Windsor Castle, Windsor, on Oct. 20, 2026, the first day of a three-day State Visit to the United Kingdom by the sultan of Oman. (Aaron Chown/POOL/AFP via Getty Images)
Vigar also wondered whether next year's 30th anniversary of Princess Diana's death could offer the brothers an opportunity to reconcile.

Diana, Princess of Wales pictured on Dec. 3, 1993. (Getty Images)
Schofield, however, disagreed with the suggestion that Diana would have pushed her sons to reconcile.

Princess Diana at a state reception in Melbourne in October 1988. (Getty Images)

"I'm always slightly uncomfortable when people invoke Princess Diana and say Diana would want the boys to reconcile," Schofield said. "None of us know what Diana would think about everything that's happened since her death. But we do know from Diana's own pattern of behavior when she believed someone had violated her trust, she was perfectly capable of cutting that person out of her life."
Still, some royal commentators hold out hope that William may eventually follow his father's lead and consider reconciling with Harry.
Prince William and Prince Harry are seen together in 2021. (Getty Images)

"It's clearly incredibly difficult. The trust has broken down," Anderson told People. "Let's hope it's not broken completely, and there's a chink in the armor on both sides, and there could be some sort of reconciliation. But that's not happening anytime soon."

title: Ashley Judd claims mom Naomi threatened to pull tuition over what she was learning and her lesbian professor
summary: Ashley Judd reveals Naomi Judd threatened to stop paying her tuition over a lesbian theologian professor on her new podcast "A Table Prepared."
story: Wynonna Judd told Fox News Digital, her and her mom Naomi Judd's shared love of music helped them "bypass the bullcrap" and build a close relationship.
Ashley Judd is opening up about a past rift with her late mother, Naomi Judd, sparked by a lesbian college professor.

On the debut episode of her new podcast, "A Table Prepared," Ashley sat down with her co-host, former Christ Church Nashville Pastor Dan Scott. During their conversation, Ashley claimed that Naomi "threatened to stop paying my tuition at the University of Kentucky" over what she was learning, and also the professor's sexual orientation.

"She didn’t like what I was learning," Ashley said. "She didn’t like [that] I had a lesbian theologian professor that was taking me through Hebrew scripture and looking at the women listed as property after the donkeys."
Ashley Judd spoke about her late mother Naomi Judd in her debut episode of her new podcast, "A Table Prepared." (Getty Images)

Ashley explained that her mother, who died by suicide in 2022, felt pressured to align politically with the country music industry out of fear of "disapproval and retaliation." Behind closed doors, however, Naomi was much more open about expressing her personal and political beliefs "in the home."
WYNONNA JUDD WISHES BOND WITH MOM WAS LIKE THEIR MUSIC, BUT 'THERE WAS A LOT OF DYSFUNCTION'
"She could share all kinds of political and social views that would surprise people if they thought Naomi Judd thought, felt, said that," Ashley said.
"She didn’t like [that] I had a lesbian theologian professor that was taking me through Hebrew scripture and looking at the women listed as property after the donkeys."
As an example of the issues that moved her mother, Ashley noted that Naomi felt "a lot of compassion" for women making headlines for harming their children.
Ashley Judd, Naomi Judd and Wynonna Judd. (Ke.Mazur/WireImage)
"She would say they need help, not punishment," Ashley recalled, adding that she wasn't sure if Naomi "would have been comfortable in her lifetime saying that."

Ashley Judd made these claims about her mother on her brand new podcast. (Getty Images)

title: Beauty queen stripped of Miss USA crown over hidden husband, kids gets unexpected spotlight decades later
summary: Justus Kelley honors Mary Leona Gage, who lost her Miss USA crown in 1957 for being married with children, as she prepares for Miss Universe.
story: Justus Kelley shares how she practiced with her baby in a carrier, squeezed in workouts during nap time and prepared for the stage around motherhood.

Nearly 70 years ago, a beauty queen lost her Miss USA crown after pageant officials learned she was married and had children. In August, Justus Kelley broke that barrier, becoming the first married woman and mother to win the title during the pageant's 75th edition.
Kelley, 31, is a foster mother who founded the nonprofit Foster Footprints to support children and families involved in foster care.
The historic victory came three years after the Miss USA pageant changed its rules to allow married women and mothers to compete.
Kelley is scheduled to compete in the 75th Miss Universe pageant, which is set to take place Nov. 24 in Puerto Rico.
FORMER MISS USA CONTESTANT MADE A LIFE-CHANGING DECISION AT 26 AFTER CANCER DEVASTATED FAMILY

Justus Kelley (left), the first married mom to win Miss USA, is paying tribute to Mary Leona Gage (right), the former Miss USA 1957, who was stripped of her title after it was revealed she was married and had two children. Kelley will be competing in the Miss Universe pageant on Nov. 24, 2026. (Ivan Apfel/Getty Images; Getty Images)
Kelley paid tribute to Gage by wearing a custom black-and-white coat featuring the former beauty queen's image as she traveled to Puerto Rico for the competition.

"Having the opportunity to represent the United States on the Miss Universe stage, I couldn't help but think about Mary Leona Gage and the circumstances under which she represented this organization," Kelley, 31, told People magazine.

"She was a woman who, in many ways, wasn't allowed to be fully herself or embrace all that she was. Her title was ultimately taken away because society wasn't ready to accept who she was as a wife and mother of two."
Justus Kelley and her husband Tyler have been licensed foster parents in the Commonwealth of Virginia for nearly two years. (Ivan Apfel/Getty Images)

On Aug. 27, the Miss USA Organization held the 75th edition of the national pageant in Miami. Kelley, who held the title of Miss Virginia USA 2026, succeeded 2025 winner Audrey Eckert. The pageant began allowing married women and mothers to compete in 2023.
WATCH: MISS USA 2026 REVEALS HOW SHE TRAINED FOR PAGEANT WITH KIDS IN TOW
In 1957, Gage represented Maryland in the Miss USA pageant and won the title, according to People.

Shortly after Gage's win, rumors circulated about her marital status and children. Gage initially denied the reports. However, it was later revealed that she had married at 14 and given birth to her first child soon afterward. She had her second child at 16, The Baltimore Sun reported.

Leona Gage, ex-Miss USA, disqualified from the Miss Universe contest because she was married rather than single, returned to California to do a television show for NBC. She later headed to Las Vegas for an engagement at the Tropicana Hotel. Gage spent the day in Hollywood with Debbie Reynolds at the Brown Derby. (Bettmann Archive)
Gage also misrepresented her age, telling pageant officials she was 21 when she was actually 18.

Mrs. Mary Leona Gage Ennis, the young lady who won the title of Miss U.S.A. in the Miss Universe contest and then lost it when it was discovered she was married and the mother of two children, is shown in this photo made in 1956 with her husband, Gene and their sons David, left, and Gene Jr. at the time she was 17 years old. (Getty Images)
Following an official investigation, Gage was disqualified and stripped of her Miss USA crown. Runner-up Charlotte Sheffield, who represented Utah, assumed the crown and received the prizes.
Gage, who lost the crown about 24 hours after her win, said she received hate mail following her disqualification.
Actress Zsa Zsa Gabor and Mary Leona Gage in Los Angeles, circa 1957. (Getty Images)

Gage had already competed in the Miss Universe preliminary round and secured a spot among the 15 semifinalists before she was disqualified. Although Sheffield inherited the Miss USA crown, she could not replace Gage in the international competition because preliminary judging had already concluded.
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS
Leona Gage of Maryland was crowned Miss USA. (Bettmann Archive)

According to The Baltimore Sun, Gage later worked as a performer at the Tropicana Hotel in Las Vegas and reportedly dated Frank Sinatra and former Mr. Universe Mickey Hargitay. She also pursued a film career but never achieved widespread success.
Despite losing her crown, Gage continued watching the Miss USA pageant every year. She died in 2010 at age 71.
Justus Kelley married her high school sweetheart. (Ivan Apfel/Getty Images)
Kelley told People that Gage has been on her mind as she prepares for the Miss Universe competition.

Miss USA 2026 winner Justus Kelley and Miss Florida Aileen Cerchiara stand on stage during the 2026 Miss USA Final Competition and Coronation at Adrienne Arsht Center for the Performing Arts in Miami, Florida., on Aug. 27, 2026. (Ivan Apfel/Getty Images)

"I think about how much has changed since then, and how grateful I am that today's American women have the opportunity to represent their country while embracing every part of who they are," Kelley said.
"I hope this moment serves as a reminder that we stand on the shoulders of women who dared to challenge what was expected of them, so that we could have the freedom to be exactly who we are today."

Justus Kelley walks the runway at the Michael Cinco show during New York Fashion Week Powered by Art Hearts Fashion at The Angel Orensanz Foundation on Sept. 12, 2026, in New York City. (Getty Images for Art Hearts Fashion)

The Miss USA pageant began in 1952 in Long Beach, California, with New York's Jackie Loughery becoming its first winner. The competition is separate from the Miss America pageant, which traces its history to a 1921 event in Atlantic City, New Jersey.
PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE
Miss USA was founded in 1952. (Bettmann Archive)
In an earlier interview with Fox News Digital, Kelley expressed a similar message about motherhood and ambition.
She said she hoped to use her reign as Miss USA to challenge the idea that women must choose between their families, careers and personal dreams.

Designer Marina Safina, Miss USA Justus Kelley and models walk the runway at the Marina Safina show during Los Angeles Fashion Week Powered By Art Hearts Fashion at The Majestic Downtown on Oct. 8, 2026. (Getty Images for Art Hearts Fashion)

"You don't have to choose one part of who you are," Kelley said. "You can be all of who you are. That, to me, is the message. We can embrace every part of who we are. It doesn't take away from the other. It doesn't mean there aren't trade-offs, and there aren't times when we have to lean on our village more heavily to get through all the things that we may be pursuing. But know that we don't have to sacrifice ourselves."

Miss Virginia USA 2026 Justus Kelley is crowned Miss USA 2026 onstage during the 2026 Miss USA Final Competition & Coronation at Adrienne Arsht Center for the Performing Arts on Aug. 27, 2026, in Miami, Florida. (Ivan Apfel/Getty Images)
Kelley said her victory gave her an opportunity to represent mothers and wives who balance family life with their own ambitions.
Miss USA 2026 Justus Kelley wants to raise awareness of providing a loving home to foster children. (Ivan Apfel/Getty Images)

"Knowing that history was made as the first mom, as the first wife, as the first woman in her 30s, my first thought was how amazing it is to get to do this and to represent women from all over the country, from all over the world that resonate with, 'Hey, we're still dreaming,'" she said.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Miss USA 2026 Justus Kelley stands on stage during the Miss USA Final Competition and Coronation at the Adrienne Arsht Center for the Performing Arts in Miami, Florida, on Aug. 27, 2026. (Ivan Apfel/Getty Images)
"We're raising our families, but we still have dreams. We still have things that we want to go after and pursue. But what an honor. I get to do this. I get to represent these women. What an honor."
Stephanie Nolasco is an Entertainment Reporter for Fox News Digital.

title: 'General Hospital' star Cameron Mathison says ‘red flags’ drove him to demand answers before cancer diagnosis
summary: Cameron Mathison opens up to Fox News Digital about kidney cancer, divorce, wildfire loss and how those struggles led him to "A Very Arctic Christmas" with Jill Wagner.
story: The "A Very Arctic Christmas" actor tells Fox News Digital he pushed for an MRI for two years before the scan saved his life and explains how cancer transformed his approach to health.
Cameron Mathison knew something was wrong — and spent two years pushing for answers before an MRI revealed he had cancer.
The "General Hospital" star told Fox News Digital the frightening experience changed how he approaches his health, including knowing when to stop pushing his body.
"I just knew something was wrong," said Mathison, who stars in Great American Media's "A Very Arctic Christmas."
'LIONESS' STAR JILL WAGNER RAISES DAUGHTERS IN TENNESSEE TOWN OF 800, WHERE HORSES AND BUGGIES STILL ROAM
Cameron Mathison told Fox News Digital he knew something was wrong with his health before an MRI revealed kidney cancer. (Christine Bartolucci/Disney via Getty Images)
Mathison was diagnosed with renal cell carcinoma, a type of kidney cancer, in 2019 after an MRI revealed a tumor.

Before his diagnosis, the actor said he had gone to extraordinary lengths to monitor his health, undergoing bloodwork, gut microbiome testing and hormone evaluations. Despite those efforts, he said, troubling results left him searching for an explanation.

"I was a guy trying to do it right, but like I was alluding to, I was very extreme," he said. "And I was doing these extreme things, and I was getting the blood tests, and … things were just off … they were like red flags."
WATCH: CAMERON MATHISON FOUGHT FOR 2 YEARS TO GET LIFE-SAVING MRI
The experience left him with a message for others facing unanswered health questions.
"One of the lessons is to be your own best advocate for your health," he said.
BUSY PHILIPPS DIAGNOSED WITH RARE BRAIN TUMOR AFTER UNDERGOING BODY SCAN HER DOCTOR TOLD HER SHE DIDN'T 'NEED'
Surviving cancer also prompted Mathison to rethink his approach to fitness. After years of pushing himself, he said he now recognizes the importance of rest and recovery.
The "General Hospital" star recalled troubling "red flags" despite his commitment to an extensive health and wellness routine. (Cameron Mathison / Instagram)
But his cancer battle was only part of a painful series of losses.

Mathison also faced his mother's death, the end of his 22-year marriage and the loss of his family home in a wildfire. He also lost his hosting job when Hallmark Channel's "Home & Family" was canceled.
'BAYWATCH' STAR NICOLE EGGERT EXPOSES FINANCIAL TOLL OF CANCER BATTLE: 'THE BILLS DON'T STOP'

"In fact, at the time, going through a divorce which was very heartbreaking for me, I had just lost my mom, I had been through my cancer journey, I had all this loss, lost my job, and I was hanging onto that house," he said.
As the losses mounted and his children left for college, Mathison found himself confronting a difficult question about his future.
Cameron Mathison lies in a hospital bed surrounded by his two children. (Cameron Mathison / Instagram)
"And it was like, ‘Now who do you want to be?’"

The actor said those experiences challenged the assumption that making the right choices guarantees decades ahead. Instead, he has found motivation in recognizing how quickly circumstances can change.

"You know, I may not make it home. Like, it sounds depressing, but it's not. It's actually very encouraging and very motivating because you don't know how short life is going to be and to make it meaningful and be kind and loving and compassionate and wise and grateful in every moment is going to make the most of it," he said.

title: Richard Sterban of The Oak Ridge Boys dead at 83
summary: Richard Sterban's iconic bass voice powered The Oak Ridge Boys' "Elvira" to No. 1. His family revealed he battled pancreatic cancer since March.
story: Richard Sterban of Oak Ridge Boys has died. He was 83. (Getty Images)
Richard Sterban, whose unmistakable voice helped make The Oak Ridge Boys’ "Elvira" a country music classic, has died. He was 83.

The singer died Saturday, Nov. 14, in Hendersonville, Tennessee, from complications of bronchitis and pneumonia following a long battle with cancer, according to an announcement from his family and The Oak Ridge Boys.

"We appreciate all of your love, support, and prayers. Please continue to lift us up in this difficult time, we find comfort knowing that he is currently face to face with Jesus," his family said in a statement obtained by Fox News Digital.

Sterban publicly announced his pancreatic cancer diagnosis in September 2025, revealing that doctors had diagnosed him that March. Despite his health struggles, the country music veteran expressed hope that his faith and medical care would help him recover and return to performing.
JOHN ANDERSON, COUNTRY MUSIC HALL OF FAMER, DEAD AT 71
Sterban announced his pancreatic cancer diagnosis last year.  (Jason Kempin/Getty Images)

"With the help of the Good Lord above, I believe I will be able to get through this," he said at the time. He also thanked fans for their prayers and said he hoped to return to the road within several months.
NEW PANCREATIC CANCER PILL COULD RESHAPE TREATMENT AS EARLY TRIAL RESULTS STUN RESEARCHERS

After stepping away from touring in May 2025, Sterban returned to the Grand Ole Opry on Jan. 30 and 31, 2026, joining his bandmates for performances of "Elvira" that brought audiences to their feet, according to the announcement.
"Having Richard on stage with us again was one of God’s greatest blessings," fellow Oak Ridge Boys singer Duane Allen said.

Richard Sterban, Tanya Tucker and William Lee Golden attend the Country Music Hall of Fame and Museum Class of 2026 Medallion Ceremony in Nashville, Tenn., on Oct. 18, 2026. (Getty Images for Country Music Hall of Fame and Museum)
GEORGE STRAIT PULLS OFF INCREDIBLE CAREER ACCOMPLISHMENT WITH STUNNING CONCERT

Born April 24, 1943, in Camden, New Jersey, Sterban began singing in Sunday school at age 6. His voice transitioned from soprano to bass by eighth grade, setting him on a path that would eventually take him from gospel quartets to some of music’s biggest stages.

Before joining The Oak Ridge Boys, Sterban performed behind Elvis Presley as a member of J.D. Sumner and the Stamps Quartet. He toured and recorded with Presley and appeared in the 1972 concert film, "Elvis on Tour."
Later that year, he left the job to become The Oak Ridge Boys’ bass singer.
"I wanted to be in the best vocal group in the world," Sterban said, according to the announcement.

Alongside lead singer Allen, baritone William Lee Golden and tenor Joe Bonsall, Sterban helped transform the Southern gospel quartet into a country and pop crossover act. Their hits included "Y’all Come Back Saloon," "Bobbie Sue," and "American Made."
The Oak Ridge Boys said it was a "blessing" to share the stage with their bandmate earlier this year.  (Omar Vega/WireImage)

But it was Sterban’s booming bass refrain on the group’s 1981 recording of "Elvira" that became his musical calling card. The song reached No. 1 on the country chart and No. 5 on the pop chart and earned a Grammy Award.
OUTLAW COUNTRY SINGER DAVID ALLAN COE DEAD AT 86
"It’s the song everyone hopes to hear at our concerts," Sterban said on its 40th anniversary, according to the announcement.
The group became Grand Ole Opry members in 2011 and entered the Country Music Hall of Fame in 2015.
DOLLY PARTON DEAD AT 80
Their decades together also forged deep personal bonds.
In January 2021, Allen reflected on his relationship with Sterban, Golden and Bonsall.

LOUISVILLE, KENTUCKY - AUGUST 22: Joe Bonsall, Duane Allen, William Lee Golden, and Richard Sterban of the Oak Ridge Boys performs during the Kentucky State Fair on August 22, 2021 in Louisville, Kentucky. (Photo by Stephen J. Cohen/Getty Images) (Stephen J. Cohen/Getty Images)
"I think the four of us have grown closer than we’ve ever been in our whole career," Allen told Fox News Digital at the time.
RANDY TRAVIS’ WIFE SAYS DOCTORS GAVE COUNTRY LEGEND 1% CHANCE OF SURVIVAL BEFORE MIRACULOUS COMEBACK

The Oak Ridge Boys also developed a lasting friendship with former President George H.W. Bush. At his request, they performed "Amazing Grace" at his funeral in Houston in December 2018, taking an overnight flight after a concert in Washington state to attend.
"There’s no way we wouldn’t do it," Sterban said, according to the announcement.

Away from the stage, Sterban was a devoted baseball fan and a part owner of the Nashville Sounds minor league team for 30 years. He continued recording late in life, contributing to several tracks on The Oak Ridge Boys’ October 2026 album, "Buried Treasures."

Sterban is survived by his wife, Donna; daughters Lauren and Tori; sons Rich, Doug and Chris; eight grandchildren; and three great-grandchildren.

title: Johnny Depp fled Hollywood spotlight for quiet Bahamas life where 'nobody’s pointing a camera at me'
summary: Johnny Depp opens up about how his 1940s Bahamas wood house with a yurt and painting studio became his sanctuary away from cameras and fame.
story: Johnny Depp says that living in the Bahamas has given him "total peace and quiet." (Getty Images)
Johnny Depp turns to the Bahamas to experience a private life.
During an interview with the Wall Street Journal, Depp opened up about craving privacy and not being able to have it in the United States.

"Today, I live most of the time in the Bahamas. It’s where I’ve found total peace and quiet. Nobody’s pointing a camera at me or staring. I bought my 1940s wood house in 2004 and added a yurt and a painting studio. Art continues to be a sanctuary that lets me process the world around me," Depp told the outlet.
‘GREASE’ STAR STOCKARD CHANNING SAYS SHE’S ‘HAPPY BEING A RECLUSE’ AFTER LEAVING AMERICA
Johnny Depp lives in the Bahamas most of the time these days, he said. (Tim P. Whitby/Getty Images for The Red Sea International Film Festival)

Depp famously purchased his own island in the Bahamas in 2004. In 2009, he told Vanity Fair that "escapism is survival to me," and that, after playing a difficult role, "my head was done in. I needed to escape. So being able to get on the boat and move allowed my head freedom again."

He continued, "Somehow, the mathematics led me here to my island. I don’t think I’d ever seen any place so pure and beautiful. You can feel your pulse rate drop about 20 beats. It’s instant freedom. And that rare beast—simplicity—can be had. And a little morsel of anonymity."
The actor added, "Whenever I was getting frustrated about being ‘novelty boy’ and making movies, I told myself, Calm down. I can come down here and disappear."

Depp told SCMP Style in 2023, "Where I feel the most myself in this world, and where I go to feel absolutely normal, I suppose, is my place in the Bahamas, because it’s an island and nobody’s looking at me. You’ve got to have some sanctuary, a safe place where you can escape the scrutiny and the interest of others, a place where you can just sit on a beach, read, paint, meditate or whatever, that’s freedom to me. That’s the only real freedom."
Johnny Depp has said in the past how much his home in the Bahamas means to him. (Gareth Cattermole/Getty Images)

Making music is also something Depp likes to do on his island. Telling WSJ about how he passes his time there, he said, "I like to grab about four or five books and flop on the couch and read. Or I play guitar in my music studio."
In the 80s, Depp was in a band – music was what originally brought him to Los Angeles in 1983, not acting.

"Soon after, I met actor Nicolas Cage at a friend’s house. Nic came to see my band several times, and we became friends," Depp said. "Six months later, he suggested I try acting. I was up for anything that would help pay the bills."

Johnny Depp transformed into Scrooge for the newly released movie "Ebenezer." (Daniel Knighton/Getty Images for Paramount Pictures)
Speaking to "CBS Mornings," Depp discussed the movie and the impact his children have had on his career.

"There was a great veil lifted when my first child was born. And suddenly, I understood exactly what everything had been for," Depp said. "There were years of that, that I thought, ‘What am I doing? Why am I doing these movies?’ This is what it's all about."

title: Sammy Kershaw accepts CMA apology after country stars speak out over red carpet access
summary: Sammy Kershaw's CMA Awards red carpet denial ignited a firestorm among country music artists who say the industry sidelines legends for influencers.
story: 'Outnumbered' panelists discuss country star Rodney Atkins' advice for young people to avoid social media fads and the impact of social media on America's youth.

Sammy Kershaw and Rodney Atkins spoke out about being denied permission to walk the red carpet at this year’s Country Music Association Awards, prompting criticism over how the organization treats veteran country artists.

Last week, Kershaw, 68, shared a statement on Instagram in which he revealed that the organization rejected his request to walk the carpet at the upcoming ceremony with his wife, Mendy, a decision that he called "extremely hurtful, embarrassing and very disappointing."

Following Kershaw's post, Atkins, 57, announced that he and his wife, Rose Falcon, were also denied red carpet access and would no longer be attending the ceremony, which will be held on Nov. 18 and marks the CMAs' milestone 60th anniversary.
COUNTRY STAR CODY JOHNSON SAYS NASHVILLE WANTED TO CHANGE HIM BEFORE SUCCESS
Country musician Sammy Kershaw spoke out after being denied access to the 2026 CMAs red carpet. (Getty Images)

After facing backlash from other country musicians and fans, the CMA issued a response in which the organization explained that its red carpet criteria helps manage limited space and security needs and apologized to those who "felt excluded by those decisions." The CMA also added that it was speaking with Kershaw's team.
On Tuesday, Kershaw shared a post in which he said that he had accepted an apology from the CMA as well as an invitation for himself and Mendy to walk the red carpet and attend the ceremony.

The controversy sparked an uproar among country artists, who argued that the CMA has welcomed influencers, actors and crossover celebrities onto the red carpet while sidelining veteran performers. In addition, other country musicians raised broader concerns about how the industry as a whole recognizes artists who helped shape the genre.

In his initial post on Nov. 5, Kershaw wrote that the denial of his request to walk the CMAs carpet "really hurts me." He explained that he learned of the rejection just two weeks ahead of the awards show after he and Mendy had already rearranged his touring schedule and booked flights and hotels.
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS
Kershaw said he and his wife, Mendy, pictured at the 2016 CMAs, had already booked flights and hotels.  (Disney General Entertainment Content via Getty Images)

"My wife, Mendy, and I don't get to attend these events very often, due to touring and schedule conflicts," Kershaw wrote at the time. "She was really looking forward to us sharing a special evening together celebrating country music. Then, to find out I was denied the red carpet two weeks before the show, after being strung along for several months and expecting we would be attending, WTF?"

Kershaw pointed to his decades-long career and longstanding relationship with the CMA to question why he was excluded. He cited his more than 50 years in the music business, millions of records sold, over two dozen Billboard hits, a past CMA Horizon Award nomination and his status as a "lifetime CMA member" since 1992.
The musician also noted that he previously "donated" his time to perform at CMA Fest, and that he hoped he had earned the right to walk the carpet alongside his wife just as they had in the past.

"I’m blessed to still be out on tour every year, performing for the greatest fans in the world doing what I love," Kershaw wrote. "I believe there should be room to recognize the artists who have spent their lives contributing to this organization’s success.

"I love country music, but never in a million years would I think that a successful country music entertainer (and I’m not the only one) would not be able to walk the red carpet. It’s extremely hurtful, embarrassing and very disappointing. I guess the next time I attend the CMA’s, it will be in tribute after I’m gone, if I’m lucky," he concluded.

Two days after Kershaw's post, Atkins shared a video in which he revealed that he and his wife, who is also a longtime CMA member, had also been excluded from the CMAs red carpet and decided to skip the event.
"Well, I found out that Sammy Kershaw and I have something in common this year. Neither one of us got approved to walk the CMA awards red carpet," he began.

"When I heard about Sammy, I thought, 'What a shame. He's a great guy, sweetheart of a dude. Spent his life representing country music.' Then I found out the same thing happened to me," Atkins continued. "And in a way, I get it. I've always been kind of an outsider, maybe a shrub in the landscape of country music."
Rodney Atkins said he and his wife, Rose Falcon, were also denied red carpet access. (Getty Images)
NATALIE MAINES’ ANTI-TRUMP TIRADE, ZACH BRYAN’S FENCE-CLIMBING CLASH FUEL COUNTRY MUSIC’S BIGGEST FEUDS

Atkins went on to emphasize that he was having his strongest touring year, that his album "True South" reached the second round of CMA voting for album of the year and that his latest single could extend his chart presence into a third decade.
In a statement the musician shared alongside the video, Atkins expressed his gratitude to his fans "who made this career possible."
"You've always made me feel welcome in country music, and that's what matters most," he wrote.

"After more than 20 years as a CMA member and countless CMA Fests I’ve played for free, Rose and I were denied red carpet clearance, just like Sammy Kershaw. So we’ve decided not to attend this year’s CMA Awards," Atkins shared. "I also believe the artists who helped build the foundation of country music, like Sammy Kershaw, deserve a place in its celebrations."

The ""She Don’t Know She’s Beautiful" singer‘s post was met with supportive comments from other country stars, including some from the younger generation that paid tribute to Kershaw for his foundational contributions to the industry.
"If you haven’t earned the right to be there then nobody has… disappointing to say the least," Riley Green wrote.
Carly Pearce commented, "Many of us wouldn’t be here without artists like you…"
Jake Owen declared himself "Team Sammy," while Granger Smith added, "So sad for country music. I grieve for the old CMA."
"This is wild! I’ll give you my spot!!," Drew Bainbridge offered. "You paved the way for all of us on that carpet."
Other artists questioned why influencers were invited to walk the carpet while Kershaw was denied.
"Ugh this makes me sad for country music. Can we please bring back the legends and not influencers?" Kylie Morgan wrote.
"They’ll let zero talent influencers walk the red carpet but not Sammy Kershaw? I hate it here," Meghan Patrick commented.
Riley Green was among the country stars who rallied behind Kershaw. (John Nacion/WireImage)

Veteran country star Mark Chesnutt reacted to Kershaw's snub by the CMA in a lengthy statement on Facebook in which he criticized the organization, arguing that it prioritizes celebrities from outside the genre over longtime country artists.
"So Sammy Kershaw won’t be allowed to walk the red carpet at the big CMA Awards," he wrote. "Well that’s about right. The CMA doesn’t care about us old 90s guys any more."

"It’s a shame they don’t respect the stars that dominated the charts in the past thirty years or before that but they sure roll out the welcome mat for pop stars and Hollywood movie stars and even hip hop artists," he continued. "Anything but country music gets the performance spots on the show."
Chesnutt also contrasted the country music industry's treatment of the genre’s history with the recognition received by rock icons.

"Rock n Roll honors its history and respects its legends while country music industry executives seem to ignore its rich history and its legends," he wrote. "Thank God there’s still a lot of people that love traditional country music. They keep coming to our shows and showing their love and respect for the music we’ve made for nearly forty years now and we’ll keep working for them and not for those who don’t matter to US!"
Mark Chesnutt said that the CMA "doesn’t care about us old 90s guys any more." (Rick Diamond/Getty Images for Country Thunder)
Country singer Pam Tillis, who also rose to fame in the 1990s, also addressed Kershaw's red carpet denial, though she clarified that her criticism was not solely directed at the CMA.

"So let’s talk about today’s drama in country music: Sammy Kershaw and the CMAs. I’m not going to single out the CMA, because this happens all the time in our business," she wrote in a post on Instagram. "It’s the nature of our industry that the rising stars get the spotlight, just as we did at one point."
Tillis emphasized the importance of preserving a legacy, pointing to her own experience growing up as the daughter of country icon Mel Tillis.
"I learned early that a legacy doesn’t keep itself," she wrote. "Somebody has to stand up and say, ‘This artist mattered. They made a contribution.’ I’ve done that for Daddy most of my life."
She acknowledged that rising stars naturally receive attention, but argued that established performers still connect with generations of fans.
PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE

"And I’ll tell you what I’ve seen: the country audience is a multigenerational audience, and ‘90s country is still very viable, even if it isn’t always visible," she wrote. "A lot of us have three generations of fans showing up to our shows, singing, whooping and hollering for our songs. Many of today’s artists are making it big with their own spin on the ‘90s sound."

"I dare say many of us have felt the sting of being passed over for this, that and the other, in order to create an image that’s only part of the picture," Tillis continued. "I know today’s new artists need all the support they can get in such a crazy, competitive market. But legacy artists who want to show up can be the bridge between where this music came from and where it’s going."
"Many of us never say anything about these slights," she added. "We just keep on doing our thing. As an artist who is a lifetime CMA member, Sammy just spoke out."
Pam Tillis said she had learned early that a "legacy doesn’t keep itself."  (Getty Images for Stagecoach)
On Monday, the CMA released a statement responding to the backlash and citing space and security criteria for red carpet management.

"In recent days, several artists and their fans have spoken out about this year’s CMA Awards red carpet guidelines," the organization wrote. "Like any major televised event, the red carpet has criteria that exists to help manage limited space and the security needs for both the artists and the media. We are deeply sorry anyone felt excluded by those decisions."

"Our organization’s mission is to honor the history and celebrate the excellence of Country Music," it continued. "With this 60th anniversary year, we are working extra hard to simultaneously spotlight the last six decades, while also celebrating what has been a tremendous year in 2026. It’s not easy to do all of that in just one night, but we are up for the challenge."

"We also know this is about more than a red carpet, and we are committed to keep listening and keep finding ways to make sure all artists feel welcome and at home here," the CMA added. "To that point, we are in touch with Sammy Kershaw’s team and look forward to continuing that conversation."

On Tuesday, Kershaw shared a positive update, revealing that CMA leadership had "extended a sincere, heartfelt apology" which he had accepted following a "sincere and meaningful private conversation."

"The CMA has also extended an invitation for my wife, Mendy, and me to walk the red carpet and attend this year's awards alongside our fellow artists," he wrote. "I am grateful for that invitation and appreciate their willingness to listen, acknowledge our concerns, and work toward a positive outcome."

Kershaw also thanked fans, fellow artists and the country music community for their support. He explained that he originally spoke publicly because he was hurt, rather than seeking attention or controversy.
The "Cadillac Style" singer emphasized that the controversy was about more than his personal invitation.

"This was never about the red carpet," he wrote. "It was about recognizing and respecting those who dedicated their lives to this music and preserving the history and legacy that makes country music so special."
Kershaw expressed his hopes that the conversations would produce lasting change in how legacy artists are recognized.
"You cannot celebrate 60 years of country music without celebrating the artists who helped build those 60 years," he wrote.

"I have nothing but respect for the incredible talent carrying country music into the future. Every generation of artists deserves its moment to shine, and I believe there’s room to celebrate all of them."

title: Kathy Ireland’s husband escapes burning boat after engine explodes 20 miles offshore

title: New organ donation rules take effect after alarming reports of patients showing ‘signs of life’
summary: New HRSA organ donation rules take effect Nov. 18, adding a five-minute waiting period after circulatory death and a formal pause process for families.
story: Dr. Raymond Lynch, director of the Division of Transplantation at HRSA, discusses how updated federal organ donation guidelines seek to protect patients and improve communication with families facing difficult end-of-life decisions.
New organ donation guidelines have taken effect as of Nov. 18, updating procedures for some donors.

The Health Resources and Services Administration (HRSA), a branch of the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS), previously announced the policy update in a press release after the changes were approved by the Organ Procurement and Transplantation Network in August.

The new guidelines apply to donation after circulatory death (DCD), in which organs are recovered after the heart and lungs stop functioning. This differs from donation after brain death, when the donor is declared dead based on the irreversible loss of brain function.
BRIDE IS WALKED DOWN WEDDING AISLE BY MAN WHO RECEIVED HER LATE FATHER'S HEART
What the new rules require

The changes include a formal process to pause donation if patient safety concerns arise. Families, medical providers and other people involved in the process must be told they can request a pause and how to do so.
New guidelines for organ donation aim to better inform families and providers. (iStock)
Procedures will also be added for handling and reporting unplanned pauses, along with more detailed records of neurological assessments.
Additionally, a minimum five-minute waiting period will be put in place after circulation stops and before organ recovery begins.
Timing concerns

While the changes are intended to strengthen patient safeguards and improve communication with families, University of Rochester bioethicist Dr. Lainie Ross told NPR that allowing organ procurement teams to approach families before they decide whether to withdraw life-sustaining care could leave them feeling pressured or distrustful of doctors’ motives.
In public comments, the American Society of Transplantation said it supports honoring requests to pause the donation process at any point.
ORGAN HARVESTING BEGAN WHILE PATIENTS STILL SHOWED 'SIGNS OF LIFE,' FEDERAL INVESTIGATION FINDS

Previous cases in which organ recovery was reportedly begun before confirmation of death have raised questions about safeguards in the donation process. HRSA Division of Transplantation Director Dr. Raymond Lynch told Fox News Digital that "does not happen" under the process governed by the new guidelines.

"The point of these policies that were put into place is to make sure that we do preserve the sanctity of that decision and make sure that the technical parts of the operation ... pose no risk to the patient," Lynch told Fox News Digital.
New guidelines implement a minimum five-minute waiting period between circulatory death and the start of organ recovery. (iStock)
The HRSA director said these new guidelines improve the "safety, quality and consistency of care that's already being delivered across the United States."

Organ donation has changed just within the last decade, according to Lynch. Historically, most donors were declared as "brain-dead," meaning they were "legally deceased" at the time the decision was made.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"Now, we're dealing with [DCD], which means that it's an individual who's not brain-dead, but they're very severely injured," he said. "The medical team and the family have come to the decision that they're going to change the goals of care and let that person have a natural, compassionate death."
"In that setting, shortly after they pass away, their organs are removed through a surgical procedure."
"The goal should always be to save lives through donation without ever compromising the care, dignity or safety of the donor."

The guidelines do not change the roles of the patient’s healthcare team or the organ procurement organization (OPO), the group that coordinates organ donation and recovery. Rather, they set clearer expectations for when donation-related discussions and procedures take place, according to Lynch.
"Historically, it was very, very late in the patient's medical course before there could be a discussion of them being an organ donor," he said. "And that really has two kinds of harm."
The HRSA aims to ensure that the quality and quantity of communication and medical care being delivered is "very high." (iStock)
One concern was that families may have felt "rushed or pressured" to decide whether to authorize organ donation before they had enough time to make an informed choice.
He said delays could deny patients "the chance to give the gift" of organ donation, as they intended when they signed up to be donors.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
The other risk was an "insufficient delivery" of information and recording of decisions, according to Lynch.
He said the new guidelines bring more thorough conversations and clearer records of what information was shared with families, and when.
These conversations are "happening in truly tragic circumstances," Lynch noted, as families and loved ones are feeling fear and grief.

"We're making sure through these regulations that there is a level of professionalism and consistency, and that the care people's loved ones get is ... compassionate and respectful," said Dr. Raymond Lynch. (iStock)
The HRSA aims to ensure that the quality and quantity of communication and medical care is "very high."

"All of this is about elevating this to the level of a medical specialty," he said. "We're making sure through these regulations that there is a level of professionalism and consistency, and that the care people's loved ones are going to get is ... compassionate and respectful."
What families should know

Dr. Stephanie Widmer, New York City emergency medicine physician and Fox News medical contributor, said families should know that "there are now clearer safeguards," including the five-minute wait and the chance to pause the process.
She added that while organ donation saves lives, protection of the donor "must always come first."
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

"I think these changes are a positive step toward improving patient safety, transparency and public trust," Widmer, who was not involved in the guideline updates, told Fox News Digital. "My concern is whether these safeguards will be consistently enforced across hospitals and organ procurement organizations."
While organ donation saves lives, protection of the donor "must always come first," said Dr. Stephanie Widmer (not pictured). (iStock)
The doctor added that a policy is "only as effective as its implementation," and that additional procedural requirements don’t "unnecessarily interfere with a patient’s wishes to donate."
Widmer said she'd like to see stronger national standards for independent neurological assessments and "greater oversight" of organ procurement practices.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

"The medical team caring for the patient should remain completely independent of the organ recovery process," she emphasized. "Families also deserve clear explanations of exactly what will happen, including any specialized procedures used to preserve organs."
"The goal should always be to save lives through donation without ever compromising the care, dignity or safety of the donor."
Angelica Stabile is a lifestyle reporter for Fox News Digital.

title: RFK Jr faces fierce backlash after US loses measles-free status for first time in 26 years
summary: Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. faces criticism after the U.S. lost measles elimination status amid over 5,400 confirmed cases this year.
story: Dr. Marc Siegel warns that dropping measles vaccination rates could cost the U.S. its elimination status. The Fox News senior medical analyst joins hosts Bill Hemmer and Dana Perino to discuss the rise to over 5,000 cases in 2026. Siegel outlines what is driving the decline and explains how communities can protect public health.

Health and Human Services (HHS) Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. is facing mounting criticism from Democrats after the United States lost its measles elimination status for the first time in more than 25 years.

The Pan American Health Organization announced Tuesday that the U.S. had lost its measles elimination designation amid a resurgence of the highly contagious virus, with more than 5,400 confirmed cases reported this year — the highest annual total in more than three decades.
The virus has spread largely among unvaccinated populations, prompting criticism from Democrats who have previously scrutinized Kennedy's stance on vaccines.
On Tuesday, Kennedy vowed to stop measles outbreaks and restore the country's measles elimination status, while continuing to recommend vaccination against the disease.
CNN'S DANA BASH SPARS WITH RFK JR OVER VACCINE EFFICACY, DEMANDS HE 'LOOK INTO THE CAMERA' AND PUSH VACCINES

Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. speaks during a news conference on the Autism report by the CDC at the Hubert Humphrey Building Auditorium in Washington, Wednesday, April 16, 2025. (AP Photo/Jose Luis Magana)
"We will stop measles outbreaks, protect American families, and work to regain U.S. measles elimination status," Kennedy said in a statement.
He added, "I continue to recommend MMR vaccination as the most effective way to prevent measles."
Several Democrats sharply criticized Kennedy following the announcement.

New York Gov. Kathy Hochul, whose state has reported its first measles-associated death in more than three decades, involving a child, accused Kennedy of contributing to declining vaccination rates through years of vaccine skepticism.
CHILD’S MEASLES DEATH MARKS NEW YORK STATE’S FIRST IN MORE THAN 30 YEARS AMID OUTBREAK
Kathy Hochul, governor of New York, speaks during a news conference at the WIN NYC family shelter in New York on Thursday, March 5, 2026. (Adam Gray/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
"RFK Jr. promised to 'Make America Healthy Again.' Now America has lost its measles-free status for the first time in 26 years," Hochul said.
"A disgraceful display of incompetence from the nation's highest public health office," she added.
Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro also blamed Kennedy, arguing that the loss of elimination status reflected the consequences of vaccine misinformation and skepticism.
"There is a clear line from the misinformation, vaccine skepticism, and incompetence of RFK Jr. to this devastating news and very real consequences," Shapiro said.
"Measles is preventable. We eliminated it in this country once, and we can do it again."
MEASLES SURGE HITS NEW MILESTONE AS US CASES SURPASS LAST YEAR'S TOTAL

Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear speaks during an event titled "How Democrats Can Connect with America" at the Center for American Progress on Feb. 19, 2026, in Washington, D.C. (Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images)
Another Democratic governor called for Kennedy's removal from office.
"This dangerous setback was 100% avoidable and is the result of one person: RFK Jr.," Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear said. "Remove him now."

The U.S., which had maintained the measles designation since 2000, is experiencing its worst measles outbreak since 1991 and has reported more than twice as many cases as in all of 2025, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).
Measles elimination means there has been no continuous local transmission of the virus for at least 12 months. The U.S. reached the status in 2000 after years of coordinated immunization campaigns.
NEW YORK DECLARES MEASLES DISASTER EMERGENCY AS CASES SURGE IN PENNSYLVANIA
HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. makes his way to the inaugural Great American Farmers Market on the National Mall on Monday, August 4, 2025. (Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc. via Getty Images)
CDC Director Dr. Erica Schwartz defended the agency's response to the ongoing outbreak, emphasizing that vaccination remains the most important tool for protecting Americans.
"The measles elimination designation is not what protects Americans. Vaccination does," Schwartz said.
She added that the CDC had invested approximately $100 million in state and local health departments to strengthen outbreak prevention and response.
The agency also noted that MMR vaccination coverage among U.S. kindergartners fell from 95.2% during the 2019–2020 school year to 92.7% in 2023–2024.

In his statement, Kennedy cited COVID-19-era disruptions as a factor in declining routine childhood vaccination coverage, noting that several other countries, including Canada, Mexico and the United Kingdom, had also lost their measles elimination status.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Fox News Digital has reached out to HHS for additional comment.
The Associated Press contributed to this report.
