"They now have a bigger navy than we do, but they fear religious freedom more than they do our aircraft carriers or our missiles," Brownback said.
Ashley J. DiMella reports on politics for Fox News Digital.

title: Beijing's hidden chokehold could derail Trump's $50B plan to fix America's aging skies
summary: Can the United States fix its air traffic control when an expert warns China's rare earth grip could bottleneck the FAA overhaul Sean Duffy wants funded?
story: As the Trump administration seeks $50 billion from Congress to replace aging air traffic control equipment after Friday’s nationwide ground stop, China’s control of the rare earth supply chain could complicate the overhaul.
Can the United States modernize its critical infrastructure without relying on China?

Amid the fallout from Friday’s nationwide ground stop that halted air travel and upended plans for millions of passengers, the Trump administration blamed aging air traffic control infrastructure, pointing fingers at past administrations and calling on lawmakers to approve billions in new modernization funding.
"Essentially, what you saw on Friday was very, very old equipment that had a heart attack," President Donald Trump told reporters Monday at the White House before departing for Asia.
DUFFY VOWS TO MODERNIZE AGING AIR TRAFFIC SYSTEM AFTER NATIONWIDE GROUND STOP

Aviation specialists work inside the FAA's SMART Center, where technology combines weather, flight path and air traffic data to help identify potential congestion and improve flight efficiency. (Courtesy Department of Transportation)

The problem, one expert told Fox News Digital, is that China holds a near-monopoly over the global rare earth supply chain. While rare earth elements are relatively abundant in nature, Beijing dominates the processing stages required to turn raw ore into usable industrial components.

"For the FAA, radars, satellite systems, complex electrical systems, precision motors, navigation systems — all of these require rare earths inside them," said Anupam Ghildyal, chief growth officer for REalloys, a North American critical minerals and rare earth company.
AMERICA DEPENDS TOO MUCH ON CHINA FOR ESSENTIAL MINERALS. WE NEED TO DIG OUR FUTURE
Rare earth magnets are displayed in the showroom at Inner Mongolia Baotou Steel Rare-Earth Hi-Tech Co. in Baotou, Inner Mongolia, China. (Bloomberg via Getty Images)

"For the FAA to upgrade the infrastructure, you need all of these components, and those components have to be manufactured here because China can limit the supply of these components to the U.S.," he added. "But to manufacture these components in the U.S., we need the basic raw materials to make them from, which is something we do not have."

Beijing's stranglehold on rare earth minerals could bottleneck U.S. efforts before they get off the ground, Ghildyal warned, noting that China has the ability to slow-walk or block much-needed materials.
THE WEST STILL DOESN’T GRASP THE DANGER OF CHINA’S RARE EARTH ENDGAME

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy discusses the Federal Aviation Administration's SMART technology, which uses flight and weather data to help air traffic controllers identify congestion and recommend more efficient routes. (Courtesy Department of Transportation)
"100% they can, and they've been doing it," he said.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy has requested $50 billion in additional funding from Congress to overhaul and modernize the nation's air traffic control system, while the White House is urging lawmakers to fund the replacement of decades-old copper wiring and aging control towers.
VETERAN PILOT: CONGRESS MUST ACT TO UPDATE 'ARCHAIC' FAA TECH THAT IS 'PUTTING AMERICANS IN DANGER'
A logo of rare earth magnets manufacturer JL Mag appears on a building in Baotou, Inner Mongolia, China, on April 6, 2026. (REUTERS)

"So you saw a telecom issue on Friday. We’re replacing old copper wires with fiber, but this is an old architecture of a network," Duffy said during an appearance on Fox News' "Hannity." "You’ve seen Newark go down. You’ve seen Dallas go down. You saw all of New York go down just a couple of months ago because of telecom issues. I want to build a brand-new architecture of a resilient telecom network that’s worthy of 2026 and worthy of America."
China didn't always dominate the rare earth minerals trade. Many companies began outsourcing those functions overseas, which China gladly took over.
GOV MIKE DUNLEAVY: CHINA IS HOLDING CRITICAL MINERALS HOSTAGE. ALASKA CAN HELP END THE THREAT

Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping are slated to meet this week while Trump is in China for a series of high-level regional summits where trade is expected to be among the main issues discussed. China has cornered the market on rare earth mineral processing, which could complicate U.S. efforts to modernize its air traffic infrastructure, one expert said. (REUTERS)

"The problem is we are starting from pretty much close to zero," said Ghildyal. "Back in the 1980s and 1990s, we actually processed a lot of rare earths, made a lot of magnets, and then we decided that these processes are too laborious and too toxic, so let's offshore them. So we taught the Chinese how to do it, and over the last 40 years they've been doing it."

Rebuilding the nation’s airspace hardware relies heavily on specialized magnets and minerals dominated by China, Ghildyal said — an issue looming large ahead of Trump’s Thursday summit with Chinese President Xi Jinping in Shenzhen.
TRUMP BRINGS TWO DIVIDED CABINET HEAVYWEIGHTS TO CHINA AS CONTROVERSY HANGS OVER HIGH-STAKES TALKS
"China uses it as leverage on the negotiating table," Ghildyal said. "I would assume they want AI chips. We want their rare earth materials, and that's how these transactions happen."
He noted that U.S. demand for neodymium magnets sits around 50,000 tons annually, far outpacing domestic production.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"We'll make about 500 tons this year, so we are making 1% of what we need," Ghildyal said. "So that 99% gap is not going away tomorrow or in the next two or three years. It's a five-to-10-year journey, but I think we should all be ashamed of ourselves if 10 years down the line, we are not independent of China for these critical materials."
Louis Casiano is a reporter for Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to louis.casiano@fox.com.

title: Trump set for economic showdown with Xi as unfulfilled promises leave billions hanging in balance
summary: Trump and Xi Jinping meet in China today as expert Ryan Yonk says years of broad promises have yielded few executed deals on trade between the nations.
story: Ryan M. Yonk, a scholar at the American Institute for Economic Research, breaks down what the U.S. needs to do if it wants concrete results on trade with China.

President Donald Trump later today will meet with President Xi Jinping in China, where the pair are expected to discuss trade between the two nations after what one expert describes as years of broad promises but few executed deals.

Tariffs, agricultural purchases and rare earth minerals are all potential topics of conversation, and are in many ways intertwined, according to Ryan Yonk, an economic scholar and research fellow at the American Institute for Economic Research who specializes in relations between the United States and China.

At a summit in Beijing in May, China agreed to purchase 25 million metric tons of American soybeans, one of its U.S. largest imports, annually. China also agreed to purchase $17 billion worth of other agricultural products this year, in 2027 and in 2028.

President Donald Trump walks on a red carpet after greeting Chinese President Xi Jinping during an arrival ceremony at Joint Base Andrews, Maryland., on Sept. 23, 2026. Trump is hosting Xi for a three-day state visit to Washington, D.C., where the leaders are expected to discuss trade practices, artificial intelligence and furthering "strategic stability" between their countries. (Getty Images)
TRUMP HEADS TO BEIJING FOR HIGH-STAKES XI TALKS AS TAIWAN TENSIONS, TRADE DISPUTES TEST US STRENGTH
"There has been a very sort of large-scale discussion, particularly about soy purchases from U.S. producers that got derailed as the tariff debate and argument increased across time," Yonk said.

Those purchases, Yonk said, were widely believed to be one area where China would make the first move in purchasing U.S. products given the current tariff arrangement, in large part because China simply lacks the domestic capability to produce soy at the quantity it needs.

When Xi visited the U.S. in September, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced that the two countries had agreed to extend a tariff truce and reduce restrictions on trade for certain products until January.
They left the door open to hammer out a more permanent deal during Trump's visit to China Wednesday.
A combine harvester during a soybean harvest at a farm in Harvard, Illinois, Oct. 17, 2025. (Christopher Dilts/Bloomberg/Getty Images)
Yonk thinks that without a "fundamental rebalancing of the trade agreements on both sides," China will not act first in making large scale purchases from the United States.
WHAT XI WANTS FROM TRUMP AS BEIJING SEEKS LEVERAGE IN HIGH-STAKES SUMMIT
"I think [it] is unrealistic, because an expectation that China will act first with very little reciprocal action on the U.S. side isn't traditionally how China has acted," he said.
That calculation is not just economic, but political, Yonk explained. Neither Trump nor Xi wants to act first for fear of the appearance that one is giving in to the other.
He is not confident that high-level talks between the two world leaders will lead to concrete change in trade policy.

"And so, if we're going to get real progress, it's going to likely have to be not simply between the two leaders meeting and agreeing, but actual trade negotiations that involve sub-cabinets, officials actually going through and identifying what specific restrictions can be lowered," he said, adding that those tactics have not yet been employed in a meaningful way between the two nations.
DOUG BURGUM SAYS TRUMP ENTERS CHINA SUMMIT IN 'STRONGEST POSITION' OF ANY US LEADER EVER
Trump already vowed on Tuesday to break China's grip on rare earth minerals, which are used to build everything from fighter jets to cell phones.

"We're doing very well," Trump said. "We're making rare earth at a level that we've never made before. We're going to catch [China] within 10 months, they say. We'll catch them. Everything we need, we'll have in 10 months."

President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping attend a bilateral meeting at the Great Hall of the People on May 14, 2026, in Beijing, China. President Trump is meeting with President Xi Jinping in Beijing to address the Iran conflict, trade imbalances and the Taiwan situation while establishing new bilateral boards for economic and AI oversight. (Alex Wong/Getty Images)
AMERICA DEPENDS TOO MUCH ON CHINA FOR ESSENTIAL MINERALS. WE NEED TO DIG OUR FUTURE

Yonk said the U.S. does have a large supply of rare earth minerals available within its borders. But it is more cautious of the environmental concerns that come along with mining and refining them than China. Thus, China has been a major source of America's rare earth minerals.

China is experiencing economic pain that keeps it coming back to the negotiating table, Yonk said, noting that the U.S. has its own share of pain with high levels of inflation. But ultimately, he surmised, China is worse off than the United States, using the analogy that if the United States catches a cold, China will catch a "fairly severe flu."

"And so the stakes are very high for China getting the trade arrangements right. It pushes us back into, if we're going make real progress, it's going be often item by item," he said. "It's going to be trade line by trade line and understanding what those bilateral trade agreements can really look like."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"It always sounds good to say we're going to solve it all at once, but most of the trade agreements we've had with China that have succeeded have been line by line, product area by product area, and it requires a holistic look at the relationship rather than mere platitudes."
Peter D'Abrosca is a politics reporter at Fox News Digital.

title: GOP chairman demands answers on Trump's costly VA technology overhaul amid US-wide outages
summary: Rep. Mike Bost demands answers from OPM on Oracle's HR 2.0 rollout, citing shifting timelines and data breach risks as alarm bells ring on Capitol Hill.
story: President Donald Trump shares his administration's efforts to support veterans on Veterans Day.
Shifting timelines and ballooning costs of the Trump administration's contracts to modernize the federal government, including programs affecting veterans, are raising alarm bells on Capitol Hill.

House Veterans Affairs Committee Chairman Mike Bost, R-Ill., wrote to the Office of Personnel Management (OPM) this month asking for more information on an Oracle software rollout for streamlining employee data and what, if any, safeguards are in place to stop potential data breaches from leaking Americans' sensitive personal information. It comes as the country has grappled with multiple outages hitting the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), big banks and Microsoft, among other entities.

"I write to you today to express concern about the pace of the Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) Federal Human Resources (HR) 2.0 implementation, uncertainty surrounding VA’s transition costs and readiness, and the risks posed by another major Oracle implementation affecting the Department," the letter said.

"The House Committee on Veterans’ Affairs supports efforts to modernize HR systems and improve how VA manages and supports its workforce. However, modernization must proceed with clear accountability, adequate resources, and safeguards against disruption."
‘BIG BALLS’ OF DOGE FAME GIVES EXCLUSIVE LOOK AT NEW TRUMP MISSION TO OVERHAUL GOVERNMENT

Illinois Republican Rep. Mike Bost speaks alongside Rep. Lisa McClain, a Republican from Michigan, and Rep. Steve Scalise, a Republican from Louisiana, during a news conference at the U.S. Capitol in Washington, D.C., on Oct. 9, 2025. (Annabelle Gordon/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

Technology firm Cerner won a $10 billion government contract in 2018 to modernize record-keeping at VA-run hospitals over 10 years. Cerner was acquired by multinational tech company Oracle four years later.
ORACLE HEALTH DATA BREACH EXPOSES NEARLY 20 MILLION PATIENTS

It was later paused for several years during the Biden administration in an effort to root out performance issues affecting veterans and healthcare providers at VA hospitals, the department said at the time.
Since then, the VA announced earlier this year it would extend that contract through 2031 — with a new total price tag of $27 billion.
OFFICE OF PERSONNEL MANAGEMENT UNCOVERS $500M IN FRAUD AND WASTE IN FEDERAL HEALTH BENEFITS PROGRAMS
It's raised concerns among lawmakers on Capitol Hill, including Bost, who referenced those issues in his questions on the VA's use of Oracle for modernizing its employee data via HR 2.0.

"More than four months after Oracle was selected to provide the governmentwide platform underpinning HR 2.0, the Committee seeks detailed evidence of implementation progress and readiness at VA. In addition, VA’s years-long experience with Oracle’s Electronic Health Record Modernization (EHRM) program reinforces the need for caution," Bost wrote.
A Department of Veterans Affairs sign is displayed outside the Washington VA Medical Center on July 17, 2026, in Washington, D.C. (Kevin Carter/Getty Images)

Bost also cited system performance issues and problems with user satisfaction with EHRM highlighted by the Government Accountability Office (GAO), but he said only four of GAO's 18 recommendations have been fully implemented as of this past August.
In June 2026, Oracle was awarded a $395.8 million contract to modernize the federal government's human resources systems.
DHS INVESTIGATES MASSIVE DATA BREACH EXPOSING 40,000 EMPLOYEES, INCLUDING ICE AND BORDER PATROL AGENTS

An independent government watchdog "identified inconsistent completion targets, concentrated security and authorization risk, vendor-dependent data migration, and persistent staffing gaps" with HR 2.0 software implementation in October, Bost noted.
"The report describes completion targets shifting from July 4, 2027, to as late as March 2028, while the Wave 2 timeline remains unset," he wrote.
He also raised concerns about the potential for a data breach after the FBI was targeted by hackers in September.

Though he noted existing reports about that hack do not link it to potential issues with Oracle's software at the VA, Bost suggested that staffing gaps and HR 2.0's "centralized authorization approach" could allow for vulnerabilities that need to be accounted for before the rollout is complete.

Fears of tech vulnerabilities are at an all-time high in the U.S. after multiple private and public entities experienced disruptions in service. Travelers were hit with chaos last week after an issue with air traffic control towers caused a nationwide ground stop of flights, while Amtrak's booking system also went offline for several hours.
Just on Monday, major banks like JPMorgan Chase and Bank of America experienced some service disruptions and transaction delays.
The incidents have not been connected so far.
In his letter, Bost also called on more transparency with HR 2.0's funding, warning it should not take away from resources aimed at Oracle's contract on veterans' healthcare systems.

"Identify VA’s projected costs, savings, funding sources, and funding gaps for fiscal years 2027 through 2029," Bost asked. "Explain how OPM and the VA will protect resources needed for EHRM and veterans’ services, avoid duplicative implementation spending, and ensure timely retirement of legacy systems."

When reached for comment, an OPM official told Fox News Digital the office "is working closely with agencies and stakeholders throughout implementation to drive adoption, manage change effectively, and continuously improve the platform over time. We take concerns over data security seriously and also want to highlight that HCM will be leveraging Oracle Fusion Cloud HCM, not PeopleSoft."

title: Dem governor’s tale of mourning fellow serviceman ripped apart after soldier's wife gives brutal fact check
summary: Maryland Democratic Gov. Wes Moore faces claims he embellished his bond with a fallen soldier in his memoir, and the widow says she never heard from him.
story: Fox News Digital spoke to Retired Lt. Col. Jamie Gottschling who pushed back against Moore’s claims that he "led paratroopers in combat" in Afghanistan.

Maryland Democratic Gov. Wes Moore – widely believed to be seriously weighing a presidential run in 2028 – is facing controversy yet again over his characterization of his military record, this time facing allegations he embellished his relationship with a fallen soldier and used an impossible timeline to tell an emotional story in his memoir.

The issue stems from a Baltimore Sun report over the weekend highlighting a passage in Moore's 2015 book, "The Work: Searching for a Life That Matters," where he told the story of breaking into tears at his grandfather's funeral when hearing about the death of his friend Tobias "Toby" Meister.
"Inside that casket, I also saw Toby," Moore wrote in his book, adding that he cried for his grandfather, Toby and other fallen soldiers.
MARYLAND GOV WES MOORE IN HOT SEAT AFTER REPORT QUESTIONS CLAIM ABOUT GRANDFATHER AND KKK
Gov. Wes Moore (D-Md.) appears on "Meet the Press" in Washington, D.C., on Sept. 7, 2025. (Shannon Finney/NBC via Getty Images)
However, Moore's grandfather's funeral was on Dec. 17, 2005. Meister was killed in a roadside bombing 11 days later, on Dec. 28, 2005.
Moore did not learn about Meister's death until January of the next year, when he returned to Afghanistan, the Baltimore Sun reported.

After Meister's death, his wife Alicia told the outlet that many of his friends from the military have reached out to her over the years and kept his memory alive with their son, who was just over a year old when his father was killed.
A group of soldiers patrols in Afghanistan. (Getty Images Creatives)

"I’ve never heard from him," his wife, Alicia, told the outlet. "I’ve never personally heard from him," she added. "I don’t know who [Moore] is. I don’t recall my late husband ever talking about him."
WES MOORE CONFRONTED ON REPORTED MISREPRESENTATIONS ABOUT MISSING OXFORD THESIS, STORY ABOUT GREAT-GRANDFATHER
Days after the Baltimore Sun reached out to Moore's office for comment, Alicia Meister said she heard from Moore.
"It was good," she told the outlet. "He paid his respects and apologized for not reaching out sooner."
She added, "I do wish, though, that my late husband would be removed from the situation completely. I just don’t like that he has been brought in the middle of it."
In a statement to Fox News Digital, Moore spokesperson Ammar Moussa pushed back.

"Governor Moore is deeply proud of his military service. He raised his hand to serve his country at 17, left his civilian career, and deployed to one of the most dangerous regions in Afghanistan, where he served with distinction and earned the praise of his superiors and fellow service members," Moussa said.

"A Republican swiftboat campaign orchestrated by Sinclair executive chairman David Smith reached a new, despicable low. Smith—a right-wing billionaire ally of Donald Trump—is now exploiting grieving families and fellow service members for a political hit job. The facts are clear and confirmed by the Governor’s fellow service members: Governor Moore knew and worked with First Sgt. Toby Meister in Afghanistan, and this shameless attempt to drag a grieving Gold Star family into the political mud is a disgrace."

Moussa also accused Sinclair of lying about Moore's response in the article and calling it a "bad-faith approach" that is "typical of an organization run by a right-wing billionaire who is using his media empire to try and intimidate the Governor into silence."
1st Lt. Anthony Del Signore, a Marine who served alongside Moore in Afghanistan, has also defended Moore against recent criticism.

"Questioning his combat record isn't just a political attack on him—it diminishes the very real dangers all of us faced out on those roads. Wes did his job, took the risks, and served honorably," he said. "Turning our deployment into a partisan hit job is an insult to everyone who wore the uniform."

Moore previously acknowledged the conflicting timeline in interviews with the Baltimore Banner in June, attributing the inaccuracy to poor editing and the effects of stress, grief and time on his memory.

Chelsea Clinton and Gov. Wes Moore speak onstage during the Clinton Global Initiative 2026 Annual Meeting at New York Hilton Midtown on Sept. 22, 2026, in New York City. (JP Yim/Getty Images for Clinton Global Initiative)

The report comes on the heels of a Baltimore Sun story earlier this month in which his former Army supervisor questioned the governor's claim that he led soldiers in combat, a story told in the same book.

In an investigative deep dive into Moore's military service, the Baltimore Sun spoke with retired Army Lt. Col. James A. "Jamie" Gottschling, who served with Moore in Afghanistan in 2005 and 2006. What Gottschling described was Moore's patriotic service and dutiful fulfillment of his role, but exaggerations — and in some cases falsehoods — about incidents that occurred overseas.

Sgt. Matthew Taylor from Orlando, Florida, 1st Lt. Wes Brockbank from Seattle, Washington, and Cpl. Matthew Moebes from Decatur, Alabama, with the U.S. Army's 4th Squadron 2nd Cavalry Regiment, walk through a village during a joint patrol with Afghan National Army soldiers near Kandahar, Afghanistan, on March 2, 2014. (Scott Olson/Getty Images)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Del Signore pushed back on that criticism as well, saying in a statement, "I’ve heard the comments from Major Gottschling claiming this didn't happen and that Wes didn't go outside the wire. I can tell you that this 100% happened because I was there."

"Wes and I were outside the wire an average amount of the time, we traveled a decent amount, and we'd be gone for a week at a time traveling around the region. It is not surprising that Major Gottschling doesn't think this happened because he was not in the chain of command that would have been reported to, and he wasn't in charge of the convoy."

Additionally, a New York Times exposé found in 2024 that Moore for years claimed to be the recipient of a Bronze Star when he had not been awarded one at the time. He included the Bronze Star claim on his resumé when applying for a White House fellowship in 2006. In 2024, he received the award after then-Sen. Laphonza Butler, D-Calif., urged the Army to give him one.
Andrew Mark Miller is a reporter from Pasadena, California, who has been with Fox News Digital since 2021. You can reach him at AndrewMark.Miller@fox.com.

title: House Dems target Trump family, JD Vance in sweeping new investigation push
summary: Rep. Robert Garcia sends document preservation letters to 12 Trump orbit figures as the House Oversight Committee readies probes into the Trump family.
story: White House counsel Will Scharf joins 'Fox News Sunday' to address incoming Democratic investigations targeting the Trump administration. Scharf warns that the Department of Justice will push back aggressively if lawmakers use their oversight powers to threaten or intimidate administration staffers.
The likely next chairman of the House Oversight Committee is officially taking the first steps to launch a wide array of investigations before Democrats take control in the new Congress.

Rep. Robert Garcia, D-Calif., is sending document preservation letters to 12 figures in President Donald Trump's orbit on Wednesday morning, including Vice President JD Vance, Donald Trump Jr., Eric Trump, Jared Kushner, former U.S. Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle and White House chief of staff Stephen Miller.

House Oversight Committee Democrats are looking to investigate the Trump family's business deals, alleged misconduct at the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) and the federal government's handling of Jeffrey Epstein's case, they said in a release.
Garcia said the probes "will lay the groundwork for legislation which helps all Americans."
THE TOP TRUMP OFFICIALS DEMOCRATS ADMIT ARE ON THEIR HIT LIST FOR INVESTIGATIONS IN THE NEW CONGRESS

Donald Trump Jr. and Eric Trump look on as President Donald Trump and President of the European Commission Ursula von der Leyen announce a U.S.-EU trade deal after a meeting at Trump Turnberry Golf Club on July 27, 2025, in Turnberry, Scotland. (Andrew Harnik/Getty Images)

The California Democrat is all but guaranteed to hold the Oversight gavel in the next Congress and has already signaled that he intends to kick off the new year with an aggressive investigation schedule.
‘LAWYER UP’: DEMS IMMEDIATELY PUT TRUMP ON NOTICE AMID REPUBLICANS' MIDTERM BLOODBATH
His committee will also be key to any potential impeachment efforts House Democrats take on in the next term.

Other investigatory targets include former DHS Secretary Kristi Noem, former DHS senior advisor Corey Lewandowski, former White House chief of staff Susie Wiles, Attorney General Todd Blanche, Federal Bureau of Prisons Director William K. Marshall III and Trust for the National Mall CEO Catherine Townsend.

"Oversight Democrats have been investigating the potential corruption, self-dealing, and abuses of power that have funneled billions of dollars to the Trump family as Americans struggle with rising costs," letters to the president's two eldest sons read.

"While the Trump Administration’s failed policies have made life increasingly unaffordable for the public, you have engaged in business pursuits that appear to have allowed you to personally profit from your father’s presidency on a massive scale and at the expense of the American people."

Rep. Robert Garcia, D-Calif., gives remarks to media outside the House Democratic Caucus meeting in the Longworth House Office Building on Nov. 10, 2026, in Washington, D.C. (Aaron Schwartz/Getty Images)

The letter to Miller reads in part, "Oversight Democrats have heard directly from the victims of the lawless conduct of President Trump’s mass deportation campaign and from whistleblowers appalled by agency behavior. There must be accountability for those responsible for orchestrating, carrying out, and covering up these abuses, at all levels of the agency."
DEMS PIVOT FROM ‘AFFORDABILITY’ PITCH TO DHS PROBE THREATS AFTER MIDTERM WINS

Democrats have positioned their investigative efforts as accountability measures long-sought by the American public. But Republicans have argued that it shows Democrats are more interested in political retribution than working on solutions to lower issues like the high cost of living that millions of Americans are dealing with.
Trump and his family have long denied any wrongdoing when it comes to their business interests.

And while Miller and Noem did face bipartisan criticism over the administration's crackdown on illegal immigration, the majority of Republicans have lined up behind the White House and maintained that it is what Americans voted for.

White House chief of staff Stephen Miller addresses the audience during opening remarks at the Ministerial on the Resurgence of Political Terrorism at the State Department on July 16, 2026, in Washington, D.C. (Finn Gomez/Getty Images)
It's not immediately clear whether the investigatory targets will comply with House Democrats' demands to preserve documents and communications.
Republicans selected House Judiciary Committee Chairman Jim Jordan, R-Ohio, as their leader in the new Congress and de facto top spokesman against Democrats' partisan activity.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Garcia's counterpart on the House Oversight Committee remains to be seen, but both Reps. Brandon Gill, R-Texas, and Pat Fallon, R-Texas, have expressed interest in the role.

title: Alaska Dem Peltola defeats Sullivan, flipping 9th GOP Senate seat after 'decoy Dan' uproar
summary: Democrats seized a 56-44 majority in the U.S. Senate after Mary Peltola defeated Alaska Republican Sen. Dan S. Sullivan in a race that featured a same-name ballot challenger.
story: Alaska Democratic Sen.-elect Mary Peltola reacted Tuesday to defeating Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan, saying "we are going to put Alaska first." (X/Mary Peltola)

Democrats flipped a ninth GOP-held Senate seat in the 2026 midterm elections, with former Democratic Rep. Mary Peltola defeating two-term Republican Sen. Dan S. Sullivan in a state that President Donald Trump carried in 2024.
Peltola's victory gives Democrats a 56-44 majority in the U.S. Senate.

"Alaskans have voted for change, and I'm so honored to be your next U.S. senator," Peltola said in a social media video released after The Associated Press called the race Tuesday two weeks after Election Day. "Together, we're gonna put an end to the era of self-serving politicians lining their own pockets at your expense. And together, we are going to put Alaska first."
Peltola defeated Sullivan with 50.1% of the vote, avoiding a ranked-choice vote count.

The contest emerged as one of the nation's most closely watched Senate races, with Republicans defending a seat in a state President Donald Trump carried by roughly 13 percentage points in 2024, and Democrats eyeing a rare opportunity to make inroads in traditionally Republican territory.

The controversy deepened just days before Election Day when The New York Times reported that Peltola campaign aides, attorneys and national Democratic operatives had participated in a secret effort to recruit a candidate sharing the Republican incumbent's name.
Alaska Democratic Senate candidate Mary Peltola speaks at an election night event Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026, in Anchorage, Alaska.  (AP Photo/Lindsey Wasson)

According to the Times, text messages and interviews revealed a broader operation, internally dubbed the "ballot composition project," aimed at recruiting candidates who could siphon votes from Sullivan. The effort reportedly involved the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee and included discussions about establishing a new right-wing political party.

Peltola's campaign denied involvement with either Sullivan campaign, while the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee (DSCC) also rejected allegations of participation. The revelations prompted Republican Gov. Michael Dunleavy to order an investigation into whether the alleged recruitment effort violated Alaska law.
The Cook Political Report rated the contest a toss-up, reflecting the unusually competitive environment in a state that has generally favored Republicans in federal elections.
Peltola, a former state lawmaker, made history in 2022 when she became the first Alaska Native elected to Congress, winning a special election to succeed the late Republican Rep. Don Young.
GOP SENATOR, EX-HOUSE DEM EMERGE FROM ALASKA’S ‘JUNGLE PRIMARY’ DESPITE FAR-LEFT MEDDLING
Sen. Dan Sullivan, R-Alaska, and former Rep. Mary Peltola, D-Alaska. (Getty Images)

She defeated former Republican Gov. Sarah Palin in that contest before winning a full term later that year. Peltola subsequently lost her 2024 reelection bid to Republican Nick Begich III, setting the stage for her Senate campaign.

Sullivan, a Marine Corps veteran and former Alaska attorney general, first won his Senate seat in 2014 by defeating Democratic incumbent Mark Begich, Nick's uncle. He secured reelection in 2020 and sought a third term emphasizing his experience, national security and Alaska's energy interests.
The 2026 race also featured an unusual ballot controversy involving Dan J. Sullivan, a retired teacher who shared nearly the same name as the Republican incumbent.

Alaska election officials initially moved to remove the second Sullivan from the ballot amid allegations that his candidacy was intended to confuse voters or siphon support from the senator. The candidate denied wrongdoing, and the Alaska Supreme Court ruled that he could remain on the ballot. The DOJ sued in October to mitigate any "misleading" impact of the newcomer Sullivan.
COURT KEEPS ‘DECOY DAN’ ON ALASKA BALLOT AS EXPERT WARNS RANKED-CHOICE SYSTEM CREATES VOTER ‘TRAPS’
The controversy added another complication to Alaska's ranked-choice voting system, which allows voters to rank candidates in order of preference.

Under the system, a candidate receiving a majority of first-choice votes wins outright. Otherwise, the lowest-performing candidate is eliminated, and ballots are redistributed according to voters' next available preferences until a winner emerges.
SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER
Anchorage, Alaska's largest city, is seen against the Chugach Range. (Getty Images/Getty Images)
Peltola had previously benefited from the system during her 2022 congressional victories, when ranked-choice tabulation helped determine the outcomes of races featuring multiple Republican opponents.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

The Alaska contest carried national significance as both parties battled over control of the Senate, with the result determining whether Republicans retained the seat or Democrats added it to their column.

title: Mamdani's luxury second home tax hits $500M milestone despite thousands of exemptions
summary: Mayor Zohran Mamdani's pied-à-terre tax has billed wealthy second-home owners more than $500 million, even as tax bills fell far below initial estimates.
story: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani announced more than $500 million in luxury second-home tax billings despite thousands of property exemptions and ongoing legal challenges.

New York City has billed wealthy second-home owners more than $500 million under Mayor Zohran Mamdani's controversial pied-à-terre tax, even as the number of homeowners receiving bills fell far below initial estimates.
"We've billed more than $500 million to owners of second homes worth more than $5 million," Mamdani wrote on X Tuesday.
"That's half a billion dollars to invest in a City that works for all New Yorkers," he continued.

According to information provided by city officials, the New York City Department of Finance mailed approximately 7,500 tax bills — a sizable drop from the roughly 17,000 initial notices sent to property owners over the summer.
APPEALS COURT HANDS MAMDANI LEGAL WIN ON NYC LUXURY SECOND-HOME TAX
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani listens to reporters' questions during a press conference at Athens Square Park on Nov. 17, 2026, in New York City. (Michael M. Santiago/Getty Images)
Officials also said roughly 8,900 exemption applications were granted, while approximately 1,600 extension applications were denied.
The surcharge is a key part of the mayor's agenda to raise taxes on wealthy New Yorkers and help close the city's budget gap.
Despite the smaller number of bills, the city said the total amount billed exceeded the $500 million target previously outlined by Gov. Kathy Hochul earlier this year.
However, officials did not immediately provide a breakdown showing how the total was calculated across the approximately 7,500 properties.

"As Mayor Mamdani has said before, owning a second home worth over 5 million dollars should come with a responsibility to the city that makes it valuable," Julia Agos, a spokesperson for the Department of Finance, said in a statement to Fox News Digital."The Department of Finance will continue to implement the pied-a-terre surcharge fairly and efficiently, ensuring that those most able to contribute do their part to build a city that works for everyone," Agos added.
The tax is assessed on a sliding scale based on property values, meaning owners of more expensive homes can face higher charges.
JIM GAFFIGAN, NEW YORK LAWMAKERS PUSH GOV HOCHUL TO AXE 'UNNECESSARY TAX' HITTING COMEDY CLUBS

New York City luxury residential towers and Mayor Zohran Mamdani amid a legal battle over the city’s pied-à-terre tax rollout. (Victor J. Blue/Bloomberg via Getty Images/Selcuk Acar/Anadolu via Getty Images)

In an April report, the New York City comptroller's office estimated that a version of the tax could generate approximately $500 million from more than 11,200 properties before accounting for exemptions and changes in homeowner behavior.
After accounting for those factors, however, the report projected that revenue could fall to between roughly $340 million and $380 million.

Still, Mamdani has continued to express confidence in the surcharge's revenue potential, telling reporters last week, "We continue to be confident in its ability to raise half a billion dollars per year."

The surcharge, approved by the New York state Legislature in May, applies to qualifying luxury second homes in New York City, including certain one- to three-family properties valued at $5 million or more and condos and co-ops valued at $1 million or more.
MAMDANI WARNING TO WEALTHY NEW YORKERS ABOUT 'FAIR SHARE' SPARKS ONLINE FIRESTORM: 'FULL BLOWN COMMUNIST'

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani announced that the city has billed more than $500 million under its luxury second-home tax, despite issuing fewer bills than the number of initial notices sent to property owners. (Lev Radin/Sipa USA)
Property owners who qualify for exemptions are not subject to the surcharge.
Tuesday's announcement comes after a state appeals court handed Mamdani a legal victory earlier this month, unanimously dismissing a lawsuit challenging the rollout of the surcharge.
The court found that the homeowners who brought the lawsuit lacked legal standing, overturning a lower court ruling that had ordered the city to restart implementation.
However, the tax continues to face separate legal challenges, including questions about its constitutionality.
Fox News Digital has reached out to the mayor's office for comment.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Fox News Digital's Brittany Miller contributed to this report.
Michael Sinkewicz is a writer for Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to michael.sinkewicz@fox.com

title: White House pulls Trump’s FDA pick Heidi Overton on eve of Senate panel vote
summary: President Donald Trump's FDA pick, Heidi Overton, saw her nomination pulled one day before a Senate committee vote, a White House official confirmed.
story: Political strategists Tiffany Smiley and Al Mottur debate whether the progressive challenge against Chuck Schumer signals a fractured Democratic Party or a routine internal disagreement.
The White House pulled Heidi Overton’s nomination to lead the Food and Drug Administration, a White House official confirmed to Fox News, one day before a Senate committee vote.
President Donald Trump hailed Overton as a "ROCKSTAR" in August when he picked the physician and White House advisor to succeed Marty Makary, who resigned in May.
At her September confirmation hearing, Overton clashed with Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., as he pressed her to endorse universal healthcare as a human right.
TRUMP TO NOMINATE DR HEIDI OVERTON AS NEXT FDA COMMISSIONER

Heidi Overton, deputy director of the White House Domestic Policy Council, during an executive order signing in the Oval Office of the White House Aug. 10, 2026. (Bonnie Cash/UPI/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

Senate health committee Chairman Bill Cassidy, R-La., pointed to Overton’s appearance alongside Trump in the Oval Office as Trump signed an executive order calling for changes to childhood vaccine recommendations, including splitting up the combined measles, mumps and rubella vaccine.
Cassidy said there was no scientific evidence for Trump’s suggestion that the combined shot could be "quite lethal" and warned the remark could discourage vaccination.
TRUMP SURGEON GENERAL PICK BACKS MMR VACCINE, REJECTS LINK BETWEEN CHILDHOOD VACCINES AND AUTISM
Dr. Heidi Overton answers questions during her confirmation hearing in Washington, D.C.

"Yes, Senator, the MMR vaccine is safe and effective," Overton told Cassidy. When he pressed her on what she would do if Trump asked her to disregard the FDA’s safety standards, Overton said she would give the president her best advice and follow the legal requirements for reviewing individual products.

Sen. Maggie Hassan, D-N.H., asked Overton directly whether Trump was wrong. Overton reiterated that the vaccine was safe and effective and called it the best tool available during the measles outbreak. Sen. Ed Markey, D-Mass., questioned why she hadn’t corrected Trump in the Oval Office.
NEW YORK DECLARES MEASLES DISASTER EMERGENCY AS CASES SURGE IN PENNSYLVANIA
"So why should we expect you to stand up to the president as FDA commissioner?" Markey asked.
Overton worked on several of the administration’s Make America Healthy Again initiatives as a White House advisor.
FOX NEWS POLL: VOTERS EMBRACE HEALTH AGENDA WHILE RATING RFK JR NEGATIVELY

President Donald Trump, joined by (L-R) National Institutes of Health Director Jay Bhattacharya, The Conservateur’s Jayme Leagh Franklin, Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., and Deputy Assistant to the President for Domestic Policy Dr. Heidi Overton, after signing an executive order updating childhood vaccine recommendations on August 10, 2026. (Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images)

Before returning to the White House, she served as vice chair and chief policy officer at the conservative America First Policy Institute, where she criticized expanded access to abortion pills in a 2023 policy brief.
Kyle Diamantas has led the agency in an acting capacity since Makary’s departure.
PRO-LIFE CEO PREDICTS TRUMP FDA NOMINEE COULD BRING RENEWED SCRUTINY TO ABORTION DRUG RISKS

Erik Baptist, senior vice president for legal strategy at SBA Pro-Life America, said the group wants the next FDA nominee to commit to ending mail-order access to abortion drugs and changing how the agency studies their safety before the Senate holds a confirmation vote.

MAJOR PRO-LIFE GROUP THREATENS TO SUE TRUMP FDA OVER ABORTION PILL'S ALLEGED ENVIRONMENTAL RISKS"The administration must immediately end the Biden FDA’s mail-order abortion-drug scheme and protect pregnant women from predators who coerce or poison women with these drugs," Baptist said in a statement to Fox News Digital. "And the FDA must fix its flawed safety study by obtaining robust data, increasing real-time transparency, and inviting external experts to help with this study."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
"Confirmation is not a coronation," he added. "It is a time to vet nominees and seek commitments before they take office."
Fox News’ Pat Ward, Caroline McKee, and James Cirrone contributed to this report.
Stepheny Price is a Writer at Fox News with a focus on West Coast and Midwest news, missing persons, national and international crime stories, homicide cases, and border security.

title: Trump administration permanently pulls funding from LA homeless agency over mounting fraud allegations
summary: The Los Angeles Homeless Services Authority will give up about $150 million in federal funding under a HUD settlement, with LA County managing the money.
story: First Assistant U.S. Attorney for the Central District of California Bill Essayli discusses the Trump administration’s crackdown on fraud in Los Angeles’ homeless funding, revealing nearly $100 million in fraud charges filed after investigators found an individual responsible for housing 300 homeless people allegedly misused funds for personal homes and vacations. Essayli says oversight agencies 'don't care.'

The Trump administration on Monday announced a landmark settlement to permanently cut the scandal-plagued Los Angeles Homeless Services Authority (LAHSA) off from federal funding, citing overwhelming evidence of fraud and years of mismanagement that wasted taxpayer dollars.

The U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) said the agreement requires LAHSA to relinquish about $150 million in federal funding and permanently sever its ties to HUD's homelessness funding programs by the end of 2027.

"Organizations that are complicit in this fraud and waste will not get one penny more of federal funding," Bill Essayli, first assistant U.S. attorney for the Central District of California, said in a statement.
LA HOMELESSNESS FRAUD CASES EXPOSE DEEPER PROBLEM THAN STOLEN MILLIONS, OVERSIGHT HAWK WARNS

A homeless encampment near Venice Beach in Los Angeles. Residents have called for stronger oversight of nearby supportive housing programs and improved public safety. (Jill Connelly/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
Los Angeles County will take over managing the funds used to combat homelessness, while HUD will closely monitor how the money is spent, according to officials.
The agreement, executed Thursday, resolves a lawsuit filed by LAHSA challenging HUD's June decision to suspend further funding to the agency.

According to HUD, investigators found that LAHSA received more federal homelessness funding than any other jurisdiction in the nation, taking in nearly $1 billion in taxpayer dollars over the last five years.
LA REAL ESTATE VET COMES AT MAYOR BASS WITH RECEIPTS OVER DAMNING HOMELESSNESS REPORT: 'SHE DOESN'T GET IT'
A homeless encampment on Skid Row Sept. 23, 2021, in Los Angeles. (Allen J. Schaben/Los Angeles Times via Getty Images)
"Los Angeles remains the epicenter of the nation’s drug-fueled homelessness crisis. On top of this, their failure has enabled record homelessness fraud," HUD said.
HUD Secretary Scott Turner said LAHSA had spent years funneling federal funding to organizations without proper oversight.
"Taxpayers will no longer bankroll an organization that fails to deliver for the Americans it was created to serve," Turner said in a statement.
HUD’S HOMELESSNESS REFORMS PUT HUMAN LIVES AHEAD OF HOUSING BUREAUCRACY

Bill Essayli, the first assistant U.S. attorney for the Central District of California, appears at a news conference at the Spring Street Courthouse on Aug. 13, 2026. (Allen J. Schaben/Los Angeles Times via Getty Images)

"For years, American taxpayers have been sending billions of dollars to Los Angeles to house the homeless and other vulnerable Americans. The result? Fraud and corruption," Scott Brady, executive director of the White House Task Force to Eliminate Fraud, added in a statement.

HUD added that it is committed to ending what it called the "harmful" "Housing First" policy, which provides permanent housing to homeless individuals without requiring them to meet preconditions such as sobriety or participation in therapy.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Under a new Treatment First approach, individuals will likely need to participate in addiction or mental health treatment and demonstrate progress toward recovery to qualify for and maintain housing assistance.

"HUD is rejecting the addiction-fueled depravity seen from LA’s Skid Row to New York’s ‘Boulevard of Broken Dreams’ and moving to Treatment First to restore lives of self-sufficiency," Turner previously said.
The settlement comes as HUD reports a 6.3% decrease in homelessness, the largest recorded decline, during the first year of Trump's administration.
"President Trump’s actions to secure the border, get criminal illegals off our streets and restore safety to our communities drove a historic decrease in homelessness," Turner previously said.
Bonny Chu is a Breaking and Trending News Writer for Fox News Digital

title: White House blasts 'Trumpcare for All' pitch from far-left El-Sayed who called president 'unserious fool'
summary: White House slammed Abdul El-Sayed's "Trumpcare for All" pitch, warning the Medicare for All plan would threaten Americans' existing health coverage.
story: Michigan Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed references an AI-generated image depicting President Donald Trump as Jesus Christ while sarcastically calling the president "Habibi" to embrace "Medicare for All." (Credit: X @AbdulElSayed)

The White House blasted far-left Michigan Democrat Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed's pitch to President Donald Trump to embrace "Trumpcare for All," warning that the Medicare for All proposal would threaten Americans' existing health coverage.

"The Radical Democrats’ socialist proposal for a government takeover of healthcare should really be called ‘Medicare for None’ as it destroys access to the life-saving care Americans rely on daily," White House spokeswoman Allison Schuster told Fox News Digital.
The sharp response came after El-Sayed, who recently called Trump an "unserious fool," posted a 16-second video Tuesday urging the president to embrace the progressive proposal.
BERNIE SANDERS THINKS MEDICARE FOR ALL BILL COULD PASS, 'NOT ABSOLUTELY CERTAIN' TRUMP WOULD VETO

Democrat Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed has said he'll call Medicare for All proposal "Trumpcare for All" if the president agrees to go along with it. (Evan Cobb for The Washington Post via Getty Images, File)

"I think there is a responsibility that we have to engage with [Trump] as the unserious fool that he is," El-Sayed said during a recent appearance on "Pod Save America," according to earlier Fox News Digital reporting.
Despite those remarks, the senator-elect struck a more conciliatory tone in his latest appeal.
"Donald. Habibi. Midterms were rough. I get it," El-Sayed said in the video posted Nov. 17, addressing Trump with the Arabic term "habibi," commonly translated as "my dear" or "my beloved."
"Trumpcare for All. It's really popular. People really want healthcare. You can put your name all over it."
EL-SAYED ADMITS FREE HEALTHCARE MEANS PAYING 'A LITTLE BIT MORE IN TAXES' REGARDLESS OF INCOME
Despite those calling President Trump "unserious," El-Sayed has seemingly struck a more conciliatory tone in his latest appeal. (Asra Q. Nomani/Fox News Digital, File)

The video featured a mock "Trumpcare" card and an AI-generated image depicting Trump as Jesus Christ, which El-Sayed, a Muslim, referenced while urging the president to embrace socialized, taxpayer-funded healthcare.
"Donald, this is your chance to heal the sick (like in that one AI image. You know the one)," El-Sayed said.
The White House instead pointed to Trump's efforts to lower prescription drug prices, contrasting those policies with the single-payer system advocated by El-Sayed.

"President Trump is focused on taking on the special interests that are driving up the costs of healthcare for all Americans including through his historic efforts to ensure American patients never pay more than those in other developed nations for all prescription drugs, which has already saved Americans well over $1 Billion," Schuster said.
MAJORITY OF AMERICANS BROADLY REJECT SOCIALIST IDEOLOGY EVEN AS FAR LEFT SURGES TO POWER
In response to El-Sayed, the White House said, in part, "The President will continue delivering real results that lower costs and put Americans first." (Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images, File)

"The President will continue delivering real results that lower costs and put Americans first, while Democrats push ideas that have devastated economies and ruined healthcare quality anywhere they have been implemented."

The administration also cited a U.S. Council of Economic Advisers' analysis estimating that Medicare for All would increase the federal budget deficit by approximately $47.4 trillion between 2027 and 2036 in the absence of additional taxes or revenues.
The White House also cited a CEA projection that Medicare for All would shift large numbers of Americans away from employer-sponsored insurance and into a new government-run coverage system.

Medicare for All, a sweeping single-payer health care proposal championed by Democratic socialists, would replace much of the nation's private health insurance system with federally financed coverage. Supporters argue it would guarantee coverage, while critics warn of substantial tax increases and massive federal spending.

Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed and other far-left Democrats are in favor of Medicare for All, a single-payer health care proposal that would replace much of the nation's private health insurance system with federally financed coverage. (Erin Kirkland/Bloomberg via Getty Images, File)
El-Sayed's public appeal was not his first attempt to recruit Trump to the idea.
During a CNN appearance earlier this month, the incoming senator suggested that the president could attach his name to a universal health care proposal.
"Donald, if you're watching, we can put your name on it. I know you like to put your name on stuff," El-Sayed said, according to a Nov. 10 social media post by CNN anchor Kaitlan Collins.
The unusual overture follows a contentious Michigan Senate race in which El-Sayed defeated Republican Mike Rogers.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

The Democrat also mocked Trump, Vice President JD Vance and Rogers during his election victory remarks, adding to the contrast between his earlier criticism of the administration and his latest invitation to collaborate.
El-Sayed is scheduled to take office Jan. 3, 2027.
El-Sayed's office did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment.
Fox News Digital's Leo Briceno contributed to this reporting.

title: POWs, teens among 6 US soldiers from Korean War identified seven decades later
summary: The DPAA identified six U.S. soldiers missing from the Korean War, including two teenagers, decades after they died as prisoners of war or in action.
story: Modern forensic analysis helped identify six Korean War soldiers, including two 18-year-olds and men who died as prisoners of war.
At least six U.S. soldiers who went missing during the Korean War, including two teenagers, have been identified decades after their deaths.

The soldiers, who ranged in age from 18 to 28, all served in the U.S. Army, the Defense POW/MIA Accounting Agency (DPAA) said. Five were junior enlisted soldiers or noncommissioned officers, including four corporals and one sergeant. The sixth was a commissioned officer, a first lieutenant.
Officials said the soldiers either died as prisoners of war or were presumed killed in action.

The soldiers identified were Cpl. Jackie Lee Thurman, 18, of Illinois; 1st Lt. Raymond Banker Gilbert, 23, of Ohio; Cpl. Richard Neal Lennox, 18, of Michigan; Cpl. William Reynold Laughlin Jr., 21, of Oregon; Sgt. Joseph Alfred Platzkoester, 28, of Illinois; and Cpl. Andrew R. Tischler, 21, of Celina, Texas.
EXPERTS FINALLY SOLVE MYSTERY OF TEENAGE REVOLUTIONARY WAR SOLDIER 246 YEARS AFTER HIS DEATH

Cpl. Jackie Lee Thurman, 18, (left) went missing while attempting to escort a wounded officer, while 1st Lt. Raymond Banker Gilbert, 23, (right) died as a prisoner of war.  (Defense POW/MIA Accounting Agency)

Most of the soldiers had been buried for decades as "Unknowns" at the National Memorial Cemetery of the Pacific, also known as the Punchbowl, in Honolulu, Hawaii. Their remains were later disinterred through DPAA initiatives between 2016 and 2024 and sent to the agency's laboratory for modern forensic analysis.
Gilbert, a member of Battery B, 503rd Field Artillery Battalion, 2nd Infantry Division, was wounded and captured before being reported missing on Dec. 1, 1950.
He died from his wounds as a prisoner of war on Jan. 31, 1951.
His remains were returned in 1954 and buried as an Unknown in Honolulu. They were disinterred in July 2024, and he was officially identified on June 4, 2026.
‘FREEDOMS ARE NEVER FREE’: A JEWISH AMERICAN SOLDIER BURIED WITH NAZIS FINALLY LAID TO REST WITH US TROOPS

Thurman, a member of Battery B, 99th Field Artillery Battalion, 1st Cavalry Division, went missing on Sept. 3, 1950, while attempting to escort a wounded officer under heavy mortar fire near Taegu and Waegwan, South Korea.
His remains were eventually recovered in 1952 and buried as an Unknown in Honolulu. They were disinterred in November 2022, and he was officially identified on May 18, 2026.
Lennox, a member of Company C, 1st Battalion, 7th Infantry Regiment, 3rd Infantry Division, was reported missing on Nov. 28, 1950, following an enemy attack near Sachang-ni, North Korea.
He was captured and taken to Prisoner of War Camp 1 in Changsong, where he died nearly a year later in October 1951.
His remains were returned in 1954 and buried as an Unknown in Honolulu. They remained there until they were disinterred on June 13, 2016. He was officially identified on Aug. 7, 2025.
Cpl. William Reynold Laughlin Jr., 21, went missing Dec. 2, 1950, during a withdrawal near the Chosin Reservoir. (Defense POW/MIA Accounting Agency)
Laughlin Jr., a member of Company D, 1st Battalion, 32nd Infantry Regiment, 7th Infantry Division, went missing on Dec. 2, 1950, during a withdrawal near the Chosin Reservoir.
He was never reported as a prisoner of war, and the Army issued a presumptive finding of death on Dec. 31, 1953.
His remains were returned in 1954 and buried as an Unknown in Honolulu. They were disinterred in July 2022, and he was officially identified on Sept. 28, 2026.
People visit the Korean War Veterans Memorial in Washington, D.C., which honors Americans who served during the conflict. (Bill O'Leary/The Washington Post via Getty Images)
Platzkoester, a member of Company H, 2nd Battalion, 38th Infantry Regiment, 2nd Infantry Division, went missing on May 30, 1951, during a convoy ambush near Inje, South Korea.
The Army issued a presumptive finding of death in December 1953 and declared his remains unrecoverable in January 1956.
Unbeknownst to officials at the time, his remains had already been recovered in the fall of 1951 and later buried as an Unknown in Honolulu in 1956.
They were disinterred in November 2023, and he was officially identified on May 29, 2026.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Tischler, a member of Company F, 2nd Battalion, 15th Infantry Regiment, 3rd Infantry Division, was reported missing in action on May 25, 1951, during a road march near Taewol Village, South Korea.
The DPAA officially accounted for him on May 5, 2026.
Each soldier is memorialized on both the Courts of the Missing in Honolulu and the Korean War Veterans Memorial Wall in Washington, D.C.
Bonny Chu is a Breaking and Trending News Writer for Fox News Digital

title: Senior US official undercuts CNN’s alarming Iran ‘dirty bomb’ report: ‘It’s not new’
summary: President Donald Trump warned Iran would pay a price "no country has ever paid" if a dirty bomb threat to Washington, D.C., proves real, amid divided assessments.
story: President Donald Trump warned Iran on Monday that it would face unprecedented retaliation if it were to carry out an attack on Washington, D.C.

A senior U.S. official is challenging a new report on Iran developing plans for a "dirty bomb" attack on Washington, D.C., which drew a warning of overwhelming retaliation from President Donald Trump this week.

The prospect of Iranian-directed violence on American soil has shadowed U.S. security officials for decades. From a plot to bomb a Washington restaurant to assassination schemes targeting former officials and dissidents, Tehran has repeatedly sought ways to reach its enemies inside U.S. borders.
"I’m not sure why this was leaked because it’s not new," a senior U.S. official told Fox News' Jennifer Griffin in response to the report.
"Iran is very aspirational, but not suicidal. If they were to attack D.C. or any other U.S. city it would cause us to have a full out war with them. Their friends would not come to their aid."

CNN reported this week that U.S. intelligence indicated Iran was developing potential plans to target senior Trump administration officials in Washington with a radiological device or chemical weapon.

Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps officers attend a memorial ceremony for IRGC commanders, nuclear scientists and civilians killed in the Iran-Israel war at the Imam Khomeini Grand Mosque in downtown Tehran on July 2, 2025. (Morteza Nikoubazl/NurPhoto via Getty Images)
BESSENT MOVED TO MILITARY BASE AS IRAN THREATS EXCEED ‘ADVANCED STAGE,’ OFFICIAL SAYS
Sources described the planning as an effort to develop options rather than evidence of an imminent attack, with officials divided over whether Tehran could or would execute it.
"We’re looking into it," Trump said in Manila on Tuesday when asked about the new report.
Pressed on whether Washington faced an imminent threat, he warned: "Well, if there is, they will pay a price the likes of which no country has ever paid before."
"I hope it’s not, but we take it very seriously because they happen to be crazy," the president added.
White House spokesperson Lauren Bis said, "We remain vigilant monitoring any and all potential threats, but at this time there are no credible threats to the homeland."

Iran could make a dirty bomb, but would need someone inside the United States with the expertise to handle the materials and carry out an attack, said Andrea Stricker, deputy director of the Foundation for Defense of Democracies’ nonproliferation program.
A dirty bomb combines conventional explosives with radioactive material, spreading contamination without producing a nuclear explosion.
The White House is seen from the Washington Monument on Nov. 4, 2026, in Washington, D.C. (Kevin Carter/Getty Images)
U.S. authorities have spent nearly two decades building defenses against that possibility.
DHS launched its Securing the Cities program in 2007 to help local agencies detect and deter nuclear and radiological threats, including dirty bombs, beginning in the New York City region.
"Making a radiological dispersal device would be within Iran’s know-how, as well as a chemical weapon," Stricker told Fox News Digital.
Iran’s chemical weapons program dates back to the 1980s. "More recently, they've been looking at how to weaponize chemical weapons like fentanyl and disperse them through the air," Stricker said.
Fentanyl can suppress breathing to the point of respiratory arrest.
"I think for an attack using chemical weapons like this, they would probably want to go with something rudimentary. Industrial scale chemicals like chlorine would be easy to obtain," she added.
President Donald Trump. (Win McNamee/Getty Images)
IRAN-BACKED TERROR SUSPECTS PLOTTED ATTACK ON US TROOPS USING VANS PACKED WITH FUEL, DOJ SAYS
Rather than risk transporting hazardous materials into the country, Tehran could look to obtain them here, she said.
"They may want to simply try to steal them or procure them from inside the United States. That would probably ease their task," Stricker said.
But the technical demands would complicate Iran’s reliance on hired criminals to execute its operations.
"In the past, they've used sort of everyday criminals for hire to execute some of their other plots, and luckily we foiled a lot of these," she said.
