title: Charlotte wants Iryna Zarutska murder lawsuit tossed, says it can’t be held responsible
summary: Charlotte argues governmental immunity shields its transit policing decisions as it asks a judge to toss Iryna Zarutska's family's wrongful-death lawsuit.
story: U.S. Attorney of North Carolina's Western District Russ Ferguson discusses the case against the man accused of killing Iryna Zarutska on a North Carolina train after he was deemed incompetent to stand trial on ‘The Story.’

The city of Charlotte is asking a judge to throw out a wrongful-death lawsuit filed by Iryna Zarutska's family over security failures they say left her unprotected aboard the city's light-rail system, arguing many of those decisions are protected by governmental immunity.

Zarutska's murder drew national attention after surveillance video showed Decarlos Brown Jr. seated behind her aboard a Lynx Blue Line train before he is accused of stabbing her in the neck about four minutes after she boarded. The 23-year-old Ukrainian refugee had just left work at a local pizzeria.

Her family alleges Charlotte failed to adequately police and secure the light-rail system. The city now argues decisions involving transit policing, crime prevention, security contractors and public safety are government functions shielded from liability under North Carolina law.
PROSECUTORS SAY CHARLOTTE TRAIN STABBING CASE WON'T BE DISMISSED REGARDLESS OF COMPETENCY RULING

Charlotte's new filing also acknowledges there was no private security guard inside Zarutska's train car when she was killed, that Brown apparently boarded without presenting a ticket or pass and that the light-rail system operates without turnstiles or fare gates.

But the city denies those circumstances caused Zarutska's death, arguing Brown acted on his own and that the attack could not have been predicted based on previous crime across the transit system.

Zarutska's family sued Charlotte and its private transit security contractor, Professional Police Services, or PSS, in August, alleging security failures left riders vulnerable to violent crime.

title: Susan Smith's ex-husband wants her ‘in prison until she dies’ after killing sons in alleged bid to win lover

Susan Smith’s ex-husband wants her to remain in prison until she dies for killing their two sons in what prosecutors say was a bid to win back her lover, as a seven-member board prepares to consider her parole request Thursday.

David Smith, 56, made the comments to CNN as the South Carolina Board of Paroles and Pardons prepares to hear his ex-wife's request for parole in the 1994 murders of her children, 3-year-old Michael and 14-month-old Alexander.
"If I have a choice, I’d want her to stay in prison until she dies," David Smith said. "32 years hasn’t changed the heartache."

While Susan Smith was convicted of two counts of murder and sentenced to life in prison in 1995, state law at the time allowed her to be considered for parole after serving 30 years. That law was changed shortly after her conviction, making people sentenced to life for a murder committed after Jan. 1, 1996 ineligible for parole.

title: Surfing legend found stabbed to death under bed – girlfriend accused of letting thugs in to wipe him out
summary: Kurt Van Dyke's girlfriend and a man were arrested in Costa Rica over the surfer's murder, as the OIJ claims she helped armed attackers enter.
story: Costa Rican authorities arrested the girlfriend of legendary California surfer Kurt Van Dyke in connection with his February killing.
A legendary California surfer's former girlfriend was among the two people arrested in Costa Rica in connection with his murder.

Kurt Van Dyke, 66, was found dead in February inside his apartment in the Costa Rican town of Hone Creek, Cahuita, Limón. He was found with signs of asphyxiation and multiple stab wounds, local authorities said at the time.

The Costa Rica Judicial Investigation Agency (OIJ) said Van Dyke's girlfriend, only identified as Arroyo, 31, helped armed attackers get into the apartment on Feb. 14, according to La Nación. A 34-year-old man identified as Gutiérrez was also arrested on Thursday morning.
Van Dyke was found dead underneath a bed and wrapped in a sheet with several stab wounds.
CALIFORNIA SURFER MURDERED IN APPARENT ROBBERY AT HIS HOME IN COSTA RICA: REPORTS
Kurt Van Dyke, 66, was murdered at his home in Costa Rica. (Facebook/ Kurt Van Dyke)
Police in Costa Rica believe both planned a robbery against Van Dyke and wanted to steal the bank card codes associated with the hotel he owned in the country.
During the raids on Thursday morning, police seized a cellphone and a vehicle allegedly used during the crime, as well as other items relevant to the investigation.

title: MICHAEL RUIZ: Tyler Robinson defense wants testing on bullet fragments paused in assassination of Charlie Kirk
summary: Tyler Robinson's lawyers want Utah ballistics testing paused as prosecutors push FBI virtual comparison microscopy on Charlie Kirk's autopsy fragments.
story: Finn reports on the upcoming court proceedings, the timeline leading up to the trial and the latest developments in the high-profile case surrounding Kirk's assassination.

Attorneys for Charlie Kirk's accused assassin Tyler Robinson are asking a Utah judge to put additional ballistics testing on pause as prosecutors attempt to conclusively link bullet fragments recovered at autopsy to the suspected murder weapon, which some experts call unnecessary and even prosecutors admit isn't central to their case.

The Utah County Attorney's Office has asked the judge to deny the motion, countering that the testing they are seeking will not consume the evidence or prevent Robinson's experts from having a look at it once the government is done — and that they have more compelling evidence to introduce at trial.

"There is no reason to believe the bullet fragments contain exculpatory evidence," Deputy Utah County Attorney Ryan McBride alleged in an opposition to the defense motion. "To the contrary, all the evidence points to the inculpatory value of the fragments."
TYLER ROBINSON JUDGE UNSEALS ATF REPORT IN ASSASSINATION OF CHARLIE KIRK

Tyler Robinson, who is accused in the fatal shooting of Charlie Kirk, listens during a preliminary hearing at the Fourth District Courthouse in Provo, Utah, Thursday, July 9, 2026. (Spenser Heaps/AP via Pool)

Robinson has allegedly admitted to the shooting, he wrote. Three unspent cartridges in the rifle were consistent with the gunshot fired at Kirk. The bullet fragments were consistent with the suspected murder weapon, although they have not been conclusively identified to it. And police recovered video evidence and a Dremel tool consistent with etchings made on brass casings recovered in the rifle at the scene.

While the fragment testing, known as virtual comparison microscopy (VCM), won't destroy the evidence, it is expected to physically alter or even damage it, according to court filings. "Petals" from the fragments may be folded out of the way as investigators look for rifling markings on the underlying surface, according to prosecutors. The fragments may be cleaned, at least in a small area. And lead fragments may be cleaned or scraped. There is a risk that pieces break off during the process.
TYLER ROBINSON'S DEFENSE TEAM FIGHTS TO SEAL EVIDENCE AND PUNISH PROSECUTORS IN CHARLIE KIRK'S ASSASSINATION

Bullet fragments are shown on a screen during a preliminary hearing for Tyler Robinson, who is accused in the fatal shooting of Charlie Kirk, at the Fourth District Courthouse in Provo, Utah, Thursday, July 9, 2026. (Spenser Heaps/AP via Pool)

Robinson's lawyers want the VCM testing placed on hold until they have a chance to examine and photograph the same evidence — or an order allowing a defense expert to observe the testing in person or via a video recording, something the FBI does not allow for a number of reasons, including contamination and national security concerns.
They argued that prior ATF testing already damaged the evidence, and the next round of testing could result in further harm.
CHARLIE KIRK JUDGE DENIES TYLER ROBINSON'S ATTEMPT TO HAVE POTENTIAL DEATH PENALTY REMOVED

Samantha Karner, a firearm and tool mark examiner for the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives, holds a model of a bullet while she testifies during a preliminary hearing for Tyler Robinson, who is accused in the fatal shooting of Charlie Kirk, at the Fourth District Courthouse in Provo, Utah, Thursday, July 9, 2026. (Spenser Heaps/AP via Pool)

"The ATF couldn’t conclusively connect the bullet fragment to the recovered rifle, but it couldn’t rule out the rifle either," said Jason Pack, a retired FBI supervisory agent who has been following the case. "That’s an important distinction, and it helps explain why prosecutors want the FBI to take another look."

He explained that VCM is a more advanced process than simply looking at the fragments under a microscope, a more traditional method. Even so, there's no guarantee that examiners will find a more conclusive link between the fragments and the suspected murder weapon.
CHARLIE KIRK'S FAMILY COMES FACE TO FACE WITH ACCUSED ASSASSIN FOR FIRST TIME
"If the markings are too damaged or simply aren’t there anymore, even the best technology can’t bring them back," Pack told Fox News Digital.

Robinson is accused of shooting Kirk at Utah Valley University during a Turning Point USA public speaking event on Sept. 10, 2025. During Kirk's autopsy, investigators recovered a bullet jacket fragment and four lead fragments from his body, according to prosecutors.

An image that shows ammunition, including a casing engraved with the words "TEST SHOT" is displayed during a preliminary hearing for Tyler Robinson, who is accused in the fatal shooting of Charlie Kirk, at the Fourth District Courthouse in Provo, Utah, Thursday, July 9, 2026. (Spenser Heaps/AP via Pool)
CHARLIE KIRK MURDER CASE AS 'STRAIGHT-FORWARD' AS IT GETS, PROSECUTORS ARGUE AS CASE NEARS TRIAL DECISION

"If the bullet fragment is again altered to the point where no independent comparison is possible, then the degree of prejudice to the defendant is severe," Robinson's lawyers wrote to the court. "The defense will be unable to independently verify conclusions, cross-examination will be unfairly limited, and the jury will hear unchallengeable expert testimony."

Bernard Zapor, a former ATF special agent in charge and faculty associate at Arizona State University, said those concerns may be overblown. The fragments were already documented meticulously during the ATF's initial examination, he said, with photographs, data and images available to the defense through discovery. If the fragments are damaged during additional testing, it may not change much, since the initial testing was inconclusive — which he said is not unusual in shootings involving similar caliber weapons.
TYLER ROBINSON HEARING ENDS WITHOUT RULING AS EVIDENCE DISMANTLES CHARLIE KIRK CONSPIRACY CLAIMS

Charlie Kirk speaks at Utah Valley University on September 10, 2025, in Orem, Utah. Kirk, founder of Turning Point USA, was speaking at his "American Comeback Tour" when he was shot in the neck and killed. (Trent Nelson/The Salt Lake Tribune/Getty Images)

"This is all distracting from the purpose of getting information to the jury so they can come to a conclusion, one way or the other," he told Fox News Digital. "This case is solid. You don’t want to do anything to disrupt it."
Robinson's lawyers previously flagged in court that they intend to challenge the ATF's findings and methodology.

During prior testing, ATF examiner Samantha Karner cleaned the jacket fragment, photographed it and then peeled the "petals" back to examine groove impressions on it. She identified the fragment as having been in the .30 caliber class, but she was unable to conclusively link it to the suspected murder weapon, Robinson's grandfather's .30-06 Mauser rifle.
TYLER ROBINSON'S AND LANCE TWIGGS' DNA BOTH ALLEGEDLY FOUND ON KEY EVIDENCE IN CHARLIE KIRK'S ASSASSINATION

"Given the limited detail that Ms. Karner observed, she could not include or exclude the fragment as having been fired from the recovered rifle," prosecutors wrote. "She testified that there was 'no further testing that [she] could do' to try to reach a conclusive result ... However, she noted 'the possibility of using a 3D system to visualize the individual characteristics on the bullet,' to obtain more conclusive results."

People run after shots were fired during an appearance by Charlie Kirk at Utah Valley University on September 10, 2025, in Orem, Utah. Kirk, founder of Turning Point USA, was speaking at his "American Comeback Tour" when he was shot in the neck and killed. (Trent Nelson/The Salt Lake Tribune/Getty Images)
For that kind of analysis, however, the fragments would need to be sent to the FBI for VCM.
TYLER ROBINSON TO FACE TRIAL IN CHARLIE KIRK ASSASSINATION AS JUDGE KEEPS DEATH PENALTY ON TABLE

"This analysis is non-destructive and uses 3D technology to capture multiple scans of the object," prosecutors wrote. "The scan data will be preserved and provided to the defense for their own analysis."
SEND US A TIP

In order to perform the scans, however, analysts may have to clean the fragments or fold back warped metal, called "petals," to expose the surface of the fragment that contacted the rifle when fired, prosecutors wrote.
Tyler Robinson, accused of the murder of Charlie Kirk, appears during a hearing in Fourth District Court in Provo, Utah, on Thursday, Dec. 11, 2025. (Rick Egan/The Salt Lake Tribune via Pool)
TYLER ROBINSON PROSECUTORS: NO DNA, NO PROBLEM — PILE OF EVIDENCE TO PUSH CHARLIE KIRK CASE TOWARD JUSTICE

Prosecutors are also seeking another type of testing, known as metallurgical testing, on the bullet jacket fragment and at least one piece of lead, according to court filings. That testing might require cleaning "around a small area," prosecutors added, before it is examined with an X-ray.
LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST

"The FBI is also proposing separate testing to compare the metal in the recovered bullet fragments with ammunition seized during the investigation," Pack said. "That could provide additional information, although it wouldn’t conclusively identify the firearm."
GET BREAKING NEWS BY EMAIL
Lastly, prosecutors want an examiner to disassemble one of the unfired .30-06 cartridges found at Robinson's home after his arrest, for comparison.

Robinson's attorneys entered not guilty pleas on his behalf to all charges. He could face the potential death penalty if convicted of the top count of aggravated murder.

title: US infrastructure crumbles as adversaries power up – leaving Americans dangerously exposed: cyber expert
summary: A wave of tech failures highlights weaknesses in America’s aging infrastructure that adversaries could exploit with increasingly accessible cyberattack tools, experts warn.
story: Charles Tango, chief strategy officer at cybersecurity company Hydden, discussed how aging U.S. infrastructure could leave critical systems vulnerable to attacks by foreign adversaries.

A string of technology failures that left flights grounded and disrupted workplace software and banking systems is renewing concerns about weaknesses in America's critical systems foreign adversaries could exploit, according to experts.

Cybersecurity professionals warn that U.S. adversaries are closely watching how the country responds to such failures for weaknesses they could exploit. A disruptive cyberattack doesn’t necessarily require sophisticated tactics, they say, and America’s foes already have the capabilities to carry one out.
The National Security Agency on Tuesday experienced disruptions to internal systems during scheduled maintenance, though officials said its critical national security functions remained operational.

Apple joined the wave of tech companies experiencing problems on Tuesday impacting services including the App Store, Apple Music and iCloud sign-ins. The tech giant attributed the disruptions to an internal update, saying many systems have since been restored.
DUFFY: INVESTIGATORS EXAMINING 2 ROUTERS AFTER NATIONWIDE FAA GROUND STOP, NO SIGNS OF FOREIGN CYBERATTACK
The Three Mile Island Nuclear power plant is seen at sunset in Middletown, Pennsylvania. (Reuters/Shannon Stapleton)
One day earlier, a technology failure forced United Airlines to delay departing flights by over 90 minutes. There was no indication of a cybersecurity issue.

The latest disruptions followed Friday's nationwide ground stop triggered by the Federal Aviation Administration, which lasted over four hours, the longest in 25 years, creating travel disruptions that took airlines days to resolve.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said on "Fox News Sunday" there was no indication of a foreign cyberattack, stating that investigators are examining if faulty equipment or an installation problem triggered the hours-long ground stop.

"We think it was the installation or the router that was the bad actor," Duffy said. "But we're open, if we see something else, we're gonna continue to investigate with our federal partners and law enforcement."
According to The Wall Street Journal, FAA radio sites in El Dorado, Arkansas, and possibly Amarillo, Texas, overloaded the communications system used by air-traffic controllers.
FAA SAYS AIR TRAVEL SHOULD BE BACK TO NORMAL SUNDAY AFTER NATIONWIDE GROUND STOP
Planes wait on the tarmac at LaGuardia Airport in New York on Nov. 13, 2026. (Charly Triballeau/AFP via Getty Images)
Meanwhile, a Microsoft Outlook outage on Thursday lasted for nearly 24 hours before service was restored Friday morning.
Microsoft executive Charles Lamanna said the issue was the result of a previously undetected software defect, increased traffic and reduced server capacity.
DAVID MARCUS: WHAT BIG TECH’S WEEKEND FROM HELL MEANS FOR THE FUTURE OF DATA CENTERS
Also on Friday, Workday — whose human resources and payroll software is used by millions of Americans — experienced a widespread outage.
"Workday is currently unavailable," a message for users said. "We are experiencing a service interruption. Your service will be restored as quickly as possible."
PERPETUAL PARALYSIS: WHY EVERYTHING IS GRINDING TO A HALT
On Monday, customers of several large banks — among them Chase, Bank of America and Wells Fargo — reported problems accessing online banking services.
FOLLOW THE FOX TRUE CRIME TEAM ON X
Passengers wait at boarding gates at Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport in Washington, D.C., on Nov. 13, 2026. (Zina Desmazes/AFP via Getty Images)
Chase acknowledged that some transactions were experiencing delays but noted that customers continued to have full access to their accounts and funds.
BILL GATES SOUNDS ALARM ON AI-POWERED CYBERATTACKS, WARNS OF 'NEGATIVE SURPRISES' WITHIN A YEAR

While officials have said there is no indication Friday’s ground stop was caused by a foreign cyberattack, U.S. adversaries have the capability to deliberately disrupt American infrastructure, Charles Tango, chief strategy officer at cybersecurity company Hydden, told Fox News Digital.
He said any of America's adversaries have the capability to deliberately cause a disruption to the nation's infrastructure, and warned it's easier to pull off than many think.

"It does not take a lot of sophistication these days to cause this type of attack, especially with the advent of AI, it's made security attacks much easier and much cheaper, but absolutely other countries like China would have immense capability of impacting our environments," Tango said. "They've spent a lot of time and a lot of effort trying to compromise our critical infrastructure."

"Not all warfare needs to be kinetic these days. A cyber warfare can be very effective. We've seen that with Russia and Ukraine. We should be very mindful of the capacities that our adversaries have when it comes to cyber capability. Many of them specialize on offensive cyber capabilities, and that's what we should be focusing on," Tango said.
"Other countries like China would have immense capability of impacting our environments. And we've seen that recently with organizations like Volt Typhoon," he added.
CHINESE HACKERS TARGET NASA AND KEY US AGENCIES, DOJ ALLEGES

Tango said aging systems, some within U.S. critical infrastructure, create vulnerabilities that capable adversaries can exploit, pointing to how a small equipment problem triggered a widespread disruption.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE FROM THE FOX TRUE CRIME HUB
A Microsoft Outlook outage on Thursday lasted for nearly 24 hours before service was restored Friday morning. (Cesc Maymo)

"What we saw here is that one very small incident led to a widespread outage. That's because a lot of these systems are old. They've been around for a while. We haven't invested in upgrading them. And that's not just for the FAA. That's across critical infrastructure," Tango said.
SEND US A TIP
"I mean, the world is watching how we respond to this, and certainly our adversaries are watching this very, very closely," he added.
HACKERS COULD ALREADY BE INSIDE AMERICAN UTILITIES, CYBER EXPERTS WARN OF 'TROJAN HORSE' THREAT

The threat from foreign adversaries extends well past aviation. In 2024, federal cybersecurity agencies warned that Chinese state-sponsored hacking group Volt Typhoon had compromised U.S. energy providers and other critical infrastructure organizations. Officials assessed the group was positioning itself to be able to disrupt essential services during a conflict or major crisis with the U.S.

Michael Balboni, a former New York homeland security adviser who also served as a New York Power Authority trustee and is currently president of Adelphi University, told Fox News Digital that reports of foreign adversaries accessing American power grids have long concerned officials.

GET BREAKING NEWS BY EMAIL

"We had reports and information that, in fact, adversaries were in the grids across the country," Balboni told Fox News Digital. "And that, again, had been there for years. The question becomes, what is their capability?"

"Imagine taking out all the traffic lights in a major city," he said. "Imagine having the power go off to a hospital. Now, most hospitals have generators, but what if they don't come back on?"

title: Major drug kingpin ‘The Kraken’ captured in California after yearslong hunt

story: Dana Perino reports on former President Donald Trump's initiative to combat drug cartels in Ecuador. The U.S. is providing military and intelligence assistance to the South American nation, which is grappling with significant drug-related violence and has become a major cocaine exporter. This joint effort reflects a broader strategy to reassert U.S. influence and target transnational criminal groups, aiming for enhanced security in the region.
An alleged Guatemalan cocaine kingpin known as "Kraken" has been arrested in San Diego, and federal officials are offering up to $10 million for information that could lead to his conviction.
Axel Bladimir Montejo Saenz, 40, is accused of helping run a cocaine trafficking network with ties to narcoterrorist cartels.
Agents seized more than 5,500 kilograms of cocaine and $3.7 million linked to him during a yearslong investigation, according to the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Southern District of California.

The State Department also announced a separate reward of up to $10 million for information leading to the arrest or conviction of Walfre Donaldo Calderon-Calderon, 44, known as "El Teniente Jr." Prosecutors say he leads a drug trafficking operation in northwestern Guatemala near the Mexican border.
EXCLUSIVE: FBI EXTRADITIONS SOAR AS PATEL RAMPS UP FOREIGN OUTREACH, VOWS 'NO SANCTUARY'

Montejo Saenz pleaded not guilty Nov. 9 in federal court in San Diego. Members of the Homeland Security Task Force arrested him on charges that he conspired to distribute cocaine bound for the United States and to distribute cocaine aboard a vessel. He faces up to life in prison if convicted.

Prosecutors allege the operation moved cocaine through at least six countries, including Colombia, Ecuador, Guatemala and Mexico, and continued through November 2018. The U.S. Treasury Department sanctioned Montejo Saenz and the Los Huistas drug trafficking organization in 2022.
DRUG CARTEL KINGPIN AMONG TARGETS IN SWEEPING TRUMP CRACKDOWN ON ALLEGED MEXICAN CORRUPTION NETWORK

Federal reward posters show Axel Bladimir Montejo Saenz, Walfre Donaldo Calderon-Calderon and Eugenio Dario Molina-Lopez, from left. (Christian Chavez, File/U.S. Attorney's Office, Southern District of California)

Calderon-Calderon was indicted in 2019 on two cocaine conspiracy charges. Prosecutors said his indictment was unsealed in June 2025 after a deadly shootout involving Mexican law enforcement in Huehuetenango, Guatemala.
5 MEXICAN CARTEL BOSSES CHARGED IN WEAPONS, DRUG TRAFFICKING, TIMESHARE FRAUD SCHEMES, DOJ SAYS

Mexican police operate to close and secure a clandestine tunnel discovered at the border between Mexico and the United States, in Ciudad Juarez, Mexico, on January 13, 2025. (David Peinado/Anadolu via Getty Images)

title: Pentagon detains senior US Army officer accused of spying for Russians after UK arrest
summary: Lt. Col. Brandon Tyner was handed to U.S. military authorities after British counterterrorism police arrested him on suspicion of spying for Russia.
story: Fox News' Gillian Turner reports on a senior U.S. Army officer detained in Britain over suspected Russian espionage. Authorities are searching two locations as U.S. officials warn about insider threats.

A U.S. Army lieutenant colonel suspected of spying for Russia was handed over to U.S. military authorities Tuesday, days after British counterterrorism police arrested him on suspicion of violating national security laws.

Lt. Col. Brandon Tyner, 41, was arrested Nov. 10 near Gloucester, England, on suspicion of assisting a foreign intelligence service and obtaining or disclosing protected information under the United Kingdom's National Security Act.
British authorities previously said the allegations involved Russia, which the Kremlin denied any connection to.
SENIOR US ARMY SOLDIER ARRESTED IN UK ON SUSPICION OF SPYING FOR RUSSIA
A U.S. Army lieutenant colonel suspected of spying for Russia was handed over to U.S. military authorities Tuesday. (Sarah Crabill/Getty Images, File)
The Associated Press, citing a U.S. official, reported that Tyner had not provided information to Russia.
Tyner's transfer followed consultations between British prosecutors, the U.K. attorney general's office and U.S. authorities, according to London's Metropolitan Police.

Assistant Commissioner Laurence Taylor, head of U.K.'s Counter Terrorism Policing, said investigators referred the case to the Crown Prosecution Service, which consulted the attorney general's office and U.S. authorities before transferring the investigation.
RUSSIAN SPIES ORCHESTRATED $40K MURDER PLOT IN NATION’S CAPITAL, US ALLEGES
Lt. Col. Brandon Tyner, 41, was arrested by British authorities Nov. 10 near Gloucester, England. (Jacob King/PA Images via Getty Images, File)

"These are extremely serious allegations, and our collective response should send a strong message that we will act swiftly and robustly where we suspect this kind of espionage activity taking place," Taylor said in a statement.

FBI Director Kash Patel said the officer was in custody following a joint espionage investigation involving the FBI's Philadelphia field office, its London legal attaché office, British counterterrorism police, MI5, U.K. defense counterintelligence officials and U.S. Army Counterintelligence Command.

"This FBI has zero tolerance for anyone who betrays their oath to the United States or puts our national security at risk. That’s been demonstrated by the 167 counterintelligence and espionage arrests we’ve made over the last 21 months, a 53% increase," Patel said.
FBI Director Kash Patel said Tyner was in custody following a joint espionage investigation. (Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images, File)
Brig. Gen. Sean Stinchon, commander of U.S. Army Counterintelligence Command, warned service members against violating their oath to defend the Constitution.
"This case should serve as a stark warning to any service member suspected of violating the oath we all take to protect and defend the Constitution," Stinchon said.
Tyner was handed over to U.S. military authorities Tuesday. (J. David Ake/Getty Images, File)
Tyner, who previously deployed to Afghanistan, Iraq and Qatar, served as a senior human resources officer with NATO's Allied Rapid Reaction Corps at Imjin Barracks near Gloucester.
The British-led multinational force, which includes personnel from 20 nations, is designed to respond rapidly to military crises and operations.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov denied Russian involvement following Tyner's arrest, according to the AP.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov has denied Russian involvement following Tyner's arrest, according to the AP. (Sputnik/Sergey Guneev/Kremlin via Reuters, File)
"This arrest does not concern us in any way," Peskov said Nov. 11. "We don’t know what it’s connected to. We have nothing to do with this."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
British police said Tyner's arrest was unrelated to other ongoing counterterrorism investigations.

According to a Nov. 13 statement from the U.S. Army, Tyner entered active-duty service in January 2008 and deployed to Afghanistan from December 2013 to December 2014, Qatar from July 2016 to July 2017, and Iraq from December 2019 to July 2020.

title: Man legally named Captain America charged with murder after allegedly giving victim’s girlfriend chilling note
summary: A man legally named Captain America allegedly gave a woman a note saying her boyfriend was dead and demanding her money. Police later found the boyfriend dead inside a home.
story: Captain C. America is charged with murder after allegedly handing his co-worker’s girlfriend a note saying her boyfriend was dead and demanding money. She escaped, and police found Khanh Dinh dead in Peoria, Illinois, prosecutors say.
An Illinois woman giving her boyfriend’s co-worker a ride escaped after he allegedly handed her a chilling note saying her boyfriend was dead and demanding all her money.
Police then went to check on her boyfriend and found his body inside a Peoria home.
The passenger, Captain C. America, 34, was charged with first-degree murder in the death of Khanh Dinh, 63, according to Peoria County State’s Attorney Jodi M. Hoos’ office.
COWORKER ACCUSED OF SLASHING WOMAN’S THROAT DURING RIDE HOME, VICTIM ESCAPED MOVING CAR: POLICE

Captain C. America, right, was charged with first-degree murder in the death of Khanh Dinh, 63. The Peoria neighborhood where police found Dinh dead is pictured at left. (Google Maps/Tazewell County Sheriff's Office)
The encounter unfolded Friday, Nov. 13, when the woman was driving America, whom she knew because he worked with Dinh, prosecutors said.
"While in the car, the defendant handed her a note that said her boyfriend was dead and demanded all of her money," Hoos’ office said.
SUSPECT IN CUSTODY FOR ALLEGED MURDER OF COLLEGE STUDENT AFTER POLICE RELEASED EERIE SURVEILLANCE PHOTOS
The North Sheridan Road area in Peoria, Illinois, where police found 63-year-old Khanh Dinh dead during a welfare check Nov. 13, 2026. (Google Maps)
The woman managed to get away and call police in neighboring Tazewell County. Officers tracked down America and took him into custody shortly afterward, prosecutors said.
When officers removed him from a squad car, they found the note the woman had described.
GYPSY ROSE BLANCHARD’S PARTNER, KEN URKER, FOUND DEAD INSIDE HIS LOUISIANA HOME: SHERIFF
A Peoria Police Department patrol vehicle is pictured in this file image. (Peoria Police Department Facebook)
The woman's account led Peoria officers to a home on North Sheridan Road, where they arrived for a welfare check at about 7:14 p.m., police said.
Inside, they found Dinh dead. A preliminary autopsy indicated he died from blunt-force head trauma, according to prosecutors.
Hoos’ office announced the murder charge Monday. Authorities have not publicly identified a motive in statements released about the case.

America, whose full legal name is Captain Cautious America, was previously known as Mark Anderson. He changed his name about a decade ago because he hoped to run for political office and wanted to stand out on the ballot, according to The Peoria Journal Star.

title: Veteran pilot: Congress must act to update 'archaic' FAA tech that is 'putting Americans in danger'
summary: Retired Air Force pilot Buzz Patterson warns the FAA ground stop will happen again, blaming "tribal" politics for delaying a $50 billion modernization.
story: With holiday travel looming, retired Lt. Col. Buzz Patterson warns that 30 years of lawmakers ‘kicking the can’ have left pilots and passengers ‘in danger’ due to outdated tech, as evidenced by the FAA's recent nationwide ground stop.

Friday's historic FAA ground stop will not be the last, a retired Air Force veteran and commercial pilot warns, unless Congress takes action and provides funds for the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) to update what he calls a "broken" and "archaic" system that is "putting Americans in danger."

"It's time for both parties to step up and say our AT system is degraded, it's old," retired Lt. Col. Buzz Patterson, who carried the nuclear football for former President Bill Clinton and is a retired 16-year Delta Air Lines pilot, told Fox News Digital in an interview this week.

"We're putting Americans in danger when they get into an airplane, and we're putting the air crews in danger when they get into an airplane, if we continue to fly under archaic system, and that's what we're doing right now, it's archaic."
FORMER TOP FAA OFFICIAL WARNS OF 48-HOUR RECOVERY AFTER AGING TECH 'OVERWHELMED' AHEAD OF GROUND STOP
Too many administrations from both parties have "kicked the can" down the road on the complex and pricy overhaul, according to Patterson.

"We've dug a big hole here, and we're trying to dig out of it," he said. "It's not going to take place overnight. It's going to be a long, grinding, devoted effort, and I think it's time for our politicians to get on board and fix it."
TRUMP'S $50B AIR TRAFFIC CONTROL OVERHAUL FACES GOP PUSHBACK AFTER NATIONWIDE GROUND STOP

Patterson, who just moved to Nevada and bought a new home he is renovating, said the $50 billion cost now laid bare by Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy this weekend is akin to buying a home and immediately renovating it: Double down for the long-term benefits, if not savings.

"Our technology, I mean, we're still using floppy disks, for God's sakes, in some of our facilities," Patterson lamented. "Last time I was in a tower, they were still using paper scripts to show what airplanes were supposed to taxi next. This should all be automated ... I mean, this should be easy-peasy, and we've made it so difficult."

"We have way, way too much traffic to have an antiquated 1970s technology trying to drive our airplanes around the skies," he added, noting he "can't tell you the number of traffic avoidance calls I've gotten from ATC over the years that if I had not heard them, I probably would have hit somebody, or they would have hit me: so, it's essential."

Patterson, who now flies frequently as a commercial passenger himself, stressed that aviation safety transcends party lines and urged Washington to abandon what he called "tribal" politics to pass comprehensive modernization funding.

"It should be bipartisan, because I think if only one party pushes it, tries to push it through, it's not going to have success," he said. "I don't care what your political affiliation is: If you want to fly safely in our country, regardless of where you're going, or who you are, then you should be able to. And right now I think it's become tribal, where Democrats don't want to do anything that supports Trump or the FAA, and Trump's trying to get some stuff done."
BUTTIGIEG TAKES SWIPE AT TRUMP ADMINISTRATION AMID FAA FLIGHT CHAOS
Even President Donald Trump is "late" to conduct the overdue modernization, but he is also facing congressional gridlock, too, Patterson lamented.
"He's late, granted, he's late, but every other president's been late too – and so Duffy asking for $50 billion, I understand that is probably too little, too late, but it's a start."

While praising the dedication of current air traffic controllers and flight crews, Patterson warned that human skill can only compensate for technological limitations for so long. He noted that pilots still rely heavily on traditional voice radio relays rather than seamless, automated cockpit-to-ground data and weather integration, recalling numerous midair traffic avoidance calls from controllers over his career that prevented potential collisions.
BUTTIGIEG TRASHES DUFFY’S GROUND STOP RESPONSE, BUT HIS DOT FAILURES DOOM HIS 2028 BID
Patterson said weather radar, FAA and ATC can all be upgraded to improve airline safety, noting the recent Learjet 60 crash in Florida.

"You don't fly through that stuff, you just don't," Patterson said of the Learjet 60 crash that featured pilots seeking a direct route through a thunderstorm. "If you do, you're going realize why you don't, because it's going to bang the crap out of you if you get through it. And in this, in this case, they didn't get through it."
FLORIDA PLANE CRASH INVESTIGATORS SAY WEATHER CONDITIONS A 'MAJOR FOCUS,' PLANE MAY HAVE STARTED TO BREAK UP
Communications, weather radar, routers and copper to fiber optic wiring upgrades all go hand-in-hand for safety, according to Patterson.

"There is an interconnectivity between the National Weather Service and the FAA," he said. "There's an interconnectivity there that could be had if we upgrade our ATC capabilities, and we can somehow connect.

"And it shouldn't be too hard to connect the National Weather Service directly to the cockpit, and I think that's where we're going to have to go, and I think that's necessary. And it's also not ironic that the same day ATC went down, the National Weather Service went down. I'm not saying it was a coordinated activity. I'm just saying that is the basis of our aviation system.

"And if we don't have the most advanced air traffic control technology and the most advanced weather technology, then we, as the world's superpower, we have failed dramatically, and I think that's where we are."
DUFFY: INVESTIGATORS EXAMINING 2 ROUTERS AFTER NATIONWIDE FAA GROUND STOP, NO SIGNS OF FOREIGN CYBERATTACK
With peak holiday travel approaching, Patterson warned that systemic meltdowns will continue to disrupt the flying public until Washington commits to a sustained, multiyear overhaul.

"I'm going to say this won't be the last one; it's going happen again," Patterson said of the nationwide ground stop. "It's probably going happen on Thanksgiving Eve or Christmas Eve, and people are going to wonder why it's happening, and I'm going tell you why it's happening: It's because our infrastructure is broken, and our ATC needs help, and the FAA needs help."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"I think Sean Duffy is doing a phenomenal job," he concluded. "He's done more as a DOT guy than anybody that I can possibly remember since I started flying, and I think that what we're seeing right now is decades of neglect on the part of both parties. I mean, I'm not going to absolve Republicans either, because I'm looking at this as a pilot and as an American with a family, and I want to be able to fly my family safely around the country, and I don't feel safe putting my family on an airplane right now until we figure this out."

During a news conference Tuesday, federal officials declined to say who built or planted the explosive device, how many devices were involved or how powerful the device was. They also would not say whether anyone else may have been involved.

title: MICHAEL RUIZ: New York's gutted police unit was more than a protest squad
summary: Zohran Mamdani is dissolving the NYPD Strategic Response Group for a civilian-led de-escalation plan critics say will embolden criminals and terrorists.
story: Terrorists and other criminals choose the path of least resistance, says retired FBI agent James Gagliano, making NYC Mayor Zohran Mamdani's decision to disband a fast-acting deterrent group risky.

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani is dissolving the NYPD's Strategic Response Group — an elite tactical unit criticized for its handling of some left-wing protests while also responding to critical threats including a mass shooting at an office building last year and an attempted bombing attack on dueling demonstrations outside the city's mayoral residence.

"I think it’s one more step towards emboldening the criminals, emboldening the anarchists and emboldening the terrorists," said James Gagliano, a retired FBI supervisory special agent and Fox News contributor who spent years working alongside the NYPD.

Mamdani announced that the group will be dissolved at a news briefing early Monday. He had campaigned on the issue in part due to the unit's role in responding to organized protests — and riots — including those that exploded after George Floyd's death in 2020, demonstrations against Immigration and Customs Enforcement and Israel's war with Palestinian Hamas terrorists.
MAMDANI GUTS ELITE NYPD TACTICAL UNIT, BACKS 'CIVILIAN-LED APPROACH' TO RESPONDING TO PROTESTS

A looter takes an armful of clothing out of a store with a broken window in Manhattan, New York on June 1, 2020, following protests in the aftermath of the death of George Floyd in Minnesota. (J. Conrad Williams Jr./Newsday via Getty Images)

"New Yorkers exercising their constitutional right to protest should not be met with the same police response as a terrorism threat," Mamdani told reporters in a news briefing announcing the changes. "We are establishing a new, civilian-led approach that prioritizes dialogue, engagement and de-escalation."

Kettling — The SRG was involved in breaking up a protest using the so-called kettling technique, which involves surrounding and corralling marchers to control their movements. A June 4, 2020, incident cost city taxpayers millions after arrestees filed a lawsuit. Some related protests involved rioting, looting and vandalism and caused an estimated $1 billion to $2 billion across the country.Anti-Israel protests at Columbia University — The SRG was involved in the NYPD's response after agitators occupied the school's Hamilton Hall building.NFL Headquarters mass shooting — The SRG helped sweep floor-by-floor after a gunman opened fire in a Park Avenue office building, killing four.ICE protests — SRG officers have arrested demonstrators at anti-immigration enforcement protests this year.Gracie Mansion bombing — The SRG responded after two alleged ISIS supporters attempted to blow up a protest outside the city's mayoral residence, according to federal prosecutors. Their bombs failed to detonate, and NYPD Chief Aaron Edwards and Sgt. Luis Navarro tackled them at the scene.

Kettling — The SRG was involved in breaking up a protest using the so-called kettling technique, which involves surrounding and corralling marchers to control their movements. A June 4, 2020, incident cost city taxpayers millions after arrestees filed a lawsuit. Some related protests involved rioting, looting and vandalism and caused an estimated $1 billion to $2 billion across the country.
Anti-Israel protests at Columbia University — The SRG was involved in the NYPD's response after agitators occupied the school's Hamilton Hall building.
NFL Headquarters mass shooting — The SRG helped sweep floor-by-floor after a gunman opened fire in a Park Avenue office building, killing four.
ICE protests — SRG officers have arrested demonstrators at anti-immigration enforcement protests this year.

Gracie Mansion bombing — The SRG responded after two alleged ISIS supporters attempted to blow up a protest outside the city's mayoral residence, according to federal prosecutors. Their bombs failed to detonate, and NYPD Chief Aaron Edwards and Sgt. Luis Navarro tackled them at the scene.

Emir Balat flees after throwing a homemade explosive device towards police as NYPD Chief Aaron Edwards and Sgt. Luis Navarro take action during a protest in front of Gracie Mansion, New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani's official residence, in New York on March 7, 2026. (CHARLY TRIBALLEAU/AFP via Getty Images)

The mayor plans to replace the SRG with several new programs by next spring. First is an unarmed Community Dialogue and De-escalation Division (CDDD). This civilian team won't have arrest authority. It will work with a new First Amendment Support Team (FAST), consisting of 30 uniformed officers with specialized training in communication and de-escalation, according to Mamdani's office.

Lastly, his overhaul includes the creation of a new Patrol Support Division consisting of officers who will be trained in crowd control but spend most of their time on patrol duties. Counterterrorism duties will be consolidated in the NYPD's Intelligence and Counterterrorism Bureau.
MAMDANI PREPARES TO FULFILL PROMISE TO AXE NYPD UNIT RESPONSIBLE FOR CONTROLLING PROTEST VIOLENCE
Emir Balat was tackled by a law enforcement officer after he allegedly threw a bomb. (FNTV)

But the SRG has a varied role. While members are on hand for crowd control at large demonstrations, they also protect the protesters from outside threats. And they are positioned at other events involving large crowds, including the city's many parades, the iconic New Year's ball drop and other large events that take place every year.
"What the Strategic Response Group was designed to do was to be a highly mobile, well-trained, well-equipped group, like a senior SWAT team," Gagliano told Fox News Digital.
Unlike the NYPD's SWAT team, known as its Emergency Services Unit, the SRG also has a public-facing role, Gagliano said.
"Part of that was being on the front lines, the deterrent effect, and I think that's something that we're losing as well," he said.
ALLEGED ISIS-INSPIRED TERROR SUSPECTS LEFT FEDS ‘VOLUMINOUS’ DIGITAL TRAIL, FAMILY BREAKS DOWN IN TEARS

This image from surveillance video obtained by The Associated Press shows Shane Tamura outside a Manhattan office building on Monday, July 28, 2025. Tamura killed himself and four others in an office building housing the NFL headquarters, and the city's medical examiner later said his brain showed "unambiguous" signs of chronic traumatic encephalopathy, also known as CTE. (AP)
Terrorists and other criminals targeting public events tend to pick soft targets and the path of least resistance, he added.
"The Strategic Response Group was a deterrent, and it probably caused some people to decide, ‘Yeah, I’m not gonna try that. I’m not gonna do that,'" he said.
POLICE GROUPS CONDEMN MAMDANI OVER AXING ELITE NYPD UNIT
The unit has also been deployed around large public events with the goal of responding rapidly when needed, Gagliano said.

"The uniform folks are there for a deterrent effect," he said. "The uniform folks kept in abeyance like SRG, that are rolled out quickly and mobilized and strategically placed so that they can get to different spots very quickly."
Students and others demonstrate during a protest outside the gates to the Columbia University main campus in New York City on April 21. (Reuters/Ryan Murphy)
MAMDANI’S FIRST 100-PLUS DAYS: FAR-LEFT MAYOR FLUNKS A KEY LEADERSHIP TEST
Vincent J. Vallelong, president of the NYPD Sergeants Benevolent Association, brought up the failed Gracie Mansion bombing Monday.

"When an alleged terrorist attack threatened lives near Gracie Mansion, NYPD Sgt. Luis Navarro and Chief Aaron Edwards ran toward danger," Vallelong said in a statement. "Their decisive actions should be a lesson for Mayor Mamdani."
HAMAS, HEZBOLLAH FLAGS FLY AT ANTI-ISRAEL PROTEST MINUTES AFTER MAMDANI CONDEMNS TERROR PLOT AGAINST JEWS

Two allegedly ISIS-inspired men, Emir Balat and Ibrahim Kayumi, were arrested after federal prosecutors say they threw improvised explosive devices at a crowd outside the mayor's home and at a group of police as left- and right-wing protesters demonstrated across from one another. The bombs failed to explode.
Protesters are arrested on Park Avenue in New York City, June 5, 2020, as they defy the 8 p.m. curfew while protesting the death of George Floyd. (TIMOTHY A. CLARY/AFP via Getty Images)
According to federal prosecutors, Balat allegedly told police he had wanted the attack to be "bigger" than the Boston Marathon Bombing, which killed three and injured hundreds in 2013.
MAMDANI UNVEILS SWEEPING NYPD USE-OF-FORCE REVIEW, BUT STOPS SHORT OF FULFILLING KEY CAMPAIGN PROMISES
The SRG also deployed to help search for the gunman floor-by-floor after the mass shooting inside a Manhattan office building that houses the NFL’s headquarters on Park Avenue.
SEND US A TIP

Shattered glass lies in front of a looted souvenir and electronics shop near Times Square after a night of protests and vandalism over the death of George Floyd early June 2, 2020, in New York City. (John Moore/Getty Images)
Vallelong scoffed at the idea that the unarmed CDDD will protect the public from similar violent plots.

"Unarmed civilians cannot talk a determined attacker out of detonating a bomb," he said. "I fear this approach will embolden violent agitators to infiltrate peaceful demonstrations, putting protesters, police and bystanders at risk."
LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST
People loot a store during demonstrations over the death of George Floyd by a Minneapolis police officer on June 1, 2020, in New York. (Bryan R. Smith / AFP)
Upcoming events like the 100th Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade and New Year's ball drop will not be impacted since the changes aren't slated to go into effect until spring 2027, he said.

NYPD Commissioner Jessica Tisch said in a statement that the restructuring would not "diminish the NYPD’s ability to protect New Yorkers, or that put our officers in a position where they lack the resources necessary to confront a serious threat."

title: Democratic judge under fire for releasing violent offenders calls bail law a ‘direct assault’ on rights
summary: Judge David Carpenter called Alabama’s Aniah’s Law a ‘direct assault’ on constitutional rights, citing defendants’ presumption of innocence.
story: Birmingham Mayor Randall Woodfin tells community that "It’s your time to step up and we need you." (Credit: WBMA)

A Democratic Alabama judge facing mounting scrutiny over past decisions to release violent offenders is criticizing a state law that allows defendants charged with certain violent crimes to be denied bail.

Circuit Court Judge David Carpenter called Alabama’s Aniah’s Law a direct assault on constitutional rights, arguing that defendants should not be held indefinitely based solely on criminal charges, citing the constitutional presumption of innocence.
In a social media post, Carpenter argued that critics of government overreach involving license plate cameras, such as Flock cameras, are not equally concerned about expanded pretrial detention laws.

"Can someone explain to me why the people who are so alarmed that a flock camera might spot their car on a public road, and they call that government overreach, are silent on the fact that voters across the country keep overwhelmingly passing new laws to empower the government to hold you in jail indefinitely on the basis of a charge only," Carpenter said.
THE SURVEILLANCE CAMERA ON YOUR STREET CORNER: LAWFUL SPYING OR CONSTITUTIONALLY PROBLEMATIC?

Damien McDaniel, 22, is connected to more than a dozen murders in the Birmingham, Alabama, area since July 2023, according to city police. Carpenter approved a plea deal for McDaniel before his alleged shooting spree left 18 dead.  (Alabama Department of Corrections / Birmingham Police Department)

"These laws, like Alabama’s Aniah’s Law, are a direct assault on the Constitutional guarantee of the presumption of innocence. But no one is talking about this at all, much less expressing the hysteria associated with having a camera see a license plate," he said.

Although Aniah’s Law was originally passed in 2022, Alabama voters approved a major constitutional amendment this year expanding the law to cover additional offenses. The expansion added attempted murder, solicitation or conspiracy to commit murder, and discharging a firearm or explosives into an occupied dwelling, building or vehicle.
"We are all one accusation away from being a criminal defendant," Carpenter said in a post on Facebook.
WHITE HOUSE CALLS DC POLICIES 'INSANITY' AFTER 19-YEAR-OLD GUNMAN GETS PROBATION IN SHOOTING

Carpenter has faced controversy over several judicial decisions over the years. Local outlet 1819 News reported that he previously described himself online as a "far left, liberal, progressive, democratic socialist."

In April 2023, Carpenter approved a plea deal for Damien McDaniel, who was arrested in 2019 for shooting two people in a car when he was 17 years old, 1819 News reported. After being released from jail, McDaniel allegedly went on a 14-month shooting spree across Alabama, killing 18 people and injuring more than 30 others.
Carpenter approved a plea deal for Damien McDaniel, 22, who was later linked to multiple shootings over 14 months. (Birmingham Police Department / WBRC)

Carpenter also granted bond to Raukeem Cunningham in connection with the 2022 shooting death of a teenage girl, the outlet reported. While out on bond, Cunningham was arrested and charged with fatally shooting three people at a Bessemer gas station in 2024, prompting the revocation of his original bond.

In addition, Carpenter reportedly dismissed a 2015 rape charge against Fredrick Terrenda Hampton in 2019, according to reports. The dismissal came just two days before Hampton met Paighton Houston, who later disappeared. Her body was found buried behind a home after she died of an accidental overdose.
CONVICTED SERIAL RAPIST ORIGINALLY SENTENCED TO 124 YEARS WALKS FREE AFTER 20, SPARKING OUTRAGE

Frederick Hampton, 50, was wanted in the disappearance of Paighton Houston, left, last seen leaving a Birmingham, Alabama, bar on Dec. 30. Her body was found two weeks later.  (Jefferson County Sheriff's Office)
Hampton pleaded guilty to abuse of a corpse in connection with Houston’s death, and Carpenter gave him a 20-year split sentence with only three years to serve in custody, the outlet said.

Houston’s mother ultimately asked Alabama Attorney General Steve Marshall to investigate Carpenter over his decision to release Hampton, whom critics described as a repeat sex offender.During his campaign for judicial office, Carpenter said one of his major goals was to "reform the criminal justice system in Alabama."
"If elected, I will work to reduce the number of repeat offenders while addressing the expensive problem of prison overcrowding in Alabama," he said.

title: Illegal alien accused of attempted murder at large after Rikers release despite ICE detainer: DHS
summary: Delon Raymond Jaundoo, a Guyanese citizen in the United States illegally, was freed from Rikers Island despite an ICE detainer, according to DHS.
story: NYC ICE official Kenneth Genalo blasts Mayor Zohran Mamdani and sanctuary policies, warning they force agents into dangerous street arrests and put public safety at risk.

A Guyanese citizen living in the United States illegally remains at large after being released from custody in New York City earlier this month, despite facing multiple violent felony charges and an active federal immigration detainer, according to the Department of Homeland Security (DHS).

DHS officials stated that Delon Raymond Jaundoo was arrested in Brooklyn on charges including attempted murder, first- and second-degree assault, criminal use of a firearm, and multiple counts of criminal possession of a loaded weapon.
His prior criminal record also includes an arrest for third-degree assault.

U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) lodged an immigration detainer for Jaundoo on April 29, which the New York City Department of Correction declined to honor, allowing him to be released from Rikers Island.
MANHUNT UNDERWAY FOR VIOLENT ILLEGAL IMMIGRANT WHO WAS RELEASED UNDER NYC SANCTUARY POLICIES

Delon Raymond Jaundoo, an illegal immigrant from Guyana, has multiple violent crime arrest, including for attempted murder. He remains at large after he was released from Rikers Island Jail in New York City under the city's sanctuary policies, the Department of Homeland Security said. (Department of Homeland Security; Getty Images)

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin criticized New York’s sanctuary policies following the release, arguing that state and local laws prevent cooperation with federal immigration authorities even in cases involving violent offenses.
Jaundoo lawfully entered the country during the Obama administration but overstayed his authorized stay, which expired in January 2015, according to DHS.

"Despite these violent charges, sanctuary politicians in New York refused to honor ICE’s detainer and released this criminal back onto the streets to put more American lives in danger," Mullin said in a statement. "Under Governor Kathy Hochul, New York has become a hotbed of illegal alien crime."
DHS SECRETARY BASHES NEW YORK LEADERSHIP AFTER ANNOUNCING THOUSANDS OF ARRESTS IN SWEEPING OPERATION

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani signs executive orders with campaign volunteers during an appearance at Grand Army Plaza in Brooklyn on January 2, 2026, in New York City. (Spencer Platt/Getty Images)
"The sooner we put an end to these reckless sanctuary policies, the sooner we can all work together to make America safe again," he added.
Jaundoo's release comes amid ongoing restrictions on local cooperation with federal immigration enforcement.
HOCHUL BOASTS 'I JUST BANNED IT' AS NEW YORK OUTLAWS LOCAL POLICE PARTNERSHIPS WITH ICE

Upon taking office, New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani signed an executive order limiting city coordination with ICE, and a state law signed by Gov. Kathy Hochul took effect in August barring local authorities from cooperating with federal immigration officials.

DHS stated that several other illegal immigrants arrested for or convicted of violent crimes, including murder, arson, assault, and rape, have similarly been released from custody under the state's current policies.

"Governor Hochul has been clear: New York State is not and never will be a sanctuary for violent criminals," a spokesperson for Hochul told Fox News Digital. "By law, New York State always notifies federal immigration enforcement of any non-citizen serving a State prison sentence. Any assertion otherwise is a blatant mischaracterization of the facts meant to distract from the cruelty and violence we’ve seen from Secretary Mullin’s ICE agents."

title: United Airlines says technology issue resolved after ‘widespread system outage’
summary: United Airlines flights were stuck on tarmacs as pilots reported a companywide IT issue preventing takeoff data, days after the nationwide FAA ground stop.
story: Fox News contributor Jonathan Turley joins ‘Special Report’ to describe his firsthand experience aboard a grounded aircraft as a nationwide FAA ground stop disrupts air travel across the country. Turley discusses the uncertainty facing stranded passengers, frustration over limited communication and the challenges travelers face as they await updates on when flights can resume.
United Airlines said Monday it resolved a technology issue that delayed departing flights, marking another disruption for travelers just days after a nationwide FAA ground stop.

"We have resolved a technology issue that delayed flight departures. While some flights were delayed, there was no impact on flights in progress, or on United Express flights," United Media Relations told Fox News Digital.
"There is no indication that this was a cybersecurity-related issue," the airline added.
Earlier Monday, passengers reported being unable to take off, with one saying their flight was returning to the gate because the crew could not obtain performance data needed for departure.
FORMER TOP FAA OFFICIAL WARNS OF 48-HOUR RECOVERY AFTER AGING TECH 'OVERWHELMED' AHEAD OF GROUND STOP
United initially acknowledged a widespread outage in a response to a passenger on X.
"We're aware of the widespread system outage, and our teams are working hard to get things back up and running as soon as possible," United’s official X account wrote in response to a passenger.
The airline apologized and urged travelers to monitor their flight status through the United app or its website. Its response did not identify the cause or provide an estimated restoration time.
One passenger reported being stuck on the tarmac, saying crews could not clear planes for takeoff because they could not connect to a weight system.
Another social media user said their flight was returning to the gate after the pilot announced a company wide IT issue that left the crew "unable to get performance data for takeoff."
"Pilot just announced ALL of United Airlines has a company wide IT issue," the user wrote. "We’re going back to the gate."
Another passenger reported a similar announcement while waiting for departure.
"Waiting to take off, on the runway, and the pilot just said we can’t take off because United is experiencing a system-wide computer outage," the user wrote.
AMERICA HITS A TECH WALL AS OUTAGES CRIPPLE EMAIL, GROUND FLIGHTS AND DISRUPT MAJOR BANKS
A United Airlines Boeing 737 MAX aircraft prepares for takeoff at Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport in Arlington, Virginia, on July 10, 2025. (Saul Loeb/AFP via Getty Images)
The X account @theATCapp also posted that it was receiving reports of a systemwide IT outage affecting the airline.
United’s response acknowledged a widespread outage but did not confirm the passengers’ descriptions of the affected systems. The number of flights and airports affected was not immediately clear.
Flight-tracking service Flightradar24 reported that United’s mainline departures were beginning to resume.
"We are seeing mainline departures resuming in the last few minutes," the service posted on X.

At Los Angeles International Airport, Fox News correspondent Max Gorden spoke with several passengers at the United counter who were able to check in for their flights. However, an agent showed Gorden her United mobile device, which appeared to be experiencing technical problems.

The outage comes after a telecommunications failure prompted the Federal Aviation Administration to issue a nationwide ground stop Friday, Nov. 13. The restriction was later lifted, but airlines faced lingering delays and cancellations as they worked to restore their schedules.

Following Friday’s ground stop, United CEO Scott Kirby praised the FAA’s decision to halt flights and thanked employees and customers for their patience. He also called for better technology and full staffing to help prevent future outages.

Scott Kirby, chief executive officer at United Airlines Holdings Inc., during a Bloomberg Television interview at Newark Liberty International Airport (EWR) in Newark, New Jersey, US, on Tuesday, Aug. 25, 2026.  (Michael Nagle/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

Kirby said he had spoken directly with Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy, FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford and aviation leaders from both parties in Congress about the impact on United’s passengers and employees.
"This moment must be a call to action," Kirby said in a statement shared with Fox News Digital.
United Airlines planes sit parked at the gate at San Francisco International Airport on April 24, 2025, in San Francisco, California. (Justin Sullivan/Getty Images)
"It is critical for safety, our passengers, and our economy that we fix our nation’s Air Traffic Control system now."
Kirby said lawmakers from both parties were committed to modernizing the system while holding the FAA accountable.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
There was no immediate confirmation that United’s outage Monday was connected to Friday’s FAA disruption.
This is a developing story. Please check back for updates.

title: TIMELINE: America hits a tech wall as outages cripple email, ground flights and disrupt major banks
summary: America’s tech troubles stretched into a sixth day as Apple, the National Weather Service and NSA reported disruptions following Microsoft, FAA, Workday and Chase issues.
story: State Secretary Marco Rubio addresses a string of major technology outages affecting companies and federal agencies across the U.S.

America’s technology troubles stretched into a sixth day Tuesday, with disruptions affecting Apple, Marriott and federal systems, but Secretary of State Marco Rubio said officials had found "zero evidence" tying the recent U.S. outages together or to malicious actors.
"In essence, the Microsoft incident has nothing to do with what we saw with the FAA. The FAA has nothing to do with what we saw with the banks a few days ago," Rubio told reporters Tuesday.
Rubio said there was no evidence linking those incidents to hackers, criminals, another nation-state or other malign actors.

Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton offered a similar assessment on FOX Business’ "The Claman Countdown," pointing to institutions installing security patches and upgrading systems, with some systems failing to restart or communicate as expected.
"We do not see the indicia of a coordinated cyber attack," Clayton said. "And we do not see the indicia of state-sponsored activity here."
PERPETUAL PARALYSIS: WHY EVERYTHING IS GRINDING TO A HALT
Chase Bank in Manhattan, New York City on July 16th, 2024. (Beata Zawrzel/NurPhoto via Getty Images)

Apple later listed all consumer services as operating normally, Marriott said its sign-in problem was resolved and the National Weather Service said its maintenance-related issues had ended. The NSA said its mission-critical capabilities remained fully operational.
Here is a timeline of the technology turmoil:
4 CRITICAL TRAVEL ISSUES FOR THOSE DELAYED AND DISRUPTED BY FAA NATIONWIDE GROUND STOP
A widespread Microsoft 365 outage disrupted Outlook, Teams and other services, leaving users struggling to access email and other functions.

The incident began Thursday and lasted nearly 24 hours, with service restored Friday morning, according to Microsoft’s preliminary incident report. Email suffered the most significant disruption, while the impact on other services varied.
Microsoft suffered a major outage that lasted nearly 24 hours. (Microsoft)
Microsoft executive Charles Lamanna attributed the failure to a combination of a previously undetected software defect, increased traffic and reduced server capacity.
Microsoft says more than 430 million people use its Microsoft 365 apps. That figure represents the platform’s user base, rather than a confirmed tally of people affected.
A person looks at a departures board showing delays and cancellations at LaGuardia airport on November 13, 2026 in the Queens borough of New York City. (Adam Gray/Getty Images)
The FAA halted departures nationwide for nearly five hours Friday after technical problems destabilized aircraft communications and radar feeds.
The disruption began around 3:30 p.m. Eastern, with air traffic resuming at 8:15 p.m., according to the agency.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said the problems began when contractor L3Harris Technologies Inc. was replacing old copper wiring with fiber wiring in the air traffic control system, causing a system overload.
BUTTIGIEG TAKES SWIPE AT TRUMP ADMINISTRATION AMID FAA FLIGHT CHAOS

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy speaks during a press briefing at Department of Transportation headquarters on Nov. 14, 2026, in Washington, D.C. The briefing followed a nationwide communications outage that grounded flights across the United States the previous day. (Aaron Schwartz / AFP via Getty Images)
The work led to intermittent communications and radar gaps. Duffy said officials were investigating whether contractor incompetence or a faulty router was responsible.
"Our contractor didn’t meet the moment or the equipment didn’t meet the moment," Duffy said.
NBA AND NHL TEAMS BATTLE DELAYS AS NATIONWIDE FAA GROUND STOP DISRUPTS WEEKEND SPORTS TRAVEL

A flight schedule board is displayed at Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport in Arlington, Va., after the Federal Aviation Administration grounded flights nationwide on Saturday, Nov. 14, 2026. (AP Photo/Tom Brenner)
Some radio frequencies and radar feeds remained operational, and every aircraft landed safely, according to the FAA.
Operators canceled approximately 12,462 flights Friday, including 9,082 by major airlines, the FAA said, while cautioning that not all cancellations were directly caused by the ground stop.
The agency said it had no indication of a cyberattack.
UPDATED START TIMES FOR COLLEGE FOOTBALL GAMES AFFECTED BY FAA GROUND STOP, BROKEN DOWN BY CONFERENCE
Workday, whose payroll and human resources software is used by millions of employees, experienced a widespread outage Friday, a day after Microsoft’s disruption.

The platform manages services for about 11,500 companies, including Walmart, Target, Netflix, Southwest Airlines and PNC Bank. Its clients also include government agencies and NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory, though not all customers reported outages.
"Workday is currently unavailable," a message shown to users said. "We are experiencing a service interruption. Your service will be restored as quickly as possible."
Outage-tracking website Downdetector recorded a spike of nearly 3,000 reports shortly after 5 p.m. Friday.

"Some of our customers are experiencing a service disruption, and we’re working urgently to investigate and resolve the issue," a Workday spokesperson told Fox News. "We sincerely apologize for the challenges this is causing impacted customers."
Customers at Chase, Bank of America and Wells Fargo reported online banking difficulties Monday, adding banking to the list of everyday services hit by technology trouble.

Chase initially said some transactions were taking longer than usual but customers retained access to their accounts and money. The bank later confirmed to Fox News that transactions were processing normally.
The incident was traced to a software release JPMorgan Chase rolled out earlier Monday that affected a subset of its systems. There was no indication of malicious or external cyber activity.
The impact was limited to JPMorgan Chase and transactions at other financial institutions in which JPMorgan Chase was a party.
Bank branch as they experience disruptions due to the banking technology outage.  (Ava Palschakov for Fox News Digital)
JPMorgan Chase initially said systems were coming back online and the incident was not malicious.

"Bank of America systems have been operating normally today. Clients experiencing delays with other providers may wish to contact them directly for the latest information," Bank of America said in a statement.
The extent and causes of the reported problems at the other banks were not immediately clear.
Zelle told FOX Business its payment network was operating normally, but problems at financial institutions could be delaying payments for some customers.

"Zelle is not down. Zelle is operating as it should," the company said. "Consumers use Zelle through participating banks and credit unions, which manage their accounts and hold their funds. Consumers do not have a separate Zelle account, and Zelle does not hold consumer funds."
"An issue at the financial institutions may be delaying Zelle payments for some of their customers. Please contact them directly," Zelle added.
Routine network maintenance caused technical problems for some users of National Weather Service websites and data services Tuesday morning, the agency said.
The disruption lasted from 11:05 a.m. to 11:45 a.m. Eastern and has been resolved. NOAA Weather Radio and NOAAPort were not affected.
"As always, NWS advises everyone to have multiple ways of receiving critical, time-sensitive warnings," the agency said in a statement.
Apple said an internal update caused outages Tuesday morning, with its system status page later showing disruptions affecting the App Store, Apple Music and AppleCare.

"Many of our systems are back up and running after an internal update caused some outages this morning. We’re working to get the remaining systems online as soon as possible," an Apple spokesperson said in a statement.
Customers at Apple's Fifth Avenue store in New York City on Sept. 18, 2026.  (Michael Nagle/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
Users also reported Apple Pay problems on outage-tracking website Downdetector, though Apple’s status page did not list an Apple Pay issue at the time.
The page later listed the App Store and Apple Music as back online as service statuses continued to change.
The National Security Agency said scheduled routine maintenance temporarily degraded some internal systems Tuesday, while its mission-critical capabilities remained fully operational.

"The National Security Agency experienced temporary degradation during scheduled routine maintenance. While some internal systems were affected, mission-critical capabilities remain fully operational and our ability to defend national security continues," the agency said in a statement.
"NSA's infrastructure is designed with multiple layers of redundancy to maintain operations during planned maintenance or unexpected events," the agency added.
Marriott International is ending its long-time Pepsi partnership and switching to Coca-Cola. (iStock)

Marriott said it resolved a technical problem that temporarily prevented travelers from signing in to Marriott.com and the Marriott Bonvoy app. A spokesperson told Fox News Digital that teams worked with technology partners to restore access and that a review found no indication the disruption was cybersecurity-related.

The FAA paused new router installations while investigating Friday’s ground stop, FOX Business confirmed. Officials traced the disruption to routers in Arkansas and Texas, isolating them to stabilize the network and disabling the broadcasting function on similar equipment.

FAA Administrator Brian Bedford called speculation that AI caused the shutdown "completely unfounded." Duffy said identifying the faulty router took longer than he wanted and demanded better performance from contractor L3Harris. Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., said oversight hearings would follow.

title: Two public safety officers shot at NYC housing complex; suspect dead
summary: Two Co-op City security guards were shot at a New York City housing complex before the suspect barricaded himself in an apartment, police said.
story: Multiple police groups condemned NYC Mayor Zohran Mamdani's order disbanding an elite unit on Monday.
Two public safety officers at a New York City housing complex were shot Monday before the suspect barricaded himself inside an apartment and took his own life, police said.
New York Police Department (NYPD) officers responded to a wellness check at a building in the Co-op City complex just before 11: 45 a.m., the NYPD told Fox News Digital.
Upon arriving at the scene, officers found two Co-op City public safety officers suffering from gunshot wounds.
TWO POLICE OFFICERS SHOT, SUSPECT 'ACTIVELY FIRING AT POLICE' IN SYRACUSE STANDOFF LASTING HOURS: REPORT

Police said two public safety officers checking on a resident at the Co-op City housing complex in the Bronx section of New York City were shot and wounded by a gunman who then barricaded himself in an apartment Monday. (Barry Williams)
Both were transported to a local hospital in stable condition.
The suspected shooter had barricaded himself inside a nearby apartment. When NYPD officers breached the unit, they found him dead from an apparent self-inflicted gunshot wound, according to police.
NYPD OFFICERS FATALLY SHOOT MAN ARMED WITH BUTCHER KNIFE AFTER HE ADVANCED TOWARD COPS: POLICE
Police arrive at the scene of the shooting at the Co-op City housing complex in the Bronx on Monday, Nov. 16, 2026. (Barry Williams)
Investigators recovered a firearm at the scene. No NYPD officers were injured during the incident, and an investigation remains ongoing.

The suspect was found dead, authorities said. (Barry Williams)
