title: Rare anti-government protests erupt in Iran over workers' deaths
summary: Hundreds of Iranians chanted "Death to the dictator!" in Abdanan after a bus crash killed 13 oil refinery employees, with at least seven people arrested.
story: Iranian protesters in the southern Iranian town of Abdanan chant 'death to the dictators!" during a protest after 13 oil refinery workers were killed in a road accident over the weekend. Credit: The Associated Press.

Hundreds of Iranians took to the streets chanting "Death to the dictator!" and other anti-government messages in the wake of a deadly bus crash over the weekend that killed 13 employees of an oil refinery company, reports said.

The rare display of anti-government anger unfolded Tuesday in Abdanan, a city in western Iran near the country's border with Iraq. Demonstrators called for the resignation of company officials blamed for the accident.

"Those who seek to exploit this incident to disrupt public order and inflame people’s emotions will be dealt with decisively," local prosecutor Amrollah Meysaei was quoted by Iran's Mizan news agency as saying, according to Radio Free Europe.

The outlet, citing Iran's Fars news agency, also reported that an estimated 1,000 people took part in the protests, making them the largest demonstrations since mass unrest swept across Iran at the beginning of this year. Some of the protesters reportedly tried to damage public property.
IRAN LAUNCHES DRONE ASSAULT ON KUWAIT AFTER US STRIKE ON IRGC MISSILE SITE
Protesters are seen marching through the streets of Abdanan, Iran, on Tuesday, Nov. 17, 2026. (UGC via AP)
A video verified by The Associated Press showed protesters chanting "Death to the dictator!"
A video shared by HRANA, a rights group based outside Iran, also showed a crowd of protesters marching through the center of Abdanan, calling for accountability for the road accident.
The Hengaw Organization for Human Rights said at least seven people were arrested in Abdanan after Tuesday's protests.
Two were later released, including a 15-year-old boy, Hengaw said.
LEAKED IRAN REPORT FINDS RECORD PUBLIC ANGER AS REGIME FOCUSES ON HOLDING POWER
People gather during a protest on Jan. 8, 2026, in Tehran, Iran. (Getty Images)
In January, Iran witnessed some of the largest anti-government protests since the 1979 Islamic Revolution and Abdanan was a hotspot of unrest.
Security forces shot thousands of protesters in the streets and arrested thousands more during those demonstrations.
Iranians block a street while gathering during a protest in Tehran, Iran, on Jan. 9. (MAHSA / Middle East Images/AFP via Getty Images)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
In late July, small protests broke out in the central city of Isfahan ahead of the public hanging of two protesters.
The Associated Press contributed to this report.
Greg Norman is a reporter at Fox News Digital.

title: Protesters call for regime change in Iran following deadly crash that killed 13 oil and gas workers
summary: Hundreds take to the streets in western Iran after 13 oil workers are killed, with demonstrations escalating into political protests against Tehran's leadership.
story: Footage from western Iran shows demonstrators taking to the streets, chanting against the Islamic Republic and calling for the return of the Pahlavi monarchy after a crash killed 13 oil and gas workers.

Hundreds of protesters poured into the streets of western Iran on Tuesday following a deadly bus crash that killed 13 oil and gas workers, with demonstrations quickly escalating into anti-government chants with some protesters calling for the return of the Pahlavi monarchy.

The unrest erupted in Abdanan, a city in Iran's Ilam province near the Iraqi border, where residents initially gathered to demand accountability for Saturday's fatal accident before turning their anger toward the Islamic Republic's leadership.
Videos obtained by Fox News Digital showed large crowds marching through the streets, chanting "Death to the dictator!"
IRANIAN PROTESTER HANGED HOURS AFTER MARRYING HIS IMPRISONED FIANCÉE OVER JAIL PHONE LINE
In this photo obtained by The Associated Press, protesters chant slogans during an anti-government protest in Tehran, Iran, Thursday, Jan. 8, 2026. (UGC via AP)

Iranian-American journalist and foreign policy analyst Lisa Daftari said the demonstrations underscore the deeper political tensions facing Tehran. "Abdanan is a reminder that the Islamic Republic sits on top of a dormant volcano," Daftari told Fox News Digital. "These uprisings start with different catalysts, and in this case it was a local grievance, but they always arrive at the same conclusion."
"The slogans we hear are ‘Death to the Dictator’ and ‘Javid Shah,’ not complaints about a policy. They are an indictment of the entire system, top to bottom," she said.
New reports Wednesday indicated that Iranian security forces arrested at least seven people, including a 15-year-old boy, during the unrest in Abdanan.

The Hengaw Organization for Human Rights said two detainees had been released, but the whereabouts of five others remained unknown. The Kurdistan Human Rights Network separately reported that security forces fired tear gas at demonstrators and that internet access was disrupted during the crackdown.

Iran's Revolutionary Guard-affiliated Fars news agency acknowledged the demonstrations, reporting that approximately 200 to 300 people initially gathered in Abdanan's Vali-e Asr Square before the crowd grew to roughly 1,000.

Fars reported that the slogans initially focused on the deadly accident but subsequently took on a political character. Police were deployed as protesters moved into surrounding streets, according to AFP's Nov. 17 report.
ONE GLARING ISSUE GOES UNADDRESSED IN UN CHIEF'S HIGH-STAKES TALKS WITH IRAN'S PRESIDENT

Reza Pahlavi, the exiled crown prince of Iran, said the Islamic Republic is "crumbling" and called for a democratic transition following recent U.S. and Israeli military strikes. (Paul Morigi/Getty Images)

The protests followed Saturday's overturning of a bus transporting workers from the Dehloran gas processing project. Thirteen people were killed and more than a dozen injured, according to Iranian media reports.

Euronews Persian reported on Nov. 17 that provincial traffic police identified driver negligence, irregularities involving the company's bus contract and inadequate road barriers as factors contributing to the accident. Prosecutors have announced legal proceedings against the company and provincial transportation officials, although responsibility has not been established in court.
Authorities warned against allowing the demonstrations to escalate.

"Individuals who seek to exploit this incident to disrupt public order or incite public sentiment will be dealt with firmly," Abdanan prosecutor Amrollah Misaie said, according to Iran's judiciary-affiliated Mizan news agency, as quoted by AFP on Nov. 17.

Daftari, The Foreign Desk editor-in-chief, argued that the Iranian government's greatest challenge may ultimately come from within, regardless of its confrontation with Washington and Jerusalem. "Whatever happens in the military standoff with the United States and Israel, Tehran will still face its most serious adversary at home," she said.

She also pointed to the protesters' willingness to return to the streets following the deadly crackdown earlier this year, saying that "despite thousands being killed by the regime for protesting in January, we still see bravery on the part of the Iranian people to tell the world of their grievances and to stand up to their murderers."

At the United Nations' daily briefing on Tuesday, Fox News Digital asked the U.N. spokesperson whether the organization was monitoring the situation, particularly the actions of Iranian security forces on the ground. "Well, we're keeping an eye on the situation and we want to make sure that all peaceful protests are allowed to proceed without obstruction and without harassment of protesters," the spokesperson said and added, "Certainly our human rights colleagues will continue to monitor the situation as we've done in the past."
IRAN TURNS CITIZENS INTO INFORMANTS AS CHILLING CRACKDOWN SPREADS BEYOND ITS BORDERS
Hundreds of protesters swarm the streets as they march against the Iranian regime. (Simay Azadi)
The demonstrations carry particular significance because Abdanan was previously a flashpoint during Iran's nationwide anti-government protests earlier this year.
Reuters reported on Jan. 9 that it had verified footage showing demonstrators marching through the city during the broader uprising against the Islamic Republic.

The city also witnessed renewed tensions during mourning ceremonies for protesters killed in the January unrest. Reuters reported on Feb. 18 that witnesses and activists said security forces opened fire on hundreds of mourners gathered at a cemetery in Abdanan.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Iranian security forces are seen near a crowd during demonstrations amid ongoing unrest, according to images released by the Iranian opposition group National Council of Resistance of Iran (NCRI). (NCRI)
Tuesday's demonstrations mark another outbreak of public anger in a city with a recent history of confrontations with Iranian authorities.

Efrat (Effie) Lachter is a reporter for Fox News Digital with more than 15 years of experience covering conflict, global affairs, human rights and political accountability. She has directed and produced more than 200 documentary segments across more than 40 countries, documenting conflicts, humanitarian crises, corruption, human trafficking, gender-based violence and the human stories behind major world events.

Lachter’s reporting has taken her into conflict zones and crisis areas across the Middle East, Europe, Asia and Africa. Her work has included uncovering human trafficking networks, revealing an ISIS underground torture prison in Syria, documenting the war in Ukraine and interviewing senior political figures and world leaders. She was also among the Western journalists who entered Russia after the war began to bring testimonies from Putin’s opposition. Lachter is the recipient of the 2022 Peres Center for Peace Award and was a 2023–2024 Knight-Wallace Journalism Fellow at the University of Michigan. She also won two Rockower Awards for Excellence in Reporting. She holds a bachelor's degree in communication and a master's degree in political science.

title: German chancellor warns Islamic immigrants, others to honor nation's Holocaust legacy or leave
summary: Chancellor Friedrich Merz told Jewish athletes that immigrants from Islamic countries and elsewhere must honor Germany's Holocaust responsibility or leave the country.
story: Author and Holocaust educator Dov Forman says Britain’s new measures are a start but warns the government must follow through with action.

Eight decades after the Holocaust, Germany's conservative Chancellor Friedrich Merz warned that accepting the nation's responsibility for the Nazi genocide is an obligation that extends fully to immigrants arriving from Islamic countries.

During an official reception for Germany’s Maccabiah Jewish sports delegation in Berlin on Nov. 6, Merz said the "historical responsibility of our country applies just as much to those who come here to Germany from Islamic countries, and anyone who fails to abide by this must leave our country."
His response came after a basketball coach told him athletes feared being attacked if they wore their red Maccabi training jackets bearing the Star of David on German streets.

The German Press Agency, dpa, reported that Merz quoted former German President Richard von Weizsäcker, who in 1985 told the Bundestag that "young people are not responsible" for the crimes of the Nazis, "but they are responsible for what becomes of it in history." Merz said the principle was "set in stone," and that, "given the current circumstances," von Weizsäcker’s words "also apply to immigrants who come to Germany," referring to recent antisemitic offenses committed by Muslim immigrants.
GERMAN OFFICIALS WARN ISLAMIST, FAR-LEFT RHETORIC DRIVING SPIKE IN ANTISEMITIC ATTACKS
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz sparked backlash while remarking about the country's migration policies. (Thomas Traasdahl/Ritzau Scanpix via AP)

The chancellor’s office released his prepared remarks from the event, but did not include comments made in a question-and-answer session with the athletes. When asked by Fox News Digital about his statement, a German government spokesperson said, "The chancellor's words speak for themselves."

"Chancellor Merz is not only right to make these remarks," said Sweden-based political scientist Daniel Schatz, "he is fulfilling Germany's historical responsibility." Schatz, who holds a doctorate from Berlin’s Humboldt University, says Merz’s statement reflects the German concept of "Staatsräson," or reason of state, "which places Germany's historical responsibility for the Holocaust and its commitment to Israel's security at the heart of German national and foreign policy."

Schatz said Merz’s remarks point to a broader challenge for Germany. "When Jewish athletes in Germany and other parts of Europe are afraid to wear clothing displaying the Star of David, we are confronting something far more serious than a failure of integration," he said. "We are witnessing a failure of the state to guarantee that Jewish citizens can live openly and securely."
"A country that has made 'Never Again' a cornerstone of its national identity cannot accept a situation in which Jewish identity must be concealed for reasons of personal safety."
ITALY’S SCHOOL VEIL BAN EXPOSES EUROPE’S ASSIMILATION FIGHT AS EXPERT WARNS US COULD BE NEXT
Protesters attend a pro-Palestinian demonstration in Leipzig, Germany, Jan. 17, 2026. (Christian Mang/Reuters)

Simone Rodan‑Benzaquen, senior envoy to Europe at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies, told Fox News Digital, "Merz is right: everyone who makes Germany their home must accept the responsibility to protect Jewish life. You do not have to inherit Germany’s guilt to share that responsibility."

"This is a fundamental question of integration," she added. "Learning German and finding a job matter, but integration also means accepting that your Jewish neighbor has the same right to live openly and safely as you do. That requires transparent foreign funding, scrutiny of what publicly supported organizations teach, enforcement against threats and violence, and support for Muslims challenging antisemitism within their own communities."
SIGN UP FOR ANTISEMITISM EXPOSED NEWSLETTER

A timeline of World War II and historical documents detailing the Holocaust are displayed at the Crossroads of Civilizations Museum in Dubai, United Arab Emirates. The exhibition commemorates the 6 million Jews murdered by Nazi Germany and its collaborators. (Efrat Lachter/Fox News Digital)

Since the Oct. 7, 2023, terrorist attack by Hamas, Janek Treiber, a Dresden University of Technology research fellow, said Germany "has seen a sort of culture war between those who argue for solidarity with Palestinians and view Israel as an oppressive state, and those who stand firmly with Israel. In Germany, this debate is naturally conducted with even greater intensity due to the country’s history."

Despite the strength of Merz's remarks, Treiber said the comments have not generated the kind of reaction that has accompanied some of Merz’s previous comments on migration. "Most people would likely agree that anyone moving to Germany… must respect the constitutional order and come to terms with Germany’s historical legacy," Treiber said.
"Merz’s words should not be a surprise to anyone," Rodan-Benzaquen said. "The measure of success will be whether those athletes can wear their team jackets on German streets without fear."

Germany's 2026 Maccabiah Games delegation was the most successful European team at the competition in Israel — a sporting event akin to the Olympics for Jewish athletes worldwide.

Tyler Speicher is an American journalist living in Slovenia after spending 25 years covering stories ranging from the Little League World Series to hurricanes, 9/11 and its aftermath for New York City news outlets, including 20 years on the Fox News Channel assignment desk.

title: Iran targets US air base in Kuwait after US defensive strikes amid criticism from Gulf states
summary: Iranian state media says Iran's army targeted U.S. assets at Ali Al Salem in Kuwait, as Kuwait's air defense intercepted hostile drone strikes.
story: Iranian protesters in the southern Iranian town of Abdanan chant 'death to the dictators!" during a protest after 13 oil refinery workers were killed in a road accident over the weekend. Credit: The Associated Press.
Iran's army targeted U.S. assets, including drone and missile sites, at Ali Al Salem base in Kuwait on Tuesday, according to Iranian state media.
Kuwait's army appeared to corroborate the attacks, reporting that its air defense systems were combating a series of hostile drone strikes.

"Kuwaiti air defenses are currently countering hostile drone attacks. The General Staff of the Army notes that any explosion sounds heard are the result of air defense systems intercepting hostile attacks. Everyone is requested to comply with the security and safety instructions issued by the relevant authorities," the army wrote in an X post.
BLINKEN WARNS US GROUND INVASION OF IRAN WOULD BE 'ABSOLUTE DISASTER' AS TEHRAN ESCALATES ATTACKS
The attacks are Iran's first on Kuwait in over two months.
Smoke rises after a reported Iranian strike near the U.S. Embassy in Kuwait City on March 2, 2026. (AFP via Getty Images)
The Islamic Republic also reportedly targeted another U.S. ally in the Gulf on Wednesday, as Bahrain's General Command reported intercepting multiple Iranian aerial attacks.
IRAN ESCALATES IN HORMUZ, CLAIMS STRIKE ON OMANI ISLAND IT SAYS 'ENEMY' USES FOR US MILITARY OPS
Iran's attacks come shortly after the U.S. struck an Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) missile site on Iran's Qeshm Island on Tuesday.
That attack was a response to Iran targeting a U.S. radar installation at the Sheikh Isa base in Bahrain.
IRAN VOWS ‘ASTONISHING’ STRIKES AND LIFTS MISSILE-RANGE LIMIT AS US TARGETS LAND ROUTES

"Earlier today, U.S. fighter aircraft used precision munitions to strike an Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) missile launch site on Qeshm Island in self-defense," a U.S. official told Fox News.

"The strike was in response to IRGC aggression targeting U.S. personnel and assets. U.S. Central Command remains highly vigilant and fully postured to protect Americans across the region," the official said in a statement.
IRAN REGIME UNDER PRESSURE AS REBEL GROUPS ESCALATE ATTACKS IN VOLATILE SOUTHEAST
An aerial view of the island of Qeshm, separated from the Iranian mainland by the Clarence Strait, Dec. 10, 2023. (Stringer/File Photo/Reuters)
Iran's escalation also occurs as the nation's leaders grapple with a reigniting of protests throughout the Islamic Republic.
On Tuesday, a demonstration erupted in the southern Iranian town of Abdanan after 13 oil refinery employees died in a road accident, according to a report from the Washington Post.
AFTER 6 MONTHS OF WAR, US MUST PREPARE FOR A FUTURE AFTER IRAN’S GOVERNMENT FALLS
Hundreds of people marched in the rally as they demanded the resignations of the company officials they deemed responsible for the accident.

A protester holds placards during the demonstration outside Downing Street in protest against executions in Iran and in support of freedom for Iran. (Vuk Valcic/SOPA Images/LightRocket via Getty Images)
Video obtained by the Associated Press shows large crowds marching through the streets chanting "death to the dictator!"
U.S. Central Command did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment.

Fox News' Emma Bussey and Reuters contributed to this report.

title: Pope Leo breaks silence on rosary striking his face in Peru, reveals details about cancer: 'Major surgery'
summary: Pope Leo XIV says his lung cancer was found in a routine check-up with no symptoms, crediting prayer and doctors for his recovery before the Peru trip.
story: Video captures the moment prayer beads hit Pope Leo near his eye as he rode through Lima in the popemobile. (Credit: Reuters)

Pope Leo XIV broke his silence Monday after being struck in the face by a rosary thrown by a worshipper in Peru, joking about the incident while also revealing details for the very first time about his cancer diagnosis and major surgery which took place before his recent trip to South America.

The pope, who had the lower lobe of his right lung removed Oct. 13, after doctors found a cancerous tumor, told reporters on the flight home to Rome that he has not fully recovered, but said he was determined to complete the long-planned 12-day journey.
"Just over a month ago, as everybody knows, I underwent rather major surgery," Leo, 71, said during a roughly 45-minute news conference on board the papal plane returning from Lima, Peru.
POPE LEO WELCOMED BACK AS HE DELIVERS ANGELUS PRAYER DAYS AFTER LUNG CANCER SURGERY

Pope Leo XIV, flanked by Director of the Holy See Press Office Matteo Bruni, meets with journalists on the return flight from Latin America, Monday, in Lima, Peru. (Elisabetta Trevisan/Vatican Media via Vatican Pool/Getty Images)
"But from the very beginning, I had in mind that this trip had been planned and that I was going to make it happen."
The pontiff credited his recovery to prayer, medical care and personal determination.

"So, with God's help — and I firmly believe in the power of prayer, as I have literally received messages from all over the world — together with a certain personal determination, which I also have, and with the help of the doctors, it proved to be possible."
Despite the demanding itinerary that included multiple flights and appearances before massive crowds in Uruguay, Argentina and Peru, Leo acknowledged that he is still regaining his strength.
POPE LEO XIV SEEN FOR FIRST TIME SINCE LUNG CANCER SURGERY AMID MAJOR RECOVERY MILESTONE
Pope Leo's 12-day tour began in Uruguay and went through Argentina before ending in Peru. (Andrew Medichini/AP Photo)
"I must say that I am not at 100%, but I am doing quite well. Stamina is a gift I have received from the Lord," he said.
The pope also revealed that his cancer diagnosis came as a shock after doctors found an abnormality during a routine annual medical examination.
"The initial news came as a surprise. There were no symptoms — I felt fine," he said.
"It was discovered during some medical tests, as part of what you might call a check-up: a routine annual examination that I have been having for many years."
Leo said the abnormality initially appeared as a shadow on his lung before additional testing revealed a tumor.
POPE LEO UNDERGOES BLOOD TESTS, X-RAY FOLLOWING CANCER SURGERY, VATICAN SAYS
Pope Leo XIV addresses the media aboard the flight from Lima to Rome.  (Simone Risoluti/Vatican Media via Vatican Pool/Getty Images)
"A biopsy then confirmed that it was a tumor," he said, before adding that he had decided to get it done "right away."
"By the grace of God, I remained calm," he added.
The surgery removed the lower lobe of his right lung after doctors diagnosed lung adenocarcinoma, a type of lung cancer. The pope was discharged four days later.
"No further treatment is necessary. However, as a precaution, I will need to continue having these routine check-ups, simply to keep an eye on things, as is normal," he explained.
The Vatican cleared the pontiff to move forward with his South American trip after medical evaluations in late October.

The journey, which began Nov. 6, marked Leo's first papal visit to Latin America. He also holds Peruvian citizenship and spent roughly two decades serving as a missionary and bishop in Peru before taking on leadership roles at the Vatican.
POPE LEO XIV HIT IN THE FACE BY FLYING ROSARY DURING FAREWELL MASS IN PERU, VIDEO SHOWS

Pope Leo XIV appeared to be struck near the eye by a rosary Monday as he reached out to catch prayer beads tossed toward his popemobile ahead of a farewell Mass in Lima, Peru. (Pilar Olivares/Reuters)
It was while riding in the popemobile through huge crowds toward the Mass in Lima on Nov. 16 that Leo was struck near the eye by a rosary thrown from the crowd.

"The affection shown by the Peruvian people, including the person who, with such great faith, simply wanted to offer me a rosary, is something one carries in one's heart — or perhaps in one's eye," he joked about the incident.
"These are experiences that leave a lasting mark on one's life."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
"They bear witness to genuine enthusiasm, deep faith, and the desire to receive the Lord's blessing," he added before describing the crowds' devotion.
"Some even tried to get past the National Police barricades. They simply wanted to live, feel, and experience this faith," he said.

Emma Bussey is a breaking news writer for Fox News Digital. Before joining Fox, she worked at The Telegraph with the U.S. overnight team, across desks including foreign, politics, news, sport and culture.

title: Kim Jong Un's daughter hits ski slopes in rare photos as North Korean dictator tours mountain resort
summary: Kim Jong Un watched from a throne-like chair, cigarette in hand, as his daughter Kim Ju Ae skied down a snowy North Korean resort during a family outing.
story: Kim Jong Un watched from an ornate armchair at a snowy North Korean ski resort as his daughter skied in an all-white outfit.

North Korean leader Kim Jong Un was photographed sitting in an ornate, throne-like armchair in the middle of a snowy ski resort while his daughter, viewed as his likely successor, carved down the slopes during an unusual family outing.

The striking images, released Monday by North Korean state media, show Kim wearing sunglasses and dress shoes while seated in the elaborate upholstered chair, holding a lit cigarette.Other photographs show his daughter skiing in an all-white outfit as officials navigate the slopes nearby.
The girl, believed to be named Kim Ju Ae, has increasingly appeared alongside her father at high-profile public events.
South Korea's National Intelligence Service has assessed that she is being positioned as his likely successor, although North Korea has not publicly confirmed a succession plan.
TRUMP ARRIVES IN PHILIPPINES AHEAD OF XI JINPING SUMMIT IN CHINA AFTER GOP MIDTERM LOSSES

North Korean leader Kim Jong Un inspects a tourist zone under development during his Nov. 15-16 visit to Samjiyon city, North Korea. The content of this image is as provided and cannot be independently verified. (KCNA via KNS via AP)

The snowy spectacle unfolded just as President Donald Trump raised the possibility that Kim could make an unexpected appearance during his upcoming high-stakes meetings with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin.
"We might have Kim Jong Un. He may come, I don't know. That's up to President Xi," Trump told reporters Monday.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Trump was serious about potentially meeting Kim, though no talks were confirmed.
"If we have a problem with North Korea, the only way we're ever going to solve it is if we engage with them," Rubio told reporters in the Philippines, adding that a meeting "may not happen."
TRUMP’S ASIA TRIP TAKES ALASKA DETOUR AS WEATHER FORCES REFUELING STOP CHANGE

In this photo provided by the North Korean government on Nov. 17, 2026, North Korean leader Kim Jong Un inspects a tourist zone under development during his Nov. 15-16 visit to Samjiyon city, North Korea. Independent journalists were not given access to cover the event. The content of this image is as provided and cannot be independently verified. (KCNA via KNS via AP)

The photographs were taken during Kim's Nov. 15–16 inspection of a tourist zone under development in Samjiyon, a mountainous city in northern North Korea, according to a report by the state-run Pyongyang Times reviewed by Fox News Digital.
Kim visited a ski resort under construction near Mount Pukphothae, where he examined skiing tracks and equipment and instructed officials to prepare the facilities for operation, the outlet reported.
His daughter was photographed skiing at the tourist zone on Nov. 15, according to an Associated Press caption accompanying the government-provided images.

The North Korean leader's visit was part of a broader effort to transform Samjiyon into a year-round mountain tourism destination, with plans for hotels, ski facilities, railway connections and an expanded airport.
TRUMP PLAYS NUCLEAR POKER WITH KIM JONG UN — BUT WHO HOLDS THE CARDS?

The daughter of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un skis at a tourist zone under development in Samjiyon city, North Korea, on Sunday, Nov. 15, 2026. Independent journalists were not given access to cover the event depicted in this image distributed by the North Korean government. The content of this image is as provided and cannot be independently verified. (KCNA via KNS via AP)
The appearance of Kim's daughter added another layer of intrigue to the ski resort visit.

South Korean intelligence officials have pointed to her increasingly prominent public role as evidence that she may eventually inherit power from her father. In an October 2026, assessment reported by KBS World, the National Intelligence Service said her position as a potential successor was strengthening.
The agency has also noted her frequent appearances at military-related events, although the North Korean government has made no formal announcement identifying her as the country's next leader.
The latest photographs offered a different setting for the young girl, showing her navigating a groomed ski slope rather than accompanying her father at an official event.

In this photo provided by the North Korean government on Nov. 17, 2026, Kim Yo Jong, sister of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, skis at a tourist zone under development in Samjiyon city on Sunday, Nov. 15, 2026. Independent journalists were not given access to cover the event. The content of this image is as provided and cannot be independently verified. (KCNA via KNS via AP)
Meanwhile, the possibility of renewed diplomacy between Trump and Kim remains uncertain.

Trump and Kim last met in 2019, when their summit in Hanoi ended without an agreement on North Korea's nuclear program. Efforts to restart negotiations have since stalled as Pyongyang has continued developing its nuclear and missile capabilities.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

A U.S. official told ABC News last week that no engagement with North Korea was planned during Trump's Asia trip, according to Fox News Digital's previous reporting.Fox News Digital's Alec Schemmel contributed to this reporting.
Jasmine Baehr is a breaking news writer for Fox News Digital, where she covers politics, the military, legal debates surrounding life and family policy, as well as faith and culture.

title: Europe assassination scheme emerges as Iran denies DC 'dirty bomb' plot amid Trump warning
summary: President Donald Trump warned Iran would pay a price like no other as Tehran's deputy foreign minister called the chemical weapons report a "shameful lie."
story: President Donald Trump warned Iran on Monday that it would face unprecedented retaliation if it were to carry out an attack on Washington, D.C.

Iran on Tuesday slammed allegations that it was plotting a chemical weapons attack in Washington, D.C., calling the claims a "shameful lie" within hours of President Donald Trump warning that Tehran would face unprecedented retaliation if it ever targeted the nation's capital.

Tehran's denial followed a CNN report that U.S. intelligence agencies had uncovered Iranian plans for potential attacks on senior administration officials, including the possible use of chemical weapons or a radioactive "dirty bomb."

The allegations also emerged amid reports of a separate Iranian-linked assassination plot targeting an Israeli executive in Greece and with Israeli security officials believing Tehran aims to target Israelis overseas as the war continues, according to news outlet Ynet Global.
Iranian Deputy Foreign Minister for Legal and International Affairs Kazem Gharibabadi immediately rejected the allegations in a post on X, invoking Iran's history as a victim of chemical warfare.
TRUMP WARNS US WOULD 'DECIMATE AND DESTROY' IRAN OVER ASSASSINATION ATTEMPT
President Donald Trump has repeatedly alluded to Iranian threats on his life this week. (Jonathan Ernst/Alkis Konstantinidis/Reuters)
"CNN's claim that Iran plans to use chemical weapons in Washington is a shameful lie and a distortion of history," Gharibabadi wrote.
Trump was asked by reporters Tuesday during the first leg of his trip across Asia about the alleged plot against administration officials and if there was an imminent threat to D.C.
"Well, if there is, they will pay a price the likes of which no country has ever paid before," Trump said.
"I hope it's not, but ... we take it very seriously because they happen to be crazy. But this is why they can't have a nuclear weapon, by the way, in case people had any questions."
SENIOR US OFFICIAL UNDERCUTS CNN'S ALARMING IRAN ‘DIRTY BOMB’ REPORT: ‘IT’S NOT NEW'

Iranian Deputy Foreign Minister for Legal and International Affairs Kazem Gharibabadi rejected the allegations of a dirty bomb plot in a post on X. (Askin Kiyagan/Anadolu Agency via Getty Images, File)
"Iran is one of the biggest victims of chemical weapons; victims who were targeted with these inhumane weapons with the support of today's accusers, especially the United States," he added.
"The truth must not become a casualty of the propaganda war," Gharibabadi warned.
TRUMP ADMIN THREATENS IRAN WITH 'CONSEQUENCES' AS ALLIES CONVENE AMID THREATS OF POST-ELECTION ESCALATION

CNN reported, citing seven officials familiar with the intelligence, that American agencies had detected Iranian efforts to develop potential attack options against senior administration officials in Washington.
White House spokesperson Lauren Bis said the administration was monitoring potential threats, but that "at this time, there are no credible threats to the homeland."
IRAN COULD MOVE SHADOW WAR IN A DANGEROUS DIRECTION, EXPERTS WARN ON BACK OF TWO POSSIBLE TERROR ATTACKS

Israeli intelligence reportedly helped foil a separate alleged Iranian-linked assassination plot Tuesday targeting an Israeli executive in Greece, leading to five arrests in Greece and North Macedonia. (Robert Atanasovski/AFP via Getty Images)

Meanwhile, Israeli intelligence reportedly helped foil a separate alleged Iranian-linked assassination plot Tuesday targeting an Israeli executive in Greece, leading to five arrests in Greece and North Macedonia, according to Ynet.
Citing sources, the outlet reported that Mossad gave intelligence to Greek and North Macedonian authorities as part of a joint effort to disrupt the plot.
North Macedonia's National Security Agency announced that authorities had uncovered the plan, with one North Macedonian national arrested in Greece last Thursday and extradited to his home country.
Four others were said to have been detained in Skopje, North Macedonia.

The alleged plot was directed by Iranian national Edris Jahangiri Mavaneh, whom the agency linked to people associated with Iranian intelligence and security services, including alleged drug trafficker Naji Sharifi Zindashti, according to Ynet.
IRAN TRIED TO ASSASSINATE ONE OF NETANYAHU'S SONS, PRIME MINISTER SAYS

Israeli security officials said Tehran considers its war with Israel as unresolved and is looking for opportunities to retaliate through attacks beyond the Middle East region. (Photo by Morteza Nikoubazl/NurPhoto via Getty Images)
Zindashti is also wanted by the FBI for operating a network that targets Iranian activists and dissidents abroad.
According to the bureau, Zindashti used encrypted, Internet-based messaging applications to hire criminal elements within North America and to murder two individuals who fled Iran.
Greek outlet Kathimerini meanwhile, also reported that the suspects allegedly planned to assassinate a senior Israeli executive working for a company operating in Greece.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Investigators seized weapons, ammunition, handwritten notes and a map, according to the report.
North Macedonia's security agency said investigators also uncovered secret meetings involving suspects in several countries, including Iran.
According to Ynet, Israeli security officials said Tehran considers its war with Israel as unresolved and is looking for opportunities to retaliate through attacks beyond the Middle East region.

Emma Bussey is a breaking news writer for Fox News Digital. Before joining Fox, she worked at The Telegraph with the U.S. overnight team, across desks including foreign, politics, news, sport and culture.

title: Iran launches drone assault on Kuwait after US strike on IRGC missile site
summary: U.S. jets struck an IRGC missile site on Iran’s Qeshm Island Tuesday in self-defense, officials told Fox News.
story: President Donald Trump warned Iran on Monday that it would face unprecedented retaliation if it were to carry out an attack on Washington, D.C.
Iran launched drone attacks against Kuwait Tuesday night after U.S. forces struck an Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) missile launch site on Qeshm Island earlier, officials said.
Kuwait's military said its air defenses were intercepting drones, while neighboring Bahrain also warned of a potential threat and urged residents to seek safety.
"Kuwaiti air defenses are currently countering hostile drone attacks," the Kuwaiti army said in a statement, without providing further details.
The army's general staff also said any explosions heard were the result of "air defense systems intercepting hostile attacks."
ARMY IDS 2 VICTIMS KILLED IN JORDAN AIR BASE ATTACK; TRUMP: IRAN WILL PAY 'MANY TIMES OVER'
"Everyone is requested to comply with the security and safety instructions issued by the relevant authorities," the army added.
Meanwhile, Bahrain's Interior Ministry urged citizens and residents to remain calm, move to the nearest safe location and follow updates through official channels, according to a Wednesday post on X.
The ministry did not specify the nature of the threat.
Fox News Chief Foreign Correspondent, Trey Yingst also confirmed that Iranian drones had been launched targeting Kuwait.

Earlier, American fighter aircraft had carried out a self-defense airstrike on an Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) missile launch site on Qeshm Island, Iran, on Tuesday, two military officials confirmed to Fox News.
"Earlier today, U.S. fighter aircraft used precision munitions to strike an Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) missile launch site on Qeshm Island in self-defense.

"The strike was in response to IRGC aggression targeting U.S. personnel and assets. U.S. Central Command remains highly vigilant and fully postured to protect Americans across the region," an official said in a statement.
The strikes came hours after Tehran claimed it targeted a U.S. radar system at the Sheikh Isa base in Bahrain.
IRAN’S DRONE HUNT ESCALATES AS TEHRAN TARGETS US SPY TECH TO EXPOSE BATTLEFIELD SECRETS
Commercial vessels are seen anchored between Iran's Qeshm and Larak islands amid disruptions to maritime traffic in the Strait of Hormuz, Iran. (Fatemeh Bahrami/Anadolu via Getty Images, File)

In a statement, the IRGC claimed its operation was in response to violations of Iran's airspace by U.S. drones and said the action was taken to counter "hostile U.S. movements in the region," according to the semi-official, state-sponsored Mehr News Agency.
CENTCOM said later the Iranian attack drones were all intercepted.

"Multiple Iranian one-way attack drones launched by the IRGC today towards Bahrain were intercepted without any damage to U.S. equipment or injury to American personnel," the command said in a post shared on X.
Qatar also went on to condemn Iran's ongoing attacks on Bahrain on Tuesday, calling them a violation of Bahraini sovereignty.

"The Ministry underscores that the continuation of these attacks constitutes a grave escalation that threatens regional security and stability and undermines diplomatic efforts aimed at easing tensions," it said in a statement on X.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Qatar also described the Iranian attacks as a "flagrant" violation of international law and the principles of good neighborliness, warning that their continuation marked a serious escalation and undermined diplomatic efforts to defuse regional tensions.

The latest attacks also followed a wave of Iranian aerial strikes repelled by Bahrain on Sunday, during which the IRGC claimed to have targeted a radar system at the Al-Riffa helicopter base with another six drones.

Emma Bussey is a breaking news writer for Fox News Digital. Before joining Fox, she worked at The Telegraph with the U.S. overnight team, across desks including foreign, politics, news, sport and culture.

title: Vance’s midterm blame game hits snag as Trump’s own Israel ambassador disputes key claim
summary: Mike Huckabee rejects JD Vance's claim that Israel cost Republicans the midterms, blaming voter apathy and low evangelical turnout for the GOP defeat.
story: U.S. Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee rejects claims that Israel contributed to GOP losses and warns of possible additional U.S. strikes on Iran in an interview with The Press Service of Israel. Credit: Yoav Dudkevitch/TPS-IL.

U.S. Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee is pushing back against Vice President JD Vance’s suggestion that America’s relationship with Israel contributed to Republicans’ crushing midterm election losses, offering a sharply different explanation from within the Trump administration.

In an exclusive interview with The Press Service of Israel (TPS-IL) published Tuesday, Huckabee rejected the argument that Israel was responsible for the GOP’s electoral defeat, instead pointing to economic concerns, voter apathy and a failure to energize the Republican base.
"Israel was not the reason the elections went wrong for Republicans last week," Huckabee told TPS-IL.
TRUMP ADMITS IRAN WAR CONTRIBUTED TO GOP MIDTERM LOSSES, INSISTS IT WAS NECESSARY
US Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee speaks to Fox News Digital during an interview at the American embassy in Jerusalem, Israel. (Yoav Dudkevitch/ TPS-IL)
The remarks come nearly two weeks after Vance blamed Republican losses on the war with Iran and dissatisfaction with Washington’s relationship with Israel.

In a Nov. 4 post on X, Vance argued, according to polling, that voters who supported the Trump-Vance ticket in 2024 had turned against Republicans over four key issues: ending the Iran war, addressing inflation and the cost of living, putting America first and changing the U.S. relationship with Israel.
"The reason we lost is the war," Vance wrote, arguing that the party needed to acknowledge the political consequences of the conflict.

But Huckabee, a former Arkansas governor and longtime Evangelical leader, offered a competing assessment, arguing that Republicans had failed to give their own supporters sufficient motivation to vote.
"To say that Israel was on the minds of most people is, I think, ludicrous," Huckabee told TPS-IL.

VIRGINIA - JULY 17: Attendees wave Israel and the United States flags at the Christians United for Israel (CUFI) summit on July 17, 2023 in Arlington, Virginia. GOP presidential hopefuls for 2024 are making their cases before the pro-Israeli group.  (Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images)

Asked about Huckabee’s comments disputing the suggestion that the relationship with the State of Israel contributed to Republican losses in the midterms, a spokesperson for Vance told Fox News Digital: "The Vice President did not blame Jews for the Republican Party’s losses in the midterms. The Vice President has forcefully condemned antisemitism on countless occasions, and he will continue to do so."

He acknowledged that the war may have influenced voters' perceptions, particularly as families struggled with higher fuel and food costs. "There’s no doubt that the war may have had some impact, not because it was the war itself, but there was such a media coverage that said that the war is what was creating the economic challenges," he said.
REPUBLICANS SUFFER HISTORIC SENATE UPSET AS DEM FLIPS DEEP-RED STATE FOR FIRST TIME IN NEARLY A CENTURY
U.S. Vice President JD Vance, meets with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu at the Prime Minister's Office in Jerusalem, on Wednesday, Oct. 22, 2025. (Marc Israel Sellem/Jerusalem Post/AP)
"But it was the economic issues," Huckabee continued, adding that the war in Iran "may have contributed to prices, but it wasn't the only thing. There were a lot of factors involved."

"If you look at the real numbers, the exit polls showed that only 17% of Evangelicals went and voted last week," Huckabee told TPS-IL. "There is no bloc of voters that is more critical to a Republican victory than Evangelical voters in the United States. They represent 80 million people. If they go vote in mass numbers, Republicans win, if they stay home, Republicans lose."

The ambassador’s remarks referred to exit polling showing that white evangelical Christians accounted for 17% of voters in the 2026 midterms, compared with 23% in 2024. That figure reflects their share of the electorate, rather than the percentage of evangelicals who voted.

"The real reason was that Republicans did not give even Republicans a good reason to go vote for them. They had the White House, they had the Senate, and they had the House. And if you ask the average American, what have they gotten done in the last two years?  They could not provide for you very many, if anything, that the Congress had passed, accomplished, that they had expected them to get done."

"So it's, it's unfortunate that Israel would factor in as a major reason for the vote in America," he added, "Because it just does not appear that that is as credible a reason as is that you had low turnout from the base of the Republican Party."
TRUMP DRAWS RED LINE AGAINST NEWLY EMPOWERED DEMOCRATS, VOWING IMMEDIATE VETOES

U.S. Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee says resentment towards the Jewish state on the right is fueled by "ignorance" of the Bible and a misunderstanding of what it means to be "America First." (Ronen Zvulun/Reuters)
"The Democrats were excited. They went and voted in mass numbers, and they voted with enthusiasm. Enthusiasm wins elections; apathy does not."

Beyond the dispute over the midterm elections, Huckabee warned that additional U.S. military action against Iran remains a possibility if Tehran refuses to abandon its nuclear ambitions, while expressing hope that a diplomatic solution could still be reached.

"It's very possible that we will end up there, because if the Iranians do not understand what the president has made very clear, at least for the U.S. position, and that is they can't have a nuclear weapon," Huckabee told TPS-IL.

"Is it possible to bring this to a resolution by diplomatic means or economic pressure? Hey, I would hope so. That would be wonderful. But if it can't be done, then the U.S, has made it clear, certainly the president, Secretary Rubio, have both said, just this week that the military option is every bit on the table."

A billboard depicting Iran's supreme leaders since 1979: (L to R) Ayatollahs Ruhollah Khomeini (until 1989), Ali Khamenei (until 2026), and Mojtaba Khamenei (incumbent) is displayed above a highway in Tehran on March 10, 2026. Iran marked the appointment of Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei to replace his father as its supreme leader on March 9, 2026.  (AFP/Via Getty Images)

Huckabee said that Trump's position on Iran has remained consistent for decades, dating back to his years as a New York businessman in the early 1980s. He also pointed to the president's response to criticism that the war had contributed to Republican losses in the midterms. "He acknowledged, he said, it may have been a factor," Huckabee said. "And then he said, ‘But I would do it all over again.’"
The ambassador defended that position, arguing that Trump's decision to confront Iran was driven by threats to American national security rather than political calculations.
"It was because, for all these years, he's recognized the threat that they pose to America, not just to Israel," Huckabee said.
PENCE DELIVERS SCATHING REBUKE OF VANCE'S IRAN WAR ASSESSMENT, BLAMES TRUMP POLICIES FOR GOP LOSSES

He cited Americans killed by Iran and Iranian-backed groups over the past several decades, including U.S. casualties in Iraq and Afghanistan, and referred to the Americans killed and taken hostage during the Oct. 7 Hamas terror attacks.
Huckabee praised Trump's willingness to accept potential political consequences, saying that even if the Iran issue had cost Republicans the election, the president would have made the same decision.
"His job is not just to win in the election, [it] is to protect Americans," Huckabee said. "That's first and foremost, and I'm happy to have a president who knows that and who practices that."

The ambassador also addressed Israel’s political future, saying Washington would work with whichever Israeli government emerges following the country’s elections, regardless of Trump’s close relationship with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. "The U.S. does not pick the government for Israel; the people do. However, it shakes up. We are committed to working with the government," he told TPS-IL.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Graphic of an Iowa asking whether the United States' decision to take military action against Iran was right or wrong. (Fox News)
He also expressed hope for expanding the Abraham Accords, pointing to the United Arab Emirates as an example of the diplomatic and economic benefits of normalization.

Efrat (Effie) Lachter is a reporter for Fox News Digital with more than 15 years of experience covering conflict, global affairs, human rights and political accountability. She has directed and produced more than 200 documentary segments across more than 40 countries, documenting conflicts, humanitarian crises, corruption, human trafficking, gender-based violence and the human stories behind major world events.

Lachter’s reporting has taken her into conflict zones and crisis areas across the Middle East, Europe, Asia and Africa. Her work has included uncovering human trafficking networks, revealing an ISIS underground torture prison in Syria, documenting the war in Ukraine and interviewing senior political figures and world leaders. She was also among the Western journalists who entered Russia after the war began to bring testimonies from Putin’s opposition. Lachter is the recipient of the 2022 Peres Center for Peace Award and was a 2023–2024 Knight-Wallace Journalism Fellow at the University of Michigan. She also won two Rockower Awards for Excellence in Reporting. She holds a bachelor's degree in communication and a master's degree in political science.

title: Ex-hostage recounts captivity in Iran-backed militia stronghold now targeted by Iraqi prime minister
summary: Israeli-Russian researcher Elizabeth Tsurkov describes where Iran-backed Iraqi terrorists held her captive for months as Iraq's Trump-backed prime minister orders a crackdown on the militia.
story: Elizabeth Tsurkov, held captive for 903 days by Kata’ib Hezbollah, urges Iraqi authorities to search the area for secret prisons and possible mass graves.

An Israeli-Russian researcher held hostage for 903 days by an Iran-backed Iraqi terrorist group revealed to Fox News Digital that she spent the first four and a half months of her captivity inside the very militia stronghold Iraq's Trump-backed prime minister has now ordered the army to reclaim.

Elizabeth Tsurkov, a senior nonresident fellow at the New Lines Institute for Strategy and Policy, said Kata’ib Hezbollah turned a private family's home in Jurf al-Sakhr, south of Baghdad, into a prison where she was held captive.

"This is where I was held for 4.5 months," Tsurkov told Fox News Digital in an interview, referring to the early months of her captivity, which began with her abduction in Baghdad in March 2023. "I was held in a private home of a family that was taken over by Kata’ib Hezbollah and turned into a prison," she said.
TRUMP ADMIN WARNS IRAQ OVER IRAN TERROR PROXIES AS US REPORTEDLY BLOCKS CASH PAYMENTS

U.S. President Donald Trump gestures toward Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi as they participate in a bilateral meeting in the Oval Office at the White House in Washington, D.C., U.S., July 14, 2026. (Evan Vucci/Reuters)

Tsurkov, who was freed in September 2025 following negotiations and sustained pressure from the Trump administration to secure her release, said that any effort to reclaim the territory must go far beyond dismantling alleged oil-smuggling operations.

She called for Iraqi authorities to search the sprawling area, including surrounding towns and villages, for "secret prisons," "mass burial sites" and "storage facilities for weapons," and to return confiscated homes to their rightful owners.

The revelations come as Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi, who has received strong public backing from President Donald Trump, ordered Iraqi armed forces into Jurf al-Sakhr, also known as Jurf al-Nasr, a stronghold of the U.S.-designated terrorist organization Kata’ib Hezbollah since 2014.
According to AFP on November 16, Baghdad has given the militia a deadline to withdraw, with a security source identifying Friday.

The order follows a Reuters investigation published Monday, citing Iraqi officials who accused Kata’ib Hezbollah of stealing hundreds of millions of dollars in state-owned oil since 2021. The government has dismissed nine security and administrative officials and referred suspects to the judiciary. The militia denies wrongdoing.
IRAN’S PROXY WAR HAS CROSSED OCEANS AND IS NOW KNOCKING ON AMERICA’S DOOR
Elizabeth Tsurkov, an Israeli-Russian researcher held hostage for 903 days by the Iran-backed Iraqi militia Kata’ib Hezbollah, was released in September 2025. (Yuri Gershberg)
For Tsurkov, the stakes go far beyond oil revenues.

She described Jurf al-Sakhr as a territory effectively closed to the Iraqi government since 2014, when Iran-backed militias helped drive ISIS from the area but prevented its predominantly Sunni population from returning.

Tsurkov estimated that between 120,000 and 180,000 people were displaced from the district and surrounding communities. "If Iraqis are allowed to return to their homes, this would signal ... restitution of state sovereignty," she said.
She explained that the current operation is being presented as an anti-corruption campaign rather than an attempt to dismantle Kata’ib Hezbollah's military infrastructure.
The organization retains bases elsewhere in Iraq and access to border crossings with Iran, she said, giving it opportunities to replenish its weapons even if it loses control of Jurf al-Sakhr.
IRAN-BACKED TERROR SUSPECTS PLOTTED ATTACK ON US TROOPS USING VANS PACKED WITH FUEL, DOJ SAYS

Masked Iran-backed Shi'ite fighters hold their weapons in Iraq's Al Hadidiya, south of Tikrit, en route to the Islamic State-controlled al-Alam town, where they are preparing to launch an offensive in March 2015. (Reuters/Thaier Al-Sudani)

Michael Knights, head of research at Horizon Engage, a New York-based strategic consultancy, and an adjunct fellow at the Washington Institute for Near East Policy, expressed skepticism that Baghdad would fundamentally challenge the militias.
"It's going to be very difficult to tell the difference between a real crackdown on Iran-backed militias and a fake one," Knights told Fox News Digital.
Previous Iraqi governments have announced crackdowns on militias, only for detainees to be released or armed groups to retain control through rebranded security arrangements.

In June 2020, when then-Prime Minister Mustafa al-Kadhimi ordered the arrest of 14 Kata’ib Hezbollah members. Armed militia supporters subsequently descended on Baghdad's fortified International Zone demanding their release. Most were later released, according to a U.S. government inspector general report.

In Nov. 2021, Kadhimi survived an explosive-drone attack targeting his residence. Reuters reported that security officials implicated Iran-backed militias, although no organization claimed responsibility.

Knights said that the Iraqi counterterrorism forces are better trained and equipped than Kata’ib Hezbollah, but the greatest danger lies in the militias' ability to threaten officials and their families.
"It's not about equipment or even training," he said, describing the danger of retaliation against commanders and their families who challenge the armed groups.

In a Nov. 16 Middle East Forum analysis, researcher Ali Mahmoud detailed competing allegations of corruption between Kata’ib Hezbollah and Asa’ib Ahl al-Haq, including claims involving companies connected to militia leaders' families.
Mahmoud reported that even the government's initial inspection of Jurf al-Sakhr required negotiations with senior militia commanders, illustrating the limits of Baghdad's authority.
IRAN HAS 'SUBSTANTIALLY INCREASED' EFFORTS TO TARGET AMERICANS ABROAD, US INTELLIGENCE MEMO WARNS
Mourners of Shi'ite group Kata'ib Hezbollah carry the coffin of a fighter during his funeral in Najaf, June 20, 2014. (Ahmad Mousa/Reuters)
Tsurkov, who has researched Iraqi armed groups for years, said her captivity gave her unusual insight into the organization's internal culture.

"I interacted with about 45 different individuals across basically three different prisons," she said, explaining that she later supplemented those observations with interviews involving former militia members and people familiar with their communities.

Her conclusion was that the organization consists of both deeply committed Iranian loyalists and a much larger group of recruits primarily motivated by salaries, status and the ability to exercise power. "They enjoy having power over others," she said, describing what she observed among her captors.

While some members embrace Iran's revolutionary ideology, Tsurkov said many joined after the major fighting against ISIS ended, attracted by government-funded salaries and relatively secure employment. "They're not interested in dying in the service of the Iranian regime," she said of many rank-and-file fighters.
She distinguished those recruits from a smaller core of ideologically committed and better-trained operatives that Iran can mobilize for sophisticated military attacks.

That distinction, she said, could offer Baghdad a path toward reducing militia power without a full-scale confrontation. She proposed allowing some fighters to join the regular Iraqi army under independent military commanders, providing alternative employment while dismantling their existing command structures.
US FACES ANOTHER MAJOR MIDDLE EAST TROOP WITHDRAWAL, BUT THREAT REMAINS

Supporters of Iraqi pro-Iran groups hold pictures of Iranian Revolutionary Guard commanders killed in the Israeli airstrikes in Tehran during a protest in Baghdad near the green zone, the ultra-secured neighborhood hosting the U.S. embassy, on June 16, 2025, amid the Israel-Iran escalating conflict. (Photo by Ahmad Al-Rubaye/AFP via Getty Images)

According to Knights, the current crackdown primarily affects the more confrontational Abu Hussein wing of Kata’ib Hezbollah, while another faction associated with senior militia commander Abu Fadak remains largely untouched. He argued that both ultimately remain responsive to Tehran.

Knights also questioned whether disrupting one oil-smuggling operation would substantially weaken the group's finances, citing its extensive investments in hotels, property and other commercial ventures.

But perhaps the clearest illustration of the contradictions facing Iraq's government, Knights said, lies in recent senior political appointments and Iran's choice of its next diplomatic representative in Baghdad.

On Oct. 15, Iraq's parliament approved Laith al-Khazali, a senior figure in the Iran-backed Asa’ib Ahl al-Haq militia, as one of three deputy prime ministers. The United States designated him and his brother Qais al-Khazali, the militia's leader, as specially designated global terrorists in 2020. Washington has accused the organization of carrying out attacks against American and coalition forces, according to al-Monitor.
IRAN'S SHADOW OPERATIONS STRETCH ACROSS EUROPE AS CHILLING SPY CONVICTIONS EXPOSE TEHRAN'S REACH
A map showing Iran's proxy terror groups around the Mideast. (Fox News)

Another newly appointed deputy prime minister, Muhsin al-Mandalawi, is the brother of two Iraqi businessmen sanctioned by the U.S. Treasury Department on Sept. 10 for facilitating financial transactions benefiting Iran. Knights also pointed to Iran's reported selection of Abdolreza Meskarian, a senior commander in the Revolutionary Guards' Quds Force, as its next ambassador to Iraq.

Alhurra reported on Nov. 9, citing an Iraqi Foreign Ministry source, that Tehran nominated Meskarian, who heads the Quds Force's Ramadan Headquarters, a unit involved in coordinating with Iran-backed armed groups in Iraq. Neither government had formally confirmed the nomination.

For Knights, these developments raise fundamental questions about how far Baghdad is prepared to go in challenging Tehran's influence. "I think on balance, we're still in a pretty bad place in Iraq when it comes to militias," he said.
IRAN’S PROXY MONEY MACHINE: HOW THE HOUTHIS BUILT A MULTIBILLION-DOLLAR NETWORK DESPITE US SANCTIONS

Members of Kata'ib Hezbollah attend the funeral of fighters from Kata'ib Hezbollah, who were killed in a U.S. airstrike in Babil province southwest of Baghdad in March 2026. (DPA / Picture Alliance via Reuters.)
Tsurkov agreed that an operation intended merely to satisfy Washington could be exposed if displaced families remained unable to return.

The broader disarmament deadline, already extended until June 2027, was "utterly unrealistic," she said, arguing that Iraqi security institutions would require years of reform before they could reliably confront the militias.
"I tend to think it will not be real," she said of the current operation, while acknowledging that successful government control could represent a meaningful breakthrough.
For the former hostage, the ultimate measure of success is straightforward: whether Iraq's military merely enters the area, or whether the territory truly returns to civilian control.
"It's either the state is there, and people can return or not," she said.

Damaged structures at the site of an airstrike on a Popular Mobilization Forces base in Mosul, Iraq, Wednesday, July 29, 2026. (AP Photo/Farid Abdulwahed)

Knights also remains skeptical that the current operation will deliver lasting results, suggesting Baghdad may reach a deal that allows the government to claim victory without substantially weakening Kata’ib Hezbollah. Still, he acknowledged the possibility that the confrontation could mark the beginning of a broader effort, even if he doubts this particular operation will prove decisive. "Every great journey starts with the first step," he said.

title: After UN peacekeeping mission ends, Morocco says Western Sahara dispute enters new phase
summary: Western Sahara talks enter a new phase as a senior Sahrawi official says Morocco will implement its autonomy proposal even if the Polisario Front refuses to agree.
story: Former State Department Foreign Service Officer Simon Hankinson joins 'Fox & Friends Weekend' to analyze dramatic footage of thousands of Moroccan migrants storming Spain's border in Ceuta. Hankinson explains how Morocco utilizes migrant surges as a hybrid threat to pressure Spain over political disputes. He details the geopolitical stakes as Spain deploys its military to secure the border.

Six years after President Donald Trump recognized Moroccan sovereignty over Western Sahara, a senior regional official says the decades-old territorial dispute has entered a new phase, with negotiations now focused on how Morocco's autonomy proposal would be implemented following the end of the United Nations peacekeeping mission.

Sidi Hamdi Ould Errachid, president of the Laâyoune–Sakia El Hamra Regional Council, told Fox News Digital in an exclusive Zoom interview that Morocco remains open to negotiations with other parties, but suggested that opposition to the plan would not necessarily prevent it from moving forward.
"The Moroccan side remains open to international engagement, and we are prepared to negotiate how the autonomy proposal will be implemented," he said through an interpreter.
US COUNTERS CHINA AS BEIJING’S ‘SHOCK WAVE’ HITS AFRICAN ECONOMIES

Sidi Hamdi Ould Errachid, right, president of the Laâyoune–Sakia El Hamra Regional Council, poses with members of a U.S. medical delegation visiting Western Sahara as part of efforts to strengthen American-Moroccan cooperation in healthcare, medical training and research. (Fox News)

Asked what remains to be negotiated with the Polisario Front, which seeks independence for Western Sahara, Ould Errachid indicated that Morocco intends to pursue its autonomy initiative regardless of whether all parties reach an agreement.
"If the other parties do not agree, we will continue implementing the autonomy proposal on the ground," he said through the interpreter.

His remarks come after Russia vetoed a U.S.-drafted Security Council resolution on Oct. 30, preventing the renewal of the U.N. Mission for the Referendum in Western Sahara, known as MINURSO. A competing Russian proposal also failed, and the mission began winding down Nov. 1.

Established in 1991, MINURSO was originally tasked with helping organize a referendum on the territory's future following a ceasefire between Morocco and the Algeria-backed Polisario Front. That referendum never took place, leaving the dispute unresolved.
TRUMP CALLS ON ARAB NATIONS TO SIGN ABRAHAM ACCORDS
U.S. and Moroccan military forces participate in the 20th edition of the African Lion military exercise in Tantan, south of Agadir, Morocco, on May 31, 2024. (Mosa'ab Elshamy/AP)
The United States recognized Moroccan sovereignty over Western Sahara in December 2020 under Trump, a position reaffirmed by his administration in July 2026.

In October 2025, the U.N. Security Council adopted Resolution 2797, establishing Morocco's autonomy proposal as the basis for negotiations while maintaining the goal of a mutually acceptable political solution providing for Sahrawi self-determination.

Ould Errachid, a Sahrawi politician who grew up in Laâyoune and participated in U.N.-convened negotiations in Geneva in 2018 and 2019, described the proposal as an opportunity for Sahrawis to govern their own affairs.
"Except for the king, the Moroccan flag, the currency, the armed forces and foreign affairs, we would have full autonomy to manage our own affairs," he explained.
Asked whether the departure of the U.N. mission raised concerns about stability, he rejected the suggestion.
TRUMP GETS MAJOR WIN AGAINST CHINA IN AFRICAN RARE EARTH MINERALS RACE
Pro-Sahwari activists hold Western Sahara flags as they take part in a demonstration on Dec. 4, 2010, during a Moroccan fair in Malag (Jorge Guerrero/AFP via Getty Images)
"We are not worried. We have a credible project that guarantees a decent future for our people and for our cousins in the Polisario Front," he said.

The Polisario Front, which seeks independence, rejects Moroccan sovereignty. Human Rights Watch warned in March 2026 that negotiations centered exclusively on Moroccan autonomy risk undermining Sahrawis' right to self-determination.

Beyond the political dispute, Ould Errachid is seeking to translate Washington's support into closer economic ties, inviting American companies to invest in renewable energy, manufacturing, agriculture, water desalination and healthcare.
TRUMP SAYS SAUDI NUCLEAR AGREEMENT WON'T MOVE FORWARD WITHOUT ABRAHAM ACCORDS: 'THEY HAVE TO BE A MEMBER'
A security guard on duty during the meeting of U.N. envoy to Western Sahara Staffan de Mistura with Polisario Front officials in Tindouf, Algeria, Jan. 15, 2022. (Ramzi Boudina/ Reuters)
He praised Trump for his 2020 recognition decision and highlighted a major highway connecting Morocco with Western Sahara that has become associated with the president's name.
"Nobody here will ever forget the moment President Donald Trump decided to support Morocco. His decision will remain engraved in the history of this region," he said.

One example of expanding American engagement is medical cooperation. Laâyoune hosted U.S. medical delegations in February 2025 and October 2026, bringing American specialists together with Moroccan doctors and students.

The first gathering produced a partnership agreement between New York's St. Francis Hospital & Heart Center and regional hospitals in Laâyoune. The second resulted in agreements between Laâyoune's Faculty of Medicine and Pharmacy and two American organizations, Celenova Fertility and the Fetal Research Fund.
According to the organizers, the partnerships are intended to expand medical training, research, student exchanges and specialized care.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

A view of the border between Morocco and Algeria, closed since 1994 due to political disputes, primarily over the Western Sahara issue, seen from Algeria on Jan. 29, 2026. Tensions that began between the Morocco-based administration and the pro-independence Polisario Front, which is supported by Algeria, have continued since Morocco annexed Western Sahara, formerly a Spanish colony, in 1975. While Morocco argues that the region should remain under its sovereignty, the Polisario Front claims that Western Sahara is an independent state. (Hamza Zait/Anadolu via Getty Images)
Ould Errachid said he is preparing further outreach to American investors in February or March, hoping to expand cooperation beyond medicine into additional economic sectors.
"We need your help," he said, describing Western Sahara as a potential gateway for American companies seeking opportunities across African markets.

title: Bahrain intercepts Iranian drones targeting US radar after 2-month lull in Gulf strikes
summary: Iran's IRGC claims it struck a U.S. radar system at the Sheikh Isa base in Bahrain, home to the Fifth Fleet, the third attack in five days after a lull.
story: Fox News chief foreign correspondent Trey Yingst reports as the Middle East braces for full-scale conflict following an Iranian drone attack targeting U.S. forces in Bahrain.
Iran fired drones toward what it said was a U.S. military radar system in Bahrain on Tuesday, marking the third strike in five days after a roughly two-month lull in the conflict, Reuters reported.
Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said its target was the radar system at the Sheikh Isa base in Bahrain, which is home to the U.S. Fifth Fleet.

Bahrain said its air defenses intercepted the incoming drones after authorities issued a security alert urging residents to seek shelter. Officials announced an all-clear later in the morning, with no deaths or injuries reported.

U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM) also addressed the Iranian drone strikes, saying they didn't hit their intended target. The drones were "intercepted without any damage to U.S. equipment or injury to American personnel," CENTCOM said.
An Iranian drone is displayed in Tehran, Iran, on Nov. 9, 2026. (Fatemeh Bahrami/Anadolu via Getty Images)
IRAN’S DRONE HUNT ESCALATES AS TEHRAN TARGETS US SPY TECH TO EXPOSE BATTLEFIELD SECRETS
The attempted attack followed another wave of Iranian aerial strikes that Bahrain repelled on Sunday, when the IRGC claimed six of its drones targeted a radar system at the Al-Riffa helicopter base.

That strike came two days after Friday's initial attempt against a U.S. radar installation in Bahrain — the first major attack after the two-month pause. U.S. Central Command said American forces shot down both drones in that incident, with no casualties or injuries.

Reuters previously reported that President Donald Trump has told advisors that he may not attack Iran again if there are no more provocations from the IRGC or the Houthis, an Iran-backed terrorist group in Yemen.
President Donald Trump attends a multilateral meeting with delegations from Japan, India and Australia at the Solaire Hotel on Nov. 17, 2026, in Manila, Philippines. (Win McNamee/Getty Images)
TRUMP KEEPS SIGNALING AN END TO IRAN WAR, BUT EXPERT WARNS A CRUCIAL PIECE OF HIS STRATEGY IS MISSING

Trump has said he plans to maintain the naval blockade on Iran, essentially putting the country's economy into a vice grip. He said the blockade will remain in place as long as Tehran seeks to disrupt traffic in the Strait of Hormuz.
In recent days, attacks on tankers have increased in the strait, still one of the world's most vital transit routes for global energy supplies.

Commercial vessels are seen anchored between Iran's Qeshm and Larak islands amid disruptions to maritime traffic in the Strait of Hormuz, Iran on Sept. 11, 2026. (Fatemeh Bahrami/Anadolu via Getty Images)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Oman and Iran have discussed ways to manage shipping through the strait, which carried roughly one-fifth of global oil supplies each day prior to the conflict.
The U.S. has not been part of those bilateral talks, and Trump has signaled he would reject any transit arrangement negotiated without Washington that gives Tehran control over the waterway.
Reuters contributed to this report.

title: State Department presses Egypt to respect religious freedom as Christian convert faces possible execution
summary: The State Department is pressing Egypt to protect religious freedom as a Christian convert faces possible execution or 25 years in prison, raising concerns over his trial.
story: Grace Drexel says her father, Pastor Ezra Jin, remains imprisoned for leading one of China’s largest independent churches.

The State Department has intensified its efforts to compel the majority Muslim state of Egypt to honor the religious liberty protections for an Egyptian who converted to Christianity and is facing either the death penalty or a lengthy prison term.

The prosecution of Said Mansour Rezk Abdelrazek has catapulted his case and has attracted publicity within the U.S., Britain and across the global Christian community. Egypt receives $1.3 billion in annual funding from the U.S.
In July, Fox News Digital reported on Abdelrazek’s trial for his embrace of Christianity in 2016.
TRUMP DOJ EXPANDS RELIGIOUS LIBERTY PROTECTIONS AFTER MAJOR SUPREME COURT RULINGS
Said Mansour Rezk Abdelrazek could face a death sentence or some 20 years in jail. (Fox News)

A State Department spokesperson told Fox News Digital that, "We are monitoring his trial closely. Religious freedom is a fundamental human value, and we encourage the Egyptian government to protect the religious freedom rights of all its citizens."

The situation for Abdelrazek has become dire, according to his attorney and human rights advocates for Coptic Christians in Egypt. He faces execution or a 25-year prison sentence for his conversion to Christianity, according to the office of his lawyer, Said Fayez.
Fayez’s office said that in early November the "Public Prosecution presented its closing arguments and requested that the maximum penalty prescribed by law be imposed upon him."
PAKISTAN’S TOP COURT UPHOLDS CHRISTIAN MAN’S DEATH SENTENCE FOR BLASPHEMY
Egyptian Coptic Christians attend the Resurrection Mass at the Monastery of Saint Simon Al-Kharaz during Holy Saturday services on April 19, 2025, in Cairo, Egypt. (Ahmad Hasaballah/Getty Images)

Fox News Digital reached out multiple times to Egypt’s Embassy in Washington, D.C., and its Foreign Ministry for a comment. According to Amnesty International, in "July 2025, security officers arrested Egyptian national and Christian convert Said Abdelrazek from his home in Cairo. After nine months of arbitrary pretrial detention, Said Abdelrazek was referred to trial before the Terrorism Circuit of the First Criminal Court in Badr on charges stemming from his conversion and religious beliefs."
Coptic Solidarity reported he faces charges that include contempt for Islam, and inciting unrest and spreading false information.

Abdelrazek’s fiancée Sophia, an Australian-Egyptian citizen, has been energetically campaigning to secure his freedom. She told Fox News Digital that she is "pleading for them to release him." She declined to use her last name because of "some extreme threats" against her.

Lindsay Rodriguez, a spokeswoman for Coptic Solidarity, told Fox News Digital that "Coptic Solidarity is deeply concerned that Egyptian prosecutors are seeking the maximum penalty against Said Abdelrazek, a Christian convert whose case has become an important test of religious freedom and judicial impartiality in Egypt."

She continued that he "has been detained since July 2025 and is being prosecuted before a terrorism court, primarily on an allegation of joining a banned terrorist organization, as well as charges of contempt for Islam, inciting unrest and spreading false information. These remain prosecution allegations, not findings of guilt. His defense will present its closing arguments on Dec. 8. Reported religious remarks attributed to the judge during the Nov. 3 hearing further heighten concerns about whether a Christian convert can receive a genuinely impartial hearing."
His supporters say the prosecution has yet to name the terrorist organization in question while noting there is no known terrorist group associated with Christians listed in Egypt.

This picture taken on Nov. 1, 2022 shows a view of the United Kingdom Embassy headquarters, left, and the United States Embassy, right background, headquarters in the Garden City district of Egypt's capital Cairo. (Amir Makar/AFP via Getty Images.)

Rodriguez added that "Peaceful religious conversion and expression must not be treated as terrorism or national-security offenses. The United States, European Union and Australia should use the Dec. 8 hearing as a clear test of Egypt's willingness to uphold basic religious-freedom and fair-trial standards."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Rodriguez said, "The U.S. Embassy in Cairo, EU Delegation and Member State embassies should seek access to monitor the hearing and raise Said's case directly with Egyptian authorities. Members of Congress and the European Parliament should publicly demonstrate that they are following the case. Australia also has a particular responsibility: Said's fiancée is an Australian citizen, and DFAT [Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade] should press his case while Home Affairs ensures a viable humanitarian pathway for reunification upon his release."
The Egyptian Christian community makes up an estimated 10% of the nation’s 120 million people.
