title: American basketball player’s Nigeria trip ends in arrest after officials spot him abandoning suspicious bags
summary: Nigerian officials say an American basketball player abandoned two checked bags containing 75 pounds of cannabis before officers arrested him in a parking lot.
story: Greene Da'monte Khiree said he visited Nigeria to build basketball connections, but officials say his phone revealed evidence of drug trafficking. (National Drug Law Enforcement )
A U.S. basketball player was arrested at a Nigerian airport last Wednesday after allegedly attempting to smuggle a large quantity of cannabis into the country in his luggage.

Greene Da'monte Khiree, 28, a native of Savannah, Georgia, was linked to two checked bags containing 75 pounds of cannabis at Murtala Muhammed International Airport, according to Nigerian officials. Khiree reportedly arrived in Lagos aboard an Emirates flight from Thailand via Dubai.
While at the airport, Khiree appeared to abandon two checked bags containing a potent strain of cannabis known as "loud," according to Nigeria's National Drug Law Enforcement Agency (NDLEA).
CBP OFFICERS SEIZE NEARLY 850 POUNDS OF KHAT PACKED INTO 12 SUITCASES AFTER FLIGHT FROM LONDON
Greene Da'monte Khiree, 28, was arrested at a Nigerian airport after officials linked him to two checked bags containing 75 pounds of cannabis. (National Drug Law Enforcement Agency)

"The suspect, who was placed under discreet surveillance upon arrival, was observed abandoning his two checked-in bags before attempting to exit the airport with only his carry-on luggage," officials said.
He was subsequently apprehended in the airport's parking lot, according to the NDLEA.
FEDS SEIZE $6.4M WORTH OF COCAINE ABOARD OIL TANKER AT PORT OF LOS ANGELES, ARREST SUSPECTED CARTEL SMUGGLER
Although Khiree claimed he was visiting Nigeria to build connections for his basketball career, a forensic examination of his phone reportedly uncovered evidence of drug trafficking.

"The suspect, a native of Savannah, Georgia, USA, who claimed he has lived in Thailand since October 2025 where he plays professional basketball, said he came to Nigeria on holiday to build networks for his basketball career," officials said.
"A forensic examination of his mobile phone revealed information pointing to his knowledge of and involvement in the drug trafficking activity."
Two checked bags at Murtala Muhammed International Airport contained 75 pounds of cannabis, along with tracking devices and the suspect’s name tags, officials said. (Jim Vondruska/Reuters)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Investigators also found that both bags bore Khiree's name tag and contained tracking devices. Authorities confirmed that the cannabis originated in Thailand.
Bonny Chu is a Breaking and Trending News Writer for Fox News Digital

title: Ecuador's president denies US operates military base despite reports of troop buildup
summary: Ecuadorian President Daniel Noboa denies the U.S. operates a military base at Taura Air Base, describing American personnel's activities as temporary.
story: Dana Perino reports on former President Donald Trump's initiative to combat drug cartels in Ecuador. The U.S. is providing military and intelligence assistance to the South American nation, which is grappling with significant drug-related violence and has become a major cocaine exporter. This joint effort reflects a broader strategy to reassert U.S. influence and target transnational criminal groups, aiming for enhanced security in the region.

Ecuadorian President Daniel Noboa denied that the United States operates a military base in his country after an Agence France-Presse (AFP) investigation signaled an expanded U.S. military presence at an air base near the port city of Guayaquil.

"Sometimes there's a specific mission. Sometimes there's a specific operation," Noboa told the news outlet Altavoz, describing U.S. personnel at Taura Air Base as carrying out "temporary activities" under a bilateral security agreement, including intelligence-gathering drone flights.
"We work together. It's not an American base. It's an Ecuadoran base," he commented.
THE UNLIKELY SOUTH AMERICAN ALLY HELPING LEAD TRUMP'S DRUG CARTEL CRACKDOWN

Ecuadorian President Daniel Noboa denied that the United States operates a military base in his country after an Agence France-Presse (AFP) investigation revealed an expanded U.S. military presence at an air base near the port city of Guayaquil. (Franklin Jacome/Agencia Press South/Getty Images)
Noboa's remarks came about a month after AFP had documented an unusual deployment of U.S. military aircraft, dozens of tents and construction of new infrastructure at the air base.
The investigation identified approximately 20 U.S. military flights arriving at Taura between June and mid-October, along with internal documents confirming the presence of American troops.

Several flights originated from U.S. military installations, including Marine Corps Air Station Cherry Point in North Carolina and Dover Air Force Base in Delaware, with stopovers in Puerto Rico and Panama.
The buildup also raised legal concerns among senior Ecuadorian military officials.

AFP cited a September letter in which then-Air Force commander Gen. Mauricio Salazar asked military leaders to clarify the legality of the deployment. Salazar was subsequently removed from his post and reassigned to a less senior role, the report said.

The increased U.S. military presence comes after Ecuadorian voters rejected a Noboa-backed referendum in November 2025 that would have amended the country's constitution to lift its ban on foreign military bases.
US MILITARY BOARDS, SEARCHES AND SINKS VESSEL ALLEGEDLY SUPPORTING LOS CHONEROS NARCO-TERRORISTS
U.S. and Ecuadorian forces launched joint operations Tuesday targeting suspected narco-terrorists in Ecuador, according to U.S. Southern Command. (U.S. Southern Command)
Despite the referendum's defeat, Quito and Washington have deepened security cooperation to combat drug trafficking and transnational organized crime.
Human Rights Watch has described the United States as Ecuador's primary security partner in its crackdown on organized crime, providing equipment, training, intelligence and direct military support.

The watchdog characterized the partnership as "perilous," warning that "both governments have engaged in serious human rights violations fuelled by their insistence on framing their confrontations with organised crime groups as a kind of war."

Since returning to the White House in January 2025, President Donald Trump has designated several Latin American cartels as foreign terrorist organizations and authorized military strikes against vessels in international waters suspected of drug trafficking.
WHITE HOUSE HIGHLIGHTS 'STEEPEST' EVER DECLINE IN US CASUALTIES FROM CARTELS AMID BOAT STRIKES
Ecuador FM Roberto Kury and Ecuadorian police forces during counterdrug mission. (Fox News Digital)

Ecuador has also emerged as a key ally in Trump's crackdown on drug cartels and narcoterrorism, with U.S. and Ecuadorian forces working together to intercept narcotics shipments and dismantle transnational criminal networks, the country's foreign minister told Fox News Digital in September.
Roberto Kury said closer cooperation with Washington had delivered "a lot of positive results" in recent months, citing drug shipments intercepted through U.S. intelligence and joint operations.

"There is an intelligence (sic) and cooperation from the United States, but there is also always the presence of Ecuadorian military or police. They work together," Kury told Fox News Digital on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly.
"Most of the drugs go to the United States. So that’s why the United States shares the problem," Kury said.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Secretary of State Marco Rubio has also praised Ecuador as the United States' most "aggressive" partner in its Western Hemisphere crackdown.
Fox News Digital has reached out to Southcom for comment.

title: French troops secretly deployed inside Ukraine as ex-NATO chief praises Macron's 'guts'
summary: President Emmanuel Macron's France reportedly runs covert "Volia" mission training Ukrainian troops as Zelenskyy holds fresh peace talks with the US.
story: Fox News chief foreign correspondent Trey Yingst reports from the outskirts of Kyiv, where Ukrainian soldiers use anti-aircraft guns and interceptor drones to defend civilians against incoming Russian attacks.

French troops have reportedly been operating secretly inside Ukraine for months, training Ukrainian forces and maintaining military equipment and, as NATO experts claim, President Emmanuel Macron is taking a more assertive role in supporting Kyiv against Russia.

The covert mission, codenamed "Volia," has operated since at least summer 2026, with small teams of French military personnel deployed on short-term assignments under the supervision of a French general, Radio France Internationale (RFI) reported Monday.
Agence France-Presse (AFP) also separately reported the French military presence, citing sources who said the troops were not involved in combat.
UKRAINE HITS PUTIN'S PRIZED BRIDGE IN RECORD DRONE BLITZ AS KREMLIN TELLS LAWMAKERS TO PREPARE FOR 'VICTORY'

New recruits of the 65th Separate Mechanized Brigade of the Ukrainian Armed Forces attend their first military training near a frontline in the Zaporizhzhia region, Ukraine, on Feb. 22, 2026. (Andriy Andriyenko/Press Service of the 65th Separate Mechanized Brigade of the Ukrainian Armed Forces/Handout via Reuters)

The reports come as the United States and European allies pursue renewed, high-stakes negotiations to end Russia's war in Ukraine, raising questions about the extent of Western military involvement in the conflict.

Former NATO Supreme Allied Commander Europe Gen. Philip Breedlove meanwhile, told Fox News Digital that the covert French mission sends a powerful message to Russian President Vladimir Putin at a critical juncture for Europe.
"The timing of what the French are doing and their announcement of what they're doing is important," Breedlove said.
"A very powerful NATO ally — both politically and militarily — is making a strong statement of support for Ukraine.
"And this is what Mr. Putin needs to see. He needs to look across the line and see that the Western alliances, NATO in this case, are standing up for Ukraine."

"It's very important to remember that if Mr. Putin stops fighting, this war ends. If Ukraine stops fighting, Ukraine ends," he said before adding that this is "an existential war that we in the West need to support to the appropriate conclusion."
UKRAINE'S ATTACKS ON RUSSIA ARE PUSHING PUTIN CLOSER TO NEGOTIATING TABLE, TRUMP NATO AMBASSADOR SAYS
A Ukrainian serviceman attends a military training in the Zaporizhzhia region of Ukraine on Monday, May 26. (Andriy Andriyenko/Ukraine's 65th Mechanized Brigade via AP)

The French mission reportedly focuses on training Ukrainian troops and maintaining French-supplied equipment, including CAESAR self-propelled howitzers, Mirage 2000 fighter jets and precision-guided missiles.
French personnel have rotated between France, Poland and Ukraine under what RFI described as a "light and flexible" operational structure.
French newspaper Le Monde separately reported Monday that personnel had also worked alongside Ukrainian intelligence units on observation missions closer to the front lines.
The deployment would mark a significant step in Macron's military support for Kyiv despite repeated Russian warnings against Western troop involvement.

"I cannot imagine the French military would deploy into Ukraine without their commander-in-chief approving it," Breedlove said of Macron while noting that Western military training missions inside Ukraine predate Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022.

"It's not new to have training facilities inside of Ukraine. But almost all of them, and almost everyone, left Ukraine when the war started, which I disagree with, but that was the decision," he said.
Breedlove also pointed to the Yavoriv military training facility in western Ukraine, where NATO countries helped train Ukrainian forces following Russia's initial intervention in 2014.
"In 2014, we had a training area called Yavoriv," he said.

"We had a large facility of NATO training ability there, and we trained Ukrainians all the time. When the war started back in 2014 — remembering this is a 12-year-long war — most of those nations left, to include the United States."
RIOT-TORN FRANCE STRUGGLES WITH CHAOS AT HOME AS MACRON EYES MILITARY MISSION THOUSANDS OF MILES AWAY
French President Emmanuel Macron reviews the troops during his visit to the nuclear submarine navy base of Ile Longue in Crozon, France, March 2, 2026 (Yoan Valat /Pool via Reuters)

"I would congratulate and thank France for having the guts to go in there and do what we all should be doing to help Ukraine fight this illegal, immoral, inhumane war that Russia is persecuting the Ukrainian people with," Breedlove said.

RFI reported that French lawmakers had not been formally informed of the deployment, with authorities maintaining that parliamentary approval was unnecessary because the mission did not involve combat operations.
France has trained approximately 25,000 Ukrainian soldiers in France and Poland since 2023, according to Le Monde.

Macron raised the possibility of sending Western military instructors into Ukraine in 2024, prompting concerns among allies, including the United States and Germany, about a potential escalation with Moscow.
France has also helped lead efforts to establish a multinational force to support a potential postwar security arrangement for Ukraine.
Russia has repeatedly opposed the presence of Western troops in Ukraine, while Putin has characterized Western military assistance to Kyiv as evidence of a proxy conflict between Russia and NATO.
TRUMP PUSHED NATO TO SPEND BIG — NOW COMES THE HARDER QUESTION: CAN EUROPE ACTUALLY FIGHT?

Russia on Thursday, Jan. 8, 2026, warned that any Western military forces deployed to Ukraine under a postwar security arrangement would be considered "legitimate combat targets." (Mikhail Metzel/Sputnik/Pool via Reuters; Stringer/Reuters)
The reports surfaced as Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy announced fresh talks Monday with American and European representatives aimed at ending the war.

Zelenskyy said Ukrainian officials held online discussions with U.S. presidential envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, along with European representatives, about prospects for a negotiated settlement with Russia.
The Ukrainian leader also warned that intelligence indicated Russia was preparing major strikes against Ukrainian targets Monday evening, overnight and Tuesday.
Breedlove suggested that France's reported mission could now encourage other NATO members to further expand their support for Ukraine.
"I think that there are more than a few NATO nations that would love to be in there helping," he said.
"They're the ones that call themselves the Eastern Front, those nations that border Russia in various parts of the eastern flank of NATO."
"And so I'm sure there are other nations that want to do this, but they're looking for leadership to go do it," he said.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
"It seems now that France may be stepping up to the task."

Emma Bussey is a breaking news writer for Fox News Digital. Before joining Fox, she worked at The Telegraph with the U.S. overnight team, across desks including foreign, politics, news, sport and culture.

title: Ukraine hits Putin's prized bridge in record drone blitz as Kremlin tells lawmakers to prepare for 'victory'
summary: Ukraine struck Vladimir Putin's prized Crimea bridge in what Russia called the war's largest drone attack, setting industrial facilities ablaze.
story: The upcoming trilateral summit in China between President Trump, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin faces critical global challenges. Alexandria Hoff reports on key agenda items, while retired Navy Captain Brent Sadler analyzes strategic threats from Iran. Discussions are expected to address nuclear talks, international trade and the potential inclusion of tech leaders.

Ukraine launched what Russia described as the largest overnight drone attack of the war Monday, striking President Vladimir Putin's prized Crimea bridge and setting industrial facilities ablaze, as separate reports revealed a covert French military mission in Ukraine and preparations in Moscow for a possible return of Russian troops.
The developments came days before President Donald Trump is expected to meet Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping in China, amid renewed U.S.-brokered efforts to end the nearly five-year conflict.

"The sheer scale and effectiveness of these drone attacks are remarkable," retired Air Force Lt. Gen. Richard Newton told Fox News Digital. "Ukraine has developed the capability to produce large numbers of drones and strike targets once considered a safe haven deep inside Russia."
UKRAINE TARGETS RUSSIA WITH OVER 1,000 DRONES, KILLING 2 AS MOSCOW HOLDS LAST DAY OF ELECTIONS
Flames engulf industrial structures as a massive fire lights up the night sky in Nizhnekamsk, Russia, Nov. 15, 2026. (Reuters)

Russia's Defense Ministry claimed its forces intercepted 1,336 Ukrainian drones across 16 regions, exceeding the previous overnight record of 1,254 on Oct. 29, Reuters reported Nov. 16. The numbers could not be independently verified.
Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said about 600 drones had been launched toward the capital region since Sunday evening, with 191 intercepted.

Russian-installed Crimean governor Sergei Aksyonov confirmed that the Kerch Strait bridge, linking occupied Crimea to mainland Russia, had been struck. The Kremlin characterized the damage as minor. Road traffic was temporarily suspended for repairs, while trains continued running, according to Russian transportation officials.
The bridge is both a strategically important supply route and a symbol of Russia's annexation of Crimea in 2014.

The strikes also hit Russia's energy sector. Rostov regional governor Yuri Slyusar reported fires at four industrial sites in Azov, where three people were injured. Officials in neighboring Krasnodar said a separate fire broke out at an industrial facility in Ilsky. Falling drone debris reportedly injured six people in the Krasnodar region.
ZELENSKYY ACCUSES PUTIN OF DEFYING TRUMP'S CEASEFIRE PUSH, SENDS POINTED MESSAGE TO WHITE HOUSE

Rescuers from the State Emergency Service of Ukraine work at a packaging facility damaged by a Russian attack in Odesa region, Ukraine, on November 16, 2026. The strike destroyed a two-storey administrative and warehouse building, damaged the roof of a production facility and shattered windows. Two people were injured in the attack. (Nina Liashonok/Ukrinform via Reuters)

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy claimed Sunday that strikes had disabled more than half of Russia's refining capacity, a figure Fox News Digital could not verify. Two industry sources separately estimated that recent attacks reduced refining capacity by approximately 30%, Reuters reported.
"Putin has a serious problem on his hands," Newton said. "Russia is enormous in terms of size; there’s simply no way to 100% defend every refinery, airfield, and military installation."
Newton said Ukraine's campaign was designed to strengthen its negotiating position while disrupting Russia's military and logistics networks.

"I don’t believe Ukraine has reached a culminating point yet, by any stretch, to change Putin’s mind, but sustained military and economic pressure just may eventually at some point force him to reconsider his position," he said.

In a separate development, Radio France Internationale reported Nov. 16 that French troops had been operating inside Ukraine since at least summer 2026 as part of a confidential mission codenamed "Volia."

The mission reportedly consists of small teams making short visits to train Ukrainian personnel and maintain equipment. RFI said French lawmakers had not been informed and alleged that an established French training operation in Poland, known as "Gerfaut," provided a gateway for deployments into Ukraine.
An anonymous source familiar with the mission confirmed French personnel's presence to AFP, while stressing that they were not combat troops.

"The rotation of French trainers supporting Ukraine in France, Poland, or occasionally in Ukraine is a reality," the source told AFP. "But this is not a military operation. There is absolutely no intention of engaging in coercive actions."
France's military general staff did not immediately comment to AFP. The number of troops involved remains unknown.
Smoke and flames rise over Moscow on June 18, 2026, following a Ukrainian drone attack that hit the Kapotnya oil refinery and other targets in the Russian capital. (East2West)

Meanwhile, Russian newspaper Vedomosti reported Nov. 16 that Kremlin officials had instructed lawmakers from Putin's United Russia party to prepare for "victory" and the return of personnel from the battlefield.

The message was reportedly delivered during a closed-door seminar attended by senior presidential administration official Sergei Kiriyenko. A source described lawmakers being told to anticipate the possibility of soldiers returning home simultaneously.
The report provided no timetable and did not establish that Putin had ordered a withdrawal or decided to end the war.
The reports emerged after U.S.-brokered talks in Abu Dhabi last week resulted in a major prisoner-exchange agreement but no breakthrough over territory.
Trump, Putin and Xi were due to meet Thursday, Nov. 19, in Shenzhen, China, with Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov describing the trilateral summit as a potentially significant event.
Newton expressed skepticism about an immediate diplomatic breakthrough. "I don't anticipate a major breakthrough on any issue, including Russia's war against Ukraine," he said.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Left to right: Russian President Vladimir Putin, U.S. President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping (Reuters)

"If President Trump has any discussions with Xi and Putin regarding Ukraine I would advise him to look those two leaders in the eye and underscore the U.S. is not backing down in our support to the Ukrainian people as they valiantly defend their homeland," he concluded.
Reuters contributed to this story.

Efrat (Effie) Lachter is a reporter for Fox News Digital with more than 15 years of experience covering conflict, global affairs, human rights and political accountability. She has directed and produced more than 200 documentary segments across more than 40 countries, documenting conflicts, humanitarian crises, corruption, human trafficking, gender-based violence and the human stories behind major world events.

Lachter’s reporting has taken her into conflict zones and crisis areas across the Middle East, Europe, Asia and Africa. Her work has included uncovering human trafficking networks, revealing an ISIS underground torture prison in Syria, documenting the war in Ukraine and interviewing senior political figures and world leaders. She was also among the Western journalists who entered Russia after the war began to bring testimonies from Putin’s opposition. Lachter is the recipient of the 2022 Peres Center for Peace Award and was a 2023–2024 Knight-Wallace Journalism Fellow at the University of Michigan. She also won two Rockower Awards for Excellence in Reporting. She holds a bachelor's degree in communication and a master's degree in political science.

title: Spain's Canary Islands flooded by thousands of migrants as country declares emergency
summary: Spain's Canary Islands processed over 2,200 migrants in two days as violent protests over housing costs and skyrocketing rents erupted nationwide.
story: Thousands of migrants flooded Spain's Canary Islands this weekend as the nation's government remains under a migration emergency.
Thousands of migrants flooded Spain's Canary Islands this weekend as the nation's government remains under a migration emergency.

The Canary Islands have received the brunt of migration from West Africa and Sub-Saharan Africa in recent months. Authorities there processed over 2,200 migrants in just two days, all arriving in dinghies and makeshift boats.
One flotilla of 14 boats landed on the island of El Hierro carrying 1,324 people. The island's Spanish population is just 12,000.
SPANISH JOURNALIST SAYS CEUTA RESIDENTS BELIEVE GOVERNMENT ISN'T DOING ENOUGH TO PREVENT ANOTHER MIGRANT RUSH

One of the migrants rescued after a cayuco capsized on May 28, 2025, in El Hierro, Canary Islands, Spain. At least seven women have died, three of them minors, following the capsizing of a cayuco with 180 people on board as it entered the port of La Restinga. (Europa Press Canarias via Getty Images)

The Spanish government declared an emergency over the archipelago last week. The latest surge comes just months after tens of thousands of migrants crossed into Spain's North African territory of Cueta in July.

The country also faced internal unrest this month after a general strike turned violent last week and rioters began clashing with police, setting fires and bashing storefronts in hotspots across the country.
WOMAN, 87, DIES AFTER BEING CARRIED FROM HOME OF 70 YEARS ON STRETCHER DURING EVICTION IN SPAIN
People light fires and throw objects during a demonstration over the housing crisis on November 11, 2026, in Barcelona, Spain. (Photo by David Ramos/Getty Images)

Violent scenes unfolded in Barcelona, where some demonstrators vandalized stores along the city's popular Paseo de Gracia shopping boulevard, set small bonfires and launched fireworks at officers arriving in riot gear and armored vehicles.
The violence erupted as Spain experienced its first general strike in 14 years, with workers demanding relief from skyrocketing rents and the rising cost of living.
TOURIST HOT SPOT FACES HOUSING REVOLT AS LOCALS DEMAND CUTS TO VACATION LODGING
A protestor holds up a poster as objects burn in the background during a demonstration over the housing crisis on November 11, 2026, in Barcelona, Spain. (Photo by David Ramos/Getty Images)

Housing activists claimed 400,000 people marched through Barcelona, while city officials estimated attendance at 55,000. Government officials reported another 120,000 demonstrators gathered in Madrid despite heavy rain, The Associated Press reported.

The nationwide walkout disrupted public transportation, forced some businesses to close and blocked major roads. Police made arrests across the country, while officers used pepper spray against demonstrators in Madrid.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Both the migration and housing crises are expected to play a major role in Spain's Nov. 29 parliamentary elections.
Fox News' Jasmine Baehr and The Associated Press contributed to this report.
Anders Hagstrom is a reporter with Fox News Digital covering national politics and major breaking news events.

title: Mexico's cartel 'godfather' convicted in American DEA agent's murder dies at age 80
summary: The Guadalajara cartel boss convicted in DEA agent Enrique "Kiki" Camarena's murder died at 80, decades after the killing triggered Operation Leyenda.
story: Miguel Angel Felix Gallardo, the Guadalajara cartel co-founder convicted in the 1985 murder of DEA agent Enrique "Kiki" Camarena, died at 80 in a Mexican hospital, The Associated Press reported, citing Jalisco authorities.
The Mexican cartel boss who helped build a drug empire supplying the United States and was convicted in the murder of Drug Enforcement Administration agent Enrique "Kiki" Camarena has died at 80.

Miguel Angel Felix Gallardo, known as the "boss of bosses," died Sunday in a Guadalajara hospital after suffering multiple organ failure, The Associated Press reported, citing Jalisco’s security ministry. He had been transferred from prison Friday.
Felix Gallardo had been behind bars since 1989, according to The AP.
JOHN KOUFOS: TRUMP’S ‘SHIELD OF THE AMERICAS’ COULD HELP DEFEND US FROM CARTELS
Miguel Angel Felix Gallardo, the Guadalajara cartel co-founder known as the "boss of bosses," appears in an archival mugshot. (The Associated Press)
His death comes more than four decades after Camarena’s abduction and torture, a killing that sparked the largest homicide investigation in DEA history, according to the agency.

In 2017, a Mexican federal judge gave Felix Gallardo a 37-year prison term for the murders of Camarena and Mexican pilot Alfredo Zavala, Excélsior reported. The judge also ordered more than 20 million pesos in compensation for the victims’ families, roughly $1.18 million at the time.

Camarena was heading to meet his wife for lunch on Feb. 7, 1985, when five men abducted him as he left the U.S. Consulate in Guadalajara, according to the DEA. One of the attackers identified himself as a Mexican law enforcement official.
DRUG CARTEL KINGPIN AMONG TARGETS IN SWEEPING TRUMP CRACKDOWN ON ALLEGED MEXICAN CORRUPTION NETWORK
A Mexican soldier stands beside a Jalisco ambulance in this file photo unrelated to Miguel Angel Felix Gallardo’s case. (Ulises Ruiz / AFP via Getty Images)
The 37-year-old agent was never seen alive again.
The DEA says Camarena was believed to have been tortured for two days before dying from a crushed skull. His body was discovered on March 5, 1985.

His killing triggered Operation Leyenda, which the agency describes as the largest homicide investigation it had ever undertaken. Felix Gallardo was among the major Mexican crime figures arrested in connection with Camarena’s torture and murder, according to the DEA.
ICE RENEWS HUNT FOR EL CHAPO'S LAST TWO FUGITIVE SONS WITH MASSIVE REWARD

U.S. Marine Corps pallbearers carry the casket holding the body of slain U.S. Drug Enforcement agent Enrique Camarena after it arrived at North Island Naval Air Station in San Diego in March 1985. (AP/Lenny Ignelzi)
The agent, a Marine Corps veteran who joined the DEA in 1974, left behind his wife and three children.

Felix Gallardo’s reach helped reshape organized crime in Mexico. A 2023 report released by Sen. Chuck Grassley’s office described the former police officer as having brought traffickers together into a large organization that became a blueprint for many of Mexico’s major criminal groups.
EXCLUSIVE: INSIDE TRUMP'S CARTEL CRACKDOWN AS WHITE HOUSE OFFICIAL DETAILS PRESIDENT'S PRIVATE BRIEFINGS

The Guadalajara cartel was among the first Mexican trafficking organizations to work with Colombian cocaine suppliers, according to a historical DEA publication. The agency said Felix Gallardo and Rafael Caro Quintero formed the cartel to ship heroin and marijuana into the United States before it prospered from the cocaine trade.
Camarena’s legacy, meanwhile, lives on through the red ribbons worn each October in his memory as part of drug prevention efforts, according to the DEA.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Fox News Digital reached out to Jalisco’s security ministry and the DEA for confirmation and comment.
The Associated Press contributed to this report.
Stepheny Price is a Writer at Fox News with a focus on West Coast and Midwest news, missing persons, national and international crime stories, homicide cases, and border security.

title: Blinken warns US ground invasion of Iran would be 'absolute disaster' as Tehran escalates attacks
summary: Former Secretary of State Antony Blinken warned a U.S. ground invasion of Iran would be an "absolute disaster" as Tehran launched drones at Bahrain.
story: Fox News chief foreign correspondent Trey Yingst has the latest on the US-Iran conflict, including Iranian attacks on US bases and an alleged plot against President Donald Trump, on ‘Fox Report with Jon Scott.’
Former Secretary of State Antony Blinken warned Saturday that airstrikes alone may not eliminate Iran's weapons capabilities, but said a U.S. ground invasion would be an "absolute disaster."

Speaking at the 24th Hindustan Times Leadership Summit in New Delhi, Blinken, who served under President Biden, pointed to Iran's massive territory, population of roughly 90 million and ability to produce weapons deep inside the country as obstacles to any military campaign aimed at dismantling its arsenal.

"The weapons that it continues to produce are back far enough, the range is great enough that you can't just take everything out," Blinken said. "You'd probably have to have a land invasion of some kind to do that, which would be an absolute disaster."
TRUMP KEEPS SIGNALING AN END TO IRAN WAR, BUT EXPERT WARNS A CRUCIAL PIECE OF HIS STRATEGY IS MISSING
Former Secretary of State Antony Blinken said President Donald Trump's 20-point ceasefire agreement was based on the one developed by the Biden administration. (ARMEND NIMANI/AFP via Getty Images)

Blinken's warning came ahead of Iran claiming Sunday to have launched six drones at a U.S. military installation in Bahrain, while reports surfaced that neighboring Iraq faced concerns that its territory could be drawn into a potential American ground operation.
Bahrain said its air defenses blocked several Iranian aerial attacks Sunday, the first such interceptions since September.

Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said it targeted a U.S. air defense radar system at the Al-Rifaa helicopter base with six drones in retaliation for what it described as "hostile US actions," according to Iranian state media, Reuters reported.
Bahraini officials said the drones were intercepted before reaching their targets.
IRAN HAS 'SUBSTANTIALLY INCREASED' EFFORTS TO TARGET AMERICANS ABROAD, US INTELLIGENCE MEMO WARNS
The locations of U.S. bases throughout the Gulf are seen in relation to Iran. (Fox News)
The latest escalation came amid further fighting in Yemen, where the Houthis made advances against Saudi-backed forces, raising additional concerns about the conflict spreading across the region.
Blinken warned that Iran retains the ability to widen the confrontation despite the United States' overwhelming conventional military superiority.

While Washington can "escalate vertically" by intensifying its bombing campaign, Blinken said, Tehran can "escalate horizontally" by targeting American military installations, regional allies and critical infrastructure, either directly or through allied armed groups.
"Even though we're much more powerful, that asymmetry in their ability to escalate horizontally as opposed to vertically is not to our advantage," Blinken said.
The former top diplomat also emphasized the geographic challenges facing U.S. forces.
"That coastline along the Strait of Hormuz goes on forever," Blinken said.
Iran is roughly four times the size of California, with a coastline and weapons production facilities that could complicate efforts to eliminate its military capabilities through air power alone.
TRUMP'S MOAB THREAT COULD PUT IRAN'S DEEPEST BUNKERS IN AMERICA'S CROSSHAIRS
Soldiers from the U.S.-led coalition forces are seen during the handover of the K1 Air Base to the Iraqi Army from the US-led coalition in Kirkuk, Iraq, on March 29, 2020. (Associated Press)
Concerns about a potential ground operation have also intensified in neighboring Iraq, where officials have resisted proposals to sharply restrict trade and movement across the Iranian border.
Iran International reported that Tehran has become concerned that Iraqi territory could be used as a staging ground for a potential U.S. operation into southern Iran.
The Iraqi newspaper Al-Mada reported Nov. 9 that Iraq's prime minister privately briefed Shiite political leaders on an alleged American military plan involving a ground offensive, the outlet said.
In an interview with France 24 published Friday, Iraqi Foreign Minister Fuad Hussein had also warned that the region's unstable security environment could not continue indefinitely.
The current state of "no war and no peace" is unsustainable, Hussein said, warning that the confrontation "either goes towards peace or it goes towards war."
AFTER 47 YEARS OF CONFRONTING IRAN, DOES AMERICA HAVE A STRATEGY FOR ENDING THIS WAR?

An MH-60R Sea Hawk helicopter lands on the flight deck of USS Rafael Peralta as it transits regional waters, in this photo released by U.S. Central Command on Oct. 15, 2026. CENTCOM said the USS Rafael Peralta is enforcing a military blockade of Iranian ports. (CENTCOM)
Hussein also said Baghdad has a responsibility to pursue diplomatic mediation because Iraq has already been drawn into the conflict.
He pointed to recent outreach to Tehran, including discussions with Iranian Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf.

The Iraqi foreign minister also rejected a reported U.S. demand that Baghdad close all but two of its land border crossings with Iran, describing the proposed restrictions as "not possible" and "a kind of sanction against the Iraqi people."
The border dispute comes as U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM) expands efforts to disrupt Iranian weapons shipments and illicit trade through Task Force Iron Gate.

CENTCOM announced the task force would coordinate with other U.S. agencies to prevent Iran from transporting advanced weapons systems, dual-use technologies, sanctioned materials and illicit revenue across its land borders and the Caspian Sea.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Iraq shares a roughly 1,000-mile border with Iran.

Emma Bussey is a breaking news writer for Fox News Digital. Before joining Fox, she worked at The Telegraph with the U.S. overnight team, across desks including foreign, politics, news, sport and culture.

title: Iran vows ‘we will find you’ to 2 US Navy officers the day warship returns from Middle East
summary: Iran's embassy in South Africa posted a "We will find you" threat targeting two USS Spruance officers as the destroyer returned to San Diego.
story: Iran threats against US officers should set off ‘alarm bells’ in Washington, Foundation for Defense of Democracies senior fellow, Behnam Taleblu, warns.

Iran’s embassy in South Africa threatened two U.S. Navy officers with a "We will find you" message online as their warship returned to San Diego on Friday after a historic 357-day deployment that included combat against Iranian forces.

The warning, posted on X on Nov. 13 alongside images identifying the USS Spruance’s commanding officer and executive officer, prompted a regional expert to warn that Iran’s public targeting of American service members should set off alarm bells in Washington.
The embassy identified Cmdr. Leigh R. Tate, commanding officer of the Spruance, and Lt. Cmdr. Jeffrey E. York, the ship’s executive officer.
IRAN MINES US TROOPS' SOCIAL MEDIA AS MILITARY CONSIDERS SEIZING CELLPHONES
(U.S. Navy) (U.S. Navy)
"We will find you," the embassy wrote on X.
The embassy had previously singled out the officers in a March 28 post accusing them of ordering Tomahawk missile launches that killed 168 children at an elementary school in Minab, Iran.
"Remember these two criminals," the earlier post began. "Don’t they have children of their own?" the embassy asked at the time.

Behnam Ben Taleblu, a senior fellow at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies, warned that the rhetoric coming out of Tehran should be taken seriously given Iran’s history of plotting attacks against American officials.

"This should be setting off alarm bells in Washington, in the White House, the Pentagon, and even within CENTCOM," Taleblu told Fox News Digital. "The Islamic Republic has literally identified personnel that they allege are involved in strikes against the regime, and they’re talking about retribution."
"If indeed there is any plot to go after these individuals, it is critical they’re detected, they are disrupted, they are defeated," Taleblu warned.
IRAN-BACKED TERROR SUSPECTS PLOTTED ATTACK ON US TROOPS USING VANS PACKED WITH FUEL, DOJ SAYS
Arleigh Burke-class guided-missile destroyer USS Spruance fires a Tomahawk Land Attack Missile in support of Operation Epic Fury. (U.S. Navy/Handout via REUTERS)
The threat from Iran came a day after President Donald Trump warned Tehran against assassinating senior American officials.
During a Nov. 12 interview with radio host Hugh Hewitt, Trump was asked what would happen if Iran killed a senior U.S. official.
"They will not exist very long, any longer," Trump responded.
His warning also followed reports that Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent had relocated from his Washington-area residence to a military base amid Iranian threats against his life.
Bessent confirmed the move during a Friday interview on CNBC, saying he was following Secret Service instructions.
"Why am I going to be afraid when the brave military personnel in the Gulf, President Trump, constantly receive death threats?" Bessent asked.
Bessent described Iran as behaving "like a dangerous cornered animal" and insisted the threats would not derail the administration’s economic pressure campaign against Tehran.
TRUMP ADMIN THREATENS IRAN WITH 'CONSEQUENCES' AS ALLIES CONVENE AMID THREATS OF POST-ELECTION ESCALATION
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent gestures while speaking at the U.S.-China Relations Gala Dinner on Nov. 10, 2026, in New York. (AP Photo/Frank Franklin II)

Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and senior White House official Stephen Miller have also reportedly moved into military or other protected housing amid security concerns.
In another post on X, the Iranian embassy in South Africa went on to mock senior administration officials over their security arrangements.

"Rubio, Bessent, Hegseth, and other U.S. officials live in constant fear, haunted by the crimes committed, and now confined to military bunkers for their own protection," the embassy wrote, suggesting they should occasionally appear in public.
The threats come as federal authorities have announced developments in alleged Iranian-backed plots targeting Americans.

On Nov. 10, the FBI added Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps operative Shahram Poursafi to its Most Wanted Terrorists list over an alleged assassination plot targeting former senior U.S. officials, including former national security adviser John Bolton.

That same day, the Justice Department announced terrorism charges against three men accused of involvement in nearly 20 attacks and attempted attacks across Europe and the United States, including an alleged plot targeting a British air base housing American forces.
The developments followed an Oct. 23 U.S. intelligence warning that Iranian efforts to target American personnel abroad had substantially increased, with some plots reaching advanced stages.
TRUMP'S TOP OFFICIALS RETREAT BEHIND MILITARY GATES AS EX-FBI DEPUTY POINTS TO WHAT'S FUELING THREATS

The Arleigh Burke-class guided-missile destroyer departed San Diego on Nov. 21, 2025, alongside the USS Abraham Lincoln Carrier Strike Group. Its deployment was extended as American forces conducted Operation Epic Fury against Iran. (Sandy HUFFAKER / AFP via Getty Images)
The embassy’s warning coincided with the Spruance’s return to Naval Base San Diego on Nov. 13, ending the longest deployment by a U.S. Navy destroyer since World War II.

The Arleigh Burke-class guided-missile destroyer departed San Diego on Nov. 21, 2025, alongside the USS Abraham Lincoln Carrier Strike Group. Its deployment was extended as American forces conducted Operation Epic Fury against Iran.

The Spruance traveled more than 88,000 nautical miles during the deployment and launched dozens of Tomahawk land-attack cruise missiles against Iranian military targets between February and August 2026, according to a statement released by the Navy.
The ship also destroyed 12 unmanned aerial vehicles and four anti-ship cruise missiles while operating under persistent threats from Iranian drones and missiles.

"Spruance, in particular, as the alternate air defense commander was, I would say, instrumental in defending the carrier, defending the force from those inbound threats," Tate said Friday in the statement.
CENTCOM COMMANDER TOUTS USS ABRAHAM LINCOLN MENTAL HEALTH RECORD AFTER MORE THAN 260 DAYS WITHOUT PORT CALL

The destroyer also participated in the U.S. blockade of Iranian ports. In April, it intercepted the Iranian-flagged cargo vessel Touska after the ship failed to comply with repeated American warnings. (CENTCOM/Handout via REUTERS )

The destroyer also participated in the U.S. blockade of Iranian ports. In April, it intercepted the Iranian-flagged cargo vessel Touska after the ship failed to comply with repeated American warnings.
U.S. Central Command said at the time that the Spruance ordered the vessel’s engine room evacuated before firing rounds that disabled the ship.
Tate called commanding the ship during the extended deployment an "honor of a lifetime."
"Spruance sailors made a difference," Tate also said in a statement Friday. "They represented their families, their ship and the United States Navy with distinction."
Meanwhile, Iranian officials have also been threatening U.S. military installations overseas.
On Nov. 11, Iranian Supreme National Security Council Secretary Mohsen Rezaei warned that Tehran could strike American bases in Europe if the United States resumed attacks on Iran.
ANOTHER TRUMP HEAVYWEIGHT REVEALED TO BE LIVING ON MILITARY BASE AS CABINET ROSTER GROWS

Mohsen Rezaei was named secretary of the Supreme National Security Council. A foremr Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps general and member of the Expediency Discernment Council, as well as the secretary of the Supreme Council for Economic Coordination and the Iranian government's Economic Committee, attends a ceremony at Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini's shrine in southern Tehran, Iran, on June 4, 2026. (Morteza Nikoubazl/NurPhoto)
"If the Americans make a mistake and attack us, we will not limit ourselves to nearby bases," Rezaei told Al Mayadeen.
Taleblu described the embassy’s latest statements as part of an escalating pattern of threats against American personnel.
"This is an escalation of the course that we’ve been on," he said, pointing to threatening rhetoric from Iranian diplomatic accounts and hard-line commentators during and after the war.
"So this is basically incitement and invective from the world’s foremost state sponsor of terrorism, one which unfortunately has a track record of carrying these things out, even with a delay."
He pointed to threats against U.S. military personnel following the accidental American shootdown of an Iranian civilian airliner in 1988.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"Something like this is not unprecedented in the 47-year shadow war between the Islamic Republic and America," Taleblu said, warning that the conflict has increasingly moved from covert operations into open warfare and increasing public threats on social media.
Fox News Digital has reached out to the Pentagon and the White House for comment.

Emma Bussey is a breaking news writer for Fox News Digital. Before joining Fox, she worked at The Telegraph with the U.S. overnight team, across desks including foreign, politics, news, sport and culture.

title: Putin's war machine tied to troubling recruitment of young women as new deals emerge
summary: Two African governments signed deals with Russia's Alabuga drone factory zone as a Ukrainian probe alleges deceptive recruitment of young African women.
story: Ukrainian investigator Solomiya Khoma tells Fox News Digital how alleged recruiters and Russian cultural groups draw young African women into Russia’s military-industrial workforce as new agreements with African governments raise concerns.

Two African governments have signed new agreements with a Russian industrial complex linked to the production of attack drones used against Ukraine, even as a Ukrainian investigation alleges Moscow is expanding a recruitment network that draws young African women into its military-industrial workforce.

The agreements, signed in late October by Ghana and the Democratic Republic of the Congo with Russia's Alabuga Special Economic Zone, come months after Britain sanctioned individuals and entities associated with the Alabuga Start program over deceptive recruitment practices. The new partnerships raise questions about whether Russia's efforts to attract foreign workers could help sustain drone production as its war against Ukraine continues.

The Ukrainian Security and Cooperation Centre says it has obtained internal documents identifying approximately 50 African women employed at Alabuga, alongside 10 Russian recruiters and two African intermediaries allegedly involved in attracting foreign workers.
OUR ADVERSARIES ARE EVEN USING THE US BANKING SYSTEM. HERE’S HOW THEY GET AWAY WITH IT

The remains of a Russian-made, Iran-designed Shahed-136 drone, known in Russia as a Geran-2, are displayed with other recovered drones, glide bombs, missiles and rockets in Kharkiv on July 30, 2025. (Scott Peterson/Getty Images)
"What we were able to do is basically to obtain internal documentation," Solomiya Khoma, the organization's head of international cooperation, told Fox News Digital in an exclusive interview.

Khoma said the investigation went beyond previous reporting by attempting to establish how recruitment operates across borders, connecting Russian cultural organizations, local intermediaries and Alabuga's human resources department. "Our case is specifically related to African countries," she said.

According to the report, the alleged network operates on three levels: Russian cultural and educational organizations cultivating relationships with young people in Africa, local recruiters promoting opportunities abroad, and Alabuga personnel arranging employment and logistics.

A satellite image shows possible planned location of UAV manufacturing plant in Russia's Alabuga Special Economic Zone, as evidence of new Russian-Iran cooperation, in this handout acquired June 9, 2023. (White House/Handout via Reuters)

The investigation identifies two women from Tunisia and Uganda as alleged recruitment coordinators and describes connections with Russian HR personnel and foreign employees. Their specific recruitment activities have not been independently verified by Fox News Digital.
Khoma said the findings relied partly on a confidential source who remains employed within the Alabuga industrial complex.
"This person is still continuing to work in the Alabuga economical zone and these factories," she said, explaining why the organization could not disclose the source's identity.
She said investigators obtained information about the workers and their identities, including internal employee passes.

The researchers also examined the involvement of Russian cultural organizations, including councils of Russian compatriots and the Russkiy Mir Foundation, in promoting educational and employment opportunities in African countries.

The report points to a September 2024 cooperation memorandum between the Russian compatriots' council in Tunisia and Alabuga, alongside Russian cultural activities in Uganda. However, the investigation does not establish that Russian diplomats or cultural organizations knowingly directed recruits into military drone production.

The findings build on an Associated Press investigation published in October 2024, which documented how African women recruited with promises of education and civilian employment were assigned to manufacture Iranian-designed attack drones. Some described long hours, lower-than-promised wages, surveillance and exposure to hazardous chemicals.

Russia's President Vladimir Putin and the Democratic Republic of the Congo's President Felix Tshisekedi arrive for their meeting on the sidelines of the Russia-Africa Summit at the Grand Kremlin Palace in Moscow, Russia, October 30, 2026. (Pavel Bednyakov/Pool via Reuters)
Khoma described a recruitment process in which women arrive in Russia expecting to combine education with paid employment, only to fail entrance examinations or Russian-language requirements.
"These people are promised a dual education opportunity," she said.

After failing examinations, she alleged, workers may find themselves with limited options and unable to afford transportation home, leaving them performing factory work instead of pursuing their expected studies.

The recruitment program has also attracted international scrutiny. On May 5, 2026, the British government sanctioned seven individuals and entities associated with Alabuga Start recruitment, accusing the operation of using deceptive practices to obtain foreign labor for facilities producing military drones.
Yet cooperation with African governments appears to be continuing.
US COMPANIES WIN BILLIONS IN AFRICAN DATA CENTER DEALS IN DIRECT COMPETITION WITH CHINA

Ghanaian broadcaster Citi News reported October 29 that Labor Minister Emmanuel Agyekum signed an agreement with Alabuga to facilitate industrial employment opportunities for Ghanaian citizens. The ministry said it would coordinate recruitment, verify job offers and provide pre-departure orientation.

title: Democrats formally nominate Rep. Hakeem Jeffries, paving way for him to be the first Black speaker
summary: Rep. Hakeem Jeffries of New York won his party’s nomination for speaker of the House, putting him on a glide path for election to the top job on the first day of the new Congress in January.
story: WASHINGTON — After leading Democrats back to the majority, Rep. Hakeem Jeffries of New York won his party’s nomination for speaker of the House, putting him on a glide path for election to the top job on the first day of the new Congress in January.

Jeffries was nominated in a closed-door, secret-ballot vote of 251-11, according to two sources in the room. It was a show of strength for Jeffries, who had faced grumbling from progressive members and activists calling for new and bolder leadership. But no challenger emerged.

Some of Jeffries’ allies had pushed for a vote by acclamation, which would not result in a tally. But Jeffries asked for a recorded vote to give his rank-and-file members an opportunity to voice their support or opposition — something he said the Democratic Caucus did when it returned Nancy Pelosi to the speaker’s office after the 2018 midterm elections amid calls for a new generation of leadership.

“It certainly seems to me to be appropriate that we take exactly the same approach,” Jeffries told reporters Tuesday, “to give every single person the opportunity to weigh in one way or the other on who the caucus feels is best positioned based on track record, experience, vision, to help move us forward in the new Congress.”
After the vote, seven of the 11 Democrats who voted against Jeffries issued a join statement explaining their position.

“Whether on Medicare for All, stopping ICE terror, getting money out of politics, or ending the genocide in Gaza, our constituents sent us to Congress with a mandate on these issues,” wrote Reps.-elect Darializa Avila Chevalier, D-N.Y., Adam Hamawy, D-N.J., Frederick Haynes, D-Texas, Melat Kiros, D-Colo., Donavan McKinney, D-Mich., Chris Rabb, D-Pa., and Claire Valdez, D-N.Y.

“We have worked to secure commitments from Leader Jeffries in good-faith conversations. While we have seen meaningful progress, there is still work to be done to ensure that the direction our party takes this coming Congress reflects what our constituents are demanding of leadership,” they said. “Those conversations are ongoing. As such, our vote in caucus today was no.”

Jeffries was nominated by five colleagues representing the broad diversity of the Democratic Caucus: Rep. Teresa Leger Fernández, D-N.M., Rep. Derek Tran, D-Calif., Rep. Mark Pocan, D-Wis., Rep.-elect Rebecca Bennett, D-N.J., and former Majority Whip Jim Clyburn, D-S.C., one of Jeffries’ political mentors.
“This is a very surreal moment for me,” Clyburn, a veteran of the Civil Rights Movement and former chair of the Black Caucus, told reporters before the vote.
Jeffries, a 56-year-old Brooklyn native, former attorney and former state lawmaker, is now poised to make history as the first Black speaker of the House.

He campaigned across the country in recent months and helped Democrats win what NBC News projects will be 259 seats — the largest majority in 35 years and well more than the 218 votes he will need to be elected speaker on the House floor on Jan. 3.

It means that Jeffries can afford roughly 40 Democratic defections that day and still be elected speaker. By contrast, in 2023, Republican Kevin McCarthy had a razor-thin 222-212 majority; he managed to win the speaker’s gavel on the 15th ballot.
For Subscribers
Last week, House Republicans elected Judiciary Committee Chairman Jim Jordan, R-Ohio, over Majority Leader Steve Scalise, R-La., to be minority leader in the next Congress.
For Subscribers

Like the speaker race, the other major Democratic leadership races are also uncontested. Rep. Katherine Clark, D-Mass., was elected by her colleagues as majority leader, the No. 2 position. She will make history as the first woman in either chamber elected to that role.
Rep. Pete Aguilar, D-Calif., was elected majority whip, the No. 3 leader and party’s top vote counter. No Hispanic American lawmaker has ever climbed higher in the House.
Rep. Ted Lieu, another California Democrat, was elected as caucus chairman, the No. 4 leader. He will make history as the first Asian American to hold that job.
And Rep. Joe Neguse, D-Colo., was elected assistant speaker.

The only significant contested leadership race is for vice chair of the Democratic Caucus, where Rep. Sara Jacobs, D-Calif., a member of the Progressive Caucus, is running against Rep. Lauren Underwood, D-Ill., a member of the Black Caucus.
Jeffries, a Pelosi protégé, had served as Democratic Caucus chairman before he was elevated to minority leader following House Democrats’ loss in the 2022 midterms.

He spent much of Tuesday holding meetings with the various factions of his massive new majority that he will need to unite to pass legislation on issues like affordability. He met separately with the leaders of the Congressional Progressive Caucus and the two moderate groups, the New Democrat Coalition and the Blue Dogs.
“It’s a great class, and they have a lot of wonderful ideas, fresh ideas, new ideas about how to advance the ball in a bold way for the American people,” Jeffries told reporters.

title: Meghan Markle’s father faces new child sex abuse complaints in the Philippines
summary: Thomas Markle, the estranged father of Meghan, the Duchess of Sussex, was charged with the possession of child abuse material, police in the Philippines said.
story: Thomas Markle, the estranged father of Meghan, the Duchess of Sussex, has had criminal complaints filed against him over alleged online child sexual abuse offences, police in the Philippines said Wednesday.

The complaints accuse Markle of violating local laws against online sexual abuse and exploitation of children, police told Reuters. They added that the complaints were filed before the prosecutor’s office in Cebu on Monday, following an investigation last month into the alleged distribution and possession of child sexual abuse materials.
Markle had lived in Cebu for a period before returning to the United States.

Prosecutors the evaluating the charges filed by police before they decide whether to issue a subpoena against Markle whose legal team would have 10 days to respond with a counter-affidavit. Prosecutors would then decide whether to proceed with a court case.
Prince Harry and Meghan’s spokesperson declined to comment when NBC News asked about the latest charges.

The announcement came less than two weeks after the 82-year-old was arrested in Florida and charged with one count of possession of child pornography, according to a criminal complaint filed by the Justice Department.

The FBI seized around 78 items from two storage units rented by Markle in Los Angeles, that contained “suspected child pornography,” according to court documents. Items seized include film negatives featuring an adult man with naked “pre-pubescent” girls, the complaint said, which added that a witness “positively identified the adult man as Markle.”
Based on background in one photo, the FBI determined the images found in California were taken in a hotel in the Philippines, according to the court document.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers
Markle was taken into custody in Tampa, Florida, and was later released under house arrest.
But after he cut off his ankle monitor, a federal judge ordered last week that Markle remain in custody for violating the conditions of his release.

Markle had been living in a senior care facility in Lakeland, Florida after he was forced to return to the U.S. from the Philippines when he suffered a stroke and a leg was amputated, according to The Associated Press.
The retired television lighting and photography director denied the allegations last month, calling them “sick lies.”

Meghan Markle asaid in a statement last month that she was “deeply distressed” by the allegations against her father. Their relationship has been limited and fraught in recent years, with her father not attending her wedding to Harry in 2018 amid widespread media scrutiny.

Her statement said that she was previously informed of “disturbing allegations” against him, with British police subsequently confirming she was passed a letter in January 2019 “containing a number of claims about alleged offending outside the United Kingdom.”

London’s Metropolitan Police said it had not informed other law enforcement agencies about the allegations in the letter at the time, referring itself to Britain’s policing watchdog over the handling of the allegations.

“The breadth of what has now been uncovered is more sickening than one could ever imagine,” said Meghan, who said she had chosen to keep her children, Prince Archie, 7, and Princess Lilibet, 5, away from her father “for one reason: to protect them.”
Meghan Markle and her husband, Prince Harry, stepped back as working royals in 2020 amid widespread reports of a royal rift and moved to, leaving Britain for California.

Harry, the second son of King Charles III and the late Princess Diana, leveled harsh criticism at Buckingham Palace and other senior royals across a series of media interviews and a tell-all memoir, “Spare.”
The couple returned to Britain two months ago, with their two children moving to schools in the country.

title: Highlights from Pope Leo’s historic, 12-day tour of South America
summary: They turned out in their millions to greet Pope Leo as he made his way around Uruguay, Argentina and Peru on a gruelling 12-day tour of the South America.
story: LIMA, Peru — They turned out in the millions to greet Pope Leo as he made his way around Uruguay, Argentina and Peru on a grueling 12-day tour of the South American nations, weeks after undergoing surgery for lung cancer.
Pope keeps energetic pace in trip to South America after surgery

For some — particularly those in Argentina, which had not received a papal visit since Pope John Paul II in 1987 — it was the first time they would get to see a pontiff in person. A record 2.5 million people flooded onto the streets of Buenos Aires last week to try and catch a glimpse of Leo.

The Vatican dubbed it a “homecoming” tour for the 71-year-old, as the Chicago-born pontiff, who is also a citizen of Peru, spent the final six days in the country where he lived for decades and served as a bishop until 2023.
NBC News takes a look at some of the highlights from his trip.
Montevideo, Uruguay

After a 17-hour flight from Rome, Leo and his entourage touched down in Uruguay’s capital, Montevideo. Praising the Lord and thanking his wonderful medical assistants, Leo said that while some had questioned whether he would be able to make the trip because of his recent surgery, he “had no doubt and was convinced that this trip had to go forward.”

title: Wondering why your friends are MIA? ‘Grand Theft Auto VI’ might be to blame
summary: Between spikes in vacation day requests and college professors reportedly granting extensions to their students, the Thursday release of Grand Theft Auto VI could bring America (or the world) to a halt.
story: Between spikes in vacation day requests and college professors reportedly granting extensions to their students, the Thursday release of Grand Theft Auto VI could bring America (or the world) to a halt.
GTA VI, which will be available on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X/S, is the first release in the Grand Theft Auto series since 2013.

Rockstar Games, the publisher behind the company, reportedly spent more than $1 billion to simply make the game. That’s more than the rumored budgets of the upcoming “Avengers” and “Dune” movies combined.

As of Wednesday, the game has notched a whopping 99/100 on Metacritic, which distills reviews from around the Internet. That ties it with Legend of Zelda Ocarina of Time for highest rated game of all time.
Here’s everything you need to know about why GTA VI is shaping up to be one of the biggest cultural events of the year.
The game made $1.5 billion in prelaunch sales

GTA VI is the eighth entry in the main Grand Theft Auto series, which doesn’t include spinoffs and expansion packs. The series began with Grand Theft Auto in 1997, but entered a new era in 2001 with the release of Grand Theft Auto III, the first in the series to feature a three-dimensional world.
Since then, Rockstar Games released Grand Theft Auto: Vice City in 2002, Grand Theft Auto: San Andreas in 2004, Grand Theft Auto IV in 2008 and Grand Theft Auto V in 2013.
The 13-year gap between V and VI is the longest wait between games in the main series.

title: Trump to hold one-on-one with Putin on the sidelines of Asia summit
summary: President Donald Trump will hold a one-on-one meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin on Thursday, a U.S. official confirmed, marking the leaders’ first in-person meeting in over a year.
story: President Donald Trump will hold a one-on-one meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin on Thursday, a U.S. official confirmed, marking the leaders’ first in-person meeting in over a year.

The bilateral meeting was not initially on Trump’s schedule for his Asia trip. The president was already scheduled to hold a trilateral meeting with Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping on Thursday, where the leaders plan to discuss nuclear disarmament, the Iran war, trade and, Trump said Monday, Russia’s war with Ukraine.
The Kremlin had said ahead of the U.S.’ confirmation that the two leaders would be meeting one-on-one.

The White House has not released information about the agenda for the bilateral meeting, which comes as major attacks continue in the Ukraine war with no end in sight. Trump’s meetings with the leaders of China and Russia — both U.S. adversaries — marks his administration’s continued shift away from traditional alliances and unconventional approach to diplomacy.

A senior U.S. official previously told reporters that while the president intended to discuss Iran with Xi and Putin during their trilateral meeting, he did not plan to focus on the war in Ukraine. The official said last week that “it doesn’t seem appropriate to have the Ukraine discussion there” with China.

Trump and Putin previously met face-to-face in Alaska in August 2025. That summit ended without an agreement to end the war in Ukraine, something Trump has been pursuing since he began his second term.
Trump continued to express optimism about ending the war after the in-person meeting in Alaska did not lead to any ceasefire or breakthrough.
Speaking to reporters on Monday, Trump said he believed Putin was “backing down a little bit” in the war in Ukraine.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers
“I think he could be tougher,” Trump said. “I think he could be a lot tougher, frankly. I think he’s backing down.”

Russia, however, has continued striking Ukraine with missiles and drones in the lead up to the meeting. Separately, on Tuesday, Ukraine damaged a key bridge that links the occupied Crimean Peninsula with Russia.
Trump repeatedly said during his 2024 presidential campaign that he could quickly end the war between Russia and Ukraine.
“I will get it settled before I even become president,” Trump said during a presidential debate.
As Trump heads into the second half of his final term, the war is entering its fifth year.
